Setup and first programs

A program is a list of steps for a computer. In this chapter you install Rust and Python. Then you write, run and fix your first program in both languages.

  • Explain what a program, a compiler and an interpreter are.
  • Install Rust with rustup and Python with uv.
  • Create and run a project with cargo and with uv.
  • Read a Rust compiler error and a Python traceback.
  • Use the Rust tab and the Python tab in this book.

What a program is

Here is one small program in two languages. It works out a total price and shows it.

fn main() {
    let price = 40;
    let count = 3;
    let total = price * count;
    println!("Total: {total}");
}
price = 40
count = 3
total = price * count
print(f"Total: {total}")
Total: 120

A program is a list of steps. The computer does the steps in order, from top to bottom. This program has four steps. It saves two numbers, multiplies them and prints the result.

You write the steps as text. This text is the source code. The CPU cannot read your text. It only runs machine code. So a tool must translate your source code.

Source code is for people. Machine code is for the CPU. A translator stands between them.

A computer does not guess. Print and print are two different names. One wrong letter stops the program. This is normal. The last section shows how to read the error.

How this book works

Rust is the main language of this book. Python stands beside it. You learn each idea in both languages.

  • Two tabs. Most examples have a Rust tab and a Python tab. Click a tab to change the language. The book remembers your choice.
  • Real output. A block marked "output" shows what the program printed. Every example in this book was run first.
  • Word help. Many hard words have a short meaning. Point at the word or tap it.
  • The same order every time. First you see an example. Then the rule. Then a common mistake.
  • Patterns and practice. Each chapter ends with a pattern table, questions and answers.
Versions on 15 November 2026
ToolNewest versionUsed to test this book
Rust (rustc, cargo)1.100.0, from 12 November 20261.99.0
Python3.15.2, from 25 October 20263.14.3
uv0.13.8, from 12 November 20260.10.12 and 0.13.8

These numbers change often. Rust gets a new version every six weeks. Python gets a new version every October. Check the official pages in the sources. With a newer version, your output can look a little different.

Compiled and interpreted

Both languages need a translator. But they translate at different times. The picture shows the two ways.

Rust is a compiled language. A compiler reads all your source code and checks it. Then it writes a new file with machine code. You run that file. The Rust compiler is named rustc.

Python is an interpreted language. A program named python reads your source code and runs it at once. This program is the interpreter. It makes no program file that runs alone.

The two ways compared
QuestionRust (compiled)Python (interpreted)
When is the code translated?One time, before the runAt every run
What does a user need?Only your program filePython and your source files
When do you see most mistakes?Before the runDuring the run
How fast is the first try?You wait for the compilerIt starts at once
How fast is the program?Very fastSlower in heavy loops

How big is the speed difference? I ran one small test. The program counts the prime numbers below 2,000,000. It has two loops and simple maths.

Show the test program 
use std::time::Instant;

// Is n a prime number? Try every divisor up to the square root.
fn is_prime(n: u32) -> bool {
    if n < 2 {
        return false;
    }
    let mut d = 2;
    while d * d <= n {
        if n % d == 0 {
            return false;
        }
        d += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn main() {
    let start = Instant::now();
    let mut count = 0;
    for n in 0..2_000_000 {
        if is_prime(n) {
            count += 1;
        }
    }
    println!("{count} primes in {:.2} s", start.elapsed().as_secs_f64());
}
import time


# Is n a prime number? Try every divisor up to the square root.
def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    if n < 2:
        return False
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return False
        d += 1
    return True


start = time.perf_counter()
count = 0
for n in range(2_000_000):
    if is_prime(n):
        count += 1
print(f"{count} primes in {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f} s")

Both programs print 148933 primes. You do not need to understand this code yet. The next chapters explain every line.

Python also translates. It first turns your file into bytecode. Then a loop inside python runs the bytecode step by step. Python saves the bytecode of imported files in a folder named __pycache__. Rust has more than one step too. rustc checks your code, a tool named LLVM makes the machine code, and a linker builds the final file.

You can look at Python bytecode yourself. This command shows the bytecode for a + b.

uv run python -c "import dis; dis.dis('a + b')"
  0           RESUME                   0

  1           LOAD_NAME                0 (a)
              LOAD_NAME                1 (b)
              BINARY_OP                0 (+)
              RETURN_VALUE

Install Rust: rustup and cargo

You install Rust with one tool named rustup. It works in a terminal.

  1. On macOS or Linux, run the command from the official install page. 
    curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
  2. The installer asks a question. Press Enter for the standard installation.
  3. Close the terminal and open it again. Now the terminal knows the new commands.
  4. Check that the tools answer. 
    rustc --version
cargo --version
    rustc 1.99.0 (b940084d7 2026-09-28)
cargo 1.99.0 (5f94df478 2026-08-27)

On Windows, download rustup-init.exe from the same page and run it. It can ask you to install the Visual Studio C++ build tools. Say yes, because Rust needs their linker. On macOS the linker comes with xcode-select --install. On Ubuntu it is in the package build-essential.

What rustup installs
ToolJob
rustupInstalls and updates Rust.
rustcThe compiler. It translates your code.
cargoCreates, builds, runs and tests projects. You use it all day.
rustfmt and clippyOne tidies your code. The other gives advice.

A new stable Rust comes out every six weeks. This command gets the newest one.

rustup update

You see "command not found: rustc". The tools are in the folder ~/.cargo/bin. Your terminal looks for commands in a list of folders named PATH. Close the terminal and open it again. Then the new folder is in the list.

Install Python with uv

Python has many install tools. This book uses one tool for everything: uv. It installs Python, creates projects and adds libraries. It comes from the company Astral. It is written in Rust.

  1. Install uv. Use the first line on macOS or Linux. Use the second line in Windows PowerShell. 
    curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
  2. Open a new terminal and check the version. 
    uv --version
    uv 0.13.8 (3d97a6aad 2026-11-12 aarch64-apple-darwin)
  3. Install Python 3.14. This book was tested with it. 
    uv python install 3.14
  4. See which Python versions uv can find. 
    uv python list

On macOS you can also use brew install uv. Step 3 is not always needed. When a project asks for a Python version that is missing, uv downloads it.

Do not type plain python or python3. On many computers that starts an old Python. On the laptop used for this book, python3 is still version 3.9. Start Python with uv run. Then you always get the right version.

Your first Rust project: cargo new, run, check

Cargo makes a new project with one command. Then you go into the new folder.

cargo new hello-rust
cd hello-rust
    Creating binary (application) `hello-rust` package
note: see more `Cargo.toml` keys and their definitions at https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html

Cargo wrote two files for you. The first file holds the settings of the project. The second file holds the code.

[package]
name = "hello-rust"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}

Read the code line by line.

  • fn main() starts a function named main. Every Rust program starts there.
  • The curly brackets { } hold the steps of the function.
  • println! prints one line of text. The ! shows that it is a macro.
  • "Hello, world!" is a string.
  • The ; ends the step.

Now build and run the program with one command.

cargo run
   Compiling hello-rust v0.1.0 (/home/you/hello-rust)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.25s
     Running `target/debug/hello-rust`
Hello, world!

Cargo did three things. It compiled your code. It saved the program as target/debug/hello-rust. Then it ran that program. The folder path in the first line is from your computer.

The cargo commands for every day
CommandWhat it doesWhen to use it
cargo new nameMakes a new project folder.One time, at the start.
cargo checkChecks the code. Makes no program file.Very often, while you write.
cargo runBuilds the program and runs it.When you want to see it work.
cargo buildBuilds the program. Does not run it.When you only need the file.
cargo build --releaseBuilds a fast program in target/release.For real use and for speed tests.

cargo check is the fastest command. It stops before the slow step that writes machine code. A normal build is a debug build. It compiles fast, but the program runs slowly. A release build compiles slowly, but the program runs fast.

The line edition = "2024" picks the Rust edition. The newest edition is 2024. This book uses it everywhere. The chapter Rust editions explains the older ones.

cargo new also starts a git repository and writes a .gitignore file. It skips this step when the folder is already inside a repository. After the first build you also see Cargo.lock. Cargo writes that file. Do not edit it by hand.

You run cargo run in the wrong folder. Cargo answers: error: could not find `Cargo.toml`. Go into the project folder first with cd hello-rust. Do not make the folder yourself before cargo new. Cargo makes it.

Your first Python project: uv init, uv run

The smallest Python program is one file with one line. Save it as hello.py and run it.

print("Hello, world!")
uv run hello.py
Hello, world!

There is no main function and no ;. Python runs the file from the first line. For real work you want a project. A project fixes the Python version and the libraries.

uv init hello-py
cd hello-py

What you get depends on your uv version. The layout changed in uv 0.12, in July 2026.

hello-py
├── .gitignore
├── .python-version
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
└── src
    └── hello_py
        └── __init__.py
def main() -> None:
    print("Hello from hello-py!")
uv run hello-py
hello-py
├── .gitignore
├── .python-version
├── README.md
├── main.py
└── pyproject.toml
def main():
    print("Hello from hello-py!")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
uv run main.py

This is the first run with uv 0.13.8. The folder paths are shortened here.

Using CPython 3.14.3
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
   Building hello-py @ file:///home/you/hello-py
      Built hello-py @ file:///home/you/hello-py
Installed 1 package in 5ms
Hello from hello-py!

uv run does more than start Python. First it reads .python-version and finds that Python. Then it makes a virtual environment in the folder .venv. It writes the exact library versions to uv.lock. Then it runs your code. The second run is fast, because all of this exists.

The settings are in pyproject.toml. This file does the same job as Cargo.toml.

[project]
name = "hello-py"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
    { name = "Your Name", email = "you@example.com" }
]
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = []

[project.scripts]
hello-py = "hello_py:main"    # the command hello-py calls main()

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.13.8,<0.14.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"

uv takes your name and email from git when it finds them. The line under [project.scripts] makes a command named hello-py. That command calls the function main. In both layouts, uv also starts a git repository and writes .gitignore, like cargo.

You like the simple layout with main.py? New uv versions still make it. Type uv init --no-package hello-py.

The file .python-version fixes the Python version for one project. Rust has the same idea. A file named rust-toolchain.toml fixes the Rust version for one project. And rustup doc opens the Rust documentation on your own computer, without internet.

The project is named hello-py. The code folder is named hello_py. This is not a typing mistake. A Python name cannot hold a minus sign, so uv writes an underscore.

How to read a compiler error

Errors are normal. You will see them every day. This program has one wrong name. Look at what each language does with it.

fn main() {
    println!("Step 1 is done.");
    let name = "Ferris";
    println!("Hello, {}!", nme);   // wrong name
    println!("Step 3 is done.");
}
print("Step 1 is done.")
name = "Ferris"
print("Hello, " + nme + "!")   # wrong name
print("Step 3 is done.")
error[E0425]: cannot find value `nme` in this scope
 --> src/main.rs:4:28
  |
4 |     println!("Hello, {}!", nme);   // wrong name
  |                            ^^^
  |
help: a local variable with a similar name exists
  |
4 |     println!("Hello, {}!", name);   // wrong name
  |                             +

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0425`.
error: could not compile `hello-rust` (bin "hello-rust") due to 1 previous error
Step 1 is done.
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/you/demo/main.py", line 3, in <module>
    print("Hello, " + nme + "!")   # wrong name
                      ^^^
NameError: name 'nme' is not defined. Did you mean: 'name'?

Rust found the mistake at compile time. No program was made. Nothing was printed. Python found it at run time. Step 1 ran. Then the program stopped at the wrong line.

A Rust error has fixed parts. Read them in this order.

Start at the first error

Scroll up to the first error line. Later errors often come from the first one. Fix one error, then check again.

Read the message and the code

error[E0425]: cannot find value `nme` in this scope

E0425 is the error code. The text after it says what is wrong.

Find the place

--> src/main.rs:4:28

This means file src/main.rs, line 4, column 28. The column counts letters from the left.

Look at the marks

The compiler prints your line again. The marks ^^^ stand under the exact problem. Sometimes a short label follows the marks.

Try the help

A help: block shows a possible fix. A + shows what to add. For a long explanation, run rustc --explain E0425.

A Python traceback is read the other way. Start at the bottom. The last line names the error and often gives a hint. The lines above it show the file and the line number.

Warnings are not errors

A warning does not stop the build. This program makes a variable and never uses it.

fn main() {
    let name = "Ferris";
    let age = 9;
    println!("Hello, {name}!");
}
warning: unused variable: `age`
 --> src/main.rs:3:9
  |
3 |     let age = 9;
  |         ^^^ help: if this is intentional, prefix it with an underscore: `_age`
  |
  = note: `#[warn(unused_variables)]` (part of `#[warn(unused)]`) on by default

warning: `hello-rust` (bin "hello-rust") generated 1 warning (run `cargo fix --bin "hello-rust" -p hello-rust` to apply 1 suggestion)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.39s
     Running `target/debug/hello-rust`
Hello, Ferris!

The program still runs. But fix warnings too. They often point at a real bug.

Three facts for later

  • Python checks the grammar of the whole file before step 1. A missing bracket gives a SyntaxError, and nothing runs.
  • When the build fails, cargo ends with exit code 101. A Python program that stops with an error ends with code 1. Scripts use these numbers to see a failure.
  • cargo check --message-format=short prints one line for each error. It looks like src/main.rs:4:28: error[E0425]: .... Editors read the same messages and show them while you type.

You forget the ! and write println("Hello"). Rust says: error[E0423]: cannot find function `println` in this scope. Then it helps: use `!` to invoke the macro. The fix is in the message. Always read the help block before you search the web.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for setup and first programs
PatternPurposeModelNote
cargo new NAMEStart a Rust projectcargo new hello-rustCargo makes the folder. Do not make it first.
cargo runBuild and runcargo runRun it inside the project folder.
cargo checkFind mistakes fastcargo checkIt makes no program file.
cargo build --releaseMake a fast programcargo build --releaseNever measure speed with a debug build.
uv init NAMEStart a Python projectuv init hello-pyuv 0.12 and newer put the code in src/.
uv run FILERun Python code with the right Pythonuv run hello.pyDo not type plain python.
uv python install VERSIONGet a Python versionuv python install 3.14uv can also download it when a project needs it.
rustup updateGet the newest Rustrustup updateA new stable version comes every six weeks.
fn main() { ... }The start of a Rust programfn main() { println!("Hi"); }Python needs no main. It starts at line 1.
println!("text")Print a line in Rustprintln!("Total: {total}");Keep the !. It is a macro.
print("text")Print a line in Pythonprint(f"Total: {total}")The f before the string lets you use {total}.
rustc --explain CODERead a long explanationrustc --explain E0425Read the help: block first.

Practice

Which tool translates Rust source code into machine code?

  • rustup
  • rustc
  • uv

rustc is the compiler. rustup only installs and updates the tools.

Which command checks your code but makes no program file?

  • cargo run
  • cargo new
  • cargo check

cargo check stops before the step that writes machine code. So it is fast.

An error shows --> src/main.rs:4:28. What is 28?

  • The error code
  • The line number
  • The column number

The order is file, line, column. So it is line 4, column 28.

A Python file has a wrong name on line 3. Lines 1 and 2 print text. What happens?

  • Nothing is printed.
  • Lines 1 and 2 print. Then Python stops with a NameError.
  • Python corrects the name and goes on.

Python finds a wrong name only at run time, when it reaches that line.

Which file tells uv which Python version a project uses?

  • .python-version
  • uv.lock
  • Cargo.toml

uv reads .python-version. The file uv.lock holds the exact versions of the libraries.

To build and run a Rust project, type cargo ?.

The ! in println! shows that it is a ?.

You read a Python traceback from the ?.

A fast Rust program comes from cargo build --?.

  1. Change the Rust program so that it prints your name. Which file do you edit? Which command do you run?
    Answer

    Edit src/main.rs. Change the text inside the quotation marks. Then run cargo run in the project folder.

  2. Remove the ! from println! and run cargo check. What does the help line say?
    Answer

    You get error E0423. The help line says: use ! to invoke the macro. It also shows the fixed line.

  3. Why is cargo check faster than cargo build?
    Answer

    Both read and check all the code. But cargo check stops there. It does not write machine code, and it does not link a program file.

  4. A friend has no Rust and no Python. You send target/release/hello-rust and hello.py. Which one can your friend run?
    Answer

    Only the Rust program. It is machine code and needs no compiler. But it only runs on the same kind of system, for example macOS on an Apple chip. The file hello.py needs a Python interpreter.

  5. Python is an interpreted language. A file has a missing bracket on line 2. Line 1 prints text. Why is nothing printed?
    Answer

    Python first turns the whole file into bytecode. It checks the grammar in that step. A missing bracket is a grammar mistake. So Python stops with a SyntaxError before line 1 runs.

  6. After a change you see twelve Rust errors. What do you do?
    Answer

    Scroll to the first error and fix only that one. Then run cargo check again. Many of the other errors come from the first one and go away.

Key takeaways

  • A program is a list of steps. Source code is its text.
  • Rust is compiled. rustc makes a machine code file before the run.
  • Python is interpreted. The python program reads and runs your file at every run.
  • rustup installs Rust. cargo creates, checks, builds and runs projects.
  • uv installs Python, creates projects and runs code with the right version.
  • Rust shows most mistakes at compile time. Python shows many of them at run time.
  • Read a Rust error from the top. Read a Python traceback from the bottom.
