Variables and types

A program keeps values under names. Every value also has a type, for example a number or a letter. In this chapter you learn how Rust and Python store values. You also see why Rust checks types before the run and Python checks them during the run.

  • Make variables with let and let mut, and use shadowing.
  • Choose the right number type and handle overflow safely.
  • Write type annotations in Rust and type hints in Python.
  • Use constants, tuples and arrays.
  • Compare static typing in Rust with dynamic typing in Python.

Names and values: let and mut

Here is a small program. It keeps an age and a score. Then it changes the score.

fn main() {
    let age = 30;          // this value cannot change
    let mut score = 10;    // mut: this value can change
    score = score + 5;
    println!("age {age}, score {score}");
}
age = 30
score = 10
score = score + 5      # every Python name can get a new value
print(f"age {age}, score {score}")
age 30, score 15

A variable is a name for a value. In Rust you make a variable with let. The value comes after the = sign.

A Rust variable is immutable by default. You cannot give it a new value. Add mut when the value must change. mut is short for mutable.

What happens when you forget mut? This program tries to change age.

fn main() {
    let age = 30;
    age = 31;
    println!("{age}");
}
error[E0384]: cannot assign twice to immutable variable `age`
 --> src/main.rs:3:5
  |
2 |     let age = 30;
  |         --- first assignment to `age`
3 |     age = 31;
  |     ^^^^^^^^ cannot assign twice to immutable variable
  |
help: consider making this binding mutable
  |
2 |     let mut age = 30;
  |         +++

The compiler stops the build. The help block shows the fix. Python has no let and no mut. You write a name, an = sign and a value. Every name can get a new value at any time.

In Rust, a value stays the same unless you say mut. In Python, every name can change. Rust makes you say your plan.

You put mut on every variable, just in case. Rust warns you: variable does not need to be mutable. Start without mut. Add it only when the compiler asks for it. Then a reader sees at once which values change.

Shadowing: the same name, a new variable

A user types the text "42". You want the number 42. Rust lets you keep the same name.

fn main() {
    let input = "42";            // text from a user
    let input: u32 = input.trim().parse().unwrap(); // same name, now a number
    let input = input * 2;       // a new variable again
    println!("input = {input}");

    let x = 5;
    {
        let x = x * 10;          // only inside these brackets
        println!("inner x = {x}");
    }
    println!("outer x = {x}");
}
user_input = "42"
user_input = int(user_input)   # the same name, now an int
user_input = user_input * 2
print(f"input = {user_input}")
input = 84
inner x = 50
outer x = 5

Each let makes a new variable. The new one hides the old one with the same name. This is shadowing. The new variable can have a different type. Here input is text first, then a number.

The curly brackets make a scope. A variable lives until the end of its scope. So the inner x is gone after the }. The outer x is still 5.

Shadowing is not the same as mut. A mut variable can change its value, but never its type.

fn main() {
    let mut spaces = "   ";
    spaces = spaces.len();   // a number into a text variable
    println!("{spaces}");
}
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:3:14
  |
2 |     let mut spaces = "   ";
  |                      ----- expected due to this value
3 |     spaces = spaces.len();   // a number into a text variable
  |              ^^^^^^^^^^^^ expected `&str`, found `usize`
Shadowing and mut side by side
Questionlet x = ... againlet mut x, then x = ...
Is it a new variable?YesNo, the same one
Can the type change?YesNo
Can it change later?No, unless the new one has mutYes
Good forSteps of one job: text, then numberA counter, a total, a buffer

In a long function you write let total = 0; a second time by accident. Now there are two variables named total. The compiler is happy, but your result is wrong. Use shadowing only for close steps, a few lines apart.

Scalar types: integers, floats, bool and char

A scalar type holds one value. Rust has four kinds: integers, floats, booleans and characters.

fn main() {
    let count = 7;               // i32, the default
    let big: u64 = 10_000_000_000;
    let byte = 255u8;            // suffix u8
    let mask = 0b1111_0000;      // binary
    let color = 0xff;            // hex
    let price = 9.99;            // f64, the default
    let ready = true;            // bool
    let letter = 'ж';            // char: one Unicode value
    let cat = '🐈';
    println!("{count} {big} {byte} {mask} {color} {price} {ready} {letter} {cat}");
    println!("i8: {} to {}", i8::MIN, i8::MAX);
    println!("u8: {} to {}", u8::MIN, u8::MAX);
    println!("i32: {} to {}", i32::MIN, i32::MAX);
}
count = 7
big = 10_000_000_000
price = 9.99
ready = True
letter = "ж"       # Python has no char type: a str of length 1
print(type(count), type(price), type(ready), type(letter))
print(2 ** 100)    # an int has no upper limit
print(isinstance(True, int), True + True)
7 10000000000 255 240 255 9.99 true ж 🐈
i8: -128 to 127
u8: 0 to 255
i32: -2147483648 to 2147483647
<class 'int'> <class 'float'> <class 'bool'> <class 'str'>
1267650600228229401496703205376
True 2

Integers

An integer type has a size in bits. The letter shows the sign. i means signed. u means unsigned.

Rust integer types
BitsSignedUnsignedUnsigned range
8i8u80 to 255
16i16u160 to 65,535
32i32u320 to about 4.3 billion
64i64u640 to about 1.8 × 1019
128i128u1280 to about 3.4 × 1038
the machine sizeisizeusize64 bits on a 64-bit computer

With n bits, a signed type holds -2^{n-1} to 2^{n-1}-1. An unsigned type holds 0 to 2^n - 1. For example, i8 holds -128 to 127. The default integer type is i32. Use usize for positions and lengths of lists. Rust uses it for every index.

You can write numbers in other forms. 1_000 is 1000, and the _ only helps your eyes. 0xff is hexadecimal. 0o77 is octal and 0b1010 is binary. b'A' is the byte 65. A suffix gives the type: 255u8.

Floats, bool and char

  • Floats. A float is f64 by default. f32 uses half the memory. Both follow the IEEE 754 standard.
  • bool. It is true or false. It uses one byte.
  • char. It holds one Unicode scalar value in single quotes: 'a', 'ж', '🐈'. It uses four bytes.

The same ideas in Python

  • Python has one integer type: int. It has no size limit. It grows as big as memory allows.
  • A Python float is the same 64-bit float as Rust's f64.
  • bool is a kind of int. So True + True is 2. Do not use this trick in real code.
  • Python has no char type. One letter is a str of length 1.

Each type has a fixed size in memory. A Python int is a full object, so it needs more room. I measured the sizes with size_of in Rust and sys.getsizeof in Python.

You write let c: char = "a";. Double quotes make a string, not a char. Rust says expected `char`, found `&str`. Use single quotes for a char: 'a'. In Python, both kinds of quotes make a str.

Type inference and annotations

You rarely write types in Rust. The compiler works them out. Look at this program.

fn main() {
    let small = 200;            // which integer type? wait and see
    let byte: u8 = small;       // this use decides: small is u8
    let ratio = 0.5;            // f64, the default
    let parsed = "7".parse::<i64>().unwrap(); // turbofish: ::<i64>
    println!("{byte} {ratio} {parsed}");
}
200 0.5 7

The compiler finds the type from the value and from later use. This is type inference. You can also write the type yourself after a colon: let byte: u8. This is a type annotation.

Read the value

let small = 200; The value is an integer. The exact type is still open.

Look at later uses

let byte: u8 = small; Now small must be a u8. Both sides of = need the same type.

Check the value

Does 200 fit in a u8? Yes, because the limit is 255. With 300 you get literal out of range for `u8`.

Use the default

No use decides the type? Then an integer becomes i32 and a float becomes f64.

Sometimes the compiler cannot decide. parse can make many types from text. So you must say which one.

fn main() {
    let number = "42".parse().unwrap();
    println!("{number}");
}
error[E0284]: type annotations needed
    --> src/main.rs:2:9
     |
   2 |     let number = "42".parse().unwrap();
     |         ^^^^^^        ----- type must be known at this point
...
help: consider giving `number` an explicit type
     |
   2 |     let number: /* Type */ = "42".parse().unwrap();
     |               ++++++++++++

Two fixes work. Write let number: i32 = ..., or write "42".parse::<i32>(). The ::<i32> form has a funny name: the turbofish.

Changing a type: as, From and try_from

Rust never changes a type on its own. You must ask. There are three ways, from risky to safe.

fn main() {
    let x: i32 = 300;
    println!("{}", x as u8);           // as cuts the value: 300 - 256
    println!("{}", 3.99_f64 as i32);   // as drops the fraction
    println!("{:?}", u8::try_from(x)); // the safe way: an error, not a wrong value
    let y: i64 = i64::from(x);         // always fits, so From exists
    println!("{y}");
}
44
3
Err(TryFromIntError(PosOverflow))
300

A cast with as never fails. But it can give a wrong number without a word. from exists only when every value fits. try_from checks and returns an error when the value does not fit. In Python you call the type like a function: int("42"), float(3), str(7).

You use as to turn a big number into a small type. 300 as u8 gives 44, and nobody warns you. Use u8::try_from(x) when the value comes from outside your program.

Overflow: when a number does not fit

A u8 holds 0 to 255. What is 250 + 10 in a u8? The value 10 comes from text, so the compiler cannot see it.

fn main() {
    let a: u8 = 250;
    let b: u8 = "10".parse().unwrap(); // the compiler cannot see the value
    let sum = a + b;                   // 260 does not fit in u8
    println!("{sum}");
}
thread 'main' (114157586) panicked at src/main.rs:4:15:
attempt to add with overflow
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
4

The result is too big for the type. This is overflow. A debug build checks every sum. It stops the program with a panic. A release build skips this check to save time. The value goes round, like a clock: 260 - 256 = 4. This is called wrapping.

When the compiler can see both numbers, it stops the build. let sum = 250u8 + 10; gives the error this arithmetic operation will overflow. But most values come from users, files or networks. So you need a plan for the run.

Four methods for a clear plan

fn main() {
    let a: u8 = 250;
    let b: u8 = 10;
    println!("{:?}", a.checked_add(b));     // None: it did not fit
    println!("{}", a.wrapping_add(b));      // goes round: 260 - 256
    println!("{}", a.saturating_add(b));    // stops at the top: 255
    println!("{:?}", a.overflowing_add(b)); // value and a flag
    println!("{:?}", a.checked_add(5));     // Some(255): it fits
}
None
4
255
(4, true)
Some(255)
Which method to choose
MethodResult for 250 + 10Use it when
checked_addNoneOverflow is an error. Money, sizes, counts.
wrapping_add4You want the clock behaviour. Hashes, random numbers.
saturating_add255A limit is fine. Volume, colour, progress.
overflowing_add(4, true)You need the value and the flag.

The same methods exist for sub, mul and more. checked_add returns an Option. The chapter Structs, enums and pattern matching explains Option.

Python numbers

A Python int never overflows. 2 ** 100 just works. But floats have limits in both languages.

fn main() {
    println!("{}", 0.1 + 0.2);         // not exactly 0.3
    println!("{}", -7 / 2);            // goes toward zero
    println!("{}", (-7_i32).div_euclid(2)); // like Python's //
    println!("{}", 1.0 / 0.0);         // infinity, no panic
    let nan = 0.0_f64 / 0.0;
    println!("{} {}", nan, nan == nan); // NaN is not equal to itself
}
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(-7 // 2)     # goes down, toward minus infinity
print(7 / 2)       # / always gives a float
print(float("inf"), float("nan") == float("nan"))
print(2.0 ** 1024) # too big for a float
0.30000000000000004
-3
-4
inf
NaN false
0.30000000000000004
-4
3.5
inf False
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/you/main.py", line 5, in <module>
    print(2.0 ** 1024) # too big for a float
          ~~~~^^~~~~~
OverflowError: (34, 'Result too large')

A float stores the number in binary. 0.1 has no exact binary form, so a tiny error remains. NaN is a special float. It is not equal to anything, not even itself.

Integer division differs. In Rust, -7 / 2 is -3. In Python, -7 // 2 is -4. Rust cuts toward zero. Python rounds down. Port maths code with care. Rust's div_euclid gives Python's answer here.

A common question: "Does Rust check overflow in release builds?" The answer is no, by default. You can turn the check on in Cargo.toml with overflow-checks = true under [profile.release]. Then the release build panics too. I tested this with Rust 1.99.

Constants and statics

Some values never change. A good name explains them.

const SECONDS_PER_HOUR: u32 = 60 * 60;   // worked out by the compiler
const MAX_USERS: usize = 1_000;
static GREETING: &str = "Hello";          // one fixed place in memory

fn main() {
    let hours = 3;
    println!("{}", hours * SECONDS_PER_HOUR);
    println!("{GREETING}, up to {MAX_USERS} users");
}
from typing import Final

SECONDS_PER_HOUR: Final = 60 * 60   # a promise, not a lock
MAX_USERS: Final = 1_000
GREETING = "Hello"                  # capitals: please do not change

hours = 3
print(hours * SECONDS_PER_HOUR)
print(f"{GREETING}, up to {MAX_USERS} users")
10800
Hello, up to 1000 users

A constant starts with const. It has four rules.

  1. You must write the type. const LIMIT = 10; gives missing type for `const` item.
  2. The value must be known at compile time. 60 * 60 is fine. A value from a user is not.
  3. The name is in capitals with underscores: MAX_USERS.
  4. It can live outside all functions, so the whole file can use it.

A static looks the same. But it has one fixed place in memory for the whole run. A const is copied into each place that uses it. Use const by default. Use static when you need one shared address.

Python has no real constant. Capital letters are only a custom. typing.Final asks a type checker for help, but Python itself ignores it. This file runs without a problem.

from typing import Final

MAX_USERS: Final = 1_000      # a promise for the type checker
count: int = "seven"          # wrong hint, but Python runs it
MAX_USERS = 2_000             # Python runs this too
print(count, MAX_USERS)
seven 2000

The type checker mypy finds both problems. Run it with uv.

uv run --with mypy mypy hints.py
hints.py:4: error: Incompatible types in assignment (expression has type "str", variable has type "int")  [assignment]
hints.py:5: error: Cannot assign to final name "MAX_USERS"  [misc]
Found 2 errors in 1 file (checked 1 source file)

You make a static mut to share a counter. In the 2024 edition, a reference to a static mut is an error: creating a shared reference to mutable static. Two threads could change it at the same time. Later chapters show safe tools, for example atomics and Mutex.

Tuples and arrays

Sometimes you want a small group of values. Rust has two simple groups.

fn main() {
    let point: (i32, f64, char) = (3, 2.5, 'A');
    let (x, y, label) = point;          // take the tuple apart
    println!("{x} {y} {label}");
    println!("{}", point.0);            // the first part
    let unit = ();                      // the empty tuple
    println!("{unit:?}");

    let days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"];   // type: [&str; 3]
    let zeros = [0u8; 4];               // four zeros
    println!("{} {:?} len={}", days[0], zeros, zeros.len());
    let mut scores: [i32; 3] = [10, 20, 30];
    scores[1] = 25;
    println!("{scores:?}");
}
point = (3, 2.5, "A")
x, y, label = point            # take the tuple apart
print(x, y, label)
print(point[0])

days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]   # a list can grow
days.append("Thu")
print(days, len(days))
zeros = [0] * 4
print(zeros)
print(days[-1])                # -1 is the last item
3 2.5 A
3
()
Mon [0, 0, 0, 0] len=4
[10, 25, 30]
3 2.5 A
3
['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu'] 4
[0, 0, 0, 0]
Thu

A tuple groups values of different types. Its length never changes. You read a part with a dot and a number: point.0. You can also take it apart with let (x, y, label) = point;. This is called destructuring.

The empty tuple () has a special name: the unit type. A function with no result returns (). You meet it again in Functions and modules.

An array holds values of one type. Its length is part of its type: [i32; 3] means three i32 values. [0u8; 4] makes four zeros. Need a list that grows? Use a Vec, from the chapter Collections.

Rust checks every index. A wrong index from outside stops the program.

fn main() {
    let scores = [10, 20, 30];
    let i: usize = "5".parse().unwrap();  // a value from outside
    println!("{}", scores[i]);
}
thread 'main' (114196521) panicked at src/main.rs:4:20:
index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 5

Python has tuples too. A Python tuple cannot change. Python has no fixed-size array in the core language. People use a list, which can grow. A wrong list index raises IndexError: list index out of range.

You think [i32; 3] and [i32; 4] are the same type. They are not. let a: [i32; 3] = [1, 2, 3, 4]; gives expected an array with a size of 3, found one with a size of 4.

Python names, dynamic types and type hints

In Python, a value has a type. A name has no type. Watch one name change its type.

age = 30
print(type(age))
age = "thirty"                # the same name, a new type
print(type(age))
other = age                   # two names, one object
print(other is age)
<class 'int'>
<class 'str'>
True

A Python name is like a label on a box. The box is the object. The object knows its type. You can move the label to another box at any time. Two labels can sit on one box. is asks: "Are these the same box?"

This is dynamic typing. Python checks a type only when it runs the line. Rust uses static typing. Each Rust variable has one type, fixed at compile time.

Type hints

You can add type hints to Python code. They look like Rust annotations.

def area(width: float, height: float) -> float:
    return width * height

print(area(3, 4))
print(area("ab", 3))          # wrong type, but it still runs
12
ababab

Python ignores the hints at run time. So area("ab", 3) repeats the text three times. A type checker reads the hints before the run. mypy says: Argument 1 to "area" has incompatible type "str"; expected "float". Pyright is another popular checker. The chapter Type hints goes deeper.

Since Python 3.14, Python does not evaluate annotations when it defines them. It waits until some code reads them. So size: UnknownType = 5 runs in Python 3.14, though UnknownType does not exist. Python 3.9 stops with NameError on the same line. The new module annotationlib reads lazy annotations. Old code with from __future__ import annotations still works.

You add hints and think Python now checks types. It does not. Hints help only when a tool reads them: mypy, Pyright or your editor. Run the checker in your tests, or the hints can be wrong for months.

Static and dynamic typing compared

Both languages refuse to mix types by accident. They only refuse at a different time.

fn main() {
    let total = 1 + 1.5;   // an integer plus a float
    println!("{total}");
}
print("1" + 1)   # a str plus an int
error[E0277]: cannot add a float to an integer
 --> src/main.rs:2:19
  |
2 |     let total = 1 + 1.5;   // an integer plus a float
  |                   ^ no implementation for `{integer} + {float}`
...
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/you/main.py", line 1, in <module>
    print("1" + 1)   # a str plus an int
          ~~~~^~~
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

Rust stops at compile time. Python stops at run time, on that line. Both are strongly typed. Neither turns text into a number on its own. In Rust, you say the change: count as f64 * price. Python mixes int and float in maths, but never str and int.

Static and dynamic typing
QuestionRust (static)Python (dynamic)
Who has the type?The variable and the valueOnly the value
When are types checked?At compile time, every lineAt run time, only lines that run
Can a name change its type?Only with shadowingYes, at any time
Do you write types?In function signatures, rarely insideNever required. Hints are optional.
Main strengthMany bugs never reach usersFast to try ideas
Main costYou must satisfy the compiler firstSome bugs appear only in production

Python with hints and a checker is called gradual typing. You add hints to one file at a time. Rust has no gradual mode. Every value has a known type before the run.

Rust inference works inside one function only. Every function signature must list its types. This is on purpose. A signature is a contract, and a change inside a function cannot break its callers. Python checkers infer more freely, so a small change can move errors far away.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for variables and types
PatternPurposeModelNote
let name = value;Make a variable that does not changelet age = 30;Start here. Add mut only when needed.
let mut name = value;Make a variable that changeslet mut total = 0;The type can never change.
let name = f(name);Shadow: a new step, the same namelet input: u32 = input.parse()?;Keep the steps close together.
let name: Type = value;Give the type yourselflet port: u16 = 8080;Needed when inference cannot decide.
expr.parse::<T>()Turn text into a number"42".parse::<i32>()The turbofish names the target type.
T::try_from(x)Change type with a checku8::try_from(300)as cuts the value without a word.
a.checked_add(b)Add without silent overflow250u8.checked_add(10)Returns None when it does not fit.
const NAME: T = value;Name a fixed valueconst MAX_USERS: usize = 1_000;The type is required. Capitals for the name.
let (a, b) = tuple;Take a tuple apartlet (x, y) = (3, 4);The count of names must match.
[value; N]An array of N copies[0u8; 4]The length is part of the type.
name: type = valueA Python hint for a checkercount: int = 0Python ignores it. Run mypy or Pyright.
NAME: Final = valueA Python constant for a checkerMAX_USERS: Final = 1_000Python itself still allows a change.

Practice

Which line makes a Rust variable that can change?

  • let count = 0;
  • let mut count = 0;
  • const count = 0;

Only mut lets you give the variable a new value. A const also needs a type and a name in capitals.

What is the type of let x = 2.5; when nothing else decides?

  • f32
  • f64
  • i32

The default float type is f64. The default integer type is i32.

A debug build adds 200 and 100 as u8 values from a file. What happens?

  • The result is 300.
  • The result is 44.
  • The program panics: attempt to add with overflow.

A debug build checks overflow and panics. A release build would give 44, because 300 - 256 = 44.

Python runs n: int = "five". What happens?

  • A TypeError at once.
  • Nothing special. The name n points to the str "five".
  • Python changes "five" into 5.

Python does not check hints at run time. A type checker like mypy reports the line.

The Rust type for one Unicode value is ?.

The type of the empty tuple () is called the ? type.

In Python, -7 // 2 gives ?.

250u8.saturating_add(10) gives ?.

  1. Write a Rust line that makes an array of 10 zeros of type i64.
    Answer

    let zeros = [0i64; 10]; or let zeros: [i64; 10] = [0; 10];

  2. Why does let n = "8".parse().unwrap(); not compile? Give two fixes.
    Answer

    parse can make many types, so the compiler cannot choose. Write let n: i32 = "8".parse().unwrap(); or let n = "8".parse::<i32>().unwrap();.

  3. Explain the difference between shadowing and mut in two sentences.
    Answer

    Shadowing makes a new variable with the same name, and its type can change. mut keeps the same variable and lets its value change, but never its type.

  4. A user sends an age as i32. You must store it as u8. Which tool do you use, and why not as?
    Answer

    Use u8::try_from(age). It returns an error for values like -5 or 300. as would give a wrong number with no warning, for example 300 as u8 is 44.

  5. Your Rust game counts points in a u32. Very big scores should stop at the top value. Which method do you use?
    Answer

    score.saturating_add(points). It stops at u32::MAX and never panics or wraps.

  6. Hard: a function works for months in Python. Then it fails in production with a TypeError. How could Rust have caught it, and what can you do in Python?
    Answer

    The bad line ran only in a rare case. Python checks types only on lines that run. Rust checks every line at compile time, so the build would fail. In Python, add type hints and run mypy or Pyright in your tests. Tests that reach the rare case help too.

Key takeaways

  • Rust variables do not change by default. mut allows a change of value, not of type.
  • Shadowing with let makes a new variable. It can have a new type.
  • Rust has many integer sizes. Python has one int with no limit.
  • Overflow panics in a Rust debug build and wraps in a release build. Use checked_, wrapping_ or saturating_ to say your plan.
  • Rust infers most types. Write a type when inference cannot decide.
  • Constants need a type in Rust. In Python, capitals and Final are only promises.
  • Rust checks types at compile time. Python checks them at run time. Type hints help only with a checker.

Sources

  • The Rust Programming Language: Variables and Mutability. let, mut, constants and shadowing.
  • The Rust Programming Language: Data Types. Scalar types, overflow, tuples and arrays.
  • The Rust Reference: Operator expressions. The exact rules for overflow and for as casts.
  • Python: Built-in Types. int, float and bool, and how division works.
  • Python: typing. Type hints and Final. Python does not check them at run time.
  • What's New in Python 3.14. Deferred evaluation of annotations.

Control flow

A program does not always run from top to bottom. It makes choices, and it repeats steps. This chapter shows how Rust and Python choose and repeat. You also learn why Python treats an empty list as false, and why Rust never does.

  • Write if and else, and use if as a value in Rust.
  • Repeat steps with loop, while and for over ranges.
  • Leave nested loops with labels, and return a value with break.
  • Read and write a first match in both languages.
  • Explain truthiness in Python and avoid its common bugs.

Choices with if and else

This program looks at a temperature. It prints one of three words.

fn main() {
    let temp = 31;
    if temp > 30 {
        println!("hot");
    } else if temp > 15 {
        println!("warm");
    } else {
        println!("cold");
    }
}
temp = 31
if temp > 30:
    print("hot")
elif temp > 15:
    print("warm")
else:
    print("cold")
hot

The part after if is the condition. When it is true, the program runs the first branch. When it is false, the program tests the next condition. else catches everything that is left. Only one branch runs.

  • Rust puts each branch in curly brackets { }. The condition needs no round brackets.
  • Python ends the condition with a colon :. The indentation shows the branch. Use four spaces.
  • Rust writes else if. Python writes elif.

The condition in Rust must be a real bool. A number is not enough.

fn main() {
    let items = 3;
    if items {
        println!("not empty");
    }
}
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:3:8
  |
3 |     if items {
  |        ^^^^^ expected `bool`, found integer

Write the test you mean: if items > 0. Python would accept if items:. The section on truthiness explains why.

The order of conditions matters. Test temp > 15 first, and 31 prints "warm". The program never reaches "hot". Put the narrow test first and the wide test later.

if gives a value

In Rust, if can give a value. You can store it in a variable.

fn main() {
    let temp = 31;
    // if gives a value: both branches have the same type
    let label = if temp % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" };
    println!("{temp} is {label}");
}
temp = 31
# a conditional expression: value if test else other value
label = "even" if temp % 2 == 0 else "odd"
print(f"{temp} is {label}")
31 is odd

An expression is code that gives a value. 2 + 3 is an expression. In Rust, if is an expression too. The last line of a block is its value, when it has no semicolon. So { "even" } gives "even".

Python has a special form for this: value if test else other. Python calls it a conditional expression. A normal Python if gives no value.

Two rules keep the Rust type clear.

fn main() {
    let temp = 31;
    let label = if temp > 30 { "hot" } else { 0 };
    println!("{label}");
}
error[E0308]: `if` and `else` have incompatible types
 --> src/main.rs:3:47
  |
3 |     let label = if temp > 30 { "hot" } else { 0 };
  |                                -----          ^ expected `&str`, found integer
  |                                |
  |                                expected because of this

Both branches must give the same type. A variable has only one type.

fn main() {
    let temp = 31;
    let label = if temp > 30 { "hot" };
    println!("{label}");
}
error[E0317]: `if` may be missing an `else` clause
 --> src/main.rs:3:17
  |
3 |     let label = if temp > 30 { "hot" };
  |                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^-----^^
  |                 |              |
  |                 |              found here
  |                 expected `&str`, found `()`
  |
  = note: `if` expressions without `else` evaluate to `()`

When the value is used, you need an else. Without it, a false condition gives (), the unit type.

You write { "even"; } with a semicolon. The semicolon throws the value away. The block now gives (), and you get a type error. Leave out the semicolon on the value line. The chapter Functions and modules explains this rule in detail.

Loops: while and for with ranges

A loop repeats steps. Here are the two most common loops.

fn main() {
    // while: repeat as long as the test is true
    let mut fuel = 3;
    while fuel > 0 {
        println!("fuel {fuel}");
        fuel -= 1;
    }
    // for: one pass for each item
    for n in 1..4 {          // 1, 2, 3 (4 is not included)
        print!("{n} ");
    }
    println!();
    for n in (1..=10).rev().step_by(3) { // 10, 7, 4, 1
        print!("{n} ");
    }
    println!();
    let days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"];
    for (i, day) in days.iter().enumerate() {
        println!("{i}: {day}");
    }
}
# while: repeat as long as the test is true
fuel = 3
while fuel > 0:
    print(f"fuel {fuel}")
    fuel -= 1
# for: one pass for each item
for n in range(1, 4):           # 1, 2, 3 (4 is not included)
    print(n, end=" ")
print()
for n in range(10, 0, -3):      # 10, 7, 4, 1
    print(n, end=" ")
print()
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
for i, day in enumerate(days):
    print(f"{i}: {day}")
fuel 3
fuel 2
fuel 1
1 2 3
10 7 4 1
0: Mon
1: Tue
2: Wed

A while loop tests its condition before each pass. When the test is false, the loop ends. One pass through a loop is an iteration.

A for loop takes one item at a time from a group. 1..4 is a range. It gives 1, 2 and 3. The end is not included. Write 1..=4 to include the end.

Ranges in Rust and Python
You wantRustPython
0, 1, 2, 3, 40..5range(5)
1, 2, 3, 4, 51..=5range(1, 6)
5, 4, 3, 2, 1(1..=5).rev()range(5, 0, -1)
0, 2, 4, 6, 8(0..10).step_by(2)range(0, 10, 2)
Index and itemlist.iter().enumerate()enumerate(list)

Watch a for loop add the numbers 1 to 4. The program prints one line in each pass.

fn main() {
    let mut total = 0;
    for n in 1..=4 {
        total += n;
        println!("n = {n}, total = {total}");
    }
}

n = 1

The range gives its first number. total was 0. Now it is 0 + 1 = 1.

n = 2

The range gives the next number. total becomes 1 + 2 = 3.

n = 3

total becomes 3 + 3 = 6.

n = 4

1..=4 includes 4. total becomes 6 + 4 = 10.

No more numbers

The range is empty. The loop ends. The program goes on after the }.

n = 1, total = 1
n = 2, total = 3
n = 3, total = 6
n = 4, total = 10

continue skips the rest of one pass. The loop goes on with the next item. This loop prints only the numbers that 3 divides.

fn main() {
    for n in 1..10 {
        if n % 3 != 0 {
            continue;          // skip to the next n
        }
        println!("{n} can be divided by 3");
    }
}
3 can be divided by 3
6 can be divided by 3
9 can be divided by 3

You want 1 to 10 and write 1..10 or range(1, 10). You get only 1 to 9. This is an off-by-one error. Use 1..=10 in Rust and range(1, 11) in Python.

You loop over a Vec with for name in names. After the loop, names is gone. Rust says borrow of moved value: `names`. The loop took the list. Write for name in &names to only look at it. The chapter Ownership and borrowing explains why.

loop and break with a value

Sometimes you do not know when to stop. You stop when you find something. Rust has a loop for this case: loop.

fn main() {
    // loop runs until break. break can carry a value out.
    let mut n: u64 = 27;
    let mut steps = 0;
    let result = loop {
        if n == 1 {
            break steps;       // the loop gives back steps
        }
        n = if n % 2 == 0 { n / 2 } else { 3 * n + 1 };
        steps += 1;
    };
    println!("27 reaches 1 after {result} steps");
}
n = 27
steps = 0
while True:                 # Python has no loop keyword
    if n == 1:
        break               # break carries no value in Python
    n = n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1
    steps += 1
print(f"27 reaches 1 after {steps} steps")
27 reaches 1 after 111 steps

The rule: halve an even number, and make an odd number 3n + 1. How many steps until 1? Nobody knows in advance. So the program uses a loop with no condition. It is an infinite loop, and only break ends it.

In Rust, break steps ends the loop and gives the value steps. So loop is an expression, like if. Only loop can do this. while and for always give (), because they can end without a break. Python writes while True:. Its break cannot carry a value.

Which loop should you choose? Follow the tree.

A while loop forgets to change its variable. Remove fuel -= 1, and the loop runs forever. Press Ctrl + C in the terminal to stop it. Then check that every pass moves toward the end.

Labels: leave nested loops

You search a grid for the number 9. When you find it, you want to stop both loops.

fn main() {
    let grid = [[1, 4, 7], [3, 9, 5], [8, 5, 6]];
    let mut found = None;
    'rows: for (r, row) in grid.iter().enumerate() {
        for (c, &value) in row.iter().enumerate() {
            if value == 9 {
                found = Some((r, c));
                break 'rows;   // leave both loops at once
            }
        }
    }
    println!("{found:?}");

    // continue with a label: skip to the next row
    'next_row: for row in grid {
        for value in row {
            if value % 2 == 0 {
                println!("first even number in {row:?} is {value}");
                continue 'next_row;
            }
        }
        println!("no even number in {row:?}");
    }
}
grid = [[1, 4, 7], [3, 9, 5], [8, 5, 6]]

def find(grid, target):
    for r, row in enumerate(grid):
        for c, value in enumerate(row):
            if value == target:
                return (r, c)      # return leaves both loops
    return None

print(find(grid, 9))

for row in grid:
    for value in row:
        if value % 2 == 0:
            print(f"first even number in {row} is {value}")
            break
    else:                          # runs only when there was no break
        print(f"no even number in {row}")
Some((1, 1))
first even number in [1, 4, 7] is 4
no even number in [3, 9, 5]
first even number in [8, 5, 6] is 8
(1, 1)
first even number in [1, 4, 7] is 4
no even number in [3, 9, 5]
first even number in [8, 5, 6] is 8

A plain break leaves only the inner loop. A label names a loop. In Rust, a label starts with a single quote: 'rows:. Then break 'rows leaves the outer loop. continue 'next_row starts the next pass of the outer loop.

Python has no labels. It has two other tools.

  • Put the loops in a function. return leaves all loops at once.
  • Use for ... else. The else part runs only when the loop ended without break.

A labelled block

A label also works on a plain block, with no loop. break then leaves the block early with a value.

fn main() {
    let score = 75;
    // a labelled block: break leaves the block with a value
    let grade = 'grade: {
        if score < 0 || score > 100 {
            break 'grade "invalid";
        }
        if score >= 90 {
            break 'grade "A";
        }
        if score >= 70 {
            break 'grade "B";
        }
        "C"                        // the normal end value
    };
    println!("{score} gives {grade}");
}
75 gives B

A labelled block runs one time only. continue is not allowed inside it. Often a small function is clearer. But a labelled block helps inside a long function.

Python's for ... else confuses many people. The else does not mean "if the loop did not run". It means "if the loop did not break". Add a short comment every time you use it.

A first look at match

A web server returns a status code. You want a short text for each code.

fn main() {
    for code in [200, 302, 404, 503, 100] {
        let text = match code {
            200 => "OK",
            301 | 302 => "moved",              // two values, one arm
            400..=499 => "client error",       // a range of values
            n if n >= 500 => "server error",   // a guard: an extra test
            _ => "something else",             // every other value
        };
        println!("{code}: {text}");
    }
}
for code in [200, 302, 404, 503, 100]:
    match code:
        case 200:
            text = "OK"
        case 301 | 302:                # two values, one case
            text = "moved"
        case n if 400 <= n <= 499:     # no range pattern: use a guard
            text = "client error"
        case n if n >= 500:
            text = "server error"
        case _:                        # every other value
            text = "something else"
    print(f"{code}: {text}")
200: OK
302: moved
404: client error
503: server error
100: something else

match compares a value with a list of patterns. It runs the first one that fits. In Rust, each line pattern => result is an arm. _ is the wildcard. A guard like if n >= 500 adds a test.

A Rust match must cover every possible value. It is exhaustive. Forget a case, and the build fails.

fn main() {
    let code: u16 = 404;
    let text = match code {
        200 => "OK",
        400..=499 => "client error",
    };
    println!("{text}");
}
error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `0_u16..=199_u16`, `201_u16..=399_u16` and `500_u16..=u16::MAX` not covered
 --> src/main.rs:3:22
  |
3 |     let text = match code {
  |                      ^^^^ patterns `0_u16..=199_u16`, `201_u16..=399_u16` and `500_u16..=u16::MAX` not covered

The compiler even lists the missing values. Python came later to match. It arrived in Python 3.10. A Python match does not need to cover every case. When no case fits, nothing happens.

Patterns can look inside a value

A pattern can also check the shape of a list. This small game reads text commands.

fn main() {
    for line in ["go north", "look", "take red key", "fly"] {
        let words: Vec<&str> = line.split_whitespace().collect();
        match words.as_slice() {
            ["go", place] => println!("you walk {place}"),
            ["look"] => println!("you see a door"),
            ["take", rest @ ..] => println!("you take {}", rest.join(" ")),
            _ => println!("unknown command: {line}"),
        }
    }
}
for line in ["go north", "look", "take red key", "fly"]:
    match line.split():
        case ["go", place]:
            print(f"you walk {place}")
        case ["look"]:
            print("you see a door")
        case ["take", *rest]:
            print(f"you take {' '.join(rest)}")
        case _:
            print(f"unknown command: {line}")
you walk north
you see a door
you take red key
unknown command: fly

["go", place] fits a list of exactly two words. The first word must be "go". The second word goes into the new variable place. rest @ .. in Rust and *rest in Python take all the words that are left. The chapter Structs, enums and pattern matching shows much more.

In Python, a plain name in a case is not a comparison. case OK_CODE: fits every value. It puts the value into a new variable OK_CODE. With more cases after it, Python stops: SyntaxError: name capture 'OK_CODE' makes remaining patterns unreachable. Without more cases, the bug is silent. Use a dotted name, for example case Status.OK: from an Enum.

Truthiness in Python, and why Rust has none

Python lets you write if items: for any value. Here is how Python decides.

values = [0, 0.0, "", [], {}, None, False, 7, "0", [0], " "]
for v in values:
    print(f"{v!r:6} -> {bool(v)}")
0      -> False
0.0    -> False
''     -> False
[]     -> False
{}     -> False
None   -> False
False  -> False
7      -> True
'0'    -> True
[0]    -> True
' '    -> True

Every Python value counts as true or false in a condition. This is truthiness. Zero, empty groups, None and False are falsy. Almost everything else is truthy. Note that "0" and [0] are truthy. They are not empty.

This is short and handy. A while loop can run until a list is empty.

tasks = ["build", "test", "deploy"]
while tasks:                   # a non-empty list counts as true
    task = tasks.pop(0)
    print("run", task)
print("all done")
fn main() {
    let mut tasks = vec!["deploy", "test", "build"];
    // while let: repeat while the pattern matches
    while let Some(task) = tasks.pop() {   // pop takes the last item
        println!("run {task}");
    }
    println!("all done");
}
run build
run test
run deploy
all done

But truthiness hides a classic bug. Zero and "missing" look the same.

for count in [None, 5, 0]:     # 0 is a real count
    if not count:              # True for None AND for 0
        print("no count")
    else:
        print(f"count = {count}")
print("---")
for count in [None, 5, 0]:
    if count is None:          # test only for None
        print("no count")
    else:
        print(f"count = {count}")
no count
count = 5
no count
---
no count
count = 5
count = 0

The first loop says "no count" for 0. That is wrong. A count of zero is a real answer. The second loop asks the exact question: is None.

Rust has no truthiness at all. A condition must be a bool. So you always write the exact question.

The same question in both languages
QuestionPython, short formRust, always exact
Is the list empty?if not items:if items.is_empty()
Is the text empty?if not name:if name.is_empty()
Is the number zero?if not count:if count == 0
Is a value missing?if value is None:if value.is_none()
Use a default for empty textname or "guest"if name.is_empty() { "guest" } else { name }

Why did Rust choose this? A missing value and a zero are different things. The type system keeps them apart. A missing value is an Option, and zero is a number. An if on a number can never ask "is it missing?" by mistake.

Python's or and and return one of their values, not always a bool. "" or "guest" gives "guest". [] and x gives []. This is why name or "guest" works as a default.

You use if not value: when 0, "" or an empty list are valid values. Use if value is None: to test for a missing value. Code reviewers look for this bug.

For experts: what for really does

A for loop is a short form of a loop with an iterator. Both versions below print the same three lines.

fn main() {
    let days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"];
    // what `for day in days.iter()` does for you
    let mut it = days.iter();
    loop {
        match it.next() {
            Some(day) => println!("{day}"),
            None => break,          // no more items: stop
        }
    }
}
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
# what `for day in days` does for you
it = iter(days)
while True:
    try:
        day = next(it)
    except StopIteration:       # no more items: stop
        break
    print(day)
Mon
Tue
Wed

Rust calls IntoIterator::into_iter one time. Then it calls next until it gets None. Python calls iter, then next until it gets StopIteration. The chapter Iterators and closures builds on this.

Prefer for x in &list to for i in 0..list.len(). The iterator form is shorter. It also cannot use a wrong index, and the compiler can often skip the index check.

Let chains (Rust 1.88, 2024 edition)

Since Rust 1.88, an if can join a pattern test and a bool test with &&. This is a let chain. It works only in the 2024 edition.

fn main() {
    for text in ["42", "-7", "abc"] {
        // a let chain: a pattern test and a bool test in one if
        if let Ok(n) = text.parse::<i32>() && n > 0 {
            println!("{text}: positive number {n}");
        } else {
            println!("{text}: not a positive number");
        }
    }
}
42: positive number 42
-7: not a positive number
abc: not a positive number

break in finally (Python 3.14)

In Python, break, continue or return inside a finally block can hide an error. Python 3.14 now warns about it. This comes from PEP 765.

for attempt in range(3):
    try:
        print("try", attempt)
        raise ValueError("bad data")
    finally:
        break              # hides the error: Python 3.14 warns
print("the error is gone")
/home/you/finally.py:6: SyntaxWarning: 'break' in a 'finally' block
  break              # hides the error: Python 3.14 warns
try 0
the error is gone

The ValueError disappeared without a trace. Never leave a finally block with break, continue or return.

A common question: "What type does a Rust loop have?" Without any break, it never ends, so its type is !, the never type. With break value, it has the type of that value. while and for always have the type ().

Patterns to remember

Patterns for control flow
PatternPurposeModelNote
if c { } else if d { } else { }Choose one of several branchesif temp > 30 { "hot" } else { "mild" }The condition must be a bool.
let x = if c { a } else { b };Choose a valuelet label = if n % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" };Same type in both branches, and no semicolon inside.
a if c else bPython: choose a valuelabel = "even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd"The test sits in the middle.
for x in a..=b { }Repeat for each numberfor n in 1..=10 { }.. leaves out the end. ..= includes it.
for x in &list { }Visit each item without taking the listfor name in &names { }Without &, the loop takes the list.
for (i, x) in list.iter().enumerate()Get the index and the itemfor (i, day) in days.iter().enumerate()Python: for i, day in enumerate(days).
while c { }Repeat while a test is truewhile fuel > 0 { fuel -= 1; }Change something in each pass, or it never ends.
let v = loop { break x; };Repeat until found, then return a valuelet steps = loop { if n == 1 { break count; } ... };Only loop can break with a value.
'name: for ... { break 'name; }Leave an outer loop'rows: for row in grid { ... break 'rows; }Python: use return in a function.
for ... elsePython: run code when no break happenedfor x in row: ... else: print("none")else means "no break", not "no items".
match v { p => e, _ => e }Compare a value with patternsmatch code { 200 => "OK", _ => "other" }Rust needs every case. Add _ at the end.
case Enum.NAME:Python: compare with a constantcase Status.OK:A plain name captures. It does not compare.
if value is None:Python: test for a missing valueif count is None:if not count: is also true for 0.

Practice

Which numbers does for n in 2..5 give?

  • 2, 3, 4, 5
  • 2, 3, 4
  • 3, 4, 5

A range with .. leaves out the end. Write 2..=5 to include 5.

Which Rust loop can return a value with break?

  • while
  • for
  • loop

while and for can end without a break. So they always give ().

Which Python value is truthy?

  • 0
  • ""
  • "0"
  • []

"0" is a string with one character. It is not empty, so it is truthy.

A Rust match on a u8 covers only 0 to 9. What happens?

  • The program panics for 10.
  • The build fails with E0004: non-exhaustive patterns.
  • Nothing happens for 10.

A Rust match must be exhaustive. Add a _ arm for the other values.

In Python, range(10, 0, -2) starts with 10 and ends with ?.

To include the end of a Rust range, write 1.?10.

Python's word for else if is ?.

  1. Write a Rust for loop that prints 10, 8, 6, 4, 2.
    Answer

    for n in (2..=10).rev().step_by(2) { println!("{n}"); }. In Python: for n in range(10, 0, -2): print(n).

  2. Fix this line: let size = if big { 100 } else { "small" };
    Answer

    Both branches must have the same type. Use two numbers, if big { 100 } else { 10 }, or two strings, if big { "big" } else { "small" }.

  3. Write a Rust loop that finds the first power of 2 above 1000 and gives it back with break.
    Answer

    let mut p = 1; let first = loop { p *= 2; if p > 1000 { break p; } };. The value is 1024.

  4. In Python, def show(limit=None): if not limit: limit = 10. A user calls show(0). What goes wrong? Fix it.
    Answer

    0 is falsy, so the limit becomes 10 instead of 0. Write if limit is None: limit = 10.

  5. Why does Python stop with a SyntaxError on case MAX: followed by case _:?
    Answer

    A plain name in a case captures every value into a new variable. So it always fits, and the cases after it can never run. Python sees this and reports it. Use a dotted name like Limits.MAX to compare.

  6. Hard: rewrite the grid search in Rust without a label. Use a labelled block or a function. Which version is clearer, and why?
    Answer

    A function is often clearer: fn find(grid: &[[i32; 3]; 3], target: i32) -> Option<(usize, usize)> with two for loops and return Some((r, c)) inside. It has a name, and you can test it alone. A label is fine for one short search inside a function.

Key takeaways

  • A Rust condition must be a bool. Python accepts any value and uses truthiness.
  • In Rust, if, match, blocks and loop give values.
  • for is the everyday loop. .. leaves out the end, ..= includes it.
  • Only loop can return a value with break.
  • Labels like 'rows: let you leave an outer loop. Python uses return or for ... else.
  • A Rust match must cover every case. A Python match can skip cases.
  • In Python, test for a missing value with is None, not with not.

Sources

  • The Rust Programming Language: Control Flow. if, loop, while, for and loop labels.
  • The Rust Reference: Loops and other breakable expressions. The exact rules for break values, labels and labelled blocks.
  • Announcing Rust 1.88.0. Let chains, for the 2024 edition only.
  • The Python Tutorial: More Control Flow Tools. if, for, range, break, loop else and match.
  • Python: Truth Value Testing. Which values are false in a condition.
  • PEP 765. Why Python 3.14 warns about break, continue and return in finally.

Functions and modules

A function gives a name to a piece of work. A module puts related functions in one place. With both, a big program becomes many small parts that you can read, test and reuse.

  • Write functions with parameters and return values in Rust and Python.
  • Explain expressions, statements and the unit type ().
  • Use default, keyword and keyword-only arguments in Python.
  • Split code into modules and files with mod, use, pub and import.
  • Write documentation comments and run their examples as tests.

Your own functions

Here are two small functions. The first one works out an area. The second one only prints a greeting.

fn area(width: f64, height: f64) -> f64 {
    width * height            // no semicolon: this is the result
}

fn greet(name: &str) {        // no -> part: the result is ()
    println!("Hello, {name}!");
}

fn main() {
    let a = area(3.0, 4.5);
    println!("area = {a}");
    let r = greet("Ann");
    println!("greet gave {r:?}");
}
def area(width: float, height: float) -> float:
    return width * height


def greet(name: str) -> None:
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")


a = area(3.0, 4.5)
print(f"area = {a}")
r = greet("Ann")
print(f"greet gave {r}")
area = 13.5
Hello, Ann!
greet gave ()
area = 13.5
Hello, Ann!
greet gave None

A function starts with fn in Rust and def in Python. The names in the brackets are parameters. The values you pass in a call are arguments. In area(3.0, 4.5), 3.0 and 4.5 are arguments.

  • Types. Every Rust parameter needs a type: width: f64. In Python, the types are only hints.
  • Result. -> f64 gives the type of the result. This result is the return value.
  • No result. greet has no -> part. In Rust it returns (). In Python it returns None.
  • Names. Both languages write function names in snake_case: read_file, not readFile.

Rust never guesses the types of parameters. This line forgets them.

fn add(a, b) -> i32 {
    a + b
}
error: expected one of `:`, `@`, or `|`, found `,`
 --> src/main.rs:1:9
  |
1 | fn add(a, b) -> i32 {
  |         ^ expected one of `:`, `@`, or `|`
  |
help: if this is a parameter name, give it a type
  |
1 | fn add(a: TypeName, b) -> i32 {
  |         ++++++++++

Write fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32. Inside a function, Rust infers types. But the first line of a function, the signature, always lists them. The signature is a promise to every caller.

In Python you forget return. The function runs, but it gives None. Then total = area(3, 4) stores None, and a later line fails. If a function computes something, end it with return.

Expressions, statements and the unit type

Look at the curly brackets in this program. They give a value.

fn main() {
    let price = 20;                 // a statement: it gives no value
    let total = {                   // a block is an expression
        let tax = price / 10;       // statement
        price + tax                 // expression: the value of the block
    };
    println!("total = {total}");
}
total = 22

Rust code has two kinds of parts.

  • An expression gives a value. price + tax, area(3.0, 4.5) and a block are expressions.
  • A statement does something, but gives no value. let tax = price / 10; is a statement.

A semicolon turns an expression into a statement. It throws the value away. So the last line of a function decides the result. With no semicolon, its value is returned. This last line is the tail expression.

One extra semicolon changes everything. Watch.

fn double(n: i32) -> i32 {
    n * 2;
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", double(4));
}
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:1:22
  |
1 | fn double(n: i32) -> i32 {
  |    ------            ^^^ expected `i32`, found `()`
  |    |
  |    implicitly returns `()` as its body has no tail or `return` expression
2 |     n * 2;
  |          - help: remove this semicolon to return this value

The body has no tail expression now. So the function gives (). That is the unit type. It has exactly one value, also written (). A function without -> returns (). So fn greet(name: &str) means the same as fn greet(name: &str) -> ().

A let is a statement, so it has no value. You cannot write let x = (let y = 6);. Rust says expected expression, found `let` statement.

The same ideas in Python
IdeaRustPython
Give back a valueTail expression, or return x;Always return x
No result(), the unit typeNone
Does a block give a value?YesNo. Blocks are only indentation.
Is if a value?YesOnly the form a if c else b

No semicolon on the last line means "this is the answer". A semicolon means "do it and forget the value".

Return early, return many values

A function can stop early with return. It can also give back two values in a tuple.

fn grade(score: u32) -> char {
    if score > 100 {
        return '?';                 // leave early
    }
    if score >= 90 { 'A' } else if score >= 70 { 'B' } else { 'C' }
}

fn min_max(values: &[i32]) -> (i32, i32) {
    let mut lo = values[0];
    let mut hi = values[0];
    for &v in values {
        if v < lo { lo = v; }
        if v > hi { hi = v; }
    }
    (lo, hi)                        // two results in one tuple
}

fn main() {
    println!("{} {} {}", grade(95), grade(75), grade(120));
    let (lo, hi) = min_max(&[4, -2, 9, 7]);
    println!("lo = {lo}, hi = {hi}");
}
def grade(score: int) -> str:
    if score > 100:
        return "?"                  # leave early
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    return "B" if score >= 70 else "C"


def min_max(values: list[int]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    lo = hi = values[0]
    for v in values:
        lo = min(lo, v)
        hi = max(hi, v)
    return lo, hi                   # two results in one tuple


print(grade(95), grade(75), grade(120))
lo, hi = min_max([4, -2, 9, 7])
print(f"lo = {lo}, hi = {hi}")
A B ?
lo = -2, hi = 9

Use return for the special cases at the top. Let the normal result be the tail expression at the end. Many Rust programmers call the top checks guard clauses.

&[i32] means "a view of some i32 values". It accepts an array or a Vec. The chapter Ownership and borrowing explains the &.

What happens inside the computer during one call? The picture and the slides show it.

Work out the arguments

area(3.0, 4.5). Both values are ready before the call starts.

Make a frame

The computer makes a stack frame for the call. width gets 3.0 and height gets 4.5.

Run the body

The body runs from top to bottom. width * height gives 13.5.

Return

The value 13.5 goes back to the caller. The frame is removed, with all its local variables.

Go on

a is now 13.5. main goes on with its next line.

You return a tuple in Python and forget to unpack it. result = min_max(data) gives (-2, 9), not two names. Write lo, hi = min_max(data). The count of names must match the count of values.

Python arguments: default and keyword

Python functions can give parameters a default value. Callers can also name the arguments.

def connect(host: str, port: int = 80, *, timeout: float = 5.0) -> str:
    return f"{host}:{port} (timeout {timeout} s)"


print(connect("example.com"))                  # use both defaults
print(connect("example.com", 8080))            # by position
print(connect("example.com", timeout=1.5))     # by keyword
print(connect(port=443, host="example.com"))   # any order with keywords
try:
    connect("example.com", 8080, 1.5)          # timeout is keyword-only
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
// Rust has no default values and no keyword arguments.
// Option says "this value may be missing".
fn connect(host: &str, port: Option<u16>) -> String {
    let port = port.unwrap_or(80);              // 80 when port is None
    format!("{host}:{port}")
}

// Or give each version its own clear name.
fn connect_tls(host: &str) -> String {
    connect(host, Some(443))
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", connect("example.com", None));
    println!("{}", connect("example.com", Some(8080)));
    println!("{}", connect_tls("example.com"));
}
example.com:80 (timeout 5.0 s)
example.com:8080 (timeout 5.0 s)
example.com:80 (timeout 1.5 s)
example.com:443 (timeout 5.0 s)
TypeError: connect() takes from 1 to 2 positional arguments but 3 were given
example.com:80
example.com:8080
example.com:443

Python has two ways to pass an argument.

  • A positional argument is matched by its place: the first value goes to the first parameter.
  • A keyword argument is matched by its name: timeout=1.5. The order of keyword arguments does not matter.

The lone * in the signature is a wall. Every parameter after it is keyword-only. So connect("example.com", 8080, 1.5) fails. A wall / does the opposite. Parameters before it are positional-only. Keyword-only parameters make calls easy to read. timeout=1.5 is clearer than a lone 1.5.

Rust has no default values, no keyword arguments and no overloading. Every call passes every argument in order. Rust programmers use three tools instead.

  1. An Option parameter, as in connect(host, None).
  2. Separate functions with clear names, as in connect_tls.
  3. A settings struct with defaults, or a builder. The chapter API design and idioms shows them.

The default value trap

def add_tag(tag, tags=[]):         # the list is made ONE time
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags


print(add_tag("rust"))
print(add_tag("python"))           # surprise: "rust" is still there


def add_tag_fixed(tag, tags=None):
    if tags is None:
        tags = []                  # a new list in every call
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags


print(add_tag_fixed("rust"))
print(add_tag_fixed("python"))
['rust']
['rust', 'python']
['rust']
['python']

Python works out a default value one time, when it runs the def line. Every call then shares the same list. So the second call still sees "rust".

Never use a list, a dict or a set as a default value. Use None and make the new object inside the function. The linter Ruff finds it with the rule B006.

Modules: mod and pub

A module groups related code under one name. In Rust you can start with a module inside one file.

mod geometry {
    pub fn square_area(side: f64) -> f64 {
        side * side
    }

    fn check(side: f64) -> bool {   // no pub: private
        side >= 0.0
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", geometry::square_area(3.0));
    println!("{}", geometry::check(3.0));
}
error[E0603]: function `check` is private
  --> src/main.rs:13:30
   |
13 |     println!("{}", geometry::check(3.0));
   |                              ^^^^^ private function
   |
note: the function `check` is defined here
  --> src/main.rs:6:5

Everything in a Rust module is private by default. pub makes an item public. Code inside a module can use the items of its parent modules. But a parent cannot see the private items of its children.

The :: separates the parts of a path. Paths can start in three places.

Where a Rust path starts
StartMeaningExample
crate::The root of your own cratecrate::geometry::square_area
self::The current moduleself::check
super::The parent modulesuper::square_area
a crate nameAnother crate, for example the standard librarystd::f64::consts::PI

A crate is one program or one library. There is also a middle level: pub(crate). It makes an item public inside your crate, but not to other crates.

You write pub mod geometry and expect all its functions to be public. They are not. pub on a module only lets others see the module name. Each function inside needs its own pub.

Files and folders

Real projects put each module in its own file. Here is the same small project in both languages.

mod geometry;                   // the code is in src/geometry.rs

use geometry::circle;           // now `circle` is a short name

fn main() {
    println!("{:.2}", circle::area(2.0));
    println!("{}", circle::box_area(2.0));
    println!("{}", geometry::square_area(3.0));
}
import geometry
from geometry import circle          # now `circle` is a short name

print(f"{circle.area(2.0):.2f}")
print(circle.box_area(2.0))
print(geometry.square_area(3.0))
pub mod circle;                 // the code is in src/geometry/circle.rs

pub fn square_area(side: f64) -> f64 {
    side * side
}
def square_area(side: float) -> float:
    return side * side
use std::f64::consts::PI;       // a name from the standard library

pub fn area(r: f64) -> f64 {
    PI * r * r
}

pub fn box_area(r: f64) -> f64 {   // the square around the circle
    super::square_area(2.0 * r)    // super: the parent module
}
import math                          # a module from the standard library

from . import square_area            # the dot: this package


def area(r: float) -> float:
    return math.pi * r * r


def box_area(r: float) -> float:     # the square around the circle
    return square_area(2.0 * r)
12.57
16
9
12.57
16.0
9.0

Rust: mod finds the file, use makes a short name

  • mod geometry; tells the compiler: a module named geometry exists. It looks in src/geometry.rs. The older place src/geometry/mod.rs also works.
  • pub mod circle; inside geometry.rs points to src/geometry/circle.rs.
  • use geometry::circle; only makes a short name. It loads no file.
  • The compiler starts at main.rs (or lib.rs). A file with no mod line pointing to it is never compiled.

The common style for use: for a function, bring in its module, then call circle::area. Then the reader sees where area comes from. For a type, bring in the type itself: use std::collections::HashMap;.

Python: every file is a module

  • Each .py file is a module. A folder with __init__.py is a package.
  • import geometry runs geometry/__init__.py one time. Later imports reuse it.
  • from geometry import circle gives the short name circle. import numpy as np gives a new name.
  • from . import square_area is a relative import. It works only inside a package.
  • Python has no pub. A name that starts with _ means "private, please do not use". It is only a custom.

The __name__ check

Python runs a whole file when you import it. Sometimes you want code that runs only when you start the file yourself.

def shout(text: str) -> str:
    return text.upper() + "!"


print("util.py runs, __name__ is", __name__)

if __name__ == "__main__":        # true only when you run this file
    print(shout("hello"))
import util                        # runs util.py one time

print(util.shout("hi"))
util.py runs, __name__ is __main__
HELLO!
util.py runs, __name__ is util
HI!

When you start a file, its __name__ is "__main__". When another file imports it, __name__ is the module name. Rust needs no such check. A Rust program always starts at fn main.

You add src/geometry.rs and write use geometry::circle;, but you forget mod geometry;. Rust says unresolved import `geometry`. Its help is clear: use `mod geometry` in this file to declare the module. Remember: mod finds the file, use only shortens a name.

You run geometry/circle.py directly. Python stops: ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package. A file you start yourself is not part of a package. Start the program from main.py, or run python -m geometry.circle from the project folder.

Documentation comments

Good code explains itself to people. Both languages have a special comment for this.

//! Small helpers for whole numbers.

/// Returns the larger of two numbers.
///
/// # Examples
///
/// ```
/// let big = numtools::larger(3, 7);
/// assert_eq!(big, 7);
/// ```
pub fn larger(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    if a > b { a } else { b }
}

/// Returns the average of the values.
///
/// # Panics
///
/// Panics when `values` is empty.
pub fn average(values: &[i32]) -> f64 {
    assert!(!values.is_empty(), "values must not be empty");
    let sum: i32 = values.iter().sum();
    sum as f64 / values.len() as f64
}
"""Small helpers for whole numbers."""


def larger(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Return the larger of two numbers.

    >>> larger(3, 7)
    7
    """
    return a if a > b else b

In Rust, a comment with three slashes /// is a doc comment. It describes the item below it. //! describes the item around it, here the whole crate. Doc comments use Markdown. Common section titles are # Examples, # Panics, # Errors and # Safety.

In Python, a string on the first line of a function, module or class is a docstring. Use three double quotes. The first line is one short sentence. A blank line follows before more text.

Both languages can run the examples in the docs as tests. In Rust, cargo test runs them in a library crate. These are doc tests.

   Doc-tests numtools

running 1 test
test src/lib.rs - larger (line 7) ... ok

test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.00s
Trying:
    larger(3, 7)
Expecting:
    7
ok
1 item had no tests:
    numtools
1 item passed all tests:
   1 test in numtools.larger
1 test in 2 items.
1 passed.
Test passed.

cargo doc --open builds web pages from the doc comments and opens them. In Python, help(numtools.larger) prints the docstring. Editors show both kinds when you point at a function.

Write the example first, then the code. A doc test that fails tells you that the docs are out of date. Docs that are tested stay true.

You write // and expect it in the docs. Only /// and //! become documentation. In Python, a # comment is not a docstring either. Only a string on the first line is.

For experts: functions are values

In both languages, a function is a value. You can pass it to another function. But the two languages read definitions at different times.

fn main() {
    println!("{}", twice(add_one, 5));   // add_one is defined below: fine
}

fn add_one(n: i32) -> i32 {
    n + 1
}

// f is a function value: fn(i32) -> i32
fn twice(f: fn(i32) -> i32, x: i32) -> i32 {
    f(f(x))
}
def twice(f, x):
    return f(f(x))

print(twice(add_one, 5))   # add_one does not exist yet

def add_one(n):
    return n + 1
7
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/you/main.py", line 4, in <module>
    print(twice(add_one, 5))   # add_one does not exist yet
                ^^^^^^^
NameError: name 'add_one' is not defined
  • A Rust fn is an item. The compiler knows all items before the run. So the order in the file does not matter.
  • A Python def is a statement. It runs from top to bottom like other lines. The name exists only after its def line has run.
  • The type fn(i32) -> i32 is a function pointer. Closures, functions that capture variables, come in Iterators and closures.

Functions that never return

The type ! is the never type. A function with -> ! never returns. It panics, exits or loops forever.

fn fail(msg: &str) -> ! {             // ! : this function never returns
    panic!("fatal: {msg}");
}

fn parse_port(text: &str) -> u16 {
    match text.parse() {
        Ok(port) => port,
        Err(_) => fail("bad port"),   // ! fits where a u16 is expected
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", parse_port("8080"));
    println!("{}", parse_port("eighty"));
}
8080

thread 'main' (114902605) panicked at src/main.rs:2:5:
fatal: bad port

A value of type ! can stand where any type is expected, because it never really arrives. That is why fail(...) fits in a match arm that must give a u16. Python has a similar hint: typing.NoReturn, or typing.Never since Python 3.11.

"What is the difference between an expression and a statement in Rust?" A good short answer: an expression gives a value, a statement does not. A semicolon turns an expression into a statement. Then give the example of a function whose last line has an extra semicolon and so returns ().

Patterns to remember

Patterns for functions and modules
PatternPurposeModelNote
fn name(p: T) -> R { expr }Define a Rust functionfn area(w: f64, h: f64) -> f64 { w * h }No semicolon on the result line.
def name(p: T) -> R:Define a Python functiondef area(w: float, h: float) -> float:Do not forget return, or you get None.
if bad { return x; }Leave early on a special caseif score > 100 { return '?'; }Keep the normal result at the end.
(a, b) as the resultReturn two valueslet (lo, hi) = min_max(&data);Unpack it with the same count of names.
p: Option<T>Rust: a parameter that may be missingport.unwrap_or(80)Rust has no default values.
def f(a, b=1, *, c=2)Python: defaults and keyword-onlyconnect("host", timeout=1.5)After *, callers must write the name.
x=None, then if x is None:Python: a safe mutable defaultdef add_tag(tag, tags=None):Never use [] or {} as a default.
mod name;Rust: add a module filemod geometry; loads src/geometry.rsuse does not load files.
pub fnRust: let other modules use an itempub fn square_area(...)pub mod alone does not make the items public.
use path::module;Rust: a short name for a moduleuse geometry::circle; then circle::area(2.0)For functions, import the module, not the function.
from package import namePython: a short namefrom geometry import circleAvoid from x import *.
