"""Text."""Python: a docstring"""Return the larger of two numbers."""The first line is one short sentence.

Practice

What does fn show(x: i32) { println!("{x}"); } return?

  • Nothing at all, not even a value
  • The unit value ()
  • The number x

A Rust function without -> returns (), the unit type.

Which line is the tail expression of a function that returns i32?

  • a + b;
  • a + b
  • let r = a + b;

The semicolon throws the value away. Only a + b without a semicolon is the result.

Which Python call fails for def f(a, *, b=0)?

  • f(1)
  • f(1, b=2)
  • f(1, 2)

b comes after *, so it is keyword-only. You must write b=2.

In src/main.rs you write mod net;. Where does Rust look first?

  • net/main.rs
  • src/net.rs
  • src/lib/net.rs

Rust looks for src/net.rs. The older place src/net/mod.rs also works.

A Python function with no return gives ?.

To use a parent module in a Rust path, start with ?.

A Rust doc comment for the item below starts with ?.

  1. Write a Rust function is_even that takes an i32 and returns a bool. Then write it in Python.
    Answer

    Rust: fn is_even(n: i32) -> bool { n % 2 == 0 }. Python: def is_even(n: int) -> bool: return n % 2 == 0.

  2. Why does this fail? fn square(n: i32) -> i32 { n * n; }
    Answer

    The semicolon makes n * n a statement. The body has no tail expression, so it returns (), but the signature promises i32. Remove the semicolon.

  3. A Python function def log(msg, lines=[]) keeps old messages between calls. Explain why and fix it.
    Answer

    Python makes the default list one time, when def runs. Every call shares it. Fix: def log(msg, lines=None): and then if lines is None: lines = [].

  4. Your Rust project has src/main.rs and src/net.rs. net.rs has fn ping(). What must you write so that main can call net::ping()?
    Answer

    Write mod net; in main.rs. Make the function public in net.rs: pub fn ping(). Then call net::ping().

  5. Rust has no default values. Show two ways to offer a call with a default port of 80.
    Answer

    One: take port: Option<u16> and use port.unwrap_or(80). Two: write two functions, for example connect(host) that calls connect_on(host, 80). A settings struct with Default is a third way.

  6. Hard: in Python, main() is called on line 3, and def main() is on line 10. The program fails. In Rust, the same order works. Explain both.
    Answer

    Python runs the file from top to bottom. A def is a statement, so the name main exists only after line 10 runs. Line 3 gives a NameError. In Rust, functions are items. The compiler reads the whole crate before the program runs, so the order does not matter. In Python, put the call at the end, often under if __name__ == "__main__":.

Key takeaways

  • A Rust signature lists every parameter type and the result type. Python types are optional hints.
  • An expression gives a value. A statement does not. A semicolon turns an expression into a statement.
  • The last expression without a semicolon is the result of a Rust function. No result means ().
  • Python has default, keyword and keyword-only arguments. Rust uses Option, clear names or a builder instead.
  • Never use a mutable default value in Python. Use None.
  • In Rust, mod finds the file, pub opens an item, and use makes a short name.
  • In Python, every file is a module, and a folder with __init__.py is a package.
  • /// and docstrings document code. Their examples can run as tests.

Sources

  • The Rust Programming Language: Functions. Parameters, statements, expressions and return values.
  • The Rust Programming Language: Paths in the module tree. crate, self, super and privacy with pub.
  • The Rust Programming Language: Modules in different files. Where the compiler looks for module files.
  • The rustdoc book: How to write documentation. Doc comments, sections and examples.
  • The Python Tutorial: Defining functions. Default values, keyword arguments, special parameters and docstrings.
  • The Python Tutorial: Modules. import, packages, relative imports and the __main__ check.

Strings and text

Almost every program reads or writes text. Rust has two main string types, and Python has one. This chapter shows how text is stored as bytes, how to cut it safely, and how to turn it into numbers.

  • Choose between String and &str in Rust, and explain why both exist.
  • Explain UTF-8 and count bytes, chars and letters in a text.
  • Slice text without a panic, and build text with format! and f-strings.
  • Use the common string methods in Rust and Python side by side.
  • Parse numbers from text and handle bad input.

Two string types: String and &str

Start with a small program. It uses both string types of Rust.

fn greet(name: &str) -> String {
    // Build a new owned String from a borrowed &str.
    format!("Hello, {name}!")
}

fn main() {
    let lit: &str = "Ann"; // a literal: borrowed, fixed text
    let mut owned: String = String::from("Bo"); // owned, can grow
    owned.push_str("b");

    println!("{}", greet(lit));
    println!("{}", greet(&owned)); // &String becomes &str
    println!("{}", greet(&owned[0..2])); // a slice is a &str too
}
Hello, Ann!
Hello, Bob!
Hello, Bo!

A String owns its text. The text lives on the heap. A String can grow and change. A &str is a slice of text. It only borrows bytes that some other value owns.

You can measure the two handles. On a 64-bit machine a String is three numbers. A &str is two numbers.

use std::mem::size_of;

fn main() {
    println!("String  {}", size_of::<String>());
    println!("&str    {}", size_of::<&str>());
    println!("char    {}", size_of::<char>());

    let mut s = String::with_capacity(10);
    s.push_str("hi");
    println!("len {} capacity {}", s.len(), s.capacity());
}
String  24
&str    16
char    4
len 2 capacity 10
String and &str side by side
QuestionString&str
Who owns the bytes?The String itselfSomeone else. It only borrows.
Can it grow?Yes, with push and push_strNo
Where do the bytes live?On the heapAnywhere: heap, program file, stack
Typical useReturn values, struct fields, text you buildFunction parameters, literals, parts of text
The same idea for listsVec<u8>&[u8]

A text in quotes, like "Ann", is a literal. Its type is &'static str. The bytes are stored inside the program file. They live as long as the program runs.

Do not write fn f(s: &String). Write fn f(s: &str). A &String turns into a &str by itself, but a literal can never become a &String. So &str accepts more inputs.

String is a notebook you own. You can write more pages. &str is a finger that points at some lines in a notebook. The finger owns nothing.

Python has only one text type: str. A Python str can never change. Every method that seems to change it returns a new str.

UTF-8: bytes and chars

How long is a word? The answer depends on what you count. This program counts in two ways.

fn main() {
    for word in ["cat", "café", "Мир", "日本", "🦀"] {
        println!(
            "{word:6} bytes {:2}  chars {}",
            word.len(),           // length in bytes
            word.chars().count()  // number of chars
        );
    }
    let w = "café";
    println!("{:?}", w.as_bytes());
    println!("{:?}", w.chars().collect::<Vec<char>>());
}
cat    bytes  3  chars 3
café   bytes  5  chars 4
Мир    bytes  6  chars 3
日本     bytes  6  chars 2
🦀      bytes  4  chars 1
[99, 97, 102, 195, 169]
['c', 'a', 'f', 'é']

Rust stores all text as UTF-8. Unicode gives every character a number. UTF-8 writes that number as 1, 2, 3 or 4 bytes. English letters need 1 byte. The letter é needs 2 bytes. The crab emoji needs 4 bytes.

So len() in Rust returns the number of bytes, not letters. A char in Rust is one Unicode code point. It is always 4 bytes in memory, but 1 to 4 bytes inside a string.

Every String and every &str holds valid UTF-8. Safe Rust cannot create one that does not. Each function that makes text from bytes checks the bytes first.

Three ways to count

People do not think in code points. They think in letters. One visible letter can be two or more code points. The standard Rust library does not count visible letters. A crate such as unicode-segmentation does it.

The word "naïve" written with a separate accent mark
UnitRustPythonCount
Bytess.len()len(s.encode())7
Code pointss.chars().count()len(s)6
Visible lettersa cratea third-party package5

Python len() counts code points. Rust len() counts bytes. Remember this difference.

Equal on the screen, different in memory

import unicodedata
a = "café"      # é as one code point
b = "café"     # e plus a combining accent
print(a, b, a == b, len(a), len(b))
na = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", a)
nb = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", b)
print(na == nb)
café café False 4 5
True

Both words look the same. But they hold different code points, so == says false. Normalization fixes this. Python has it in unicodedata. Rust needs a crate, for example unicode-normalization. Rust gives the same false for a == b.

Do not use len() to limit what a user sees. A limit of 10 bytes can cut a Japanese name after three letters. Decide first: do you limit bytes (for storage) or chars (for the screen)?

Slicing safely

In many languages s[0] gives the first letter. In Rust it does not compile.

fn main() {
    let s = String::from("hello");
    let c = s[0];
    println!("{c}");
}
error[E0277]: the type `str` cannot be indexed by `{integer}`
 --> index_err.rs:3:15
  |
3 |     let c = s[0];
  |               ^ string indices are ranges of `usize`
  |
  = note: you can use `.chars().nth()` or `.bytes().nth()`

The output above is shortened. Why does Rust say no? A byte is not always a letter. And finding the fifth char means walking through all the bytes before it. Rust does not hide that cost behind [ ].

You can slice with a byte range. The range must start and end on char boundaries. If not, the program stops with a panic.

fn main() {
    let s = "café";
    println!("{}", &s[0..3]); // bytes 0, 1, 2: "caf"
    println!("{}", &s[0..4]); // byte 4 is in the middle of 'é'
}
caf

thread 'main' (115075776) panicked at slice_panic.rs:4:22:
end byte index 4 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 3..5 of string)
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace

The number after 'main' is a thread id. It changes on every run. The panic happens at run time. The compiler cannot see it. So use the safe tools below when the text comes from users.

fn main() {
    let s = "café au lait";

    // 1. get() returns None instead of a panic.
    println!("{:?}", s.get(0..4)); // byte 4 is inside 'é'
    println!("{:?}", s.get(0..5)); // a real boundary

    // 2. Ask if a byte index is a boundary.
    println!("{} {}", s.is_char_boundary(4), s.is_char_boundary(5));

    // 3. Cut after the first 4 chars, whatever their size.
    let end = s.char_indices().nth(4).map(|(i, _)| i).unwrap_or(s.len());
    println!("{}", &s[..end]);

    // 4. Move a byte index down to the nearest boundary (Rust 1.91).
    let i = s.floor_char_boundary(4);
    println!("{i} {}", &s[..i]);

    // 5. The first char, as a char.
    println!("{:?}", s.chars().next());
}
None
Some("café")
false true
café
3 caf
Some('c')
  • get(range) returns an Option. You get None instead of a crash. The chapter Structs, enums and pattern matching explains Option.
  • char_indices() gives pairs: the byte index and the char. Its indexes are always boundaries.
  • floor_char_boundary became stable in Rust 1.91. Older compilers do not have it.

Python counts code points

s = "café au lait"
print(s[0], s[3], s[:4])   # indexes count code points
print(s[:100])             # a slice past the end is fine
try:
    s[0] = "C"             # str cannot change
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
c é café
café au lait
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment

Python indexes count code points, so s[3] is é. A slice that goes past the end is not an error. A single index past the end raises IndexError. You cannot change a char in place. Build a new string instead.

A classic question: why can Rust not index a string with s[i]? Give two reasons. A byte may be only part of a char. And reaching char number i costs time that grows with i, not a fixed cost.

Building text: push, +, format! and f-strings

There are several ways to build a String. They differ in ownership.

fn main() {
    let mut s = String::new();
    s.push('R'); // one char
    s.push_str("ust"); // a &str
    s += " 2024"; // same as push_str

    let a = String::from("tic");
    let b = String::from("tac");
    let c = a + "-" + &b; // a moves into c; b is only borrowed
    // println!("{a}"); // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `a`

    let d = format!("{c}-{}", "toe"); // format! borrows, never moves
    println!("{s} | {c} | {d} | {b}");
}
Rust 2024 | tic-tac | tic-tac-toe | tac

The + operator takes the left String by value. It moves it, adds the right side, and returns it. The right side must be a &str. A macro like format! only borrows its arguments. Prefer format! when you join more than two parts. It is easier to read.

The format language

Rust format!, println! and Python f-strings share almost the same small language. Text inside { } is a placeholder. After a colon you can give a width, an alignment and a precision.

fn main() {
    let name = "Ann";
    let score = 7.256_f64;
    let items = vec!["pen", "cup"];

    println!("[{name}]");          // inline capture
    println!("[{name:>6}]");       // right-align in 6 chars
    println!("[{name:<6}]");       // left-align
    println!("[{name:*^7}]");      // center, fill with *
    println!("[{score:.1}]");      // 1 digit after the point
    println!("[{score:8.3}]");     // width 8, 3 digits
    println!("[{:05}]", 42);       // pad with zeros
    println!("[{:+}]", 42);        // always show the sign
    println!("[{:x} {:#b}]", 255, 5); // hex and binary
    println!("[{items:?}]");       // Debug form
    println!("[{name:?}]");        // Debug adds quotes
    println!("{{ and }}");         // literal braces
    let w = 6;
    println!("[{name:>w$}]");      // width from a variable
    println!("[{:.2}]", "hello");  // precision cuts text
}
name = "Ann"
score = 7.256
items = ["pen", "cup"]

print(f"[{name}]")

print(f"[{name:<6}]")

print(f"[{255:x} {5:#b}]")
print(f"[{items!r}]")
print(f"[{name!r}]")

w = 6
print(f"[{name:>{w}}]")
print(f"[{'hello':.2}]")

This is the Rust output. Python prints the same, except that it uses single quotes: ['pen', 'cup'] and 'Ann'.

  • {} uses the Display form, for people. {:?} uses the Debug form, for programmers. In Python, !r plays the role of :?.
  • Your own types need Display or Debug before they can print. See Traits and generics.
  • A Rust placeholder can hold a variable name only, like {name}. A Python f-string can hold any expression, like {score * 2}.

println!("{user.name}") does not compile. Rust captures plain names only. Write println!("{}", user.name) or println!("{n}", n = user.name).

Python 3.14: template strings (t-strings)

Python 3.14 added a new prefix: t. A t-string looks like an f-string. But it does not give a str. It gives a Template object. Your code then decides how to join the parts. This is useful for escaping user data in HTML or SQL.

from string.templatelib import Template, Interpolation
import html

def safe_html(t: Template) -> str:
    parts = []
    for part in t:
        if isinstance(part, Interpolation):
            parts.append(html.escape(str(part.value)))  # escape user data
        else:
            parts.append(part)  # keep the fixed text as it is
    return "".join(parts)

user = "<b>Bo</b>"
print(f"<p>{user}</p>")           # f-string: a plain str
print(safe_html(t"<p>{user}</p>")) # t-string: a Template
print(type(t"<p>{user}</p>").__name__)
<p><b>Bo</b></p>
<p><b>Bo</b></p>
Template

The chapter Python versions lists the other news of 3.14.

Common methods in both languages

Here is one messy line of text. Both programs clean it and take it apart.

fn main() {
    let line = "  Rust, Python ,Go  ";
    let t = line.trim(); // remove spaces at both ends
    println!("{t:?}");
    println!("{}", t.contains("Py"));
    println!("{}", t.starts_with("Rust"));
    println!("{:?}", t.find(',')); // byte index of the first ','
    println!("{}", t.replace(" ", ""));
    println!("{}", t.to_uppercase());

    // split, trim each part, collect into a Vec
    let langs: Vec<&str> = t.split(',').map(|p| p.trim()).collect();
    println!("{langs:?}");
    println!("{}", langs.join(" / "));

    // split_once: one cut, two parts
    println!("{:?}", "key=value=x".split_once('='));

    let text = "one two\n  three\n";
    println!("{:?}", text.split_whitespace().collect::<Vec<_>>());
    println!("{:?}", text.lines().collect::<Vec<_>>());
}

Many Rust methods return an iterator, not a list. split, lines and chars do no work until you use them. Call .collect() to get a Vec. The chapter Iterators and closures goes deeper.

Notice the slices. trim and split return &str values. They point into the original text. No bytes are copied.

Python "v1.2".strip("v.") removes any of the chars v and . from both ends. It does not remove the prefix "v.". Use removeprefix for an exact prefix. In Rust, use strip_prefix.

Upper case is not one char to one char (expert)

"straße".to_uppercase() gives "STRASSE" in Rust. Python upper() gives the same. One ß became two letters. So upper case can make a text longer. For a case-free compare, Python has casefold(). Rust has eq_ignore_ascii_case, which only knows English letters.

Parsing numbers from text

Text from a file or a user is only text. You must turn it into a number. Rust uses parse.

fn main() {
    let a: i32 = "42".parse().unwrap(); // type from the annotation
    let b = "3.5".parse::<f64>().unwrap(); // type with turbofish
    println!("{a} {b}");

    // parse returns a Result. Look at the errors.
    println!("{:?}", "42".parse::<i32>());
    println!("{:?}", " 42".parse::<i32>()); // space: error
    println!("{:?}", " 42 ".trim().parse::<i32>()); // trim first
    println!("{:?}", "".parse::<i32>());
    println!("{:?}", "300".parse::<u8>()); // too big for u8
    println!("{:?}", "1_000".parse::<i32>());

    let s: String = 255.to_string(); // number back to text
    println!("{s} {}", s.len());

    match "abc".parse::<i32>() {
        Ok(n) => println!("number {n}"),
        Err(e) => println!("not a number: {e}"),
    }
    println!("{:?}", i64::from_str_radix("ff", 16));
}

parse needs to know the target type. Give it with a type annotation, or with the turbofish ::<i32>. It returns a Result: Ok(value) or Err(error). The chapter Error handling shows how to pass such errors on with ?.

A line read from the keyboard ends with \n. In Rust "42\n".parse::<i32>() is an error. Always call trim() before parse().

Bytes and text

Files and networks deliver bytes, not text. You must check that the bytes are valid UTF-8.

fn main() {
    let text = "héllo";
    let bytes: &[u8] = text.as_bytes(); // borrow the bytes
    println!("{bytes:?}");

    let raw: &[u8; 3] = b"abc"; // a byte string literal
    println!("{raw:?}");

    // Bytes to text: the bytes must be valid UTF-8.
    let good = vec![104, 105];
    println!("{:?}", String::from_utf8(good));
    let bad = vec![104, 0xFF, 105];
    println!("{:?}", String::from_utf8(bad.clone()).is_err());
    // Lossy: bad bytes become U+FFFD, the replacement char.
    println!("{}", String::from_utf8_lossy(&bad));
}
text = "héllo"
data = text.encode("utf-8")  # str -> bytes
print(data, len(text), len(data))
print(data[0], data[1:3])    # one item is an int; a slice is bytes

print(b"hi".decode("utf-8"))  # bytes -> str
bad = bytes([104, 0xFF, 105])
try:
    bad.decode("utf-8")
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    print("UnicodeDecodeError:", e.reason)
print(bad.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"))

[97, 98, 99]

hi

  • String::from_utf8 returns a Result. Bad bytes give an error, never broken text.
  • from_utf8_lossy puts the replacement character where bytes are bad.
  • To encode means text to bytes. To decode means bytes to text. Python has str.encode() and bytes.decode().
  • In Python, "A" == b"A" is False. A str and a bytes are never equal.

Other text types in Rust (expert)

Not all text from the system is UTF-8. A file name on Linux can hold any bytes. So Rust has more owned and borrowed pairs.

A C string ends with a zero byte. The chapter Unsafe Rust and FFI uses CString. Python hides most of this. It turns bad bytes in file names into special code points, so you rarely see an error.

Why Rust has two string types

Now the full picture. The two types follow the same rule as all Rust data: one owner, many borrowers. See Ownership and borrowing.

  1. Ownership. Someone must free the bytes. A String does it. A &str never does.
  2. No copies. trim, split and slices return &str. They reuse the bytes that already exist.
  3. Literals. Text in quotes is in the program file. Nobody needs to free it. So it is a &'static str.
  4. Speed you can see. A new String asks for heap memory. In Rust you see each one in the code.

Python made a different choice. Its str can never change, so many names can share one object safely. A slice like s[1:4] makes a new str with copied data.

use std::borrow::Cow;

// Four ways to turn a &str into a String. All give the same result.
fn four_ways(s: &str) -> [String; 4] {
    [String::from(s), s.to_string(), s.to_owned(), s.into()]
}

// Accept String, &String and &str alike.
fn shout(s: impl AsRef<str>) -> String {
    s.as_ref().to_uppercase()
}

// Return the input unchanged when no work is needed.
fn no_tabs(s: &str) -> Cow<'_, str> {
    if s.contains('\t') {
        Cow::Owned(s.replace('\t', "    ")) // allocate only here
    } else {
        Cow::Borrowed(s) // no allocation
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", four_ways("hi"));
    let name = String::from("ann");
    println!("{} {} {}", shout("bo"), shout(&name), shout(name.clone()));
    for s in ["plain", "a\tb"] {
        let r = no_tabs(s);
        let kind = if matches!(r, Cow::Borrowed(_)) { "borrowed" } else { "owned" };
        println!("{r:?} {kind}");
    }
}
["hi", "hi", "hi", "hi"]
BO ANN ANN
"plain" borrowed
"a    b" owned

Cow means "clone on write". A Cow<str> holds either a borrowed &str or an owned String. You pay for a new String only when you change something. The chapter Smart pointers and interior mutability explains Cow fully.

Which to use for a parameter, a return value, a field?

Parameter: &str. Return a new text: String. Return a part of the input: &str. Struct field: String in most cases. A &str field needs a lifetime, see Lifetimes.

How do I build a big text fast?

In Rust, reserve space with String::with_capacity(n) and call push_str. In Python, collect the parts in a list and call "".join(parts) once. Many += in a Python loop can copy the text again and again.

Why is char 4 bytes but a string char 1 to 4 bytes?

A single char must hold any code point. The biggest one needs 21 bits, so Rust uses 4 bytes. Inside a string, UTF-8 saves space for common chars.

From one line of input to numbers

A real task joins all these ideas. The input is " 3, 4, x, 10 ,". We want the sum of the good numbers and a list of the bad parts.

// Read numbers like "3, 4, x, 10" and sum the good ones.
fn sum_line(line: &str) -> (i64, Vec<String>) {
    let mut total = 0;
    let mut bad = Vec::new();
    for part in line.split(',') {
        let part = part.trim(); // shadow: a smaller &str
        match part.parse::<i64>() {
            Ok(n) => total += n,
            Err(_) => bad.push(part.to_string()), // own a copy
        }
    }
    (total, bad)
}

fn main() {
    let (total, bad) = sum_line(" 3, 4, x, 10 ,");
    println!("total {total}, bad {bad:?}");
}
# Read numbers like "3, 4, x, 10" and sum the good ones.
def sum_line(line: str) -> tuple[int, list[str]]:
    total = 0
    bad = []
    for part in line.split(","):
        part = part.strip()
        try:
            total += int(part)
        except ValueError:
            bad.append(part)
    return total, bad


total, bad = sum_line(" 3, 4, x, 10 ,")
print(f"total {total}, bad {bad}")
total 17, bad ["x", ""]

Python prints the same with single quotes. The empty string at the end comes from the last comma. Follow one part through the Rust code, step by step.

Borrow the line

fn sum_line(line: &str)

The function borrows the text. The caller keeps it. No bytes are copied.

Split

for part in line.split(',')

Each part is a &str inside the line. The second one is " 4".

Trim

let part = part.trim();

A smaller slice of the same bytes: "4". Still no copy.

Parse

part.parse::<i64>()

The result is Ok(4). For "x" it would be an Err.

Keep or report

bad.push(part.to_string())

A bad part must outlive the line, so we copy it into a String. Only here does the program allocate.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for strings and text
PatternPurposeModelNote
fn f(s: &str)Accept any text for readingfn greet(name: &str) -> StringNot &String. A literal cannot become one.
format!("{a}-{b}")Join values into a new Stringformat!("{user}: {score:.1}")Only plain names inside braces, no fields.
s.push_str(t)Add text to an owned Stringlog.push_str("done\n");Needs let mut.
s.chars().count()Count chars, not bytes"café".chars().count() is 4len() counts bytes.
s.get(a..b)Slice without a panics.get(0..4) gives None&s[a..b] panics off a char boundary.
s.char_indices().nth(n)Find the byte index of char n&s[..i] keeps n charsThe index is always a boundary.
s.trim().parse::<T>()Turn text into a number"42\n".trim().parse::<i32>()It returns a Result. Handle the error.
s.split(',').map(str::trim)Cut text into clean parts.collect::<Vec<&str>>()The parts borrow the original text.
s.split_once('=')Cut into exactly two partslet (k, v) = line.split_once('=')?;Gives None when the separator is missing.
String::from_utf8(bytes)Check bytes and make textString::from_utf8(vec![104, 105])Use from_utf8_lossy to accept bad bytes.
Python f"{x:>8.2f}"Format numbers for a tablef"{price:>8.2f}"Same mini-language as Rust, plus any expression.
Python "".join(parts)Build big text fast", ".join(names)The separator comes first, before .join.

Practice

What is "héllo".len() in Rust?

  • 5
  • 6
  • 10

Rust len() counts bytes. The letter é takes 2 bytes, so the total is 6.

s is a String. Which line compiles and gives the first char?

  • let c = s[0];
  • let c = s.chars().next();
  • let c = s.first();

Strings cannot be indexed with a number. chars().next() returns an Option<char>.

What does " 7 ".parse::<i32>() return?

  • Ok(7)
  • An Err, because of the spaces
  • A panic

Rust parse does not skip spaces. Call trim() first. Python int(" 7 ") would give 7.

After let c = a + &b;, where a and b are both String, which names can you still use?

  • a and b
  • b and c
  • Only c

+ takes a by value and moves it into c. b is only borrowed.

In Python, len("🦀") is ? and len("🦀".encode()) is ?.

To show a number with two digits after the point, write format!("{x:?}").

  1. Write initials in Rust. initials("Ada Lovelace") returns "AL". Note the two spaces.
    Answer 
    fn initials(name: &str) -> String {
    name.split_whitespace()
        .filter_map(|w| w.chars().next()) // first char of each word
        .collect()
}

    split_whitespace skips the empty part between the two spaces. In Python: "".join(w[0] for w in name.split()).

  2. Write first_chars(s: &str, n: usize) -> &str. It returns the first n chars and never panics. Test it with "Здравствуйте" and 3.
    Answer 
    fn first_chars(s: &str, n: usize) -> &str {
    match s.char_indices().nth(n) {
        Some((i, _)) => &s[..i], // i is a char boundary
        None => s,               // the text is shorter than n
    }
}

    It returns "Здр". Those are 3 chars and 6 bytes. first_chars("hi", 5) returns "hi".

  3. Why does &"café"[0..4] panic, but &"cafe"[0..4] works?
    Answer

    In "café" the é uses bytes 3 and 4. Index 4 is in the middle of it, so it is not a char boundary. In "cafe" every char is 1 byte, so every index is a boundary.

  4. A function only reads a name and prints it. A teammate wrote fn show(name: String). What is wrong, and what is better?
    Answer

    The function takes ownership. The caller loses the name or must clone it. Write fn show(name: &str). Then it accepts literals, &String and slices.

  5. Expert. Write capitalize in Rust. It makes the first char upper case. capitalize("ölçek") gives "Ölçek". Hint: to_uppercase on a char returns an iterator.
    Answer 
    fn capitalize(s: &str) -> String {
    let mut chars = s.chars();
    match chars.next() {
        Some(first) => first.to_uppercase().chain(chars).collect(),
        None => String::new(),
    }
}

    One char can become more than one in upper case, like ß to SS. That is why it returns an iterator. chain adds the rest of the chars.

  6. Expert. Two strings look the same on screen, but == says false. Give a likely reason and a fix in Python.
    Answer

    One string may use é as one code point. The other may use e plus a combining accent. Normalize both before you compare: unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s).

Key takeaways

  • String owns text and can grow. &str borrows text and is the best parameter type.
  • Rust text is always UTF-8. One char is 1 to 4 bytes, and len() counts bytes.
  • Slice ranges count bytes. Use get, char_indices or chars for safe cuts.
  • format! and f-strings share one small format language for width, alignment and precision.
  • parse returns a Result. Trim the text first. Python int() raises ValueError instead.
  • Python has one immutable str and a separate bytes type. encode and decode move between them.

Sources

  • The Rust Programming Language, 8.2: Storing UTF-8 text with strings. The official book on String, &str, indexing and slicing.
  • Rust standard library: str. All str methods, with the version where each became stable.
  • Rust standard library: std::fmt. The full format language for format! and println!.
  • Python documentation: Built-in types. The str and bytes types and all their methods.
  • What's new in Python 3.14. Template strings (PEP 750) and other changes.
  • Python Unicode HOWTO. Code points, encodings and normalization.

Collections

A collection holds many values in one place. The right collection makes code short and fast. The wrong one makes it slow. This chapter shows the main collections of Rust and Python and how to choose between them.

  • Use Vec, arrays and slices, and their Python twins list and tuple.
  • Count, group and update data with HashMap and the entry API.
  • Use HashSet, BTreeMap and VecDeque for the right jobs.
  • Loop over a collection by borrowing, by changing, or by moving it.
  • Choose a collection with a decision tree and the cost of each operation.

Vec: a list that grows

A shop keeps a list of prices. New prices arrive while the program runs. Both programs below build and change such a list.

fn main() {
    let mut v: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    v.push(10);
    v.push(20);
    v.push(30);
    let w = vec![1, 2, 3]; // the vec! macro

    println!("{v:?} len {}", v.len());
    println!("{}", v[0]); // index: panics if out of range
    println!("{:?} {:?}", v.get(1), v.get(9)); // get: Some or None
    println!("{:?}", v.pop()); // remove the last item
    v.insert(0, 5); // shift all items one step right
    println!("{v:?} {w:?}");
    println!("{}", v.contains(&20));
    v[1] = 99; // change one item
    v.extend([7, 8]);
    v.sort();
    println!("{v:?} first {:?} last {:?}", v.first(), v.last());
}
v = []
v.append(10)
v.append(20)
v.append(30)
w = [1, 2, 3]

print(v, "len", len(v))
print(v[0])
print(v[1], v[-1])          # Python allows negative indexes
print(v.pop())
v.insert(0, 5)
print(v, w)
print(20 in v)
v[1] = 99
