This is the Rust output. Python prints the same list values. Where Rust gives Some(20), Python gives just 20.

A Vec<T> is a collection of values of one type T, side by side in memory. Python's list is the same idea. But a Python list can mix types, like [1, "a", None]. A Rust Vec cannot.

When the spare slots run out, push asks for a bigger block. It copies all items there and frees the old block. Watch the capacity jump.

fn main() {
    let mut v: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    let mut last = v.capacity();
    println!("len 0 capacity {last}");
    for i in 1..=40 {
        v.push(i);
        if v.capacity() != last {
            last = v.capacity();
            println!("len {} capacity {}", v.len(), last); // a new block
        }
    }
    let w: Vec<i32> = Vec::with_capacity(40);
    println!("with_capacity: len {} capacity {}", w.len(), w.capacity());
}
len 0 capacity 0
len 1 capacity 4
len 5 capacity 8
len 9 capacity 16
len 17 capacity 32
len 33 capacity 64
with_capacity: len 0 capacity 40

Today the capacity doubles each time. The documentation does not promise this exact rule. It only promises that push is fast on average. If you know the size, use Vec::with_capacity(n). Then the Vec allocates only once.

Check the space

Is the length smaller than the capacity? With length 5 and capacity 8 the answer is yes.

Write the item

The new item goes into slot 5. The length becomes 6. No new memory was needed.

Space is full

Later the length is 8 and the capacity is 8. The next push cannot write in place.

Grow

The Vec asks the allocator for 16 slots. It copies the 8 old items into the new block.

Free and finish

The old block is freed. The new item goes into slot 8. Any old reference into the Vec is now invalid. That is why the borrow checker forbids them.

The copy in step 4 costs time. But it happens rarely, and each time the block doubles. So on average one push costs a small, fixed amount of work. This average is called amortized cost.

Index or get?

fn main() {
    let v = vec![10, 20, 30];
    let i = 5;
    println!("{}", v[i]);
}
thread 'main' (115398501) panicked at panic_idx.rs:4:21:
index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 5
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace

v[i] stops the program when i is too big. v.get(i) returns None instead. Python raises IndexError. Use v[i] when a bad index is a bug. Use get when a bad index can really happen, like with user input.

Python v[-1] is the last item. Rust has no negative indexes. The index type is usize, which cannot be negative. Write v.last() or v[v.len() - 1].

Arrays, slices and tuples

An array like [f64; 7] has a fixed size. A slice &[f64] borrows some items of an array or a Vec. Write your functions for slices. Then they work for both.

// Works for an array, a Vec, or a part of either.
fn average(xs: &[f64]) -> Option<f64> {
    if xs.is_empty() {
        return None;
    }
    Some(xs.iter().sum::<f64>() / xs.len() as f64)
}

fn main() {
    let week: [f64; 7] = [3.0, 5.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0, 7.0, 9.0]; // fixed size
    let more: Vec<f64> = vec![1.0, 2.0];

    println!("{:?}", average(&week));      // &[f64; 7] becomes &[f64]
    println!("{:?}", average(&more));      // &Vec<f64> becomes &[f64]
    println!("{:?}", average(&week[5..])); // the weekend only
    println!("{:?}", average(&[]));

    // Slice methods: windows, chunks, binary_search
    for w in week.windows(3).take(2) {
        print!("{w:?} ");
    }
    println!();
    for c in week.chunks(3) {
        print!("{c:?} ");
    }
    println!();
    let sorted = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32];
    println!("{:?} {:?}", sorted.binary_search(&8), sorted.binary_search(&5));
}
Some(6.0)
Some(1.5)
Some(8.0)
None
[3.0, 5.0, 4.0] [5.0, 4.0, 6.0]
[3.0, 5.0, 4.0] [6.0, 8.0, 7.0] [9.0]
Ok(2) Err(2)
  • windows(3) gives every group of 3 neighbours. They overlap.
  • chunks(3) cuts the slice into groups of 3. The last group can be smaller.
  • binary_search needs sorted data. Err(2) means "not found, but it would go at index 2".

A Python slice like week[5:] is different. It makes a new list and copies the items. A Rust slice copies nothing. Arrays are explained in Variables and types. Slices are explained in Ownership and borrowing.

Python has one more sequence: the tuple. A tuple cannot change, so it can be a dict key. A list cannot.

point_names = {(0, 0): "origin", (1, 2): "home"}  # a tuple can be a key
print(point_names[(1, 2)])
try:
    bad = {[1, 2]: "home"}  # a list cannot
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
home
TypeError: cannot use 'list' as a dict key (unhashable type: 'list')

This exact message comes from Python 3.14. Older versions print only unhashable type: 'list'.

HashMap and the entry API

A phone book finds a number by a name. A map does the same in code. Rust has HashMap. Python has dict.

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    let mut ages: HashMap<String, u32> = HashMap::new();
    ages.insert("Ann".to_string(), 31);
    ages.insert("Bo".to_string(), 25);
    ages.insert("Ann".to_string(), 32); // same key: the value is replaced

    println!("{:?}", ages.get("Ann")); // Some(&32)
    println!("{:?}", ages.get("Cy")); // None
    println!("{}", ages.contains_key("Bo"));
    println!("{}", ages["Bo"]); // panics if the key is missing
    println!("{:?}", ages.remove("Bo")); // Some(25)
    println!("len {}", ages.len());

    // Update a value in place
    if let Some(age) = ages.get_mut("Ann") {
        *age += 1;
    }
    println!("{ages:?}");
}
ages = {}
ages["Ann"] = 31
ages["Bo"] = 25
ages["Ann"] = 32

print(ages.get("Ann"))
print(ages.get("Cy"))          # None, no error
print("Bo" in ages)
print(ages["Bo"])              # KeyError if the key is missing
print(ages.pop("Bo"))
print("len", len(ages))
ages["Ann"] += 1
print(ages)
Some(32)
None
true
25
Some(25)
len 1
{"Ann": 33}

This is the Rust output. Python prints plain values: 32 instead of Some(32), and True instead of true.

A HashMap turns each key into a number with a hash function. The number points to a slot in a table. So finding a key does not mean looking at every pair. Python's dict works in the same way.

ages["Cy"] panics in Rust and raises KeyError in Python. Use get when the key may be missing.

Counting with the entry API

Counting words is the classic map task. Each word needs "find it, or add it with zero, then add one".

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    let text = "the cat and the dog and the bird";
    let mut counts: HashMap<&str, usize> = HashMap::new();
    for word in text.split_whitespace() {
        // One lookup: find the slot, or make it with 0.
        *counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }
    // A HashMap has no order. Sort the pairs to print them.
    let mut pairs: Vec<(&str, usize)> = counts.into_iter().collect();
    pairs.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(&a.1).then(a.0.cmp(b.0)));
    println!("{pairs:?}");
}
from collections import Counter

text = "the cat and the dog and the bird"
counts = {}
for word in text.split():
    counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1
print(counts)  # a dict keeps insertion order

# The standard library already has a counter.
print(Counter(text.split()).most_common(2))
[("the", 3), ("and", 2), ("bird", 1), ("cat", 1), ("dog", 1)]

Python prints this:

{'the': 3, 'cat': 1, 'and': 2, 'dog': 1, 'bird': 1}
[('the', 3), ('and', 2)]

entry(key) looks up the key one time. It returns an Entry. An entry is either occupied (the key is there) or vacant (it is not). or_insert(0) fills a vacant entry with 0. Then it gives you a &mut to the value. The * lets you change the value behind that reference.

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    // Group words by their first letter.
    let mut groups: HashMap<char, Vec<&str>> = HashMap::new();
    for w in ["apple", "bean", "avocado", "beet", "corn"] {
        let first = w.chars().next().unwrap();
        groups.entry(first).or_default().push(w); // or_default: empty Vec
    }
    let mut keys: Vec<_> = groups.keys().collect();
    keys.sort();
    for k in keys {
        println!("{k}: {:?}", groups[k]);
    }

    // and_modify: change the value if it exists, else insert.
    let mut stock: HashMap<&str, i32> = HashMap::from([("pen", 3)]);
    for item in ["pen", "cup"] {
        stock.entry(item).and_modify(|n| *n += 10).or_insert(1);
    }
    println!("pen {} cup {}", stock["pen"], stock["cup"]);
}
from collections import defaultdict

groups = defaultdict(list)  # a missing key gets an empty list
for w in ["apple", "bean", "avocado", "beet", "corn"]:
    groups[w[0]].append(w)
for k in sorted(groups):
    print(f"{k}: {groups[k]}")

stock = {"pen": 3}
for item in ["pen", "cup"]:
    if item in stock:
        stock[item] += 10
    else:
        stock[item] = 1
print("pen", stock["pen"], "cup", stock["cup"])
a: ["apple", "avocado"]
b: ["bean", "beet"]
c: ["corn"]
pen 13 cup 1

Python prints the same lines with single quotes.

The entry methods and their Python twins
RustWhat it doesPython
entry(k).or_insert(v)Insert v if missing, then give the valued.setdefault(k, v)
entry(k).or_default()Insert the default value (0, empty Vec) if missingdefaultdict(list)
entry(k).or_insert_with(f)Call f only when the key is missingif k not in d: d[k] = f()
entry(k).and_modify(f)Change the value only if the key is thereif k in d: d[k] = f(d[k])

Do not write if !m.contains_key(k) { m.insert(k, 0); } and then get_mut. That looks up the key two or three times. One entry call does it all.

Python's dict keeps the order in which you inserted the keys. The language promises this since Python 3.7. Rust's HashMap has no order at all. You will see that in the next sections.

HashSet: is it there?

Sometimes you need no value. You only want to know if you have seen a thing. Then use a set.

use std::collections::{BTreeSet, HashSet};

fn main() {
    let tags = ["rust", "web", "rust", "cli", "web"];
    let unique: HashSet<&str> = tags.into_iter().collect();
    println!("{} unique, has cli: {}", unique.len(), unique.contains("cli"));

    let a: BTreeSet<i32> = [1, 2, 3, 4].into();
    let b: BTreeSet<i32> = [3, 4, 5].into();
    println!("union        {:?}", a.union(&b).collect::<Vec<_>>());
    println!("intersection {:?}", a.intersection(&b).collect::<Vec<_>>());
    println!("difference   {:?}", a.difference(&b).collect::<Vec<_>>());
    println!("symmetric    {:?}", a.symmetric_difference(&b).collect::<Vec<_>>());

    let mut seen = HashSet::new();
    for x in [3, 1, 3, 2, 1] {
        // insert returns false when the value was already there
        if !seen.insert(x) {
            println!("duplicate {x}");
        }
    }
}
tags = ["rust", "web", "rust", "cli", "web"]
unique = set(tags)
print(len(unique), "unique, has cli:", "cli" in unique)

a = {1, 2, 3, 4}
b = {3, 4, 5}
print("union       ", sorted(a | b))
print("intersection", sorted(a & b))
print("difference  ", sorted(a - b))
print("symmetric   ", sorted(a ^ b))

seen = set()
for x in [3, 1, 3, 2, 1]:
    if x in seen:
        print("duplicate", x)
    seen.add(x)
3 unique, has cli: true
union        [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
intersection [3, 4]
difference   [1, 2]
symmetric    [1, 2, 5]
duplicate 3
duplicate 1

Python prints the same, with True on the first line. A HashSet<T> is a HashMap<T, ()> inside: keys with empty values. So the cost of each operation is the same as for the map. Python writes set operations with |, &, - and ^. Rust has named methods.

The example uses BTreeSet for a and b. It keeps its items sorted, so the output order is stable. A HashSet would print them in any order.

BTreeMap: sorted keys and ranges

Run this program three times. Look at the first line each time.

use std::collections::{BTreeMap, HashMap};

fn main() {
    let pairs = [("pear", 3), ("apple", 5), ("fig", 1), ("kiwi", 2)];
    let h: HashMap<&str, i32> = HashMap::from(pairs);
    let b: BTreeMap<&str, i32> = BTreeMap::from(pairs);
    println!("hash  {h:?}"); // arbitrary order
    println!("btree {b:?}"); // always sorted by key
}
hash  {"fig": 1, "pear": 3, "kiwi": 2, "apple": 5}
btree {"apple": 5, "fig": 1, "kiwi": 2, "pear": 3}
hash  {"kiwi": 2, "apple": 5, "pear": 3, "fig": 1}
btree {"apple": 5, "fig": 1, "kiwi": 2, "pear": 3}
hash  {"apple": 5, "pear": 3, "fig": 1, "kiwi": 2}
btree {"apple": 5, "fig": 1, "kiwi": 2, "pear": 3}

The HashMap order changes from run to run. Rust starts each HashMap with a random seed. A BTreeMap is a B-tree. It always keeps the keys sorted. So it can answer questions about order and ranges.

use std::collections::BTreeMap;

fn main() {
    // Temperature by hour of the day, kept sorted by hour.
    let mut temps: BTreeMap<u32, f64> = BTreeMap::new();
    for (hour, t) in [(14, 21.5), (6, 12.0), (9, 15.5), (18, 19.0), (12, 20.0)] {
        temps.insert(hour, t);
    }
    println!("{temps:?}");
    println!("first {:?}", temps.first_key_value());
    println!("last  {:?}", temps.last_key_value());

    // Range query: all hours from 9 up to (not including) 15.
    for (h, t) in temps.range(9..15) {
        println!("{h:2}:00 {t:.1}");
    }
    // The last reading before 13:00.
    println!("{:?}", temps.range(..13).next_back());
}
import bisect

temps = {14: 21.5, 6: 12.0, 9: 15.5, 18: 19.0, 12: 20.0}
hours = sorted(temps)                 # sort the keys when you need order
print([(h, temps[h]) for h in hours])
print("first", hours[0], "last", hours[-1])

lo = bisect.bisect_left(hours, 9)     # binary search in the sorted keys
hi = bisect.bisect_left(hours, 15)
for h in hours[lo:hi]:
    print(f"{h:2}:00 {temps[h]:.1f}")
{6: 12.0, 9: 15.5, 12: 20.0, 14: 21.5, 18: 19.0}
first Some((6, 12.0))
last  Some((18, 19.0))
 9:00 15.5
12:00 20.0
14:00 21.5
Some((12, 20.0))

Python prints this:

[(6, 12.0), (9, 15.5), (12, 20.0), (14, 21.5), (18, 19.0)]
first 6 last 18
 9:00 15.5
12:00 20.0
14:00 21.5

Python has no sorted map in its standard library. You sort the keys when you need them, and use bisect for a binary search. A third-party package, sortedcontainers, gives a real sorted dict.

Do not write tests that expect a fixed HashMap order. They pass on one run and fail on the next. Sort the output, or use a BTreeMap.

VecDeque: both ends

A print queue takes jobs from the front and adds jobs at the back. A Vec is bad at the front. Removing item 0 moves every other item. A deque is fast at both ends.

use std::collections::VecDeque;

fn main() {
    // A queue of print jobs: add at the back, take from the front.
    let mut jobs: VecDeque<&str> = VecDeque::new();
    jobs.push_back("report");
    jobs.push_back("photo");
    jobs.push_front("urgent"); // jump the line
    while let Some(job) = jobs.pop_front() {
        println!("printing {job}");
    }

    // Keep only the last 3 readings.
    let mut last3: VecDeque<i32> = VecDeque::with_capacity(3);
    for r in [5, 7, 9, 11, 13] {
        if last3.len() == 3 {
            last3.pop_front(); // drop the oldest
        }
        last3.push_back(r);
    }
    println!("{last3:?} front {:?} index 1: {}", last3.front(), last3[1]);
}
from collections import deque

jobs = deque()
jobs.append("report")
jobs.append("photo")
jobs.appendleft("urgent")
while jobs:
    print("printing", jobs.popleft())

last3 = deque(maxlen=3)   # old items fall off by themselves
for r in [5, 7, 9, 11, 13]:
    last3.append(r)
print(last3, "front", last3[0], "index 1:", last3[1])
printing urgent
printing report
printing photo
[9, 11, 13] front Some(9) index 1: 11

Python prints deque([9, 11, 13], maxlen=3) front 9 index 1: 11 on the last line. Its maxlen drops old items for you. In Rust you drop them yourself.

BinaryHeap: always take the biggest (a look ahead)

A BinaryHeap gives you the biggest item first. It is a priority queue. Python has the module heapq, which gives the smallest first. The chapter Algorithms 2 uses both.

Iterating: borrow, change or move

A for loop over a Rust collection can do three different things. The & decides which.

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    let mut prices = vec![10, 20, 30];

    for p in &prices {          // borrow: read each item
        print!("{p} ");
    }
    println!();
    for p in &mut prices {      // borrow mutably: change each item
        *p += 1;
    }
    for (i, p) in prices.iter().enumerate() {
        print!("{i}:{p} ");
    }
    println!();
    let total: i32 = prices.iter().sum();
    let doubled: Vec<i32> = prices.iter().map(|p| p * 2).collect();
    println!("total {total} doubled {doubled:?}");

    for p in prices {           // move: the Vec is used up
        print!("{p} ");
    }
    println!();
    // println!("{prices:?}"); // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value

    let stock = HashMap::from([("pen", 3)]);
    for (name, n) in &stock {   // pairs of (&key, &value)
        println!("{name} {n}");
    }
}
prices = [10, 20, 30]

for p in prices:
    print(p, end=" ")
print()
for i in range(len(prices)):   # change items through the index
    prices[i] += 1
for i, p in enumerate(prices):
    print(f"{i}:{p}", end=" ")
print()
total = sum(prices)
doubled = [p * 2 for p in prices]
print("total", total, "doubled", doubled)

stock = {"pen": 3}
for name, n in stock.items():
    print(name, n)
10 20 30
0:11 1:21 2:31
total 63 doubled [22, 42, 62]
11 21 31
pen 3

Python prints the same, without the line 11 21 31. Python has no loop that uses up a list.

Three ways to loop in Rust
You writeSame asEach item isAfter the loop
for x in &vv.iter()&T, read onlyv is unchanged
for x in &mut vv.iter_mut()&mut T, can changev holds the changes
for x in vv.into_iter()T, ownedv is gone

A Python for p in prices gives each item, but p += 1 only changes the local name. To change the list, go through the index, or build a new list. The chapter Iterators and closures explains map, filter and collect in depth.

Changing a collection inside its own loop

Both languages stop you, in different ways.

stock = {"pen": 0, "cup": 4, "ink": 0}
try:
    for name, n in stock.items():
        if n == 0:
            del stock[name]  # change the dict during the loop
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("RuntimeError:", e)

stock = {"pen": 0, "cup": 4, "ink": 0}
stock = {k: v for k, v in stock.items() if v > 0}  # build a new dict
print(stock)
RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration
{'cup': 4}

Python finds the problem at run time. Rust finds it at compile time, as a borrow error. In Rust, use retain.

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    let mut stock = HashMap::from([("pen", 0), ("cup", 4), ("ink", 0)]);
    stock.retain(|_, n| *n > 0); // keep the pairs where the test is true
    println!("{stock:?}");

    // Two mutable values from one map at once (Rust 1.86).
    let mut acc = HashMap::from([("ann", 100), ("bo", 50)]);
    if let [Some(a), Some(b)] = acc.get_disjoint_mut(["ann", "bo"]) {
        *a -= 30; // move 30 from ann to bo
        *b += 30;
    }
    println!("ann {} bo {}", acc["ann"], acc["bo"]);
}
{"cup": 4}
ann 70 bo 80

Two get_mut calls on one map fail with error E0499. The checker cannot see that the keys are different. get_disjoint_mut became stable in Rust 1.86. It checks at run time that the keys differ, and panics if two are the same.

The cost of common operations

Search for a missing number in a list, then in a set. The list must look at every item. The set does one hash lookup. These times come from this machine. Yours will differ, but the shape stays.

use std::collections::HashSet;
use std::hint::black_box;
use std::time::Instant;

fn main() {
    for n in [1_000, 10_000, 100_000] {
        let data: Vec<i64> = (0..n).collect();
        let set: HashSet<i64> = data.iter().copied().collect();
        let reps = 200;

        let t = Instant::now();
        for _ in 0..reps {
            black_box(data.contains(black_box(&-1))); // scan every item
        }
        let vec_us = t.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1e6 / reps as f64;

        let t = Instant::now();
        for _ in 0..reps {
            black_box(set.contains(black_box(&-1))); // one hash lookup
        }
        let set_us = t.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1e6 / reps as f64;
        println!("n={n:>7}  Vec {vec_us:8.2} µs   HashSet {set_us:5.2} µs");
    }
}
import timeit

for n in [1_000, 10_000, 100_000]:
    data = list(range(n))
    as_set = set(data)
    missing = -1  # the worst case: not in the collection
    t_list = timeit.timeit(lambda: missing in data, number=200) / 200
    t_set = timeit.timeit(lambda: missing in as_set, number=200) / 200
    print(f"n={n:>7}  list {t_list * 1e6:9.2f} µs   set {t_set * 1e6:5.2f} µs")
n=   1000  Vec     0.09 µs   HashSet  0.01 µs
n=  10000  Vec     0.86 µs   HashSet  0.01 µs
n= 100000  Vec     9.32 µs   HashSet  0.01 µs

The Rust program was built with rustc -O. Without -O it is much slower. Python printed this:

n=   1000  list      6.04 µs   set  0.03 µs
n=  10000  list     58.51 µs   set  0.03 µs
n= 100000  list    609.17 µs   set  0.04 µs

Programmers describe this growth with big-O notation. O(1) means the cost does not grow with the size. O(n) means it grows in step with the size. O(\log n) means it grows very slowly: double the size, and you add one step.

Typical cost of common operations
OperationRustPythonCost
Read item iv[i]v[i]O(1)
Add at the endv.push(x)v.append(x)O(1) amortized
Remove from the endv.pop()v.pop()O(1)
Insert or remove at the frontv.insert(0, x)v.insert(0, x)O(n)
Find a value in a listv.contains(&x)x in vO(n)
Sortv.sort()v.sort()O(n \log n)
Add or remove at either end of a dequepush_front, pop_frontappendleft, popleftO(1)
Look up, insert, remove by keyHashMap, HashSetdict, setO(1) expected
Look up, insert, remove by key, sortedBTreeMap, BTreeSetno built-in typeO(\log n)
Biggest or smallest keyfirst_key_value()min(d), a full scanO(\log n) or O(n)

"Expected" means: on average, with a good hash function. If many keys land in the same slot, a lookup can become O(n). The Rust and Python documentation both say this.

A loop with if x in my_list inside a loop over another list is O(n \cdot m). With 10,000 items each, that is 100 million steps. Turn the inner list into a set first. Then it is about 10,000 steps.

Why does Rust use a slow-looking hash function? (expert)

The default hasher today is SipHash 1-3, with a random seed. The documentation says this can change. It protects against HashDoS. An attacker who knows the hash function can send many keys for one slot. Then every lookup becomes slow. A random seed stops that. For trusted data, a faster hasher from a crate can help.

What does the table inside look like? (expert)

The Rust documentation says HashMap is a port of Google's SwissTable design. It uses quadratic probing and SIMD to check many slots at once. CPython's dict uses its own open-addressing design. It also keeps a separate array in insertion order. That is how it remembers the order.

Why is a Vec usually faster than a linked list? (expert)

The items of a Vec sit next to each other. The CPU loads neighbours together into its cache. A linked list jumps around in memory. The Rust documentation says Vec and VecDeque are generally faster than LinkedList.

Choosing a collection

The Rust documentation gives simple advice: you probably want Vec or HashMap. Use the others when you need their special skill. Walk down the tree from the top.

Each Rust collection and its nearest Python twin
RustPythonMain difference
Vec<T>listA Python list can mix types.
[T; N], tupletupleA Python tuple can have any length and mix types.
HashMap<K, V>dictdict keeps insertion order. HashMap has none.
HashSet<T>setPython has set operators: | & - ^.
BTreeMap<K, V>none built inSort the keys, or use sortedcontainers.
VecDeque<T>collections.dequedeque has maxlen.
BinaryHeap<T>heapq on a listRust gives the biggest first, heapq the smallest.

What can be a key?

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    let mut m: HashMap<f64, &str> = HashMap::new();
    m.insert(0.5, "half");
}
error[E0599]: the method `insert` exists for struct `HashMap<f64, &str>`, but its trait bounds were not satisfied
 --> f64key.rs:5:7
  |
5 |     m.insert(0.5, "half");
  |       ^^^^^^
  |
  = note: the following trait bounds were not satisfied:
          `f64: Eq`
          `f64: Hash`

A HashMap key must have the traits Eq and Hash. A f64 has neither, because NaN is not equal to itself. Use integers, strings, tuples of them, or your own type with #[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]. A BTreeMap key needs Ord instead. In Python, a key must be hashable.

Interviewers love "two sum": find two numbers that add up to a target. The slow answer tries every pair: O(n^2). The fast answer stores each number in a HashMap as you go and asks the map for target - x: O(n). Most "make it faster" questions end with a hash map or a set.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for collections
PatternPurposeModelNote
Vec::with_capacity(n)Allocate once when you know the sizelet mut out = Vec::with_capacity(lines.len());The length is still 0.
v.get(i)Read an index that may be missingif let Some(x) = v.get(i) { ... }v[i] panics when i is too big.
fn f(xs: &[T])Accept arrays, Vecs and parts of themfn average(xs: &[f64])Not &Vec<T>.
*m.entry(k).or_insert(0) += 1Count things*counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;One lookup, not two.
m.entry(k).or_default().push(x)Group items under a keygroups.entry(first).or_default().push(w);Python: defaultdict(list).
set.insert(x) returns boolFind repeatsif !seen.insert(x) { dup }It is false for a repeat.
btree.range(a..b)Find all keys in a rangetemps.range(9..15)Only BTreeMap, not HashMap.
VecDeque as a queueFirst in, first outpush_back, then pop_frontVec::remove(0) is O(n).
v.retain(|x| test)Remove items while loopingstock.retain(|_, n| *n > 0);Python: build a new list or dict.
for x in &vLoop without using up vfor p in &prices { ... }for x in v moves v.
Python Counter(items)Count in one lineCounter(words).most_common(3)It is a dict subclass.
Python deque(maxlen=n)Keep the last n itemsrecent = deque(maxlen=100)Old items fall off silently.

Practice

You must keep the last 100 log lines. New lines arrive all the time. Which Rust collection fits best?

  • Vec with remove(0)
  • VecDeque
  • HashSet

You add at the back and drop at the front. A VecDeque does both in O(1). Vec::remove(0) moves every item.

What does x in my_list cost in Python for a list of n items?

  • O(1)
  • O(\log n)
  • O(n)

A list does not know where x is. It checks the items one by one.

You print a HashMap in a test and compare it with fixed text. What happens?

  • The test always passes.
  • The test can pass on one run and fail on the next.
  • The code does not compile.

The order of a HashMap is arbitrary. It changes because of the random seed. Sort the items or use a BTreeMap.

Which type can be a HashMap key?

  • f64
  • (String, u32)
  • Vec<f32>

A key needs Eq and Hash. A tuple of a String and a u32 has both. Floats have neither.

Count a word in one line: *counts.entry(w).? += 1;

Python promises that a dict keeps insertion order since version ?.

  1. After for x in v { } you try v.len(). Why does it fail? How do you fix the loop?
    Answer

    for x in v calls into_iter() and moves v into the loop. The Vec is gone after it. Write for x in &v to borrow it instead.

  2. Remove repeats from a Vec<i32> and keep the first order. [3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 4] becomes [3, 1, 2, 4]. Write it in Rust and in Python.
    Answer 
    use std::collections::HashSet;

fn dedup_keep_order(v: &mut Vec<i32>) {
    let mut seen = HashSet::new();
    v.retain(|x| seen.insert(*x)); // insert is false for a repeat
}

    In Python: list(dict.fromkeys(v)). It works because a dict keeps insertion order. Note that v.dedup() in Rust only removes repeats that stand next to each other.

  3. You have 50,000 user ids in a list and 50,000 order records. For each order you check if order.user in ids. The program is slow. Why, and what is the fix?
    Answer

    Each check scans the list: O(n). Together it is about 2.5 billion steps. Put the ids in a set first: ids = set(ids). Then each check is O(1) on average.

  4. Expert. Group anagrams. ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"] gives [["bat"], ["eat", "tea", "ate"], ["tan", "nat"]].
    Answer 
    use std::collections::HashMap;

fn group_anagrams<'a>(words: &[&'a str]) -> Vec<Vec<&'a str>> {
    let mut groups: HashMap<Vec<char>, Vec<&'a str>> = HashMap::new();
    for w in words {
        let mut key: Vec<char> = w.chars().collect();
        key.sort_unstable(); // "eat" and "tea" both give [a, e, t]
        groups.entry(key).or_default().push(w);
    }
    let mut out: Vec<Vec<&str>> = groups.into_values().collect();
    out.sort(); // a fixed order for printing
    out
}

    The sorted letters are the key. Words with the same letters land in the same group. Python: use defaultdict(list) with the key "".join(sorted(w)).

  5. Expert. Why does HashMap<f64, V> not work? Give two ways to store prices as keys.
    Answer

    f64 is not Eq, because NaN != NaN. It also has no Hash. Store prices as whole cents in a u64. Or use f64::to_bits(), which gives a u64 key. But then 0.0 and -0.0 become different keys.

Key takeaways

  • Start with Vec and HashMap. Pick another collection only for a clear reason.
  • A Vec has a length and a capacity. push is O(1) amortized. Inserting at the front is O(n).
  • The entry API looks up a key once: or_insert, or_default, and_modify.
  • HashMap has no order. BTreeMap keeps keys sorted and answers range questions. Python dict keeps insertion order.
  • for x in &v borrows, for x in &mut v changes, for x in v moves.
  • Membership in a list is O(n). In a set it is O(1) on average. This one change often fixes slow code.

Sources

  • Rust standard library: std::collections. When to use each collection, and the cost table.
  • Rust standard library: HashMap. The entry API, the default hasher, and get_disjoint_mut.
  • The Rust Programming Language, chapter 8. The official book on vectors, strings and hash maps.
  • Python documentation: Built-in types. list, tuple, dict and set, and the insertion order promise.
  • Python documentation: collections. deque, defaultdict and Counter.
  • Python documentation: Time complexity of built-in types. The cost of list, dict and set operations.

Structs, enums and pattern matching

Real programs work with users, orders and shapes, not only with numbers. Structs and enums let you build your own types for them. Pattern matching takes those types apart again, and the compiler checks that you handled every case.

  • Define structs and add methods with impl.
  • Use tuple structs and the newtype idea to keep units and ids apart.
  • Build enums whose variants carry data, and use Option instead of null.
  • Write match, if let, let else and while let, and read every kind of pattern.
  • Model data so that wrong states cannot exist, in Rust and in Python.

Structs: group related data

A user has a name, an email, an age and a flag. You want to keep the four values together. Here is the same type in both languages.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct User {
    name: String,
    email: String,
    age: u32,
    active: bool,
}

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("Ann");
    let mut ann = User {
        name, // shorthand for name: name
        email: String::from("ann@example.com"),
        age: 31,
        active: true,
    };
    ann.age += 1; // the whole value is mut, so every field is
    println!("{} is {}", ann.name, ann.age);

    // Struct update: copy the other fields from ann.
    let bo = User {
        name: String::from("Bo"),
        email: String::from("bo@example.com"),
        ..ann.clone()
    };
    println!("{bo:#?}"); // pretty Debug: one field per line
    println!("{}", ann == bo);
}
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace


@dataclass
class User:
    name: str
    email: str
    age: int
    active: bool = True  # a default value


ann = User("Ann", "ann@example.com", 31)
ann.age += 1
print(ann.name, "is", ann.age)

bo = replace(ann, name="Bo", email="bo@example.com")  # a changed copy
print(bo)
print(ann == bo)  # @dataclass writes __eq__ for you
Ann is 32
User {
    name: "Bo",
    email: "bo@example.com",
    age: 32,
    active: true,
}
false

Python prints User(name='Bo', email='bo@example.com', age=32, active=True) on one line, and then False.

A struct is a type with named fields. Each field has a type. You make a value of the struct with all fields filled. Python's @dataclass is the closest twin. It writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for you.

  • #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)] asks the compiler to write three traits. Then you can print with {:?}, call .clone() and compare with ==. See Traits and generics.
  • ..ann.clone() fills the remaining fields from another value. Without clone(), the String fields of ann would move into bo.
  • Rust has no default values for fields. Write a constructor, or derive Default.

You cannot make one field mut. Mutability belongs to the whole binding: let mut ann. If only some data should change, put it in a separate value.

Methods with impl

Functions that belong to a type go into an impl block. Look at the first parameter of each method.

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Account {
    owner: String,
    cents: i64,
}

impl Account {
    // An associated function: no self. Call it with Account::new.
    fn new(owner: &str) -> Self {
        Self { owner: owner.to_string(), cents: 0 }
    }

    // &self: read only
    fn balance(&self) -> f64 {
        self.cents as f64 / 100.0
    }

    // &mut self: may change the fields
    fn deposit(&mut self, cents: i64) {
        self.cents += cents;
    }

    // self: takes the value; the caller cannot use it after this
    fn close(self) -> String {
        format!("closed {} with {:.2}", self.owner, self.balance())
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut acc = Account::new("Ann");
    acc.deposit(1250);
    acc.deposit(199);
    println!("{:.2}", acc.balance());
    println!("{}", acc.close());
    // println!("{acc:?}"); // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `acc`
}
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Account:
    owner: str
    cents: int = 0

    @classmethod
    def new(cls, owner: str) -> "Account":  # Python usually calls Account(...)
        return cls(owner)

    def balance(self) -> float:
        return self.cents / 100

    def deposit(self, cents: int) -> None:
        self.cents += cents

    def close(self) -> str:
        return f"closed {self.owner} with {self.balance():.2f}"


acc = Account.new("Ann")
acc.deposit(1250)
acc.deposit(199)
print(f"{acc.balance():.2f}")
print(acc.close())
print(acc)  # still usable: Python has no moves
14.49
closed Ann with 14.49

Python prints one more line: Account(owner='Ann', cents=1449). The object still exists after close().

The first parameter decides what a method may do
First parameterMeansThe caller needsAfter the call
&selfBorrow and readAny bindingThe value is unchanged
&mut selfBorrow and changelet mutThe value holds the changes
selfTake the valueAny bindingThe value is gone (unless it is Copy)
noneAn associated functionType::name(...)Often a constructor like new

Self with a capital S is the type of the impl block. Here it means Account. Python always writes self and can change any field. It has no read-only methods.

Rust has no constructors in the language. new is just a name that everyone uses. A type can have several, like Account::with_balance.

Tuple structs and the newtype idea

A distance in meters and a distance in feet are both f64. Mix them up and a program computes nonsense. Give each its own type.

// Tuple structs: fields have no names, only positions.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Meters(f64);
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Feet(f64);
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8);
// A unit struct: no fields at all.
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Marker;

fn add(a: Meters, b: Meters) -> Meters {
    Meters(a.0 + b.0) // .0 is the first field
}

fn to_meters(f: Feet) -> Meters {
    Meters(f.0 * 0.3048)
}

fn main() {
    let run = add(Meters(400.0), Meters(100.0));
    let jump = to_meters(Feet(10.0));
    let Rgb(r, g, b) = Rgb(255, 128, 0); // take the fields apart
    println!("{run:?} {jump:?} {r} {g} {b} {Marker:?}");
}
Meters(500.0) Meters(3.048) 255 128 0 Marker

Now try to add feet to meters.

struct Meters(f64);
struct Feet(f64);

fn add(a: Meters, b: Meters) -> Meters {
    Meters(a.0 + b.0)
}

fn main() {
    let total = add(Meters(400.0), Feet(3.0));
}
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> newtype_err.rs:9:36
  |
9 |     let total = add(Meters(400.0), Feet(3.0));
  |                 ---                ^^^^^^^^^ expected `Meters`, found `Feet`
  |                 |
  |                 arguments to this function are incorrect

The output above is shortened. The compiler stops the mistake before the program runs.

A tuple struct has fields with positions, not names. You read them with .0, .1 and so on. A tuple struct with one field around another type is a newtype. It costs nothing at run time. Meters is exactly as big as an f64.

Python has typing.NewType("Meters", float). Only a type checker such as mypy sees the difference. At run time a Meters value is a plain float.

Do not use a tuple struct with many fields of the same type, like struct Size(u32, u32). Which one is the width? Use named fields when the meaning is not clear from the position.

Enums: one of several kinds, each with its own data

A shape is a circle, a rectangle, a triangle or a dot. Each kind needs different data. An enum says exactly that.

use std::f64::consts::PI;

#[derive(Debug)]
enum Shape {
    Circle { r: f64 },        // a variant with named fields
    Rect { w: f64, h: f64 },
    Triangle(f64, f64, f64),  // a variant with unnamed fields
    Dot,                      // a variant with no data
}

impl Shape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 {
        match self {
            Shape::Circle { r } => PI * r * r,
            Shape::Rect { w, h } => w * h,
            Shape::Triangle(a, b, c) => {
                let s = (a + b + c) / 2.0; // Heron's formula
                (s * (s - a) * (s - b) * (s - c)).sqrt()
            }
            Shape::Dot => 0.0,
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let shapes = [
        Shape::Circle { r: 1.0 },
        Shape::Rect { w: 2.0, h: 3.0 },
        Shape::Triangle(3.0, 4.0, 5.0),
        Shape::Dot,
    ];
    for s in &shapes {
        println!("{:<34} area {:.2}", format!("{s:?}"), s.area());
    }
}
import math
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Circle:
    r: float


@dataclass
class Rect:
    w: float
    h: float


@dataclass
class Triangle:
    a: float
    b: float
    c: float


@dataclass
class Dot:
    pass


type Shape = Circle | Rect | Triangle | Dot  # a union of classes (3.12 syntax)


def area(s: Shape) -> float:
    match s:
        case Circle(r=r):
            return math.pi * r * r
        case Rect(w, h):  # positional: uses __match_args__
            return w * h
        case Triangle(a, b, c):
            p = (a + b + c) / 2
            return math.sqrt(p * (p - a) * (p - b) * (p - c))
        case Dot():
            return 0.0


for s in [Circle(1.0), Rect(2.0, 3.0), Triangle(3.0, 4.0, 5.0), Dot()]:
    print(f"{s!r:<34} area {area(s):.2f}")
Circle { r: 1.0 }                  area 3.14
Rect { w: 2.0, h: 3.0 }            area 6.00
Triangle(3.0, 4.0, 5.0)            area 6.00
Dot                                area 0.00

Python prints Circle(r=1.0), Rect(w=2.0, h=3.0) and so on, with the same areas.

An enum lists its variants. A value is always exactly one variant. Each variant can carry its own data. Some languages call this a tagged union or a sum type.

Python has no single feature for this. The usual way is one dataclass per variant, a union type, and match. Python's Enum class is for simple names without data. You will see it below.

A struct says "this AND this AND this". An enum says "this OR this OR this". Most data in the real world needs both.

Option: no null in Rust

A search can fail. In many languages it then returns null or None. Rust returns an Option.

// Find the first word that starts with a capital letter.
fn first_name(text: &str) -> Option<&str> {
    for w in text.split_whitespace() {
        if w.chars().next()?.is_uppercase() { // ? returns None if no char
            return Some(w);
        }
    }
    None
}

fn main() {
    let a = first_name("today ann met Bo");
    let b = first_name("no names here");
    println!("{a:?} {b:?}");

    // Ways to get the value out
    match a {
        Some(n) => println!("found {n}"),
        None => println!("nobody"),
    }
    println!("{}", b.unwrap_or("nobody"));           // a default
    println!("{:?}", a.map(|n| n.len()));            // change the inside
    println!("{}", a.is_some());
    let len = a.map_or(0, |n| n.len());              // default and change
    println!("{len}");
    println!("{:?}", a.filter(|n| n.len() > 5));     // keep only if true
    println!("{}", a.unwrap());                       // panics on None!
}
Some("Bo") None
found Bo
nobody
Some(2)
true
2
None
Bo

Option<T> is a normal enum from the standard library. It has two variants: Some(T) and None. The key point: an Option<i32> is not an i32. You cannot use it as a number by accident.

fn main() {
    let x: i32 = 5;
    let y: Option<i32> = Some(5);
    let sum = x + y;
}
error[E0277]: cannot add `Option<i32>` to `i32`
 --> option_err.rs:4:17
  |
4 |     let sum = x + y;
  |                 ^ no implementation for `i32 + Option<i32>`

The output above is shortened. The compiler forces you to handle None first. Python's None can appear anywhere. A missing check fails only at run time.

def first_name(text: str) -> str | None:
    for w in text.split():
        if w[0].isupper():
            return w
    return None


a = first_name("today ann met Bo")
b = first_name("no names here")
print(a, b)
print(b or "nobody")            # careful: "" is also false
try:
    print(len(b))               # the checker can warn; Python fails at run time
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
Bo None
nobody
TypeError: object of type 'NoneType' has no len()

The hint str | None tells a type checker that None is possible. The checker can then warn about len(b). Python itself does not check hints.

unwrap() on None panics. Use it in tests and quick experiments. In real code, use match, if let, unwrap_or, or ?. The chapter Error handling does the same for Result.

Why is Option free for references and Box? (expert)

A reference or a Box can never be zero. So Rust uses the zero value to mean None. No extra tag is needed. This is called the niche optimization.

use std::mem::size_of;

#[allow(dead_code)]
enum Direction { North, East, South, West }

fn main() {
    println!("Direction        {}", size_of::<Direction>());
    println!("Option<u32>      {}", size_of::<Option<u32>>());
    println!("Box<u32>         {}", size_of::<Box<u32>>());
    println!("Option<Box<u32>> {}", size_of::<Option<Box<u32>>>());
    println!("&str             {}", size_of::<&str>());
    println!("Option<&str>     {}", size_of::<Option<&str>>());
}
Direction        1
Option<u32>      8
Box<u32>         8
Option<Box<u32>> 8
&str             16
Option<&str>     16

A u32 can be any bit pattern, so Option<u32> needs a tag and grows from 4 to 8 bytes.

match: every case, checked

Forget one case of a traffic light. Rust refuses to compile.

enum Light {
    Red,
    Yellow,
    Green,
}

fn action(l: Light) -> &'static str {
    match l {
        Light::Red => "stop",
        Light::Green => "go",
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", action(Light::Yellow));
}
error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `Light::Yellow` not covered
  --> e0004.rs:8:11
   |
 8 |     match l {
   |           ^ pattern `Light::Yellow` not covered
   |
help: ensure that all possible cases are being handled by adding a match arm with a wildcard pattern or an explicit pattern as shown
   |
10 ~         Light::Green => "go",
11 ~         Light::Yellow => todo!(),

The output above is shortened. Note the help: the compiler even writes the missing arm for you.

A Rust match must be exhaustive. Every possible value must fit some arm. When you add a new variant later, the compiler shows every match you must update. This is one of the best tools for changing big programs safely.

Python's match (since 3.10) does not check this. A missed case simply does nothing.

from enum import Enum, auto


class Light(Enum):
    RED = auto()
    YELLOW = auto()
    GREEN = auto()


def action(l: Light) -> str:
    match l:
        case Light.RED:
            return "stop"
        case Light.GREEN:
            return "go"


print(action(Light.YELLOW))  # no error: the function returns None
print(list(Light), Light.RED.value, Light["GREEN"])
None
[<Light.RED: 1>, <Light.YELLOW: 2>, <Light.GREEN: 3>] 1 Light.GREEN

Python's Enum gives names to fixed values. auto() picks the values for you. To get a check like Rust's, add a last arm with typing.assert_never. A type checker such as mypy or pyright then reports the missed case before the program runs. At run time, the same line fails loudly:

from enum import Enum, auto
from typing import assert_never


class Light(Enum):
    RED = auto()
    YELLOW = auto()
    GREEN = auto()


def action(l: Light) -> str:
    match l:
        case Light.RED:
            return "stop"
        case Light.GREEN:
            return "go"
        case _:
            assert_never(l)  # a type checker flags this line


print(action(Light.YELLOW))
AssertionError: Expected code to be unreachable, but got: <Light.YELLOW: 2>

The output shows the last line of the error only.

A wildcard _ => arm turns off the check. Add a new variant, and it silently lands in _. For your own enums, prefer to list every variant.

A bare name in a pattern catches everything

STOP = 0
GO = 1

def action(signal: int) -> str:
    match signal:
        case STOP:          # not a compare: this binds a NEW name STOP
            return "stop"
        case GO:
            return "go"
  File "capture_trap.py", line 6
    case STOP:          # not a compare: this binds a NEW name STOP
         ^^^^
SyntaxError: name capture 'STOP' makes remaining patterns unreachable

A plain name in a pattern is a binding, not a compare. Python compares only dotted names like Light.RED. Rust has the same rule for lowercase names. A Rust const like MAX in a pattern does compare.

if let, let else and while let

Sometimes you care about one pattern only. A full match is then too long.

use std::collections::HashMap;

// let else: get the value or leave the function early.
fn parse_pair(line: &str) -> Option<(String, i32)> {
    let Some((key, value)) = line.split_once('=') else {
        return None; // the else block must leave: return, break, panic
    };
    let Ok(n) = value.trim().parse::<i32>() else {
        return None;
    };
    Some((key.trim().to_string(), n))
}

fn main() {
    let ports = HashMap::from([("web", 8080)]);

    // if let: one pattern, and you do not care about the rest
    if let Some(p) = ports.get("web") {
        println!("web on {p}");
    }
    if let Some(p) = ports.get("db") {
        println!("db on {p}");
    } else {
        println!("no db");
    }

    println!("{:?} {:?} {:?}", parse_pair("x = 5"), parse_pair("x5"), parse_pair("x=a"));

    // while let: loop while the pattern matches
    let mut stack = vec![1, 2, 3];
    while let Some(top) = stack.pop() {
        print!("{top} ");
    }
    println!();
}
ports = {"web": 8080}

if (p := ports.get("web")) is not None:   # the walrus operator
    print("web on", p)
if (p := ports.get("db")) is not None:
    print("db on", p)
else:
    print("no db")


def parse_pair(line: str) -> tuple[str, int] | None:
    key, sep, value = line.partition("=")
    if not sep:
        return None
    try:
        return key.strip(), int(value)
    except ValueError:
        return None


print(parse_pair("x = 5"), parse_pair("x5"), parse_pair("x=a"))

stack = [1, 2, 3]
while stack:
    print(stack.pop(), end=" ")
print()
web on 8080
no db
Some(("x", 5)) None None
3 2 1

Python prints ('x', 5) None None on the third line.

Four ways to use a pattern
FormUse it whenIf the pattern does not match
match x { ... }Several cases, all handledNot possible. Every case has an arm.
if let P = x { } else { }One case mattersThe else block runs, or nothing
let P = x else { ... };Get a value or leave earlyThe else block must return, break or panic
while let P = x { }Repeat while values comeThe loop ends

let else came in Rust 1.65. It keeps the "happy path" flat, without deep nesting. Since Rust 1.88, in the 2024 edition, you can also chain conditions: if let Some(x) = a && x > 0. The chapter Control flow shows let chains.

if let Some(n) = name moves the String out of name. After that, name cannot be used, and you get error E0382. Match on &name instead. Then n is a &String, and name stays whole.

Pattern syntax: the full toolbox

Patterns are not only for enums. They work on numbers, tuples, structs, slices and nested values. This program uses most kinds.

struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}

fn describe(n: i32) -> &'static str {
    match n {
        0 => "zero",                    // a literal
        1 | 2 | 3 => "small",           // several patterns
        4..=9 => "medium",              // inclusive range
        10..100 => "large",             // exclusive range (Rust 1.80)
        i32::MIN..0 => "negative",
        _ => "huge",                    // anything else
    }
}

fn where_is(p: &Point) -> String {
    match p {
        Point { x: 0, y: 0 } => "origin".to_string(),
        Point { x: 0, y } => format!("on the y axis at {y}"),
        Point { x, y: 0 } => format!("on the x axis at {x}"),
        Point { x, y } if x == y => format!("on the diagonal at {x}"), // guard
        Point { x, .. } => format!("somewhere with x = {x}"),        // ignore y
    }
}

fn slice_info(v: &[i32]) -> String {
    match v {
        [] => "empty".to_string(),
        [one] => format!("one item: {one}"),
        [first, .., last] => format!("{first} ... {last}"),
    }
}

The main function calls them with a few values. The rest of the file is below, with its output.

fn main() {
    for n in [0, 2, 7, 42, -5, 1000] {
        print!("{} ", describe(n));
    }
    println!();
    for p in [Point { x: 0, y: 0 }, Point { x: 0, y: 4 }, Point { x: 3, y: 0 },
              Point { x: 5, y: 5 }, Point { x: 1, y: 9 }] {
        println!("{}", where_is(&p));
    }
    println!("{} | {} | {}", slice_info(&[]), slice_info(&[7]), slice_info(&[1, 2, 3, 4]));

    // @ binds the value and tests it at the same time
    let age = 15;
    match age {
        a @ 13..=19 => println!("teen, {a}"),
        a => println!("not a teen, {a}"),
    }
    // Patterns in let and in function parameters
    let (a, (b, c)) = (1, (2, 3));
    let add = |(x, y): (i32, i32)| x + y;
    println!("{} {}", a + b + c, add((4, 5)));
}
zero small medium large negative huge
origin
on the y axis at 4
on the x axis at 3
on the diagonal at 5
somewhere with x = 1
empty | one item: 7 | 1 ... 4
teen, 15
6 9
Every kind of pattern, in Rust and Python
KindRustPython
Literal0, "yes", 'a'0, "yes"
Bind a namenn
Anything, no name__
Several1 | 2 | 31 | 2 | 3
Range4..=9, 10..100none. Use a guard: case _ if 4 <= n <= 9
Tuple(a, (b, c))(a, (b, c))
Struct or classPoint { x: 0, y }Point(x=0, y=y)
Enum variantShape::Rect { w, h }Rect(w, h)
Slice or list[first, .., last][first, *_, last]
Ignore the restPoint { x, .. }Point(x=x)
Bind and testa @ 13..=19int(a) if 13 <= a <= 19
GuardSome(x) if x > 0case x if x > 0

A pattern that can fail is refutable, like Some(x). A pattern that always matches is irrefutable, like (a, b) for a pair. let and function parameters need irrefutable patterns. if let, let else and match arms accept refutable ones.

A guard turns off part of the exhaustiveness check. The compiler does not read the condition if x == y. So after guarded arms you usually need a last arm without a guard.

Matching on a reference: binding modes (expert)

When you match a &Point against Point { x, y }, Rust borrows the fields for you. Then x is a &i32. People call this "match ergonomics". The 2024 edition made one rule stricter. Inside such an implicit borrow, you may not write mut, ref or & on a binding.

fn main() {
    let opt = &Some(5);
    if let Some(mut x) = opt {
        x += 1;
        println!("{x}");
    }
}
error: cannot mutably bind by value within an implicitly-borrowing pattern
 --> ergo.rs:3:17
  |
3 |     if let Some(mut x) = opt {
  |                 ^^^ `mut` binding modifier not allowed when implicitly borrowing

The output above is shortened. The edition 2021 compiler accepts this code and prints 6. In 2024, write &Some(mut x) to copy the number out.

if let guards in match arms (Rust 1.95)

Since Rust 1.95, a match guard can hold an if let: Some(t) if let Ok(n) = t.parse::<i32>() => .... Both t and n are usable in that arm. See Rust recent releases.

Modelling data: make wrong states impossible

A network connection can be idle, connecting, connected or failed. Here is a first design with flags.

#[allow(dead_code)]
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Conn {
    connecting: bool,
    connected: bool,
    attempt: u32,
    session: Option<u64>,
    reason: Option<String>,
}

fn main() {
    // This compiles, but it makes no sense:
    // connected and failed at the same time, with no session.
    let nonsense = Conn {
        connecting: true,
        connected: true,
        attempt: 0,
        session: None,
        reason: Some("timeout".into()),
    };
    println!("{nonsense:?}");
}
Conn { connecting: true, connected: true, attempt: 0, session: None, reason: Some("timeout") }

Two flags and two options give 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 16 combinations. Only four of them make sense. Every function must check for the other twelve, and one day someone forgets. The fix is to make the wrong states impossible to build.

List the real states

Ask: what can this thing be? Here: idle, connecting, connected, failed. Four states, not sixteen.

One variant per state

enum Conn { Idle, Connecting, Connected, Failed }

The two flags are gone. A value is always exactly one state.

Move each field to its state

Connecting { attempt: u32 }
Connected { session: u64 }
Failed { reason: String }

A session exists only when connected. No Option is needed any more.

List the events

enum Event { Start, Ok(u64), Timeout, Close }

Events are also an enum. Some carry data, like the session id.

Match on the pair

match (state, event) { ... }

One arm per allowed change. A last arm keeps the state for any other event.

#[allow(dead_code)] // some fields are only printed
#[derive(Debug)]
enum Conn {
    Idle,
    Connecting { attempt: u32 },
    Connected { session: u64 },
    Failed { reason: String },
}

#[derive(Debug)]
enum Event {
    Start,
    Ok(u64),
    Timeout,
    Close,
}

const MAX_TRIES: u32 = 3;

// Every pair of (state, event) has one clear answer.
fn step(state: Conn, event: Event) -> Conn {
    match (state, event) {
        (Conn::Idle, Event::Start) => Conn::Connecting { attempt: 1 },
        (Conn::Connecting { .. }, Event::Ok(id)) => Conn::Connected { session: id },
        (Conn::Connecting { attempt }, Event::Timeout) if attempt < MAX_TRIES => {
            Conn::Connecting { attempt: attempt + 1 }
        }
        (Conn::Connecting { .. }, Event::Timeout) => Conn::Failed {
            reason: format!("no answer after {MAX_TRIES} tries"),
        },
        (Conn::Connected { .. }, Event::Close) => Conn::Idle,
        (state, _) => state, // any other event changes nothing
    }
}

The main function sends some events and prints each new state.

fn main() {
    let mut s = Conn::Idle;
    for e in [Event::Start, Event::Timeout, Event::Ok(42), Event::Start, Event::Close] {
        print!("{e:?} -> ");
        s = step(s, e);
        println!("{s:?}");
    }
    let mut s = Conn::Connecting { attempt: 1 };
    for _ in 0..3 {
        s = step(s, Event::Timeout);
    }
    println!("{s:?}");
}
Start -> Connecting { attempt: 1 }
Timeout -> Connecting { attempt: 2 }
Ok(42) -> Connected { session: 42 }
Start -> Connected { session: 42 }
Close -> Idle
Failed { reason: "no answer after 3 tries" }

This is a state machine. The enum makes it visible in the types. The Python version uses frozen dataclasses and a union.

from dataclasses import dataclass

MAX_TRIES = 3

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Idle: pass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Connecting:
    attempt: int

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Connected:
    session: int

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Failed:
    reason: str

type Conn = Idle | Connecting | Connected | Failed

def step(state: Conn, event: str, value: int = 0) -> Conn:
    match state, event:
        case Idle(), "start":
            return Connecting(1)
        case Connecting(), "ok":
            return Connected(value)
        case Connecting(attempt=n), "timeout" if n < MAX_TRIES:
            return Connecting(n + 1)
        case Connecting(), "timeout":
            return Failed(f"no answer after {MAX_TRIES} tries")
        case Connected(), "close":
            return Idle()
        case _:
            return state

s: Conn = Idle()
for event, value in [("start", 0), ("timeout", 0), ("ok", 42), ("start", 0), ("close", 0)]:
    s = step(s, event, value)
    print(event, "->", s)
start -> Connecting(attempt=1)
timeout -> Connecting(attempt=2)
ok -> Connected(session=42)
start -> Connected(session=42)
close -> Idle()

frozen=True makes each state unchangeable, like a Rust value without mut. But Python does not stop you from building a strange object at run time. The type hints and a type checker are your safety net there.

Parse, do not validate

The same idea works for single values. Check the input once, when you build the type. After that, the type itself is the proof.

mod email {
    #[derive(Debug)]
    pub struct Email(String); // the field is private to this module

    impl Email {
        // The only way to make an Email. It checks the text once.
        pub fn parse(s: &str) -> Result<Email, String> {
            match s.split_once('@') {
                Some((user, host)) if !user.is_empty() && host.contains('.') => {
                    Ok(Email(s.to_lowercase()))
                }
                _ => Err(format!("not an email: {s:?}")),
            }
        }
        pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
            &self.0
        }
    }
}

use email::Email;

// This function never needs to check again.
fn send_welcome(to: &Email) -> String {
    format!("welcome mail to {}", to.as_str())
}

fn main() {
    match Email::parse("Ann@Example.com") {
        Ok(e) => println!("{}", send_welcome(&e)),
        Err(msg) => println!("{msg}"),
    }
    println!("{:?}", Email::parse("ann.example.com"));
}
welcome mail to ann@example.com
Err("not an email: \"ann.example.com\"")

Code outside the module cannot write Email(String::from("x")). The compiler says: error[E0603]: tuple struct constructor `Email` is private. So every Email in the program went through parse. The check here is simple on purpose. Real email rules are much longer.

A common design question: "How do you stop invalid data in your system?" A strong answer names three tools. Enums for states, newtypes with private fields for checked values, and exhaustive match so new cases cannot be forgotten. The chapter Advanced traits and types adds the type-state pattern.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for structs, enums and matching
PatternPurposeModelNote
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]Get printing, copying and comparing for freestruct User { name: String, age: u32 }Python: @dataclass does the same.
fn new(...) -> SelfA constructor by conventionAccount::new("Ann")It is a normal associated function.
&self / &mut self / selfRead, change or consumefn deposit(&mut self, cents: i64)Pick the weakest one that works.
struct Meters(f64);Give a plain number a meaningfn add(a: Meters, b: Meters)No run-time cost.
enum E { A { x: T }, B(U), C }One of several kinds, each with dataenum Shape { Circle { r: f64 }, Dot }Python: one dataclass per variant and a union.
Option<T>A value that may be missingfn find(id: u32) -> Option<User>Never unwrap() in real code paths.
match x { ... }Handle every caseLight::Red => "stop",Avoid _ for your own enums.
if let P = x { }Handle one caseif let Some(p) = ports.get("web")Match on &x to avoid a move.
let P = x else { return };Get a value or leave earlylet Some((k, v)) = line.split_once('=') else { return None };The else must not continue.
while let P = x { }Loop while values comewhile let Some(top) = stack.pop()Python: while stack:
[first, .., last]Look at the ends of a slicematch v { [] => ..., [one] => ..., [a, .., z] => ... }Python: [first, *_, last].
match (state, event)Write a state machine(Conn::Idle, Event::Start) => ...Keep a last arm for "no change".

Practice

A method must add money to an account. Which first parameter does it need?

  • &self
  • &mut self
  • self

It changes a field and the caller keeps the account. That is a mutable borrow.

A match on an enum forgets one variant. What happens in Rust and in Python?

  • Both raise an error at run time.
  • Rust does not compile. Python silently does nothing for that case.
  • Both refuse to run the program.

Rust checks exhaustiveness (E0004). Python's match does not. Use assert_never and a type checker.

What does size_of::<Option<Box<u32>>>() print on a 64-bit machine?

  • 16
  • 8
  • 12

A Box is never zero, so Rust stores None as zero. No extra tag is needed.

In Python, STOP = 0 at the top of a file. What does case STOP: do?

  • It compares the value with 0.
  • It binds the value to a new name STOP.
  • It raises NameError.

A bare name is a capture pattern. Use a dotted name like Signal.STOP to compare.

The else block of let Some(x) = v else { ... }; must leave, for example with ?.

The part if x == y after a pattern is called a match ?.

  1. Write an enum Coin with Penny, Nickel, Dime and Quarter, and a method cents. A purse holds a quarter, a dime and two pennies. What is the total?
    Answer 
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
enum Coin { Penny, Nickel, Dime, Quarter }

impl Coin {
    fn cents(self) -> u32 {
        match self {
            Coin::Penny => 1,
            Coin::Nickel => 5,
            Coin::Dime => 10,
            Coin::Quarter => 25,
        }
    }
}

    [Coin::Quarter, Coin::Dime, Coin::Penny, Coin::Penny].iter().map(|c| c.cents()).sum::<u32>() gives 37. The method takes self by value. That is fine because Coin is Copy.

  2. A payment is a card (with the last four digits), cash, or a bank transfer (with an IBAN). Write the enum and a function describe.
    Answer 
    enum Payment {
    Card { last4: String },
    Cash,
    Transfer { iban: String },
}

fn describe(p: &Payment) -> String {
    match p {
        Payment::Card { last4 } => format!("card ending {last4}"),
        Payment::Cash => "cash".to_string(),
        Payment::Transfer { iban } => format!("transfer from {iban}"),
    }
}

    Cash needs no data, so it has no fields. A card value cannot have an IBAN by accident.

  3. A struct has is_admin: bool and is_guest: bool. What is wrong? Write a better type.
    Answer

    Both flags can be true at once, which makes no sense. Use enum Role { Guest, Member, Admin } and a field role: Role. Now there are exactly three states.

  4. Why does if let Some(n) = name { } followed by println!("{name:?}") fail when name is an Option<String>? Give the fix.
    Answer

    The pattern moves the String out of name. That is a partial move, so name is no longer whole (E0382). Write if let Some(n) = &name. Then n is a &String.

  5. Expert. Write shape(v: &[i32]) -> &'static str with slice patterns. It returns "empty", "one item", "starts with zero", "ends with a negative" or "something else".
    Answer 
    fn shape(v: &[i32]) -> &'static str {
    match v {
        [] => "empty",
        [_] => "one item",
        [0, ..] => "starts with zero",
        [.., x] if *x < 0 => "ends with a negative",
        _ => "something else",
    }
}

    For [0, 1, 2] it gives "starts with zero". For [3, -1] it gives "ends with a negative". The order of arms matters: the first matching arm wins.

  6. Expert. In state.rs, someone adds a new variant Conn::Paused. What does the compiler say, and why might it say nothing?
    Answer

    step ends with the arm (state, _) => state. That arm also catches Paused, so the compiler says nothing. Every event in Paused is silently ignored. Other match blocks without a wildcard would fail with E0004. This is why you should be careful with catch-all arms.

Key takeaways

  • A struct groups named fields. Methods live in impl and take &self, &mut self or self.
  • A newtype like Meters(f64) keeps units and ids apart at no run-time cost.
  • An enum is "one of these", and each variant can carry its own data. Option replaces null.
  • Rust's match must cover every case. Python's match does not check, so add assert_never.
  • if let, let else and while let are short forms for one pattern.
  • Design types so that wrong states cannot be built. Then the compiler guards your rules.
