  • The Rust Programming Language, 6.1: Defining an enum. Enums with data and the Option type.
  • The Rust Programming Language, 19.3: Pattern syntax. Every kind of pattern with examples.
  • The Rust Reference: Patterns. Exact rules for ranges, slices, binding modes and the 2024 edition.
  • Rust Blog: Announcing Rust 1.95.0. If let guards in match arms.
  • Python documentation: dataclasses. frozen, slots, match_args and replace.
  • PEP 636: Structural pattern matching tutorial. How Python's match statement works.

Error handling

Real programs meet bad input, missing files and lost networks. Rust and Python handle these problems in two different ways. Rust returns an error as a normal value. Python throws an exception. This chapter shows both models, from the first unwrap to error types for real libraries.

  • Tell a bug from an expected problem, and choose a panic or a Result.
  • Handle a Result with match, helper methods, unwrap, expect and ?.
  • Build your own error enum with Display, Error and From.
  • Use thiserror in a library and anyhow in an application.
  • Catch, raise and chain exceptions in Python, and compare the two models.

Two kinds of failure: panic and Result

Here are two problems in one program. The first one is expected. The second one is a bug.

fn main() {
    let good = "42".parse::<i32>();     // a Result
    let bad = "4x2".parse::<i32>();     // a Result too
    println!("{good:?}");
    println!("{bad:?}");

    let scores = vec![10, 20, 30];
    let i: usize = "7".parse().unwrap(); // a value from outside
    println!("{}", scores[i]);           // a bug: panic
}
print(int("42"))
try:
    int("4x2")
except ValueError as e:
    print("ValueError:", e)

scores = [10, 20, 30]
print(scores[7])
Ok(42)
Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit })

thread 'main' (115169755) panicked at src/main.rs:9:26:
index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 7
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
42
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '4x2'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/you/main.py", line 8, in <module>
    print(scores[7])
          ~~~~~~^^^
IndexError: list index out of range

Text from a user can be wrong. That is normal, so parse returns a Result. The program goes on and can react. An index past the end is different. It is a bug. Rust stops the program at once. This stop is a panic.

A Result is a normal enum from the standard library. It has two variants.

enum Result<T, E> {
    Ok(T),    // success: holds the value
    Err(E),   // failure: holds the error
}

Python has one tool for both cases: the exception. A bad int() and a bad index both throw one. If nobody catches it, Python prints a traceback and stops.

Which tool for which problem
ProblemKindRustPython
The user types "abc" for an ageExpectedResultValueError
The config file is missingExpectedResultFileNotFoundError
Your code reads index 7 of 3 itemsBugpanicIndexError
A value that "cannot happen" happensBugpanicAssertionError

A panicking Rust program ends with exit code 101. A Python program with an uncaught exception ends with exit code 1. I checked both numbers on this Mac.

You call panic! when the user types a wrong value. Now one bad key press stops a whole server. Bad input is not a bug. Return a Result and let the caller decide.

Working with a Result

This function can fail. The caller must look inside the Result before it gets the number.

use std::num::ParseIntError;

fn parse_age(text: &str) -> Result<u8, ParseIntError> {
    text.trim().parse::<u8>()
}

fn main() {
    for input in ["31", "abc", "300"] {
        match parse_age(input) {
            Ok(age) => println!("{input}: age {age}"),
            Err(e) => println!("{input}: error: {e}"),
        }
    }
    let a = parse_age("x").unwrap_or(0);               // a default value
    let b = parse_age("12").map(|age| age + 1);        // change the Ok value
    let c = parse_age("x").map_err(|e| e.to_string()); // change the Err value
    let d = parse_age("abc").ok();                     // Result to Option
    let e: Result<u8, &str> = None.ok_or("no age");    // Option to Result
    if let Ok(age) = parse_age("40") {
        println!("if let: {age}");
    }
    println!("{a} {b:?} {c:?} {d:?} {e:?}");
}
def parse_age(text: str) -> int:
    age = int(text.strip())
    if not 0 <= age <= 255:
        raise ValueError(f"age out of range: {age}")
    return age

for text in ["31", "abc", "300"]:
    try:
        print(f"{text}: age {parse_age(text)}")
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"{text}: error: {e}")
31: age 31
abc: error: invalid digit found in string
300: error: number too large to fit in target type
if let: 40
0 Ok(13) Err("invalid digit found in string") None Err("no age")
31: age 31
abc: error: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
300: error: age out of range: 300

The return type Result<u8, ParseIntError> tells the full story. Success gives a u8. Failure gives a ParseIntError. The Python signature says only int. You must read the code or the docs to learn about ValueError.

A match handles both variants. When you need only one case, the helper methods are shorter. They are called combinators.

Common Result methods
MethodWhat it doesExample result
unwrap_or(v)Gives v on error0
unwrap_or_else(f)Calls f on error, only thena value from f
unwrap_or_default()Gives the type's default on error0 for numbers
map(f)Changes the Ok valueOk(13)
map_err(f)Changes the Err valueErr("invalid digit...")
and_then(f)Runs another step that can failOk or the first Err
ok()Turns a Result into an OptionNone
ok_or(e)Turns an Option into a ResultErr("no age")

What if you call a function and ignore its Result? The compiler warns you. Result is marked #[must_use].

warning: unused `Result` that must be used
 --> src/main.rs:3:5
  |
3 |     parse("5");
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = note: this `Result` may be an `Err` variant, which should be handled

You write let _ = save_file(); to make the warning go away. Now a failed save is silent. Write let _ = only when you really do not care. Leave a comment that says why.

unwrap and expect

Sometimes you want the value now, and a crash is fine if it is missing. Two methods do this.

use std::env;

fn main() {
    let text = env::var("PORT").unwrap_or_else(|_| "8080".to_string());
    let port: u16 = text
        .parse()
        .expect("PORT should be a whole number from 0 to 65535");
    println!("listening on port {port}");
}
cargo run                 # no PORT set
PORT=abc cargo run        # a bad PORT
listening on port 8080

thread 'main' (115183580) panicked at src/main.rs:7:10:
PORT should be a whole number from 0 to 65535: ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit }
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace

unwrap gives the Ok value or panics. expect does the same, but it adds your message to the panic. Compare the plain unwrap message for the same kind of error.

called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: ParseIntError { kind: PosOverflow }

The expect message tells the reader what went wrong and why you thought it could not. The Rust book suggests a style for it. Say what should be true: "PORT should be a whole number".

When is a panic with unwrap or expect fine?

  • Tests. A failure must fail the test. A panic does exactly that.
  • Quick examples and prototypes. Each unwrap marks a place to fix later.
  • You know more than the compiler. "127.0.0.1".parse::<IpAddr>() is fixed text. It cannot fail. Use expect and say why.
  • A broken promise in your own code. This is an invariant. If it breaks, going on could do harm.

Python has no unwrap. An exception that nobody catches has the same effect. For invariants Python has assert. But python -O removes every assert, so never use it to check user input.

You write .unwrap() on every network call in a web server. One slow partner service now crashes your server many times a day. In code that serves users, return the error with ?. The next section shows how.

The ? operator

A function often calls three steps that can fail. Each step needs the same work: on error, stop and pass the error up. The ? operator does this in one character.

use std::error::Error;
use std::fs;

// Return the number after "port=".
fn read_port(path: &str) -> Result<u16, Box<dyn Error>> {
    let text = fs::read_to_string(path)?;         // io::Error goes up
    let line = text
        .lines()
        .find(|l| l.starts_with("port="))
        .ok_or("no port line")?;                  // &str error goes up
    let port = line["port=".len()..].parse::<u16>()?; // ParseIntError goes up
    Ok(port)
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    println!("port = {}", read_port("app.conf")?);
    println!("port = {}", read_port("missing.conf")?);
    println!("never printed");
    Ok(())
}
def read_port(path: str) -> int:
    with open(path) as f:          # OSError goes up by itself
        for line in f:
            if line.startswith("port="):
                return int(line.removeprefix("port="))  # ValueError goes up
    raise LookupError("no port line")

print("port =", read_port("app.conf"))
print("port =", read_port("missing.conf"))
port = 8080
Error: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }
port = 8080
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/you/main.py", line 9, in <module>
    print("port =", read_port("missing.conf"))
                    ~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/you/main.py", line 2, in read_port
    with open(path) as f:          # OSError goes up by itself
         ~~~~^^^^^^
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'missing.conf'

The file app.conf holds the line port=8080. Passing an error up to the caller is called propagating it. In Python, exceptions propagate by themselves. In Rust, you write ?. Every place that can fail is visible.

Look at the Result

fs::read_to_string(path)? gives a Result<String, io::Error>.

Ok: take the value

It is Ok(text)? Then the whole expression becomes text. The function goes on.

Err: convert the error

It is Err(e)? Then Rust calls From::from(e). This turns e into the function's error type.

Return at once

The function returns Err(converted). The lines below never run.

The long form

match r { Ok(v) => v, Err(e) => return Err(From::from(e)) }. The ? is short for this.

The rules of ?

  • The function must return a Result or an Option.
  • On a Result, the error must convert into the function's error type with From.
  • Box<dyn Error> accepts almost any error. The &str "no port line" converts too.
  • When main returns Err, Rust prints the error with {:?} and exits with code 1.

Box<dyn Error> is a trait object. It means "some error type, decided at run time". The chapter Traits and generics explains dyn.

? also works on Option. None returns early.

fn first_word_len(text: &str) -> Option<usize> {
    let word = text.split_whitespace().next()?; // None if text is empty
    Some(word.len())
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", first_word_len("hello world"));
    println!("{:?}", first_word_len("   "));
}
Some(5)
None

Two errors are very common. First, ? in a main that returns nothing.

error[E0277]: the `?` operator can only be used in a function that returns `Result` or `Option` (or another type that implements `FromResidual`)
 --> src/main.rs:4:46
  |
3 | fn main() {
  | --------- this function should return `Result` or `Option` to accept `?`
4 |     let text = fs::read_to_string("app.conf")?;
  |                                              ^ cannot use the `?` operator in a function that returns `()`

Second, ? on an Option inside a function that returns a Result. The compiler even gives the fix.

error[E0277]: the `?` operator can only be used on `Result`s, not `Option`s, in a function that returns `Result`
 --> src/main.rs:2:22
  |
1 | fn first(v: &[i32]) -> Result<i32, String> {
  | ------------------------------------------ this function returns a `Result`
2 |     let x = v.first()?;
  |                      ^ use `.ok_or(...)?` to provide an error compatible with `Result<i32, String>`

You forget the final Ok(...). A function that returns Result<u16, E> must end with Ok(port), not port. The compiler says expected `Result<u16, ...>`, found `u16`. Wrap the last value in Ok.

Your own error type

Box<dyn Error> is easy. But the caller cannot see which error happened. An enum fixes this. Each variant is one kind of failure.

use std::error::Error;
use std::fmt;
use std::io;
use std::num::ParseIntError;

#[derive(Debug)]
enum ConfigError {
    Io(io::Error),               // the file could not be read
    Missing(&'static str),       // a key is not in the file
    BadPort(ParseIntError),      // the port is not a number
}

impl fmt::Display for ConfigError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            ConfigError::Io(_) => write!(f, "cannot read the config file"),
            ConfigError::Missing(key) => write!(f, "the key `{key}` is missing"),
            ConfigError::BadPort(_) => write!(f, "the port is not a valid number"),
        }
    }
}

impl Error for ConfigError {
    fn source(&self) -> Option<&(dyn Error + 'static)> {
        match self {
            ConfigError::Io(e) => Some(e),      // the cause below this error
            ConfigError::BadPort(e) => Some(e),
            ConfigError::Missing(_) => None,
        }
    }
}

A good error type has three parts.

  1. Debug is for developers. #[derive(Debug)] writes it for you.
  2. Display is for users. It is one short line, with no capital letter at the start and no full stop at the end.
  3. The Error trait marks the type as an error. Its source method returns the lower error that caused this one, the source.

Now add From. Then ? converts the low errors into ConfigError by itself.

impl From<io::Error> for ConfigError {
    fn from(e: io::Error) -> Self { ConfigError::Io(e) }
}
impl From<ParseIntError> for ConfigError {
    fn from(e: ParseIntError) -> Self { ConfigError::BadPort(e) }
}

fn read_port(path: &str) -> Result<u16, ConfigError> {
    let text = std::fs::read_to_string(path)?;          // uses From<io::Error>
    let line = text.lines().find(|l| l.starts_with("port="))
        .ok_or(ConfigError::Missing("port"))?;
    Ok(line["port=".len()..].parse::<u16>()?)           // uses From<ParseIntError>
}

fn main() {
    for path in ["app.conf", "missing.conf", "noport.conf", "badport.conf"] {
        match read_port(path) {
            Ok(port) => println!("{path}: port {port}"),
            Err(ConfigError::Missing(key)) => println!("{path}: using default for {key}"),
            Err(e) => {
                print!("{path}: {e}");
                if let Some(cause) = e.source() { print!(" (cause: {cause})"); }
                println!();
            }
        }
    }
}
app.conf: port 8080
missing.conf: cannot read the config file (cause: No such file or directory (os error 2))
noport.conf: using default for port
badport.conf: the port is not a valid number (cause: invalid digit found in string)

Look at the match in main. The caller reacts to Missing in a special way and uses a default. A string error could not do this safely. The errors also form a chain: ConfigError on top, the io::Error below it.

You return Result<T, String> from a library. The caller can only compare text, and text changes. Use an enum. Then a caller can match on ConfigError::Missing, and the compiler checks every case.

thiserror and anyhow

The enum above needs about 40 lines of boilerplate. Two popular crates remove most of it. The versions below were the newest on crates.io on 2026-11-15.

[dependencies]
anyhow = "1.0.104"
thiserror = "2.0.21"

thiserror: error types for libraries

use std::{fs, io, num::ParseIntError};
use thiserror::Error;

#[derive(Debug, Error)]
pub enum ConfigError {
    #[error("cannot read the config file")]
    Io(#[from] io::Error),                  // From and source, made for you
    #[error("the key `{0}` is missing")]
    Missing(&'static str),
    #[error("the port `{text}` is not a valid number")]
    BadPort { text: String, source: ParseIntError }, // a field named source is the cause
}

pub fn read_port(path: &str) -> Result<u16, ConfigError> {
    let text = fs::read_to_string(path)?;
    let line = text.lines().find(|l| l.starts_with("port="))
        .ok_or(ConfigError::Missing("port"))?;
    let raw = &line["port=".len()..];
    raw.parse::<u16>().map_err(|source| ConfigError::BadPort {
        text: raw.to_string(),
        source,
    })
}

thiserror is a derive macro. It writes the same Display, Error and From code that you wrote by hand. Your public type stays a normal enum.

  • #[error("...")] makes the Display text. {0} and {text} use the fields.
  • #[from] makes a From impl and marks the field as the source.
  • A field named source, or marked #[source], becomes the source.
  • #[error(transparent)] passes the message and source of the inner error through unchanged.

anyhow: one easy error type for applications

mod config;

use anyhow::{Context, Result, bail, ensure};

fn start(path: &str) -> Result<u16> {
    let port = config::read_port(path)
        .with_context(|| format!("loading settings from {path}"))?;
    ensure!(port >= 1024, "port {port} needs admin rights");
    if port == 9999 {
        bail!("port 9999 is reserved for tests");
    }
    Ok(port)
}

fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let port = start("app.conf")?;
    println!("started on {port}");
    if let Err(e) = start("badport.conf") {
        println!("short: {e}");          // only the top message
        println!("chain: {e:#}");        // all messages on one line
        let inner = e.downcast_ref::<config::ConfigError>();
        println!("is a ConfigError? {}", inner.is_some());
    }
    start("missing.conf")?;              // main prints the full report
    Ok(())
}
started on 8080
short: loading settings from badport.conf
chain: loading settings from badport.conf: the port `80a` is not a valid number: invalid digit found in string
is a ConfigError? true
Error: loading settings from missing.conf

Caused by:
    0: cannot read the config file
    1: No such file or directory (os error 2)

anyhow::Result<T> is short for Result<T, anyhow::Error>. anyhow::Error holds any error type. So ? works on almost everything.

  • .context("...") and .with_context(|| ...) add a new message on top. This message is the context.
  • bail!("...") returns a new error at once. ensure!(cond, "...") returns one when the condition is false.
  • {e} shows the top message. {e:#} shows the whole chain on one line.
  • downcast_ref::<T>() looks for the original error type inside. Use it when you must react to one case.
  • Set RUST_BACKTRACE=1 or RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1 to get a backtrace with the error.
thiserror or anyhow?
Questionthiserroranyhow
Where?Libraries and modules with a public APIApplications, scripts, main
What do callers get?A typed enum they can matchOne error type with a message chain
Add context?New variants or fields.context() on any line
Can they work together?Yes. The library uses thiserror. The application wraps it with anyhow.

You write .context(format!("loading {path}")). The format! runs every time, even on success. Use .with_context(|| format!(...)). The closure runs only when there is an error.

Both crates come from the same author, David Tolnay. thiserror writes only normal Rust code, so it does not appear in your public API. You can switch between hand-written impls and thiserror without breaking callers. anyhow should stay inside applications.

Python exceptions: try, raise, finally

Here is the same config reader in Python. It has its own exception classes and every part of try.

class ConfigError(Exception):
    """The base class for all config problems."""

class MissingKey(ConfigError):
    def __init__(self, key: str) -> None:
        super().__init__(f"the key {key!r} is missing")
        self.key = key                      # extra data for the caller

def read_port(path: str) -> int:
    try:
        with open(path) as f:               # with closes the file for you
            text = f.read()
    except OSError as e:
        raise ConfigError(f"cannot read {path}") from e   # keep the cause
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if line.startswith("port="):
            return int(line.removeprefix("port="))
    raise MissingKey("port")

for path in ["app.conf", "noport.conf", "missing.conf"]:
    try:
        port = read_port(path)
    except MissingKey as e:                 # the most specific class first
        print(f"{path}: default for {e.key}")
    except ConfigError as e:
        print(f"{path}: {e} (cause: {e.__cause__!r})")
    else:
        print(f"{path}: port {port}")       # runs only with no exception
    finally:
        print("  checked", path)            # always runs
app.conf: port 8080
  checked app.conf
noport.conf: default for port
  checked noport.conf
missing.conf: cannot read missing.conf (cause: FileNotFoundError(2, 'No such file or directory'))
  checked missing.conf
  • try holds the code that can fail.
  • except Type as e is a handler. It catches that class and all its subclasses. Python checks the handlers from top to bottom.
  • else runs only when try raised nothing. Keep normal code here, not inside try.
  • finally always runs: after success, after an error, even after return.
  • raise X from e throws a new exception and stores e as its __cause__. This is the Python twin of source().
  • with closes the file even when an exception flies. Rust does this with Drop.

Your exception classes inherit from Exception. Their names end in Error by custom. A base class like ConfigError lets callers catch your whole family with one handler. This is the Python twin of a Rust error enum.

Notes, groups and Python 3.14

def load(path: str) -> int:
    try:
        return int("80a")
    except ValueError as e:
        e.add_note(f"while reading {path}")   # extra context
        raise                                 # the same exception goes up

def check_all() -> None:
    problems = [ValueError("bad port"), KeyError("name"), ValueError("bad size")]
    raise ExceptionGroup("config has 3 problems", problems)

try:
    check_all()
except* ValueError as group:
    print("value errors:", [str(e) for e in group.exceptions])
except* KeyError as group:
    print("key errors:", len(group.exceptions))

try:
    int("x")
except ValueError, TypeError:   # 3.14: no brackets without "as"
    print("caught")

load("badport.conf")
value errors: ['bad port', 'bad size']
key errors: 1
caught
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/you/more.py", line 24, in <module>
    load("badport.conf")
    ~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/you/more.py", line 3, in load
    return int("80a")
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '80a'
while reading badport.conf
  • add_note adds a line of context. It is like anyhow's .context(). A bare raise throws the same exception again.
  • An ExceptionGroup holds many exceptions at once. except* takes out the ones of one class. This came in Python 3.11.
  • Since Python 3.14, except A, B: works without brackets. With as e you still need except (A, B) as e:.

You write except Exception: pass. Now every bug is silent, even a typo in a name. Catch the narrowest class you can handle. Let the rest go up. Also, never return inside finally. It throws away the exception. Python 3.14 warns: SyntaxWarning: 'return' in a 'finally' block.

Errors as values and exceptions compared

Both models solve the same problem. They make different things easy.

Rust Result and Python exceptions
QuestionRust: errors as valuesPython: exceptions
Can I see that a call can fail?Yes. It is in the return type.No. Read the docs or the code.
How does an error go up?You write ? at each stepBy itself, through every call
Can I forget to handle it?The compiler warns youYes, until it happens at run time
Context and causesource(), .context()raise ... from, add_note
Clean-upDrop runs on every pathfinally and with
Bugspanican exception too
Cost on the happy pathOne small check per ?Almost zero since Python 3.11

Python's style has a name: EAFP. You try the action and catch the exception. The other style is LBYL. You check first, then act. Python code usually prefers EAFP. Rust makes you look at every Result, but ? keeps it short.

For experts: panics in real systems

A panic in a thread does not stop the whole program. join returns it as an Err.

use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let worker = thread::spawn(|| {
        let v: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
        v[0]                      // panics inside the thread
    });
    match worker.join() {         // the panic becomes an Err here
        Ok(n) => println!("result {n}"),
        Err(_) => println!("the worker panicked, main goes on"),
    }
}
thread '<unnamed>' (115241394) panicked at src/main.rs:6:10:
index out of bounds: the len is 0 but the index is 0
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
the worker panicked, main goes on
  • By default a panic unwinds. Each value on the way is cleaned up with Drop.
  • In Cargo.toml, panic = "abort" under [profile.release] stops the process at once. The binary gets smaller, but threads can no longer catch panics.
  • std::panic::catch_unwind exists. It is for borders, for example a C library calling Rust. It is not a try block for normal errors.
  • Errors that cross threads or async tasks need Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>. anyhow::Error is already Send and Sync.
  • A library enum can carry #[non_exhaustive]. Then you may add variants later without a breaking change. Callers must write a _ arm.

A common question: "When do you panic and when do you return a Result?" A good answer: return a Result when the caller can do something useful, like bad input or a missing file. Panic when your own invariant is broken and going on is unsafe. Mention tests and expect with a "should" message.

You use the type system too little. A function checks 1 <= n <= 100 on every call. Make a type Percent whose constructor returns Result. After that one check, every Percent is valid. The chapter API design and idioms calls this the newtype pattern.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for error handling
PatternPurposeModelNote
fn f() -> Result<T, E>Say that a function can failfn parse_age(s: &str) -> Result<u8, ParseIntError>Do not panic on bad input.
match r { Ok(v) => .., Err(e) => .. }Handle both casesmatch parse_age(s) { ... }The compiler checks that both arms exist.
r.unwrap_or(default)Use a default on errorparse_age(s).unwrap_or(0)Use unwrap_or_else when the default costs work.
r.expect("X should ...")Panic with a clear reason.expect("PORT should be a number")Only for tests, prototypes and true invariants.
let v = step()?;Pass the error uplet text = fs::read_to_string(p)?;The function must return Result or Option.
opt.ok_or(err)?Use ? on an Option in a Result function.ok_or(ConfigError::Missing("port"))?ok_or_else builds the error lazily.
fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>Use ? in mainOk(()) at the endAn Err gives exit code 1.
impl From<Low> for MyErrorLet ? convert errorsimpl From<io::Error> for ConfigErrorthiserror's #[from] writes it.
#[derive(Error)] #[error("..")]A typed error enum for a library#[error("the key `{0}` is missing")]Lower case, no full stop at the end.

Practice

A user types "abc" where your program wants a number. What should a Rust function do?

  • Call panic! with a clear message.
  • Return an Err so the caller can react.
  • Return 0 and say nothing.

Bad input is expected, not a bug. A Result lets the caller show a message or use a default.

What does ? do with an Err(e)?

  • It panics with the error.
  • It ignores the error and goes on.
  • It converts e with From and returns it at once.

? is short for a match that returns Err(From::from(e)).

Which crate fits a public library that needs a typed error enum?

  • thiserror
  • anyhow
  • Neither. Use String.

thiserror writes Display, Error and From for your own enum. Callers can match on it.

In Python, when does the else block of a try run?

  • Always.
  • Only when the try block raised no exception.
  • Only when an exception was caught.

finally always runs. else runs only after success.

A panicking Rust program ends with exit code ?.

The Error trait method that returns the lower cause is e.<span class="blank" data-answer="source|source()">?</span>.

In Python, raise ConfigError("x") from e stores e in the attribute ?.

To turn an Option into a Result, call .<span class="blank" data-answer="ok_or|ok_or_else">?</span>(err).

  1. Rewrite let n = s.parse::<i32>().unwrap(); so it gives -1 on error.
    Answer

    let n = s.parse::<i32>().unwrap_or(-1);

  2. Why does fn main() { let t = std::fs::read_to_string("a.txt")?; } not compile? Give the fix.
    Answer

    main returns (), so ? has nowhere to send the error. Write fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> and end with Ok(()).

  3. Write a function fn double(s: &str) -> Result<i64, std::num::ParseIntError> that parses s and returns twice the number. Use ?.
    Answer

    fn double(s: &str) -> Result<i64, std::num::ParseIntError> { let n: i64 = s.trim().parse()?; Ok(n * 2) }

  4. Your function calls fs::read_to_string and str::parse::<u16>. It returns Result<u16, AppError>. What must exist so that ? works on both calls?
    Answer

    impl From<std::io::Error> for AppError and impl From<std::num::ParseIntError> for AppError. With thiserror, add a variant with #[from] for each.

  5. Write a Python function to_port(text) that raises ValueError("port out of range") for numbers above 65535. Keep the first error as the cause when int() fails.
    Answer

    def to_port(text): then try: n = int(text), except ValueError as e: raise ValueError(f"not a port: {text!r}") from e, then if n > 65535: raise ValueError("port out of range") and return n.

  6. Hard: a team uses anyhow::Result in the public API of its library. Users complain. What is the problem, and what should the team do?
    Answer

    Users cannot match on an anyhow::Error. They must guess with downcast_ref or compare text. The library should define its own error enum with thiserror. Users can then match on variants. Applications can still wrap it with anyhow and add context.

  7. Hard: why is return inside finally dangerous in Python? What does Python 3.14 do about it?
    Answer

    The return in finally wins over everything. An exception from try is thrown away without a word. Python 3.14 shows a SyntaxWarning for return, break or continue that leaves a finally block (PEP 765).

Key takeaways

  • Use a Result for expected problems. Use a panic only for bugs and broken invariants.
  • ? returns the error early and converts it with From. The function must return Result or Option.
  • unwrap and expect panic on error. Keep them for tests, prototypes and true invariants.
  • A good error type has Debug, Display, Error with source, and From impls.
  • Use thiserror in libraries and anyhow in applications. They work well together.
  • Python exceptions propagate by themselves. Use specific except classes, raise ... from, finally and with.
  • Rust shows every failure in the type. Python hides it, but needs less code.

Sources

  • The Rust Programming Language: Error Handling. panic, Result, the ? operator and when to panic.
  • Rust standard library: the Error trait. Display, Debug and the source method.
  • thiserror on docs.rs. The error, from, source and transparent attributes.
  • anyhow on docs.rs. Result, context, bail, downcasting and backtraces.

  • What's New in Python 3.14. except without brackets and the warning for return in finally.

Ownership and borrowing

Rust has no garbage collector. You also never free memory by hand. Rust uses ownership: a few rules that the compiler checks before the program runs.

  • Explain where a value lives: on the stack or on the heap.
  • Predict if a line moves, copies or clones a value.
  • Use & and &mut and follow the two borrow rules.
  • Read the common borrow checker errors and fix them.
  • Compare Rust ownership with Python references and garbage collection.

Stack and heap: where values live

Every value needs a place in memory. Rust uses two places. Look at these two lines.

let n = 5;                     // a number with a fixed size
let s = String::from("hello"); // text that can grow

The number n lives on the stack. The text of s lives on the heap. The variable s itself is a small handle on the stack.

The handle has three parts. A pointer says where the text is. The length says how many bytes are in use. The capacity says how many bytes are reserved.

You can measure the stack part of a type. This program prints sizes in bytes.

use std::mem::size_of;

fn main() {
    println!("i32       {}", size_of::<i32>());
    println!("String    {}", size_of::<String>());
    println!("Vec<i32>  {}", size_of::<Vec<i32>>());
    println!("&String   {}", size_of::<&String>());
    println!("&str      {}", size_of::<&str>());
    println!("Box<i32>  {}", size_of::<Box<i32>>());
}
i32       4
String    24
Vec<i32>  24
&String   8
&str      16
Box<i32>  8

These numbers come from a 64-bit machine. There a String handle is always 24 bytes. The text can be five bytes or five million bytes. The handle does not grow.

Stack and heap side by side
QuestionStackHeap
Size of the dataFixed and known before the program runsCan change while the program runs
Cost to get spaceAlmost zeroHigher. The allocator must find a free block.
When the space is freedWhen the function returnsWhen the owner goes away
Examplesi32, bool, (f64, f64), [u8; 4]The text of a String, the items of a Vec

The allocator manages the heap. Asking it for memory takes time. So Rust keeps small fixed values on the stack.

People say "a String is on the heap". Only the text is there. The handle sits on the stack, or inside the value that owns it.

The three ownership rules

Heap memory must be freed exactly one time. Rust gives this job to an owner. This program shows the moment when Rust frees a value.

struct Noisy(&'static str);

impl Drop for Noisy {
    // Rust calls this when the owner goes away.
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        println!("drop {}", self.0);
    }
}

fn main() {
    let _a = Noisy("a");
    {
        let _b = Noisy("b");
        println!("inner scope ends");
    } // _b is dropped here
    let _c = Noisy("c");
    println!("main ends");
} // _c is dropped, then _a
inner scope ends
drop b
main ends
drop c
drop a

A scope is a block between { and }. When a scope ends, Rust cleans up each owner in it. To drop a value means to clean it up and free it. You did not write any call to drop. The compiler added the calls for you.

Rust checks three rules for every value.

  1. Every value has an owner.
  2. A value has exactly one owner at a time.
  3. When the owner leaves its scope, Rust drops the value.

Rule 2 stops a double free. One owner means one clean-up. Rule 3 stops leaks. You cannot forget to free, because you never free by hand.

More about drop order (expert)

Rust drops local variables in reverse order. The newest variable goes first. In the program above _c is dropped before _a.

The fields of a struct are dropped in the order you wrote them. If you assign a new value to a variable, Rust drops the old value at once. You can also drop early with drop(x).

Move, Copy and Clone

What happens when you assign one variable to another? It depends on the type. Start with a String.

fn main() {
    let s1 = String::from("hello");
    let s2 = s1; // the String moves to s2
    println!("{s1} {s2}");
}
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s1`
 --> move_err.rs:4:16
  |
2 |     let s1 = String::from("hello");
  |         -- move occurs because `s1` has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
3 |     let s2 = s1; // the String moves to s2
  |              -- value moved here
4 |     println!("{s1} {s2}");
  |                ^^ value borrowed here after move

The line let s2 = s1; is a move. Rust copies the 24-byte handle into s2. It does not copy the text. Then it marks s1 as dead.

Why is s1 dead? Two live handles would mean two owners. Both would free the same text. That is a double free. So Rust allows only one of them.

Now the three cases. The same = sign can do three different things.

What an assignment does
You writeType of the valueWhat happensOld name after it
let b = a;String, Vec, Box, most structsMove. Only the handle is copied.Dead
let b = a;A Copy type: integers, floats, bool, charCopy. The bits are copied.Still usable
let b = a.clone();Any Clone typeClone. Heap data is copied too.Still usable
 
fn main() {
    let a = 5;
    let b = a; // i32 is Copy. Both names are valid.

    let s1 = String::from("hi");
    let s2 = s1.clone(); // a second String on the heap

    println!("{a} {b} {s1} {s2}");
}
5 5 hi hi

Copy and Clone are traits. A type is Copy when a plain copy of its bits is safe. That is true for numbers, bool, char and shared references. It is also true for tuples and arrays of such types. A type that owns heap data can never be Copy.

You can make your own small types Copy. All fields must be Copy too.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}

fn main() {
    let p = Point { x: 1, y: 2 };
    let q = p; // a copy, because Point is Copy
    println!("{p:?} {q:?} {}", p.x + q.y);
}
Point { x: 1, y: 2 } Point { x: 1, y: 2 } 3

Moves into and out of functions

A function call follows the same rules. Passing a value is like an assignment to the parameter.

fn consume(s: String) -> usize {
    s.len()
} // s is dropped here

fn add_mark(mut s: String) -> String {
    s.push('!');
    s // ownership moves out to the caller
}

fn main() {
    let a = String::from("abc");
    let n = consume(a); // a moves into the function
    // println!("{a}"); // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value

    let b = add_mark(String::from("hey"));
    println!("{n} {b}");
}
3 hey!

Do not add .clone() to every line that fails. Each clone of a String asks the allocator for memory. First ask one question: can I lend the value instead?

Partial moves (expert)

You can move one field out of a struct. The other fields stay usable. The struct as a whole is not usable after that.

struct User {
    name: String,
    age: u32,
}

fn main() {
    let u = User { name: String::from("Ann"), age: 30 };
    let name = u.name; // only the field `name` moves out
    println!("{name} is {}", u.age); // `age` is still usable
}
Ann is 30

A common question: what is the difference between Copy and Clone? Copy happens without any call and only copies bits. Clone needs a call to .clone() and can run any code.

Borrowing: shared and mutable references

Often a function only needs to look at a value. It should not take the value away. Then you lend the value.

// A shared borrow: the function may read, not change.
fn count_a(text: &str) -> usize {
    text.chars().filter(|c| *c == 'a').count()
}

// A mutable borrow: the function may change the value.
fn add_mark(text: &mut String) {
    text.push('!');
}

fn main() {
    let mut s = String::from("banana");
    let n = count_a(&s); // lend s for reading
    add_mark(&mut s); // lend s for writing
    println!("{s} has {n} a");
} // s is dropped here, one time
banana! has 3 a

A reference is a pointer that is always valid. To borrow means to make a reference. The owner keeps the value. The reference only visits it.

The two kinds of reference
Question&T (shared)&mut T (mutable)
Can it read?YesYes
Can it write?NoYes
How many at the same time?As many as you wantOnly one, and no shared ones
Is it Copy?YesNo

Rust checks two rules for every reference.

  1. At one moment a value has many shared references or one mutable reference. Never both.
  2. A reference never lives longer than the value it points to.

The part of the compiler that checks these rules is the borrow checker. It works before the program runs. It costs nothing at run time.

Do not keep a reference around "for later". A long borrow blocks every change of the owner. Borrow late and finish early.

A borrow ends at its last use

This program has shared and mutable borrows of the same value. It still compiles.

fn main() {
    let mut s = String::from("hello");

    let r1 = &s;
    let r2 = &s;
    println!("{r1} {r2}"); // last use of r1 and r2

    let r3 = &mut s; // fine: the shared borrows are finished
    r3.push_str(" world");
    println!("{r3}");
}
hello hello
hello world

A borrow does not last until the closing }. It lasts until the last line that uses the reference. The Rust team calls this non-lexical lifetimes. It came with the 2018 edition in Rust 1.31. Since Rust 1.63 all editions use it.

Why the rules exist

Now break rule 1 and see what the compiler protects you from.

fn main() {
    let mut scores = vec![10, 20, 30];
    let first = &scores[0]; // shared borrow starts
    scores.push(40); // needs a mutable borrow
    println!("{first}"); // shared borrow is still in use
}
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `scores` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
 --> e0502.rs:4:5
  |
3 |     let first = &scores[0]; // shared borrow starts
  |                  ------ immutable borrow occurs here
4 |     scores.push(40); // needs a mutable borrow
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ mutable borrow occurs here
5 |     println!("{first}"); // shared borrow is still in use
  |                ----- immutable borrow later used here

The vector is full. So push must move all items to a bigger block. The old block is freed. Then first would point to freed memory. That is a dangling reference. In C or C++ this bug compiles and breaks at run time. In Rust it does not compile.

  1. Find the line where the first borrow starts. Here it is line 3.
  2. Find the line that needs a second borrow. Here it is line 4.
  3. Find the line that uses the first borrow later. Here it is line 5.
  4. Fix it: finish step 3 before step 2, or do not keep the first borrow.
Why do threads need the same rule? (expert)

A data race needs three things. Two pointers reach the same data at the same time. At least one of them writes. Nothing puts the two in order. Rule 1 makes the first two things impossible together. So safe Rust has no data races. See Threads and shared state.

Why does v.push(v.len()) compile? (expert)

This line reads v and changes v. Rust allows it with two-phase borrows. The mutable borrow is first only reserved. It acts like a shared borrow while the arguments are computed. It becomes a real mutable borrow when push starts. This works only for borrows that Rust adds for you, like the one in a method call.

Why can I use a &mut again after a call? (expert)

A &mut reference is not Copy. But you can pass r to a function two times. Rust lends it again for each call. This is a reborrow. The first loan ends when the call returns.

fn add_mark(s: &mut String) {
    s.push('!');
}

fn main() {
    let mut text = String::from("hi");
    let r = &mut text;
    add_mark(r); // Rust lends r again for this call
    add_mark(r); // so r still works here
    println!("{r}");
}
hi!!

Slices: borrowing a part

A reference can also point to a part of a value. That is a slice.

// Return the part of the text before the first space.
fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str {
    match text.find(' ') {
        Some(i) => &text[..i], // a slice of the same bytes
        None => text,
    }
}

fn main() {
    let sentence = String::from("borrow checker");
    let word = first_word(&sentence);
    println!("{word}");

    let nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];
    let middle = &nums[1..4]; // items 1, 2 and 3
    println!("{middle:?} has {} items", middle.len());

    let mut data = [1, 2, 3, 4];
    // Two mutable slices. They do not overlap.
    let (left, right) = data.split_at_mut(2);
    left[0] = 10;
    right[0] = 30;
    println!("{data:?}");
}
borrow
[20, 30, 40] has 3 items
[10, 2, 30, 4]

A slice of a list has the type &[T]. A slice of text has the type &str. Both are 16 bytes on a 64-bit machine: one pointer and one length.

  • Use &str for a text parameter, not &String. Use &[T], not &Vec<T>. Then the function accepts more kinds of input.
  • A slice borrows the whole owner. While word is in use, you cannot change sentence.
  • A range outside the data stops the program with a panic. This check happens at run time.
  • Text ranges count bytes, not letters. Read Strings and text before you slice text with other alphabets.

Common borrow checker errors and their fixes

You will see the same few errors again and again. Each one has a code. Run rustc --explain E0382 to read a long explanation of a code.

The errors you meet most
CodeThe compiler saysWhat you didUsual fix
E0382borrow of moved valueYou used a name after its value moved.Lend with &. Or clone. Or return the value.
E0499cannot borrow as mutable more than once at a timeTwo &mut are alive together.Finish with the first one. Or split the data.
E0502cannot borrow as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutableYou write while a & is still in use.Change the order. Or copy the value out.
E0505cannot move out because it is borrowedYou move the owner while a borrow lives.Use the borrow first. Move after that.
E0507cannot move out of index of Vec<String>You take a value from behind a reference.Borrow it, clone it, or use std::mem::take.
E0596cannot borrow as mutable, as it is not declared as mutableThe owner has no mut.Write let mut.
E0597does not live long enoughThe owner is dropped while a borrow is in use.Declare the owner in the outer scope.
E0515cannot return reference to local variableThe function returns a dangling reference.Return the owned value.

The last two errors are about how long values live. The chapter Lifetimes explains them in depth.

The tree names Rc. It lets several owners share one value. The chapter Smart pointers and interior mutability explains it.

Worked example: change a list inside its own loop

You want to add every even number one more time. The first try loops over the list and pushes into it.

fn main() {
    let mut nums = vec![1, 2, 3, 4];
    for n in &nums {
        if n % 2 == 0 {
            nums.push(*n);
        }
    }
    println!("{nums:?}");
}
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `nums` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
 --> iter_mut_err.rs:5:13
  |
3 |       for n in &nums {
  |       -        -----
  |       |        |
  |       |        immutable borrow occurs here
  |  _____|        immutable borrow later used here
  | |
4 | |         if n % 2 == 0 {
5 | |             nums.push(*n);
  | |             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ mutable borrow occurs here
6 | |         }
7 | |     }
  | |_____- this for loop borrows `nums` immutably, preventing mutation within its body
  |
  = help: consider using an index-based loop instead, or collecting modifications into a separate collection

The loop borrows nums for all its rounds. A push inside the loop needs a mutable borrow. The fixes below never hold two borrows at once.

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    // Fix 1: copy the small value out. No borrow stays alive.
    let mut scores = vec![10, 20, 30];
    let first = scores[0]; // i32 is Copy
    scores.push(40);
    println!("{first} {scores:?}");

    // Fix 2: do not change a list inside its own loop.
    let mut nums = vec![2, 4, 6, 7];
    nums.retain(|n| n % 2 != 0); // keep only the odd numbers
    println!("{nums:?}");

    // Fix 3: take the value out and leave an empty one.
    let mut names = vec![String::from("Ann"), String::from("Bo")];
    let first_name = std::mem::take(&mut names[0]);
    println!("{first_name} {names:?}");

    // Fix 4: one lookup with the entry API.
    let mut hits: HashMap<&str, u32> = HashMap::new();
    *hits.entry("home").or_insert(0) += 1;
    *hits.entry("home").or_insert(0) += 1;
    println!("{hits:?}");
}
10 [10, 20, 30, 40]
[7]
Ann ["", "Bo"]
{"home": 2}
Fields and methods (expert)

Inside one function the checker looks at each field alone. You can read self.hits and change self.total together. A method call is different. A call like self.bump() borrows all of self. So it clashes with a loop over self.hits.

struct Counter {
    hits: Vec<u32>,
    total: u32,
}

impl Counter {
    fn run(&mut self) {
        for h in &self.hits {
            self.total += h; // a different field: allowed
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut c = Counter { hits: vec![1, 2], total: 0 };
    c.run();
    println!("{}", c.total);
}
3

Sometimes safe code is rejected. One known case: return a borrow in one branch, then change the owner in the other branch. Rust 1.99 rejects it with E0502. In August 2026 the Rust team turned on a new checker, Polonius alpha, in the nightly compiler. It accepts this case. Check the Rust blog: this can change soon.

How Python does it

Python has no owners. A Python variable is a name that refers to an object. An assignment adds a second name for the same object.

Compare the same idea in both languages. Rust moves the list. Python shares it.

fn main() {
    let a = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let mut b = a; // move: only b owns the list now
    b.push(4);
    // println!("{a:?}"); // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `a`
    println!("{b:?}");
}
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a  # no move and no copy: two names, one list
b.append(4)
# Both names still work. They show the same list.
print(a)
[1, 2, 3, 4]

In Python the change through b is visible through a. Two names for one object are called an alias. Aliases are normal in Python. A function argument is an alias too. For a real copy you call a.copy() or copy.deepcopy(a).

Who frees the memory?

CPython keeps a reference count in every object. A new name adds one. A removed name takes one away. At zero, CPython frees the object at once. Other Python programs may free it later.

import sys

a = [1, 2, 3]
print(sys.getrefcount(a))  # one name, plus the call itself
b = a
print(sys.getrefcount(a))  # two names, plus the call itself
2
3

The next pair shows the moment of clean-up in both languages. Rust decides it at compile time. Python counts at run time.

struct Noisy(&'static str);

impl Drop for Noisy {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        println!("free {}", self.0);
    }
}

fn main() {
    let a = Noisy("a");
    let b = a; // move: b is the one owner
    println!("still alive");
    drop(b); // free the value now
    println!("end");
}
class Noisy:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def __del__(self):  # runs when the object is freed
        print("free", self.name)


a = Noisy("a")
b = a  # two names, one object
del a  # one name is gone, the object stays
print("still alive")
del b  # no name is left: CPython frees it now
print("end")
still alive
free a
end

Counting has one weak point. Two objects can point to each other. Then their counts never reach zero. This is a reference cycle. A second tool, the cycle collector, finds such groups later. You reach it through the gc module. Its inner design changes between Python versions. The chapter Performance and how CPython works has the details.

The bug that Rust refuses

Python lets you change a list inside its own loop. The program runs. The result is wrong.

nums = [2, 4, 6, 7]
for n in nums:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        nums.remove(n)  # changes the list during its own loop
print(nums)  # we wanted [7]
[4, 7]

The loop skips the number 4. Each remove shifts the items to the left, and the loop steps over one. Rust rejects the same idea with E0502. The correct way looks similar in both languages.

fn main() {
    let mut nums = vec![2, 4, 6, 7];
    // Keep the items for which the test is true.
    nums.retain(|n| n % 2 != 0);
    println!("{nums:?}");
}
nums = [2, 4, 6, 7]
# Build a new list. Do not change the old one in a loop.
nums = [n for n in nums if n % 2 != 0]
print(nums)
[7]
Rust and Python side by side
QuestionRustPython (CPython)
What is a variable?The owner of a valueA name that refers to an object
What does b = a do with a list?It moves the list. a is dead.It adds a second name. Both work.
Who frees memory?The compiler adds the clean-up code.The reference count and the cycle collector.
When are the rules checked?Before the program runsThere are no such rules.
Cost at run timeNone for the rulesCount updates and collector runs
Two names that can both writeNot allowedAllowed. You must be careful.

Python says: share everything, and I clean up later. Rust says: one owner, clear loans, and I check it before the program starts.

The life of one value

These slides follow one String from start to end. Each step uses one idea from this chapter.

Create

let mut s = String::from("hi");

The allocator gives a block on the heap. The variable s is the owner.

Lend for reading

let n = s.len();

The method takes &s. Many readers are fine. The owner does not change.

Lend for writing

s.push('!');

The method takes &mut s. No other borrow may be alive at this moment.

Move

let t = s;

The handle is copied to t. The name s is dead from now on.

Clone

let u = t.clone();

A second block appears on the heap. Now there are two values with two owners.

Drop

} // end of scope

Rust drops u and then t. Each block is freed exactly one time.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for ownership and borrowing
PatternPurposeModelNote
fn f(x: &T)Read a value without taking itfn total(v: &[i32]) -> i32Prefer &str and &[T] as parameter types.
fn f(x: &mut T)Change the value of the callerfn add_mark(s: &mut String)The caller needs let mut and writes &mut s.
fn f(x: T)Take the value for goodfn send(msg: String)The caller cannot use the value after the call.
fn f() -> TGive a new value to the callerfn make() -> StringNever return a reference to a local variable.
let b = a.clone();Get a second, independent valuelet backup = names.clone();It allocates. Try a borrow first.
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]Let a small type copy itselfstruct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }Every field must be Copy.
&x[a..b]Borrow a part&nums[1..4]A range outside the data panics at run time.
Copy the value outEnd a borrow earlylet first = scores[0];Works only for Copy types.
v.retain(|x| test)Remove items while you visit themnums.retain(|n| n % 2 != 0);Do not push or remove inside a for over the same list.
std::mem::take(&mut x)Move a value out of a borrowed placelet old = std::mem::take(&mut names[0]);It leaves the default value behind.
map.entry(k).or_insert(v)Look up and insert with one borrow*hits.entry("home").or_insert(0) += 1;It replaces "get, then insert".
split_at_mut(i)Get two mutable parts of one slicelet (a, b) = data.split_at_mut(2);The two parts never overlap.

Practice

a is a String. What is true after let b = a;?

  • Both names own the same text.
  • Only b is usable. The value moved.
  • The text was copied to a new heap block.

A String is not Copy. The handle moves to b and a is dead.

Which type is Copy?

  • String
  • Vec<u8>
  • (i32, bool)
  • Box<i32>

A tuple is Copy when all its parts are. The other three types own heap data.

A value has one live &mut reference. How many shared references can be in use at the same moment?

  • Zero
  • One
  • As many as you want

Rule 1: many shared references or one mutable reference. Never both.

Where does the borrow r end?

let mut v = vec![1, 2];
let r = &v;        // line 2
println!("{r:?}"); // line 3
v.push(3);         // line 4
  • At the end of the scope
  • After line 3, its last use
  • At line 2

A borrow lasts until its last use. So the push on line 4 is fine.

Each value has exactly how many? owner at a time.

On a 64-bit machine a &str is how many? bytes: a pointer and a length.

The error code for "borrow of moved value" is code.

  1. This function takes the list away from the caller. Change one type so the caller keeps it. 
    fn total_len(names: Vec<String>) -> usize {
    names.iter().map(|n| n.len()).sum()
}
    Answer

    Borrow a slice. The body stays the same. The caller writes total_len(&names).

    fn total_len(names: &[String]) -> usize {
    names.iter().map(|n| n.len()).sum()
}
  2. Write last_word. It returns the part after the last space as a slice.
    Answer 
    fn last_word(text: &str) -> &str {
    match text.rfind(' ') {
        Some(i) => &text[i + 1..],
        None => text,
    }
}

    For "the borrow checker" it returns "checker". No text is copied.

  3. Why does Rust reject a push while first = &scores[0] is still in use? Say what could happen at run time.
    Answer

    A push can move all items to a new block. The old block is freed. Then first would point to freed memory. Rule 1 stops this before the program runs.

  4. What does this Python program print? Explain the difference between the two parts. 
    a = [1]
b = a
b += [2]
print(a)

t = (1,)
u = t
u += (2,)
print(t, u)
    Answer 
    [1, 2]
(1,) (1, 2)

    A list can change, so += changes the one shared list. A tuple cannot change. Python makes a new tuple and binds only u to it.

  5. Expert. What does this program print? Use the rules for drop order. 
    struct Noisy(&'static str);

impl Drop for Noisy {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        println!("drop {}", self.0);
    }
}

struct Pair {
    first: Noisy,
    second: Noisy,
}

fn main() {
    let p = Pair { first: Noisy("first"), second: Noisy("second") };
    let _x = Noisy("x");
    println!("{} and {}", p.first.0, p.second.0);
}
    Answer 
    first and second
drop x
drop first
drop second

    Variables are dropped in reverse order, so _x goes before p. Fields are dropped in the order of their declaration.

  6. Expert. A method loops over &self.hits and calls self.bump() inside the loop. The method bump takes &mut self. Why does this fail, and how do you fix it?
    Answer

    The loop holds a shared borrow of one field. The call needs a mutable borrow of all of self. That breaks rule 1 with error E0502. Fix it by changing the field directly in the loop, like self.total += 1. The checker sees that the two fields are different.

Key takeaways

  • Small fixed values live on the stack. Data that can grow lives on the heap, behind a handle.
  • Every value has one owner. When the owner leaves its scope, Rust drops the value.
  • An assignment moves a value, unless the type is Copy. A clone is always a visible call.
  • You can have many & or one &mut. A reference never outlives its value.
  • A borrow ends at its last use. Many errors go away when you reorder lines.
  • Python shares objects and counts references at run time. Rust checks ownership at compile time.

Sources

  • The Rust Programming Language, chapter 4. The official book on ownership, references and slices.
  • The Rust Reference: Destructors. The exact rules for drop order and scopes.
  • Rust Blog: Non-lexical lifetimes fully stable. When borrows started to end at the last use.
  • Rust Blog: Enabling the next iteration of the borrow checker on nightly. The state of Polonius alpha in August 2026.
  • Python documentation: Data model. Objects, names, identity and when objects are freed.
  • Python documentation: the gc module. The collector for reference cycles.

Lifetimes

A borrow must never live longer than the value it points to. Rust checks this with lifetimes. Most of the time the compiler finds them alone. This chapter shows when you must write them, and how to read the errors.

  • Explain what a lifetime is with a picture of two scopes.
  • Add lifetime annotations to functions, structs and impl blocks.
  • Apply the three elision rules to any function signature.
  • Fix the common lifetime errors, including the 2024 rules for impl Trait.
  • Decide when a struct or a function should own data instead of borrowing it.

What a lifetime is

Start with a program that Rust refuses. Read it slowly.

fn main() {
    let r;
    {
        let x = 5;
        r = &x; // borrow x
    } // x is dropped here
    println!("r = {r}");
}
error[E0597]: `x` does not live long enough
 --> dangle.rs:5:13
  |
4 |         let x = 5;
  |             - binding `x` declared here
5 |         r = &x; // borrow x
  |             ^^ borrowed value does not live long enough
6 |     } // x is dropped here
  |     - `x` dropped here while still borrowed
7 |     println!("r = {r}");
  |                    - borrow later used here

The value x dies at the inner }. But r is used one line later. So r would point to dead memory. This is a dangling reference. Rust stops it before the program runs.

A lifetime is the part of the code where a reference must be valid. The borrow checker compares two regions. One region is where the value lives. The other is where the reference is used.

The rule is short. A reference may only be used while its value is alive. In the picture, region 'a must fit inside region 'b.

People think a lifetime annotation makes a value live longer. It never does. An annotation only describes how borrows relate. The value still dies at the end of its scope.

A lifetime is a promise: "this reference is good from here to there." The compiler checks every promise.

Lifetime annotations on functions

Inside one function the compiler sees everything. It finds all lifetimes alone. The problem starts when a function returns a reference. Try this function. It returns the longer of two texts.

fn longest(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", longest("borrow", "own"));
}
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
 --> longest_err.rs:1:33
  |
1 | fn longest(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str {
  |               ----     ----     ^ expected named lifetime parameter
  |
  = help: this function's return type contains a borrowed value, but the signature does not say whether it is borrowed from `a` or `b`
help: consider introducing a named lifetime parameter
  |
1 | fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
  |           ++++     ++          ++          ++

The caller only sees the signature. It does not read the body. So the signature must say where the result comes from. From a? From b? Rust will not guess.

The fix is a lifetime parameter. You write it like a generic, with an apostrophe: 'a.

// 'a is a name for "some region of code".
fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}

fn main() {
    let first = String::from("lifetime");
    let answer;
    {
        let second = String::from("scope");
        answer = longest(&first, &second);
        println!("inside: {answer}");
    }
    let s = longest("borrow", "own");
    println!("literals: {s}");
}
# No lifetimes: names refer to objects that live on.
def longest(a: str, b: str) -> str:
    return a if len(a) >= len(b) else b

first = "lifetime"
second = "scope"
answer = longest(first, second)
print(f"inside: {answer}")
del second              # the name goes, the object may stay
s = longest("borrow", "own")
print(f"literals: {s}")
inside: lifetime
literals: borrow

Python has no lifetime annotations. Every object stays alive while any name refers to it. A Python function can even return a list it made inside. That safety costs time at run time. Rust does the work before the program runs.

Read the Rust signature like this. "There is a region 'a. Both inputs are valid in it. The result is valid in it too." The compiler picks the biggest 'a that fits inside both inputs. So the result lives as long as the shorter input.

Find the regions

first lives to the end of main. second lives to the inner }.

Fit 'a inside both

'a must be inside both regions. So 'a ends at the inner }, the shorter one.

Give 'a to the result

The signature says the result is &'a str. So answer is valid only until the inner }.

Check every use

The println! inside the block is in 'a. It is fine.

A use outside 'a fails

Move the println! after the block. Now the use is outside 'a. You get error E0597.

Here is step 5 for real. The answer is "lifetime", from first. But the checker only reads the signature. The signature says the result may come from second.

fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}

fn main() {
    let first = String::from("lifetime");
    let answer;
    {
        let second = String::from("scope");
        answer = longest(&first, &second);
    } // second is dropped here
    println!("{answer}");
}
error[E0597]: `second` does not live long enough
  --> longest_scope_err.rs:10:34
   |
 9 |         let second = String::from("scope");
   |             ------ binding `second` declared here
10 |         answer = longest(&first, &second);
   |                                  ^^^^^^^ borrowed value does not live long enough
11 |     } // second is dropped here
   |     - `second` dropped here while still borrowed
12 |     println!("{answer}");
   |                ------ borrow later used here

Tie only the inputs that the result really uses. This function returns a part of a. It only reads the length of b. So b gets no 'a.

// Only `a` is tied to the result. `b` has its own, free lifetime.
fn prefix_of<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &str) -> &'a str {
    let n = b.len().min(a.len());
    &a[..n]
}

fn main() {
    let text = String::from("lifetimes");
    let cut;
    {
        let ruler = String::from("life"); // dropped soon
        cut = prefix_of(&text, &ruler);
    }
    println!("{cut}"); // fine: cut borrows only text
}
life

Do not put the same 'a on every reference by habit. Each extra tie makes the result shorter-lived for the caller. Tie the output only to the inputs it can come from.

The three elision rules

You wrote fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str in earlier chapters. It has no 'a. Why does it compile? Because of lifetime elision. The compiler fills in the lifetimes with three fixed rules.

Two words first. An input lifetime is on a parameter. An output lifetime is on the return type.

The compiler applies these rules in order to every function and method.

  1. Each elided lifetime in the parameters becomes its own input lifetime.
  2. If there is exactly one input lifetime, every output lifetime gets it.
  3. If there are many input lifetimes, but one is &self or &mut self, every output lifetime gets the lifetime of self.

If an output lifetime is still unknown after the three rules, you get error E0106.

In simple words: one input borrow means the output borrows from it. A method usually returns something from self. In every other case you must say it.

  1. Start with fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str.
  2. Rule 1 gives the input its own name: fn first_word<'a>(s: &'a str) -> &str.
  3. Rule 2: there is one input lifetime. The output gets it: -> &'a str. Done. It compiles.
  4. Now take fn longest(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str.
  5. Rule 1 gives two names: a: &'a str, b: &'b str.
  6. Rule 2 does not apply. There are two inputs. Rule 3 does not apply. There is no self.
  7. The output is still unknown. The compiler stops with E0106.
What the compiler fills in
You writeThe compiler readsRule
fn len(s: &str) -> usizefn len<'a>(s: &'a str) -> usize1 (no output borrow)
fn trim(s: &str) -> &strfn trim<'a>(s: &'a str) -> &'a str1 and 2
fn get(&self, key: &str) -> &strthe output gets the lifetime of self1 and 3
fn pick(a: &str, b: &str) -> &strerror E0106none fits
fn words(t: &str) -> Words<'_>fn words<'a>(t: &'a str) -> Words<'a>1 and 2

The last row uses '_, the anonymous lifetime. It says "a borrow is here, use the rules". It makes a hidden borrow visible to the reader. Use it when a struct with a lifetime appears in a signature.

Rule 3 can surprise you. In fn get(&self, key: &str) -> &str the output is tied to self. If the body returns a part of key, the compiler complains. Then write the lifetimes by hand.

Elision outside functions (expert)

The same rules apply to function pointer types and closure traits. fn(&str) -> &str works for every lifetime of the input.

A reference in a const or static is 'static by default. So const NAME: &str = "x"; is a &'static str.

Trait objects have their own defaults. Box<dyn Trait> means Box<dyn Trait + 'static>. &'a dyn Trait means &'a (dyn Trait + 'a).

Lifetimes in structs and impl blocks

A struct can hold a reference. Then the struct needs a lifetime parameter. The parameter says: "this struct cannot outlive the data it borrows."

// The struct holds a borrow, so it needs a lifetime parameter.
struct Excerpt<'a> {
    part: &'a str,
}

impl<'a> Excerpt<'a> {
    fn len(&self) -> usize {
        self.part.len()
    }
    // Elision rule 3: the result gets the lifetime of &self.
    fn first_word(&self) -> &str {
        self.part.split(' ').next().unwrap_or("")
    }
}

fn main() {
    let notes = String::from("Rust frees memory early. It has no GC.");
    let first = notes.split('.').next().unwrap();
    let e = Excerpt { part: first };
    println!("{} chars, first word: {}", e.len(), e.first_word());
}
23 chars, first word: Rust

Look at the impl line. You declare 'a after impl. Then you use it in Excerpt<'a>. The lifetime is part of the type, like a generic type parameter.

  • Every reference field needs a lifetime: part: &'a str.
  • The struct name carries it: Excerpt<'a>.
  • Methods often need no annotations. Rule 3 handles them.

Expert: tie the result to the data, not to self

This is a tiny word reader. It hands out one word at a time. Watch the return type of next_word.

struct Words<'a> {
    text: &'a str,
}

impl<'a> Words<'a> {
    // Returns &'a str: the word borrows the text, not self.
    fn next_word(&mut self) -> Option<&'a str> {
        let t = self.text.trim_start();
        if t.is_empty() {
            return None;
        }
        let end = t.find(' ').unwrap_or(t.len());
        self.text = &t[end..];
        Some(&t[..end])
    }
}

fn main() {
    let line = String::from("own borrow move");
    let mut w = Words { text: &line };
    let a = w.next_word().unwrap();
    let b = w.next_word().unwrap(); // a is still alive here
    println!("{a} + {b}");
}
own + borrow

Now remove the 'a and write Option<&str>. Rule 3 ties the word to &mut self. So a keeps w borrowed as mutable. The second call needs a second mutable borrow.

error[E0499]: cannot borrow `w` as mutable more than once at a time
  --> parser_err.rs:22:13
   |
21 |     let a = w.next_word().unwrap();
   |             - first mutable borrow occurs here
22 |     let b = w.next_word().unwrap(); // a is still alive here
   |             ^ second mutable borrow occurs here
23 |     println!("{a} + {b}");
   |                - first borrow later used here

The word really comes from line, not from the reader. &'a str says exactly that. Elision gave a correct answer, but a too strict one.

Ask one question for each returned reference. "Where does this data live?" Put that lifetime on the return type.

The 'static lifetime

'static is a special lifetime name. It means "valid until the program ends". Every string literal is &'static str. Its text is stored inside the program file.

use std::fmt::Debug;

static GREETING: &str = "hello"; // type is &'static str

// T: 'static means "T holds no short borrows".
fn keep<T: Debug + 'static>(x: T) -> Box<dyn Debug> {
    Box::new(x) // Box<dyn Debug> means Box<dyn Debug + 'static>
}

fn main() {
    let owned = String::from("owned text");
    let a = keep(owned);    // String owns its data: ok
    let b = keep(GREETING); // &'static str: ok
    let c = keep(42);       // i32: ok
    println!("{a:?} {b:?} {c:?}");
}
"owned text" "hello" 42

'static appears in two places. They mean different things.

Two meanings of 'static
FormMeaningExamples that fit
&'static TA reference to data that lives until the end"hello", a static item
T: 'staticA bound: the type holds no short borrowsString, i32, Vec<u8>, &'static str

So a String is 'static in the second sense. It owns its text. You can keep it as long as you like. But &owned is a short borrow. It fails the bound.

error[E0597]: `owned` does not live long enough
  --> static_err.rs:9:18
   |
 8 |     let owned = String::from("owned text");
   |         ----- binding `owned` declared here
 9 |     let b = keep(&owned); // a short borrow
   |             -----^^^^^^-
   |             |    |
   |             |    borrowed value does not live long enough
   |             argument requires that `owned` is borrowed for `'static`

Threads need this bound. std::thread::spawn asks for a 'static closure. The new thread may run longer than the function that started it. So the closure must own what it uses.

error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `name`, which is owned by the current function
...
help: to force the closure to take ownership of `name` (and any other referenced variables), use the `move` keyword
  |
5 |     let h = thread::spawn(move || {
  |                           ++++

Write move || and the closure owns name. The chapter Threads and shared state goes deeper.

An error says "borrowed for 'static". You add 'static to your own signature. Now the error moves to the caller. The real fix is usually to own the data or to use move.

Lifetime errors and how to fix them

Lifetime errors look scary. But there are only a few kinds. Each one has a usual fix. Open each one below.

E0106: missing lifetime specifier

A function returns a reference. The rules cannot find its source.

error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
 --> e0106b.rs:1:19
  |
1 | fn make_name() -> &str {
  |                   ^ expected named lifetime parameter
  |
  = help: this function's return type contains a borrowed value, but there is no value for it to be borrowed from

Fix: if the output comes from an input, name the lifetime. If there is no input to borrow from, return an owned value like String. The compiler gives both hints.

E0515: cannot return reference to local variable

You wrote -> &'static str to quiet E0106. But the body returns &name, and name is local.

error[E0515]: cannot return reference to local variable `name`
 --> e0515.rs:3:5
  |
3 |     &name
  |     ^^^^^ returns a reference to data owned by the current function

Fix: return the owner. Change the type to String and the last line to name. The value moves out. Nothing dangles.

E0597: borrowed value does not live long enough

A reference is used after its value was dropped. You saw it with dangle.rs and with longest.

Fix: move the value to an outer scope. Or move the last use earlier. Or keep an owned copy, for example with to_string().

E0716: temporary value dropped while borrowed 
error[E0716]: temporary value dropped while borrowed
 --> e0716.rs:3:13
  |
3 |     words = String::from("a b c").split(' ').collect();
  |             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^                     - temporary value is freed at the end of this statement
  |             |
  |             creates a temporary value which is freed while still in use

A temporary has no name. It dies at the end of the statement. Fix: give it a name with let. Then it lives to the end of the block.

E0621: explicit lifetime required 
error[E0621]: explicit lifetime required in the type of `s`
 --> mismatch.rs:7:9
  |
7 |         self.last = s; // s may live shorter than 'a
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ lifetime `'a` required
  |
help: add explicit lifetime `'a` to the type of `s`
  |
6 |     fn remember(&mut self, s: &'a str) {
  |                                ++

You store a parameter inside a struct that borrows for 'a. The parameter must live for 'a too. Fix: write s: &'a str. Or make the field an owned String.

"lifetime may not live long enough" 
error: lifetime may not live long enough
 --> outlive.rs:2:23
  |
1 | fn pick<'a, 'b>(x: &'a str, y: &'b str) -> &'a str {
  |         --  -- lifetime `'b` defined here
  |         |
  |         lifetime `'a` defined here
2 |     if x.is_empty() { y } else { x }
  |                       ^ function was supposed to return data with lifetime `'a` but it is returning data with lifetime `'b`
  |
  = help: consider adding the following bound: `'b: 'a`

The function promises 'a but may return data from 'b. Fix: use one lifetime for both. Or add an outlives bound: 'b: 'a. Read it as "'b lasts at least as long as 'a".

// 'b: 'a reads "'b lives at least as long as 'a".
fn pick<'a, 'b: 'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'b str) -> &'a str {
    if x.is_empty() { y } else { x }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", pick("", "fallback"));
}
fallback

Types can have outlives bounds too. T: 'a means "every borrow inside T lives at least as long as 'a". The 'static bound from the last section is the longest case.

Interviewers like this question: "Does 'a on a function make the data live longer?" The answer is no. Lifetimes describe. They never change when a value is dropped.

impl Trait and the 2024 capture rules

A function can return impl Iterator<Item = i32>. The caller does not see the real type. It is an opaque type. The question is: may the hidden type keep a borrow of the inputs? This is called capturing.

A lifetime was captured only if it was written in the bounds. This function returns an iterator that still reads nums. The lifetime is not written, so Rust 2021 rejects it.

error[E0700]: hidden type for `impl Iterator<Item = i32>` captures lifetime that does not appear in bounds
 --> capture_under.rs:7:5
  |
6 | fn doubled(nums: &[i32]) -> impl Iterator<Item = i32> {
  |                  ------     ------------------------- opaque type defined here
...
help: add a `use<...>` bound to explicitly capture `'_`

Every lifetime in scope is captured by default. The same code compiles. This is usually what you want.

// Returns an iterator that reads from `nums`.
fn evens(nums: &[i32]) -> impl Iterator<Item = &i32> {
    nums.iter().filter(|n| *n % 2 == 0)
}

fn doubled(nums: &[i32]) -> impl Iterator<Item = i32> {
    nums.iter().map(|n| n * 2) // still borrows nums
}

fn main() {
    let v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4];
    let e: Vec<_> = evens(&v).collect();
    let d: Vec<_> = doubled(&v).collect();
    println!("{e:?} {d:?}");
}
[2, 4] [2, 4, 6, 8]

In the 2024 edition, a return-position impl Trait captures every generic parameter in scope. This includes all lifetimes. An explicit use<..> bound replaces the default with an exact list.

The new default can capture too much. This function only uses the length of nums. The iterator holds no borrow. But Rust 2024 assumes it does.

// The result does not borrow `nums`. It only uses its length.
fn indices<T>(nums: &[T]) -> impl Iterator<Item = usize> {
    0..nums.len()
}

fn main() {
    let mut v = vec![10, 20, 30];
    let idx = indices(&v);
    v.push(40); // change v while idx is alive
    for i in idx {
        print!("{i} ");
    }
    println!();
}
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `v` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
  --> capture_over.rs:9:5
   |
 8 |     let idx = indices(&v);
   |                       -- immutable borrow occurs here
 9 |     v.push(40); // change v while idx is alive
   |     ^^^^^^^^^^ mutable borrow occurs here
10 |     for i in idx {
   |              --- immutable borrow later used here
   |
note: this call may capture more lifetimes than intended, because Rust 2024 has adjusted the `impl Trait` lifetime capture rules

The fix is precise capturing. Write + use<..> and list what the hidden type may keep. Leave out the lifetime of nums.

// use<T> lists what the hidden type may capture.
// The lifetime of `nums` is not in the list.
fn indices<T>(nums: &[T]) -> impl Iterator<Item = usize> + use<T> {
    0..nums.len()
}

fn main() {
    let mut v = vec![10, 20, 30];
    let idx = indices(&v);
    v.push(40); // fine: idx does not borrow v
    for i in idx {
        print!("{i} ");
    }
    println!("(len now {})", v.len());
}
0 1 2 (len now 4)
