Practice

What does next return when an iterator has no more items?

  • It panics.
  • None
  • The last item again

next returns Option<Item>. None means the end.

Which line prints something?

  • v.iter().map(|x| println!("{x}"));
  • v.iter().for_each(|x| println!("{x}"));
  • let m = v.iter().map(|x| x * 2);

map is lazy. for_each is a consumer, so it runs the closure.

A closure pushes items into a Vec it captured. Which trait fits it best?

  • Fn
  • FnMut
  • Only FnOnce

It changes a capture, so it is not Fn. It can be called many times, so it is FnMut.

In Python, what does [f() for f in [lambda: i for i in range(3)]] give?

  • [0, 1, 2]
  • [2, 2, 2]
  • An error

Late binding: every lambda reads i when it runs, and then i is 2.

The only required method of Iterator is method.

v.iter() on a Vec<String> gives items of type type.

To give a closure ownership of the variables it uses, write the keyword keyword before it.

  1. Rewrite this loop as one iterator chain. 
    let mut total = 0;
for n in &nums {
    if n % 3 == 0 {
        total += n * n;
    }
}
    Answer 
    let total: i32 = nums.iter().filter(|n| *n % 3 == 0).map(|n| n * n).sum();

    Python: total = sum(n * n for n in nums if n % 3 == 0).

  2. You have names: Vec<&str> and scores: Vec<u32>. Print 1. ann: 90, 2. bo: 75 and so on.
    Answer 
    for (i, (name, score)) in names.iter().zip(scores.iter()).enumerate() {
    println!("{}. {name}: {score}", i + 1);
}

    zip pairs the two lists. enumerate adds the position, which starts at 0.

  3. Write make_multiplier(k: i32) that returns a closure. The closure multiplies its input by k.
    Answer 
    fn make_multiplier(k: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    move |x| x * k
}

    move is needed. Otherwise the closure would borrow k, which dies when the function returns.

  4. Write an iterator Countdown(u32) that yields 3, 2, 1 for Countdown(3) and then stops.
    Answer 
    struct Countdown(u32);

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.0 == 0 {
            return None;
        }
        self.0 -= 1;
        Some(self.0 + 1)
    }
}

    Python: def countdown(n): with while n > 0: yield n; n -= 1.

  5. Expert. Why does a function that calls its closure twice need Fn or FnMut, and not FnOnce?
    Answer

    An FnOnce closure may move a captured value out when it runs. After that the value is gone. A second call would use a moved value. So the compiler allows only one call through FnOnce.

  6. Expert. A teammate writes let lens = words.iter().map(|w| w.len()); and then calls lens.sum() twice. What happens in Rust, and what happens with the same idea in Python?
    Answer

    Rust refuses to compile. sum takes the iterator by value, so the second call is E0382, "use of moved value". Python runs. The second sum silently returns 0, because the generator is empty. Fix in Rust: lens.clone().sum() for the first pass, or build the chain again.

Key takeaways

  • An iterator has one required method, next. It returns Some(item) or None.
  • iter borrows, iter_mut borrows to change, into_iter moves. A for loop uses into_iter.
  • Adapters like map and filter are lazy. Consumers like collect and sum do the work, one item at a time.
  • A closure captures by borrow, by mutable borrow or by move. move forces ownership.
  • Fn reads, FnMut changes, FnOnce consumes. Ask for the weakest one you need.
  • Python generators and comprehensions match Rust iterators. A generator works only once, and nothing warns you.

Sources

  • The Rust Programming Language, chapter 13. Closures, the Fn traits and iterators.
  • Rust standard library: std::iter. The Iterator trait, laziness, from_fn and successors.
  • The Rust Reference: Closure types. Capture modes, disjoint capture and the call traits.
  • Python documentation: itertools. Lazy building blocks, including batched and pairwise.
  • Python documentation: Functional Programming HOWTO. Iterators, generators and comprehensions.

Smart pointers and interior mutability

A normal reference only borrows a value. A smart pointer owns a value and adds a skill: heap storage, shared owners or safe changes through a shared reference. Rust has a small family of them, and each one has one job. This chapter shows each pointer, when to choose it, and how Python does the same work with reference counting.

  • Use Box for heap values, recursive types and trait objects.
  • Explain Deref and Drop, and write a tiny smart pointer.
  • Share data with Rc and Arc, and break cycles with Weak.
  • Change data behind & with Cell, RefCell and Mutex.
  • Choose the right pointer, and build a linked list and a tree.

Box: a value on the heap

Here is a list where each item holds the next one. Without a box, Rust cannot build it.

#[derive(Debug)]
enum List {
    Cons(i32, Box<List>),   // a value and a box with the rest
    Nil,                    // the end
}
use List::{Cons, Nil};

fn sum(list: &List) -> i32 {
    match list {
        Cons(value, rest) => value + sum(rest), // rest is &Box<List>
        Nil => 0,
    }
}

trait Shape { fn area(&self) -> f64; }
struct Square(f64);
struct Circle(f64);
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }
impl Shape for Circle { fn area(&self) -> f64 { 3.14 * self.0 * self.0 } }

fn main() {
    let b = Box::new(5);            // the 5 lives on the heap
    println!("b = {b}, b + 1 = {}", *b + 1);
    let list = Cons(1, Box::new(Cons(2, Box::new(Nil))));
    println!("{list:?} sum = {}", sum(&list));
    let shapes: Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> = vec![Box::new(Square(2.0)), Box::new(Circle(1.0))];
    for s in &shapes {
        println!("area {:.2}", s.area());
    }
}
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Cons:
    value: int
    rest: "Cons | None"     # a reference, no Box needed

def total(node: Cons | None) -> int:
    return 0 if node is None else node.value + total(node.rest)

items = Cons(1, Cons(2, None))
print(items, "sum =", total(items))
b = 5, b + 1 = 6
Cons(1, Cons(2, Nil)) sum = 3
area 4.00
area 3.14
Cons(value=1, rest=Cons(value=2, rest=None)) sum = 3

A pointer holds an address. A smart pointer also owns the value and does extra work. Box<T> is the simplest one. It puts a T on the heap. The box itself is one address on the stack. When the box goes away, the value on the heap goes away too.

Why does List need a box? The compiler must know the size of every type. Without the box, a List holds a List, which holds a List, and so on forever.

error[E0072]: recursive type `List` has infinite size
 --> src/main.rs:1:1
  |
1 | enum List {
  | ^^^^^^^^^
2 |     Cons(i32, List),
  |               ---- recursive without indirection
  |
help: insert some indirection (e.g., a `Box`, `Rc`, or `&`) to break the cycle
  |
2 |     Cons(i32, Box<List>),
  |               ++++    +

A box always has the size of one address. So the size of List is known. Use Box in three cases:

  • Recursive types, like lists and trees.
  • Trait objects, like Box<dyn Shape>. One Vec can then hold many types.
  • Big values that you want to move without copying many bytes.

Python needs no box. Every Python object already lives on the heap. A name or a field holds only a reference to it.

You put small values in a Box "to be faster". Box::new(5) is slower than 5. It asks the heap for memory and adds one more jump. Use a box only for the three cases above.

Deref and Drop: what makes a pointer smart

Two traits turn a normal struct into a smart pointer. Let us write a tiny one that prints a line when it dies.

use std::ops::Deref;

struct Loud<T> {               // a tiny smart pointer of our own
    name: &'static str,
    value: T,
}

impl<T> Deref for Loud<T> {
    type Target = T;
    fn deref(&self) -> &T { &self.value }   // *x gives the inner value
}

impl<T> Drop for Loud<T> {
    fn drop(&mut self) { println!("drop {}", self.name); } // runs at the end of scope
}

fn greet(name: &str) { println!("hello, {name}"); }

fn main() {
    let a = Loud { name: "a", value: String::from("Ann") };
    let _b = Loud { name: "b", value: 7 };
    greet(&a);                     // &Loud<String> -> &String -> &str
    println!("len = {}", a.len()); // String methods work through Deref
    {
        let _c = Loud { name: "c", value: () };
        println!("inner scope ends");
    }
    let d = Loud { name: "d", value: 1.5 };
    drop(d);                       // std::mem::drop: drop it now
    println!("main ends");
}
hello, Ann
len = 3
inner scope ends
drop c
drop d
main ends
drop b
drop a
  • Deref says what *x means. Then Loud<String> acts like a String.
  • Deref coercion: Rust follows Deref by itself when the types do not match. &Loud<String> becomes &String, then &str. This is deref coercion.
  • Drop runs clean-up code when the owner goes out of scope. Values drop in reverse order: b before a.
  • drop(x) ends a value early. It is a normal function that takes ownership.

This idea has a name: RAII. A file closes, a lock unlocks and memory goes back when the owner dies. You cannot forget it. Python uses with for the same goal. Python also has __del__, but its timing is less certain.

You call the method yourself: guard.drop(). Rust refuses with error[E0040]: explicit use of destructor method. A double clean-up could free memory twice. Write drop(guard) instead.

Rc and Weak: many owners

Sometimes one value has many owners. A config is read by many parts of a program. Nobody knows who finishes last. Rc counts the owners.

use std::rc::{Rc, Weak};

fn main() {
    let shared = Rc::new(String::from("config"));
    println!("count = {}", Rc::strong_count(&shared));
    let a = Rc::clone(&shared);          // a new owner, no copy of the text
    {
        let b = Rc::clone(&shared);
        println!("count = {}, b = {b}", Rc::strong_count(&shared));
    }                                    // b is gone: count goes down
    println!("count = {}, a = {a}", Rc::strong_count(&shared));
    println!("same place? {}", Rc::ptr_eq(&a, &shared));

    let w: Weak<String> = Rc::downgrade(&shared);  // does not keep it alive
    println!("weak = {}", Rc::weak_count(&shared));
    println!("upgrade: {:?}", w.upgrade());
    drop(a);
    drop(shared);                         // the last strong owner is gone
    println!("upgrade after drop: {:?}", w.upgrade());
}
import sys, weakref

class Config:
    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name
    def __del__(self) -> None:
        print("freed", self.name)

shared = Config("config")
print("refs =", sys.getrefcount(shared))   # the call itself adds one
a = shared
print("refs =", sys.getrefcount(shared))
w = weakref.ref(shared)                    # does not keep it alive
print("weak ->", w().name)
del a
del shared                                 # count reaches 0: freed now
print("weak ->", w())
count = 1
count = 3, b = config
count = 2, a = config
same place? true
weak = 1
upgrade: Some("config")
upgrade after drop: None
refs = 2
refs = 3
weak -> config
freed config
weak -> None

Rc means reference counted. The heap block holds two counters and the value. Rc::clone adds one to the strong count. It does not copy the text. When the strong count reaches zero, the value is freed.

Create

Rc::new(value) moves the value to the heap. Strong count: 1.

Clone

Rc::clone(&rc) adds an owner. Strong count: 2. No data is copied.

An owner leaves

At the end of its scope, an Rc runs Drop. Strong count goes down by one.

Downgrade

Rc::downgrade(&rc) gives a Weak. Weak count goes up. Strong count stays.

The last owner leaves

Strong count reaches 0. The value is dropped. weak.upgrade() now returns None.

A weak pointer watches the value but does not own it. upgrade() returns Some(Rc) while the value lives, and None after. Python has the same tool: weakref.ref.

You write shared.clone() and think the text is copied. For an Rc, it only adds one to the count. Many teams write Rc::clone(&shared) so that a reader sees at once: this clone is cheap.

Interior mutability: Cell and RefCell

An Rc gives only shared access. Shared means read-only in Rust. But sometimes you must change a value behind &. Here a counter counts hits in a method that takes &self.

use std::cell::{Cell, RefCell};
use std::rc::Rc;

struct Counter {
    hits: Cell<u32>,              // change a Copy value through &self
    log: RefCell<Vec<String>>,    // borrow rules checked at run time
}

impl Counter {
    fn hit(&self, page: &str) {   // note: &self, not &mut self
        self.hits.set(self.hits.get() + 1);
        self.log.borrow_mut().push(page.to_string());
    }
}

fn main() {
    let c = Counter { hits: Cell::new(0), log: RefCell::new(Vec::new()) };
    c.hit("/home");
    c.hit("/about");
    println!("hits = {}, log = {:?}", c.hits.get(), c.log.borrow());

    let cart = Rc::new(RefCell::new(vec!["tea"])); // many owners, all can change it
    let alice = Rc::clone(&cart);
    let bob = Rc::clone(&cart);
    alice.borrow_mut().push("milk");
    bob.borrow_mut().push("bread");
    println!("cart = {:?}", cart.borrow());
}
class Counter:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.hits = 0
        self.log: list[str] = []

    def hit(self, page: str) -> None:
        self.hits += 1                # any reference can change the object
        self.log.append(page)

c = Counter()
c.hit("/home")
c.hit("/about")
print("hits =", c.hits, "log =", c.log)

cart = ["tea"]
alice = bob = cart                    # three names, one list
alice.append("milk")
bob.append("bread")
print("cart =", cart)
hits = 2, log = ["/home", "/about"]
cart = ["tea", "milk", "bread"]

Without a cell, the compiler refuses the change.

error[E0594]: cannot assign to `self.hits`, which is behind a `&` reference
 --> src/main.rs:3:21
  |
3 |     fn hit(&self) { self.hits += 1; }
  |                     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ `self` is a `&` reference, so it cannot be written to

Changing a value through a shared reference is called interior mutability. The cell types make it safe.

  • Cell<T> moves values in and out with get and set. It never hands out a reference to the inside. So it needs no checks at all. get works only for Copy types like numbers.
  • RefCell<T> hands out references with borrow() and borrow_mut(). It checks the borrow rules at run time: many readers or one writer.
  • Rc<RefCell<T>> is a common pair. Rc gives many owners. RefCell lets them change the value.

What happens when you break the rules of a RefCell? Add these lines at the end of main above. The program panics at run time.

let first = cart.borrow();                         // a reader is alive
println!("{:?}", cart.try_borrow_mut().is_err());  // true: no writer now
drop(first);
let _again = cart.borrow();
let _oops = cart.borrow_mut();                     // panics
true

thread 'main' (115626972) panicked at src/main.rs:32:22:
RefCell already borrowed

The borrow rules did not go away. They moved from compile time to run time. try_borrow_mut returns a Result instead of panicking.

Two more cells set a value only once. OnceCell (stable since Rust 1.70) is filled once and then read. LazyCell (stable since Rust 1.80) runs a function on the first read. Their thread-safe twins are OnceLock and LazyLock.

You keep a borrow_mut() alive in a variable and then call a function that also borrows. The code compiles, but it panics with RefCell already borrowed. Keep borrows short. Borrow, change, and let the guard drop at once.

Arc and Mutex: sharing between threads

Four threads add numbers to one total. Rc and RefCell cannot do this. Their counters are not safe when two threads change them at once.

use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let total = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0u64));  // shared by threads, changed safely
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for id in 1..=4u64 {
        let total = Arc::clone(&total);      // each thread gets one owner
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            let mut guard = total.lock().unwrap(); // wait for the lock
            *guard += id * 10;                     // guard derefs to u64
        }));                                       // guard dropped: unlocked
    }
    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
    println!("total = {}", *total.lock().unwrap());
    println!("owners = {}", Arc::strong_count(&total));
}
import threading

total = 0
lock = threading.Lock()          # Python's Mutex

def work(n: int) -> None:
    global total
    with lock:                   # unlocked again at the end of with
        total += n * 10

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work, args=(n,)) for n in range(1, 5)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print("total =", total)
total = 100
owners = 1

Arc is an atomic Rc. Its counter uses special CPU steps that are safe across threads. They cost a little more, so use Rc in one thread and Arc across threads.

A Mutex is interior mutability for threads. lock() waits until no other thread holds the lock. It returns a guard. The guard derefs to the value. When the guard drops, the lock opens. This is RAII again.

The compiler stops you if you send an Rc to a thread.

error[E0277]: `Rc<i32>` cannot be sent between threads safely
   --> src/main.rs:7:19
    |
  7 |     thread::spawn(move || println!("{copy}")).join().unwrap();
    |     ------------- -------^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
    |     |             |
    |     |             `Rc<i32>` cannot be sent between threads safely
...
    = help: within `{closure@src/main.rs:7:19: 7:26}`, the trait `Send` is not implemented for `Rc<i32>`

Types that may move to another thread are Send. Types that may be shared between threads are Sync. Rc, Cell and RefCell are not Sync. Arc<Mutex<T>> is both, when T is Send.

One-thread tools and their thread-safe twins
One threadMany threadsNote
Rc<T>Arc<T>Atomic counter, a bit slower
RefCell<T>Mutex<T>, RwLock<T>RwLock allows many readers
Cell<u64>AtomicU64No lock at all, for numbers and flags
OnceCell<T>, LazyCell<T>OnceLock<T>, LazyLock<T>Set once, read many times

A thread panics while it holds the lock. Now the mutex is poisoned, and every later lock() returns Err. That is why you see lock().unwrap(). It turns one panic into a clear chain of panics, not silent bad data. The chapter Threads and shared state goes deeper.

Cow: copy only when you must

A function cleans text. Most texts are already clean. Why copy them?

use std::borrow::Cow;

// Replace tabs with spaces. Copy the text only when there is a tab.
fn no_tabs(input: &str) -> Cow<'_, str> {
    if input.contains('\t') {
        Cow::Owned(input.replace('\t', "    "))  // a new String
    } else {
        Cow::Borrowed(input)                     // no copy at all
    }
}

fn main() {
    for text in ["plain text", "a\tb"] {
        let out = no_tabs(text);
        let kind = match &out {
            Cow::Borrowed(_) => "borrowed",
            Cow::Owned(_) => "owned",
        };
        println!("{kind:8} {out:?} len={}", out.len()); // Cow derefs to &str
    }
    let mut name: Cow<str> = Cow::Borrowed("ann");
    name.to_mut().make_ascii_uppercase();        // clones on the first write
    println!("{name} is owned: {}", matches!(name, Cow::Owned(_)));
    let s: String = name.into_owned();           // get a String out
    println!("{s}");
}
borrowed "plain text" len=10
owned    "a    b" len=6
ANN is owned: true
ANN

Cow means clone on write. It is an enum with two variants: Borrowed(&T) and Owned(T). It derefs to the borrowed form, so you read it like a &str. to_mut() clones the value the first time you change it. Python strings cannot change, so Python has no need for Cow.

You return String from every text helper "to be safe". Each call now copies the text, even when nothing changes. In a hot loop that is many wasted copies. Return Cow<'_, str> when most inputs pass through unchanged.

Reference cycles, a linked list and a tree

Two nodes point to each other with Rc. Watch what happens at the end of main.

use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

struct Node {
    name: &'static str,
    next: RefCell<Option<Rc<Node>>>,
}
impl Drop for Node {
    fn drop(&mut self) { println!("drop {}", self.name); }
}

fn main() {
    let a = Rc::new(Node { name: "a", next: RefCell::new(None) });
    let b = Rc::new(Node { name: "b", next: RefCell::new(Some(Rc::clone(&a))) });
    *a.next.borrow_mut() = Some(Rc::clone(&b));   // a -> b -> a: a cycle
    println!("a strong = {}, b strong = {}", Rc::strong_count(&a), Rc::strong_count(&b));
    println!("main ends");
}   // each count only drops to 1: no "drop" lines
import gc

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name
        self.next = None
    def __del__(self) -> None:
        print("freed", self.name)

gc.collect()                 # start clean
a, b = Node("a"), Node("b")
a.next, b.next = b, a        # a cycle
del a, b                     # counts stay at 1: nothing freed yet
print("before collect")
found = gc.collect()         # the cycle collector finds them
print("unreachable objects found:", found)
a strong = 2, b strong = 2
main ends
before collect
freed a
freed b
unreachable objects found: 2

No "drop" line appears in Rust. Each node keeps the other alive. This is a reference cycle, and the memory leaks. Rust calls a leak memory safe, so the compiler does not stop it. Python has a second helper, the cycle garbage collector. It finds such rings and frees them.

The fix in Rust: one direction owns, the other direction is Weak. In a tree, a parent owns its children. A child only points back to its parent.

use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::{Rc, Weak};

struct TreeNode {
    name: String,
    parent: RefCell<Weak<TreeNode>>,          // up: weak, no cycle
    children: RefCell<Vec<Rc<TreeNode>>>,     // down: strong, owns
}

fn node(name: &str) -> Rc<TreeNode> {
    Rc::new(TreeNode {
        name: name.to_string(),
        parent: RefCell::new(Weak::new()),
        children: RefCell::new(Vec::new()),
    })
}

fn add_child(parent: &Rc<TreeNode>, child: Rc<TreeNode>) {
    *child.parent.borrow_mut() = Rc::downgrade(parent);
    parent.children.borrow_mut().push(child);
}

fn main() {
    let root = node("src");
    let leaf = node("main.rs");
    add_child(&root, Rc::clone(&leaf));
    add_child(&root, node("lib.rs"));
    let up = leaf.parent.borrow().upgrade();   // Option<Rc<TreeNode>>
    println!("parent of {} = {:?}", leaf.name, up.map(|p| p.name.clone()));
    let names: Vec<_> = root.children.borrow().iter().map(|c| c.name.clone()).collect();
    println!("children of {} = {names:?}", root.name);
    println!("root strong = {}, weak = {}", Rc::strong_count(&root), Rc::weak_count(&root));
    drop(root);
    println!("after drop: parent = {:?}", leaf.parent.borrow().upgrade().is_some());
}
parent of main.rs = Some("src")
children of src = ["main.rs", "lib.rs"]
root strong = 1, weak = 2
after drop: parent = false

A linked list with Option<Box<Node>>

A list where each node has one owner needs no Rc. A Box is enough. Here is a stack.

struct Node {
    value: i32,
    next: Option<Box<Node>>,      // the next node, or None at the end
}

pub struct Stack {
    head: Option<Box<Node>>,
    len: usize,
}

impl Stack {
    pub fn new() -> Self { Stack { head: None, len: 0 } }

    pub fn push(&mut self, value: i32) {
        let old = self.head.take();             // take the head, leave None
        self.head = Some(Box::new(Node { value, next: old }));
        self.len += 1;
    }

    pub fn pop(&mut self) -> Option<i32> {
        self.head.take().map(|node| {           // move the first node out
            self.head = node.next;
            self.len -= 1;
            node.value
        })
    }

    pub fn peek(&self) -> Option<&i32> {
        self.head.as_ref().map(|node| &node.value)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut s = Stack::new();
    for v in [1, 2, 3] { s.push(v); }
    println!("peek = {:?}, len = {}", s.peek(), s.len);
    println!("{:?} {:?} {:?} {:?}", s.pop(), s.pop(), s.pop(), s.pop());
}
peek = Some(3), len = 3
Some(3) Some(2) Some(1) None

The key tool is Option::take(). It moves the value out and leaves None behind. Without it, you try to move out of &mut self.

error[E0507]: cannot move out of `self.head` which is behind a mutable reference
 --> src/main.rs:5:55
  |
5 |         self.head = Some(Box::new(Node { value, next: self.head }));
  |                                                       ^^^^^^^^^ move occurs because `self.head` has type `Option<Box<Node>>`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait

You try a doubly linked list with Rc<RefCell<Node>> in both directions. You get cycles, leaks and borrow panics. Use Weak for the back links. Or, for real work, use Vec, VecDeque or std::collections::LinkedList. A Vec is usually faster because its items sit side by side in memory.

Choosing a pointer, and how Python counts references

Start from the question "who owns this value, and who changes it?". Then walk down the tree.

Each pointer has a cost in memory. I measured these sizes with std::mem::size_of on this Mac with Rust 1.99.

Python: every name is an Rc

CPython, the normal Python, counts references on every object. Each object has a counter, like a Rust Rc. When the count reaches zero, the object is freed at once. That is why freed config printed right after del shared.

  • sys.getrefcount(x) shows the count. The call itself adds one, so expect one more than you think.
  • Reference counting cannot free cycles. The gc module finds and frees them from time to time.
  • weakref.ref is Python's Weak. Caches often use weakref.WeakValueDictionary.
  • Python has no RefCell. Any reference can change a mutable object. Nothing checks it, so bugs with shared lists are common.

Some objects are immortal since Python 3.12. On Python 3.14.3 here, sys.getrefcount(None) printed 3221225472, a fixed marker. Python 3.14 also skips some count updates, so getrefcount numbers can differ from older versions. Python 3.14.0 to 3.14.4 shipped a new incremental garbage collector. Python 3.14.5 went back to the older generational one because of memory problems in production. Check the official page: this can change again.

A common question: "What is the difference between Rc<RefCell<T>> and Arc<Mutex<T>>?" Answer: both give shared owners that can change the value. The first is for one thread and panics on a borrow conflict. The second works across threads and blocks until the lock is free.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for smart pointers
PatternPurposeModelNote
Box<T> in a recursive typeGive the type a known sizeCons(i32, Box<List>)Without it: E0072, infinite size.
Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>Keep many types in one listVec<Box<dyn Shape>>Each call goes through a method table.
impl Deref for PMake your type act like the inner onetype Target = T;Only for pointer-like types.
impl Drop for GClean up when the owner diesfn drop(&mut self) { ... }Call drop(x), never x.drop().
Rc::clone(&rc)Add an owner in one threadlet a = Rc::clone(&shared);Cheap: only a counter changes.
Rc::downgrade(&rc)Point back without owningparent: RefCell<Weak<Node>>upgrade() may return None.
Cell<T>Change a Copy value behind &self.hits.set(self.hits.get() + 1)No references to the inside.
Rc<RefCell<T>>Many owners that all change itcart.borrow_mut().push("milk")Keep borrows short or it panics.
Arc<Mutex<T>>Share and change across threads*total.lock().unwrap() += 1The guard unlocks when dropped.
Cow<'_, str>Copy only when you changeCow::Borrowed(input)Good for text that is often unchanged.
opt.take()Move out of a field, leave Nonelet old = self.head.take();The key move in linked lists.
weakref.ref(obj)Python: watch without owningw = weakref.ref(shared)w() returns None after free.

Practice

Why does enum List { Cons(i32, List), Nil } not compile?

  • Enums cannot hold numbers.
  • The type would have infinite size.
  • Nil is a keyword.

A List would contain a whole List. A Box<List> has a fixed size of one address.

What does Rc::clone(&a) do?

  • It copies the value on the heap.
  • It adds one to the strong count.
  • It makes a weak pointer.

All clones point to the same heap block. Only the counter changes.

You need many owners and changes, across four threads. Which type?

  • Rc<RefCell<T>>
  • Box<Cell<T>>
  • Arc<Mutex<T>>

Rc and RefCell are not safe across threads. Arc counts atomically and Mutex locks.

A RefCell has an active borrow(). You call borrow_mut(). What happens?

  • A compile error.
  • A panic at run time: RefCell already borrowed.
  • The first borrow ends by itself.

RefCell checks the rules at run time. Use try_borrow_mut to get a Result.

To end a value early, call the function <span class="blank" data-answer="drop">?</span>(x).

A weak pointer turns into an Option<Rc<T>> with the method <span class="blank" data-answer="upgrade|upgrade()">?</span>.

The thread-safe twin of Rc is ?.

In Python, the module that frees reference cycles is ?.

  1. Write the type of a vector that holds boxed values of any type that implements Display.
    Answer

    Vec<Box<dyn std::fmt::Display>>

  2. A struct has a method fn record(&self) that must add one to a u32 field. Which cell do you use, and how does the line look?
    Answer

    Use Cell<u32>, because u32 is Copy. The line is self.count.set(self.count.get() + 1);.

  3. In a tree, children hold Rc pointers to their parent, and parents hold Rc pointers to their children. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
    Answer

    Parent and child keep each other alive. Their strong counts never reach zero, so the memory leaks. Make the parent link a Weak. Parents own children. Children only watch the parent.

  4. Write a function fn trim_dots(s: &str) -> Cow<'_, str> that removes a final "." only if there is one, without copying otherwise.
    Answer

    match s.strip_suffix('.') { Some(t) => Cow::Borrowed(t), None => Cow::Borrowed(s) }. A slice is enough here, so you never need Owned. Use Owned only when you must build new text.

  5. Add a method fn is_empty(&self) -> bool to the Stack above.
    Answer

    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool { self.head.is_none() }. You could also check self.len == 0.

  6. Hard: why is Rc<T> not Send, while Arc<T> is (for a T that is Send and Sync)?
    Answer

    Two threads could clone or drop an Rc at the same moment. Its counter uses normal adds, so updates could be lost. The value might be freed too early or never. Arc uses atomic adds, which the CPU makes safe across threads.

  7. Hard: in Python, del x printed "freed" at once for a simple object, but not for two objects in a cycle. Explain both cases.
    Answer

    For the simple object, the reference count dropped to zero, so CPython freed it at once. In a cycle, each object still holds a reference to the other. The counts stay at one. Only the cycle garbage collector, run by gc.collect() or on its own, can find and free them.

Key takeaways

  • Box puts one value on the heap with one owner. Use it for recursive types, trait objects and big values.
  • Deref makes a pointer act like its value. Drop runs clean-up when the owner dies.
  • Rc counts owners in one thread. Arc does it across threads. Weak watches without owning.
  • Cell, RefCell and Mutex allow changes behind &. RefCell checks at run time and can panic.
  • Cow borrows first and copies only when you change the value.
  • Rc cycles leak. Use Weak for back links, as in a tree's parent pointer.
  • CPython counts references on every object and adds a cycle collector. Rust has no collector, so you choose the pointer.

Sources

  • The Rust Programming Language: Smart Pointers. Box, Deref, Drop, Rc, RefCell and reference cycles.
  • Rust standard library: std::cell. Cell, RefCell, OnceCell, LazyCell and their thread-safe twins.
  • Rust standard library: Cow. Clone-on-write, to_mut and into_owned.
  • Rust standard library: Mutex. Locking, guards and poisoning.
  • Python: gc, the garbage collector interface. Cycle collection in CPython.
  • What's New in Python 3.14. Reference count changes and the garbage collector revert in 3.14.5.

Cargo, crates and workspaces

A real project has many files, many dependencies and often many crates. Cargo is the tool that holds it all together. This chapter goes from one module to a workspace you can publish. It ends with the same job in Python: pyproject.toml, uv, virtual environments and wheels.

  • Explain packages, crates and modules, and control visibility with pub, pub(crate) and pub use.
  • Read and write a full Cargo.toml with dependencies, features and profiles.
  • Use semver requirements, Cargo.lock, rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver.
  • Build a workspace with a build script, and prepare a crate for cargo publish.
  • Set up a Python package with pyproject.toml and uv, and build a wheel.

Packages, crates and modules

Here is a small shop project. It has two parts: a library with the shop logic and a command-line program that uses it.

shop/
├── Cargo.toml            # the workspace root
├── Cargo.lock            # exact versions for the whole workspace
└── crates/
    ├── shop-core/        # package 1: a library
    │   ├── Cargo.toml
    │   └── src/
    │       ├── lib.rs    # crate root of the library
    │       ├── cart.rs   # module cart
    │       └── tax.rs    # module tax (private)
    └── shop-cli/         # package 2: a program
        ├── Cargo.toml
        ├── build.rs      # build script
        └── src/main.rs   # crate root of the binary
cargo run -p shop-cli
total with tax: 770 cents
as JSON: {"cents":770}
shop-cli 0.3.0 (debug)

Three words describe this structure. They go from big to small.

  • A package is a folder with a Cargo.toml. It holds one or more crates.
  • A crate is what rustc compiles in one go. A library crate starts at src/lib.rs. A binary crate starts at src/main.rs or at a file in src/bin/. That first file is the crate root.
  • A module groups code inside one crate. mod cart; loads src/cart.rs.

A package has at most one library crate, but any number of binary crates. A workspace groups several packages.

The chapter Functions and modules showed mod, use and files. This chapter builds on that.

You think a crate is a file. It is not. A crate is a whole tree of modules, starting from one root file. Your package can be one crate made of fifty files.

Visibility: who can see what

Here is the library of the shop. Look at the words before each item.

//! Prices and carts for a tiny shop.
pub mod cart;                    // public module
mod tax;                         // private: only this crate sees it

pub use cart::Cart;              // re-export: users write shop_core::Cart

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
#[cfg_attr(feature = "serde", derive(serde::Serialize))]
pub struct Price {
    cents: u64,                  // private field: use Price::new
}

impl Price {
    pub fn new(cents: u64) -> Self { Price { cents } }
    pub fn cents(&self) -> u64 { self.cents }
    pub(crate) fn with_tax(self) -> Price {   // visible in this crate only
        Price { cents: self.cents + tax::vat(self.cents) }
    }
}
// src/cart.rs
use crate::Price;                // crate:: is the root of this crate

#[derive(Default)]
pub struct Cart {
    items: Vec<(String, Price)>,
}

impl Cart {
    pub fn add(&mut self, name: &str, price: Price) {
        self.items.push((name.to_string(), price));
    }
    pub fn total(&self) -> Price {
        let sum = self.items.iter().map(|(_, p)| p.cents()).sum();
        Price::new(sum).with_tax()   // pub(crate) is fine here
    }
}

// src/tax.rs
const VAT_PERCENT: u64 = 10;

pub(crate) fn vat(cents: u64) -> u64 {
    cents * VAT_PERCENT / 100
}

Everything in Rust is private by default. You open it step by step.

The visibility levels
KeywordWho can see itExample
nothingThis module and its child modulesmod tax;
pub(super)The parent module tooa helper for the parent
pub(in crate::a)Everything inside the path crate::arare, for big crates
pub(crate)The whole crate, but no other cratepub(crate) fn with_tax
pubEveryone, if the path to it is public toopub fn new

A struct can be public while its fields stay private. Then nobody outside can build a Price with a wrong value. They must call Price::new. The line pub use cart::Cart; is a re-export. Users write shop_core::Cart, and you may move the file later without breaking them.

The program shop-cli tries to reach private items. The compiler stops it.

error[E0603]: module `tax` is private
 --> crates/shop-cli/src/main.rs:6:31
  |
6 |     println!("{}", shop_core::tax::vat(100));
  |                               ^^^  --- function `vat` is not publicly re-exported
  |                               |
  |                               private module

error[E0616]: field `cents` of struct `Price` is private
 --> crates/shop-cli/src/main.rs:5:22
  |
5 |     println!("{}", p.cents);
  |                      ^^^^^ private field
  |
help: a method `cents` also exists, call it with parentheses

Python has no private keyword. A leading underscore, like _vat, means "please do not use". The list __all__ sets what from pyshop import * brings in. Nothing is enforced at run time.

You mark a function pub, but its module is private. Outsiders still cannot reach it. Every step of the path must be public, or you need a pub use at the top. Start private, then open only what users need. Everything that is pub becomes a promise.

Cargo.toml in detail

Every package has a manifest. Here is the one of shop-cli, and below it a table of the common keys.

[package]
name = "shop-cli"
version.workspace = true        # take the value from the workspace
edition.workspace = true
rust-version.workspace = true
license.workspace = true
publish = false                 # never upload this one

[dependencies]
shop-core = { path = "../shop-core", version = "0.3.0", features = ["serde"] }
serde_json.workspace = true

[lints]
workspace = true
Common Cargo.toml tables and keys
Table or keyWhat it doesExample
name, versionThe package name and its semver versionversion = "0.3.0"
editionThe language editionedition = "2024"
rust-versionThe oldest Rust you supportrust-version = "1.85"
description, licenseNeeded by crates.iolicense = "MIT OR Apache-2.0"
repository, readme, keywords, categoriesShown on crates.iokeywords = ["shop"]
[dependencies]Crates your code usesserde = "1.0"
[dev-dependencies]Only for tests, examples and benchmarksproptest = "1"
[build-dependencies]Only for build.rscc = "1"
[target.'cfg(unix)'.dependencies]Only on some platformslibc = "0.2"
[features]Optional parts of your crateserde = ["dep:serde"]
[lib], [[bin]]Change the default crate targets[[bin]] name = "shop"
[profile.release]Compiler settings for a build modelto = "thin"
[lints]Lint levels for this packageunsafe_code = "forbid"

A dependency can come from four places.

[dependencies]
serde = "1.0"                                     # crates.io, the default
shop-core = { path = "../shop-core" }             # a folder on your disk
regex = { git = "https://github.com/rust-lang/regex.git", tag = "1.10.3" } # a git repo
anyhow = { version = "1", default-features = false }  # turn off default features

A path dependency with a version works in both worlds. On your disk, Cargo uses the folder. After publishing, users get the version from crates.io.

You add a test helper crate under [dependencies]. Now every user of your library downloads it. Put tools for tests under [dev-dependencies]. cargo add --dev proptest does it for you.

Dependencies, semver and Cargo.lock

You write serde = "1.0". Cargo picks 1.0.229. Why that number?

cargo tree -p shop-cli --depth 1
shop-cli v0.3.0 (/home/you/shop/crates/shop-cli)
├── serde_json v1.0.154
└── shop-core v0.3.0 (/home/you/shop/crates/shop-core)

Crates use semver. A version is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. A new PATCH fixes bugs. A new MINOR adds features. A new MAJOR may break your code. The text "1.0" is a version requirement, not one exact version.

Version requirements in Cargo.toml
You writeCargo allowsName
"1.2.3">=1.2.3, <2.0.0caret, the default
"0.2.3">=0.2.3, <0.3.0caret on 0.x: MINOR acts like MAJOR
"0.0.3">=0.0.3, <0.0.4caret on 0.0.x: only this one
"~1.2.3">=1.2.3, <1.3.0tilde: patch updates only
"1.2.*">=1.2.0, <1.3.0wildcard
"=1.2.3"exactly 1.2.3exact
">=1.2, <1.5"both rules at oncea range

Cargo takes the newest version that fits. Then it writes the exact choice into Cargo.lock.

# This file is automatically @generated by Cargo.
# It is not intended for manual editing.
version = 4

[[package]]
name = "serde"
version = "1.0.229"
source = "registry+https://github.com/rust-lang/crates.io-index"
checksum = "4148590afebada386688f18773da617792bf2ef03ffc1e4cbd2b1d45b023e0ba"

The lock file makes builds repeatable. Your laptop and CI get the same versions. The checksum proves the download is the right file.

  • cargo update moves to newer versions inside your requirements.
  • cargo update -p serde updates only one crate.
  • cargo tree -d lists crates that appear in two versions, like rand 0.8 and rand 0.9.

Should you commit Cargo.lock? cargo new now tracks it by default. The Cargo FAQ says it depends on your needs. It does not affect people who use your library. Only your Cargo.toml requirements do.

You write serde = "=1.0.200" in a library to be safe. Another crate in the user's project needs 1.0.210. Now Cargo cannot find one version for both and fails. In libraries, use the normal caret form. Exact versions belong in Cargo.lock.

Features: optional parts of a crate

shop-core can turn a Price into JSON. But most users do not need serde. So JSON support is a feature.

[package]
name = "shop-core"
description = "Prices and carts for a tiny shop"
version.workspace = true
edition.workspace = true
rust-version.workspace = true
license.workspace = true

[dependencies]
serde = { workspace = true, optional = true }

[features]
default = []
serde = ["dep:serde"]           # turn on JSON support only when asked

[lints]
workspace = true

In the code, one line uses the feature: #[cfg_attr(feature = "serde", derive(serde::Serialize))]. Without the feature, the derive is gone and serde is never compiled.

  • A feature is a name in [features]. It lists what it turns on.
  • optional = true makes a dependency optional. "dep:serde" turns it on without making a public feature with the same name.
  • default lists the features that are on unless the user says default-features = false.
  • "other?/feat" turns on feat of other only if something else already turned on other.
  • On the command line: --features serde, --no-default-features, --all-features.

Features are unified. If two crates in one build use shop-core, one with serde and one without, Cargo builds it once with serde. So a feature must only add code. It must never remove or change code.

You make a feature called no_std that removes standard library code. Another crate in the build turns it on, and your code breaks for everyone. Make it positive: a feature called std, on by default. Removing a default feature later is a breaking change.

Workspaces

The root Cargo.toml of the shop has no [package]. It only lists members and shared settings.

[workspace]
members = ["crates/*"]          # every folder in crates/ is a member
resolver = "3"                  # the default for edition 2024

[workspace.package]             # shared fields, members inherit them
version = "0.3.0"
edition = "2024"
rust-version = "1.85"
license = "MIT OR Apache-2.0"

[workspace.dependencies]        # one version for the whole workspace
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1.0"

[workspace.lints.rust]
unsafe_code = "forbid"

[profile.release]
lto = "thin"
codegen-units = 1

A root without [package] is a virtual workspace. All members share three things: one Cargo.lock, one target/ folder and one set of profiles. So a crate used by two members is built only once.

  • [workspace.package]: members write version.workspace = true to inherit a field.
  • [workspace.dependencies]: members write serde = { workspace = true, optional = true }. They may add features and optional, but not change the version.
  • [workspace.lints]: one lint policy. Each member opts in with [lints] workspace = true.
  • Commands: cargo build --workspace, cargo test -p shop-core, cargo run -p shop-cli.

You put [profile.release] in a member's Cargo.toml. Cargo ignores it and warns: profiles for the non root package will be ignored. Profiles live only in the workspace root. The resolver setting also counts only in the root.

Build scripts and profiles

Sometimes code must run before the build: to compile C code, find a system library or make Rust code. That is the job of a build script.

fn main() {
    // PROFILE is "debug" or "release". Cargo sets it for build scripts.
    let profile = std::env::var("PROFILE").unwrap();
    println!("cargo::rustc-env=SHOP_PROFILE={profile}");
    println!("cargo::rerun-if-changed=build.rs"); // do not rerun on every edit
}
use shop_core::{Cart, Price};

fn main() {
    let mut cart = Cart::default();
    cart.add("tea", Price::new(450));
    cart.add("milk", Price::new(250));
    let total = cart.total();
    println!("total with tax: {} cents", total.cents());
    println!("as JSON: {}", serde_json::to_string(&total).unwrap());
    println!("{} {} ({})", env!("CARGO_PKG_NAME"), env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"), env!("SHOP_PROFILE"));
}
total with tax: 770 cents
as JSON: {"cents":770}
shop-cli 0.3.0 (debug)
total with tax: 770 cents
as JSON: {"cents":770}
shop-cli 0.3.0 (release)

A build script talks to Cargo by printing lines that start with cargo::.

  • cargo::rustc-env=KEY=VALUE sets a value for env! in your code.
  • cargo::rerun-if-changed=PATH reruns the script only when that file changes. Without any rerun line, Cargo reruns it after every change in the package.
  • cargo::rustc-cfg=NAME turns on #[cfg(NAME)]. Pair it with cargo::rustc-check-cfg so the compiler knows the name.
  • Write generated files only into the folder in OUT_DIR.
  • The double colon form needs Rust 1.77 or newer. Old scripts use one colon: cargo:rerun-if-changed.

Profiles

A profile is a set of compiler settings. cargo build uses dev. cargo build --release uses release.

Default settings of the two main profiles
SettingdevreleaseWhat it means
opt-level03How hard the compiler optimises
debugtruefalseDebug info for debuggers
debug-assertionstruefalsedebug_assert! runs or not
overflow-checkstruefalsePanic on integer overflow
incrementaltruefalseReuse work between builds
codegen-units25616More units: faster build, slower code
ltofalsefalseOptimise across crates at link time
panic"unwind""unwind""abort" makes smaller binaries

test inherits from dev, and bench inherits from release. You can add your own profile and override settings for dependencies.

[profile.dist]                  # cargo build --profile dist
inherits = "release"
lto = "fat"
strip = "symbols"

[profile.dev.package."*"]       # all dependencies, not your own crates
opt-level = 2                   # fast dependencies, quick rebuilds of your code

You measure speed with cargo run. That is the dev profile, with no optimisation. Rust code can be many times slower there. Always measure with --release.

cargo publish and the MSRV

Your library is ready. Try a publish without really uploading.

cargo publish --dry-run -p shop-core
warning: manifest has no documentation, homepage or repository
   Packaging shop-core v0.3.0 (/home/you/shop/crates/shop-core)
    Packaged 6 files, 4.3KiB (1.9KiB compressed)
   Verifying shop-core v0.3.0 (/home/you/shop/crates/shop-core)
   Compiling shop-core v0.3.0 (/home/you/target/package/shop-core-0.3.0)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.64s
   Uploading shop-core v0.3.0 (/home/you/shop/crates/shop-core)
warning: aborting upload due to dry run

Fill in the metadata

crates.io refuses a crate with no description or no license. Add repository and readme too.

Check the files

cargo package --list shows what goes into the upload. Use include or exclude to change it. The limit is 10 MB.

Dry run

cargo publish --dry-run packs the crate and builds it from the packed copy.

Log in

Make an API token on crates.io. cargo login stores it. The token is a secret.

Publish

cargo publish uploads it. Since Rust 1.90, cargo publish --workspace uploads all members in the right order.

It is permanent

You can never change or delete a version. cargo yank --version 0.3.0 only stops new projects from choosing it.

rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver

The MSRV goes in rust-version. With an older compiler, Cargo stops with a clear error. Since Rust 1.84, the resolver can also use it. Resolver "3" does this by default, and edition 2024 uses resolver 3.

Watch it work. This package says rust-version = "1.85" and depends on time = "0.3".

cargo generate-lockfile
    Updating crates.io index
     Locking 13 packages to highest Rust 1.85 compatible versions
      Adding time v0.3.45 (available: v0.3.55, requires Rust 1.88.0)
      Adding time-core v0.1.7 (available: v0.1.9, requires Rust 1.88.0)

The newest time needs Rust 1.88. So Cargo picks 0.3.45, the newest version that works on 1.85. cargo add does the same. Here an old package says rust-version = "1.70".

warning: ignoring clap@4.6.7 (which requires rustc 1.85) to maintain old's rust-version of 1.70
      Adding clap v4.4.18 to dependencies

If no version fits, the resolver does not fail. It picks a newer one anyway, and the build may break on the old compiler. The Cargo docs treat a higher MSRV as a minor change, not a major one. Test your MSRV in CI with that exact compiler, for example cargo +1.85 check.

You set rust-version = "1.85" but test only on the newest Rust. You use a new API by accident, and users on 1.85 break. Run CI on the MSRV too. Clippy's incompatible_msrv lint can warn you about APIs that are too new.

Python: pyproject.toml, uv, virtual environments and wheels

Now the same shop library in Python. uv 0.13.8 was the newest version on 2026-11-15.

uv init --lib --vcs none --author-from none --python 3.14 pyshop
cd pyshop
uv add 'httpx>=0.28'          # a normal dependency
uv add --dev pytest           # only for development
uv run python -c "import pyshop; print(pyshop.total_with_tax([450, 250]))"
uv build
Initialized project `pyshop` at `/home/you/pyshop`
770
Building source distribution...
Building wheel from source distribution...
Successfully built dist/pyshop-0.1.0.tar.gz
Successfully built dist/pyshop-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
[project]
name = "pyshop"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "httpx>=0.28",
]

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.13.8,<0.14.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "pytest>=9.2.0",
]
"""Prices and carts for a tiny shop."""

VAT_PERCENT = 10


def total_with_tax(cents: list[int]) -> int:
    subtotal = sum(cents)
    return subtotal + subtotal * VAT_PERCENT // 100
  • pyproject.toml is Python's manifest. [project] holds the name, version and dependencies. requires-python is the twin of rust-version.
  • [build-system] names the build backend. uv uses its own backend, uv_build, by default.
  • [dependency-groups] holds development tools. It is the twin of [dev-dependencies].
  • uv.lock records exact versions, like Cargo.lock.
  • .venv/ is a virtual environment. Each project gets its own packages, so two projects never fight over versions. uv run uses it for you.

A wheel is a zip file that installs without a build step. Its name tells where it works.

Reading a wheel file name
WheelPython tagABI tagPlatform tag
pyshop-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whlpy3: any Python 3none: no compiled codeany: every system
numpy-2.5.4-cp314-cp314-macosx_14_0_arm64.whlcp314: CPython 3.14cp314macOS 14 or newer on Apple chips

Pure Python code makes one wheel for all systems. Code with compiled parts, written in C or Rust, needs one wheel per platform. The chapter Rust and Python together builds such wheels with maturin. uv publish uploads the files in dist/ to PyPI.

uv also has workspaces. The root pyproject.toml lists [tool.uv.workspace] members = ["packages/*"]. A member uses another member with [tool.uv.sources] pyshop = { workspace = true }. The whole workspace shares one uv.lock, just like Cargo.

Cargo and uv side by side
JobRust and CargoPython and uv
ManifestCargo.tomlpyproject.toml
Lock fileCargo.lockuv.lock
Add a dependencycargo add serdeuv add httpx
Dev-only tools[dev-dependencies][dependency-groups] dev
Optional parts[features][project.optional-dependencies]
Oldest supported versionrust-versionrequires-python
Where packages goa shared cache and target/the project's .venv/
Package file.crate (source only)wheel and sdist
Publishcargo publish to crates.iouv publish to PyPI

You run pip install into the system Python. Now your tools and your projects share one set of packages, and versions clash. Use one virtual environment per project. With uv, uv add and uv run take care of it.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for Cargo, crates and workspaces
PatternPurposeModelNote
pub(crate) fnShare inside the crate onlypub(crate) fn with_tax(self)Not part of your public API.
pub use path::Item;Give users a short, stable pathpub use cart::Cart;You can move files freely later.
Private field + pub fn newKeep values validpub struct Price { cents: u64 }Outsiders must use the constructor.
name = "1.2"Allow compatible updatesserde = "1.0"On 0.x, the MINOR number breaks.
{ path = "..", version = ".." }Local now, crates.io after publishshop-core = { path = "../shop-core", version = "0.3.0" }Needed to publish a crate with path deps.
feat = ["dep:x"]An optional dependency behind a featureserde = ["dep:serde"]Features must only add code.
#[cfg(feature = "x")]Compile code only with a feature#[cfg_attr(feature = "serde", derive(Serialize))]Test both with and without it.
[workspace.dependencies]One version for all membersserde.workspace = trueMembers may add features only.
cargo::rerun-if-changed=..Rerun a build script only when neededcargo::rerun-if-changed=build.rsWithout it, any change reruns it.
[profile.X] inherits = ".."Your own build mode[profile.dist] inherits = "release"Only in the workspace root.
rust-version = ".."State your MSRVrust-version = "1.85"Resolver 3 picks versions that fit it.
cargo publish --dry-runCheck before a permanent uploadcargo publish --dry-run -p shop-coreA version can never be replaced.
uv add / uv run / uv buildPython dependencies, run and packageuv add 'httpx>=0.28'uv keeps .venv and uv.lock in sync.

Practice

How many library crates can one package have?

  • None
  • At most one
  • As many as you like

A package has at most one library crate, but any number of binary crates.

Which versions does regex = "0.2.3" allow?

  • >=0.2.3, <1.0.0
  • >=0.2.3, <0.3.0
  • exactly 0.2.3

For 0.x versions, the MINOR number counts as breaking. So 0.3.0 is not allowed.

Two crates in one build use shop-core. One turns on the serde feature. What does Cargo build?

  • Two copies of shop-core.
  • One copy, with serde on.
  • One copy, with serde off.

Features are unified. Cargo builds the crate once with every requested feature.

Your package has rust-version = "1.85" and edition 2024. The newest version of a dependency needs Rust 1.88. What does cargo generate-lockfile do?

  • It fails with an error.
  • It picks an older version that works on 1.85, if one fits the requirement.
  • It upgrades your rust-version.

Edition 2024 uses resolver 3, which prefers versions that match your MSRV.

To make a function visible in the whole crate but not outside, write <span class="blank" data-answer="pub(crate)">?</span> fn.

The requirement "~1.2.3" allows versions below ?.

The Python twin of [dev-dependencies] in uv is the table ?.

In the wheel tag py3-none-any, the word any is the ? tag.

  1. Write the line in lib.rs that lets users write mylib::Parser although the type lives in src/parse/parser.rs (module parse::parser).
    Answer

    pub use parse::parser::Parser; The modules parse and parser may stay private.

  2. Add an optional dependency chrono behind a feature named time. Write both tables.
    Answer

    [dependencies] with chrono = { version = "0.4", optional = true }, and [features] with time = ["dep:chrono"].

  3. A workspace has three members that all use tokio. How do you make sure they all use the same version requirement?
    Answer

    Put tokio = "1" under [workspace.dependencies] in the root. In each member, write tokio.workspace = true, or tokio = { workspace = true, features = ["rt"] }.

  4. Your build script generates a file from schema.json. It reruns on every edit and slows the build. Fix it.
    Answer

    Print cargo::rerun-if-changed=schema.json and cargo::rerun-if-changed=build.rs. Then Cargo reruns the script only when one of these files changes. Write the output into OUT_DIR.

  5. You published version 1.4.0 with a bad bug. Can you replace it? What do you do?
    Answer

    No. A published version can never be changed or deleted. Publish a fixed 1.4.1. Then run cargo yank --version 1.4.0 so that new projects do not pick it. Old lock files keep working.

  6. Hard: why must Cargo features be additive? Give a concrete case that goes wrong.
    Answer

    Cargo unifies features, so one crate in the build can turn a feature on for everyone. If a feature no_std removed the standard library parts, crate A could turn it on while crate B still calls those parts. B would fail to compile, though B never asked for no_std. A positive std feature avoids this.

  7. Hard: why does pure Python code ship one wheel, but numpy ships many wheels per release?
    Answer

    Pure Python runs on any interpreter, so the tags are py3-none-any. numpy contains compiled code. That code depends on the CPython version (ABI) and on the operating system and CPU. So numpy builds one wheel for each mix, like cp314-cp314-macosx_14_0_arm64.

Key takeaways

  • A workspace holds packages. A package holds at most one library crate and any number of binaries. A crate is a tree of modules.
  • Everything is private by default. Open it with pub(super), pub(crate) or pub, and give a clean path with pub use.
  • Requirements like "1.2" allow compatible updates. Cargo.lock records the exact versions.
  • Features are optional, unified and must only add code.
  • A workspace shares one lock file, one target folder, profiles and inherited fields.
  • Set rust-version. Resolver 3, the default in edition 2024, picks dependencies that fit it.
  • A publish is permanent. Dry-run first. Yank only stops new users.
  • Python uses pyproject.toml, uv.lock and one .venv per project. Wheels carry tags for Python version, ABI and platform.

Sources

  • The Cargo Book: The Manifest Format. Every key of Cargo.toml.
  • The Cargo Book: Specifying Dependencies. Version requirements, git, path and workspace dependencies.
  • The Cargo Book: Features. Optional dependencies, dep: and feature unification.
  • The Cargo Book: Dependency Resolution. Resolver versions and the MSRV-aware resolver.
  • The Cargo Book: Build Scripts. The cargo:: instructions and OUT_DIR.
  • uv: Creating projects. uv init, the uv_build backend and the project layout.

Testing and tooling

A test is a small program that checks your program. Good tests let you change code without fear. Rust ships a test runner, a formatter and a linter with the toolchain. Python has the same jobs done by pytest, ruff and a type checker. This chapter shows all of them on one small library, and it ends with a CI pipeline.

  • Write unit, integration and doc tests, and organise them well.
  • Use the assert macros, test attributes and the most useful cargo test flags.
  • Find hidden bugs with property tests, and measure speed with a benchmark.
  • Keep code clean with rustfmt, clippy and rust-analyzer, and with ruff and mypy in Python.
  • Measure coverage and run everything in a CI pipeline.

Your first tests

Here is a small library called textkit. It turns titles into URL slugs and parses times like "2m". The tests live in the same file.

pub fn slugify(title: &str) -> String {
    let mut out = String::new();
    for c in title.chars() {
        if c.is_ascii_alphanumeric() {
            out.push(c.to_ascii_lowercase());
        } else if !out.is_empty() && !out.ends_with('-') {
            out.push('-');                 // one dash for any run of other chars
        }
    }
    while out.ends_with('-') {
        out.pop();
    }
    out
}

#[cfg(test)]                               // compiled only for cargo test
mod tests {
    use super::*;                          // see private items too

    #[test]
    fn slug_basic() {
        assert_eq!(slugify("Rust 2024 Edition"), "rust-2024-edition");
    }

    #[test]
    fn slug_trims_dashes() {
        assert_eq!(slugify("  --Hi!--  "), "hi");
    }
}
from textkit import slugify


def test_slug_basic() -> None:
    assert slugify("Rust 2024 Edition") == "rust-2024-edition"


def test_slug_trims_dashes() -> None:
    assert slugify("  --Hi!--  ") == "hi"
cargo test
running 7 tests
test tests::slug_many ... ignored, slow: runs a million inputs
test tests::seconds_units ... ok
test tests::seconds_errors ... ok
test tests::slug_trims_dashes ... ok
test tests::slug_basic ... ok
test tests::wrap_pieces ... ok
test tests::wrap_zero_width_panics - should panic ... ok

test result: ok. 6 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.00s

The full file has a few more tests. You will meet them in the next sections.

  • A test in Rust is a function with #[test] above it. It passes if it returns without a panic.
  • #[cfg(test)] means: compile this module only for tests. Your normal build stays small.
  • use super::*; brings in everything from the parent module, even private functions.
  • Tests run in parallel, on many threads. So their order in the output changes from run to run.

In Python, pytest finds files named test_*.py and functions named test_*. A plain assert is enough. pytest 9.2.0 was the newest version on 2026-11-15. Run it with uv run pytest.

You forget #[test] above a function in mod tests. The function compiles, but it never runs. Cargo even warns: function `checks_one` is never used. Count the tests in the output. If a new test is missing, look for the attribute.

Assert macros and test attributes

A test needs a way to say "this is wrong". Here is a failing test in both languages. Compare the messages.

use textkit::slugify;

#[test]
fn ampersand_word() {
    assert_eq!(slugify("Rust & Python"), "rust-and-python", "input had an &");
}
from textkit import slugify


def test_ampersand() -> None:
    assert slugify("Rust & Python") == "rust-and-python"
thread 'ampersand_word' (116135230) panicked at tests/fail_demo.rs:5:5:
assertion `left == right` failed: input had an &
  left: "rust-python"
 right: "rust-and-python"
>       assert slugify("Rust & Python") == "rust-and-python"
E       AssertionError: assert 'rust-python' == 'rust-and-python'
E
E         - rust-and-python
E         ?     ----
E         + rust-python

test_fail.py:5: AssertionError

pytest rewrites your plain assert so it can show both values. Rust uses macros instead.

Rust assert macros
MacroChecksExample
assert!(cond)The condition is trueassert!(err.contains("unit"))
assert_eq!(a, b)The values are equal. Shows both on failure.assert_eq!(wrap("abcdef", 4), ["abcd", "ef"])
assert_ne!(a, b)The values are not equalassert_ne!(wrap("abc", 1).len(), 1)
assert!(matches!(v, pat))A value fits a patternassert!(matches!(r, Err(_)))
debug_assert!(cond)Like assert!, but only in debug buildscheap checks inside hot code

Every macro takes an extra message, like format!: assert!(ok, "got: {err}"). assert_eq! needs both values to implement PartialEq and Debug.

Test attributes

#[test]
fn seconds_errors() -> Result<(), String> {
    let err = parse_seconds("5x").unwrap_err();
    assert!(err.contains("unknown unit"), "got: {err}");
    parse_seconds("1m")?;              // a test can use ? too
    Ok(())
}

#[test]
#[should_panic(expected = "width must be at least 1")]
fn wrap_zero_width_panics() {
    wrap("abc", 0);
}

#[test]
#[ignore = "slow: runs a million inputs"]
fn slug_many() {
    for i in 0..1_000_000 {
        assert!(!slugify(&format!("item {i}")).is_empty());
    }
}
  • A test can return Result<(), E>. An Err fails the test, and you can use ? inside.
  • #[should_panic(expected = "...")] passes only if the code panics with that text in the message.
  • #[ignore = "reason"] skips a slow test. Run it on purpose with cargo test -- --ignored.

pytest has the same tools. with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="unknown unit"): expects an exception. @pytest.mark.skip skips a test. @pytest.mark.parametrize runs one test with many inputs.

You write #[should_panic] with no expected. Now the test passes for any panic, even an index error in the wrong line. Always add expected = "..." with a piece of the real message.

Unit, integration and doc tests

Rust has three kinds of tests. Each kind sees a different part of your crate.

  • A unit test lives in mod tests next to the code. It can test private helpers.
  • An integration test lives in the tests/ folder. Each file there is its own crate. It sees only pub items.
  • A doc test is a code example in a /// comment. Your docs can never go out of date, because the examples must pass.
mod common;                       // loads tests/common/mod.rs

use textkit::slugify;             // only the public API is visible here

#[test]
fn every_title_gives_a_slug() {
    for t in common::titles() {
        let s = slugify(t);
        assert!(!s.is_empty(), "empty slug for {t:?}");
    }
}

Doc tests

/// Splits `text` into pieces of at most `width` chars.
///
/// ```
/// # use textkit::wrap;          // a hidden line: it runs, but docs do not show it
/// assert_eq!(wrap("abcdef", 4), ["abcd", "ef"]);
/// ```
///
/// # Panics
///
/// Panics if `width` is 0.
///
/// ```should_panic
/// textkit::wrap("abc", 0);
/// ```
///
/// ```compile_fail
/// let n: u64 = textkit::wrap("abc", 2); // a Vec is not a u64
/// ```
pub fn wrap(text: &str, width: usize) -> Vec<String> {
    assert!(width > 0, "width must be at least 1");
    let chars: Vec<char> = text.chars().collect();
    chars.chunks(width).map(|piece| piece.iter().collect()).collect()
}
   Doc-tests textkit

running 4 tests
test src/lib.rs - parse_seconds (line 26) ... ok
test src/lib.rs - wrap (line 54) - should panic ... ok
test src/lib.rs - slugify (line 5) ... ok
test src/lib.rs - wrap (line 45) ... ok

test result: ok. 4 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.02s

running 1 test
test src/lib.rs - wrap (line 58) - compile fail ... ok

test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.10s

all doctests ran in 0.97s; merged doctests compilation took 0.47s

Tags after the three backticks change the rules. should_panic expects a panic. compile_fail expects a compile error. no_run compiles but does not run, which is good for network code. ignore skips the example. A line that starts with # runs but is hidden in the docs.

Look at the last line of the output. Since the 2024 edition, rustdoc merges doc tests into one binary. That is much faster. A compile_fail test still builds alone, so it has its own block. Python has the same idea: pytest --doctest-modules runs the >>> examples in docstrings.

Your crate is only a binary, with all code in main.rs. Integration tests cannot import anything from it. Move the logic into src/lib.rs and keep main.rs thin. Then tests/ can use the library.

cargo test flags

You can choose which tests run. A word after cargo test is a filter. Only tests whose names contain it run.

cargo test --lib slug
running 3 tests
test tests::slug_many ... ignored, slow: runs a million inputs
test tests::slug_trims_dashes ... ok
test tests::slug_basic ... ok

test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored; 0 measured; 4 filtered out; finished in 0.00s

Flags before -- go to Cargo. Flags after -- go to the test harness, the built-in test runner.

Useful cargo test flags
CommandWhat it does
cargo test slugRuns tests whose name contains slug
cargo test --libOnly unit tests in the library
cargo test --test apiOnly the integration file tests/api.rs
cargo test --docOnly doc tests
cargo test -p shop-coreOnly one package of a workspace
cargo test --no-fail-fastKeeps going after a test binary fails
cargo test -- --exact tests::slug_basicOnly the test with exactly this name
cargo test -- --ignoredOnly ignored tests. --include-ignored runs all.
cargo test -- --nocaptureShows println! output of passing tests too
cargo test -- --test-threads=1One test at a time, for tests that share a file or port
cargo test -- --listLists the tests without running them

pytest has the twins: pytest -k slug filters by name, -x stops at the first failure, -s shows prints, and -v lists every test.

Two tests write the same file out.txt. They pass alone but fail together, because tests run in parallel. Give each test its own temporary folder. As a quick check, run -- --test-threads=1. If the failure goes away, the tests share state.

Property tests with proptest

Your examples test the inputs you thought of. A property test tries inputs you did not think of. Here is parse_seconds. Its unit tests pass.

pub fn parse_seconds(text: &str) -> Result<u64, String> {
    let (num, unit) = text.split_at(text.len().saturating_sub(1));
    let n: u64 = num.parse().map_err(|_| format!("bad number in {text:?}"))?;
    let factor = match unit {
        "s" => 1,
        "m" => 60,
        "h" => 3600,
        _ => return Err(format!("unknown unit in {text:?}")),
    };
    Ok(n * factor)
}

Now write rules that must hold for every input. proptest 1.12.0 was the newest version on 2026-11-15. Add it with cargo add --dev proptest.

use proptest::prelude::*;
use textkit::{parse_seconds, slugify};

proptest! {
    #[test]
    fn slug_has_only_safe_chars(s in ".*") {   // any string
        let slug = slugify(&s);
        prop_assert!(slug.chars().all(|c| c.is_ascii_lowercase() || c.is_ascii_digit() || c == '-'));
        prop_assert!(!slug.starts_with('-') && !slug.ends_with('-'));
        prop_assert!(!slug.contains("--"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn slug_twice_is_slug_once(s in ".*") {
        let once = slugify(&s);
        prop_assert_eq!(slugify(&once), once);
    }

    #[test]
    fn parse_never_panics(s in "\\PC{0,6}") {  // up to 6 printable chars
        let _ = parse_seconds(&s);
    }
}
test parse_never_panics ... FAILED
test slug_twice_is_slug_once ... ok
test slug_has_only_safe_chars ... ok

---- parse_never_panics stdout ----
end byte index 2 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'נ' (bytes 1..3 of string)
end byte index 1 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'נ' (bytes 0..2 of string)
...
end byte index 1 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'א' (bytes 0..2 of string)
Test failed: end byte index 1 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'א' (bytes 0..2 of string).
minimal failing input: s = "א"

A property test makes hundreds of random inputs from a strategy. Here the strategy is a regex: ".*" means any string. After a failure, proptest shrinks the input. It found a Hebrew text, then cut it down to one letter: "א".

The bug: split_at cuts by bytes. The letter א takes two bytes in UTF-8, so the cut lands inside it and Rust panics. A user could crash the program with one letter. Here is the fix.

pub fn parse_seconds(text: &str) -> Result<u64, String> {
    let unit = text.chars().last().ok_or("empty input")?;
    let num = &text[..text.len() - unit.len_utf8()];   // cut on a char boundary
    let n: u64 = num.parse().map_err(|_| format!("bad number in {text:?}"))?;
    let factor = match unit {
        's' => 1,
        'm' => 60,
        'h' => 3600,
        _ => return Err(format!("unknown unit in {text:?}")),
    };
    n.checked_mul(factor).ok_or_else(|| format!("too big: {text:?}"))
}

Now all three properties pass. The fix also uses checked_mul, so a huge number gives an error, not an overflow. Good properties to test:

  • It never panics on any input.
  • Doing it twice changes nothing: slugify(slugify(s)) == slugify(s).
  • A round trip gives back the start: parse(format(x)) == x.
  • An output rule: only safe characters, sorted, no duplicates.

Python's twin is Hypothesis. @given(st.text()) plays the role of s in ".*".

from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

from textkit import slugify


@given(st.text())                      # hypothesis: any string
def test_slug_twice_is_slug_once(s: str) -> None:
    once = slugify(s)
    assert slugify(once) == once

You write a property that copies the code: assert_eq!(slugify(s), my_own_slugify(s)). If both have the same bug, the test passes. Test rules that are simpler than the code: "only safe characters", "no double dash".

Benchmarks

How fast is slugify? Guessing is not enough. A benchmark measures it. The built-in #[bench] works only on nightly Rust, so most projects use the criterion crate. Version 0.8.2 was the newest on 2026-11-15.

[dev-dependencies]
criterion = "0.8.2"
proptest = "1.12.0"

[[bench]]
name = "slug"
harness = false                 # criterion brings its own main
use criterion::{Criterion, criterion_group, criterion_main};
use std::hint::black_box;
use textkit::slugify;

fn bench_slugify(c: &mut Criterion) {
    let title = "Rust 2024 Edition: What Changed, and Why It Matters";
    c.bench_function("slugify 50 chars", |b| {
        b.iter(|| slugify(black_box(title)))   // black_box: do not optimise away
    });
}

criterion_group!(benches, bench_slugify);
criterion_main!(benches);
cargo bench
Benchmarking slugify 50 chars: Warming up for 3.0000 s
Benchmarking slugify 50 chars: Collecting 100 samples in estimated 5.0008 s (26M iterations)
Benchmarking slugify 50 chars: Analyzing
slugify 50 chars        time:   [195.08 ns 197.01 ns 199.36 ns]
Found 4 outliers among 100 measurements (4.00%)
  3 (3.00%) high mild
  1 (1.00%) high severe

The three times are a range. The middle one, 197 ns, is the best guess. The outer two show how sure criterion is. cargo bench uses the bench profile, which inherits release. Run it again after a change, and criterion reports the change in percent.

std::hint::black_box hides a value from the optimiser. Without it, the compiler may see that the result is never used and remove the work. Then you measure nothing. In Python, use python -m timeit for small code, or the pytest-benchmark plugin.

You benchmark on a laptop while a video call runs. The numbers jump by 30%. Close other programs, plug in the power, and compare runs on the same machine. A single number from one run means little.

rustfmt, clippy and rust-analyzer

Three tools come with the Rust toolchain. Here is some messy but working code.

pub fn count_long(words: &Vec<String>) -> usize {
    let mut n = 0;
    for i in 0..words.len() {
        if (words[i].len() > 5) == true {
            n = n + 1;
        }
    }
    n
}

pub fn is_blank(s: &str) -> bool {
    s.len() == 0
}
cargo clippy
warning: writing `&Vec` instead of `&[_]` involves a new object where a slice will do
 --> src/lib.rs:1:26
  |
1 | pub fn count_long(words: &Vec<String>) -> usize {
  |                          ^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = help: for further information visit https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/rust-1.99.0/index.html#ptr_arg

 --> src/lib.rs:3:14

warning: equality checks against true are unnecessary
 --> src/lib.rs:4:12
  |
4 |         if (words[i].len() > 5) == true {
  |            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ help: try: `words[i].len() > 5`

 --> src/lib.rs:5:13

  --> src/lib.rs:12:5
   |
12 |     s.len() == 0
   |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^ help: using `is_empty` is clearer and more explicit: `s.is_empty()`

warning: `lintme` (lib) generated 5 warnings (run `cargo clippy --fix --lib -p lintme -- ` to apply 3 suggestions)

Clippy is a linter. Its README says it has over 800 lints. They come in groups:

  • correctness (an error by default), suspicious, style, complexity and perf (warnings by default).
  • pedantic, nursery, restriction and cargo are off. Turn on the ones you want.
  • Set levels in Cargo.toml under [lints.clippy], for example pedantic = "warn".
  • cargo clippy --fix applies the safe suggestions for you.

rustfmt formats code in one standard style. Nobody argues about spaces any more.

cargo fmt --check
Diff in /home/you/lintme/src/fmt_demo.rs:1:
-pub fn area(w:f64,h:f64)->f64{ if w<0.0||h<0.0 {return 0.0} w*h }
+pub fn area(w: f64, h: f64) -> f64 {
+    if w < 0.0 || h < 0.0 {
+        return 0.0;
+    }
+    w * h
+}

cargo fmt rewrites the files. cargo fmt --check only reports and fails, which is what CI needs. A rustfmt.toml file holds the few options, but most projects keep the default style.

rust-analyzer is the language server for Rust. Your editor talks to it. It shows types inline, jumps to definitions, renames safely, and puts a "Run test" button above each #[test]. It can run clippy instead of cargo check on every save.

The Python twins: ruff, mypy and pyright

import os
import json


def total(prices: list[int]) -> int:
    result = 0
    for p in prices:
        result = result + p
    return result


def label(n: int) -> str:
    if n == None:
        return "none"
    return "count: " + n
uv run --with ruff ruff check messy.py
uv run --with mypy mypy messy.py
messy.py:1:1: I001 [*] Import block is un-sorted or un-formatted
messy.py:1:8: F401 [*] `os` imported but unused
messy.py:2:8: F401 [*] `json` imported but unused
Found 3 errors.
[*] 3 fixable with `--fix`.

messy.py:15: error: Unsupported operand types for + ("str" and "int")  [operator]
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
  • ruff is a linter and formatter for Python, written in Rust. ruff check is the clippy twin. ruff format is the rustfmt twin. Version 0.17.5 was the newest on 2026-11-15.
  • Ruff 0.16.0 raised its default rule set from 59 to 413 rules. On 0.17.5 I counted 407 rules on by default. Pin the version and choose rules under [tool.ruff.lint], or a new release can break your CI.
  • mypy (2.4.1) and pyright (1.1.414) check type hints. They find type errors that Rust's compiler would find. Use mypy --strict for new code.

You add #[allow(clippy::all)] at the top of a file to make the warnings go away. Now real bugs hide too. Fix the code, or allow one lint on one item with a comment that says why: #[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)] // matches the C API.

Coverage and CI

Which lines did your tests run? A coverage tool tells you. Here is the Python version, with the pytest-cov plugin.

uv run --with pytest --with hypothesis --with pytest-cov pytest --cov=textkit --cov-report=term-missing
Name         Stmts   Miss  Cover   Missing
------------------------------------------
textkit.py      13      0   100%
------------------------------------------
TOTAL           13      0   100%
7 passed in 1.28s

For Rust, the common tool is cargo-llvm-cov. It wraps the compiler flag -C instrument-coverage. Install it with cargo +stable install cargo-llvm-cov --locked, then run cargo llvm-cov for a summary or cargo llvm-cov --html for a report. I did not run it on this machine, because it needs an extra toolchain part, llvm-tools-preview.

100% coverage does not mean no bugs. The first parse_seconds had full line coverage from its unit tests. The property test still found a crash. Coverage shows what you did not test. It cannot show that a test is good.

A CI pipeline
