CI runs your checks on a server for every push and pull request. Here is a GitHub Actions workflow for a project with Rust and Python.

name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  rust:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: clippy, rustfmt
      - run: cargo fmt --all --check
      - run: cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features
        env:
          CARGO_BUILD_WARNINGS: deny    # any warning fails the job
      - run: cargo test --all-features

  msrv:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@1.85.0   # the rust-version in Cargo.toml
      - run: cargo check --all-features

  python:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.3
      - run: uv run ruff check
      - run: uv run ruff format --check
      - run: uv run mypy src
      - run: uv run pytest

Get the code

actions/checkout copies your repository onto a fresh machine.

Install Rust

dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable installs stable Rust with clippy and rustfmt.

Check the format

cargo fmt --all --check fails in a second if someone forgot to format. Cheap checks go first.

Lint

CARGO_BUILD_WARNINGS=deny turns every warning into an error. Cargo respects this setting since 1.97.

Test

cargo test --all-features runs unit, integration, property and doc tests.

Check the MSRV

A second job builds with the oldest Rust you promise in rust-version.

I checked the YAML with a parser, and the versions were the newest on 2026-11-15: actions/checkout v7 and astral-sh/setup-uv v10.3.3. I could not run the workflow itself here. Check the action pages before you copy it: versions change.

You use cargo clippy -- -D warnings in CI and plain cargo clippy on your laptop. The flags differ, so Cargo rebuilds everything each time you switch. The Clippy README now suggests CARGO_BUILD_WARNINGS=deny, which keeps the build cache. On Cargo older than 1.97, -- -D warnings is still the way.

"How do you test a Rust library?" A strong answer names all layers: unit tests for private logic, integration tests for the public API, doc tests for examples, property tests for edge cases, clippy and rustfmt in CI, and an MSRV job.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for testing and tooling
PatternPurposeModelNote
#[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; }Unit tests next to the code#[test] fn slug_basic() { ... }They may test private items.
assert_eq!(got, want, "msg")Compare two valuesassert_eq!(slugify("A B"), "a-b")Both sides need Debug and PartialEq.
fn t() -> Result<(), E>Use ? in a testparse_seconds("1m")?; Ok(())An Err fails the test.
#[should_panic(expected = "..")]Expect a panic with this textexpected = "width must be at least 1"Never leave out expected.
#[ignore = "reason"]Skip a slow test by defaultcargo test -- --ignoredRun ignored tests in CI at night.
tests/name.rsIntegration test, public API onlycargo test --test apiShared code goes in tests/common/mod.rs.
/// ``` ... ```Doc test: docs that are checked/// assert_eq!(wrap("ab", 1).len(), 2);# hides setup lines.
proptest! { fn p(s in ".*") }Check a rule on random inputsprop_assert_eq!(slugify(&once), once)Read the shrunk minimal input.
b.iter(|| f(black_box(x)))Benchmark with criterionc.bench_function("slugify", ...)Set harness = false.
cargo fmt --checkFail CI on unformatted codecargo fmt --all --checkRun cargo fmt locally first.
CARGO_BUILD_WARNINGS=deny cargo clippyLint with no warnings allowed--all-targets --all-featuresCargo 1.97 or newer.
with pytest.raises(E, match=".."):Python: expect an exceptionpytest.raises(ValueError, match="unit")The twin of should_panic.
uv run ruff check / mypy --strictPython lint and type checkuv run ruff format --checkPin tool versions in CI.

Practice

Where do integration tests live in a Cargo package?

  • In src/tests.rs
  • In the tests/ folder
  • In mod tests inside lib.rs

Each file in tests/ is its own crate and sees only the public API.

Which command shows the println! output of passing tests?

  • cargo test --verbose
  • cargo test -- --nocapture
  • cargo test --print

Flags after -- go to the test harness. --nocapture turns off output capture.

What does proptest do after it finds a failing input?

  • It stops at once and prints the random input.
  • It shrinks the input to a small, simple case that still fails.
  • It fixes the code.

Shrinking turned a long Hebrew string into one letter, "א". Small inputs are easy to debug.

Why use black_box in a benchmark?

  • To make the code run faster.
  • To stop the optimiser from removing the work you measure.
  • To hide the result from the user.

If the compiler sees an unused result, it may delete the whole call. Then the benchmark measures nothing.

A test module is compiled only for tests because of the attribute #[<span class="blank" data-answer="cfg(test)">?</span>].

To run only doc tests, write cargo test --<span class="blank" data-answer="doc">?</span>.

A line in a doc test that starts with <span class="blank" data-answer="#">?</span> runs but is hidden in the docs.

The Python twin of clippy is ruff <span class="blank" data-answer="check">?</span>.

  1. Write a unit test that checks slugify("") returns an empty string.
    Answer

    #[test] fn slug_empty() { assert_eq!(slugify(""), ""); } inside mod tests.

  2. Write a test that expects parse_seconds("7d") to fail with a message that contains "unknown unit". Use a test that returns nothing.
    Answer

    #[test] fn days_unknown() { let err = parse_seconds("7d").unwrap_err(); assert!(err.contains("unknown unit"), "got: {err}"); }

  3. Your binary crate has all its code in main.rs. You want integration tests. What do you change?
    Answer

    Move the logic into src/lib.rs as public functions. Keep main.rs small: it calls the library. Then files in tests/ can write use mycrate::....

  4. Write a property for a function reverse(s: &str) -> String.
    Answer

    Reversing twice gives the start back: prop_assert_eq!(reverse(&reverse(&s)), s);. Another one: the length in chars stays the same.

  5. Your CI fails on cargo fmt --check, but the code compiles. What happened, and how do you fix it?
    Answer

    Someone pushed code that is not in the standard format. Run cargo fmt locally and commit the result. Many people also set their editor to format on save.

  6. Hard: why did split_at(text.len() - 1) panic on "א", and why did the unit tests not catch it?
    Answer

    split_at takes a byte index. "א" is two bytes in UTF-8, so index 1 is inside the letter, and Rust panics. The unit tests used only ASCII inputs like "90s", where each char is one byte. Only random inputs with other letters showed the bug.

  7. Hard: your team wants "100% coverage" as a CI rule. Give one good and one bad effect.
    Answer

    Good: no code is left without any test, and dead code becomes visible. Bad: people write weak tests that only run lines but check nothing. Our first parse_seconds had full coverage and still crashed. A coverage floor helps, but it does not replace property tests and review.

Key takeaways

  • Unit tests live in #[cfg(test)] mod tests and see private items. Integration tests live in tests/ and see only the public API.
  • Doc tests keep examples true. Since the 2024 edition, rustdoc merges them into one binary.
  • assert_eq! shows both values. Add expected to should_panic. Tests can return Result.
  • Use filters and flags after -- to run the tests you need.
  • Property tests find inputs you never thought of, and shrink them to a small case.
  • Benchmark in release mode with criterion and black_box.
  • rustfmt, clippy and rust-analyzer come with Rust. ruff, mypy and pyright do the same jobs for Python.
  • CI runs format, lint, tests and the MSRV build on every push. Pin tool versions.

Sources

  • The Rust Programming Language: Writing Automated Tests. Unit and integration tests, attributes and test organisation.
  • The Edition Guide: Rustdoc combined tests. Merged doc tests in the 2024 edition.
  • Clippy on GitHub. Lint groups, levels and CARGO_BUILD_WARNINGS.
  • proptest on docs.rs. Strategies, prop_assert and shrinking.
  • cargo-llvm-cov on GitHub. Source-based code coverage for Rust.
  • Ruff: Default rules. The rules ruff turns on without any configuration.

The 15 patterns of Rust and Python

A pattern is a shape of code that solves one problem again and again. This page collects fifteen patterns that you will use every week. Each one has a Rust model, a Python twin and one warning.

  • Name the fifteen patterns and the problem that each one solves.
  • Write each pattern in Rust and find its twin in Python.
  • Choose between two close patterns, for example a generic and a trait object.
  • Spot the common mistake of each pattern before it reaches production.

How this page works

Think of an English book with sentence patterns. "I would like + noun" is a shape. You fill it with your own words. Code works the same way.

A pattern is such a shape. You learn it one time. Then you see it in every project. It also gives you a name to use in a code review.

This page has fifteen patterns in five groups. Each group has three patterns. Click the tree to open a group.

Every pattern below has the same four parts.

  1. Use it when. The problem in one sentence.
  2. Example. Working code in a Rust tab and a Python tab, with the real output.
  3. Rule. The pattern in a few short lines.
  4. Mistake. The one error that people make most often.

All code on this page ran on rustc 1.99.0 and Python 3.14. Most patterns also have their own chapter. This page is the short version. The links lead to the long version.

Rust often puts a rule into the type. The compiler then checks it. Python often puts the same rule into a habit. You or a type checker must remember it.

Group 1: Missing values and errors

Pattern 1: Option instead of null

Use it when a value may be absent. A search may find nothing. A field may be empty.

// Return Some(name) or None. There is no null in Rust.
fn find_user(id: u32) -> Option<&'static str> {
    match id {
        1 => Some("Ann"),
        2 => Some("Bo"),
        _ => None,
    }
}

fn main() {
    // 1. match: handle both cases
    match find_user(1) {
        Some(name) => println!("found {name}"),
        None => println!("no user"),
    }
    // 2. a default value
    let name = find_user(9).unwrap_or("guest");
    println!("hello {name}");
    // 3. let else: leave early when there is no value
    let Some(name) = find_user(2) else {
        return;
    };
    println!("{} letters", name.len());
}
found Ann
hello guest
2 letters
def find_user(id: int) -> str | None:
    users = {1: "Ann", 2: "Bo"}
    return users.get(id)  # None when the key is missing


name = find_user(1)
if name is not None:
    print(f"found {name}")

name = find_user(9) or "guest"
print(f"hello {name}")

name = find_user(2)
if name is None:
    raise SystemExit
print(f"{len(name)} letters")
found Ann
hello guest
2 letters

Rule. Return Option<T>. The type says "maybe". The value is Some(x) or None. The compiler does not let you use x before you check. Python writes str | None. There, only a type checker reminds you to check.

You open an Option with match, if let, let else, unwrap_or or ?.

Do not write .unwrap() everywhere. It stops the program with a panic when the value is None. In Python, do not write if name: for this check. An empty string is false too. Write if name is None:.

Pattern 2: Result and the ? operator

Use it when an action can fail and the caller should decide what to do.

use std::num::ParseIntError;

// The ? returns the error to the caller at once.
fn parse_port(text: &str) -> Result<u16, ParseIntError> {
    let port: u16 = text.trim().parse()?;
    Ok(port)
}

fn sum_ports(a: &str, b: &str) -> Result<u32, ParseIntError> {
    let total = parse_port(a)? as u32 + parse_port(b)? as u32;
    Ok(total)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", parse_port(" 8080 "));
    println!("{:?}", sum_ports("80", "443"));
    match sum_ports("80", "http") {
        Ok(n) => println!("total {n}"),
        Err(e) => println!("error: {e}"),
    }
}
Ok(8080)
Ok(523)
error: invalid digit found in string
def parse_port(text: str) -> int:
    port = int(text.strip())  # raises ValueError on bad text
    if not 0 <= port <= 65535:
        raise ValueError(f"port out of range: {port}")
    return port


def sum_ports(a: str, b: str) -> int:
    return parse_port(a) + parse_port(b)  # errors rise on their own


print(parse_port(" 8080 "))
print(sum_ports("80", "443"))
try:
    print(sum_ports("80", "http"))
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"error: {e}")
8080
523
error: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'http'

Rule. Return Result<T, E>. Put ? after each call that can fail. On Ok(v), the ? gives you v. On Err(e), the ? returns Err(e) from your function at once. In Python an exception rises on its own. So the twin of ? is simply "do nothing".

The Rust version shows the risk in the type. A reader sees Result and knows the call can fail. In Python you must read the code or the documentation.

The ? works only in a function that returns Result or Option. In a plain fn main() you get an error. Give main a return type.

error[E0277]: the `?` operator can only be used in a function that returns `Result` or `Option` (or another type that implements `FromResidual`)
help: consider adding return type
  |
1 ~ fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {

With that return type, main prints the error and the program ends with exit code 1. The Box<dyn Error> type holds any error. It is fine in main and in small tools.

Pattern 3: Error enum

Use it when a function can fail in more than one way, and callers must tell the ways apart.

use std::{collections::HashMap, fmt, num::ParseIntError};

#[derive(Debug)]
enum ConfigError {
    Missing(String),        // a key is not there
    BadPort(ParseIntError), // the text is not a number
}

impl fmt::Display for ConfigError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            ConfigError::Missing(key) => write!(f, "missing key: {key}"),
            ConfigError::BadPort(e) => write!(f, "bad port: {e}"),
        }
    }
}

impl std::error::Error for ConfigError {}

// With this From, the ? turns a ParseIntError into a ConfigError.
impl From<ParseIntError> for ConfigError {
    fn from(e: ParseIntError) -> Self {
        ConfigError::BadPort(e)
    }
}

fn read_port(cfg: &HashMap<&str, &str>) -> Result<u16, ConfigError> {
    let text = cfg.get("port").ok_or(ConfigError::Missing("port".into()))?;
    Ok(text.parse()?)
}
port 8080
error: bad port: invalid digit found in string
error: missing key: port
class ConfigError(Exception):
    """The base class: callers can catch all config errors."""


class MissingKey(ConfigError):
    pass


class BadPort(ConfigError):
    pass


def read_port(cfg: dict[str, str]) -> int:
    if "port" not in cfg:
        raise MissingKey("missing key: port")
    try:
        return int(cfg["port"])
    except ValueError as e:
        raise BadPort(f"bad port: {cfg['port']}") from e  # keep the cause


for cfg in [{"port": "8080"}, {"port": "80x"}, {}]:
    try:
        print(f"port {read_port(cfg)}")
    except ConfigError as e:
        print(f"error: {e}")
port 8080
error: bad port: 80x
error: missing key: port

The Rust output comes from a main that calls read_port with three maps: a good one, a bad one and an empty one.

Rule. Make one enum for one area of failure. Give each way to fail its own variant. Implement Display and Error. Add one From for each lower error. Then ? converts the lower error for you. Python uses one base exception class with a subclass for each case. raise ... from e keeps the first error as the cause.

Do not return Result<T, String> from a library. A caller cannot match on a string. It can only print it. The crate thiserror writes the Display and From code for you. The chapter Error handling shows it.

Group 2: Data with types

Pattern 4: Match on enum

Use it when a value is one of a few kinds, and each kind has its own data.

enum Shape {
    Circle { r: f64 },
    Rect { w: f64, h: f64 },
    Triangle { base: f64, height: f64 },
}

fn area(s: &Shape) -> f64 {
    // The compiler checks that every variant has an arm.
    match s {
        Shape::Circle { r } => 3.14159 * r * r,
        Shape::Rect { w, h } => w * h,
        Shape::Triangle { base, height } => 0.5 * base * height,
    }
}

fn main() {
    let shapes = [
        Shape::Circle { r: 1.0 },
        Shape::Rect { w: 2.0, h: 3.0 },
        Shape::Triangle { base: 4.0, height: 5.0 },
    ];
    for s in &shapes {
        println!("{:.2}", area(s));
    }
}
3.14
6.00
10.00
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import assert_never


@dataclass
class Circle:
    r: float


@dataclass
class Rect:
    w: float
    h: float


type Shape = Circle | Rect


def area(s: Shape) -> float:
    match s:
        case Circle(r=r):
            return 3.14159 * r * r
        case Rect(w=w, h=h):
            return w * h
        case _:
            assert_never(s)  # a type checker warns if a case is missing


for s in [Circle(1.0), Rect(2.0, 3.0)]:
    print(f"{area(s):.2f}")
3.14
6.00

Rule. Put all kinds into one enum. A match must cover every variant. This is an exhaustive check. Now add a variant and forget one arm. The compiler lists every place to update.

error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `&Shape::Triangle { .. }` not covered
 --> p04_err.rs:8:11
  |
8 |     match s {
  |           ^ pattern `&Shape::Triangle { .. }` not covered

Python's match does not check this when the program runs. A type checker does. With assert_never, mypy reports the missing case.

p04_err.py:32: error: Argument 1 to "assert_never" has incompatible type "Triangle"; expected "Never"  [arg-type]

Do not add a _ => arm to a match on your own enum. It catches every new variant without a word. You lose the compiler's best help.

Pattern 5: Newtype

Use it when two values have the same raw type but a different meaning. A user id and an order id are both numbers. Metres and feet are both floats.

use std::mem::size_of;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
struct UserId(u32);

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
struct OrderId(u32);

fn cancel(order: OrderId, by: UserId) {
    println!("order {} cancelled by user {}", order.0, by.0);
}

fn main() {
    let user = UserId(7);
    let order = OrderId(1042);
    cancel(order, user);
    // cancel(user, order); // error[E0308]: arguments are incorrect
    println!("{} {}", size_of::<UserId>(), size_of::<u32>());
}
order 1042 cancelled by user 7
4 4
from typing import NewType

UserId = NewType("UserId", int)
OrderId = NewType("OrderId", int)


def cancel(order: OrderId, by: UserId) -> None:
    print(f"order {order} cancelled by user {by}")


user = UserId(7)
order = OrderId(1042)
cancel(order, user)
cancel(user, order)  # runs! Only mypy or pyright reports it.
print(type(user))  # at run time it is a plain int
order 1042 cancelled by user 7
order 7 cancelled by user 1042
<class 'int'>

Rule. Wrap the raw value in a struct with one field. Now the compiler sees two different types. The wrong order of arguments does not compile. The cost is zero. The output 4 4 shows that both types have the same size. Python's NewType exists only for the type checker. Python itself still sees a plain int.

Do not implement Deref on a newtype just to get all methods of the inner type back. Then UserId acts like a u32 again, and the safety is gone. Add only the methods that make sense.

Pattern 6: Builder

Use it when a type has many settings, and most callers change only one or two.

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Request {
    url: String,
    timeout_s: u32,
    retries: u32,
}

struct RequestBuilder {
    url: String,
    timeout_s: u32,
    retries: u32,
}

impl Request {
    fn builder(url: &str) -> RequestBuilder {
        // Good defaults. The caller changes only what it needs.
        RequestBuilder { url: url.to_string(), timeout_s: 30, retries: 0 }
    }
}

impl RequestBuilder {
    fn timeout(mut self, s: u32) -> Self {
        self.timeout_s = s;
        self // give the builder back, so calls can chain
    }
    fn retries(mut self, n: u32) -> Self {
        self.retries = n;
        self
    }
    fn build(self) -> Request {
        Request { url: self.url, timeout_s: self.timeout_s, retries: self.retries }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let req = Request::builder("https://example.com").retries(3).build();
    println!("{req:?}");
}
Request { url: "https://example.com", timeout_s: 30, retries: 3 }
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Request:
    url: str
    timeout_s: int = 30  # defaults do the job of a builder
    retries: int = 0


req = Request("https://example.com", retries=3)  # keyword arguments
print(req)
fast = replace(req, url="https://example.org", timeout_s=5, retries=0)
print(fast.url, fast.timeout_s, fast.retries)
Request(url='https://example.com', timeout_s=30, retries=3)
https://example.org 5 0

Rule. A builder() function starts with good defaults. Each setter takes self and returns Self, so the calls form a chain. build() makes the final value. It can also check the settings and return a Result. Rust has no default values for arguments, so the builder fills that gap. Python has keyword arguments with defaults. So Python rarely needs a builder.

Do not write a builder for a struct with two fields. A plain new(a, b) is shorter. For a few public fields, derive Default and write Config { port: 8080, ..Default::default() }.

Group 3: Ownership and data flow

Pattern 7: Borrow, do not clone

Use it when a function only needs to read the data.

// Bad: takes the Vec. The caller loses it, or must clone it.
fn total_len_owned(words: Vec<String>) -> usize {
    words.iter().map(|w| w.len()).sum()
}

// Good: borrows a slice. No copy. The caller keeps the data.
fn total_len(words: &[String]) -> usize {
    words.iter().map(|w| w.len()).sum()
}

fn shout(word: &str) -> String {
    word.to_uppercase() // a new String only when we need one
}

fn main() {
    let words = vec!["red".to_string(), "green".to_string()];
    let a = total_len_owned(words.clone()); // a full copy of the list
    let b = total_len(&words); // just a pointer and a length
    println!("{a} {b} {}", shout(&words[0]));
    println!("{words:?}"); // still ours
}
8 8 RED
["red", "green"]
def total_len(words: list[str]) -> int:
    return sum(len(w) for w in words)  # reads, never changes


def add_word_bad(words: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    words.append("blue")  # changes the caller's list!
    return words


def add_word(words: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    return [*words, "blue"]  # a new list. The input stays the same.


words = ["red", "green"]
print(total_len(words))  # no copy: the function gets the same list
print(add_word(words), words)
add_word_bad(words)
print(words)
8
['red', 'green', 'blue'] ['red', 'green']
['red', 'green', 'blue']

Rule. Take &str, &[T] or &T when you only read. Take T only when you keep the value. Clone only when you really need a second, independent value. Python never copies an argument. It passes the same object. So the Python risk is the opposite one: a function that changes the caller's list by surprise.

Do not add .clone() just to silence the borrow checker. The Rust design patterns book lists this as an anti-pattern. First try to reorder the lines or to borrow. Note: cloning an Rc or Arc is cheap. It only adds one to a counter.

Pattern 8: Iterator chain

Use it when you filter, change or sum the items of a collection.

struct Order {
    amount: u32,
    paid: bool,
}

fn main() {
    let orders = vec![
        Order { amount: 120, paid: true },
        Order { amount: 80, paid: false },
        Order { amount: 45, paid: true },
    ];
    // filter, then map, then sum. No index, no mut counter.
    let paid_total: u32 = orders.iter().filter(|o| o.paid).map(|o| o.amount).sum();
    println!("{paid_total}");

    let big: Vec<u32> = orders.iter().map(|o| o.amount).filter(|&a| a > 50).collect();
    println!("{big:?}");
}
165
[120, 80]
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Order:
    amount: int
    paid: bool


orders = [Order(120, True), Order(80, False), Order(45, True)]
paid_total = sum(o.amount for o in orders if o.paid)  # a generator expression
print(paid_total)
big = [o.amount for o in orders if o.amount > 50]  # a list comprehension
print(big)
165
[120, 80]

Rule. A chain has three parts. A source like iter(). One or more adapters like filter and map. One consumer like sum, count or collect. Adapters are lazy. The chain is as fast as a hand-written loop. Python uses a comprehension or a generator expression.

A chain without a consumer does nothing. Rust warns you. Python's map(print, items) also does nothing, but without a warning.

warning: unused `Map` that must be used
 --> p08_lazy.rs:3:5
  |
3 |     v.iter().map(|x| println!("{x}")); // nothing runs
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = note: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed

The chapter Iterators and closures has all the adapters.

Pattern 9: RAII guard

Use it when something must always be undone: unlock a lock, close a file, restore a setting, roll back a change.

// A guard: setup in enter(), clean-up in drop().
struct Span {
    name: &'static str,
}

impl Span {
    fn enter(name: &'static str) -> Span {
        println!("enter {name}");
        Span { name }
    }
}

impl Drop for Span {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        println!("leave {}", self.name); // runs on every way out
    }
}

fn work() -> Result<(), String> {
    let _span = Span::enter("work"); // lives until the function ends
    Err("disk full".to_string())?; // an early return still runs drop
    println!("never printed");
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", work());
    let _ = Span::enter("oops"); // `_` drops the guard at once!
    println!("after oops");
}
enter work
leave work
Err("disk full")
enter oops
leave oops
after oops
from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def span(name: str):
    print(f"enter {name}")
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        print(f"leave {name}")  # runs on every way out


def work() -> None:
    with span("work"):
        raise OSError("disk full")


try:
    work()
except OSError as e:
    print(f"error: {e}")
enter work
leave work
error: disk full

RAII ties a resource to a value. You get the resource when you make the value. Rust frees it when the value is dropped. A value that does this job is a guard.

Rule. Do the setup in a constructor. Do the clean-up in Drop. The clean-up then runs on every way out: a normal end, a return, a ?, even a panic. The standard library is full of guards: MutexGuard, File and the Ref of a RefCell. Python uses the with statement and a context manager.

Look at the output again. let _ = Span::enter("oops") drops the guard at once. The pattern _ keeps nothing. Write let _span = .... A name that starts with _ still keeps the value alive.

Rust 1.100 came out on 12 November 2026. It adds std::mem::DropGuard. It runs any closure when it is dropped, so you need no custom struct. This machine has rustc 1.99, so this page does not run it.

Group 4: Conversions and traits

Pattern 10: From and Into

Use it when a value of one type can become a value of another type.

struct Celsius(f64);
struct Fahrenheit(f64);

// Write From. Into comes for free.
impl From<Celsius> for Fahrenheit {
    fn from(c: Celsius) -> Self {
        Fahrenheit(c.0 * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0)
    }
}

struct User {
    name: String,
}

impl User {
    // Accept &str, String, or anything that turns into a String.
    fn new(name: impl Into<String>) -> User {
        User { name: name.into() }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let f = Fahrenheit::from(Celsius(100.0));
    let g: Fahrenheit = Celsius(-40.0).into(); // the same, written with into
    println!("{} {}", f.0, g.0);

    let a = User::new("Ann"); // a &str
    let b = User::new(String::from("Bo")); // a String, no extra copy
    println!("{} {}", a.name, b.name);

    let small = u8::try_from(300_i32); // TryFrom: this one can fail
    println!("{small:?}");
}
212 -40
Ann Bo
Err(TryFromIntError(PosOverflow))
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Celsius:
    value: float


@dataclass
class Fahrenheit:
    value: float

    @classmethod
    def from_celsius(cls, c: Celsius) -> "Fahrenheit":
        return cls(c.value * 9 / 5 + 32)  # a named constructor


print(Fahrenheit.from_celsius(Celsius(100.0)))
print(Fahrenheit.from_celsius(Celsius(-40.0)))
print(int("42"), str(42), float("2.5"))  # built-in conversions


def to_byte(n: int) -> int:
    if not 0 <= n <= 255:
        raise ValueError(f"{n} does not fit in a byte")
    return n


try:
    to_byte(300)
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
Fahrenheit(value=212.0)
Fahrenheit(value=-40.0)
42 42 2.5
300 does not fit in a byte

Rule. Implement From<A> for B. The standard library then gives you Into<B> for A for free. A parameter of type impl Into<String> accepts both &str and String. Use TryFrom when the conversion can fail, like 300 into a u8. Python has no conversion trait. It uses named constructors like from_celsius and the built-in calls int() and str().

Do not implement Into by hand. Implement From. Also, never use From for a conversion that can fail or lose data. From must always work.

Pattern 11: Generic with a bound

Use it when one function should work for many types that share an ability.

use std::fmt::Display;

// T can be any type that can be compared and copied.
fn largest<T: PartialOrd + Copy>(items: &[T]) -> Option<T> {
    let mut best = *items.first()?;
    for &x in items {
        if x > best {
            best = x;
        }
    }
    Some(best)
}

// A where clause is easier to read when bounds are long.
fn show_all<T>(items: &[T]) -> String
where
    T: Display,
{
    items.iter().map(|x| x.to_string()).collect::<Vec<_>>().join(", ")
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", largest(&[3, 9, 4]));
    println!("{:?}", largest(&[1.5, 0.2]));
    println!("{:?}", largest::<char>(&[]));
    println!("{}", show_all(&["a", "b"]));
}
Some(9)
Some(1.5)
None
a, b
from typing import Protocol, Self


class Comparable(Protocol):
    def __lt__(self, other: Self, /) -> bool: ...


# Python 3.12+ syntax: T must support "<".
def largest[T: Comparable](items: list[T]) -> T | None:
    if not items:
        return None
    best = items[0]
    for x in items:
        if best < x:
            best = x
    return best


print(largest([3, 9, 4]))
print(largest([1.5, 0.2]))
print(largest([]))
9
1.5
None

A generic function has a type parameter T. A bound like T: PartialOrd says what T must be able to do. Without the bound the compiler refuses the > sign.

error[E0369]: binary operation `>` cannot be applied to type `T`
help: consider further restricting type parameter `T` with trait `PartialOrd`

Rule. Write <T: Trait>, or a where clause for long bounds. The compiler makes one copy of the function for each type you use. This is monomorphisation. Each copy is as fast as hand-written code. Python 3.12 has the same syntax, def f[T: Bound]. There only the type checker uses it.

Ask only for what you use. A bound like T: Clone + Debug + Default "just in case" blocks callers for no reason. Many large generic functions also make the program file bigger.

Pattern 12: Trait object

Use it when different types must live in one collection, or the type is chosen while the program runs.

trait Shape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64;
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        "shape".to_string() // a default method
    }
}

struct Square(f64);
struct Circle(f64);

impl Shape for Square {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 }
    fn name(&self) -> String { "square".to_string() }
}

impl Shape for Circle {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 { 3.14159 * self.0 * self.0 }
}

fn main() {
    // Different types in one Vec, behind one trait.
    let shapes: Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> = vec![Box::new(Square(2.0)), Box::new(Circle(1.0))];
    for s in &shapes {
        println!("{} {:.2}", s.name(), s.area()); // chosen at run time
    }
    let total: f64 = shapes.iter().map(|s| s.area()).sum();
    println!("total {total:.2}");
}
square 4.00
shape 3.14
total 7.14
from typing import Protocol


class Shape(Protocol):
    def area(self) -> float: ...


class Square:
    def __init__(self, side: float) -> None:
        self.side = side

    def area(self) -> float:
        return self.side * self.side


class Circle:
    def __init__(self, r: float) -> None:
        self.r = r

    def area(self) -> float:
        return 3.14159 * self.r * self.r


shapes: list[Shape] = [Square(2.0), Circle(1.0)]  # no common base class
for s in shapes:
    print(type(s).__name__.lower(), f"{s.area():.2f}")
print(f"total {sum(s.area() for s in shapes):.2f}")
square 4.00
circle 3.14
total 7.14

A trait object like Box<dyn Shape> hides the real type. It holds two pointers: one to the data and one to a vtable. Each call looks up the method in the vtable. This is dynamic dispatch.

Rule. Use Box<dyn Trait>, &dyn Trait or Arc<dyn Trait>. The trait must be dyn compatible. In Python every call is dynamic. A Protocol lets the type checker check the shape without a base class.

Do not pick dyn by habit from other languages. If all items have the same type, a generic is simpler and faster. Pick dyn when the types really mix. The chapter Advanced traits and types explains the dyn rules.

Group 5: Threads and tests

Pattern 13: Shared state with Arc and Mutex

Use it when several threads must read and change the same value.

use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    // Arc: many owners across threads. Mutex: one writer at a time.
    let hits = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..4 {
        let hits = Arc::clone(&hits); // one more owner, no data copy
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for _ in 0..1000 {
                *hits.lock().unwrap() += 1; // lock, add, unlock at once
            }
        }));
    }
    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
    println!("{}", *hits.lock().unwrap());
}
4000
import threading

hits = 0
lock = threading.Lock()


def worker() -> None:
    global hits
    for _ in range(1000):
        with lock:  # the lock is released at the end of the block
            hits += 1


threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print(hits)
4000

Rule. Arc gives many owners across threads. Mutex lets one thread at a time touch the data. lock() returns a guard (pattern 9). The lock opens again when the guard is dropped. Python uses threading.Lock with with lock:. In Python hits += 1 is not one step. Without the lock, two threads can lose an update.

Do not keep the guard while you do slow work. Copy the data out, drop the guard, then work. And never lock two mutexes in a different order in two threads. That can cause a deadlock. See Threads and shared state.

Pattern 14: Channel

Use it when one thread makes work or results and another thread uses them.

use std::sync::mpsc;
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();
    for id in 0..3 {
        let tx = tx.clone(); // each worker gets its own sender
        thread::spawn(move || {
            tx.send(format!("worker {id} done")).unwrap();
        });
    }
    drop(tx); // drop the first sender, or the loop below never ends

    let mut msgs: Vec<String> = rx.iter().collect(); // waits for all
    msgs.sort(); // threads finish in any order
    println!("{msgs:?}");
}
["worker 0 done", "worker 1 done", "worker 2 done"]
import queue
import threading

q: queue.Queue[str | None] = queue.Queue()


def worker(id: int) -> None:
    q.put(f"worker {id} done")


threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(i,)) for i in range(3)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
q.put(None)  # a stop signal: Python has no "all senders are gone"

msgs = []
while (msg := q.get()) is not None:
    msgs.append(msg)
print(sorted(msgs))
['worker 0 done', 'worker 1 done', 'worker 2 done']

A channel moves values between threads. No data is shared. Each message moves from the sender to the receiver.

Rule. mpsc::channel() gives a Sender and a Receiver. The name means "many producers, single consumer". Clone the sender for each producer. A loop over rx ends when every sender is gone. Python uses queue.Queue and a sentinel like None.

Forget drop(tx) and the program hangs forever. The first sender is still alive, so the receiver keeps waiting. In Python, forget the sentinel and you get the same hang.

Pattern 15: Test first

Use it when you start a new function, or before you fix a bug.

  1. Red. Write one small test. Run it. It must fail.
  2. Green. Write just enough code to pass the test.
  3. Refactor. Clean up the code. The tests stay green.

Here is step 1 for a slug function. The first, too simple version fails, and the test shows why.

---- simple_title stdout ----
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: "hello,-world"
 right: "hello-world"
test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

After steps 2 and 3, the code and its tests look like this.

/// Turn a title into a URL slug: "Hello, World" -> "hello-world".
pub fn slug(title: &str) -> String {
    title
        .split(|c: char| !c.is_alphanumeric()) // cut at every non-letter
        .filter(|w| !w.is_empty())
        .map(|w| w.to_lowercase())
        .collect::<Vec<_>>()
        .join("-")
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn simple_title() {
        assert_eq!(slug("Hello, World"), "hello-world");
    }

    #[test]
    fn extra_spaces_and_signs() {
        assert_eq!(slug("  Rust -- 2024!  "), "rust-2024");
    }

    #[test]
    fn empty_title() {
        assert_eq!(slug(""), "");
    }
}
running 3 tests
test tests::empty_title ... ok
test tests::extra_spaces_and_signs ... ok
test tests::simple_title ... ok

test result: ok. 3 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.00s
# slug.py
import re


def slug(title: str) -> str:
    words = re.split(r"[\W_]+", title)  # cut at every non-letter
    return "-".join(w.lower() for w in words if w)


# test_slug.py
from slug import slug


def test_simple_title():
    assert slug("Hello, World") == "hello-world"


def test_extra_spaces_and_signs():
    assert slug("  Rust -- 2024!  ") == "rust-2024"


def test_empty_title():
    assert slug("") == ""
...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 0.01s

Rule. In Rust, tests live next to the code in a #[cfg(test)] module. Run them with cargo test. In Python, pytest finds files named test_*.py and runs plain assert lines. A test first makes you design the interface from the caller's side.

A test that never failed may test nothing. Watch it fail one time. Also test what the function does, not how it does it. Then you can rewrite the inside without changing the tests. More in Testing and tooling.

Choosing between close patterns

Some patterns solve almost the same problem. Experts know when to pick which one. This table gives the usual answer.

Six choices you make every week
ChoicePick the first whenPick the second when
Option or Result"Nothing" is a normal answer, like an empty search.The caller needs a reason. Convert with opt.ok_or(err).
Generic or trait objectOne type per call, and speed matters.Types mix in one list, or plugins load at run time.
Arc<Mutex<T>> or channelMany threads update one small value.Work flows one way, like a pipeline of steps.
Borrow or cloneYou read for a short time.You need an independent copy that lives on.
Builder or DefaultMany options, or build() must check them.Few public fields with good defaults.
Error enum or Box<dyn Error>A library: callers must match on cases.An application's main: you only report.

The patterns also work together. One pattern often uses another one inside it. Drag the nodes to see the links.

Anti-patterns to unlearn

An anti-pattern feels helpful today and hurts tomorrow. Open each one to see the fix.

Clone everything until it compiles

Each clone of a String or Vec allocates new memory. It also hides a design problem. Fix: borrow, reorder lines, or move the value once (pattern 7).

Unwrap everywhere

Every unwrap() is a possible crash. Fix: return Result and use ? (pattern 2). Keep unwrap for tests. Use expect("reason") where a failure is truly impossible.

Strings for everything

A String for an error, an id or a state accepts any text, even wrong text. Fix: an error enum (pattern 3), a newtype (pattern 5) or an enum of states (pattern 4).

Deref on a newtype

It makes the wrapper act like the inner type again. The safety of pattern 5 is gone. Fix: write the few methods you need. Deref is for smart pointers.

Rc and RefCell everywhere

People copy object graphs from Java or Python. Every object points to every other object. Fix: one owner for each value, and ids or indexes for the links. See Smart pointers.

A catch-all arm on your own enum

_ => hides new variants. Fix: list every variant (pattern 4). A catch-all is fine for numbers and strings.

A common question is "generic or trait object?". Name three things in your answer. Static or dynamic dispatch. Code size, because generics make copies. Mixed types, because only dyn allows them in one Vec.

The fifteen patterns in fifteen slides

Use these slides to review. Each slide starts with the problem you see. Then it names the pattern you write.

1. Option instead of null

You see: a search may find nothing.

You write: fn find(id: u32) -> Option<User>

Python: def find(id: int) -> User | None

2. Result and ?

You see: a step can fail, and the caller decides.

You write: let n: u16 = text.parse()?;

Python: let the exception rise.

3. Error enum

You see: there are several ways to fail.

You write: enum ConfigError { Missing(String), BadPort(ParseIntError) }

Python: a base exception with subclasses.

4. Match on enum

You see: a value is one of a few kinds.

You write: match s { Shape::Circle { r } => ..., ... }

Python: match plus assert_never.

5. Newtype

You see: two numbers that people mix up.

You write: struct UserId(u32);

Python: UserId = NewType("UserId", int)

6. Builder

You see: many settings, most with defaults.

You write: Request::builder(url).retries(3).build()

Python: keyword arguments with defaults.

7. Borrow, do not clone

You see: a function that only reads.

You write: fn total(words: &[String]) -> usize

Python: do not change the argument.

8. Iterator chain

You see: a loop with an index and a counter.

You write: v.iter().filter(..).map(..).sum()

Python: sum(x.a for x in v if x.ok)

9. RAII guard

You see: a step that must always be undone.

You write: impl Drop for Span { ... }

Python: with and a context manager.

10. From and Into

You see: one type turns into another.

You write: impl From<Celsius> for Fahrenheit

Python: a from_x class method.

11. Generic with bound

You see: the same code for many types.

You write: fn largest<T: PartialOrd + Copy>(v: &[T])

Python: def largest[T: Comparable](v: list[T])

12. Trait object

You see: different types in one list.

You write: Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>

Python: a Protocol, or plain duck typing.

13. Arc and Mutex

You see: threads that change one value.

You write: Arc::new(Mutex::new(0))

Python: with lock:

14. Channel

You see: workers that send back results.

You write: let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();

Python: queue.Queue and a stop value.

15. Test first

You see: a new function or a bug report.

You write: #[test] fn ... and watch it fail.

Python: def test_...(): with pytest.

Patterns to remember

This is the one table to keep. Switch to cards to learn one pattern at a time.

The 15 patterns of Rust and Python
PatternPurposeRust modelPython modelNote
1. Option instead of nullSay "maybe there is no value"fn find(id: u32) -> Option<User>def find(id: int) -> User | NoneNo unwrap() in normal code. In Python test with is None.
2. Result and ?Pass a failure up to the callerlet port: u16 = text.parse()?;Let the exception rise? needs a function that returns Result or Option.
3. Error enumName each way to failenum ConfigError { Missing(String), BadPort(ParseIntError) }class BadPort(ConfigError): ...Add From so ? converts. No String errors in libraries.
4. Match on enumHandle each kind of valuematch s { Shape::Rect { w, h } => w * h, ... }match s: case Rect(w=w, h=h): ...No _ => on your own enum. Python needs assert_never and mypy.
5. NewtypeStop mix-ups of same-typed valuesstruct UserId(u32);UserId = NewType("UserId", int)Zero cost in Rust. Python checks it only with a type checker.
6. BuilderBuild a value with many optional settingsRequest::builder(url).retries(3).build()Request(url, retries=3)Not for two fields. Then use new or Default.
7. Borrow, do not cloneRead data without copying itfn total(words: &[String]) -> usizedef total(words: list[str]) -> intClone is not a fix for borrow errors. Python: never change an argument by surprise.
8. Iterator chainFilter, change and sum a collectionv.iter().filter(|o| o.paid).map(|o| o.amount).sum()sum(o.amount for o in v if o.paid)Lazy: no consumer, no work.
9. RAII guardUndo a step on every way outlet _span = Span::enter("work");with span("work"): ...let _ = guard drops at once. Use a name.
10. From and IntoTurn one type into anotherimpl From<Celsius> for FahrenheitFahrenheit.from_celsius(c)Write From, get Into. Use TryFrom if it can fail.
11. Generic with boundOne function for many typesfn largest<T: PartialOrd + Copy>(v: &[T]) -> Option<T>def largest[T: Comparable](v: list[T]) -> T | NoneAsk only for the traits you use.
12. Trait objectMixed types behind one interfaceVec<Box<dyn Shape>>list[Shape] with a ProtocolCosts one vtable lookup per call. The trait must be dyn compatible.
13. Arc and MutexMany threads change one valuelet hits = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0));with lock: hits += 1Keep the lock short. Lock several mutexes in one fixed order.
14. ChannelSend values from thread to threadlet (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();q = queue.Queue()Drop the last sender, or the receiver waits forever.
15. Test firstDesign and check behaviour#[test] fn simple_title() { assert_eq!(...) }def test_simple_title(): assert ...See the test fail one time. Test behaviour, not the inside.

Practice

A function looks up a user by id. Often no user exists. Which return type fits best?

  • User, and return a user with an empty name
  • Option<User>
  • Result<User, String>

"No user" is a normal answer here. Option says exactly that. An empty user is a hidden null.

Which line keeps the lock until the end of the block?

  • let _ = data.lock().unwrap();
  • let _guard = data.lock().unwrap();
  • data.lock().unwrap();

A plain _ and a bare call drop the guard at once. A named variable keeps it alive.

You need one list that holds a Square and a Circle. What do you write?

  • Vec<T> where T: Shape
  • Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>
  • Vec<impl Shape>

A generic T is one type for the whole list. Only a trait object lets the types mix.

The loop for msg in rx { ... } never ends. All workers are done. What is the most likely cause?

  • The channel is full.
  • One Sender is still alive, often the first tx.
  • The receiver was cloned.

The receiver ends only when every sender is dropped. Call drop(tx) after you clone it for the workers.

You implement trait and the standard library gives you Into for free.

The Python twin of an RAII guard is the keyword statement.

A chain of iterator adapters does no work until a word like sum or collect runs.

  1. This function takes the list away from its caller. Fix it with one change. 
    fn count_long(words: Vec<String>) -> usize {
    words.iter().filter(|w| w.len() > 5).count()
}
    Answer

    Borrow a slice: fn count_long(words: &[String]) -> usize. The body stays the same. The caller writes count_long(&words) and keeps the list.

  2. An old Python function returns -1 when it finds nothing. Rewrite its signature in both languages with pattern 1. 
    def index_of(items: list[str], target: str) -> int:
    for i, x in enumerate(items):
        if x == target:
            return i
    return -1
    Answer

    Python: def index_of(items: list[str], target: str) -> int | None, and return None at the end. Rust: fn index_of(items: &[String], target: &str) -> Option<usize>. The body can be items.iter().position(|x| x == target). Now the caller cannot use -1 as an index by mistake.

  3. A function send(from: u64, to: u64, cents: u64) has had two bugs. Callers swapped the arguments. Which pattern helps? Write the new signature.
    Answer

    Pattern 5, newtype: struct AccountId(u64); struct Cents(u64); and fn send(from: AccountId, to: AccountId, cents: Cents). Now an amount cannot go into an account slot. Two accounts can still be swapped. For that, name the step: transfer().from(a).to(b), a small builder.

  4. Write an error enum for a parser of lines like key=value. It fails when there is no = or when the key is empty.
    Answer 
    #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
enum LineError {
    NoEquals,
    EmptyKey,
}

fn parse_line(line: &str) -> Result<(&str, &str), LineError> {
    let (key, value) = line.split_once('=').ok_or(LineError::NoEquals)?;
    if key.trim().is_empty() {
        return Err(LineError::EmptyKey);
    }
    Ok((key.trim(), value.trim()))
}

    parse_line("a = 1") gives Ok(("a", "1")). parse_line("a") gives Err(NoEquals). A real version also implements Display and Error.

  5. Expert. Thread A locks accounts and then log. Thread B locks log and then accounts. Sometimes the program freezes. Why, and what is the simplest fix?
    Answer

    A holds accounts and waits for log. B holds log and waits for accounts. Each waits for the other forever: a deadlock. Fix: every thread locks the two mutexes in the same fixed order. Or keep each lock only for one short step, and never hold both at once.

  6. Expert. A program loads "exporters" by name from a config file: CSV, JSON or Parquet. Should run take a generic E: Exporter or a Box<dyn Exporter>? Give two reasons.
    Answer

    Box<dyn Exporter>. First, the type is chosen at run time from text, so the compiler cannot know it. Second, you may keep a list of several exporters, and only dyn lets types mix in one list. The cost of one vtable lookup is tiny next to writing a file.

Key takeaways

  • Rust puts many rules into types: Option, Result, enums and newtypes. Python keeps them in habits and type hints.
  • ?, an error enum and From work as a team for clean error code.
  • Borrow by default. Clone on purpose. Let a guard undo every setup step.
  • Generics give speed and one type per call. Trait objects give mixed types and run-time choice.
  • Share state with Arc and Mutex, or send messages on a channel. Keep locks short.
  • Write a test that fails first. Then make it pass, then clean up.

Sources

  • Rust API Guidelines: checklist. The official advice on conversions, newtypes, builders and generic parameters.
  • Rust Design Patterns: RAII with guards. The guard pattern and how the borrow checker supports it.
  • Rust Design Patterns: Clone to satisfy the borrow checker. Why extra clones are an anti-pattern.
  • The Rust Programming Language: Recoverable errors with Result. The ? operator and a main that returns Result.
  • Python documentation: typing. NewType, Protocol, assert_never and the generic syntax.
  • Python documentation: contextlib. Context managers, the Python twin of a guard.

Threads and shared state

A modern laptop has many cores. Threads let one program use them at the same time. Rust checks thread safety before the program runs. Python has a lock inside the interpreter, and that lock is starting to go away.

  • Start threads with spawn and scope, and collect their results with join.
  • Explain Send and Sync, and read the errors they cause.
  • Protect shared data with Mutex, RwLock, Condvar, atomics and channels.
  • Find and prevent a deadlock.
  • Choose between Python threads, the free-threaded build, processes and interpreters.

Spawn and join

Start with a program that does two things at once.

use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

fn main() {
    // spawn starts a new thread. It returns a JoinHandle.
    let handle = thread::spawn(|| {
        let mut sum = 0u64;
        for i in 1..=1_000_000 {
            sum += i;
        }
        sum // the thread's result
    });

    println!("main keeps working");
    thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(10));

    // join waits for the thread and gives back its result.
    let sum = handle.join().unwrap();
    println!("sum = {sum}");
    println!("cores: {}", thread::available_parallelism().unwrap());
}
main keeps working
sum = 500000500000
cores: 10
import os
import threading
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor


def total() -> int:
    return sum(range(1, 1_000_001))


# A plain Thread has no return value. A pool gives a Future.
with ThreadPoolExecutor() as pool:
    future = pool.submit(total)  # like thread::spawn
    print("main keeps working")
    time.sleep(0.01)
    print(f"sum = {future.result()}")  # like join

t = threading.Thread(target=print, args=("hello from a thread",))
t.start()
t.join()
print(f"cores: {os.cpu_count()}")
main keeps working
sum = 500000500000
hello from a thread
cores: 10

A thread runs its code beside the other threads. The operating system decides when each one runs. thread::spawn takes a closure and starts it on a new thread. It returns a JoinHandle<T>. join() waits for the thread to end and gives back its value.

A thread can also panic. Then join() returns Err, and the main thread decides what to do. Python's future.result() raises the error of the worker in the same way.

Do not forget join. When main returns, the whole process ends. Running threads stop in the middle. This program never prints "worker finished".

use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

fn main() {
    thread::spawn(|| {
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(100));
        println!("worker finished"); // never printed
    });
    println!("main ends");
} // main returns: the whole process stops, workers too
main ends

Move closures and scoped threads

A thread wants to print a list from main. The first try does not compile.

use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let names = vec!["Ann", "Bo"];
    let h = thread::spawn(|| {
        println!("{names:?}");
    });
    h.join().unwrap();
}
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `names`, which is owned by the current function
 --> t02_err.rs:5:27
  |
5 |     let h = thread::spawn(|| {
  |                           ^^ may outlive borrowed value `names`
6 |         println!("{names:?}");
  |                    ----- `names` is borrowed here
  |
help: to force the closure to take ownership of `names` (and any other referenced variables), use the `move` keyword

Why? A spawned thread may run longer than main. Then it would read a list that is already freed. So spawn wants a closure that owns all its data. In the signature this is the bound F: 'static. There are two fixes.

use std::thread;

fn main() {
    // Fix 1: move. The thread now owns `names`.
    let names = vec!["Ann", "Bo"];
    let h = thread::spawn(move || {
        println!("{names:?}");
        names.len()
    });
    println!("len {}", h.join().unwrap());

    // Fix 2: a scope. Threads may borrow, because the scope
    // joins them all before it returns.
    let nums: Vec<u64> = (1..=10).collect();
    let (left, right) = nums.split_at(nums.len() / 2);
    let (a, b) = thread::scope(|s| {
        let ha = s.spawn(|| left.iter().sum::<u64>());
        let hb = s.spawn(|| right.iter().sum::<u64>());
        (ha.join().unwrap(), hb.join().unwrap())
    });
    println!("{a} + {b} = {}", a + b);
    println!("nums is still here: {}", nums.len());

    // A scope can also give each thread a &mut to its own part.
    let mut data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for chunk in data.chunks_mut(2) {
            s.spawn(move || chunk.iter_mut().for_each(|x| *x *= 10));
        }
    }); // all threads are joined here
    println!("{data:?}");
}
["Ann", "Bo"]
len 2
15 + 40 = 55
nums is still here: 10
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
  • A move closure takes the variables it uses. The old name is not usable after that.
  • A scoped thread lives inside thread::scope. The scope joins every thread before it returns. So the threads may borrow local data, even with &mut. Scoped threads are stable since Rust 1.63.

Python has no such rule. Every thread can read every object, because the garbage collector keeps objects alive. The price: Python does not check who changes what.

Prefer thread::scope for "split the work, then wait for all parts". You need no Arc, no move of big data, and no forgotten join.

Send and Sync

Now try to send an Rc to another thread.

use std::rc::Rc;
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let shared = Rc::new(5);
    let h = thread::spawn(move || {
        println!("{shared}");
    });
    h.join().unwrap();
}
error[E0277]: `Rc<i32>` cannot be sent between threads safely
   --> t03_err.rs:6:27
    |
  6 |       let h = thread::spawn(move || {
    |               ------------- ^------
    |               |             |
    |               |             within this `{closure@t03_err.rs:6:27: 6:34}`
    |               required by a bound introduced by this call
    = help: within `{closure@t03_err.rs:6:27: 6:34}`, the trait `Send` is not implemented for `Rc<i32>`

Rc counts its owners with a plain number. Two threads could change that number at the same moment. Then the count is wrong, and memory is freed too early. The compiler stops this with two marker traits.

  • A type is Send when you can move a value of it to another thread.
  • A type is Sync when many threads can share a &T to it. Exactly: T is Sync if and only if &T is Send.

You almost never write these traits. They are auto traits. A struct is Send when all its fields are Send. thread::spawn requires F: Send, and that is the whole trick.

Common types and their thread safety
TypeSendSyncWhy
i32, String, Vec<T>YesYesNormal owned data (when T is too)
Rc<T>NoNoThe count is not atomic
Arc<T>YesYesAtomic count (when T is Send + Sync)
Cell<T>, RefCell<T>YesNoChanges through & without a lock
Mutex<T>YesYesThe lock makes sharing safe (when T: Send)
MutexGuard<T>NoYesIt must unlock on the thread that locked
*const T, *mut TNoNoRaw pointers carry no promise

This is how Rust prevents a data race before the program runs. A data race needs shared data, a writer and no order. The borrow rules and Send and Sync together forbid that mix.

Do not write unsafe impl Send for MyType {} to silence this error. It is a promise that the compiler cannot check. A wrong promise gives undefined behaviour. First change the type: Rc to Arc, RefCell to Mutex.

Rust stops data races. It does not stop a race condition in your logic, and it does not stop deadlocks. You see both later in this chapter.

Locks: Mutex, RwLock and Condvar

Mutex

Ten threads add money to one balance.

use std::sync::Mutex;
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let balance = Mutex::new(100);
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for _ in 0..10 {
            s.spawn(|| {
                let mut b = balance.lock().unwrap(); // wait for the lock
                *b += 10; // only this thread can touch it now
            }); // the guard `b` is dropped here: unlock
        }
    });
    println!("balance {}", balance.lock().unwrap());

    // Poisoning: a thread panics while it holds the lock.
    let m = Mutex::new(vec![1, 2]);
    let _ = thread::scope(|s| {
        s.spawn(|| {
            let mut v = m.lock().unwrap();
            v.push(3);
            panic!("oops"); // the data may be half changed
        })
        .join()
    });
    println!("poisoned: {}", m.is_poisoned());
    let v = m.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner()); // take it anyway
    println!("{v:?}");
}
balance 200

thread '<unnamed>' (115694551) panicked at t04.rs:22:13:
oops
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
poisoned: true
[1, 2, 3]
import threading

balance = 100
lock = threading.Lock()


def deposit() -> None:
    global balance
    with lock:  # wait for the lock, unlock at the end of the block
        balance += 10


threads = [threading.Thread(target=deposit) for _ in range(10)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print(f"balance {balance}")

# No poisoning in Python: an error inside "with" just unlocks.
items = [1, 2]
try:
    with lock:
        items.append(3)
        raise RuntimeError("oops")  # the data may be half changed
except RuntimeError:
    pass
print(lock.locked(), items)
balance 200
False [1, 2, 3]

A mutex (mutual exclusion) holds the data inside it. You cannot reach the data without lock(). lock() returns a guard. The guard unlocks when it is dropped. In C you must remember to unlock. In Rust you cannot forget.

A panic while a thread holds the guard poisons the mutex. Later calls to lock() return Err. That is why you see .unwrap() after lock(). Python has no poisoning. The lock simply opens.

RwLock

Many threads read a setting. One thread sometimes changes it.

use std::sync::RwLock;
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let config = RwLock::new(String::from("v1"));
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for id in 0..3 {
            let config = &config;
            s.spawn(move || {
                let c = config.read().unwrap(); // many readers at once
                println!("reader {id} sees {c}");
            });
        }
    });
    {
        let mut c = config.write().unwrap(); // one writer, no readers
        c.push_str("-patched");
    }
    println!("now {}", config.read().unwrap());
}
reader 0 sees v1
reader 1 sees v1
reader 2 sees v1
now v1-patched

An RwLock (read-write lock) allows many readers or one writer. This is the borrow rule again, checked at run time. The order of the reader lines can change from run to run. Python's standard library has no read-write lock.

Condvar: sleep until something changes

A worker waits for jobs. It should sleep, not spin in a loop.

use std::collections::VecDeque;
use std::sync::{Condvar, Mutex};
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let queue = Mutex::new(VecDeque::new());
    let not_empty = Condvar::new();

    thread::scope(|s| {
        // Consumer: sleep until there is work.
        s.spawn(|| {
            for _ in 0..3 {
                let mut q = queue.lock().unwrap();
                // wait_while unlocks, sleeps, and locks again on wake-up.
                q = not_empty.wait_while(q, |q| q.is_empty()).unwrap();
                let job = q.pop_front().unwrap();
                drop(q); // unlock before the slow part
                println!("got job {job}");
            }
        });
        // Producer: add work and wake the consumer.
        for job in 1..=3 {
            queue.lock().unwrap().push_back(job);
            not_empty.notify_one();
        }
    });
}
got job 1
got job 2
got job 3
import threading
from collections import deque

queue: deque[int] = deque()
not_empty = threading.Condition()  # a lock plus a wait list


def consumer() -> None:
    for _ in range(3):
        with not_empty:
            not_empty.wait_for(lambda: len(queue) > 0)  # unlock, sleep, relock
            job = queue.popleft()
        print(f"got job {job}")  # the lock is free here


t = threading.Thread(target=consumer)
t.start()
for job in range(1, 4):
    with not_empty:
        queue.append(job)
        not_empty.notify()
t.join()
got job 1
got job 2
got job 3

A Condvar always works with a mutex. wait_while unlocks the mutex and sleeps. A notify_one wakes it. Then it locks again and checks the condition again.

Do not use a plain wait() without a loop or a condition. A thread can wake up with no notify at all. This is a spurious wake-up. wait_while in Rust and wait_for in Python check the condition for you.

Deadlock

Two threads need the same two locks. Watch the order.

use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

fn main() {
    let a = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0));
    let b = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0));

    let (a1, b1) = (Arc::clone(&a), Arc::clone(&b));
    let t1 = thread::spawn(move || {
        let _x = a1.lock().unwrap(); // thread 1: a, then b
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50));
        let _y = b1.lock().unwrap();
    });
    let (a2, b2) = (Arc::clone(&a), Arc::clone(&b));
    let t2 = thread::spawn(move || {
        let _y = b2.lock().unwrap(); // thread 2: b, then a
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50));
        let _x = a2.lock().unwrap();
    });

    thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(500));
    println!("t1 done: {}, t2 done: {}", t1.is_finished(), t2.is_finished());
    println!("deadlock: each thread waits for the other");
    std::process::exit(1); // the threads would wait forever
}
t1 done: false, t2 done: false
deadlock: each thread waits for the other

A deadlock compiles fine. Rust cannot see it. The slides show how it forms.

Thread 1 locks A

Thread 1 holds lock A. All is fine so far.

Thread 2 locks B

At the same time, thread 2 holds lock B.

Thread 1 wants B

B is taken. Thread 1 sleeps and waits. It still holds A.

Thread 2 wants A

A is taken. Thread 2 sleeps and waits. It still holds B.

Nobody moves

Each thread waits for a lock that the other one holds. No error, no crash. The program just stops.

One fixed order

Every thread locks A first, then B. Now step 2 cannot happen while thread 1 holds A.

A deadlock needs all four of these at the same time.

  1. Mutual exclusion. A lock has only one owner.
  2. Hold and wait. A thread holds one lock and waits for another.
  3. No preemption. Nobody can take a lock away from a thread.
  4. Circular wait. The waiting threads form a circle.

Break any one condition and the deadlock cannot happen. In practice you break number 2 or number 4.

  • Fixed order breaks the circle. Always lock in the same order, for example by account id.
  • Short locks break hold and wait. Never hold one lock while you take another.
  • One lock for data that always changes together.
  • try_lock fails at once instead of waiting. You can let go and try again.

Locking the same Mutex two times in one thread is also a deadlock. The Rust docs say the second lock() never returns: it may panic or hang. Python has the same trap with Lock. Python's RLock allows one thread to lock again.

Atomics and memory ordering

A counter does not need a mutex. Look at two ways to count with four threads.

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
use std::thread;

static HITS: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0);   // no Mutex, no Arc
static BROKEN: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0);

fn main() {
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for _ in 0..4 {
            s.spawn(|| {
                for _ in 0..100_000 {
                    // Right: one atomic step reads, adds and writes.
                    HITS.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
                    // Wrong: two steps. Another thread can run between them.
                    let v = BROKEN.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
                    BROKEN.store(v + 1, Ordering::Relaxed);
                }
            });
        }
    });
    println!("fetch_add:    {}", HITS.load(Ordering::Relaxed));
    println!("load + store: {}", BROKEN.load(Ordering::Relaxed));
}
fetch_add:    400000
load + store: 193097

The second line was 227419 in the next run. It changes every time. The code has no data race, so it is safe Rust. But it has a race condition: two threads read the same old value, and one update is lost.

An atomic type changes in one step that no other thread can split. fetch_add, swap and compare_exchange read and write in that one step. Atomics are the building blocks of Arc, Mutex and channels.

Ordering in simple words

Every atomic call takes an Ordering. Why? The compiler and the CPU may reorder memory work. One thread can see the writes of another thread in a different order. The ordering says which order is promised.

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, AtomicU64, Ordering};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

static DATA: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0);
static READY: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);

fn main() {
    thread::scope(|s| {
        s.spawn(|| {
            DATA.store(42, Ordering::Relaxed); // 1. write the data
            READY.store(true, Ordering::Release); // 2. then raise the flag
        });
        s.spawn(|| {
            // Acquire pairs with Release: once we see the flag,
            // we also see every write made before it.
            while !READY.load(Ordering::Acquire) {
                thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));
            }
            println!("data = {}", DATA.load(Ordering::Relaxed)); // always 42
        });
    });
}
data = 42

Think of a letter and a flag on a mailbox. The writer puts the letter in, then raises the flag with Release. The reader sees the flag with Acquire. Now the reader is sure to find the letter. With Relaxed on the flag, the reader could see the flag first and an old letter.

The five orderings
OrderingPromise in simple wordsTypical use
RelaxedOnly this one value is safe. No order with other memory.Counters and statistics
ReleaseMy earlier writes become visible with this store.Raise a "ready" flag, unlock
AcquireAfter this load, I see the writes before the paired release.Read the flag, lock
AcqRelBoth, for one read-and-write step.fetch_add or compare_exchange in a lock
SeqCstAcquire and release, plus one order that all threads agree on.When you are not sure

Rust uses the same memory model as C++20. Release is only for stores and Acquire only for loads. A wrong pair, like load(Ordering::Release), panics at run time.

Do not build your own lock out of atomics in normal code. It is very easy to get wrong, and tests rarely show the bug. Use Mutex, channels or a crate. Use atomics for counters and flags.

What about Python? (expert)

Python's standard library has no atomic integer type. Use a Lock. On the normal build, counter += 1 from four threads gave the right total here. That is a detail of the interpreter, not a promise. The operation is still three steps: read, add, write. On the free-threaded build, updates can be lost. Always use a lock.

Channels

The book's pattern page showed an unbounded channel. Now limit its size.

use std::sync::mpsc;
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

fn main() {
    // A bounded channel: at most 2 messages wait in it.
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::sync_channel::<u32>(2);
    let producer = thread::spawn(move || {
        for i in 1..=5 {
            tx.send(i).unwrap(); // blocks while the channel is full
            println!("sent {i}");
        }
    }); // tx is dropped here, so the receiver loop can end

    thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)); // a slow consumer
    for v in rx {
        println!("got {v}");
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(20));
    }
    producer.join().unwrap();
}
sent 1
sent 2
sent 3
got 1
got 2
sent 4
got 3
sent 5
got 4
got 5
import queue
import threading
import time

q: queue.Queue[int | None] = queue.Queue(maxsize=2)  # a bounded queue


def producer() -> None:
    for i in range(1, 6):
        q.put(i)  # blocks while the queue is full
        print(f"sent {i}")
    q.put(None)  # the stop signal


threading.Thread(target=producer).start()
time.sleep(0.1)  # a slow consumer
while (v := q.get()) is not None:
    print(f"got {v}")
    time.sleep(0.02)
sent 1
sent 2
got 1
sent 3
got 2
sent 4
got 3
sent 5
got 4
got 5

The producer sends 1 and 2 at once. Then the channel is full, and send waits. Each recv frees one place. In the Rust run, "sent 3" was printed just before "got 1". The free place appeared before main could print. This waiting is back-pressure. It keeps memory small when the consumer is slow.

  • mpsc::channel() has no limit. A fast producer can fill the memory.
  • mpsc::sync_channel(n) holds at most n messages. sync_channel(0) makes every send wait for a receive.
  • The name mpsc means many producers, single consumer. The receiver cannot be cloned.
  • The docs of Rust 1.100 list a module std::sync::mpmc (many consumers) as experimental. It is not stable yet. The crate crossbeam-channel offers many consumers today.

A send fails when the receiver is gone. send(..).unwrap() then panics. In a long-running program, handle that Err: it usually means "stop working, nobody listens".

Data parallelism with rayon

Many jobs look like this: do the same work on a million items. The crate rayon makes that a one-word change.

[dependencies]
rayon = "1.12"
use rayon::prelude::*;
use std::time::Instant;

fn is_prime(n: u64) -> bool {
    n >= 2 && (2..).take_while(|d| d * d <= n).all(|d| n % d != 0)
}

fn main() {
    let limit = 5_000_000u64;

    let t = Instant::now();
    let seq = (0..limit).filter(|&n| is_prime(n)).count();
    let seq_ms = t.elapsed().as_millis();

    let t = Instant::now();
    let par = (0..limit).into_par_iter().filter(|&n| is_prime(n)).count();
    let par_ms = t.elapsed().as_millis();

    println!("primes: {seq} and {par}");
    println!("iter: {seq_ms} ms, par_iter: {par_ms} ms");
    println!("threads in the pool: {}", rayon::current_num_threads());

    let mut v: Vec<u32> = (0..1_000_000).rev().collect();
    v.par_sort_unstable(); // a parallel sort
    println!("sorted: {}", v.windows(2).all(|w| w[0] <= w[1]));
}
primes: 348513 and 348513
iter: 717 ms, par_iter: 127 ms
threads in the pool: 10
sorted: true

This ran with cargo run --release and rayon 1.12.0 on a laptop with 10 cores. The times change a lot from run to run, so read them as "several times faster", not as exact numbers.

Data parallelism means one operation on many items at once. Rayon keeps one thread per core. It cuts the work into pieces. An idle thread takes pieces from a busy thread. This is work stealing.

  • iter() becomes par_iter(), and into_iter() becomes into_par_iter(). Most adapters keep their names.
  • The closures must be Send and Sync. So the compiler still prevents data races.
  • rayon::join(a, b) runs two closures, maybe in parallel. It is good for divide and conquer.

Do not use par_iter for tiny work. Splitting the work costs time too. A sum of 1,000 numbers is faster on one thread. Measure first.

Which tool for which job

The last branch belongs to the next chapter, Async and await. Threads are best for work that uses the CPU. Async is best for many tasks that mostly wait.

Python: threads, the GIL and other options

Python threads behave differently. Look at the same CPU-heavy job in four ways.

import sys
import time
from concurrent.futures import (InterpreterPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor,
                                ThreadPoolExecutor)


def count_primes(lo: int, hi: int) -> int:
    count = 0
    for n in range(max(lo, 2), hi):
        d = 2
        while d * d <= n:
            if n % d == 0:
                break
            d += 1
        else:
            count += 1
    return count


def run(name: str, executor_cls) -> None:
    parts = [(i * 300_000, (i + 1) * 300_000) for i in range(4)]
    start = time.perf_counter()
    if executor_cls is None:
        total = sum(count_primes(lo, hi) for lo, hi in parts)
    else:
        with executor_cls(max_workers=4) as ex:
            total = sum(ex.map(count_primes, *zip(*parts)))
    ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
    print(f"{name:<12} {total} primes in {ms:5.0f} ms")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("GIL enabled:", sys._is_gil_enabled())
    run("one thread", None)
    run("4 threads", ThreadPoolExecutor)
    run("4 processes", ProcessPoolExecutor)
    run("4 interps", InterpreterPoolExecutor)
GIL enabled: True
one thread   92938 primes in  3315 ms
4 threads    92938 primes in  3230 ms
4 processes  92938 primes in  1604 ms
4 interps    92938 primes in  1574 ms

Why are four threads no faster? The normal Python build has a GIL. Only one thread runs Python code at a time. The others wait. The last part of the range has the most work, so four workers do not give four times the speed.

Threads still help when the work mostly waits. A thread lets go of the GIL while it waits for the network or the disk.

import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor


def fetch(url: str) -> str:
    time.sleep(0.5)  # waiting for the network: the GIL is released
    return f"{url}: ok"


urls = ["a.example", "b.example", "c.example", "d.example"]
start = time.perf_counter()
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    for line in pool.map(fetch, urls):
        print(line)
print(f"{time.perf_counter() - start:.1f} s, not 2.0 s")
a.example: ok
b.example: ok
c.example: ok
d.example: ok
0.5 s, not 2.0 s

The four ways to run Python in parallel

Python concurrency options in 2026
WayUses many cores for Python code?Shares memory?Good for
threading, normal buildNo, the GIL allows one at a timeYesWaiting for network and disk
threading, free-threaded buildYesYesCPU work, if your libraries support it
multiprocessing, ProcessPoolExecutorYesNo, data is copiedCPU work with little data to send
InterpreterPoolExecutor (new in 3.14)Yes, one GIL per interpreterNo, by defaultCPU work, lighter than processes
  • Free-threaded build. Python 3.13 added a build without the GIL as an experiment (PEP 703). In Python 3.14 it is officially supported (PEP 779), but it is not the default. With uv you install it as uv python install 3.14t. The 3.14 notes say one thread runs about 5 to 10 percent slower on it. Some C extensions turn the GIL back on.
  • Check your build with sys._is_gil_enabled(). The normal build prints True, as above.
  • Processes. On macOS and Windows a new process starts fresh (the spawn method). Since Python 3.14, other Unix systems use forkserver by default, not fork.
  • Interpreters. Python 3.14 added concurrent.interpreters (PEP 734) and InterpreterPoolExecutor. Each interpreter has its own GIL inside one process.

This machine has only the normal build of Python 3.14, so the free-threaded results are not shown. Python 3.15 came out on 9 October 2026. Its free-threaded build is still a separate build. Check python.org: this changes fast.

Do not use threads to speed up pure Python math on the normal build. Use processes, interpreters, numpy, or a Rust extension (see Rust and Python together). Also, keep the code that starts processes under if __name__ == "__main__":. With spawn, each new process imports your file again.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for threads and shared state
PatternPurposeModelNote
thread::spawn(move || ...)Start a thread that owns its datalet h = thread::spawn(move || work(data));Keep the handle and call join().
thread::scope(|s| ...)Split work that borrows local datathread::scope(|s| { s.spawn(|| sum(left)); });All threads are joined at the end of the scope.
Arc<Mutex<T>>Share changing data between owned threadslet hits = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0));In a scope, a plain Mutex<T> is enough.
let mut g = m.lock().unwrap();Get exclusive access*g += 1;Keep the guard short. Drop it before slow work.
RwLock<T>Many readers, rare writerslet c = config.read().unwrap();Not faster for short reads. Measure.
cv.wait_while(guard, cond)Sleep until a condition holdsq = cv.wait_while(q, |q| q.is_empty()).unwrap();Never a plain wait() without a check.
