AtomicU64::fetch_addCount without a lockHITS.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);Never load, then store. That loses updates.
Release store, Acquire loadPublish data with a flagREADY.store(true, Ordering::Release);Use SeqCst when you are not sure.
mpsc::sync_channel(n)Pass work with back-pressurelet (tx, rx) = mpsc::sync_channel(100);The receiver loop ends when all senders are dropped.
Lock in one fixed orderPrevent deadlocksLock the lower account id firstRust does not detect deadlocks.
par_iter()Same work on many items, all coresv.par_iter().map(f).sum()Not for tiny work. Measure first.
ThreadPoolExecutorPython: many waiting taskspool.map(fetch, urls)No CPU speed-up on the normal build.
ProcessPoolExecutorPython: CPU work on many coresex.map(count_primes, los, his)Put start-up code under if __name__ == "__main__":.

Practice

Why does thread::spawn(|| println!("{names:?}")) fail to compile?

  • Vec is not Send.
  • The thread may outlive names, so it may not borrow it.
  • println! cannot run in a thread.

E0373. Add move, or use thread::scope, which joins the thread before names is dropped.

Which type can you not send to another thread?

  • Arc<String>
  • Rc<String>
  • Mutex<Vec<u8>>

Rc changes its count without atomic steps. So it is neither Send nor Sync.

Four threads each run let v = c.load(Relaxed); c.store(v + 1, Relaxed); 1,000 times. What is the final value?

  • Always 4000
  • 4000 or less, different on each run
  • The program does not compile.

It compiles, and there is no data race. But two threads can read the same value, so updates are lost. Use fetch_add.

A pure-Python function counts primes. On the normal Python 3.14 build, which option uses four cores?

  • ThreadPoolExecutor(4)
  • ProcessPoolExecutor(4)
  • asyncio.gather with four tasks

The GIL lets one thread run Python code at a time. Processes each have their own interpreter and GIL.

A type is trait when &T is Send.

A store with Ordering::<span class="blank" data-answer="Release">name</span> pairs with a load with Ordering::Acquire.

The Python function sys.<span class="blank" data-answer="_is_gil_enabled">name</span>() tells you if the GIL is on.

  1. Sum a Vec<u64> with four scoped threads. Each thread sums one quarter.
    Answer 
    fn par_sum(v: &[u64]) -> u64 {
    let size = v.len().div_ceil(4).max(1); // at least 1, so chunks() works
    std::thread::scope(|s| {
        let handles: Vec<_> = v
            .chunks(size)
            .map(|part| s.spawn(move || part.iter().sum::<u64>()))
            .collect(); // start all threads first
        handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).sum()
    })
}

    For (1..=100).collect() it returns 5050. The collect matters. Without it, the lazy chain would start and join one thread at a time.

  2. This code holds the lock while it sleeps. Change it so other threads can work during the sleep. 
    let mut q = queue.lock().unwrap();
let job = q.pop_front();
std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(100)); // slow work
    Answer

    Take the job in a short block, so the guard is dropped before the slow part.

    let job = queue.lock().unwrap().pop_front(); // the guard drops at the end of this line
std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(100));
  3. A bank moves money between two accounts. Each account has its own Mutex. A transfer locks from, then to. Two opposite transfers sometimes freeze. Fix the order.
    Answer

    Lock the account with the lower id first, in every transfer. Then all threads use one fixed order, and there is no circle.

    let (first, second) = if from.id < to.id { (from, to) } else { (to, from) };
let mut a = first.balance.lock().unwrap();
let mut b = second.balance.lock().unwrap();

    After that, add and take the amount on the right guard.

  4. Expert. Why is MutexGuard not Send?
    Answer

    Some operating systems require that the thread that locked a mutex also unlocks it. The guard unlocks in its drop. If you could move the guard to another thread, that other thread would unlock. So the guard must stay on its thread.

  5. Expert. Your Python web scraper downloads 200 pages and then parses each page with slow pure-Python code. Which tools do you use for each part on the normal build?
    Answer

    Downloads mostly wait, so threads (or asyncio) are fine. Parsing uses the CPU, so a ProcessPoolExecutor or InterpreterPoolExecutor helps. On the free-threaded build, threads could do both, if the parser library supports it.

Key takeaways

  • spawn needs a closure that owns its data. scope lets threads borrow and joins them for you.
  • Send and Sync are auto traits. They make data races a compile error.
  • A Mutex holds its data. The guard unlocks on drop. A panic poisons the mutex.
  • Deadlocks compile. Prevent them with one fixed lock order and short locks.
  • Atomics do one step that cannot be split. Release and Acquire form a handshake.
  • In Python, the GIL limits threads to waiting work. Use processes or interpreters for CPU work, or the free-threaded build.

Sources

  • Rust std::thread. Spawn, join, scoped threads and available_parallelism.
  • The Rustonomicon: Send and Sync. The exact meaning of the two traits and which types have them.
  • Rust std::sync::atomic::Ordering. The five orderings and the C++20 memory model.
  • rayon on docs.rs. Parallel iterators, join and the thread pool (version 1.12.0).
  • Python HOWTO: free-threaded CPython. How to check the build and what is still limited.
  • What's new in Python 3.14. PEP 779, InterpreterPoolExecutor and the new process start method.

Async and await

A web server waits most of the time. It waits for the network, the disk and the database. Async code lets one thread handle thousands of waiting tasks. This chapter shows how Rust does it with tokio, and how Python does it with asyncio.

  • Explain what a future is and what poll, Pending and a waker do.
  • Write async code with tokio: tasks, join!, JoinSet, select! and timeouts.
  • Use async closures and async functions in traits, and know their limits.
  • Explain why Pin exists and what cancellation safety means.
  • Keep blocking code out of async code, in Rust and in Python.

What async solves

Start ten thousand tasks. Each one waits one second, like a slow network call.

use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let start = Instant::now();
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for i in 0..10_000u64 {
        // Each task "waits for the network" for one second.
        handles.push(tokio::spawn(async move {
            tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1)).await;
            i
        }));
    }
    let mut sum = 0;
    for h in handles {
        sum += h.await.unwrap();
    }
    println!("10000 tasks, sum {sum}, {:.2} s", start.elapsed().as_secs_f64());
}
10000 tasks, sum 49995000, 1.01 s
import asyncio
import time


async def task(i: int) -> int:
    await asyncio.sleep(1)  # "wait for the network" for one second
    return i


async def main() -> None:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(task(i) for i in range(10_000)))
    print(f"10000 tasks, sum {sum(results)}, {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f} s")


asyncio.run(main())
10000 tasks, sum 49995000, 1.06 s

Ten thousand seconds of waiting finished in about one second. The tasks waited at the same time. With threads you would need ten thousand threads. Each spawned Rust thread reserves a 2 MiB stack by default. An async task is a small object, often a few hundred bytes.

A task runs until it must wait. At that point it gives the thread back. The thread runs another task. This is concurrency. It is not the same as parallelism.

Threads and async tasks
QuestionThreadsAsync tasks
Who switches?The operating system, at any momentThe task itself, only at .await
Cost of oneA stack of megabytes, a system call to startA small object on the heap
How many are fine?Hundreds or a few thousandHundreds of thousands
Best forCPU workWaiting: network, timers, many connections

Async does not make CPU work faster. A loop that counts primes never waits, so it never gives the thread back. For CPU work use threads or rayon, as in Threads and shared state.

Future and poll in simple words

Here is a future written by hand. It says "not yet" two times. Then it gives 42.

use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::task::{Context, Poll};

// A hand-made future: it says "not yet" two times, then gives 42.
struct Countdown {
    left: u32,
}

impl Future for Countdown {
    type Output = u32;

    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<u32> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            println!("poll: ready");
            Poll::Ready(42)
        } else {
            println!("poll: pending, {} left", self.left);
            self.left -= 1;
            cx.waker().wake_by_ref(); // "poll me again soon"
            Poll::Pending
        }
    }
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let fut = Countdown { left: 2 }; // nothing runs yet: futures are lazy
    println!("created");
    let v = fut.await; // the runtime calls poll until Ready
    println!("got {v}");
}
created
poll: pending, 2 left
poll: pending, 1 left
poll: ready
got 42

The Future trait has one method, poll. To poll means to ask "are you ready?". The answer is Poll::Ready(value) or Poll::Pending.

  • A future that returns Pending must arrange a wake-up. It keeps the waker from cx. When its data arrives, it calls wake().
  • The runtime then polls the task again. It never polls in a busy loop.
  • Real futures, like a socket read, give the waker to the operating system's event system. The countdown calls it at once, only to keep the example small.

The slides show what happens at one .await.

Poll

The runtime polls the task. The task runs until it reaches socket.read(..).await.

Not ready

No data has arrived. The read future gives the waker to the system and returns Pending.

Give the thread back

The task returns Pending too. The thread is free. The runtime polls other tasks.

Data arrives

The operating system reports the socket as readable. The runtime calls wake() on the saved waker.

Poll again

The task goes back into the run queue. The runtime polls it, maybe on another thread.

Ready

The read returns Ready(bytes). The code after .await runs.

An async fn becomes a state machine. Each .await is one state. The local variables that live across an .await are stored inside the future.

Futures are lazy. Call an async function without .await, and its body never runs. Both languages warn you, and both programs print only "done".

warning: unused implementer of `Future` that must be used
 --> src/bin/lazy.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     greet(); // forgot .await: the body never runs
  |     ^^^^^^^
  |
  = note: futures do nothing unless you `.await` or poll them
lazy.py:9: RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'greet' was never awaited
  greet()  # forgot await: the body never runs

async fn, .await and the tokio runtime

Rust's standard library has the Future trait, but no runtime. You choose one. Tokio is the most used. This chapter uses tokio 1.54.1, the newest version on crates.io in November 2026, and futures 0.3.34.

[dependencies]
tokio = { version = "1.54", features = ["full"] }
futures = "0.3"

The attribute #[tokio::main] is only a short way to write this:

fn main() {
    tokio::runtime::Builder::new_multi_thread()
        .enable_all() // timers and network I/O
        .build()
        .unwrap()
        .block_on(async {
            // the body of your async main
        })
}
  • async fn f() -> T returns a future of T. The body runs when you .await it.
  • .await works only inside an async function or an async block.
  • block_on is the bridge from normal code into async code. Call it one time, in main.
  • The multi-thread runtime starts one worker thread per core. #[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")] uses one thread only.

Do not call block_on inside async code. Tokio stops the program with a panic.

Cannot start a runtime from within a runtime. This happens because a function (like `block_on`) attempted to block the current thread while the thread is being used to drive asynchronous tasks. If you are in an async function, use `.await` on the future instead of blocking on it.

Tasks: spawn, join! and JoinSet

Two downloads can wait at the same time. Compare three ways.

use std::time::{Duration, Instant};
use tokio::task::JoinSet;
use tokio::time::sleep;

async fn fetch(name: &str, ms: u64) -> String {
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(ms)).await; // pretend to wait for the network
    format!("{name} ({ms} ms)")
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let t = Instant::now();
    let a = fetch("users", 300).await;
    let b = fetch("orders", 200).await; // starts only after a is done
    println!("one by one: {a}, {b} in {:.1} s", t.elapsed().as_secs_f64());

    let t = Instant::now();
    let (a, b) = tokio::join!(fetch("users", 300), fetch("orders", 200));
    println!("join!: {a}, {b} in {:.1} s", t.elapsed().as_secs_f64());

    // JoinSet: spawn many tasks, take results as they finish.
    let mut set = JoinSet::new();
    for (name, ms) in [("slow", 300), ("fast", 100), ("mid", 200)] {
        set.spawn(fetch(name, ms));
    }
    while let Some(res) = set.join_next().await {
        println!("finished: {}", res.unwrap());
    }
}
one by one: users (300 ms), orders (200 ms) in 0.5 s
join!: users (300 ms), orders (200 ms) in 0.3 s
finished: fast (100 ms)
finished: mid (200 ms)
finished: slow (300 ms)
import asyncio
import time


async def fetch(name: str, ms: int) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(ms / 1000)  # pretend to wait for the network
    return f"{name} ({ms} ms)"


async def main() -> None:
    t = time.perf_counter()
    a = await fetch("users", 300)
    b = await fetch("orders", 200)  # starts only after a is done
    print(f"one by one: {a}, {b} in {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f} s")

    t = time.perf_counter()
    a, b = await asyncio.gather(fetch("users", 300), fetch("orders", 200))
    print(f"gather: {a}, {b} in {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f} s")

    # TaskGroup (3.11+): all tasks end before the block ends.
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tasks = [tg.create_task(fetch(n, ms))
                 for n, ms in [("slow", 300), ("fast", 100), ("mid", 200)]]
        for coro in asyncio.as_completed(tasks):  # in the order they finish
            print("finished:", await coro)


asyncio.run(main())
one by one: users (300 ms), orders (200 ms) in 0.5 s
gather: users (300 ms), orders (200 ms) in 0.3 s
finished: fast (100 ms)
finished: mid (200 ms)
finished: slow (300 ms)
  • Two .await lines in a row run one after the other. 300 ms plus 200 ms is 0.5 s.
  • tokio::join! polls both futures in the same task. They wait together, so it takes 0.3 s. try_join! stops at the first Err.
  • tokio::spawn makes a new task. The runtime can run it on another core. It returns a JoinHandle, like a thread.
  • A JoinSet holds many tasks. join_next() gives results in the order they finish. When the set is dropped, it cancels all its tasks.

Like thread::spawn, tokio::spawn needs a future that is Send and 'static. The task may move between threads and may outlive the caller.

Do not hold a std::sync::MutexGuard across an .await. The guard is not Send, so the whole future is not Send.

error: future cannot be sent between threads safely
  = help: within `{async block@src/bin/send_err.rs:7:26: 7:36}`, the trait `Send` is not implemented for `std::sync::MutexGuard<'_, i32>`
note: future is not `Send` as this value is used across an await
  8 |         let mut n = hits.lock().unwrap(); // a std MutexGuard
    |             ----- has type `std::sync::MutexGuard<'_, i32>` which is not `Send`
  9 |         tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(10)).await; // held across .await
    |                                                       ^^^^^ await occurs here, with `mut n` maybe used later

Fix it in one of two ways. Drop the guard before the .await, for example with a small block. Or, when you really must hold the lock while you wait, use tokio::sync::Mutex. Its lock() is itself async.

select!, timeouts and cancellation

Often you want "the first of these to finish". Here are a timeout and a loop that stops on a signal.

use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::sync::mpsc;
use tokio::time::{sleep, timeout};

async fn slow_query() -> u32 {
    sleep(Duration::from_secs(5)).await;
    7
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // 1. A time limit on one future.
    match timeout(Duration::from_millis(100), slow_query()).await {
        Ok(v) => println!("result {v}"),
        Err(_) => println!("timed out after 100 ms"),
    }

    // 2. select!: wait for the first of several futures.
    let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<String>(8);
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        for i in 1..=3 {
            tx.send(format!("job {i}")).await.unwrap();
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(30)).await;
        }
    });
    let shutdown = sleep(Duration::from_millis(70)); // pretend: Ctrl+C
    tokio::pin!(shutdown); // select! in a loop needs a pinned future
    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            Some(job) = rx.recv() => println!("got {job}"), // cancel safe
            _ = &mut shutdown => {
                println!("shutdown signal: stop the loop");
                break;
            }
        }
    }
}
timed out after 100 ms
got job 1
got job 2
got job 3
shutdown signal: stop the loop

select! polls all its branches. The first branch that is ready wins. The other futures are dropped. A dropped future is cancelled. It never runs again. timeout is the same idea: the work or the timer, whichever comes first.

Cancellation safety

Cancellation can only happen at an .await. That sounds harmless. Now look at a transfer with two steps.

use std::sync::Mutex;
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::time::{sleep, timeout};

// Two steps with an .await between them. Not cancel safe!
async fn transfer(log: &Mutex<Vec<&'static str>>) {
    log.lock().unwrap().push("took 10 from Ann");
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(200)).await; // cancellation can happen here
    log.lock().unwrap().push("gave 10 to Bo");
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let log = Mutex::new(Vec::new());
    let r = timeout(Duration::from_millis(100), transfer(&log)).await;
    println!("timed out: {}", r.is_err());
    println!("log: {:?}", log.lock().unwrap()); // only half the work!
}
timed out: true
log: ["took 10 from Ann"]
import asyncio


async def slow_query() -> int:
    await asyncio.sleep(5)
    return 7


async def transfer(log: list[str]) -> None:
    log.append("took 10 from Ann")
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)  # cancellation can happen here
    log.append("gave 10 to Bo")


async def main() -> None:
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.1):  # Python 3.11+
            print(await slow_query())
    except TimeoutError:
        print("timed out after 100 ms")

    log: list[str] = []
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.1):
            await transfer(log)
    except TimeoutError:
        print("timed out: True")
    print("log:", log)  # only half the work!


asyncio.run(main())
timed out after 100 ms
timed out: True
log: ['took 10 from Ann']

Ann lost 10 and Bo got nothing. A future is cancel safe when you can drop it at any .await and lose nothing. The tokio docs list which methods are cancel safe.

Cancel safe or not (from the tokio select! docs)
Cancel safe: fine in a select! loopNot cancel safe: can lose data or a place in line
mpsc::Receiver::recvAsyncReadExt::read_exact
TcpListener::acceptAsyncReadExt::read_to_end
AsyncReadExt::readAsyncWriteExt::write_all
StreamExt::nexttokio::sync::Mutex::lock (loses its place in the queue)

Do not put a two-step operation directly into a select! branch in a loop. Spawn it as its own task, or keep its future outside the loop and poll it by &mut. Then a lost race does not stop it in the middle.

Rust and Python cancel in different ways (expert)

In Rust, cancellation means "drop the future". No more code of the task runs. Only destructors run. In Python, the event loop throws CancelledError into the coroutine at its await. Your finally blocks and except blocks still run. A coroutine can even catch the error and go on, but then TaskGroup and timeout may misbehave. Always re-raise CancelledError.

Async closures and async fn in traits

A retry helper takes "some async operation" as an argument. Since Rust 1.85 this is an async closure.

use std::time::Duration;

// Takes an async closure. AsyncFnMut is in the prelude since Rust 1.85.
async fn retry<T, E: std::fmt::Display>(
    times: u32,
    mut op: impl AsyncFnMut(u32) -> Result<T, E>,
) -> Result<T, E> {
    let mut attempt = 1;
    loop {
        match op(attempt).await {
            Ok(v) => return Ok(v),
            Err(e) if attempt < times => {
                println!("attempt {attempt} failed: {e}");
                tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(10 * attempt as u64)).await;
                attempt += 1;
            }
            Err(e) => return Err(e),
        }
    }
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let mut calls = Vec::new(); // the closure borrows this mutably
    let result = retry(5, async |n| {
        calls.push(n);
        if n < 3 { Err(format!("server busy ({n})")) } else { Ok("data") }
    })
    .await;
    println!("{result:?} after calls {calls:?}");
}
attempt 1 failed: server busy (1)
attempt 2 failed: server busy (2)
Ok("data") after calls [1, 2, 3]

An async closure is written async |n| { ... }. The three traits AsyncFn, AsyncFnMut and AsyncFnOnce match Fn, FnMut and FnOnce. The old way was a closure that returns an async block: |n| async move { ... }. That future could not borrow from the closure's captures. So calls.push(n) above was impossible with the old way.

async fn in traits

// async fn in a trait: stable since Rust 1.75.
trait Store {
    async fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String>;
}

struct MemStore;

impl Store for MemStore {
    async fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String> {
        tokio::task::yield_now().await; // pretend to do I/O
        (key == "a").then(|| "apple".to_string())
    }
}

// Generic use works: static dispatch.
async fn show(store: &impl Store, key: &str) {
    println!("{key} -> {:?}", store.get(key).await);
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let s = MemStore;
    show(&s, "a").await;
    show(&s, "b").await;
}
a -> Some("apple")
b -> None

This works well with generics. It has two limits today.

  1. No dyn. A trait with an async fn is not dyn compatible. Each implementation returns a future of a different size.
  2. No Send bound on the returned future. Generic code cannot easily say "the future of get must be Send". So tokio::spawn may refuse it.
error[E0038]: the trait `Store` is not dyn compatible
  |
1 | trait Store {
  |       ----- this trait is not dyn compatible...
2 |     async fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String>;
  |              ^^^ ...because method `get` is `async`

Workarounds exist. For dyn, write the method by hand to return Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = T> + Send + '_>>, or use the async-trait crate. For Send, the Rust team's trait-variant crate (version 0.1.3) makes a second trait whose futures are Send. A real fix, "return type notation" like T::get(..): Send, is a 2026 project goal. It is still unstable as far as I could check. Check the Rust blog: this can change.

Do not write |x| async { ... } when you need to borrow from the closure. Write async |x| { ... }. And take it as impl AsyncFn(T) -> R, not as impl Fn(T) -> Fut with a second generic.

Pin and why it exists

An async fn keeps its local variables inside its future. A local variable can be a reference to another local variable. Then the future points into itself. That is a self-referential value.

Pin<P> wraps a pointer, like Pin<&mut T> or Pin<Box<T>>. It promises that the value behind the pointer stays at one address until it is dropped. That is why poll takes self: Pin<&mut Self>. Most types do not care about their address. They have the auto trait Unpin, and for them Pin changes nothing.

You meet Pin in two places in normal code.

use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::{pin, Pin};
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::time::sleep;

async fn step(name: &str, ms: u64) -> String {
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(ms)).await;
    name.to_string()
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // 1. Different futures in one Vec: box and pin each one.
    let jobs: Vec<Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = String>>>> = vec![
        Box::pin(step("download", 20)),
        Box::pin(async { "cached".to_string() }),
    ];
    for job in jobs {
        println!("{}", job.await);
    }

    // 2. Await the same future in many rounds: pin it on the stack.
    let mut deadline = pin!(sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)));
    let mut rounds = 0;
    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            _ = &mut deadline => break, // needs Pin<&mut Sleep>
            _ = sleep(Duration::from_millis(40)) => rounds += 1,
        }
    }
    println!("{rounds} rounds before the deadline");
}
download
cached
2 rounds before the deadline
  • Box::pin(fut) puts the future on the heap and pins it there. Use it for trait objects and for futures you return from a function.
  • std::pin::pin!(fut) pins it on the stack. It costs nothing. Use it for a future that you poll many times by &mut.

Awaiting a future by &mut without pinning gives a long error. The key line is "cannot be unpinned". The compiler even suggests the fix.

error[E0277]: `PhantomPinned` cannot be unpinned
 --> src/bin/pin_err.rs:6:18
  |
6 |     (&mut sleep).await; // await by reference, without pinning
  |                  ^^^^^ within `(PhantomData<&()>, PhantomPinned)`, the trait `Unpin` is not implemented for `PhantomPinned`
  |
  = note: consider using the `pin!` macro
          consider using `Box::pin` if you need to access the pinned value outside of the current scope

Streams and blocking code

Streams

A future gives one value. A stream gives many values over time. The trait lives in the futures crate. The standard library has an AsyncIterator trait, but it is not stable.

use futures::stream::{self, StreamExt};
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::time::Duration;

static IN_FLIGHT: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);
static MAX_SEEN: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);

async fn fetch(id: u32) -> u32 {
    let now = IN_FLIGHT.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) + 1;
    MAX_SEEN.fetch_max(now, Ordering::SeqCst);
    tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50)).await;
    IN_FLIGHT.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
    id * 10
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // A stream: values that arrive one by one, over time.
    let mut evens = stream::iter(1..=10).filter(|n| std::future::ready(n % 2 == 0));
    while let Some(n) = evens.next().await {
        print!("{n} ");
    }
    println!();

    // 20 downloads, but at most 3 at the same time.
    let results: Vec<u32> = stream::iter(1..=20)
        .map(fetch) // a stream of futures, nothing runs yet
        .buffer_unordered(3) // run up to 3 of them at once
        .collect()
        .await;
    println!("{} results, max in flight: {}", results.len(), MAX_SEEN.load(Ordering::SeqCst));
}
2 4 6 8 10
20 results, max in flight: 3
import asyncio

in_flight = 0
max_seen = 0


async def evens(limit: int):  # an async generator: a stream
    for n in range(1, limit + 1):
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        if n % 2 == 0:
            yield n


async def fetch(id: int, limit: asyncio.Semaphore) -> int:
    global in_flight, max_seen
    async with limit:  # at most 3 inside at the same time
        in_flight += 1
        max_seen = max(max_seen, in_flight)
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        in_flight -= 1
        return id * 10


async def main() -> None:
    print(*[n async for n in evens(10)])
    limit = asyncio.Semaphore(3)
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(i, limit) for i in range(1, 21)))
    print(f"{len(results)} results, max in flight: {max_seen}")


asyncio.run(main())
2 4 6 8 10
20 results, max in flight: 3

buffer_unordered(3) is a very useful tool. It limits how many futures run at once. Without a limit, 10,000 downloads would open 10,000 connections. Python uses a semaphore for the same job. Tokio has tokio::sync::Semaphore too.

Blocking code inside async code

One slow call that does not .await can stop a whole runtime. This example uses a runtime with one thread.

use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

// One worker thread, so a blocked task blocks everything.
#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]
async fn main() {
    let start = Instant::now();
    let ticker = tokio::spawn(async move {
        for _ in 0..3 {
            tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)).await;
            println!("tick at {} ms", start.elapsed().as_millis());
        }
    });

    // Wrong: std::thread::sleep blocks the only worker thread.
    std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(350));
    println!("blocking work done at {} ms", start.elapsed().as_millis());
    ticker.await.unwrap();

    // Right: move blocking work to the blocking thread pool.
    let start = Instant::now();
    let ticker = tokio::spawn(async move {
        for _ in 0..3 {
            tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)).await;
            println!("tick at {} ms", start.elapsed().as_millis());
        }
    });
    let n = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| {
        std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(350)); // or heavy CPU work
        42
    })
    .await
    .unwrap();
    println!("spawn_blocking gave {n} at {} ms", start.elapsed().as_millis());
    ticker.await.unwrap();
}
blocking work done at 357 ms
tick at 460 ms
tick at 563 ms
tick at 666 ms
tick at 103 ms
tick at 206 ms
tick at 309 ms
spawn_blocking gave 42 at 355 ms
import asyncio
import time


async def ticker(start: float) -> None:
    for _ in range(3):
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
        print(f"tick at {(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.0f} ms")


def blocking_work() -> int:
    time.sleep(0.35)  # or heavy CPU work
    return 42


async def main() -> None:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    t = asyncio.create_task(ticker(start))
    time.sleep(0.35)  # wrong: blocks the event loop
    print(f"blocking work done at {(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.0f} ms")
    await t

    start = time.perf_counter()
    t = asyncio.create_task(ticker(start))
    n = await asyncio.to_thread(blocking_work)  # right: run it in a thread
    print(f"to_thread gave {n} at {(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.0f} ms")
    await t


asyncio.run(main())
blocking work done at 356 ms
tick at 458 ms
tick at 560 ms
tick at 663 ms
tick at 104 ms
tick at 206 ms
tick at 308 ms
to_thread gave 42 at 358 ms

In the wrong half, the ticker could not even start. Its first sleep began only at about 357 ms, when main reached an .await. In the right half, the ticks come on time. The exact numbers change a little from run to run.

Code between two .await points should finish quickly. A common rule of thumb from a tokio maintainer is 10 to 100 microseconds at most. Send slow file calls and blocking libraries to spawn_blocking in Rust or asyncio.to_thread in Python. Send heavy CPU work to rayon or to a process pool.

The usual blockers are std::thread::sleep, std::fs, a blocking HTTP client, a sync database driver and heavy loops. Use the async versions: tokio::time::sleep, tokio::fs and async clients.

Python asyncio and TaskGroup compared

Python has had async and await since 3.5, and asyncio is in the standard library. The ideas match Rust's. The details differ in important ways.

tokio and asyncio side by side
JobRust with tokioPython asyncio
RuntimeA crate you chooseBuilt in, one event loop per thread
Start#[tokio::main]asyncio.run(main())
Start a tasktokio::spawn(fut)tg.create_task(coro)
Wait for alljoin!, JoinSetTaskGroup, gather
First one winsselect!asyncio.wait(..., return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)
Time limittokio::time::timeoutasync with asyncio.timeout(s)
Blocking workspawn_blockingasyncio.to_thread
StreamStream from futuresAsync generator, async for
Many coresYes, tasks move between worker threadsNo, one loop runs on one thread
CancellationDrop the futureCancelledError raised inside the task

TaskGroup: structured concurrency

asyncio.TaskGroup came in Python 3.11. All tasks end before the async with block ends. If one task fails, the group cancels the others. It raises the errors together as an ExceptionGroup. This idea is structured concurrency. In Rust, a JoinSet is the closest twin. It cancels its tasks when it is dropped.

Python 3.15 came out on 9 October 2026. It adds TaskGroup.cancel(), an early exit without an error. This program asks three servers and keeps the first answer.

import asyncio


async def search(server: str, ms: int, found: asyncio.Future) -> None:
    await asyncio.sleep(ms / 1000)
    if not found.done():
        found.set_result(server)


async def main() -> None:
    found = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        for server, ms in [("eu", 300), ("us", 100), ("asia", 200)]:
            tg.create_task(search(server, ms, found))
        print("first answer from", await found)
        tg.cancel()  # new in 3.15: stop the other tasks, no error
    print("group closed")


asyncio.run(main())
first answer from us
group closed

This ran on the 3.15.0b2 beta that is installed here. On Python 3.14, TaskGroup has no cancel method.

Do not start a task with asyncio.create_task(...) and forget it. The event loop keeps only a weak reference, so the task can disappear before it finishes, and its errors are lost. Start tasks inside a TaskGroup.

Python 3.14 added python -m asyncio ps PID and python -m asyncio pstree PID. They show the tasks of a running program and what each one awaits. Use them when an async program hangs.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for async and await
PatternPurposeModelNote
#[tokio::main] async fn main()Start the runtime once#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]Never block_on inside async code.
tokio::join!(a, b)Wait for a few futures togetherlet (u, o) = join!(users(), orders());Two .await lines in a row run one after the other.
tokio::spawn(async move { .. })Start an independent tasklet h = tokio::spawn(work(id));The future must be Send + 'static.
JoinSetMany tasks, results as they finishwhile let Some(r) = set.join_next().awaitDropping the set cancels its tasks.
timeout(d, fut)Put a time limit on worktimeout(Duration::from_secs(2), query()).awaitThe work is dropped at an .await. Is it cancel safe?
select! in a loopReact to the first of several eventsselect! { Some(m) = rx.recv() => .., _ = &mut stop => break }Only cancel safe futures in the branches.
async |x| { .. }Pass async behaviour as an argumentop: impl AsyncFnMut(u32) -> Result<T, E>Stable since 1.85. Can borrow from captures.
async fn in a traitAn async interfacetrait Store { async fn get(&self, k: &str) -> Option<String>; }Not dyn compatible. No easy Send bound yet.
pin!(fut)Poll one future many times by &mutlet mut d = pin!(sleep(t));Box::pin for trait objects and returns.
buffer_unordered(n)Limit how many futures run at oncestream::iter(urls).map(fetch).buffer_unordered(8)Python: an asyncio.Semaphore.
spawn_blocking(f)Run blocking or CPU workspawn_blocking(|| hash(file)).awaitPython: await asyncio.to_thread(f).
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tgPython: structured concurrencytg.create_task(fetch(u))Errors arrive as an ExceptionGroup.

Practice

What does a future do before anyone awaits or polls it?

  • It starts in the background.
  • Nothing. Futures are lazy.
  • It runs until its first .await.

A future is only a state machine. The runtime must poll it. tokio::spawn hands it to the runtime.

let a = f().await; let b = g().await; Each takes 1 second. How long does it take?

  • About 1 second
  • About 2 seconds
  • It depends on the number of cores.

The second line starts after the first one ends. Use join!(f(), g()) for about 1 second.

Which call is cancel safe inside a select! loop?

  • stream.read_exact(&mut buf)
  • rx.recv() on a tokio mpsc receiver
  • stream.write_all(&data)

If recv loses the race, no message is taken. read_exact and write_all may stop after part of the data.

An async handler calls std::fs::read_to_string on a big file. What is the risk?

  • A compile error
  • It blocks a worker thread, so other tasks on it wait.
  • The file is read two times.

It compiles. But it never gives the thread back. Use tokio::fs or spawn_blocking.

The method of the Future trait is called name.

A future that is not ready returns Poll::<span class="blank" data-answer="Pending">variant</span>.

In Python, run a blocking function from async code with asyncio.<span class="blank" data-answer="to_thread">name</span>.

  1. Rewrite with join! so both calls wait at the same time: let u = users().await; let o = orders().await;
    Answer

    let (u, o) = tokio::join!(users(), orders());. If both return Result and you want to stop at the first error, use let (u, o) = tokio::try_join!(users(), orders())?;.

  2. Put a 2 second limit on fetch(url), and print "too slow" when it fails.
    Answer 
    match tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(2), fetch(url)).await {
    Ok(body) => println!("{body}"),
    Err(_elapsed) => println!("too slow"),
}

    In Python: async with asyncio.timeout(2): body = await fetch(url), inside try with except TimeoutError: print("too slow").

  3. This task does not compile. Why, and what are two fixes? 
    tokio::spawn(async move {
    let mut n = counter.lock().unwrap(); // std::sync::Mutex
    save(&n).await;
    *n += 1;
});
    Answer

    The MutexGuard lives across save(..).await. The guard is not Send, so the future is not Send, and tokio::spawn refuses it. Fix 1: copy the value out and drop the guard before the .await, then lock again to add. Fix 2: use tokio::sync::Mutex and write counter.lock().await.

  4. Download 500 URLs with at most 10 requests at the same time. Sketch it in Rust and in Python.
    Answer

    Rust: stream::iter(urls).map(fetch).buffer_unordered(10).collect::<Vec<_>>().await. Python: make limit = asyncio.Semaphore(10), wrap the body of fetch in async with limit:, and run all of them in a TaskGroup or with gather.

  5. Expert. Why does poll take self: Pin<&mut Self> and not &mut self?
    Answer

    The future of an async fn can hold a reference to its own local variables. With &mut self, safe code could move the future between two polls, for example with std::mem::swap. The inner reference would then point to the old place. Pin forbids the move after the first poll, so the references stay valid.

  6. Expert. A select! loop has a branch msg = read_frame(&mut socket), where read_frame calls read_exact two times. Sometimes frames are broken. Explain the bug and a fix.
    Answer

    When another branch wins, the read_frame future is dropped. It may have read the first part of a frame already. Those bytes are lost, so the next read starts in the middle of a frame. Fix: move reading into its own task that sends whole frames on an mpsc channel, and select on rx.recv(), which is cancel safe. Or keep one buffered reader whose state lives outside the loop.

Key takeaways

  • Async is for many tasks that mostly wait. Threads are for CPU work.
  • A future is a lazy state machine. The runtime polls it, and a waker says when to poll again.
  • Tokio gives tasks, join!, JoinSet, select! and timeouts. Spawned futures must be Send + 'static.
  • Cancellation in Rust drops the future at an .await. Keep two-step work out of select! branches.
  • Pin keeps self-referential futures in place. Use pin! or Box::pin.
  • Never block the executor. Python's asyncio has the same rule, and TaskGroup gives structured concurrency.

Sources

  • Alice Ryhl: Async: What is blocking?. A tokio maintainer on blocking code, spawn_blocking and rayon.
  • tokio::select! on docs.rs. How select works and the list of cancel safe methods (tokio 1.54.1).
  • Rust std::pin. Why pinning exists, Unpin, pin! and Box::pin.
  • Announcing Rust 1.85.0. Async closures and the AsyncFn traits.
  • Inside Rust: Stabilizing async fn in traits. The plan, the limits and the Send bound problem.
  • Python asyncio: Coroutines and Tasks. TaskGroup, TaskGroup.cancel (3.15), timeout and to_thread.

Advanced traits and types

Rust lets you put rules into types. The compiler then checks the rules for free, before the program runs. This chapter shows the advanced tools for that: associated items, const generics, trait objects, marker types and type-level patterns.

  • Choose between an associated type and a generic parameter, and use GATs and const generics.
  • Check if a trait is dyn compatible, and use trait upcasting.
  • Read and write higher-ranked trait bounds like for<'a> Fn(&'a str).
  • Build safe APIs with PhantomData, the type-state pattern and sealed traits.
  • Explain the never type ! and why specialisation is not stable.

Associated types and associated consts

Two sensors give different kinds of readings. A thermometer gives a float. A people counter gives a whole number.

use std::ops::Add;

// An associated type and an associated const.
trait Sensor {
    type Reading; // each sensor picks ONE reading type
    const UNIT: &'static str; // each sensor picks ONE unit
    fn read(&self) -> Self::Reading;
}

struct Thermometer;
struct Counter(u32);

impl Sensor for Thermometer {
    type Reading = f64;
    const UNIT: &'static str = "°C";
    fn read(&self) -> f64 { 21.5 }
}

impl Sensor for Counter {
    type Reading = u32;
    const UNIT: &'static str = "people";
    fn read(&self) -> u32 { self.0 }
}

fn report<S: Sensor>(s: &S) -> String
where
    S::Reading: std::fmt::Display,
{
    format!("{} {}", s.read(), S::UNIT)
}

// A generic parameter allows MANY impls: Meters + Meters, Meters + f64.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Meters(f64);

impl Add for Meters {
    type Output = Meters; // the result type is fixed per impl
    fn add(self, o: Meters) -> Meters { Meters(self.0 + o.0) }
}

impl Add<f64> for Meters {
    type Output = Meters;
    fn add(self, o: f64) -> Meters { Meters(self.0 + o) }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", report(&Thermometer));
    println!("{}", report(&Counter(12)));
    println!("{:?} {:?}", Meters(1.0) + Meters(2.0), Meters(1.0) + 0.5);
}
21.5 °C
12 people
Meters(3.0) Meters(1.5)
from typing import ClassVar, Protocol


class Sensor[R](Protocol):
    UNIT: ClassVar[str]  # like an associated const

    def read(self) -> R: ...  # R plays the part of the associated type


class Thermometer:
    UNIT: ClassVar[str] = "°C"

    def read(self) -> float:
        return 21.5


class Counter:
    UNIT: ClassVar[str] = "people"

    def __init__(self, n: int) -> None:
        self.n = n

    def read(self) -> int:
        return self.n


def report[R](s: Sensor[R]) -> str:
    return f"{s.read()} {s.UNIT}"


print(report(Thermometer()))
print(report(Counter(12)))
21.5 °C
12 people

An associated type is a type slot in a trait. Each implementation fills it one time. Iterator uses one: type Item. An associated const is the same idea for a value. Code reads it as S::UNIT, with no object needed.

Associated type or generic parameter?
QuestionAssociated type: trait Sensor { type Reading; }Generic parameter: trait Add<Rhs>
How many impls per type?One. A thermometer has one reading type.Many. Meters + Meters and Meters + f64.
Who chooses?The implementerThe caller, by the types it uses
Type annotations for callersRarely neededSometimes needed

Python has no associated types. A generic Protocol with a type parameter does a similar job for the type checker. ClassVar marks a class-level constant.

Do not use a generic parameter when one choice per type makes sense. trait Sensor<R> would let one type have many sensors. Then every caller must write the type: Sensor::<f64>::read(&t).

The rest of the chapter uses the tools in this tree. Open a branch to see its parts.

Generic associated types and const generics

GATs

A normal iterator cannot give items that borrow from the iterator itself. A "lending" iterator can. Here each item is a mutable window into the same array.

// A lending iterator: each item borrows from the iterator itself.
// That needs a generic associated type (GAT), stable since Rust 1.65.
trait LendingIterator {
    type Item<'a>
    where
        Self: 'a; // an item cannot outlive the iterator
    fn next<'a>(&'a mut self) -> Option<Self::Item<'a>>;
}

// Gives overlapping mutable windows: [0,1], [1,2], [2,3] ...
struct WindowsMut<'s, T> {
    data: &'s mut [T],
    pos: usize,
    size: usize,
}

impl<'s, T> LendingIterator for WindowsMut<'s, T> {
    type Item<'a> = &'a mut [T] where Self: 'a;

    fn next<'a>(&'a mut self) -> Option<&'a mut [T]> {
        let w = self.data.get_mut(self.pos..self.pos + self.size)?;
        self.pos += 1;
        Some(w)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];
    let mut it = WindowsMut { data: &mut nums, pos: 0, size: 2 };
    // Each window adds its first item to its second one.
    while let Some(w) = it.next() {
        w[1] += w[0];
    }
    println!("{nums:?}"); // running sums
}
[1, 3, 6, 10]

A GAT is an associated type with its own generic parameters. Here Item<'a> takes a lifetime. Each call to next borrows the iterator for 'a, and the window lives only that long. The standard Iterator cannot do this, because its Item has no lifetime parameter. Overlapping &mut windows would then be alive together.

Do not forget where Self: 'a on the GAT. The compiler asks for it, because an item must not outlive the value it borrows from.

Const generics

A matrix type can carry its size in its type. Then a wrong multiplication does not compile.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Matrix<const R: usize, const C: usize> {
    cells: [[i32; C]; R],
}

impl<const R: usize, const C: usize> Matrix<R, C> {
    // (R x C) times (C x K) gives (R x K). The sizes are part of the type.
    fn mul<const K: usize>(&self, other: &Matrix<C, K>) -> Matrix<R, K> {
        let mut cells = [[0; K]; R];
        for i in 0..R {
            for j in 0..K {
                cells[i][j] = (0..C).map(|x| self.cells[i][x] * other.cells[x][j]).sum();
            }
        }
        Matrix { cells }
    }
}

fn sum<const N: usize>(values: [i32; N]) -> i32 {
    values.iter().sum()
}

fn zeros<const N: usize>() -> [i32; N] {
    [0; _] // `_` here: Rust 1.89+ infers N from the return type
}

fn main() {
    let a = Matrix { cells: [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] }; // 2 x 3
    let b = Matrix { cells: [[1], [0], [2]] }; // 3 x 1
    println!("{:?}", a.mul(&b).cells); // 2 x 1
    println!("{} {}", sum([1, 2, 3]), sum([10; 5]));
    let z: [i32; 4] = zeros();
    println!("{z:?}");
}
[[7], [16]]
6 50
[0, 0, 0, 0]

Now multiply in the wrong order: a 3 x 1 matrix times a 2 x 3 matrix.

error[E0308]: mismatched types
  --> a03_err.rs:30:28
   |
30 |     println!("{:?}", b.mul(&a).cells); // 3 x 1 times 2 x 3
   |                        --- ^^ expected `1`, found `2`
   |
   = note: expected reference `&Matrix<1, _>`
              found reference `&Matrix<2, 3>`

A const generic is a parameter that is a value. It came in Rust 1.51. On stable Rust the value must be an integer, a bool or a char.

  • Since Rust 1.89 you can write _ for a const argument inside a body, like [0; _]. The compiler infers it.
  • You cannot compute with a parameter in a type yet. [i32; N + 1] fails with "generic parameters may not be used in const operations". That feature is still unstable.
  • Python has no twin. numpy checks array shapes when the program runs.

Dyn compatibility and trait upcasting

Try to put a trait with a generic method behind dyn.

trait Shape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64;
    fn scaled<T: Into<f64>>(&self, k: T) -> f64; // generic method
    fn bigger(&self) -> Self; // returns Self
}

fn total(shapes: &[Box<dyn Shape>]) -> f64 {
    shapes.iter().map(|s| s.area()).sum()
}
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
 --> a04_err.rs:7:24
  |
7 | fn total(shapes: &[Box<dyn Shape>]) -> f64 {
  |                        ^^^^^^^^^ `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  |
3 |     fn scaled<T: Into<f64>>(&self, k: T) -> f64; // generic method
  |        ^^^^^^ ...because method `scaled` has generic type parameters
4 |     fn bigger(&self) -> Self; // returns Self
  |                         ^^^^ ...because method `bigger` references the `Self` type in its return type

A dyn Shape value is a wide pointer. It holds a pointer to the data and a pointer to a vtable. The vtable has one entry per method. The compiler builds it once for each type.

That explains the rules. A vtable needs a fixed list of functions with known types. So a trait is dyn compatible only under these conditions. The old name was "object safe".

  1. All supertraits are dyn compatible, and Sized is not a supertrait.
  2. No associated consts and no GATs.
  3. Each method has a receiver like &self, &mut self, Box<Self> or Pin<&mut Self>.
  4. No method has type parameters, and no method uses Self outside the receiver.
  5. No method is async or returns impl Trait.
  6. Escape hatch: a method with where Self: Sized is left out of the vtable. Then the rest of the trait stays dyn compatible.

The fix, and trait upcasting

use std::any::Any;
use std::fmt::Debug;

trait Shape: Debug + Any {
    fn area(&self) -> f64;
    // A generic method would break dyn. `where Self: Sized`
    // keeps it out of the vtable, so the trait stays dyn compatible.
    fn scaled<T: Into<f64>>(&self, k: T) -> f64
    where
        Self: Sized,
    {
        self.area() * k.into()
    }
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);

impl Shape for Square {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 }
}

fn main() {
    let sq = Square(3.0);
    println!("{}", sq.scaled(2)); // fine on the concrete type

    let s: Box<dyn Shape> = Box::new(Square(2.0));
    println!("{}", s.area()); // through the vtable

    // Trait upcasting (Rust 1.86+): dyn Shape -> dyn Debug, dyn Any.
    let d: &dyn Debug = &*s;
    println!("{d:?}");
    let a: &dyn Any = &*s;
    if let Some(square) = a.downcast_ref::<Square>() {
        println!("it is a Square with side {}", square.0);
    }
}
18
4
Square(2.0)
it is a Square with side 2
class Shape:
    def area(self) -> float:
        raise NotImplementedError


class Square(Shape):
    def __init__(self, side: float) -> None:
        self.side = side

    def area(self) -> float:
        return self.side * self.side

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"Square({self.side})"


s: Shape = Square(2.0)
print(s.area())
print(repr(s))  # every object can be printed: no upcast needed
if isinstance(s, Square):  # the twin of downcast_ref
    print(f"it is a Square with side {s.side}")
4.0
Square(2.0)
it is a Square with side 2.0

Trait upcasting turns &dyn Shape into &dyn Debug or &dyn Any, because both are supertraits. It is stable since Rust 1.86. Before that, you needed a helper method like fn as_any(&self) -> &dyn Any in every implementation. In Python every object is already dynamic, and isinstance does the downcast.

Do not add where Self: Sized to the trait itself. That makes the whole trait not dyn compatible. Put it on single methods only.

Higher-ranked trait bounds

A function calls a closure on a string that it makes itself. The first try does not compile.

// The caller picks 'a. But `local` lives only inside the function.
fn apply_to_local<'a, F>(f: F) -> usize
where
    F: Fn(&'a str) -> &'a str,
{
    let local = String::from("  hello  ");
    f(&local).len()
}
error[E0597]: `local` does not live long enough
  --> a05_err.rs:7:7
   |
 2 | fn apply_to_local<'a, F>(f: F) -> usize
   |                   -- lifetime `'a` defined here
...
 7 |     f(&local).len()
   |     --^^^^^^-
   |     | |
   |     | borrowed value does not live long enough
   |     argument requires that `local` is borrowed for `'a`

The lifetime 'a belongs to the caller. The caller could choose a long one, even 'static. But local dies at the end of the function. What we mean is different: "F works for any lifetime".

// for<'a>: F must work for EVERY lifetime, also a short local one.
fn apply_to_local<F>(f: F) -> usize
where
    F: for<'a> Fn(&'a str) -> &'a str,
{
    let local = String::from("  hello  ");
    f(&local).len()
}

// The short form Fn(&str) -> &str means exactly the same bound.
fn apply_short(f: impl Fn(&str) -> &str) -> usize {
    let local = String::from("  hi  ");
    f(&local).len()
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", apply_to_local(|s| s.trim()));
    println!("{}", apply_short(|s| s.trim()));
}
5
2

A higher-ranked trait bound (HRTB) is written for<'a>. Read it as "for all 'a". You rarely type it, because Fn(&str) -> &str is short for the same thing. You meet it in three places: bounds on Fn traits with references, error messages, and traits with a lifetime parameter like for<'de> Deserialize<'de> in serde.

Do not add a lifetime parameter to a function just to name the closure's argument. If the function makes the reference itself, the caller cannot choose its lifetime. Use Fn(&T) or for<'a>.

Marker traits and PhantomData

Marker traits

Some traits have no methods. They only say something about a type. They are marker traits.

use std::fmt::Debug;
use std::mem::size_of_val;

// ?Sized: T may be a type without a fixed size, like str or [i32].
fn describe<T: ?Sized + Debug>(x: &T) {
    println!("{x:?} uses {} bytes", size_of_val(x));
}

// Marker traits as bounds: T can move to another thread and live forever.
fn run_later<T: Send + 'static + Debug>(value: T) {
    std::thread::spawn(move || println!("later: {value:?}")).join().unwrap();
}

fn main() {
    describe("hello"); // str: 5 bytes
    describe(&[1, 2, 3][..]); // [i32]: 12 bytes
    describe(&7u8); // u8: 1 byte
    run_later(vec![1, 2]);
}
"hello" uses 5 bytes
[1, 2, 3] uses 12 bytes
7 uses 1 bytes
later: [1, 2]
The marker traits you meet most
TraitMeaningWho adds it
SendCan move to another threadThe compiler, when all fields are Send
Sync&T can be shared between threadsThe compiler, when all fields are Sync
SizedThe size is known at compile timeThe compiler. Every generic T has it unless you write ?Sized.
UnpinSafe to move even when pinnedThe compiler, for almost all types
CopyA plain bit copy is a correct copyYou, with #[derive(Clone, Copy)]

Send, Sync and Unpin are auto traits. The chapter Threads and shared state shows Send and Sync at work.

PhantomData

One generic id type can replace many newtypes. The type parameter is only a label.

use std::marker::PhantomData;
use std::mem::size_of;

struct User;
struct Order;

// One generic id type. T is only a label: no T is stored.
struct Id<T> {
    raw: u64,
    _kind: PhantomData<T>, // zero bytes, but the compiler sees T
}

impl<T> Id<T> {
    fn new(raw: u64) -> Self {
        Id { raw, _kind: PhantomData }
    }
}

fn cancel(order: Id<Order>, by: Id<User>) {
    println!("order {} cancelled by user {}", order.raw, by.raw);
}

fn main() {
    let u: Id<User> = Id::new(7);
    let o: Id<Order> = Id::new(1042);
    cancel(o, u);
    // cancel(u, o); // error[E0308]: expected `Id<Order>`, found `Id<User>`
    println!("size of Id<User>: {} bytes", size_of::<Id<User>>());
}
order 1042 cancelled by user 7
size of Id<User>: 8 bytes
from dataclasses import dataclass


class User: ...


class Order: ...


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Id[T]:  # T is only a label for the type checker
    raw: int


def cancel(order: Id[Order], by: Id[User]) -> None:
    print(f"order {order.raw} cancelled by user {by.raw}")


u: Id[User] = Id(7)
o: Id[Order] = Id(1042)
cancel(o, u)
cancel(u, o)  # runs, but mypy reports it
order 1042 cancelled by user 7
order 7 cancelled by user 1042

Without the PhantomData field, Rust refuses the struct.

error[E0392]: type parameter `T` is never used
  = help: consider removing `T`, referring to it in a field, or using a marker such as `PhantomData`

PhantomData<T> is a zero-sized type. It tells the compiler "act as if I own a T". That matters for three things: type checks, as above, the auto traits Send and Sync, and drop checking. Python's type checker reports the swapped call. Python itself runs it.

PhantomData<T> makes your type Send only when T is Send. For a pure label, PhantomData<fn() -> T> is a common choice. It is always Send and Sync, and it does not claim to own a T.

Newtype and type-state patterns

Newtype against the orphan rule

You want Display for a Vec<String>. Rust says no, because neither the trait nor the type is yours.

error[E0117]: only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for types defined outside of the crate
  = note: define and implement a trait or new type instead
use std::fmt;

// impl fmt::Display for Vec<String> is not allowed: both are foreign.
// A newtype makes a local type, so the impl is allowed.
struct Lines(Vec<String>);

impl fmt::Display for Lines {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        for (i, line) in self.0.iter().enumerate() {
            writeln!(f, "{:>2}: {line}", i + 1)?;
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}

fn main() {
    let text = Lines(vec!["fn main() {".into(), "}".into()]);
    print!("{text}");
}
 1: fn main() {
 2: }

The orphan rule keeps two crates from writing the same impl. A newtype is your own type, so the rule is happy. The pattern page shows the other job of a newtype: stopping mix-ups.

Type-state

A connection must be opened before you send. Make "send on a closed connection" a compile error.

use std::marker::PhantomData;

// The states are empty types. They exist only for the compiler.
struct Closed;
struct Open;

struct Conn<State> {
    addr: String,
    sent: u32,
    _state: PhantomData<State>,
}

impl Conn<Closed> {
    fn new(addr: &str) -> Self {
        Conn { addr: addr.to_string(), sent: 0, _state: PhantomData }
    }
    // open() eats the closed connection and returns an open one.
    fn open(self) -> Conn<Open> {
        println!("open {}", self.addr);
        Conn { addr: self.addr, sent: self.sent, _state: PhantomData }
    }
}

impl Conn<Open> {
    fn send(&mut self, msg: &str) {
        self.sent += 1;
        println!("send {msg:?}");
    }
    fn close(self) -> Conn<Closed> {
        println!("close after {} messages", self.sent);
        Conn { addr: self.addr, sent: self.sent, _state: PhantomData }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let c = Conn::new("db:5432");
    let mut c = c.open();
    c.send("SELECT 1");
    c.send("SELECT 2");
    let _c = c.close();
    // _c.send("too late"); // error[E0599]: no method named `send` found
}
open db:5432
send "SELECT 1"
send "SELECT 2"
close after 2 messages
class OpenConn:
    def __init__(self, addr: str) -> None:
        self.addr, self.sent = addr, 0

    def send(self, msg: str) -> None:
        self.sent += 1
        print(f"send {msg!r}")

    def close(self) -> "ClosedConn":
        print(f"close after {self.sent} messages")
        return ClosedConn(self.addr)


class ClosedConn:  # no send method at all
    def __init__(self, addr: str) -> None:
        self.addr = addr

    def open(self) -> OpenConn:
        print(f"open {self.addr}")
        return OpenConn(self.addr)


c = ClosedConn("db:5432").open()
c.send("SELECT 1")
c.send("SELECT 2")
closed = c.close()
# closed.send("too late")  # mypy: "ClosedConn" has no attribute "send"
open db:5432
send 'SELECT 1'
send 'SELECT 2'
close after 2 messages

The slides walk through it one step at a time.

Start closed

let c: Conn<Closed> = Conn::new("db:5432");

Only the methods in impl Conn<Closed> exist: new and open.

Open moves the value

let mut c: Conn<Open> = c.open();

open(self) takes the old value. The closed connection cannot be used again.

Send is now possible

c.send("SELECT 1");

send lives in impl Conn<Open>. It takes &mut self, so the state stays open.

Close moves it back

let c: Conn<Closed> = c.close();

The open connection is gone. A closed one comes back.

A wrong call does not compile

c.send("too late"); // E0599

The error even says: "the method was found for Conn<Open>".

In the type-state pattern, each state is a type. A method that changes the state takes self by value and returns the value in the new type. The state types are zero-sized, so they cost nothing at run time. Python can split states into classes too. Only a type checker enforces it.

error[E0599]: no method named `send` found for struct `Conn<Closed>` in the current scope
  --> a07_err.rs:41:8
   |
41 |     _c.send("too late");
   |        ^^^^ method not found in `Conn<Closed>`
   |
   = note: the method was found for `Conn<Open>`

Type-state fits states that you know at compile time. If the state comes from outside, like a network message, you cannot know the type in advance. Then use a normal enum and a match.

Sealed traits and the never type

Sealed traits

A library offers a trait for units of length. Users may use the trait, but only the library may implement it.

mod private {
    pub trait Sealed {} // public trait in a PRIVATE module
}

/// A unit of length. This trait is sealed: only this crate implements it.
pub trait Unit: private::Sealed {
    const NAME: &'static str;
    fn to_meters(v: f64) -> f64;
}

pub struct Meter;
pub struct Foot;

impl private::Sealed for Meter {}
impl private::Sealed for Foot {}

impl Unit for Meter {
    const NAME: &'static str = "m";
    fn to_meters(v: f64) -> f64 { v }
}

impl Unit for Foot {
    const NAME: &'static str = "ft";
    fn to_meters(v: f64) -> f64 { v * 0.3048 }
}

pub fn show<U: Unit>(v: f64) -> String {
    format!("{v} {} = {:.3} m", U::NAME, U::to_meters(v))
}
10 ft = 3.048 m
2.5 m = 2.500 m
class Unit:
    """Sealed: only this module may define units."""

    def __init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs) -> None:
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        if cls.__module__ != __name__:  # a class from another module
            raise TypeError(f"{cls.__name__}: Unit is sealed")


class Meter(Unit):
    factor = 1.0


class Foot(Unit):
    factor = 0.3048
3.048
TypeError: Mile: Unit is sealed

The Python output comes from a second file. It prints 10 * Foot.factor, then tries class Mile(Unit). In Rust, a second crate that writes impl Unit for Mile gets this error.

error[E0277]: the trait bound `Mile: units::private::Sealed` is not satisfied
  --> user.rs:6:15
   |
 6 | impl Unit for Mile {
   |               ^^^^ unsatisfied trait bound

A sealed trait has a supertrait that nobody outside can name. Why do this? The library can add a method to Unit later without breaking anyone. No outside implementation exists that would miss the new method. The Rust API guidelines call this C-SEALED. Say in the docs that the trait is sealed.

The never type

use std::convert::Infallible;
use std::process;

// `!` as a return type: this function never returns.
fn fail(msg: &str) -> ! {
    panic!("{msg}");
}

fn port_or_exit(text: &str) -> u16 {
    match text.parse() {
        Ok(p) => p,
        // process::exit returns `!`, and `!` fits where a u16 is expected.
        Err(_) => {
            eprintln!("bad port");
            process::exit(2)
        }
    }
}

// Infallible: an error type with no values. This Result is always Ok.
fn double(n: u32) -> Result<u32, Infallible> {
    Ok(n * 2)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", port_or_exit("8080"));
    let Ok(v) = double(21); // no Err arm needed: Err cannot exist
    println!("{v}");
    let n: u32 = if v > 0 { v } else { fail("impossible") };
    println!("{n}");
}
8080
42
42

The never type ! has no values. An expression of type ! never finishes: panic!, return, break, loop {} and process::exit. Because it never gives a value, it fits anywhere. That is why the Err arm above can be a u16. Infallible is an enum with no variants, so a Result<T, Infallible> can only be Ok.

On Rust 1.99, the version on this machine, ! works only as a return type. In other places it is refused.

error[E0658]: the `!` type is experimental
 --> a09_err.rs:1:28
  |
1 | fn certain<T>(r: Result<T, !>) -> T {
  |                            ^

Rust 1.100 came out on 12 November 2026. It makes ! a full type that you can write anywhere, like Result<T, !>. Infallible becomes another name for !. The "fallback" type for ! also changes from () to ! in all editions. The release post says this rarely breaks code. This page did not run 1.100 code.

Python's twin is typing.Never, or the older typing.NoReturn, for a function that always raises. Only the type checker uses it.

Specialisation: what it is and why it is not stable

You want a general impl for every Debug type, and a faster impl for String.

use std::fmt::Debug;

trait Describe {
    fn describe(&self) -> String;
}

// One general impl for every Debug type ...
impl<T: Debug> Describe for T {
    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        format!("{self:?}")
    }
}

// ... and a better one for String. Stable Rust refuses the overlap.
impl Describe for String {
    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        format!("text of {} bytes", self.len())
    }
}
error[E0119]: conflicting implementations of trait `Describe` for type `String`
  --> a10_err.rs:15:1
   |
 8 | impl<T: Debug> Describe for T {
   | ----------------------------- first implementation here
...
15 | impl Describe for String {
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ conflicting implementation for `String`

String is Debug, so two impls apply. Specialisation would let the more specific impl win. The nightly feature marks the general method with default fn. On stable Rust that word gives "specialization is experimental".

Why is it still not stable after ten years? The tracking issue is rust-lang/rust#31844. It says the full feature is unsound as it is built today. The main problem is lifetimes. The compiler erases lifetimes before it picks an impl, so an impl "only for 'static" cannot be chosen safely. A smaller feature, min_specialization, avoids most problems. The standard library uses it inside, for example to make to_string() on a &str fast. You cannot use it on stable Rust.

from functools import singledispatch


@singledispatch
def describe(x: object) -> str:  # the general version
    return repr(x)


@describe.register
def _(x: str) -> str:  # a more specific version for str
    return f"text of {len(x)} chars"


print(describe([1, 2]))
print(describe("hello"))
print(describe(3.5))
[1, 2]
text of 5 chars
3.5
Stable Rust has no twin of this.
Workarounds:
  1. No blanket impl. Implement the trait for each type you need.
  2. A narrower blanket impl, over a trait that String does not have.
  3. A wrapper type (newtype) with its own impl.

Python's functools.singledispatch picks the most specific function at run time. That is the nearest Python idea.

Do not plan a library design around specialisation "coming soon". It has been unstable since 2016. Design with separate traits or with no blanket impl.

Asked "what is object safety?", give the new name too: dyn compatibility. Then give the reason in one line: a vtable needs a fixed list of methods with known types. Generic methods and Self returns break that.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for advanced traits and types
PatternPurposeModelNote
type Item; in a traitOne output type per implementationtrait Sensor { type Reading; fn read(&self) -> Self::Reading; }Use a generic parameter when many impls per type make sense.
const NAME: T; in a traitA value per implementationconst UNIT: &'static str = "°C";A trait with an associated const is not dyn compatible.
type Item<'a> where Self: 'a;Items that borrow from the trait's valuefn next<'a>(&'a mut self) -> Option<Self::Item<'a>>GATs: stable since 1.65.
struct M<const N: usize>Put a size into a typefn mul<const K: usize>(&self, o: &Matrix<C, K>) -> Matrix<R, K>No N + 1 in types on stable.
where Self: Sized on a methodKeep a trait dyn compatiblefn scaled<T>(&self, k: T) -> f64 where Self: SizedNever on the trait itself.
Upcast &dyn Sub to &dyn SuperUse a supertrait objectlet a: &dyn Any = &*shape;Stable since 1.86. Then downcast_ref.
F: for<'a> Fn(&'a T) -> &'a UA closure that works for any borrowf: impl Fn(&str) -> &strThe short form means the same thing.
T: ?SizedAlso accept str, [T], dyn Traitfn describe<T: ?Sized + Debug>(x: &T)Then use T only behind a pointer.
PhantomData<T>Use a type parameter without storing itstruct Id<T> { raw: u64, _kind: PhantomData<T> }PhantomData<fn() -> T> for a pure label.
Newtype wrapperImplement a foreign trait for a foreign typestruct Lines(Vec<String>); impl Display for LinesThe orphan rule allows it, because the wrapper is local.
Type-stateMake wrong call order a compile errorfn open(self) -> Conn<Open>Only for states known at compile time.
Sealed traitAdd trait methods later without breaking userspub trait Unit: private::Sealed {}Write "sealed" in the docs.
-> ! and InfallibleSay "this never returns" or "this never fails"let Ok(v) = double(21);! as a full type needs Rust 1.100.

Practice

A trait Parser should give one output type for each parser. What do you write?

  • trait Parser { type Output; }
  • trait Parser<Output> {}
  • trait Parser { const Output: Type; }

One choice per implementer means an associated type. A generic parameter allows many impls per type.

Which method makes a trait not dyn compatible?

  • fn name(&self) -> String
  • fn convert<T>(&self, x: T) -> T
  • fn clone_box(&self) -> Box<dyn Shape>

A generic method needs one vtable entry per T. Returning Box<dyn Shape> is fine, because it does not name Self.

What does PhantomData<T> cost at run time?

  • One pointer
  • The size of T
  • Nothing: zero bytes

Id<User> was 8 bytes, the size of its u64 alone.

Is specialisation available on stable Rust 1.99?

  • Yes, with default fn
  • No. It is unstable, and the full feature is unsound today.
  • Yes, since the 2024 edition

default fn gives "specialization is experimental". Only the standard library uses min_specialization inside.

Trait upcasting became stable in Rust 1.number.

The bound for<'a> Fn(&'a str) is a word trait bound.

A generic T has the marker trait Sized unless you write <span class="blank" data-answer="?Sized">bound</span>.

  1. Write a function first_and_last<const N: usize> that takes [i32; N] and returns the first and last item. What should happen when N is 0?
    Answer 
    fn first_and_last<const N: usize>(a: [i32; N]) -> Option<(i32, i32)> {
    Some((*a.first()?, *a.last()?))
}

    For [4, 5, 6] it gives Some((4, 6)). For an empty array it gives None. Stable Rust cannot forbid N = 0 in the type, so the return type is an Option.

  2. This trait is not dyn compatible. Make it dyn compatible and keep with_label for concrete types. 
    trait Widget {
    fn draw(&self) -> String;
    fn with_label(self, label: &str) -> Self;
}
    Answer

    Add where Self: Sized to with_label: fn with_label(self, label: &str) -> Self where Self: Sized;. Now Box<dyn Widget> works. You can call draw on it, but not with_label.

  3. Design type-states for an email: Draft, then Ready (it has a recipient), then Sent. Which method moves between which states?
    Answer

    impl Email<Draft> has new() and to(self, addr) -> Email<Ready>. impl Email<Ready> has send(self) -> Email<Sent>. impl Email<Sent> has only getters, like sent_at(). Now "send without a recipient" and "send two times" do not compile.

  4. Why must a generic lifetime parameter 'a fail in apply_to_local, while for<'a> works?
    Answer

    A lifetime parameter of the function is chosen by the caller, and it is longer than the whole call. A reference to a local variable cannot live that long, so E0597. With for<'a>, the closure must accept every lifetime, including the short one of the local variable.

  5. Expert. Your library has a public trait Backend. You plan to add methods in the next minor version. Users only need to use the backends you provide. What do you do, and what do you write in the docs?
    Answer

    Seal the trait: pub trait Backend: private::Sealed, with Sealed in a private module and implemented only for your types. Then new methods are not a breaking change. The docs should say that the trait is sealed and cannot be implemented outside the crate.

  6. Expert. Why is it unsound to allow an impl that is chosen only when a lifetime is 'static?
    Answer

    The compiler erases lifetimes before it generates code and picks impls. It cannot know at that point if a reference was 'static. So it might pick the 'static impl for a short-lived reference. That impl could then keep the reference too long, which is undefined behaviour in safe code. This is the main reason the full feature is still unstable.

Key takeaways

  • Associated types fix one type per impl. Generic parameters allow many impls. GATs give associated types their own parameters.
  • Const generics put sizes into types. Arithmetic on them in types is still unstable.
  • A trait is dyn compatible when a vtable can describe it. where Self: Sized keeps single methods out.
  • for<'a> means "for every lifetime". Fn(&T) already means that.
  • PhantomData, type-states and sealed traits move rules into types at zero run-time cost.
  • ! is a full type since Rust 1.100. Specialisation is still unstable and partly unsound.

Sources

  • The Rust Reference: Traits. The exact dyn compatibility rules and associated items.
  • Announcing Rust 1.86.0. Trait upcasting and upcasting to dyn Any.
  • Announcing Rust 1.100.0. The never type as a full type, Infallible and the fallback change.
  • The Rustonomicon: Higher-rank trait bounds. The for<'a> syntax and the Fn sugar.
  • Rust API Guidelines: Future proofing. C-SEALED, the sealed trait pattern.
  • rust-lang/rust#31844. The tracking issue for specialisation and its soundness problems.

Macros

A macro is code that writes code. Rust runs it while it compiles your program. Macros give you println!, vec! and #[derive(Debug)]. This chapter shows how to read them, how to write them, and when to say no.

  • Write macro_rules! macros with fragments, repetition and many rules.
  • Explain hygiene and fix the common macro errors.
  • Build a small derive macro with syn and quote.
  • Look inside any macro with cargo expand.
  • Choose between a function, a generic, a macro and a Python decorator.

Why macros exist

Look at three lines you already know.

println!("hi");                 // one argument
println!("{} + {} = {}", 2, 3, 5); // four arguments
let v = vec![1, 2, 3];          // a list of any length

A Rust function has a fixed number of parameters. So println! cannot be a function. The ! tells you it is a macro. The compiler replaces each macro call with new code. This step is called expansion.

Expansion happens early. It happens before the compiler checks types. So a macro can do things a function cannot.

  • Take any number of arguments, like println!.
  • Create new items, like structs, functions and impl blocks.
  • Read the code of a type and write a trait for it, like #[derive(Debug)].
  • Check a format string at compile time.

Rust has two families of macros.

A macro is not a function call. Its arguments are not computed first. The macro pastes the argument code into new code. You will see the danger in the next section.

macro_rules! step by step

Here is a first declarative macro. It has one rule. Then a second macro has three rules.

// A macro with one rule. It takes an expression.
macro_rules! square {
    ($x:expr) => {
        $x * $x
    };
}

// Three rules. The first rule that matches wins.
macro_rules! max {
    ($a:expr) => { $a };
    ($a:expr, $b:expr) => {
        if $a > $b { $a } else { $b }
    };
    ($a:expr, $($rest:expr),+) => {
        max!($a, max!($($rest),+)) // calls itself on the rest
    };
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", square!(7));
    println!("{}", square!(2 + 3)); // $x is one expression: (2 + 3)
    println!("{}", max!(4));
    println!("{}", max!(4, 9));
    println!("{}", max!(4, 9, 2, 11, 5));
}
# Python functions can take any number of arguments.
# So Python does not need a macro here.
def max_of(first, *rest):
    best = first
    for x in rest:
        best = x if x > best else best
    return best

print(max_of(4), max_of(4, 9), max_of(4, 9, 2, 11, 5))
49
25
4
9
11

Each rule has two parts. The left part is the matcher. The right part is the transcriber. Between them is =>.

  • $x:expr means: "match one expression and call it $x".
  • The compiler tries the rules from top to bottom. The first match wins.
  • A macro can call itself. max! uses this to handle long lists.
  • square!(2 + 3) gives 25, not 11. The macro keeps 2 + 3 as one expression. It does not paste plain text.

When no rule matches, you get a clear error.

error: no rules expected `,`
 --> nomatch.rs:4:31
  |
1 | macro_rules! pair {
  | ----------------- when calling this macro
...
4 | fn main() { let p = pair!(1, 2, 3); println!("{p:?}"); }
  |                               ^ no rules expected this token in macro call

The double evaluation trap

Now pass a function call with a side effect to square!.

macro_rules! square_bad {
    ($x:expr) => { $x * $x }; // $x is pasted two times
}

macro_rules! square {
    ($x:expr) => {
        match $x {
            v => v * v, // evaluate once, then use the value
        }
    };
}

fn next(counter: &mut i32) -> i32 {
    *counter += 1;
    *counter
}

fn main() {
    let mut c = 0;
    println!("bad:  {}", square_bad!(next(&mut c))); // 1 * 2
    let mut c = 0;
    println!("good: {}", square!(next(&mut c)));     // 1 * 1
}
bad:  2
good: 1

The bad macro writes next(&mut c) * next(&mut c). The function runs twice. The fix is to compute the value once. A match or a let inside a block does it. The standard assert_eq! and dbg! use the same trick.

Never use $x two times in a transcriber when $x may be a call. Bind it once: match $x { v => ... }.

Fragments and repetition

The word after the colon in $x:expr is a fragment specifier. It says what kind of code to match. This macro uses ident and literal to build a whole enum.

use std::fmt;

// Build an enum and its Display impl from one list.
macro_rules! named_enum {
    ($name:ident { $($variant:ident => $text:literal),+ $(,)? }) => {
        #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
        enum $name {
            $($variant),+
        }

        impl fmt::Display for $name {
            fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
                let s = match self {
                    $( $name::$variant => $text ),+
                };
                f.write_str(s)
            }
        }

        impl $name {
            const ALL: &[$name] = &[$($name::$variant),+];
        }
    };
}

named_enum!(Level { Low => "low", Mid => "medium", High => "high", });

fn main() {
    for l in Level::ALL {
        print!("{l} ({l:?}) ");
    }
    println!();
}
low (Low) medium (Mid) high (High)

One list made three things: the enum, the Display code and a const array. You add a new level in one place only. That is a good reason for a macro.

The fragment specifiers
SpecifierMatchesExample input
expran expression2 + 3, f(x)
expr_2021an expression, old rules (no _, no const {})a * b
identa nametotal, Level
tya typeVec<u8>
patha type pathstd::io::Error
literala literal, maybe with a minus"low", -5
pat / pat_parama pattern (with or without top-level |)Some(x)
stmta statement without the last ;let a = 1
blocka block in braces{ a + 1 }
iteman itemfn f() {}, struct S;
lifetimea lifetime'a
metathe inside of an attributederive(Debug)
visa visibility, maybe emptypub, pub(crate)
ttone token tree+, (a b c)
