Some fragments must be followed by special tokens. This is the follow-set rule. It keeps old macros working when the language grows.

error: `$a:expr` is followed by `and`, which is not allowed for `expr` fragments
 --> follow_err.rs:2:14
  |
2 |     ($a:expr and $b:expr) => { println!("{} {}", $a, $b) };
  |              ^^^ not allowed after `expr` fragments
  |
  = note: allowed there are: `=>`, `,` or `;`

Fix: write $a:expr, $b:expr. Or match $a:tt, which has no follow rule.

The 2024 edition changed expr

In the 2024 edition, expr also matches _ and const { ... } blocks. The same macro can behave differently in two editions.

macro_rules! kind {
    ($e:expr) => { "an expression" };
    (_) => { "an underscore" };
}
fn main() { println!("{}", kind!(_)); }
an underscore
an expression

Fix: put the (_) rule first. Or write $e:expr_2021 to keep the old meaning. cargo fix --edition does the second fix for you.

Repetition

A repetition looks like $( ... ) sep op. The separator is often , or ;. The operator says how many times.

  • * means zero or more.
  • + means one or more.
  • ? means zero or one. It takes no separator.
use std::collections::HashMap;

macro_rules! hashmap {
    // zero or more "key => value" pairs, split by commas,
    // then an optional comma at the end
    ($($k:expr => $v:expr),* $(,)?) => {{
        #[allow(unused_mut)] // not needed when there are no pairs
        let mut m = HashMap::new();
        $( m.insert($k, $v); )* // one insert per pair
        m
    }};
}

fn main() {
    let ages = hashmap! {
        "ana" => 31,
        "bo" => 27, // trailing comma is fine
    };
    let empty: HashMap<&str, i32> = hashmap! {};
    let mut keys: Vec<_> = ages.keys().collect();
    keys.sort();
    println!("{keys:?} {} {}", ages["ana"], empty.len());
}
["ana", "bo"] 31 0

Start the repetition

The matcher sees $( ... ),*. It tries to match one pair: $k:expr => $v:expr.

First pair

"ana" becomes $k. Then it finds =>. Then 31 becomes $v.

Separator

It sees ,. So it tries one more pair: "bo" => 27.

The last comma

After 27 comes , and then nothing. The $(,)? part eats this last comma.

Write the output

The transcriber $( m.insert($k, $v); )* runs once per pair. It writes two insert lines.

Without the #[allow], hashmap! {} gives a warning. The empty call never changes m. So the mut is not needed there. Macro warnings point at your call, so test the empty case too.

A variable must repeat in the transcriber as deep as in the matcher.

error: variable `k` is still repeating at this depth
 --> depth_err.rs:2:37
  |
2 |     ($($k:expr => $v:expr),*) => { [$k] };
  |                                     ^^

Fix: wrap it in a repetition, [$($k),*].

To count items on stable Rust, build an array and ask its length: [$(stringify!($x)),*].len(). It works in a const. The nicer ${count($x)} is still unstable on Rust 1.99.

Hygiene and scope

Can a macro's local variable clash with yours? Try it.

macro_rules! double_it {
    ($e:expr) => {{
        let x = 2;   // this x belongs to the macro
        x * $e       // $e comes from the caller
    }};
}

macro_rules! make_var {
    ($name:ident, $val:expr) => {
        let $name = $val; // the caller gave the name, so the caller sees it
    };
}

fn main() {
    let x = 10;
    println!("{}", double_it!(x)); // the caller's x is 10
    make_var!(total, 5 + 1);
    println!("{total}");
}
20
6

There are two different x. The macro's x is 2. The caller's x is 10. The answer is 2 times 10. This is hygiene. A name written inside the macro stays inside the macro.

The other direction also holds. The caller cannot see a variable that the macro made up.

error[E0425]: cannot find value `x` in this scope
 --> hygiene_err.rs:9:16
  |
9 |     println!("{x}");
  |                ^ not found in this scope
  |
help: an identifier with the same name is defined here, but is not accessible due to macro hygiene

If you want the caller to see a name, let the caller pass it in. make_var!(total, ...) does that with $name:ident.

In a macro_rules! macro, local variables and loop labels are looked up where the macro is defined. All other names (functions, types, modules, other macros) are looked up where the macro is called.

So hygiene protects let names only. A function name inside a macro is found at the call site. The caller may not have it in scope. The fix is $crate. It always means "the crate that defines this macro".

pub mod util {
    pub fn tag(s: &str) -> String {
        format!("[{s}]")
    }
}

// #[macro_export] puts the macro at the crate root: crate::tagged!
#[macro_export]
macro_rules! tagged {
    ($($s:expr),+ $(,)?) => {
        // $crate always means "the crate that defines this macro"
        [$($crate::util::tag($s)),+]
    };
}

mod other {
    pub fn run() {
        // the caller does not need `use util::tag`
        let t = crate::tagged!("a", "b");
        println!("{t:?}");
    }
}

fn main() {
    other::run();
}
["[a]", "[b]"]

Two kinds of scope apply to macro_rules!:

  • Textual scope. A macro works only after its definition in the file. Order matters, unlike functions.
  • Path scope. #[macro_export] puts the macro at the crate root. Other crates call it as my_crate::tagged!. Inside the crate you can also write pub(crate) use tagged; after the definition.

An exported macro calls helper() or HashMap::new(). It works in your crate. In the user's crate it fails, because they did not import the name. Always write $crate::helper() and full paths like ::std::collections::HashMap.

Useful standard macros

The standard library has many macros. Most of them exist because a function could not do the job.

Standard macros you will use
MacroWhat it doesExample
println!, format!, write!Format text. The format string is checked at compile time.format!("{name}: {age}")
vec!Make a Vec from a list or a repeatvec![0u8; 1024]
assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne!Stop with a clear message when a check failsassert_eq!(sum, 10)
debug_assert!A check only in debug buildsdebug_assert!(i < len)
dbg!Print file, line, code and value. Returns the value.let y = dbg!(x * 2);
matches!Test a value against a pattern. Gives a bool.matches!(c, 'a'..='z')
todo!, unimplemented!, unreachable!Panic with a message that says whytodo!("parse dates")
include_str!, include_bytes!Put a file into the program at compile timeinclude_str!("schema.sql")
env!, option_env!Read an environment variable at compile timeenv!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")
cfg!Ask about the build target. Gives a bool.cfg!(target_os = "linux")
stringify!, concat!Turn code into text, join literalsstringify!(a + b)
compile_error!Stop the build with your own messageinside a macro rule that should never match
file!, line!, column!The place in the source codeline!()

Some macro features are not stable yet. On rustc 1.99 these three give error E0658 ("unstable"). I tested each one:

  • macro_rules! macros used as attributes, with attr() rules.
  • macro_rules! macros used in derive, with derive() rules.
  • Meta-variable expressions like ${count($x)}.

Unstable features can become stable in any release. Check the release notes before you rely on this list.

Procedural macros and a derive with syn and quote

A procedural macro is a normal Rust function. The compiler calls it while it compiles your crate. It gets a TokenStream and returns a new one.

The three kinds of procedural macros
KindHow you use itFunction signatureOutput
Derive#[derive(Describe)]fn(TokenStream) -> TokenStreamNew items added after the type
Attribute#[log_call]fn(TokenStream, TokenStream) -> TokenStreamReplaces the item
Function-likesquares!(5)fn(TokenStream) -> TokenStreamReplaces the call

Most authors use two helper crates. syn turns tokens into a syntax tree. quote turns Rust code with holes back into tokens.

Now build a real one. #[derive(Describe)] adds a describe() method. It lists each field with its value. A helper attribute #[describe(skip)] hides a field, for example a password.

  1. Make a workspace with two crates: describe (the macro) and app (the user).
  2. Mark describe as a macro crate with proc-macro = true.
  3. Parse the input into a DeriveInput with syn.
  4. Read the fields. Skip the ones marked #[describe(skip)].
  5. Write the impl with quote!. Return errors as compile errors.
[package]
name = "describe"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[lib]
proc-macro = true   # this crate makes macros, not normal code

[dependencies]
syn = { version = "3", features = ["full"] }  # "full" is needed for ItemFn
quote = "1"
proc-macro2 = "1"

The lock file picked syn 3.0.10, quote 1.0.47 and proc-macro2 1.0.107. syn 3.0.0 came out in July 2026. The official Rust book still shows syn = "2.0". Both work for this code. Only the derive needs the default features. The attribute macro later needs "full".

use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, Data, DeriveInput, Fields};

// attributes(describe) allows #[describe(...)] on fields.
#[proc_macro_derive(Describe, attributes(describe))]
pub fn derive_describe(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    let ast = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput); // tokens -> tree
    match expand(&ast) {
        Ok(tokens) => tokens.into(),
        Err(e) => e.to_compile_error().into(), // a clear compile error
    }
}

fn is_skipped(f: &syn::Field) -> syn::Result<bool> {
    let mut skip = false;
    for attr in &f.attrs {
        if attr.path().is_ident("describe") {
            attr.parse_nested_meta(|meta| {
                if meta.path.is_ident("skip") {
                    skip = true;
                    Ok(())
                } else {
                    Err(meta.error("expected `skip`"))
                }
            })?;
        }
    }
    Ok(skip)
}
fn expand(ast: &DeriveInput) -> syn::Result<proc_macro2::TokenStream> {
    let name = &ast.ident;
    let Data::Struct(data) = &ast.data else {
        return Err(syn::Error::new_spanned(name, "Describe works only on structs"));
    };
    let Fields::Named(fields) = &data.fields else {
        return Err(syn::Error::new_spanned(name, "Describe needs named fields"));
    };
    let mut parts = Vec::new();
    for f in &fields.named {
        if is_skipped(f)? {
            continue; // #[describe(skip)] hides this field
        }
        let id = f.ident.as_ref().unwrap();
        parts.push(quote! { format!("{} = {:?}", stringify!(#id), self.#id) });
    }
    // Keep the generics: impl<T: Debug> ... for Pair<T>
    let (impl_g, type_g, where_c) = ast.generics.split_for_impl();
    Ok(quote! {
        impl #impl_g crate::Describe for #name #type_g #where_c {
            fn describe(&self) -> ::std::string::String {
                let parts: &[::std::string::String] = &[#(#parts),*];
                format!("{} {{ {} }}", stringify!(#name), parts.join(", "))
            }
        }
    })
}

Read the quote! block like a template. #name puts in a value from your code. #(#parts),* is a repetition, like $(...),* in macro_rules!. Paths start with ::std because procedural macros are not hygienic.

use describe::Describe; // the derive macro

trait Describe {        // the trait it implements
    fn describe(&self) -> String;
}

#[derive(Describe)]
struct User {
    name: String,
    age: u32,
    #[describe(skip)]
    password: String,
}

#[derive(Describe)]
struct Pair<T: std::fmt::Debug> {
    left: T,
    right: T,
}

fn main() {
    let u = User { name: "Ana".into(), age: 31, password: "secret".into() };
    println!("{}", u.describe());
    println!("{}", Pair { left: 1.5, right: 2.0 }.describe());
}
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, fields

def describe(cls):                  # a class decorator
    def describe(self):
        parts = [f"{f.name} = {getattr(self, f.name)!r}"
                 for f in fields(self) if not f.metadata.get("skip")]
        return f"{type(self).__name__} {{ {', '.join(parts)} }}"
    cls.describe = describe         # add a method at run time
    return cls

@describe
@dataclass
class User:
    name: str
    age: int
    password: str = field(metadata={"skip": True})

print(User("Ana", 31, "secret").describe())
User { name = "Ana", age = 31 }
Pair { left = 1.5, right = 2.0 }

Python prints User { name = 'Ana', age = 31 } with single quotes. The idea is the same. The timing is not. Rust writes the method once, while it compiles. Python adds it when the class is created, at run time.

Wrong input gives errors that point at the user's code, not at your macro:

error: Describe works only on structs
 --> app/examples/bad.rs:5:6
  |
5 | enum Color { Red, Green }
  |      ^^^^^

error: expected `skip`
 --> app/examples/bad.rs:9:16
  |
9 |     #[describe(hide)]
  |                ^^^^

Do not call panic! or unwrap() on bad user input. A panic in a macro becomes an ugly error with no good position. Return a syn::Error with a span, and call to_compile_error().

A procedural macro runs with the same rights as the compiler. It can read files and use the network, like a build script. Only depend on macro crates you trust.

Attribute and function-like macros

An attribute macro gets two inputs. The first is the text inside its brackets. The second is the item under it. This one prints a line when a function starts and ends.

#[proc_macro_attribute]
pub fn log_call(attr: TokenStream, item: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    if !attr.is_empty() {
        let msg = "log_call takes no arguments";
        return syn::Error::new(proc_macro2::Span::call_site(), msg)
            .to_compile_error()
            .into();
    }
    let f = parse_macro_input!(item as syn::ItemFn);
    let (attrs, vis, sig, body) = (&f.attrs, &f.vis, &f.sig, &f.block);
    let name = sig.ident.to_string();
    quote! {
        #(#attrs)* #vis #sig {
            println!("enter {}", #name);
            let result = #body; // the old body, as one block
            println!("leave {}", #name);
            result
        }
    }
    .into()
}

// In app/src/main.rs:
// #[log_call]
// fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }
import functools

def log_call(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)          # keep the name and docstring
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print(f"enter {func.__name__}")
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print(f"leave {func.__name__}")
        return result
    return wrapper

@log_call                           # same as: add = log_call(add)
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

print("sum =", add(2, 3))
enter add
leave add
sum = 5

Both print the same lines. The Rust version writes new source code once. The Python version wraps the function in another function. That wrapper runs on every call.

A return inside the old body jumps out of the whole function. Then "leave" is never printed. Real tracing macros handle this, for example with a guard value that prints in its Drop. Think about early returns, ? and async fn when you rewrite a body.

A function-like macro looks like name!(...). It can do real work at compile time. This one makes a table of squares.

#[proc_macro]
pub fn squares(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    let lit = parse_macro_input!(input as syn::LitInt);
    let n: u64 = match lit.base10_parse() {
        Ok(n) => n,
        Err(e) => return e.to_compile_error().into(),
    };
    let items = (0..n).map(|i| i * i); // runs inside the compiler
    quote! { [#(#items),*] }.into()
}

// In app/src/main.rs:
// const SQ: [u64; 5] = squares!(5);
// println!("{SQ:?}");
[0, 1, 4, 9, 16]

Here a const fn could do the same job. That is a hint for the last section.

Debugging macros and when not to write one

The best tool is cargo expand. It prints your crate after all macros ran. Install it with cargo install cargo-expand. It is a wrapper around a longer compiler command, cargo rustc --profile=check -- -Zunpretty=expanded. That flag needs a nightly compiler. I did not install the tool here. I ran the compiler command with RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=1 on stable 1.99, then formatted the result by hand.

cargo expand            # the whole crate
cargo expand path::to::item   # one module, type or function
cargo expand --test my_test   # one test target
impl crate::Describe for User {
    fn describe(&self) -> ::std::string::String {
        let parts: &[::std::string::String] = &[
            ::alloc::__export::must_use({
                ::alloc::fmt::format(format_args!("{0} = {1:?}", "name", self.name))
            }),
            ::alloc::__export::must_use({
                ::alloc::fmt::format(format_args!("{0} = {1:?}", "age", self.age))
            }),
        ];
        ::alloc::__export::must_use({
            ::alloc::fmt::format(format_args!("{0} {{ {1} }}", "User", parts.join(", ")))
        })
    }
}
fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    { ::std::io::_print(format_args!("enter {0}\n", "add")); };
    let result = { a + b };
    { ::std::io::_print(format_args!("leave {0}\n", "add")); };
    result
}
const SQ: [u64; 5] = [0u64, 1u64, 4u64, 9u64, 16u64];

You can see three facts. password is gone. format! itself is a macro and expanded too. squares!(5) left only an array of numbers.

Do not paste expanded code back into your project. The text loses hygiene information. The cargo-expand page warns that such code may not compile, or may behave differently. Use it to read, not to copy.

More debugging tricks

Write the smallest call that fails. Add one rule at a time. In rust-analyzer, the command "Expand macro recursively" shows the expansion of the macro under the cursor. For procedural macros, unit test your expand function with proc_macro2::TokenStream. That type works outside the compiler.

Testing compile errors

Your error messages are part of the macro. The trybuild crate compiles small files that should fail. It compares the error text with a saved file. Many macro crates test their errors this way.

Nightly-only helpers

trace_macros! and log_syntax! print each step of macro_rules! matching. They need a nightly compiler. The error note "run with -Z macro-backtrace" is nightly-only too.

When not to write a macro

Macros have real costs:

  • Readers must learn a small new language for each macro.
  • Error messages get harder to follow.
  • Editors give weaker help inside macro calls.
  • Procedural macros compile syn, which adds build time to a clean build.

A classic question: "Why is println! a macro and not a function?" Give two reasons. It takes any number of arguments. It checks the format string against the arguments at compile time.

Python: decorators and metaclasses

Python has no macros in the language. Its nearest tools change functions and classes at run time.

  • A decorator like @log_call is like an attribute macro.
  • A class decorator like @dataclass is like a derive macro. It adds methods to a class.
  • A metaclass controls how a class is built. Python calls it for every new class.
class Registered(type):             # a metaclass: the class of a class
    plugins = {}

    def __new__(mcs, name, bases, ns):
        cls = super().__new__(mcs, name, bases, ns)
        if bases:                   # skip the base class itself
            mcs.plugins[name.lower()] = cls
        return cls

class Plugin(metaclass=Registered):
    pass

class Csv(Plugin): pass
class Json(Plugin): pass

print(sorted(Registered.plugins))

class Base:                         # the simpler modern way
    found = []
    def __init_subclass__(cls, **kw):
        super().__init_subclass__(**kw)
        Base.found.append(cls.__name__)

class Toml(Base): pass
print(Base.found)
['csv', 'json']
['Toml']

Every subclass registers itself. Today most people use __init_subclass__ for this. It is shorter, and it does not clash with other metaclasses.

Rust macros and their nearest Python tool
RustPythonBig difference
macro_rules!*args, **kwargsRust writes code. Python only takes more values.
derive macroclass decorator, @dataclassCompile time versus class creation time
attribute macrofunction decoratorRust rewrites the code once. Python wraps it, and the wrapper runs on each call.
function-like macrono real twinPython can build code with ast and exec, but at run time
a crate that registers typesmetaclass, __init_subclass__Python sees each class as it is created

A Rust macro edits your code before the program exists. A Python decorator edits objects while the program runs.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for macros
PatternPurposeModelNote
($x:expr) => { ... }A one-rule macromacro_rules! square { ($x:expr) => { $x * $x }; }Use each $x once, or bind it first.
match $x { v => ... }Evaluate an argument only oncematch $x { v => v * v }Stops double side effects.
Many rules, top to bottomDifferent shapes of input(_) => ...; ($e:expr) => ...;Put the special rules first.
$($x:expr),* $(,)?A list with an optional last commahashmap! { "a" => 1, "b" => 2, }Test the empty call too.
$name:identLet the caller choose a namenamed_enum!(Level { Low => "low" })Names made inside the macro stay hidden.
$crate::pathReach your own items from an exported macro$crate::util::tag($s)Never rely on the caller's imports.
#[macro_export]Let other crates call the macromy_crate::tagged!("a")Define before use inside the file.
$e:expr_2021Keep the pre-2024 meaning of expr($e:expr_2021) => ...2024 expr also matches _.
proc-macro = trueMake a procedural macro crate[lib] proc-macro = trueThe crate can export only macros.
parse_macro_input! + quote!Read tokens, write tokenslet ast = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);syn 3 is current. The Rust book shows 2.
split_for_impl()Support generic types in a deriveimpl #impl_g Tr for #name #type_g #where_cForgetting it breaks Pair<T>.
syn::Error::new_spannedReport a clear error at the right placeErr(syn::Error::new_spanned(name, "only structs"))Do not panic on user input.
cargo expandSee the code a macro wrotecargo expand path::to::itemRead it. Do not paste it back.

Practice

Why can println! not be a normal Rust function?

  • Functions cannot print text.
  • It takes any number of arguments and checks the format string at compile time.
  • Macros run faster than functions.

Rust functions have a fixed list of parameters. A macro can accept many shapes of input.

macro_rules! sq { ($x:expr) => { $x * $x }; }. What does sq!(1 + 1) give?

  • 3
  • 4
  • It does not compile.

$x is one expression. The macro keeps it grouped, so it is (1 + 1) times (1 + 1).

A macro does let x = 2; and the caller already has x = 10. What happens?

  • The caller's x becomes 2.
  • Compile error: x is defined twice.
  • Two separate variables. Hygiene keeps them apart.

Local variables in macro_rules! are looked up where the macro is defined.

Which procedural macro kind gets two TokenStream inputs?

  • Derive
  • Attribute
  • Function-like

The first input is the attribute's arguments. The second is the item under it.

The repetition operator for "one or more" is symbol.

In an exported macro, write word to mean "the crate that defines this macro".

A fragment that matches a name like total is specifier.

  1. Write a macro min! that accepts one or more expressions, like max!.
    Answer 
    macro_rules! min {
    ($a:expr) => { $a };
    ($a:expr, $($rest:expr),+) => {
        match ($a, min!($($rest),+)) {
            (x, y) => if x < y { x } else { y },
        }
    };
}

    The match evaluates each part once. min!(4, 9, 2) gives 2.

  2. This macro fails in a user's crate but works in yours. Why? macro_rules! ids { () => { make_ids() }; }
    Answer

    The name make_ids is looked up at the call site. The user did not import it. Write $crate::make_ids() and mark the macro #[macro_export].

  3. A macro has the rules ($e:expr) then (_). After moving to edition 2024, m!(_) takes the first rule. Give two fixes.
    Answer

    Put the (_) rule first. Or change the fragment to $e:expr_2021, which keeps the old meaning.

  4. Your derive macro works on struct A but fails on struct B<T>. What did you forget?
    Answer

    The generics. Use ast.generics.split_for_impl() and write impl #impl_g Trait for #name #type_g #where_c.

  5. Extend Describe so #[describe(rename = "user_name")] prints another name. Which syn call reads the value?
    Answer

    Inside parse_nested_meta, check meta.path.is_ident("rename"). Then call meta.value()?.parse::<syn::LitStr>()?. Use the string in place of stringify!(#id).

  6. Expert. A teammate wants a derive macro that only adds fn new() -> Self with default values. What do you suggest instead?
    Answer

    Use #[derive(Default)] from the standard library, or write a normal impl by hand. A new macro crate adds build time and harder errors for no real gain.

Key takeaways

  • A macro writes code at compile time. It sees tokens, not types.
  • macro_rules! matches patterns. Rules go top to bottom. Fragments say what each $var can be.
  • Repetitions $(...),* must repeat in the output at the same depth.
  • Hygiene hides local variables. Other names are found at the call site, so use $crate and full paths.
  • Procedural macros are Rust functions in a proc-macro crate. syn reads, quote writes.
  • Use cargo expand to see the result. Prefer a function, a generic or const fn when they work.

Sources

  • The Rust Programming Language, 20.5: Macros. The official introduction, with a derive example.
  • The Rust Reference: Macros by example. Fragments, repetition, follow sets, hygiene and scope.
  • The Rust Reference: Procedural macros. The three kinds, helper attributes and error reporting.
  • syn 3.0.0 release notes. What changed from syn 2. Versions checked on crates.io.
  • cargo-expand. How to install and use it, and why expanded text is lossy.
  • Python data model: customizing class creation. Metaclasses and __init_subclass__.

Unsafe Rust and FFI

Safe Rust cannot express everything. Talking to C, writing a fast data structure or touching hardware needs a few extra powers. The unsafe keyword gives you those powers, and with them the duty to keep the rules yourself. This chapter shows how to use it in small, checked pieces.

  • Name the five unsafe powers and explain what unsafe does not turn off.
  • Use raw pointers, &raw and MaybeUninit without undefined behaviour.
  • Wrap unsafe code in a safe function with a clear SAFETY comment.
  • Apply the 2024 edition rules: unsafe extern, unsafe attributes and unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn.
  • Call C from Rust and Rust from C, with bindgen, cbindgen and Miri as helpers.

What unsafe means

Start with code that Rust refuses.

fn main() {
    let n = 1;
    let p = &raw const n; // a raw pointer to n
    println!("{}", *p);   // read through it
}
error[E0133]: dereference of raw pointer is unsafe and requires unsafe block
 --> noblock.rs:4:20
  |
4 |     println!("{}", *p);
  |                    ^^ dereference of raw pointer
  |
  = note: raw pointers may be null, dangling or unaligned; they can violate aliasing rules and cause data races: all of these are undefined behavior

The compiler cannot prove that p is good. So it asks you to write unsafe { ... }. With that block you say: "I checked this myself." The compiler trusts you.

An unsafe block unlocks exactly five powers. Nothing else changes.

  1. Dereference a raw pointer.
  2. Call an unsafe function or method, including C functions.
  3. Read or write a mutable static.
  4. Implement an unsafe trait, like Send or Sync.
  5. Read a field of a union.

The borrow checker still runs inside unsafe. Types are still checked. Array indexing with v[i] still checks bounds. Only the five actions above become allowed.

People think unsafe turns off all checks. It does not. It only allows five actions. If your code breaks a rule inside the block, the program is still wrong. The compiler just cannot tell you.

Safe Rust: the compiler checks the rules. Unsafe Rust: you check the rules. The rules stay the same.

Raw pointers and &raw

There are two raw pointer types. *const T is for reading. *mut T is for writing. Making a raw pointer is safe. Using it is not.

fn main() {
    let mut n = 10;
    let p = &raw const n; // *const i32: making it is safe
    let q = &raw mut n;   // *mut i32: two pointers to n are fine

    unsafe {
        // SAFETY: n is alive, aligned and nobody else uses it now.
        *q += 5;
        println!("{}", *p);
    }

    let nums = [1, 2, 3];
    let first = nums.as_ptr();
    // SAFETY: index 2 is inside the array of 3.
    let third = unsafe { *first.add(2) };
    println!("{third}");

    let null: *const i32 = std::ptr::null();
    println!("{}", null.is_null());
}
import ctypes

n = ctypes.c_int(10)                  # a C int inside Python
p = ctypes.pointer(n)                 # like *mut i32
p.contents.value += 5                 # write through the pointer
print(n.value)

nums = (ctypes.c_int * 3)(1, 2, 3)    # a C array
first = ctypes.cast(nums, ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_int))
print(first[2])                       # no bounds check: first[300] reads garbage

null = ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_int)()  # a null pointer
print(bool(null))                      # False means null
15
3
true

(Python prints False on the last line. It answers "is it set?", not "is it null?".)

A raw pointer is different from a reference in four ways:

  • It may be null.
  • It may point to freed or wrong memory.
  • Many *mut pointers to one place may exist at once.
  • It frees nothing when it goes away.

Python's ctypes module is Python's unsafe corner. A wrong address crashes the whole interpreter. ctypes.string_at(0) reads address 0. The process stops with "Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault" and exit code 139. No exception can catch that.

Why &raw exists

&raw const x and &raw mut x make a raw pointer without making a reference first. They are stable since Rust 1.82. This matters when a reference would already be wrong. A packed struct is the classic case.

#[repr(C, packed)] // no padding: fields may be misaligned
struct Header {
    tag: u8,
    len: u32, // starts at byte 1, not at byte 4
}

fn main() {
    let h = Header { tag: 7, len: 1000 };
    // let r = &h.len;          // error E0793: reference to packed field
    let p = &raw const h.len;   // a raw pointer is allowed
    // SAFETY: p points to a live u32; read_unaligned allows any address.
    let len = unsafe { p.read_unaligned() };
    let tag = h.tag;
    println!("tag={tag} len={len} size={}", size_of::<Header>());
}
tag=7 len=1000 size=5

A u32 wants an address that is a multiple of 4. This is its alignment. Here len starts at byte 1. A &u32 to it would be misaligned. A misaligned reference is undefined behaviour, even if you never read it. So the compiler stops you:

error[E0793]: reference to field of packed struct is unaligned
 --> packed_err.rs:9:13
  |
9 |     let r = &h.len;
  |             ^^^^^^
  |
  = note: creating a misaligned reference is undefined behavior (even if that reference is never dereferenced)
  = help: copy the field contents to a local variable, or replace the reference with a raw pointer and use `read_unaligned`/`write_unaligned`

*p on a raw pointer still needs an aligned address. For packed fields, use p.read_unaligned() and p.write_unaligned(v). Or copy the field into a local: let len = h.len;.

Undefined behaviour in simple words

Undefined behaviour (UB) means the program broke a rule of the language. The compiler optimises as if the rules always hold. So after UB, anything can happen. The program may crash. It may print a wrong number. It may work today and fail after the next compiler update.

The main kinds of undefined behaviour
Rule brokenSmall example
Read memory that is freed or outside the objecta pointer to a dropped Vec
Use a misaligned pointer or reference&h.len in a packed struct
Break the borrow rules with pointerstwo live &mut to one value
Change data behind a &Twriting to a string literal
Make an invalid valuea bool that is 2, a null reference
A data racetwo threads write a static mut
Call a function with the wrong ABIa wrong signature in an extern block

The Rust Reference says its list "is not exhaustive". So read it as the minimum. When you are not sure, assume it is UB.

Debug builds catch some UB for you. Since Rust 1.78, many standard library functions check their rules when debug assertions are on. Here is a wrong index on purpose.

fn main() {
    let v = vec![1, 2, 3];
    // Wrong on purpose: index 5 is outside the vector.
    let x = unsafe { *v.get_unchecked(5) };
    println!("{x}");
}
thread 'main' panicked at precond.rs:4:25:
unsafe precondition(s) violated: slice::get_unchecked requires that the index is within the slice

This indicates a bug in the program. This Undefined Behavior check is optional, and cannot be relied on for safety.

A release build removes this check. Then the same code reads random memory. Never use a debug check as your safety plan.

A function is sound if no safe code can cause undefined behaviour by calling it. A function that safe code can misuse to cause UB is unsound, even if no one misuses it today.

A common interview question: "Is a crate with unsafe inside unsafe to use?" Answer: not if its safe API is sound. The standard library is full of unsafe. Vec and String are built on raw pointers.

Safe wrappers around unsafe code

You want two &mut to different items of one slice. The borrow checker cannot see that they differ.

error[E0499]: cannot borrow `v[_]` as mutable more than once at a time
 --> twomut_err.rs:4:13
  |
3 |     let a = &mut v[0];
  |             --------- first mutable borrow occurs here
4 |     let b = &mut v[2];
  |             ^^^^^^^^^ second mutable borrow occurs here

So write a small safe function with an unsafe core.

/// Returns mutable references to two different items.
/// Panics if `i == j` or an index is out of bounds.
fn two_mut<T>(v: &mut [T], i: usize, j: usize) -> (&mut T, &mut T) {
    assert!(i != j, "indexes must differ");
    assert!(i < v.len() && j < v.len(), "index out of bounds");
    let p = v.as_mut_ptr();
    // SAFETY: both indexes are in bounds (checked above), and they differ,
    // so the two references never point to the same item.
    unsafe { (&mut *p.add(i), &mut *p.add(j)) }
}

fn main() {
    let mut scores = [10, 20, 30];
    let (a, b) = two_mut(&mut scores, 0, 2);
    std::mem::swap(a, b);
    println!("{scores:?}");

    // The standard library has this since Rust 1.86:
    if let Ok([x, y]) = scores.get_disjoint_mut([0, 1]) {
        *x += 1;
        *y += 1;
    }
    println!("{scores:?}");
}
# Python has no borrow rules. Two names may change one list.
scores = [10, 20, 30]
scores[0], scores[2] = scores[2], scores[0]
print(scores)
scores[0] += 1
scores[1] += 1
print(scores)
[30, 20, 10]
[31, 21, 10]

The two assert! lines make the function sound. Delete assert!(i != j) and call two_mut(&mut v, 1, 1). Now safe code gets two &mut to one item. That is UB. The function would be unsound.

Try safe code first

Look in the standard library. split_at_mut, get_disjoint_mut or swap may already do it.

Write down the rules

List what must be true. For two_mut: both indexes in bounds, and different.

Check the rules in safe code

Use assert! or return an error. Do this before the unsafe block.

Keep the unsafe block tiny

Put only the dangerous lines inside. Add a // SAFETY: comment that says why each rule holds.

Test it, then test it with Miri

Write tests for the edge cases. Run them under Miri, which finds UB at run time.

Unsafe functions and unsafe traits

Sometimes you cannot check the rules inside. Then the function itself is unsafe fn. Its doc comment gets a # Safety part. It tells the caller what they must promise.

An unsafe trait works the same way. Send and Sync are the famous ones. A type with a raw pointer inside is not Send by default. If you know it is safe to move to another thread, write unsafe impl Send for MyType {}. Now you carry that promise, not the compiler.

Mutable statics and unions

A static mut is one global value that anyone may change. Two threads can write it at once. In the 2024 edition, even making a & to it is an error by default:

error: creating a shared reference to mutable static
  --> ed2024b.rs:17:17
   |
17 |         let r = &COUNT;
   |                 ^^^^^^ shared reference to mutable static
   |
   = note: `#[deny(static_mut_refs)]` (part of `#[deny(rust_2024_compatibility)]`) on by default
help: use `&raw const` instead to create a raw pointer

The better fix is no static mut at all. Use an atomic like AtomicU32, a Mutex, or OnceLock. They are safe and work across threads.

A union stores one of its fields at a time. Reading a field is unsafe, because Rust does not know which one was written. Unions exist mainly for C code.

#[repr(C)]
union Bits {
    f: f32,
    u: u32,
}

fn main() {
    let b = Bits { f: 1.0 };
    // SAFETY: every bit pattern is a valid u32.
    let raw = unsafe { b.u };
    println!("{raw:#010x} {}", 1.0f32.to_bits() == raw);
}
0x3f800000 true

Safe code does the same with 1.0f32.to_bits(). Prefer it.

A SAFETY comment that says "this is fine" is not enough. Name each rule and say why it holds: "in bounds because of the assert on line 5".

The 2024 edition changes

The 2024 edition made unsafe code easier to spot. Compare the same file in two editions.

extern "C" {
    fn abs(x: i32) -> i32;
}

#[no_mangle]
pub extern "C" fn rust_add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }

unsafe fn first(v: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    *v.get_unchecked(0) // no unsafe block needed in 2021
}
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, Ordering};

// SAFETY: these signatures match the C library.
unsafe extern "C" {
    safe fn abs(x: i32) -> i32;            // callable without unsafe
    unsafe fn strlen(s: *const std::ffi::c_char) -> usize;
}

// SAFETY: no other global symbol in the program is named rust_add.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn rust_add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }

/// # Safety
/// `v` must not be empty.
unsafe fn first(v: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    // SAFETY: the caller promised that index 0 exists.
    unsafe { *v.get_unchecked(0) }
}

static COUNT: AtomicU32 = AtomicU32::new(0); // no static mut needed

fn main() {
    COUNT.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
    // SAFETY: the C string literal ends with a 0 byte.
    let n = unsafe { strlen(c"hello".as_ptr()) };
    // SAFETY: the slice has one item.
    let f = unsafe { first(&[9]) };
    println!("{} {} {} {} {}", abs(-3), n, f, rust_add(2, 2), COUNT.load(Ordering::Relaxed));
}
3 5 9 4 1

Four rules changed. The old file fails in 2024 with these messages:

What 2024 asks for
Old code2024 messageNew code
extern "C" { ... }error: extern blocks must be unsafeunsafe extern "C" { ... }
#[no_mangle], #[export_name], #[link_section]error: unsafe attribute used without unsafe#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
unsafe calls inside unsafe fn with no blockwarning: unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fnunsafe { ... } inside the body
&COUNT on a static muterror: static_mut_refs (deny by default)an atomic, or &raw const COUNT

Why the unsafe on extern? The compiler cannot read the C code. If your signature is wrong, calls are UB. So writing the block is the unsafe act. Inside it you mark each item safe or unsafe. No mark means unsafe.

Why #[unsafe(no_mangle)]? Two functions with the same exported name can clash in the final program. That can be UB too.

Why unsafe { } inside an unsafe fn? The old rule mixed two meanings. unsafe fn now only means "callers must keep a promise". The body is safe code again, and each dangerous line needs its own block.

  1. 2 May 2024 Rust 1.78. Many standard library precondition checks run in debug builds of your code.
  2. 5 Sep 2024 Rust 1.81. A panic that leaves an extern "C" function now aborts the program.
  3. 17 Oct 2024 Rust 1.82. &raw const, &raw mut, unsafe extern with safe items, and unsafe(...) attributes, in every edition.
  4. 20 Feb 2025 Rust 1.85. The 2024 edition is stable and makes these forms required.
  5. 3 Apr 2025 Rust 1.86. get_disjoint_mut for slices and HashMap.

cargo fix --edition adds the unsafe keywords for you. It cannot check that your C signatures are right. Read each extern block again after the fix. The chapter Rust editions shows the full migration.

MaybeUninit: memory that is not set yet

Rust assumes every variable holds a valid value. An unset bool or i32 breaks that rule. MaybeUninit<T> is a box of bytes that may not be a valid T yet. A C function that fills a struct for you is the usual case.

use std::mem::MaybeUninit;

// Pretend this is a C function that fills a struct for us.
fn fill(out: *mut [u32; 4]) {
    // SAFETY: the caller gives a valid, writable pointer.
    unsafe { out.write([1, 2, 3, 4]) };
}

fn main() {
    // 1. Space for a value that is not set yet.
    let mut slot = MaybeUninit::<[u32; 4]>::uninit();
    fill(slot.as_mut_ptr());             // 2. someone writes it
    // SAFETY: fill wrote all 4 numbers.
    let nums = unsafe { slot.assume_init() }; // 3. now it is a real value
    println!("{nums:?}");

    // An array of Strings, one element at a time.
    let mut names: [MaybeUninit<String>; 3] = [const { MaybeUninit::uninit() }; 3];
    for (i, slot) in names.iter_mut().enumerate() {
        slot.write(format!("user{i}"));
    }
    // SAFETY: all 3 elements were written in the loop.
    let names: [String; 3] = unsafe { std::mem::transmute(names) };
    println!("{names:?}");

    // Most of the time a safe tool does the same job:
    let same: [String; 3] = std::array::from_fn(|i| format!("user{i}"));
    println!("{}", same == names);
}
[1, 2, 3, 4]
["user0", "user1", "user2"]
true

The steps are always the same: uninit(), then write, then assume_init(). The last step is the unsafe promise: "every byte is set now".

  • MaybeUninit never runs the destructor of its content. If you never call assume_init, the String values leak.
  • write does not drop an old value. Writing twice leaks the first one.
  • Do not make a &mut T to unset memory, even to fill it. Write through as_mut_ptr() or write.

MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init() for an i32 is UB, even if you never read the number. The old mem::uninitialized() made this mistake easy. Use std::array::from_fn or a Vec when you can. Reach for MaybeUninit only for real speed or for C.

Calling C from Rust

FFI means calling code from another language. C is the common language of operating systems. So most FFI goes through the C ABI. Here is a small C library.

#include <stddef.h>

typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

double mean(const double *xs, size_t n);
size_t count_vowels(const char *s);
double dist(Point a, Point b);

The cc crate compiles the C file from a build script. Then Rust declares the functions and wraps them.

fn main() {
    // Compile c/stats.c and link it into this crate.
    cc::Build::new().file("c/stats.c").compile("stats");
    println!("cargo::rerun-if-changed=c/stats.c");
}
use std::ffi::{c_char, CString, NulError};

#[repr(C)] // same field order and padding as the C struct
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Point {
    x: f64,
    y: f64,
}

// SAFETY: these signatures match c/stats.h exactly.
unsafe extern "C" {
    fn mean(xs: *const f64, n: usize) -> f64;
    fn count_vowels(s: *const c_char) -> usize;
    safe fn dist(a: Point, b: Point) -> f64; // plain values: no pointer rules
}

// Safe wrappers: the rest of the program never sees a raw pointer.
fn mean_of(xs: &[f64]) -> Option<f64> {
    if xs.is_empty() {
        return None; // C would divide by zero
    }
    // SAFETY: the pointer and length come from a real slice.
    Some(unsafe { mean(xs.as_ptr(), xs.len()) })
}

fn vowels(s: &str) -> Result<usize, NulError> {
    let c = CString::new(s)?; // adds the 0 byte, fails on inner 0
    // SAFETY: c is a valid C string and lives until the end of the call.
    Ok(unsafe { count_vowels(c.as_ptr()) })
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", mean_of(&[1.0, 2.0, 6.0]));
    println!("{:?}", mean_of(&[]));
    println!("{:?}", vowels("unsafe rust"));
    println!("{:?}", vowels("bad\0text").is_err());
    let d = dist(Point { x: 0.0, y: 0.0 }, Point { x: 3.0, y: 4.0 });
    println!("{d}");
}
import ctypes

lib = ctypes.CDLL("./libstats.dylib")   # libstats.so on Linux

class Point(ctypes.Structure):          # like #[repr(C)]
    _fields_ = [("x", ctypes.c_double), ("y", ctypes.c_double)]

# Without these lines ctypes guesses int for every type.
lib.mean.argtypes = [ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_double), ctypes.c_size_t]
lib.mean.restype = ctypes.c_double
lib.count_vowels.argtypes = [ctypes.c_char_p]
lib.count_vowels.restype = ctypes.c_size_t
lib.dist.argtypes = [Point, Point]
lib.dist.restype = ctypes.c_double

xs = (ctypes.c_double * 3)(1.0, 2.0, 6.0)  # a C array
print(lib.mean(xs, len(xs)))
print(lib.count_vowels(b"unsafe rust"))     # bytes, not str
print(lib.dist(Point(0, 0), Point(3, 4)))
Some(3.0)
None
Ok(4)
true
5

The Python version prints 3.0, 4 and 5.0. I built libstats.dylib with clang -shared on macOS.

Three ideas make this work:

  • #[repr(C)] gives a struct the C layout. Without it, Rust may reorder fields. Never pass a plain Rust struct to C.
  • C strings end with a 0 byte. Rust strings do not. CString adds the 0 byte. CStr reads one. A literal c"hello" is a ready &CStr.
  • Ownership crosses by agreement. Memory from C malloc must go back to C free. Memory from Rust must go back to Rust.

CString::new(s).unwrap().as_ptr() in one line gives a dangling pointer. The CString is a temporary. It dies at the end of the statement. Keep it in a let, as in vowels above.

bindgen writes the extern block for you

Writing signatures by hand is slow and easy to get wrong. bindgen reads a C header and writes the extern block. It needs libclang. On macOS the Xcode command line tools provide it.

use std::{env, path::PathBuf};

fn main() {
    cc::Build::new().file("c/stats.c").compile("stats");
    let bindings = bindgen::Builder::default()
        .header("c/stats.h")
        .allowlist_function("mean|count_vowels|dist") // only what we need
        .parse_callbacks(Box::new(bindgen::CargoCallbacks::new()))
        .generate()
        .expect("bindgen failed");
    let out = PathBuf::from(env::var("OUT_DIR").unwrap());
    bindings.write_to_file(out.join("bindings.rs")).unwrap();
}
/* automatically generated by rust-bindgen 0.73.2 */

#[repr(C)]
#[derive(Debug, Copy, Clone)]
pub struct Point {
    pub x: f64,
    pub y: f64,
}
// (compile-time checks of size, alignment and offsets cut here)
unsafe extern "C" {
    pub fn mean(xs: *const f64, n: usize) -> f64;
}
unsafe extern "C" {
    pub fn count_vowels(s: *const ::std::os::raw::c_char) -> usize;
}
unsafe extern "C" {
    pub fn dist(a: Point, b: Point) -> f64;
}

You load it with include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/bindings.rs")) inside a module. bindgen marks every function unsafe. It cannot know which ones are safe. Your safe wrappers are still your job.

Calling Rust from C

Now the other direction. Build a Rust library that a C program links. Three things are needed:

  • crate-type = ["staticlib"] (a .a file) or ["cdylib"] (a shared library).
  • pub extern "C" fn, so the function uses the C ABI.
  • #[unsafe(no_mangle)], so the symbol keeps its plain name.
use std::ffi::{c_char, CStr};

/// Counts of a text, shared with C.
#[repr(C)]
pub struct Stats {
    pub words: u32,
    pub bytes: u32,
}

/// Count words and bytes of a C string.
///
/// # Safety
/// `text` must be a valid, 0-terminated C string, or null.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub unsafe extern "C" fn text_stats(text: *const c_char) -> Stats {
    if text.is_null() {
        return Stats { words: 0, bytes: 0 };
    }
    // SAFETY: the caller promised a valid C string.
    let s = unsafe { CStr::from_ptr(text) };
    let s = s.to_string_lossy(); // bad UTF-8 becomes U+FFFD
    Stats {
        words: s.split_whitespace().count() as u32,
        bytes: s.len() as u32,
    }
}

/// Safe for C to call: plain numbers in and out.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn add_u32(a: u32, b: u32) -> u32 {
    a.wrapping_add(b)
}

cbindgen writes the C header from this code. I ran it from build.rs with cbindgen 0.29 and Language::C. Here is the header it made, without the comments:

#include <stdint.h>

typedef struct Stats {
  uint32_t words;
  uint32_t bytes;
} Stats;

struct Stats text_stats(const char *text);

uint32_t add_u32(uint32_t a, uint32_t b);
#include <stdio.h>
#include "include/textstats.h"

int main(void) {
    Stats s = text_stats("Rust called from C");
    printf("words=%u bytes=%u\n", s.words, s.bytes);
    printf("null words=%u\n", text_stats(NULL).words);
    printf("sum=%u\n", add_u32(40, 2));
    return 0;
}
cargo build --release
clang main.c target/release/libtextstats.a -o main_c
./main_c
words=4 bytes=18
null words=0
sum=42

Panics must not cross the border

What if a Rust function called by C panics? Since Rust 1.81 the program aborts. This program shows it.

extern "C" fn parse(n: i32) -> i32 {
    if n < 0 {
        panic!("negative input"); // cannot unwind into C
    }
    n * 2
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", parse(4));
    println!("{}", parse(-1));
}
8

thread 'main' panicked at abort.rs:3:9:
negative input
...
panic in a function that cannot unwind
...

The second ... hides a long backtrace. Then the process aborts with exit code 134.

An abort is safe, but your C caller dies. The polite fix is std::panic::catch_unwind. Catch the panic at the border and return an error code. In my test, parse_safe(-1) with catch_unwind(...).unwrap_or(-1) returned -1. If you really need a panic to travel through C frames, use the extern "C-unwind" ABI.

Do not give C a String, a Vec or a Box by value. C does not know their layout. Give a pointer and a length, or a #[repr(C)] struct. Also give C a function to free what Rust allocated.

Checking unsafe code with Miri

Miri is an interpreter for Rust. It runs your program or tests slowly, and it checks every memory access. It reports these problems.

  • Reads outside an object, and use after free.
  • Reads of memory that was never set.
  • Misaligned pointers and invalid values, like a bool that is 2.
  • Breaks of the borrow rules through raw pointers.
  • Data races and memory leaks.
rustup +nightly component add miri   # Miri needs a nightly toolchain
cargo +nightly miri test             # run your tests under Miri
cargo +nightly miri run              # run the program under Miri
MIRIFLAGS="-Zmiri-tree-borrows" cargo +nightly miri test   # other aliasing model

When Miri finds UB, it stops and points at the line. I could not run Miri for this chapter. This machine has no nightly toolchain, and the rules for this book do not allow new global installs. So no Miri output is shown here.

What Miri cannot do

Miri checks only the paths your tests run. It does not support most system calls, networking or most FFI calls. So it cannot test the C examples in this chapter. A clean Miri run does not prove that your code is sound. A Miri error does prove a bug.

Stacked Borrows and Tree Borrows

Rust has no final rule yet for when raw pointers and references may mix. Miri has two models of these rules. Stacked Borrows is the default. Tree Borrows is newer and allows more code. Both are still experimental.

Other tools

Debug builds run the standard library checks you saw earlier. Clippy has lints for unsafe code, like clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks. It asks for a SAFETY comment on every block.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for unsafe Rust and FFI
PatternPurposeModelNote
unsafe { ... } // SAFETY: ...Use one of the five powers// SAFETY: i < len, checked aboveName each rule and why it holds.
Safe fn, unsafe coreHide raw pointers from callersfn two_mut<T>(v: &mut [T], i: usize, j: usize) -> (&mut T, &mut T)The checks before the block make it sound.
unsafe fn + # Safety docPass a promise to the caller/// # Safety: v must not be emptyIn 2024 the body still needs unsafe { }.
&raw const xPoint to a place without a referencelet p = &raw const h.len;Use read_unaligned on packed fields.
MaybeUninit::uninit() then assume_init()Fill memory later, often from Cfill(slot.as_mut_ptr()); slot.assume_init()Try array::from_fn first.
unsafe extern "C" { safe fn ... }Declare C functions (2024)safe fn abs(x: i32) -> i32;safe is your promise, not a check.
#[repr(C)]Share a struct with C#[repr(C)] struct Point { x: f64, y: f64 }Plain Rust structs have no fixed layout.
CString::new(s)? in a letPass text to Clet c = CString::new(s)?; f(c.as_ptr())A temporary CString dangles.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fnLet C call Rustpub extern "C" fn add_u32(a: u32, b: u32) -> u32Unique names. Catch panics at the border.
bindgen in build.rsMake Rust declarations from a C headerBuilder::default().header("c/stats.h")Needs libclang. Add an allowlist.
cbindgen in build.rsMake a C header from RustBuilder::new().with_crate(dir).with_language(Language::C)Only repr(C) types and extern "C" functions go out.
cargo +nightly miri testFind UB in testsMIRIFLAGS="-Zmiri-tree-borrows"Silence is not proof.

Practice

Inside an unsafe block, is the borrow checker still active?

  • No, unsafe turns it off.
  • Yes. Only five extra actions become allowed.
  • Only in debug builds.

References keep their rules. Raw pointers are the way around them, and using them is one of the five powers.

Which line needs an unsafe block?

  • let p = &raw const x;
  • let p: *const i32 = std::ptr::null();
  • let v = *p;

Making a raw pointer is safe. Dereferencing it is one of the five powers.

In the 2024 edition, what does an item with no mark inside unsafe extern "C" { } mean?

  • It is safe to call.
  • It is unsafe to call.
  • It is a compile error.

Items default to unsafe. Write safe fn only when the function has no memory rules for the caller.

A safe function with an unsafe block inside lets safe callers cause UB with some input. What is the right word?

  • Unsound
  • Unstable
  • Undefined

Soundness is about the safe API. If any safe call can cause UB, the function is unsound.

To give a struct the same layout as in C, write attribute.

In the 2024 edition, #[no_mangle] must be written as attribute.

The tool that writes a C header from Rust code is tool.

  1. Find the bug: let p = CString::new("hi").unwrap().as_ptr(); unsafe { puts(p) };
    Answer

    The CString is a temporary. It is freed at the end of the first statement. p dangles. Fix: let c = CString::new("hi").unwrap(); then unsafe { puts(c.as_ptr()) };.

  2. Write a SAFETY comment for unsafe { *v.get_unchecked(i) } inside if i < v.len() { ... }.
    Answer 
    if i < v.len() {
    // SAFETY: i < v.len() was checked on the line above,
    // so the index is in bounds.
    let x = unsafe { *v.get_unchecked(i) };
}
  3. Move this 2021 code to the 2024 edition: extern "C" { fn sqrt(x: f64) -> f64; }. Can sqrt be safe?
    Answer

    Write unsafe extern "C" { safe fn sqrt(x: f64) -> f64; }. Yes, it can be safe. It takes a plain number and touches no memory you give it.

  4. A teammate wrote unsafe impl Send for Handle {}. Handle holds a raw pointer to a C object. What must be true?
    Answer

    It must be safe to use and drop the C object from another thread. Many C libraries are not thread-safe. Check the C documentation. Write the reason in a SAFETY comment above the impl.

  5. Why does let x: bool = unsafe { MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init() }; count as UB, even if x is never used?
    Answer

    A bool must be 0 or 1. Unset memory has no fixed value. Making an invalid value is UB at the moment it is made. The optimiser may already use the "0 or 1" rule.

  6. Expert. A Rust function called from C can panic. Name two ways to handle it, and what happens with neither.
    Answer

    With neither, a panic in an extern "C" function aborts the process (since Rust 1.81). Way one: wrap the body in std::panic::catch_unwind and return an error code. Way two: use extern "C-unwind" if the C side is built to let unwinding pass through.

Key takeaways

  • unsafe unlocks five powers. It never turns off the borrow checker or the rules.
  • Undefined behaviour means anything can happen. Debug checks catch only a little of it.
  • Put a tiny unsafe block inside a safe function. Check the rules first. Explain them in a SAFETY comment.
  • The 2024 edition asks for unsafe extern, #[unsafe(no_mangle)] and unsafe { } inside unsafe fn.
  • FFI needs #[repr(C)], C strings and clear ownership. bindgen and cbindgen write the boring parts.
  • Run tests of unsafe code under Miri. A clean run is good news, not proof.

Sources

  • The Rust Programming Language, 20.1: Unsafe Rust. The five powers, safe abstractions, FFI and Miri.
  • The Rust Reference: Behavior considered undefined. The official list of UB.
  • Edition Guide: Unsafe extern blocks. The 2024 rules, with the pages on unsafe attributes and unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn next to it.
  • The bindgen user guide: build.rs. How to make bindings from a C header.
  • cbindgen on GitHub. Making C headers from Rust code.
  • Miri on GitHub. What Miri detects and how to run it.

Memory and performance

Rust is fast by default, but not magic. Speed comes from how your data sits in memory and from what the compiler can see. This chapter shows how values are laid out, what costs time, and how to measure before you change anything.

  • Read the size, alignment and padding of any type with size_of and offset_of!.
  • Explain the cost of heap allocation, dynamic dispatch and cache misses with real numbers.
  • Measure code with criterion and find hot spots with a profiler.
  • Tune release builds with profiles, LTO and PGO.
  • Spot common slow patterns and fix them in Rust and Python.

All timings come from one run on one laptop (Apple M2 Pro, Rust 1.99, Python 3.14). Other programs were running at the same time. Your numbers will be different. Look at the ratios, not the exact values.

Size, alignment and layout

Every type has a size in bytes. Ask the compiler.

use std::mem::{align_of, size_of};

#[allow(dead_code)]
struct Rusty { a: u8, b: u32, c: u8 }   // Rust may reorder fields

#[allow(dead_code)]
#[repr(C)]
struct CLike { a: u8, b: u32, c: u8 }   // fields stay in this order

fn main() {
    println!("u8={} u32={} u64={} char={} bool={}",
        size_of::<u8>(), size_of::<u32>(), size_of::<u64>(),
        size_of::<char>(), size_of::<bool>());
    println!("align: u32={} u64={}", align_of::<u32>(), align_of::<u64>());
    println!("Rusty={} CLike={}", size_of::<Rusty>(), size_of::<CLike>());
    println!("&u8={} &[u8]={} &str={} Box<dyn Fn()>={}",
        size_of::<&u8>(), size_of::<&[u8]>(), size_of::<&str>(),
        size_of::<Box<dyn Fn()>>());
    println!("String={} Vec<u64>={}", size_of::<String>(), size_of::<Vec<u64>>());
    println!("Option<u32>={} Option<&u32>={} Option<Box<u8>>={}",
        size_of::<Option<u32>>(), size_of::<Option<&u32>>(),
        size_of::<Option<Box<u8>>>());
    println!("()={} [u16; 5]={}", size_of::<()>(), size_of::<[u16; 5]>());
}
import sys

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

class SlotPoint:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y")          # no per-object dict
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

print(sys.getsizeof(1), sys.getsizeof(2**100), sys.getsizeof(True))
print(sys.getsizeof([]), sys.getsizeof([1, 2, 3]), sys.getsizeof((1, 2, 3)))
p, s = Point(1, 2), SlotPoint(1, 2)
print(sys.getsizeof(p) + sys.getsizeof(p.__dict__), sys.getsizeof(s))
u8=1 u32=4 u64=8 char=4 bool=1
align: u32=4 u64=8
Rusty=8 CLike=12
&u8=8 &[u8]=16 &str=16 Box<dyn Fn()>=16
String=24 Vec<u64>=24
Option<u32>=8 Option<&u32>=8 Option<Box<u8>>=8
()=0 [u16; 5]=10

Python printed 28 40 28, then 56 88 72, then 344 48. A small Python int takes 28 bytes. A Rust i64 takes 8. Every Python value is a full object on the heap. __slots__ shrinks a Python object a lot, from 344 to 48 bytes here.

Three words explain the Rust numbers:

  • Size: how many bytes one value uses.
  • Alignment: the address of a value must be a multiple of this number. A u32 wants a multiple of 4.
  • Padding: empty bytes the compiler adds to keep fields aligned.

std::mem::offset_of! shows where each field starts.

println!("Rusty: a={} b={} c={}", offset_of!(Rusty, a), offset_of!(Rusty, b), offset_of!(Rusty, c));
println!("CLike: a={} b={} c={}", offset_of!(CLike, a), offset_of!(CLike, b), offset_of!(CLike, c));
Rusty: a=4 b=0 c=5
CLike: a=0 b=4 c=8

More rules you can see in the output:

  • A reference to a sized type is one machine word, 8 bytes here.
  • &[u8], &str and Box<dyn Fn()> are fat pointers: an address plus a length or a vtable pointer.
  • String and Vec are three words on the stack: pointer, capacity, length. The text itself is on the heap.
  • Option<&u32> is still 8 bytes. A reference is never null, so None can use the null value. This trick is called a niche.

Do not depend on the field order of a normal struct. The default layout has almost no guarantees, and it may change between compiler versions. When order matters (C code, files, network bytes), write #[repr(C)].

A big enum is as large as its largest variant. If one variant holds a 1 KB array, every value takes 1 KB. Put the big variant in a Box. Clippy warns about this with large_enum_variant.

Stack, heap and the cost of allocation

The stack holds local variables. Making space there costs almost nothing: the CPU moves one pointer. The heap holds data that can grow or outlive a function. Getting heap memory means a call to the allocator.

A Vec grows by asking for a bigger block and copying. Watch the capacity.

fn main() {
    let mut v: Vec<u64> = Vec::new();
    let mut last = usize::MAX;
    for i in 0..100 {
        v.push(i);
        if v.capacity() != last {
            last = v.capacity();
            print!("{last} "); // a new, bigger heap block was allocated
        }
    }
    println!();
    let w: Vec<u64> = Vec::with_capacity(100); // one allocation up front
    println!("{} {}", w.len(), w.capacity());
}
import sys
v, last = [], None
for i in range(100):
    v.append(i)
    size = sys.getsizeof(v)
    if size != last:
        last = size
        print((size - sys.getsizeof([])) // 8, end=" ")  # slots for items
print()
4 8 16 32 64 128
0 100

Here Rust doubled the capacity each time: 6 allocations for 100 pushes. Python grows more slowly and printed 4 8 16 24 32 40 52 64 76 92 108: 11 allocations. Both are smart. Neither is free. If you know the size, use Vec::with_capacity.

How much does one allocation cost? This benchmark builds a small 16-item list 10,000 times. One version makes a new Vec each time. The other reuses one buffer.

pub fn new_vec_each_time(rows: &[u32]) -> u64 {
    let mut total = 0;
    for &r in rows {
        let mut tmp = Vec::new(); // a new heap block every time
        tmp.extend((0..16).map(|i| r + i));
        total += tmp.iter().map(|&x| x as u64).sum::<u64>();
    }
    total
}

pub fn reuse_buffer(rows: &[u32]) -> u64 {
    let mut total = 0;
    let mut tmp = Vec::with_capacity(16); // one heap block
    for &r in rows {
        tmp.clear(); // keeps the capacity
        tmp.extend((0..16).map(|i| r + i));
        total += tmp.iter().map(|&x| x as u64).sum::<u64>();
    }
    total
}
alloc/new_each_time     time:   [308.49 µs 309.99 µs 311.70 µs]
alloc/reuse_buffer      time:   [24.588 µs 24.865 µs 25.191 µs]

Reusing the buffer was about 12 times faster. The work is the same. Only the allocations changed. Each new Vec also starts small and grows, so it allocates more than once.

Do not fear every allocation. One String per request is fine. Look for allocations inside hot loops: Vec::new(), to_string(), clone() and format!.

Measure first: criterion and profilers

Guessing about speed is usually wrong. So the first rule is: measure, change one thing, measure again. Before anything else, check the build mode. I timed one word-count program in two modes. With cargo run (the dev profile, no optimisation) the counting took 408 ms. With cargo run --release it took 36 ms.

That is about 11 times. The performance book says release builds are often 10 to 100 times faster. Never time a debug build.

Benchmarks with criterion

A benchmark runs code many times and reports a statistic. criterion is the common tool. Version 0.8.2 is current. It needs Rust 1.86 or newer.

// Cargo.toml:
// [dev-dependencies]
// criterion = "0.8"
// [[bench]]
// name = "perf"
// harness = false   # criterion brings its own main
use criterion::{criterion_group, criterion_main, Criterion};
use perfbench::{new_vec_each_time, reuse_buffer};
use std::hint::black_box;

fn benches(c: &mut Criterion) {
    let rows: Vec<u32> = (0..10_000).collect();
    c.bench_function("alloc/new_each_time", |b| {
        b.iter(|| new_vec_each_time(black_box(&rows)))
    });
    c.bench_function("alloc/reuse_buffer", |b| {
        b.iter(|| reuse_buffer(black_box(&rows)))
    });
}

criterion_group!(perf, benches);
criterion_main!(perf);
import timeit

def join_plus(n):
    s = ""
    for i in range(n):
        s = s + f"{i},"          # may copy the string each time
    return s

def join_list(n):
    return "".join(f"{i}," for i in range(n))   # one final copy

for f in (join_plus, join_list):
    t = min(timeit.repeat(lambda: f(2_000), number=200, repeat=5)) / 200
    print(f.__name__, f"{t * 1e6:.0f} µs")
cargo bench                                    # run all benchmarks
cargo bench -- alloc                           # only names with "alloc"
cargo bench -- --warm-up-time 1 --measurement-time 3   # shorter runs

Criterion prints three numbers: a low bound, the best guess and a high bound. On the next run it also says if the code got faster or slower. Python's timeit printed join_plus 212 µs and join_list 171 µs. Take the minimum of several repeats. The minimum is the run with the least noise.

black_box hides a value from the optimiser. Without it, the compiler may compute the answer once at compile time. Then you measure nothing. Since criterion 0.6, use std::hint::black_box, not criterion::black_box.

Measure the real program

Time it in release mode with real input. Write the number down.

Profile it

A profiler shows which functions use the time. Usually one or two places matter.

Write a benchmark for the hot spot

Put the hot function in a criterion benchmark. Now you can test ideas in seconds.

Change one thing

Only one. Then run the benchmark again.

Keep it or throw it away

If it is not clearly faster, undo it. Simple code is worth more than 2 percent.

Profilers and flame graphs

A flame graph draws the call stacks of many samples. A wide box means much time. Look for wide boxes near the top.

Common profilers
ToolSystemsCommand
perfLinuxperf record -g ./app then perf report
cargo flamegraphLinux, macOScargo flamegraph --bin app (makes an SVG)
samplyLinux, macOS, Windowssamply record ./target/release/app (opens the Firefox Profiler)
InstrumentsmacOSthe Time Profiler from Xcode

Add debug = true to [profile.release] while you profile. Then the profiler can show function names and lines. I ran samply record --save-only on the word-count program. It saved a profile file for the Firefox Profiler. A browser picture cannot be shown in this book.

A benchmark that runs 5 percent faster once proves nothing. The noise on a busy laptop is often bigger than that. Run it several times, close other programs, and trust only clear differences.

Zero-cost abstractions and monomorphisation

A zero-cost abstraction is a nice tool with no hidden price. Iterators are the famous example. Compare an index loop with an iterator chain.

pub fn dot_index(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    let mut s = 0i32;
    for i in 0..a.len() {
        s = s.wrapping_add(a[i].wrapping_mul(b[i])); // b[i] is checked
    }
    s
}

pub fn dot_iter(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    a.iter().zip(b).fold(0i32, |s, (x, y)| s.wrapping_add(x.wrapping_mul(*y)))
}
dot/index               time:   [9.9599 µs 11.229 µs 13.256 µs]
dot/iter                time:   [9.2675 µs 9.3797 µs 9.5034 µs]

Both are about the same. The iterator is not slower. The ranges overlap, so the difference is mostly noise.

Generics: one copy per type

Generic code is fast because of monomorphisation. The compiler writes one copy of the function for each type you use. Each copy is optimised for its type. The price is a bigger binary and longer builds.

use std::fmt::Debug;

#[inline(never)]
fn show_generic<T: Debug>(x: T) -> usize {
    format!("{x:?}").len() // one copy of this code per type T
}

#[inline(never)]
fn show_dyn(x: &dyn Debug) -> usize {
    format!("{x:?}").len() // one copy, a vtable call inside
}

fn main() {
    let g = show_generic(1u8) + show_generic(2i64) + show_generic(3.5f64)
        + show_generic("four") + show_generic('5') + show_generic([6u16; 2]);
    let d = show_dyn(&1u8) + show_dyn(&2i64) + show_dyn(&3.5f64)
        + show_dyn(&"four") + show_dyn(&'5') + show_dyn(&[6u16; 2]);
    println!("{g} {d}");
}
rustc --edition 2024 -O mono.rs -o mono && ./mono
nm mono | grep -c show_generic   # count the copies in the binary
nm mono | grep -c show_dyn
20 20
6
1

Six types gave six copies of show_generic. show_dyn has one copy. It uses a vtable to find the right fmt at run time. This is dynamic dispatch.

Now the speed side. The same closure runs over 100,000 numbers, first as a generic, then as &dyn Fn.

dispatch/generic        time:   [8.2188 µs 8.7335 µs 9.2573 µs]
dispatch/dyn            time:   [92.319 µs 93.832 µs 95.283 µs]

The generic version was about 11 times faster. The compiler could see the closure, put it inline and use vector instructions. Through &dyn Fn it had to make 100,000 real calls.

Generic or dyn?
QuestionGeneric T: Traitdyn Trait
Speed in a hot loopbest: inlining is possibleone indirect call each time
Binary sizeone copy per typeone copy
Build timelongershorter
Mixed types in one Vecnot possibleyes: Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>

A common trick for big generic functions: make a thin generic wrapper that converts the input, then call one non-generic inner function. For example, fn open<P: AsRef<Path>>(p: P) calls fn open_inner(p: &Path). You get a friendly API and only one big copy.

"Zero cost" does not mean "free". It means "not slower than writing it by hand". A .clone() inside an iterator chain still clones.

Inlining and bounds checks

Inlining removes a call. It also lets the optimiser see both sides at once. That is why the generic closure above was fast. The compiler decides alone most of the time. You can give hints:

  • #[inline]: a hint, and it allows inlining into other crates.
  • #[inline(always)] and #[inline(never)]: stronger hints. Use them only after measuring.
  • #[cold]: this function runs rarely, like an error path. The compiler moves it out of the hot path.

Since Rust 1.75, small functions are inlined across crates automatically. Generic functions could always be inlined, because each crate makes its own copy. LTO, later in this chapter, opens all functions to inlining.

Bounds checks

Every v[i] checks that i is less than the length. A failed check panics instead of reading wrong memory. This is safe, and often cheap. Look at the optimised machine code of three versions of the dot product.

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub fn dot_index(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    let mut s = 0i32;
    for i in 0..a.len() {
        s = s.wrapping_add(a[i].wrapping_mul(b[i])); // is b[i] in bounds?
    }
    s
}

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub fn dot_slice(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    let b = &b[..a.len()]; // one check here, before the loop
    let mut s = 0i32;
    for i in 0..a.len() {
        s = s.wrapping_add(a[i].wrapping_mul(b[i]));
    }
    s
}

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub fn dot_iter(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    a.iter().zip(b).fold(0, |s, (x, y)| s.wrapping_add(x.wrapping_mul(*y)))
}
rustc --edition 2024 -O --crate-type=lib --emit asm bounds.rs -o bounds.s
What the ARM64 assembly showed (rustc 1.99, -O)
FunctionPanic calls in the functionChecks inside the loopVector instructions
dot_index1 bounds-check panicnoneyes (mla.4s)
dot_slice1 slice-length panicnoneyes
dot_iternonenoneyes

The compiler was clever. In dot_index it compared the two lengths once, before the loop. All three loops became vector code. That is why the benchmark showed almost no difference.

The compiler cannot always do this. When it fails, try these, in this order:

  1. Use iterators: iter(), zip, chunks_exact, windows.
  2. Slice before the loop: let b = &b[..a.len()];. One check, then none.
  3. Add an assert! on the lengths before the loop. The optimiser can use it.
  4. Only as a last step, use unsafe { get_unchecked(i) } with a SAFETY comment. See Unsafe Rust and FFI.

Do not replace every v[i] with get_unchecked "for speed". The check is often already gone, as you just saw. You add risk and win nothing. Read the assembly or measure first.

Cache friendliness

The CPU does not read one byte from memory. It reads a cache line. The cache keeps recent lines close. Reading the next bytes in memory is cheap. Jumping around is expensive. Sum a 2048 by 2048 matrix of u32 in two orders.

pub fn sum_rows(m: &[u32], n: usize) -> u64 {
    let mut s = 0u64;
    for r in 0..n {
        for c in 0..n {
            s += m[r * n + c] as u64; // next number is next in memory
        }
    }
    s
}

pub fn sum_cols(m: &[u32], n: usize) -> u64 {
    let mut s = 0u64;
    for c in 0..n {
        for r in 0..n {
            s += m[r * n + c] as u64; // jumps n * 4 bytes each step
        }
    }
    s
}
cache/rows              time:   [219.47 µs 238.90 µs 266.03 µs]
cache/cols              time:   [9.5580 ms 9.8207 ms 10.158 ms]
cache/vec               time:   [9.0516 µs 9.1239 µs 9.2072 µs]
cache/linked_list       time:   [81.641 µs 84.893 µs 88.350 µs]

Same numbers, same sum, different order: about 41 times slower by columns. The matrix is 16 MB, bigger than the cache. By rows, every loaded line is fully used. By columns, each step loads a new line for 4 bytes.

The last two lines sum 100,000 numbers. A Vec keeps them side by side. A LinkedList keeps each number in its own heap block, behind a pointer. The Vec was about 9 times faster.

Data-oriented layout

Suppose a game updates only positions, but each struct also holds a name and a colour. An array of structs loads the name and colour too. A struct of arrays keeps all positions together.

struct Particle {
    pos: [f32; 3],
    vel: [f32; 3],
    name: String,   // 24 bytes we do not need
}
let parts: Vec<Particle> = Vec::new();
struct Particles {
    pos: Vec<[f32; 3]>,  // read together
    vel: Vec<[f32; 3]>,
    name: Vec<String>,   // only when needed
}

The same idea makes Python fast. A NumPy array stores raw numbers side by side, like a Vec<f64>. A Python list stores pointers to separate number objects. The chapter Performance and how CPython works goes deeper.

Release profiles, LTO and PGO

A profile is a set of build settings. Cargo has dev for cargo build and release for cargo build --release.

Default settings (Cargo reference)
Settingdevrelease
opt-level03
debugtruefalse
debug-assertions, overflow-checkstruefalse
ltofalsefalse (thin LTO inside the crate only)
codegen-units25616
incrementaltruefalse
panicunwindunwind

You can add your own profiles. Each one starts from another with inherits.

[profile.release-fast]   # for speed
inherits = "release"
lto = "fat"              # optimise across all crates
codegen-units = 1        # one unit: slower build, better code
panic = "abort"          # no unwinding code

[profile.release-small]  # for a small binary
inherits = "release"
opt-level = "z"          # optimise for size
lto = "fat"
codegen-units = 1
panic = "abort"
strip = "symbols"        # remove symbol names

LTO lets the compiler inline and remove code across crate borders. codegen-units = 1 gives the optimiser the whole crate at once. Both make builds slower. I built the word-count program with each profile, ran it three times and kept the middle time.

One program, four profiles (macOS, ARM64)
CommandBinary sizeCounting time
cargo build635,144 bytes408 ms
cargo build --release456,592 bytes36 ms
cargo build --profile release-fast395,360 bytes24 ms
cargo build --profile release-small302,688 bytes37 ms

Here the speed profile was about one third faster than plain release. The size profile made the smallest file at about release speed. Your program may react differently. The performance book reports 10 to 20 percent or more from LTO.

PGO: optimise for real use

PGO uses data from real runs. The compiler learns which branches are hot. The steps:

  1. Install the tool: rustup component add llvm-tools-preview.
  2. Build with counters: RUSTFLAGS="-Cprofile-generate=/tmp/pgo-data" cargo build --release.
  3. Run the program on typical input. It writes .profraw files.
  4. Merge them: llvm-profdata merge -o /tmp/pgo-data/merged.profdata /tmp/pgo-data.
  5. Rebuild: RUSTFLAGS="-Cprofile-use=/tmp/pgo-data/merged.profdata" cargo build --release.

The community tool cargo-pgo does these steps for you. I could not finish PGO on this machine. The llvm-profdata from Xcode is too old for the LLVM inside rustc 1.99:

warning: pgo-data/default_3357610195662263501_0.profraw: raw profile version mismatch: Profile uses raw profile format version = 11; expected version = 10
error: no profile can be merged

This is a real lesson. Use the llvm-profdata from llvm-tools-preview. It matches your compiler.

-C target-cpu=native makes code for your exact CPU. It can be faster, but the binary may crash on an older CPU. Do not ship it to users unless you control their machines.

The SIMD idea

SIMD means one instruction works on several numbers at once. A 128-bit register holds four f32 values. One add instruction adds four pairs. The compiler often does this alone. That is auto-vectorisation, like the mla.4s lines in the dot product.

But not for this float sum:

fn sum_simple(v: &[f32]) -> f32 {
    v.iter().sum() // one running total: each add waits for the last one
}

fn sum_lanes(v: &[f32]) -> f32 {
    let mut acc = [0.0f32; 8]; // 8 independent totals, one per lane
    let chunks = v.chunks_exact(8);
    let rest = chunks.remainder();
    for c in chunks {
        for i in 0..8 {
            acc[i] += c[i]; // the compiler turns this into vector adds
        }
    }
    acc.iter().sum::<f32>() + rest.iter().sum::<f32>()
}

fn main() {
    let v: Vec<f32> = (0..100_000).map(|i| (i % 100) as f32 * 0.5).collect();
    println!("{} {}", sum_simple(&v), sum_lanes(&v));
    let tiny = [1e8f32, 1.0, -1e8, 1.0];
    println!("{} {}", sum_simple(&tiny), tiny[0] + tiny[2] + tiny[1] + tiny[3]);
}
2475000 2475000
1 2
simd/f32_simple         time:   [92.462 µs 94.285 µs 96.595 µs]
simd/f32_lanes          time:   [11.290 µs 11.335 µs 11.378 µs]

Eight totals were about 8 times faster. Why does the compiler not do it alone? Look at the second output line. Float addition depends on the order. Adding the same four numbers in two orders gave 1 and 2. The compiler must keep your order, so it cannot split the sum. When you write 8 totals, you allow the new order yourself.

std::arch: CPU instructions by name

The std::arch module has stable functions for the instructions of each CPU, for example NEON on ARM and SSE or AVX on x86. They are unsafe, because the CPU must support them. Check first at run time with is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2") on x86.

std::simd: portable SIMD

std::simd gives types like f32x8 that work on every CPU. It is still unstable. On rustc 1.99, use std::simd::f32x8; fails with error E0658 (feature portable_simd). Check the release notes for its status.

Help the auto-vectoriser

Use simple loops over slices. Use chunks_exact so the length is known. Avoid early break and function calls inside the loop. Integer math vectorises more easily than float math.

Common slow patterns and their fixes
