Most slow Rust code has a few well-known causes. Two of them have numbers from this chapter's runs.

use std::fmt::Write;

pub fn join_format(n: u32) -> String {
    let mut s = String::new();
    for i in 0..n {
        s = format!("{s}{i},"); // copies the whole string each time
    }
    s
}

pub fn join_write(n: u32) -> String {
    let mut s = String::with_capacity(n as usize * 6);
    for i in 0..n {
        write!(s, "{i},").unwrap(); // appends in place
    }
    s
}
// string/format_each_time  time: [444.27 µs 459.71 µs 476.67 µs]
// string/write_in_place    time: [27.658 µs 27.847 µs 28.116 µs]
import time
from collections import Counter

words = ["rust", "python", "memory", "cache", "heap", "stack", "simd"]
text = [words[(i * 7 + i // 3) % len(words)] for i in range(2_000_000)]

start = time.perf_counter()
freq = {}
for w in text:                       # a plain loop with a dict
    freq[w] = freq.get(w, 0) + 1
loop_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000

start = time.perf_counter()
freq2 = Counter(text)                # the counting loop runs in C
counter_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000

top = sorted(freq.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:2]
print(top, f"loop {loop_ms:.0f} ms, Counter {counter_ms:.0f} ms", freq == freq2)
[('rust', 285716), ('cache', 285714)] loop 134 ms, Counter 44 ms True

The Python output is from wordfreq.py. The same count took 36 ms in Rust release mode. Python's Counter runs its loop in C, so it came close. The Rust HashMap uses SipHash 1-3 by default. It protects servers from hash-flooding attacks, but it is not the fastest. I wrote a second test program to compare hashers. There the default HashMap took about 24 ms and HashMap<&str, u32, foldhash::fast::RandomState> about 10 ms. The faster hasher comes from the foldhash crate, version 0.2.

Slow pattern, fix
Slow patternWhy it is slowFix
Timing a debug buildno optimisationcargo run --release
Vec::new() or String::new() inside a hot loopone allocation per roundmake it once, clear() it each round
s = format!("{s}...")copies the whole string each timewrite!(s, ...) or push_str
.clone() to calm the borrow checkercopies databorrow (&T) or move
.collect() then loop againan extra Veckeep the iterator chain going
println! in a big looplocks stdout each calllet mut out = BufWriter::new(stdout().lock());
Reading a file byte by byteone system call each timeBufReader, or fs::read_to_string
Default HashMap with small keysSipHash is slow but safefoldhash or rustc-hash for trusted keys
Vec<Vec<T>> for a gridone heap block per rowone flat Vec<T> with r * n + c
Box<dyn Fn> in a hot loopno inlininga generic F: Fn
LinkedList for a list of numberspointer chasing, cache missesVec or VecDeque

Do not use a fast non-random hasher for keys that come from users of a web service. An attacker can send keys that all collide. Then every lookup gets slow. Keep the default hasher for untrusted input.

Interviewers often ask: "Your Rust service is slow. What do you do first?" A strong answer: check it runs a release build, measure with real input, profile to find the hot spot, then fix allocations or data layout there. Do not start with unsafe.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for memory and performance
PatternPurposeModelNote
size_of::<T>(), offset_of!(T, f)See the layout of a typesize_of::<Option<&u32>>() == 8Default layout may change. Do not rely on it.
#[repr(C)]Fix field order for C or files#[repr(C)] struct Header { .. }May add padding. Order fields big to small.
Box the big variantKeep an enum smallenum Msg { Ping, Data(Box<[u8; 4096]>) }Clippy: large_enum_variant.
Vec::with_capacity(n)Allocate once when the size is knownlet mut v = Vec::with_capacity(rows.len());Capacity is not length.
buf.clear() and reuseAvoid allocations in a looptmp.clear(); tmp.extend(..)12 times faster in this chapter.
--releaseMeasure optimised codecargo run --releaseDebug builds can be 10 to 100 times slower.
criterion + black_boxBenchmark one functionb.iter(|| f(black_box(&data)))Use std::hint::black_box.
Profile, then optimiseFind the real hot spotsamply record ./target/release/appSet debug = true while profiling.
Generic F: Fn in hot loopsAllow inliningfn apply<F: Fn(u32) -> u32>(v: &[u32], f: F)Costs binary size per type.
Iterators over indexingRemove bounds checksa.iter().zip(b)Often the compiler already removed them.
Row-major loops, flat VecUse the cache wellm[r * n + c] with c inside41 times faster than by columns here.
Several accumulatorsLet float sums use SIMDlet mut acc = [0.0f32; 8];The result can change in the last digits.
lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1Faster release binary[profile.release-fast] inherits = "release"Builds get slower.
PGO with -Cprofile-generate/useOptimise for real inputcargo pgo buildllvm-profdata must match rustc's LLVM.

Practice

What is size_of::<Option<&u64>>() on a 64-bit machine?

  • 16
  • 8
  • 9

A reference is never null. None uses the null value, so no extra tag byte is needed. This is the niche trick.

Why can't the compiler turn v.iter().sum::<f32>() into SIMD by itself?

  • SIMD does not support floats.
  • Float addition depends on the order, and the compiler must keep your order.
  • Iterators block all optimisation.

Splitting the sum into lanes changes the order of additions. That can change the result, as 1 versus 2 showed.

Which change is the most likely to speed up a hot loop that calls a closure through &dyn Fn?

  • Take the closure as a generic F: Fn.
  • Add #[inline(never)].
  • Use Box<dyn Fn> instead.

A generic lets the compiler see the closure body and inline it. The dyn version makes a real call each time.

Your benchmark shows the new code is 3 percent faster on a busy laptop. What do you do?

  • Ship it. Faster is faster.
  • Run again in a quiet setting. Keep it only if the gain is clear and the code is not worse.
  • Switch to a debug build to see more detail.

Noise is often bigger than 3 percent. Small gains must be checked again before you trust them.

The default codegen-units for the release profile is number.

A struct #[repr(C)] struct S { a: u8, b: u64 } has size bytes.

To hide a value from the optimiser in a benchmark, use std::hint::function.

  1. Order the fields of #[repr(C)] struct R { a: u8, b: u64, c: u16 } to make it as small as possible. What are the old and new sizes?
    Answer

    Old: a at 0, padding to 8, b at 8, c at 16, padding to 24. Size 24. New order b, c, a: 8 + 2 + 1 = 11, padded to 16. Size 16. Rule: big fields first.

  2. This function is slow. Find two problems and fix them. 
    fn names(users: &[User]) -> String {
    let mut out = String::new();
    for u in users {
        out = format!("{out}{}\n", u.name.clone());
    }
    out
}
    Answer

    format! copies the whole string each round. clone() copies each name for nothing.

    use std::fmt::Write;

fn names(users: &[User]) -> String {
    let mut out = String::new();
    for u in users {
        writeln!(out, "{}", u.name).unwrap(); // append, no clone
    }
    out
}
  3. A grid is stored as Vec<Vec<f64>>, and you sum it column by column. Give two changes for better cache use.
    Answer

    Store it as one flat Vec<f64> with index r * n + c. Then loop rows outside and columns inside, so you read memory in order.

  4. When would you choose dyn Trait over generics even if it is slower?
    Answer

    When you need different types in one collection, like Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>. Also when the function is not hot and you want a smaller binary and faster builds.

  5. Write a Cargo.toml profile named profiling for use with a profiler.
    Answer 
    [profile.profiling]
inherits = "release"
debug = true    # keep names and lines for the profiler

    Build it with cargo build --profile profiling. The binary is in target/profiling/.

  6. Expert. A teammate wants to replace all v[i] with get_unchecked in a hot loop. What do you ask for first?
    Answer

    A profile that shows the loop is hot, and the assembly or a benchmark that shows the checks are still there. Often the compiler already moved the check out of the loop. If a check stays, try iterators, slicing before the loop or an assert! first. Use get_unchecked only with a SAFETY comment and a test under Miri.

Key takeaways

  • Size, alignment and padding decide how much memory a type uses. The default Rust layout reorders fields to save space.
  • Heap allocation costs real time in hot loops. Reuse buffers and use with_capacity.
  • Always measure release builds. Use criterion for small parts and a profiler for the whole program.
  • Generics are fast because of monomorphisation and inlining. dyn is smaller and more flexible.
  • Memory order matters a lot: flat Vecs and row-by-row loops use the cache well.
  • Profiles, LTO and PGO tune the final binary. SIMD often comes free from simple loops.

Sources

  • The Rust Reference: Type layout. Size, alignment, repr(C) and what the default layout promises.
  • The Rust Performance Book. Build settings, profiling, bounds checks and heap allocations.
  • The Cargo Book: Profiles. Default dev and release settings, LTO values and custom profiles.
  • The rustc book: Profile-guided optimization. The PGO steps and the tools they need.
  • criterion.rs on GitHub. The benchmark library, its changelog and its user guide.
  • Python docs: timeit. Measuring small pieces of Python code.

API design and idioms

Other people see only the public face of your code. A good public face is easy to use well and hard to use wrong. This chapter shows the habits that Rust and Python developers expect from a library.

  • Name types, methods and conversions the way the Rust API guidelines ask.
  • Accept flexible input with AsRef, Into and impl IntoIterator, and return iterators.
  • Build complex values with a builder, and catch a missing step at compile time with typestate.
  • Design error types for libraries and for applications.
  • Tell a breaking change from a safe one, and write documentation with tested examples.

What a good API looks like

Read this call. Can you say what true and false mean?

send(addr.clone(), text.clone(), true, false)

send(&addr, text, Retry::Yes, Format::Html)

The first call forces you to open the source code. The second call explains itself. It also needs no clone(), because the function borrows what it only reads.

An API is the set of public types, functions and traits of your code. An idiom is the way most people write a thing in one language. Idiomatic APIs feel familiar, so users guess right.

The Rust library team wrote the Rust API guidelines. It is a checklist with more than 50 items in 11 groups. Each item has a short id, like C-GETTER. The items are advice, not laws. They matter most for crates that other people use.

Making everything pub "just in case". Every public item is a promise. You cannot remove it later without a major release. Start private and open things up when a user needs them.

Naming: the name tells the cost

Here is a small type. Look at the first word of each method name.

/// A short label, stored in lower case.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Default)]
pub struct Tag(String);

impl Tag {
    pub fn new(s: &str) -> Self {
        Tag(s.trim().to_lowercase())
    }
    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
        &self.0 // as_: free, borrowed to borrowed
    }
    pub fn to_upper(&self) -> String {
        self.0.to_uppercase() // to_: does work, makes a new String
    }
    pub fn into_inner(self) -> String {
        self.0 // into_: takes self, gives the inside away
    }
    pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
        self.0.len() // a getter: no get_ prefix
    }
    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        self.0.is_empty()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let t = Tag::new("  Rust ");
    println!("{} {} {}", t.as_str(), t.to_upper(), t.len());
    let s: String = t.into_inner(); // t is gone after this
    println!("{s} {}", Tag::default().is_empty());
}
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Tag:
    """A short label, stored in lower case."""

    _value: str  # leading _ means "private, do not touch"

    @classmethod
    def new(cls, s: str) -> "Tag":
        return cls(s.strip().lower())

    @property
    def value(self) -> str:  # a property, not get_value()
        return self._value

    def to_upper(self) -> str:
        return self._value.upper()

    def __len__(self) -> int:  # len(tag) works
        return len(self._value)


t = Tag.new("  Rust ")
print(t.value, t.to_upper(), len(t))
print(len(Tag("")) == 0)
rust RUST 4
rust true

Python prints rust RUST 4 and then True.

In Rust, the prefix of a conversion method tells the reader two things. Does it cost work? Who owns the result?

Conversion prefixes (guideline C-CONV)
PrefixCostOwnershipExample from std
as_Freeborrowed to borrowedString::as_str
to_Does workusually borrowed to ownedstr::to_lowercase
into_Variesowned to owned, consumes selfString::into_bytes

More naming rules from the guidelines:

  • Case. Types, traits and enum variants use UpperCamelCase. Functions, methods, modules and local names use snake_case. Constants and statics use SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE.
  • Acronyms are one word. Write Uuid and HttpClient, not UUID and HTTPClient.
  • No get_. A getter is just the field name: len(), first(), first_mut(). Use get alone only when there is one obvious thing to get, like Cell::get.
  • Iterator methods. A collection has iter(), iter_mut() and into_iter(). They give &T, &mut T and T.
  • Word order. Error types follow verb, object, "Error": ParseIntError, ParseAddrError.
  • Features. Name a feature std or serde, not use-std or with-serde.

Python follows PEP 8. Functions are snake_case, classes are CapWords, constants are UPPER_CASE. A leading underscore marks a private name. Python uses a @property where Rust uses a getter method.

An as_ method that allocates memory. Users call as_ methods in hot loops because the name promises "free". If the method builds a new value, name it to_.

Flexible input: AsRef, Into and IntoIterator

These functions accept many input types. The caller does not need to convert anything first.

use std::io;
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};

// AsRef<Path>: accepts &str, String, &Path, PathBuf ...
fn name_len<P: AsRef<Path>>(p: P) -> usize {
    p.as_ref().file_name().map_or(0, |n| n.len())
}

struct User {
    name: String,
}

impl User {
    // Into<String>: accepts &str and String. A String moves in, no copy.
    fn new(name: impl Into<String>) -> Self {
        User { name: name.into() }
    }
}

// IntoIterator: accepts Vec, arrays, ranges and iterators.
fn total(xs: impl IntoIterator<Item = u32>) -> u32 {
    xs.into_iter().sum()
}

// The generic part is tiny. The real work is compiled only once.
pub fn read_text<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> io::Result<String> {
    fn inner(path: &Path) -> io::Result<String> {
        std::fs::read_to_string(path)
    }
    inner(path.as_ref())
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", name_len("data/report.csv"));
    println!("{}", name_len(String::from("/tmp/a.txt")));
    println!("{}", name_len(PathBuf::from("notes.md")));
    let (a, b) = (User::new("Ann"), User::new(String::from("Bo")));
    println!("{} {}", a.name, b.name);
    println!("{} {} {}", total(vec![1, 2, 3]), total([4, 5]), total(1..=4));
    println!("{}", total([1, 2, 3].iter().copied()));
    println!("{}", read_text("no-such-file").is_err());
}
import os
from collections.abc import Iterable
from pathlib import Path


def name_len(p: str | os.PathLike[str]) -> int:
    return len(Path(p).name)  # Path() accepts str and Path


def total(xs: Iterable[int]) -> int:  # list, tuple, range, generator
    return sum(xs)


print(name_len("data/report.csv"), name_len(Path("notes.md")))
print(total([1, 2, 3]), total((4, 5)), total(range(1, 5)))
print(total(x for x in [1, 2, 3]))
10
5
8
Ann Bo
6 9 10
6
true

Python prints 10 8, 6 9 10 and 6.

The rule is simple. Ask for the weakest thing that does the job.

  • Only reading text? Take &str, not &String. Only reading items? Take &[T], not &Vec<T>.
  • Opening a file? Take P: AsRef<Path>. Then strings and paths both work.
  • Storing a String? Take impl Into<String> or a plain String. The caller can move a value in. If you take &str and copy inside, every caller pays for the copy. The guidelines call this "the caller decides where to copy" (C-CALLER-CONTROL).
  • Many items? Take impl IntoIterator<Item = T>. Vectors, arrays, ranges and iterator chains all fit.

Generics have a cost. The compiler makes one copy of a generic function for each concrete type. This is called monomorphisation. It is fast at run time, but the binary grows. The read_text function shows the fix. The generic outer part only converts. A private inner function with a plain &Path does the real work, and it is compiled once. The standard library uses this trick in functions like fs::read_to_string. The chapter Memory and performance measures the effect.

Python has no compile step, so one function already accepts anything. Type hints say what is allowed. Iterable[int] is the twin of impl IntoIterator<Item = u32>. str | os.PathLike[str] is the twin of AsRef<Path>.

Taking &String, &Vec<T> or &PathBuf as a parameter. Then a caller with a &str or an array cannot call you. Clippy warns with the lint ptr_arg. Take &str, &[T] or &Path.

Returning iterators

An inventory can list the items in stock. It returns an iterator, not a Vec.

struct Inventory {
    items: Vec<(String, u32)>,
}

impl Inventory {
    // Edition 2024: the returned iterator may borrow from &self.
    // No `+ '_` is needed any more.
    fn in_stock(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = &str> {
        self.items
            .iter()
            .filter(|(_, n)| *n > 0)
            .map(|(name, _)| name.as_str())
    }

    // Two different iterator types: box them behind one trait object.
    fn names(&self, only_stock: bool) -> Box<dyn Iterator<Item = &str> + '_> {
        if only_stock {
            Box::new(self.in_stock())
        } else {
            Box::new(self.items.iter().map(|(n, _)| n.as_str()))
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let inv = Inventory {
        items: vec![("pen".into(), 3), ("cup".into(), 0), ("ink".into(), 9)],
    };
    // The caller decides: take two, count, or collect.
    let first: Vec<&str> = inv.in_stock().take(2).collect();
    println!("{first:?} {}", inv.in_stock().count());
    println!("{:?}", inv.names(false).collect::<Vec<_>>());
}
from collections.abc import Iterator
from itertools import islice


class Inventory:
    def __init__(self, items: list[tuple[str, int]]) -> None:
        self._items = items

    def in_stock(self) -> Iterator[str]:
        # A generator: lazy, like a Rust iterator.
        for name, n in self._items:
            if n > 0:
                yield name


inv = Inventory([("pen", 3), ("cup", 0), ("ink", 9)])
print(list(islice(inv.in_stock(), 2)), sum(1 for _ in inv.in_stock()))
["pen", "ink"] 2
["pen", "cup", "ink"]

Python prints ['pen', 'ink'] 2.

Return impl Iterator<Item = T> when you produce a sequence. The iterator is lazy. The caller may want only the first item, or only a count. A Vec would force every caller to pay for the memory. Since the 2024 edition, an impl Trait return type may borrow from every input automatically. The chapter Lifetimes explains these capture rules and use<..>.

One impl Iterator must be one concrete type. Two branches with different iterator chains do not compile:

error[E0308]: `if` and `else` have incompatible types
...
help: you could change the return type to be a boxed trait object

You have three ways out:

  1. Box it, as in names. A trait object costs one allocation and a small indirect call per item.
  2. Write a named iterator type, like std::collections::hash_map::Keys. The guideline C-ITER-TY says the type name matches the method name.
  3. Use an enum with one variant per branch, and implement Iterator for it.

In Python, a generator runs only once. After list(gen), a second list(gen) gives [], with no error. Return a fresh generator from a method each time, as in_stock() does. A Rust iterator moves into collect(), so the compiler stops you from reusing it.

Builders and typestate

A request has one required value and several optional ones. A builder keeps the call short and readable.

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Request {
    url: String,
    method: String,
    timeout_ms: u64,
    headers: Vec<(String, String)>,
}

pub struct RequestBuilder {
    url: String,          // required: asked for in new()
    method: String,       // optional: has a default
    timeout_ms: u64,
    headers: Vec<(String, String)>,
}

impl RequestBuilder {
    pub fn new(url: impl Into<String>) -> Self {
        RequestBuilder { url: url.into(), method: "GET".into(), timeout_ms: 5_000, headers: vec![] }
    }
    // Non-consuming: take &mut self, give &mut self back.
    pub fn method(&mut self, m: &str) -> &mut Self {
        self.method = m.to_string();
        self
    }
    pub fn timeout_ms(&mut self, ms: u64) -> &mut Self {
        self.timeout_ms = ms;
        self
    }
    pub fn header(&mut self, k: &str, v: &str) -> &mut Self {
        self.headers.push((k.into(), v.into()));
        self
    }
    // &self: the same builder can build many requests.
    pub fn build(&self) -> Request {
        Request {
            url: self.url.clone(),
            method: self.method.clone(),
            timeout_ms: self.timeout_ms,
            headers: self.headers.clone(),
        }
    }
}

The main function uses it in one line, and then step by step.

fn main() {
    // One line:
    let r = RequestBuilder::new("https://example.com").method("POST").build();
    println!("{} {} {} {}", r.method, r.url, r.timeout_ms, r.headers.len());
    // Step by step, with an if in the middle:
    let mut b = RequestBuilder::new("https://example.com/items");
    b.timeout_ms(800);
    let debug = true;
    if debug {
        b.header("x-debug", "1");
    }
    println!("{:?}", b.build());
}
POST https://example.com 5000 0
Request { url: "https://example.com/items", method: "GET", timeout_ms: 800, headers: [("x-debug", "1")] }

The rule (C-BUILDER): new takes only the required values. Each setter sets one option and returns the builder, so calls can chain. A last method, often build, makes the value. There are two styles.

Two builder styles
Non-consumingConsuming
Setterfn x(&mut self) -> &mut Selffn x(mut self) -> Self
Steps with ifEasy: b.x();Must reassign: b = b.x();
Build many valuesYesNo, the builder is used up
Use it whenThe default choice of the guidelinesThe result must own something the builder holds
Known examplestd::process::Commandstd::thread::Builder

Python rarely needs builders. Keyword arguments with defaults do the same job. A frozen dataclass with kw_only=True forces callers to name every argument.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field, replace


@dataclass(frozen=True, kw_only=True)
class Request:
    url: str  # required: no default
    method: str = "GET"
    timeout_ms: int = 5_000
    headers: tuple[tuple[str, str], ...] = field(default_factory=tuple)


r = Request(url="https://example.com", method="POST")
print(r.method, r.url, r.timeout_ms)
r2 = replace(r, timeout_ms=800)  # a changed copy, like a builder step
print(r2)
try:
    Request(method="POST")  # the url is missing
except TypeError as e:
    print(e)
try:
    Request("https://example.com")  # kw_only: names are required
except TypeError as e:
    print(e)
POST https://example.com 5000
Request(url='https://example.com', method='POST', timeout_ms=800, headers=())
Request.__init__() missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'url'
Request.__init__() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given

Typestate: a missing step is a compile error

Sometimes the required value comes later in the chain. A typestate builder changes its type when you set it. The build method exists only on the finished type.

// Two marker states. HasUrl carries the url it needs.
pub struct NoUrl;
pub struct HasUrl(String);

pub struct ClientBuilder<S> {
    state: S,
    retries: u32,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Client {
    url: String,
    retries: u32,
}

impl ClientBuilder<NoUrl> {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        ClientBuilder { state: NoUrl, retries: 0 }
    }
    // Consuming: the old builder goes in, a new type comes out.
    pub fn url(self, u: &str) -> ClientBuilder<HasUrl> {
        ClientBuilder { state: HasUrl(u.to_string()), retries: self.retries }
    }
}

Next come the methods for every state, and build for the finished state only.

// Methods for every state.
impl<S> ClientBuilder<S> {
    pub fn retries(mut self, n: u32) -> Self {
        self.retries = n;
        self
    }
}

// build() exists only when the url is set.
impl ClientBuilder<HasUrl> {
    pub fn build(self) -> Client {
        Client { url: self.state.0, retries: self.retries }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let c = ClientBuilder::new().retries(3).url("https://api.example.com").build();
    println!("{} {}", c.url, c.retries);
    // ClientBuilder::new().retries(3).build(); // does not compile
}
https://api.example.com 3

Remove the comment marks on the last line, and the compiler stops you:

error[E0599]: no method named `build` found for struct `ClientBuilder<NoUrl>` in the current scope
   = note: the method was found for `ClientBuilder<HasUrl>`

A builder whose build() panics when a required value is missing. The bug shows up only at run time. Ask for required values in new(), use typestate, or make build() return a Result.

Types that carry meaning

Plain bool and u64 values say nothing. Small types of your own make each call clear.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Overwrite {
    Allow,
    Deny,
}

// Two ids with the same inner type, but they cannot be mixed up.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct UserId(u64);
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct OrderId(u64);

fn save(path: &str, mode: Overwrite) -> String {
    format!("save {path}: {mode:?}")
}

fn cancel(order: OrderId, by: UserId) -> String {
    format!("order {} cancelled by user {}", order.0, by.0)
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
pub struct Price(u64); // cents

impl Price {
    #[must_use = "this returns a new Price and does not change self"]
    pub fn with_tax(self, percent: u64) -> Price {
        Price(self.0 + self.0 * percent / 100)
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", save("notes.txt", Overwrite::Deny)); // not save("notes.txt", false)
    println!("{}", cancel(OrderId(77), UserId(5)));
    // cancel(UserId(5), OrderId(77)); // error[E0308]: mismatched types
    let p = Price(1000);
    p.with_tax(10); // warning: the new Price is thrown away
    println!("{:?} {:?}", p, p.with_tax(10));
}
from enum import Enum
from typing import NewType

UserId = NewType("UserId", int)
OrderId = NewType("OrderId", int)


class Overwrite(Enum):
    ALLOW = "allow"
    DENY = "deny"


def save(path: str, *, mode: Overwrite) -> str:  # * : mode must be named
    return f"save {path}: {mode.name}"


def cancel(order: OrderId, by: UserId) -> str:
    return f"order {order} cancelled by user {by}"


print(save("notes.txt", mode=Overwrite.DENY))
print(cancel(OrderId(77), UserId(5)))
print(cancel(UserId(5), OrderId(77)))  # runs! only a type checker complains
print(type(UserId(5)))  # at run time it is a plain int
warning: unused return value of `Price::with_tax` that must be used
  --> types.rs:36:5
   = note: this returns a new Price and does not change self

save notes.txt: Deny
order 77 cancelled by user 5
Price(1000) Price(1100)

Python prints DENY, then the two cancel lines with the ids in the wrong order, then <class 'int'>.

  • Enums, not bool (C-CUSTOM-TYPE). Overwrite::Deny reads well. You can add a third variant later, like AskUser.
  • Newtypes (C-NEWTYPE). A newtype like UserId(u64) costs nothing at run time. The compiler rejects a swapped call. See Structs, enums and pattern matching.
  • Private fields (C-STRUCT-PRIVATE). Then you can change the inside later, and you can check values in the constructor.
  • #[must_use] warns when a caller drops a result. Use it on methods that return a new value instead of changing self.

Python's NewType exists only for the type checker. At run time, UserId(5) is a plain int, so the swapped call runs. The bare * in save makes mode a keyword-only argument. The caller must write mode=.

Using Option<bool> for three states, like "yes, no, not asked yet". Nobody remembers what None means. Write enum Consent { Given, Refused, NotAsked }.

Errors for libraries and for applications

A small library reads key=value settings. It defines its own error type with the thiserror crate.

use std::num::ParseIntError;

/// Everything that can go wrong while reading settings.
#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
#[non_exhaustive] // we may add variants later without a major release
pub enum ConfigError {
    /// A line has no `=` sign.
    #[error("line {line}: expected `key=value`")]
    Syntax { line: usize },
    /// A key the caller asked for is not there.
    #[error("missing key `{0}`")]
    Missing(String),
    /// A value is not a valid number.
    #[error("key `{key}` is not a valid number")]
    BadNumber {
        key: String,
        #[source] // the cause, reachable with Error::source()
        source: ParseIntError,
    },
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    // The error can cross threads and be boxed: check it at compile time.
    fn assert_good_error<E: std::error::Error + Send + Sync + 'static>() {}

    #[test]
    fn error_is_send_sync() {
        assert_good_error::<super::ConfigError>();
    }
}

An application uses the library. It does not define new error types. It adds context with anyhow.

use anyhow::{Context, Result};
use apilib::{Config, ConfigError};

fn load(text: &str) -> Result<u16> {
    let cfg = Config::parse(text).context("could not read the settings")?;
    let port = cfg.port().context("settings have no usable port")?;
    Ok(port)
}

fn main() {
    for text in ["port=8080", "port=http", "name=demo", "oops"] {
        match load(text) {
            Ok(p) => println!("ok: port {p}"),
            Err(e) => println!("error: {e:#}"), // {:#} prints the whole chain
        }
    }
    // A library error is an enum, so callers can match on it.
    // #[non_exhaustive] forces a `_` arm in other crates.
    match Config::parse("name=demo").map(|c| c.port()) {
        Ok(Err(ConfigError::Missing(k))) => println!("no {k}, using 3000"),
        Ok(Err(other)) => println!("other: {other}"),
        Ok(Ok(p)) => println!("port {p}"),
        Err(e) => println!("bad file: {e}"),
    }
}
ok: port 8080
error: settings have no usable port: key `port` is not a valid number: invalid digit found in string
error: settings have no usable port: missing key `port`
error: could not read the settings: line 1: expected `key=value`
no port, using 3000

Look at the second line of output. Each layer adds one piece: the context, the library message, and the cause from the standard library. No layer repeats another.

Library errors and application errors
LibraryApplication
Who reads the error?Other code, which may handle itA person, in a log or a terminal
TypeYour own enum, often with thiserroranyhow::Result or Box<dyn Error>
Main toolVariants the caller can match.context("what we were doing")
Future proofing#[non_exhaustive]Not needed

A well-behaved library error (C-GOOD-ERR) follows these rules:

  • It implements std::error::Error, Display and Debug.
  • It is Send + Sync + 'static. Then it works across threads and inside anyhow. The small test above checks this at compile time.
  • Its Display message is short, in lower case, with no full stop at the end.
  • It gives the cause through source(). It does not also copy the cause into its own message. Otherwise a chain printer shows the cause twice.
  • It is never (). A unit error has no message and no Error impl.

Python libraries define one base exception class. Callers can catch all errors of the library with it, or catch one subclass. raise ... from err keeps the cause, like #[source].

class ConfigError(Exception):
    """Base class: callers can catch every error of this library."""


class SyntaxProblem(ConfigError):
    def __init__(self, line: int) -> None:
        super().__init__(f"line {line}: expected `key=value`")
        self.line = line


class MissingKey(ConfigError):
    def __init__(self, key: str) -> None:
        super().__init__(f"missing key `{key}`")
        self.key = key

The functions raise these errors, and the caller catches them:

def parse(text: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    values = {}
    for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), start=1):
        if not line.strip():
            continue
        if "=" not in line:
            raise SyntaxProblem(i)
        k, v = line.split("=", 1)
        values[k.strip()] = v.strip()
    return values


def port(values: dict[str, str]) -> int:
    if "port" not in values:
        raise MissingKey("port")
    try:
        return int(values["port"])
    except ValueError as err:
        # "from err" keeps the cause, like #[source] in Rust
        raise ConfigError("key `port` is not a valid number") from err


for text in ["port=8080", "port=http", "name=demo", "oops"]:
    try:
        print("ok: port", port(parse(text)))
    except MissingKey as e:
        print("no", e.key, "-> using 3000")
    except ConfigError as e:
        print("error:", e, "| cause:", repr(e.__cause__))
ok: port 8080
error: key `port` is not a valid number | cause: ValueError("invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'http'")
no port -> using 3000
error: line 1: expected `key=value` | cause: None

Returning Box<dyn Error> or String errors from a public library function. The caller cannot match on a missing key and choose a default. Keep anyhow for applications. The chapter Error handling covers thiserror and anyhow from the start.

Semver: what breaks your users

Your crate is at version 1.4.2. A user's Cargo.toml says apilib = "1.4". Cargo reads this as "1.4.0 or newer, but below 2.0.0". So every 1.x release must keep the user's code compiling.

Semver has three numbers: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. A breaking change needs a new major version. New features need a new minor version. Bug fixes need a new patch version. Before 1.0, the rules shift one place left. In 0.y.z, a change of y counts as major. In 0.0.z, every release counts as major.

Some changes and their size (from the Cargo SemVer guide)
ChangeSizeWhy
Rename, move or remove a public itemMajorUser code names it
Add a public itemMinorOld code does not know it
Add a variant to a normal enumMajorUser match blocks are no longer complete
Add a variant to a #[non_exhaustive] enumMinorUsers already have a _ arm
Add a public field to a struct with only public fieldsMajorStruct literals in user code break
Add a private field when a private field existsMinorUsers could never build it with a literal
Add a trait method without a default bodyMajorUser impls are now incomplete
Add or remove a function parameterMajorEvery call breaks
Tighten a generic bound, like adding T: CopyMajorSome types no longer fit
Loosen a generic boundMinorOld types still fit
Raise the minimum Rust versionPossibly breakingProjects disagree

Three tools keep your future changes small:

  • #[non_exhaustive] on enums and structs. In other crates, it forces a _ arm and forbids struct literals. In your own crate it changes nothing. Here is what a user crate sees when it lists every variant of ConfigError:
error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `&_` not covered
   = note: `ConfigError` is marked as non-exhaustive, so a wildcard `_` is necessary to match exhaustively
  • Private fields. Users build the value with new or a builder. You may add fields later.
  • Sealed traits. A sealed trait lets users call its methods but not implement it. Then you may add methods later.
mod shapes {
    mod private {
        pub trait Sealed {} // public trait in a private module
    }

    /// Users can call `area`, but only this module can add new shapes.
    pub trait Shape: private::Sealed {
        fn area(&self) -> f64;
    }

    pub struct Square(pub f64);
    impl private::Sealed for Square {}
    impl Shape for Square {
        fn area(&self) -> f64 {
            self.0 * self.0
        }
    }
}

use shapes::Shape;

fn main() {
    println!("{}", shapes::Square(3.0).area());
}
9

Outside code cannot name private::Sealed, so it cannot satisfy the supertrait. An impl Shape for Circle outside the module fails with error[E0277]: the trait bound `Circle: Sealed` is not satisfied.

Add the new API

Add parse_port next to the old get_port. Adding is a minor change: release 1.5.0.

Mark the old one

#[deprecated(since = "1.5.0", note = "use `parse_port` instead")]

Users now see a warning with the way out. Their code still builds.

Write release notes

Say what changed, why, and what to do. Guideline C-RELNOTES asks for this.

Check before you publish

Run cargo semver-checks. It compares your API with the last release on crates.io and reports breaking changes.

Remove it in the next major

Collect several removals. Then release 2.0.0 once, not five majors in a year.

Here is the warning a user sees for a deprecated function:

warning: use of deprecated function `get_port`: use `parse_port` instead
  --> deprecated.rs:11:22
   = note: `#[warn(deprecated)]` on by default

cargo-semver-checks is a separate tool. You install it with cargo install cargo-semver-checks. The Rust project has a 2026 goal to move it into Cargo itself. At the time of writing, this has not happened yet. Check the project goals page: this can change.

Python has no compiler to break, but users still break. Python package versions follow PEP 440. Many projects use semver ideas, but pip does not enforce them. Mark the public names of a module in __all__. Since Python 3.13, the decorator warnings.deprecated marks old functions. Type checkers flag the calls. At run time, Python emits a DeprecationWarning, and test runners like pytest show it.

Thinking that adding things is always safe. Adding a method with a default body to a public trait can still break users. Their own trait may have a method with the same name, and calls become unclear. The Cargo guide calls this "possibly breaking".

Documentation that runs

Here is the port method of the settings library. The comment has a summary line, an Errors section and an example.

//! Read small `key=value` settings files.
//!
//! ```
//! let cfg = apilib::Config::parse("port=8080\nname=demo")?;
//! assert_eq!(cfg.port()?, 8080);
//! # Ok::<(), apilib::ConfigError>(())
//! ```

impl Config {
    /// Returns the `port` value as a number.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    ///
    /// [`ConfigError::Missing`] if there is no `port` key, and
    /// [`ConfigError::BadNumber`] if it is not a number from 0 to 65535.
    ///
    /// ```
    /// let cfg = apilib::Config::parse("port=99999")?;
    /// assert!(cfg.port().is_err());
    /// # Ok::<(), apilib::ConfigError>(())
    /// ```
    pub fn port(&self) -> Result<u16, ConfigError> {
        let raw = self.get("port").ok_or_else(|| ConfigError::Missing("port".into()))?;
        raw.parse().map_err(|source| ConfigError::BadNumber { key: "port".into(), source })
    }
}
cargo test --doc
   Doc-tests apilib

running 2 tests
test src/lib.rs - (line 3) ... ok
test src/lib.rs - Config::port (line 67) ... ok

test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.01s

Every code block in a doc comment is a doc test. cargo test compiles and runs it. So your examples cannot quietly go out of date.

  • //! documents the crate or module. /// documents the next item.
  • The first line is a one-line summary. Search results and module lists show it.
  • Use the usual headings: # Examples, # Errors, # Panics, and # Safety for unsafe functions (C-FAILURE).
  • Examples use ?, not unwrap() (C-QUESTION-MARK). A line that starts with # runs but is hidden on the page. The hidden line Ok::<(), E>(()) lets ? work.
  • [`ConfigError::Missing`] is an intra-doc link. Rustdoc turns it into a real link and warns if the target is gone.
  • Add #![warn(missing_docs)] at the top of lib.rs. Then every public item without docs gives a warning.

Python has the same idea. A docstring can hold examples, and the doctest module runs them.

"""Read small ``key=value`` settings files."""

import warnings

__all__ = ["parse_port"]  # the public names of this module


def parse_port(text: str) -> int:
    """Return the port from a ``port=N`` line.

    Raises ValueError if the number is not valid.

    >>> parse_port("port=8080")
    8080
    >>> parse_port("port=x")
    Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
    ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'x'
    """
    return int(text.split("=", 1)[1])


@warnings.deprecated("use parse_port() instead")
def get_port(text: str) -> int:
    return parse_port(text)
python3.14 -m doctest -v settings.py
1 item passed all tests:
   2 tests in settings.parse_port
2 tests in 3 items.
2 passed.
Test passed.

"How do you design a library API?" A strong answer has five parts. Small public surface with private fields. Flexible input and lazy iterator output. Custom types instead of bool. A matchable error enum that is Send + Sync. Tested examples and a semver check before each release.

Examples that call unwrap() everywhere. Readers copy examples into real code. Show the ? style, and hide the setup lines with #.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for API design
PatternPurposeModelNote
as_x / to_x / into_xTell the cost of a conversionfn as_str(&self) -> &stras_ must be free.
Getter without get_Read a fieldfn len(&self) -> usizePython: a @property.
P: AsRef<Path>Accept any path-like valuefn open<P: AsRef<Path>>(p: P)Put the real work in a non-generic inner function.
impl Into<String>Store text without forcing a copyUser::new("Ann")Do not take &str and clone inside.
impl IntoIterator<Item = T>Accept many items of any collectiontotal([4, 5])Python: Iterable[T].
-> impl Iterator<Item = T>Return a lazy sequencefn in_stock(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = &str>Different branches: box it.
BuilderMany optional settingsRequestBuilder::new(url).method("POST").build()Required values go in new.
TypestateMake a missing step a compile errorimpl ClientBuilder<HasUrl> { fn build(self) }Each state is a type.
Enum instead of boolClear call sitessave(p, Overwrite::Deny)Python: Enum plus keyword-only.
Newtype idStop mixed-up argumentsstruct UserId(u64);Python NewType checks nothing at run time.
Library error enumLet callers handle each case#[derive(thiserror::Error)] #[non_exhaustive] enum ConfigErrorLower-case message, cause via source().
.context("...")Explain errors in an applicationcfg.port().context("no usable port")?Print with {:#}.
Sealed traitAdd trait methods later safelypub trait Shape: private::SealedUsers can call but not implement.
#[deprecated(since, note)]Retire an item gently#[deprecated(note = "use parse_port")]Remove it only in the next major.
Doc test with hidden linesExamples that stay correct# Ok::<(), E>(())Use ?, not unwrap().

Practice

A method returns the inner &[u8] of a type, with no copy. What should it be called?

  • get_bytes
  • to_bytes
  • as_bytes

Free and borrowed to borrowed means as_. to_ promises work, and get_ is not used for getters.

Which parameter type accepts the most callers for a function that only reads names?

  • names: &Vec<String>
  • names: &[String]
  • names: Vec<String>

A slice accepts vectors, arrays and parts of them. &Vec accepts only vectors, and Vec takes ownership it does not need.

You add a new variant to a public enum without #[non_exhaustive]. Your crate is at 1.3.0. What is the next version?

  • 1.3.1
  • 1.4.0
  • 2.0.0

User match blocks without a _ arm stop compiling. That is a breaking change, so the major number goes up.

Your crate is at 0.7.3. You remove a public function. What is the next version?

  • 0.7.4
  • 0.8.0
  • 1.0.0

Before 1.0, the middle number acts as the major number. Cargo treats 0.7 and 0.8 as incompatible.

In a doc example, a line that starts with the sign ? runs, but the page hides it.

One attribute warns when a caller ignores a returned value. Its name is ?.

  1. Rewrite this signature so the call is clear: fn resize(img: &Image, w: u32, h: u32, keep: bool, fast: bool).
    Answer

    Group width and height into a type, and replace each bool with an enum: fn resize(img: &Image, size: Size, ratio: Ratio, quality: Quality). A call reads resize(&img, Size { w: 800, h: 600 }, Ratio::Keep, Quality::Fast). If more options come, a builder is the next step.

  2. Write fn longest(words: impl IntoIterator<Item = ...>) -> usize that works for a Vec<&str> and for a Vec<String>.
    Answer 
    fn longest<S: AsRef<str>>(words: impl IntoIterator<Item = S>) -> usize {
    words.into_iter().map(|w| w.as_ref().len()).max().unwrap_or(0)
}
// longest(vec!["a", "abc"]) == 3
// longest(vec![String::from("hello")]) == 5

    The item type is a generic S with the bound AsRef<str>. Both &str and String meet it.

  3. A library function returns Result<User, String>. List two problems and the fix.
    Answer

    Callers cannot match on the kind of error. They would have to compare text, which breaks when you reword a message. Also, String does not implement std::error::Error, so there is no source() chain. Fix: an error enum with thiserror, for example enum LoadError { NotFound(UserId), Db(#[source] DbError) }, marked #[non_exhaustive].

  4. Why does the guideline prefer a non-consuming builder? When must you use a consuming one?
    Answer

    With &mut self setters, you can configure step by step with if blocks, and you can build many values from one builder. Use a consuming builder when build must move something out of the builder, for example an owned writer or a closure. Typestate builders are always consuming, because each step changes the type.

  5. Expert. Your crate exports pub struct Point { pub x: f64, pub y: f64 }. You want to add a z field in a minor release next year. What can you do today?
    Answer

    Adding a public field to a struct with only public fields is major, because user struct literals break. Today, mark it #[non_exhaustive] or make the fields private and add Point::new(x, y) with getters. Both changes are breaking themselves, so do them now, before 1.0 or in your next major. After that, a new field is a minor change.

  6. Expert. A generic public function fn load<P: AsRef<Path>>(p: P) -> Result<Data> has 200 lines. Users call it with &str, String and PathBuf. What happens to the binary, and how do you fix it?
    Answer

    Monomorphisation makes three copies of the 200 lines, one per type. Move the body into a private fn inner(p: &Path) -> Result<Data> and call inner(p.as_ref()). Now only the one-line wrapper is copied. The API stays the same, so it is not a breaking change.

Key takeaways

  • Every public item is a promise. Start private, use private fields, and open up only what users need.
  • Names tell cost and ownership: as_ is free, to_ does work, into_ consumes. Getters have no get_.
  • Take the weakest input (&str, &[T], AsRef, IntoIterator) and return lazy iterators.
  • Builders handle many options. Typestate turns a forgotten step into a compile error.
  • Libraries return matchable, #[non_exhaustive], Send + Sync error enums. Applications add context with anyhow.
  • Know which changes are major. Deprecate first, check with cargo semver-checks, and keep examples tested with doc tests.

Sources

  • Rust API Guidelines: checklist. All guideline ids, from C-CASE to C-PERMISSIVE.
  • Rust API Guidelines: naming. Casing, as_ to_ into_, getters and iterator names.
  • The Cargo Book: SemVer compatibility. Which changes are major, minor or possibly breaking.
  • The rustdoc book: how to write documentation. Crate docs, summary lines and examples.
  • Rust project goals 2026: cargo-semver-checks. The plan to merge the tool into Cargo.
  • Python documentation: warnings. The deprecated decorator, new in 3.13.

Web services with axum

Most backend work is a web service: a program that answers HTTP requests with JSON. In this chapter you build a small to-do API with axum and tokio, step by step. Then you build the same API in Python with FastAPI, and you test both without starting a server.

  • Read an HTTP request and response, and choose the right method and status code.
  • Build a JSON API with axum routes, extractors, shared state and serde.
  • Turn errors and bad input into clear JSON responses.
  • Add tower middleware for logging, timeouts and an API key, and shut down gracefully.
  • Test the router in-process, and write the same service in FastAPI.

HTTP in one page

A client sends a request. The server sends back a response. Both are plain text at the start, and both have the same three parts.

POST /todos HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Content-Type: application/json
x-api-key: dev-key
Content-Length: 20

{"title":"Buy milk"}
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
content-type: application/json
content-length: 40

{"id":1,"title":"Buy milk","done":false}
  1. The first line. A request has a method, a path and the version. A response has a status code and a short reason.
  2. The headers. Each header is a name and a value. Content-Type says the body is JSON.
  3. An empty line, then the body. The body may be empty, as in most GET requests.
The main methods (RFC 9110)
MethodUseSafeIdempotent
GETRead somethingyesyes
POSTCreate, or run an actionnono
PUTReplace something completelynoyes
PATCHChange part of somethingnonot promised
DELETERemove somethingnoyes

A safe method only reads. An idempotent method can be retried with no extra effect. Deleting item 7 twice still leaves item 7 deleted. Creating with POST twice makes two items. So clients and proxies may retry a timed-out GET, but not a POST.

Status codes come in five classes: 1xx information, 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error. This chapter uses 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found, 408 Request Timeout, 415 Unsupported Media Type and 422. RFC 9110 calls 422 "Unprocessable Content". Older names, like "Unprocessable Entity" in the Rust http crate, mean the same code.

Returning 200 OK with {"error": "not found"} in the body. Clients, proxies and monitoring tools read the status code first. A missing item is a 404. A server bug is a 500.

A first axum service

Start with the smallest service: one route that answers "ok". Here is the Cargo.toml of the project. The versions were the newest on crates.io on 2026-11-15.

[package]
name = "todo-api"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
axum = { version = "0.8.9", features = ["macros"] }
tokio = { version = "1.54", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread", "net", "signal"] }
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1"
tower-http = { version = "0.7", features = ["trace", "timeout"] }
tracing = "0.1"
tracing-subscriber = { version = "0.3", features = ["env-filter"] }

[dev-dependencies]
tower = { version = "0.5", features = ["util"] }  # for oneshot() in tests
http-body-util = "0.1"                              # to read bodies in tests
use axum::{Router, routing::get};

async fn health() -> &'static str {
    "ok"
}

#[tokio::main] // starts the tokio runtime, then runs main
async fn main() {
    let app = Router::new().route("/health", get(health));
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:3000").await.unwrap();
    axum::serve(listener, app).await.unwrap();
}
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/health")
def health() -> str:
    return "ok"

# To run it, you start a server (not done in this book):
#   uv run --with "fastapi[standard]" fastapi dev app.py

axum sits on three layers. tokio is the async runtime. It runs many requests at the same time on a few threads. hyper speaks the HTTP protocol. tower gives the Service trait: "take a request, return a future of a response". axum adds routing and nice handler functions on top.

A handler is an async fn. Its return type must implement IntoResponse. A &str becomes a 200 text response. A Json<T> becomes a JSON response. A tuple like (StatusCode, Json<T>) sets the status too.

FastAPI plays the same role in Python. It sits on Starlette (the web toolkit) and Pydantic (data checks). A server program like Uvicorn runs it. The book tests the services in-process, so neither server is started in this chapter.

axum 0.8.9 is from April 2026, and it needs Rust 1.80 or newer. tower-http 0.7.1 is from August 2026. FastAPI here is 0.163.0, which needs Python 3.11 or newer. Check crates.io and PyPI before you start: these numbers change.

Calling std::thread::sleep or slow blocking code inside a handler. It blocks a runtime thread, and other requests wait. Use tokio::time::sleep, async libraries, or tokio::task::spawn_blocking for heavy work. See Async and await.

Routing and extractors

Here is the router of the to-do API. Each line joins a path and a method to a handler.

pub fn app(state: AppState) -> Router {
    // Writes need the key. route_layer runs only when a route matched.
    let writes = Router::new()
        .route("/todos", axum::routing::post(create_todo))
        .route("/todos/{id}", axum::routing::delete(delete_todo))
        .route_layer(middleware::from_fn_with_state(state.clone(), require_key));

    Router::new()
        .route("/health", get(health))
        .route("/todos", get(list_todos))
        .route("/todos/{id}", get(get_todo))
        .merge(writes)
        .layer(TimeoutLayer::with_status_code(StatusCode::REQUEST_TIMEOUT, Duration::from_secs(10)))
        .layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http())
        .with_state(state)
}

{id} is a capture. It matches one path segment, like /todos/7. {*rest} would match all the remaining segments. merge joins two routers into one.

A handler gets its input from extractors. You just list them as arguments, and axum fills them in.

Common extractors
ExtractorReadsExampleFastAPI twin
Path<T>Captures in the pathPath(id): Path<u64>todo_id: int in the path
Query<T>The query string ?done=trueQuery(p): Query<ListParams>Other plain arguments
Json<T>A JSON bodyJson(new): Json<NewTodo>An argument with a Pydantic model type
State<S>Shared app stateState(state): State<AppState>Depends(...)
HeaderMapAll headersheaders: HeaderMapHeader()

The body is a stream. It can be read only once. So axum has one rule: the extractor that reads the body must be the last argument. Extractors that read the body implement FromRequest. All others implement FromRequestParts. If you break the rule, the handler does not compile.

Copying a route like "/todos/:id" from an old tutorial. axum 0.8 changed the syntax to {id}. The old form compiles, but the program panics when it builds the router:

Path segments must not start with `:`. For capture groups, use `{capture}`. If you meant to literally match a segment starting with a colon, call `without_v07_checks` on the router.

Shared state

All handlers need the same list of to-dos. The state holds it. axum clones the state for each request, so the clone must be cheap.

#[derive(Default)]
struct Store {
    next_id: u64,
    todos: BTreeMap<u64, Todo>,
}

#[derive(Clone)] // cloned for every request: keep it cheap with Arc
pub struct AppState {
    store: Arc<Mutex<Store>>,
    api_key: Arc<str>,
}

impl AppState {
    pub fn new(api_key: &str) -> Self {
        AppState { store: Arc::default(), api_key: api_key.into() }
    }
}
class Store:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.next_id = 0
        self.todos: dict[int, Todo] = {}


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    app.state.store = Store()  # startup
    yield
    log.info("shutting down")  # shutdown


app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
API_KEY = "dev-key"


def store(request: Request) -> Store:
    return request.app.state.store  # used with Depends(store)

The rule: put the shared data behind Arc. Cloning an Arc only adds one to a counter. Data that changes also needs a lock, here a Mutex. Pass the state once with .with_state(state), and read it with the State extractor. A real service keeps a database pool here instead. The chapter Data, serde and databases does that.

In FastAPI, the lifespan function creates the state at startup. A dependency, Depends(store), hands it to each handler.

Holding a std::sync::Mutex guard across an .await. Other tasks can then wait on the lock forever, and the future is no longer Send. Lock, copy what you need, and drop the guard before any .await. The tokio tutorial says a plain std Mutex is fine when no .await happens while it is locked. Use tokio::sync::Mutex only when you must hold it across an .await.

JSON, serde and validation

The API reads a new to-do from JSON and writes to-dos back as JSON. serde does both with two derives.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize)]
pub struct Todo {
    id: u64,
    title: String,
    done: bool,
}

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] // reject {"titel": ...} instead of ignoring it
pub struct NewTodo {
    title: String,
    #[serde(default)] // missing "done" means false
    done: bool,
}

impl NewTodo {
    // Validation: check the meaning after serde checked the shape.
    fn validate(&self) -> Result<(), AppError> {
        let t = self.title.trim();
        if t.is_empty() || t.chars().count() > 100 {
            return Err(AppError::Invalid("title must have 1 to 100 characters".into()));
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
pub struct ListParams {
    done: Option<bool>,
    #[serde(default = "default_limit")]
    limit: usize,
}
fn default_limit() -> usize {
    20
}
class NewTodo(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")  # like deny_unknown_fields
    title: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=100)
    done: bool = False

    @field_validator("title")
    @classmethod
    def strip_title(cls, v: str) -> str:
        v = v.strip()
        if not v:
            raise ValueError("title must not be blank")
        return v


class Todo(BaseModel):
    id: int
    title: str
    done: bool

There are two kinds of checks. Shape: is it JSON, is title a string? serde does this while it reads. Meaning: is the title between 1 and 100 characters? That is validation, and your code does it. Here a small validate method is enough. For many rules, crates like validator and garde add derive macros. Pydantic does both kinds in one model with Field limits and validators.

What does axum send back when the shape is wrong? These results come from the tests of this chapter.

How the Json extractor rejects bad bodies (tested)
Request bodyStatusWhy
{not json400 Bad RequestNot valid JSON
Valid JSON, no Content-Type415 Unsupported Media TypeThe header is missing
{"title": 5}422JSON is fine, but the type is wrong
{"titel": "typo"}422Unknown field, because of deny_unknown_fields

By default, axum sends these errors as plain text. The API should answer in JSON every time. So it uses its own extractor. It works like Json, but turns the rejection into the app's error type.

// Same as axum::Json, but a rejection becomes an AppError.
// The derive needs the "macros" feature of axum.
#[derive(FromRequest)]
#[from_request(via(axum::Json), rejection(AppError))]
pub struct AppJson<T>(T);

impl From<JsonRejection> for AppError {
    fn from(r: JsonRejection) -> Self {
        AppError::BadJson(r)
    }
}

Forgetting deny_unknown_fields or extra="forbid". By default, serde and Pydantic ignore unknown keys. A client sends "titel", the real field gets its default, and nobody notices the typo. With a required field you get an error anyway. With an optional field, the typo is silent.

Errors as responses

Handlers return Result<T, AppError>. The ? operator works as usual. One IntoResponse impl turns every error into JSON with the right status.

#[derive(Debug)]
pub enum AppError {
    NotFound(u64),
    Invalid(String),
    BadJson(JsonRejection),
    Unauthorized,
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ErrorBody {
    error: &'static str,
    message: String,
}

impl IntoResponse for AppError {
    fn into_response(self) -> Response {
        let (status, error, message) = match self {
            AppError::NotFound(id) => (StatusCode::NOT_FOUND, "not_found", format!("no todo {id}")),
            AppError::Invalid(m) => (StatusCode::UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY, "invalid", m),
            // keep axum's status code (400, 415 or 422) and its text
            AppError::BadJson(r) => (r.status(), "bad_json", r.body_text()),
            AppError::Unauthorized => {
                (StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED, "unauthorized", "missing or wrong x-api-key".into())
            }
        };
        (status, Json(ErrorBody { error, message })).into_response()
    }
}

Now the handlers stay short. Each one returns either data or an AppError.

#[tracing::instrument(skip(state))]
async fn list_todos(State(state): State<AppState>, Query(p): Query<ListParams>) -> Json<Vec<Todo>> {
    let store = state.store.lock().unwrap();
    let items = store.todos.values()
        .filter(|t| p.done.is_none_or(|d| t.done == d))
        .take(p.limit)
        .cloned()
        .collect();
    Json(items)
}

async fn create_todo(
    State(state): State<AppState>,
    AppJson(new): AppJson<NewTodo>, // the body extractor must come last
) -> Result<(StatusCode, Json<Todo>), AppError> {
    new.validate()?;
    let mut store = state.store.lock().unwrap();
    store.next_id += 1;
    let todo = Todo { id: store.next_id, title: new.title.trim().to_string(), done: new.done };
    store.todos.insert(todo.id, todo.clone());
    tracing::info!(id = todo.id, "todo created");
    Ok((StatusCode::CREATED, Json(todo)))
}

async fn get_todo(State(state): State<AppState>, Path(id): Path<u64>) -> Result<Json<Todo>, AppError> {
    let store = state.store.lock().unwrap();
    store.todos.get(&id).cloned().map(Json).ok_or(AppError::NotFound(id))
}

async fn delete_todo(State(state): State<AppState>, Path(id): Path<u64>) -> Result<StatusCode, AppError> {
    let mut store = state.store.lock().unwrap();
    match store.todos.remove(&id) {
        Some(_) => Ok(StatusCode::NO_CONTENT),
        None => Err(AppError::NotFound(id)),
    }
}
@app.get("/todos")
def list_todos(
    s: Annotated[Store, Depends(store)], done: bool | None = None, limit: int = 20
) -> list[Todo]:
    items = [t for t in s.todos.values() if done is None or t.done == done]
    return items[:limit]


@app.post("/todos", status_code=201, dependencies=[Depends(require_key)])
def create_todo(new: NewTodo, s: Annotated[Store, Depends(store)]) -> Todo:
    s.next_id += 1
    todo = Todo(id=s.next_id, title=new.title, done=new.done)
    s.todos[todo.id] = todo
    log.info("todo created id=%d", todo.id)
    return todo


@app.get("/todos/{todo_id}")
def get_todo(todo_id: int, s: Annotated[Store, Depends(store)]) -> Todo:
    if todo_id not in s.todos:
        raise HTTPException(404, f"no todo {todo_id}")
    return s.todos[todo_id]


@app.delete("/todos/{todo_id}", status_code=204, dependencies=[Depends(require_key)])
def delete_todo(todo_id: int, s: Annotated[Store, Depends(store)]) -> None:
    if s.todos.pop(todo_id, None) is None:
        raise HTTPException(404, f"no todo {todo_id}")

FastAPI raises HTTPException for errors. An exception handler can give it the same JSON shape as the Rust API:

@app.exception_handler(HTTPException)
async def http_error(request: Request, exc: HTTPException) -> JSONResponse:
    return JSONResponse({"error": exc.status_code, "message": exc.detail}, exc.status_code)

FastAPI's own validation errors stay in its standard 422 format, with a detail list. That list names each problem, for example missing and extra_forbidden.

Sending internal error text to the client, like a database error with table names. Log the details on the server. Send the client a short, safe message and a 500 status.

Middleware with tower

Some work is the same for many routes: logging, timeouts, checking a key. Middleware does this work in one place. In axum, middleware is a tower layer.

async fn require_key(
    State(state): State<AppState>,
    req: Request,
    next: Next,
) -> Result<Response, AppError> {
    let sent = req.headers().get("x-api-key").and_then(|v| v.to_str().ok());
    if sent != Some(&*state.api_key) {
        return Err(AppError::Unauthorized); // the handler never runs
    }
    let mut res = next.run(req).await; // run the inner layers and the handler
    res.headers_mut().insert("x-checked", HeaderValue::from_static("yes"));
    Ok(res)
}
def require_key(x_api_key: Annotated[str | None, Header()] = None) -> None:
    # Header() reads the "x-api-key" header (underscores become dashes)
    if x_api_key != API_KEY:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED, "missing or wrong x-api-key")

# used on a route: @app.post("/todos", dependencies=[Depends(require_key)])

The router adds three layers. Read the request path through them:

  • TraceLayer from tower-http logs each request and response with its status and time.
  • TimeoutLayer answers 408 when a handler takes longer than 10 seconds. In tower-http 0.6.7 and newer, use TimeoutLayer::with_status_code. The older TimeoutLayer::new is deprecated.
  • route_layer runs only when a route matched. So an unknown path still gets a 404, not a 401.

Order matters. Each .layer(...) call wraps everything added before it. So the last .layer runs first on the request. Here TraceLayer is last, so it sees every request, even one that times out. With tower::ServiceBuilder, the order is the other way: top to bottom. The axum docs suggest ServiceBuilder because it reads more easily.

axum gives several ways to write middleware. from_fn is the easiest and uses plain async code. A full tower Service and Layer is more work, but other tower projects can reuse it.

Putting the key check with .layer on the whole app. Then /health needs a key too, and the load balancer's health check fails. Group the protected routes in their own router, and use route_layer there.

Tracing and graceful shutdown

The tests can turn on the log output. A test sent one POST, and this is what tracing printed:

DEBUG request{method=POST uri=/todos version=HTTP/1.1}: tower_http::trace::on_request: started processing request
 INFO request{method=POST uri=/todos version=HTTP/1.1}: todo_api: todo created id=1
DEBUG request{method=POST uri=/todos version=HTTP/1.1}: tower_http::trace::on_response: finished processing request latency=0 ms status=201

tracing writes structured logs. The part request{method=POST ...} is a span from TraceLayer. Every log line inside the request carries it. Your own line tracing::info!(id = todo.id, "todo created") adds a field id=1. #[tracing::instrument] on a handler opens a span with the handler's arguments.

The main function sets up the logger, binds the port and serves until a stop signal comes.

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    tracing_subscriber::fmt()
        .with_env_filter(
            tracing_subscriber::EnvFilter::try_from_default_env()
                .unwrap_or_else(|_| "info,tower_http=debug".into()),
        )
        .init();
    let key = std::env::var("API_KEY").unwrap_or_else(|_| "dev-key".into());
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:3000").await.unwrap();
    tracing::info!("listening on {}", listener.local_addr().unwrap());
    axum::serve(listener, app(AppState::new(&key)))
        .with_graceful_shutdown(shutdown_signal())
        .await
        .unwrap();
}

async fn shutdown_signal() {
    let ctrl_c = async {
        tokio::signal::ctrl_c().await.expect("install Ctrl+C handler");
    };
    #[cfg(unix)]
    let terminate = async {
        tokio::signal::unix::signal(tokio::signal::unix::SignalKind::terminate())
            .expect("install SIGTERM handler")
            .recv()
            .await;
    };
    #[cfg(not(unix))]
    let terminate = std::future::pending::<()>();
    tokio::select! {
        _ = ctrl_c => {},
        _ = terminate => {},
    }
    tracing::info!("shutting down: finishing open requests");
}

Graceful shutdown matters in containers. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM before it stops a pod. The service then stops accepting new connections and finishes the open requests. The environment variable RUST_LOG can change the log level without a new build, for example RUST_LOG=debug.

This main function was compiled with cargo check and cargo clippy. It was not run here, because the book does not start servers. In FastAPI, the lifespan function's code after yield runs at shutdown. Uvicorn handles the signals.

Using println! for logs. It has no levels, no fields and no request span. You cannot filter it in production. Use tracing in Rust and the logging module in Python.

Testing without a server

A Router is a tower Service. So a test can call it directly with one request. No port and no network are needed.

use super::*;
use axum::body::Body;
use axum::http::Request;
use http_body_util::BodyExt; // for .collect()
use serde_json::{Value, json};
use tower::ServiceExt; // for .oneshot()

const KEY: &str = "test-key";

// Send one request to the router. No socket, no port.
async fn send(app: &Router, method: &str, uri: &str, body: Option<Value>) -> (StatusCode, Value) {
    let mut req = Request::builder().method(method).uri(uri).header("x-api-key", KEY);
    let body = match body {
        Some(v) => {
            req = req.header("content-type", "application/json");
            Body::from(v.to_string())
        }
        None => Body::empty(),
    };
    let res = app.clone().oneshot(req.body(body).unwrap()).await.unwrap();
    let status = res.status();
    let bytes = res.into_body().collect().await.unwrap().to_bytes();
    (status, serde_json::from_slice(&bytes).unwrap_or(Value::Null))
}

#[tokio::test]
async fn create_then_get() {
    let app = app(AppState::new(KEY));
    let (s, body) = send(&app, "POST", "/todos", Some(json!({"title": " Buy milk "}))).await;
    assert_eq!(s, StatusCode::CREATED);
    assert_eq!(body, json!({"id": 1, "title": "Buy milk", "done": false}));
    let (s, body) = send(&app, "GET", "/todos/1", None).await;
    assert_eq!((s, body["title"].as_str()), (StatusCode::OK, Some("Buy milk")));
}

#[tokio::test]
async fn writes_need_the_key() {
    let app = app(AppState::new("other-key"));
    let (s, _) = send(&app, "POST", "/todos", Some(json!({"title": "x"}))).await;
    assert_eq!(s, StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED);
    let (s, _) = send(&app, "GET", "/todos", None).await; // reads stay open
    assert_eq!(s, StatusCode::OK);
}

Two more tests check the error bodies (404, 422) and the query string. The test show_logs turns on the log output that you saw above. The query ?limit=many is not a number, so the Query extractor answers 400.

cargo test
running 5 tests
test tests::writes_need_the_key ... ok
test tests::create_then_get ... ok
test tests::show_logs ... ok
test tests::errors_are_json ... ok
test tests::list_with_query ... ok

test result: ok. 5 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.00s

oneshot sends one request and consumes the service. That is why each call clones the router first. The clone is cheap, because the state inside is an Arc. Each test builds a fresh AppState, so tests do not share data.

FastAPI has TestClient. It also calls the app directly, without a server.

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from app import app

H = {"x-api-key": "dev-key"}


def test_create_then_get():
    with TestClient(app) as client:  # "with" runs the lifespan
        r = client.post("/todos", json={"title": " Buy milk "}, headers=H)
        assert r.status_code == 201
        assert r.json() == {"id": 1, "title": "Buy milk", "done": False}
        assert client.get("/todos/1").json()["title"] == "Buy milk"


def test_errors():
    with TestClient(app) as client:
        r = client.get("/todos/42")
        assert r.status_code == 404 and r.json()["message"] == "no todo 42"
        r = client.post("/todos", json={"titel": "typo"}, headers=H)
        assert r.status_code == 422
        print([e["type"] for e in r.json()["detail"]])
        assert client.post("/todos", json={"title": "x"}).status_code == 401
uv run --with fastapi --with httpx2 --with pytest pytest -v -s test_app.py
test_app.py::test_create_then_get PASSED
test_app.py::test_errors ['missing', 'extra_forbidden']
PASSED
test_app.py::test_list_with_query PASSED

============================== 3 passed in 1.31s ===============================

FastAPI's testing page says to install httpx. The Starlette version used here (1.10.0) prefers httpx2, a fork of httpx 0.28.1 with the same API. With only httpx installed, the tests still pass, but Starlette prints a deprecation warning. Check the Starlette release notes: this is changing right now.

TraceLayer

Opens a span request{method=POST uri=/todos} and logs "started processing request".

TimeoutLayer

Starts a 10-second clock. If the inner work is slower, it answers 408.

Router

Finds the route POST /todos. No match would give 404. A wrong method would give 405.

require_key

Checks x-api-key. A wrong key returns a 401 JSON error, and the handler never runs.

Extractors

State clones the Arc. AppJson reads the body. Bad JSON becomes a 400, 415 or 422 JSON error.

Handler

validate() checks the title. The handler stores the to-do and returns (201, Json(todo)).

Back out

require_key adds a header. TraceLayer logs "finished processing request" with the status and the time.

"How do you test an HTTP service?" A strong answer: test the router in-process with oneshot or a test client. These tests are fast and need no port. Use a fresh state per test. Keep a few end-to-end tests against a real server and database for the last check.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for web services
PatternPurposeModelNote
.route(path, get(h).post(h2))Join a path and methods to handlers.route("/todos/{id}", get(get_todo))axum 0.8 uses {id}, not :id.
Path(x): Path<T>Read a typed path capturePath(id): Path<u64>A non-number gives 400.
Query(p): Query<T>Read the query string into a struct?done=true&limit=1Use Option and serde defaults.
Body extractor lastRead the body onceasync fn h(State(s): State<S>, Json(b): Json<B>)Otherwise it does not compile.
#[derive(Clone)] struct AppState { x: Arc<...> }Share data with all handlers.with_state(state)Cloned per request: keep it cheap.
Result<T, AppError>Use ? in handlersimpl IntoResponse for AppErrorOne place maps errors to status codes.
(StatusCode, Json<T>)Set status and bodyOk((StatusCode::CREATED, Json(todo)))POST that creates: 201.
#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]Catch typos in client JSON{"titel": ...} gives 422Pydantic: extra="forbid".
from_fn_with_state + route_layerCheck something on some routesAPI key on write routesUnknown paths still get 404.
.layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http())Log every request with a spanRUST_LOG=info,tower_http=debugThe last .layer runs first.
with_graceful_shutdown(signal)Finish open requests on stopWait for Ctrl+C or SIGTERMNeeded for rolling deploys.
app.clone().oneshot(req)Test without a serveruse tower::ServiceExt;FastAPI: TestClient(app).

Practice

A client sends a valid JSON body, but forgets the Content-Type header. What does axum's Json extractor answer?

  • 400 Bad Request
  • 415 Unsupported Media Type
  • 422

The body is not checked at all. The missing JSON content type gives 415. Bad JSON syntax gives 400, and a wrong type gives 422.

Which method can a client safely retry after a timeout, without creating a second item?

  • POST
  • PUT
  • Both

PUT is idempotent: it replaces the item, so twice is the same as once. POST may create a new item each time.

The code says .layer(A).layer(B). Which layer sees the request first?

  • A
  • B
  • It depends on the route.

Each .layer wraps everything before it. B is the outer layer, so it runs first on the request and last on the response.

Why does this handler not compile? async fn h(Json(b): Json<B>, State(s): State<S>)

  • State needs Arc.
  • The body extractor Json is not the last argument.
  • Handlers cannot take two arguments.

Only the last argument may implement FromRequest and read the body. Swap the two arguments.

A successful DELETE with no body returns status code ?.

In axum 0.8, the route for one user by id is written "/users/?".

  1. Add a route GET /todos/count that returns {"open": 2, "done": 1}.
    Answer 
    #[derive(Serialize)]
struct Count { open: usize, done: usize }

async fn count(State(state): State<AppState>) -> Json<Count> {
    let store = state.store.lock().unwrap();
    let done = store.todos.values().filter(|t| t.done).count();
    Json(Count { open: store.todos.len() - done, done })
}
// in app(): .route("/todos/count", get(count))

    axum prefers the fixed segment count over the capture {id}, so the two routes do not clash.

  2. Write the FastAPI version of the same route.
    Answer 
    @app.get("/todos/count")
def count(s: Annotated[Store, Depends(store)]) -> dict[str, int]:
    done = sum(1 for t in s.todos.values() if t.done)
    return {"open": len(s.todos) - done, "done": done}

    Careful: FastAPI checks routes in the order you declare them. Declare /todos/count before /todos/{todo_id}. Otherwise "count" goes to get_todo and fails the int check with a 422.

  3. Write a test for DELETE /todos/99 on an empty store. Which status and which error value do you expect?
    Answer 
    #[tokio::test]
async fn delete_missing() {
    let app = app(AppState::new(KEY));
    let (s, body) = send(&app, "DELETE", "/todos/99", None).await;
    assert_eq!(s, StatusCode::NOT_FOUND);
    assert_eq!(body["error"], "not_found");
}

    The key is correct, so require_key passes. The handler finds nothing and returns AppError::NotFound(99).

  4. A handler locks the store, then calls fetch_price().await, then unlocks. What can go wrong? How do you fix it?
    Answer

    The std::sync::MutexGuard lives across the .await. The future is then not Send, and axum refuses the handler at compile time. Even with a tokio mutex, other requests would wait during the slow call. Fix: call fetch_price().await first, then lock, change the data, and drop the lock.

  5. Expert. Your service runs in Kubernetes. During a deploy, some clients get "connection reset". Name two causes on the service side and the fixes.
    Answer

    First, the program ignores SIGTERM or exits at once, so open requests die. Fix: with_graceful_shutdown with a signal handler, as in this chapter. Second, the load balancer still sends new traffic for a short time after SIGTERM. Fix: let a readiness check fail first, or wait a few seconds before you stop accepting connections. Also keep the pod's grace period longer than your slowest request.

  6. Expert. Why is TraceLayer added after TimeoutLayer in the router, and not before?
    Answer

    The last .layer is the outermost one. With TraceLayer outside, it also sees the 408 that the timeout layer makes, and it logs the full time. If it were inside, a timed-out request would end inside the trace span with no response logged.

Key takeaways

  • An HTTP message has a first line, headers and a body. Pick methods by safety and idempotency, and use honest status codes.
  • An axum handler is an async fn with extractors as arguments. The body extractor goes last.
  • Share state with Arc and .with_state. Never hold a std lock across an .await.
  • serde checks the shape of JSON. Your code or Pydantic checks the meaning. One IntoResponse impl gives every error a JSON body.
