  • Middleware is a tower layer. The last .layer runs first. Use route_layer for checks on some routes only.
  • Test the router in-process with oneshot, and FastAPI with TestClient. Add tracing and graceful shutdown before production.

Sources

  • axum 0.8.9 documentation. Routing, extractors, state, middleware ordering and feature flags.
  • Tokio blog: Announcing axum 0.8.0. The new path syntax and the Option extractor change.
  • tower-http releases. Version 0.7 and the deprecation of TimeoutLayer::new.
  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics. Methods, safe and idempotent, and status codes.
  • Tokio tutorial: Shared state. When a std Mutex is fine in async code.
  • FastAPI: Testing. TestClient without a running server.

Command-line tools

Many useful programs have no window at all. They read arguments and text, and they write text and an exit code. In this chapter you build tgrep, a tiny grep, step by step in Rust. Then you build the same tool in Python.

  • Define arguments, flags and help text with clap derive, argparse and Typer.
  • Read files and standard input, and write results to standard output without losing speed.
  • Use exit codes, error messages, config files and logs the way other tools expect.
  • Show progress only when a person is watching.
  • Test a tool end to end, and package it as a small binary or a Python command.

The contract of a command-line tool

Here is the finished tool at work. Look at what goes where.

$ tgrep -i -n rust langs.txt
1:Rust is fast.
3:rust and python work well together.
$ echo $?
0
$ tgrep rust langs.txt missing.txt
tgrep: missing.txt: No such file or directory (os error 2)
langs.txt:rust and python work well together.
$ echo $?
2

Every command-line tool has the same contract with the shell. It has four parts.

  • stdin and stdout carry data. Then tgrep x a.txt | sort works.
  • stderr carries messages. They show on the screen even when stdout goes into a file or a pipe.
  • The exit code lets scripts react, for example with && or if.

Arguments

A Cli struct with clap derive. Help text comes from doc comments.

The search core

A function that reads any BufRead and writes to any Write. Easy to test.

Output

One locked, buffered stdout. Quiet exit on a broken pipe. Color only on a terminal.

Exit codes

0 for a match, 1 for none, 2 for an error, like grep.

Config

Defaults from a TOML file. Flags win over the file.

Logs and progress

--verbose logs to stderr. Progress bars only for people.

Tests

Unit tests for the core. End-to-end tests that run the real binary.

Packaging

A small release binary, cargo install, and a Python wheel.

Printing errors or progress to stdout. Then tool > out.txt puts error text into the data, and the next program in the pipe reads garbage. Results go to stdout. Everything else goes to stderr.

Step 1: arguments with clap derive

You describe the arguments as a struct. clap reads the struct and writes the parser and the help page.

use std::path::PathBuf;

use clap::{ArgAction, Parser, ValueEnum};

/// Print lines that match a pattern.
///
/// Reads standard input when no FILE is given, or when FILE is "-".
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version)] // about and long_about come from the doc comment
pub struct Cli {
    /// The regular expression to look for
    pub pattern: String,
    /// Files to search
    pub files: Vec<PathBuf>,
    /// Ignore upper and lower case
    #[arg(short, long)]
    pub ignore_case: bool,
    /// Treat the pattern as plain text, not a regex
    #[arg(short = 'F', long)]
    pub fixed_strings: bool,
    /// Print lines that do NOT match
    #[arg(short = 'v', long)]
    pub invert_match: bool,
    /// Show line numbers
    #[arg(short = 'n', long)]
    pub line_number: bool,
    /// Only print the number of matching lines
    #[arg(short, long)]
    pub count: bool,
    /// When to color the matches
    #[arg(long, value_enum, value_name = "WHEN")]
    pub color: Option<ColorWhen>,
    /// More log output on stderr (repeat for even more)
    #[arg(long, action = ArgAction::Count)]
    pub verbose: u8,
    /// Config file to read
    #[arg(long, env = "TGREP_CONFIG", value_name = "PATH")]
    pub config: Option<PathBuf>,
}
import argparse
import os
from pathlib import Path


def parse_args(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> argparse.Namespace:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="pygrep", description=__doc__)
    p.add_argument("pattern", help="the regular expression to look for")
    p.add_argument("files", nargs="*", type=Path, help="files to search")
    p.add_argument("-i", "--ignore-case", action="store_true")
    p.add_argument("-F", "--fixed-strings", action="store_true")
    p.add_argument("-v", "--invert-match", action="store_true")
    p.add_argument("-n", "--line-number", action="store_true")
    p.add_argument("-c", "--count", action="store_true")
    p.add_argument("--verbose", action="count", default=0)
    p.add_argument("--config", type=Path, default=os.environ.get("PYGREP_CONFIG"))
    return p.parse_args(argv)  # bad arguments: prints usage, exits with 2

The ColorWhen type is an enum. Each variant becomes one allowed value.

#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, ValueEnum, serde::Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]
pub enum ColorWhen {
    /// Color only when stdout is a terminal
    Auto,
    /// Always color
    Always,
    /// Never color
    Never,
}
$ tgrep -h
Print lines that match a pattern

Usage: tgrep [OPTIONS] <PATTERN> [FILES]...

Arguments:
  <PATTERN>   The regular expression to look for
  [FILES]...  Files to search

Options:
  -i, --ignore-case    Ignore upper and lower case
  -F, --fixed-strings  Treat the pattern as plain text, not a regex
  -v, --invert-match   Print lines that do NOT match
  -n, --line-number    Show line numbers
  -c, --count          Only print the number of matching lines
      --color <WHEN>   When to color the matches [possible values: auto, always, never]
      --verbose...     More log output on stderr (repeat for even more)
      --config <PATH>  Config file to read [env: TGREP_CONFIG=]
  -h, --help           Print help (see more with '--help')
  -V, --version        Print version

The field type decides the kind of argument. This table is the heart of clap derive.

Field types in clap derive (clap 4.6)
Field typeMeaningExample here
T without #[arg]A required positional argumentpattern: String
Vec<T>Zero or more valuesfiles: Vec<PathBuf>
bool with short/longA flag-i
Option<T> with longAn optional option with a value--color never
u8 with ArgAction::CountCounts how often a flag appears--verbose --verbose gives 2
env = "NAME"Falls back to an environment variableTGREP_CONFIG

A typo gets a helpful message and exit code 2. clap even suggests the right name:

$ tgrep --colour never x
error: unexpected argument '--colour' found

  tip: a similar argument exists: '--color'

Usage: tgrep --color <WHEN> <PATTERN> [FILES]...

For more information, try '--help'.

Python's standard argparse does the same job without extra packages. It also exits with code 2 on bad arguments. Python 3.14 added the options color (on by default) and suggest_on_error (off by default). Typer is the third-party twin of clap derive. It reads type hints instead of a struct.

import re
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Annotated

import typer

app = typer.Typer()


@app.command()
def main(
    pattern: Annotated[str, typer.Argument(help="The regular expression to look for")],
    files: Annotated[list[Path], typer.Argument(help="Files to search")],
    ignore_case: Annotated[bool, typer.Option("--ignore-case", "-i")] = False,
    line_number: Annotated[bool, typer.Option("--line-number", "-n")] = False,
) -> None:
    rx = re.compile(pattern, re.IGNORECASE if ignore_case else 0)
    matched = False
    for path in files:
        for i, line in enumerate(path.read_text().splitlines(), start=1):
            if rx.search(line):
                matched = True
                typer.echo(f"{i}:{line}" if line_number else line)
    raise typer.Exit(code=0 if matched else 1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app()

Since version 0.26 (May 2026), Typer ships its own copy of Click. It no longer installs Click as a separate package.

Giving -v two meanings. In grep, -v means "invert". Many tools use -v for "verbose". Users bring habits from the tools they know. For a grep-like tool, keep -v as invert and use a long --verbose.

Step 2: the search core and reading input

The core of the tool knows nothing about files or the terminal. It reads lines from any reader and writes to any writer.

use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

use regex::{Regex, RegexBuilder};

pub struct Options {
    pub invert: bool,
    pub line_number: bool,
    pub count: bool,
    pub color: bool,
}

pub fn build_regex(pattern: &str, fixed: bool, ignore_case: bool) -> Result<Regex, regex::Error> {
    let pat = if fixed { regex::escape(pattern) } else { pattern.to_string() };
    RegexBuilder::new(&pat).case_insensitive(ignore_case).build()
}

Here is the search function itself, next to its Python twin.

/// Reads `input` line by line and writes the selected lines to `out`.
/// Returns the number of selected lines.
pub fn grep<R: BufRead, W: Write>(
    input: R,
    out: &mut W,
    re: &Regex,
    opts: &Options,
    name: Option<&str>, // Some(file name) when we search several files
) -> io::Result<u64> {
    let mut selected = 0;
    for (i, line) in input.lines().enumerate() {
        let line = line?; // fails on bytes that are not UTF-8
        if re.is_match(&line) == opts.invert {
            continue; // not selected
        }
        selected += 1;
        if opts.count {
            continue; // only count, print nothing
        }
        if let Some(n) = name {
            write!(out, "{n}:")?;
        }
        if opts.line_number {
            write!(out, "{}:", i + 1)?;
        }
        if opts.color && !opts.invert {
            writeln!(out, "{}", re.replace_all(&line, "\x1b[1;31m$0\x1b[0m"))?;
        } else {
            writeln!(out, "{line}")?;
        }
    }
    Ok(selected)
}
import re


def grep(lines, out, rx: re.Pattern, args, name: str | None) -> int:
    selected = 0
    for i, line in enumerate(lines, start=1):
        line = line.rstrip("\n")
        if bool(rx.search(line)) == args.invert_match:
            continue
        selected += 1
        if not args.count:
            prefix = (f"{name}:" if name else "") + (f"{i}:" if args.line_number else "")
            print(prefix + line, file=out)
    return selected

The generic bounds are the trick. R: BufRead accepts a file, stdin, or a &[u8] in a test. W: Write accepts stdout, a file, or a Vec<u8>. A BufRead reads big blocks and hands out lines, so a 5 GB file never sits in memory at once. The regex crate promises that search time grows only in a straight line with the input. A strange pattern cannot freeze the tool.

The caller picks the reader. By convention, no file or the file - means stdin.

let result = if path.as_os_str() == "-" {
    search::grep(io::stdin().lock(), &mut out, &re, &opts, label)
} else {
    File::open(path).and_then(|f| search::grep(BufReader::new(f), &mut out, &re, &opts, label))
};
$ printf 'one\ntwo\nthree\n' | tgrep -v o
three

Reading a whole file with fs::read_to_string in a tool that may meet huge logs. It also stops on the first byte that is not UTF-8. lines() has the same UTF-8 limit: tgrep reports stream did not contain valid UTF-8 for a Latin-1 file. Real grep tools read bytes. The regex::bytes module searches &[u8] for this reason.

Step 3: writing output fast and safely

This little program prints numbers. It is fine alone. In a pipe to head, it crashes.

fn main() {
    for i in 0..1_000_000 {
        println!("{i}"); // panics when the reader has gone away
    }
}
$ ./pipe | head -2
0
1

thread 'main' (117073993) panicked at /rustc/b940084d7eb6a299eb4bfeb8e34901bc051e7ac4/library/std/src/io/stdio.rs:1168:9:
failed printing to stdout: Broken pipe (os error 32)
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace

head reads two lines and closes the pipe. The next write fails with a broken pipe. C programs like grep are killed by the signal SIGPIPE, with exit code 141. Rust ignores that signal, so the write returns an error, and println! turns it into a panic. tgrep writes with writeln!, checks for this one error, and exits quietly:

let mut out = BufWriter::new(io::stdout().lock()); // one lock, few system calls

fn is_broken_pipe(e: &anyhow::Error) -> bool {
    e.downcast_ref::<io::Error>().is_some_and(|e| e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::BrokenPipe)
}
$ seq 1 200000 | tgrep 1 | head -3
1
10
11

Three rules for stdout:

  1. Lock once. println! locks stdout for every line. io::stdout().lock() locks it once for the whole run.
  2. Buffer. Rust's stdout is line-buffered. Each line can become one system call. BufWriter collects about 8 KB first.
  3. Flush at the end. Call out.flush()? so that a write error shows up as an error, not as lost output.

Buffering has one visible effect. Look again at the first example. The error for missing.txt came before the result from langs.txt, although langs.txt was searched first. stderr is not buffered, but our stdout is. Both streams are fine. Only their order on one screen can mix.

Color is for people, not for files. --color auto checks io::stdout().is_terminal() from the IsTerminal trait. When stdout is a pipe, the tool writes no escape codes.

Python has the same problem with a different face. A BrokenPipeError is raised, and Python complains again when it flushes at exit. The fix sends the rest of the output to /dev/null:

def run() -> None:
    """Entry point: exit with main's code, and stay quiet on a broken pipe."""
    try:
        sys.exit(main())
    except BrokenPipeError:  # the reader went away, e.g. | head -1
        devnull = os.open(os.devnull, os.O_WRONLY)
        os.dup2(devnull, sys.stdout.fileno())  # stop Python's error at exit
        sys.exit(0)

In Python, BrokenPipeError is a subclass of OSError. A per-file except OSError catches it too, and the tool prints a strange "Broken pipe" message for a file. pygrep first has except BrokenPipeError: raise, then except OSError.

Step 4: exit codes and error messages

Here is the whole main.rs logic. main only turns the result of run into an exit code.

fn main() -> ExitCode {
    let cli = Cli::parse(); // bad arguments: clap prints usage and exits with 2
    init_logging(cli.verbose);
    match run(&cli) {
        Ok(code) => ExitCode::from(code),
        Err(e) if is_broken_pipe(&e) => ExitCode::SUCCESS, // e.g. `tgrep x f | head -1`
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("tgrep: {e:#}"); // errors go to stderr, never stdout
            ExitCode::from(2)
        }
    }
}

/// Exit code like grep: 0 = a line was selected, 1 = none, 2 = an error.
fn run(cli: &Cli) -> anyhow::Result<u8> {
    let cfg = config::load(cli.config.as_deref())?;
    // A command-line flag wins over the config file.
    let ignore_case = cli.ignore_case || cfg.ignore_case;
    let re = search::build_regex(&cli.pattern, cli.fixed_strings, ignore_case)
        .context("invalid pattern")?;
    let color = match cli.color.or(cfg.color).unwrap_or(ColorWhen::Auto) {
        ColorWhen::Always => true,
        ColorWhen::Never => false,
        ColorWhen::Auto => io::stdout().is_terminal(),
    };
    let opts = search::Options {
        invert: cli.invert_match,
        line_number: cli.line_number || cfg.line_number,
        count: cli.count,
        color,
    };
    let files = if cli.files.is_empty() { vec![PathBuf::from("-")] } else { cli.files.clone() };
    // ... the loop over files: see the next block ...
}

The loop searches each file. A file that fails is reported, and the loop goes on.

    let many = files.len() > 1;
    let mut out = BufWriter::new(io::stdout().lock()); // one lock, few system calls
    let (mut matched, mut failed) = (false, false);
    for path in &files {
        let name = if path.as_os_str() == "-" { "(standard input)".into() } else { path.display().to_string() };
        tracing::debug!(file = %name, "searching");
        let label = many.then_some(name.as_str());
        let result = /* stdin or file, as in step 2 */;
        match result {
            Ok(n) => {
                matched |= n > 0;
                if opts.count {
                    match label {
                        Some(l) => writeln!(out, "{l}:{n}")?,
                        None => writeln!(out, "{n}")?,
                    }
                }
            }
            Err(e) if e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::BrokenPipe => return Err(e.into()),
            Err(e) => {
                eprintln!("tgrep: {name}: {e}"); // report, then go on with the next file
                failed = true;
            }
        }
    }
    out.flush()?;
    Ok(if failed { 2 } else if matched { 0 } else { 1 })
$ tgrep java langs.txt; echo "exit=$?"
exit=1
$ tgrep 'a(b' langs.txt; echo "exit=$?"
tgrep: invalid pattern: regex parse error:
    a(b
     ^
error: unclosed group
exit=2
Exit codes you will meet
CodeMeaningWho uses it
0SuccessEvery tool
1A general failure, or "nothing found"grep: no line selected
2Wrong usage, or a real errorgrep, clap, argparse
64 to 78Detailed codes from sysexits.h, for example 64 usage, 66 no input, 78 configBSD tools, the exitcode crate
101A Rust panicAny Rust program that panics
128 + NKilled by signal N, for example 141 for SIGPIPEThe shell reports it

A good error message has the tool name, the thing, and the problem: tgrep: missing.txt: No such file or directory. With anyhow, {e:#} prints the whole chain on one line. If main returns anyhow::Result<()> instead, Rust prints Error: and the debug form, and exits with 1. That is fine for small scripts. A tool with documented exit codes needs ExitCode.

Python follows the same shape. main returns a number, and sys.exit(main()) hands it to the shell.

def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    args = parse_args(argv)
    level = [logging.WARNING, logging.INFO, logging.DEBUG][min(args.verbose, 2)]
    logging.basicConfig(level=level, format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s")  # stderr
    try:
        cfg = load_config(args.config)
        flags = re.IGNORECASE if args.ignore_case or cfg.get("ignore_case") else 0
        args.line_number = args.line_number or cfg.get("line_number", False)
        pattern = re.escape(args.pattern) if args.fixed_strings else args.pattern
        rx = re.compile(pattern, flags)
    except (OSError, tomllib.TOMLDecodeError, re.error) as e:
        print(f"pygrep: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    files = args.files or [Path("-")]
    many = len(files) > 1
    matched = failed = False
    for path in files:
        name = "(standard input)" if str(path) == "-" else str(path)
        log.debug("searching %s", name)
        try:
            if str(path) == "-":
                n = grep(sys.stdin, sys.stdout, rx, args, name if many else None)
            else:
                with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
                    n = grep(f, sys.stdout, rx, args, name if many else None)
        except BrokenPipeError:
            raise  # a subclass of OSError: let main's caller handle it
        except (OSError, UnicodeDecodeError) as e:
            print(f"pygrep: {name}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
            failed = True
            continue
        matched = matched or n > 0
        if args.count:
            print(f"{name}:{n}" if many else n)
    return 2 if failed else 0 if matched else 1
$ python3.14 pygrep.py rust langs.txt missing.txt; echo "exit=$?"
pygrep: missing.txt: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'missing.txt'
langs.txt:rust and python work well together.
exit=2

Calling std::process::exit(2) deep inside the program. It ends the process at once, and destructors do not run. A BufWriter then never flushes, and the last lines of output are lost. Return an ExitCode from main instead.

Step 5: config files and the environment

Some users always want -i and -n. They can put defaults in a TOML file.

ignore_case = true
line_number = true
color = "never"
use std::fs;
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};

use anyhow::Context;
use serde::Deserialize;

use crate::cli::ColorWhen;

/// Defaults from a TOML file. Every field may be missing.
#[derive(Debug, Default, Deserialize)]
#[serde(default, deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct Config {
    pub ignore_case: bool,
    pub line_number: bool,
    pub color: Option<ColorWhen>,
}

/// $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/tgrep/config.toml, else ~/.config/tgrep/config.toml
fn default_path() -> Option<PathBuf> {
    let base = std::env::var_os("XDG_CONFIG_HOME")
        .map(PathBuf::from)
        .or_else(|| std::env::home_dir().map(|h| h.join(".config")))?;
    Some(base.join("tgrep").join("config.toml"))
}

/// A path given by the user must exist. The default path may be missing.
pub fn load(given: Option<&Path>) -> anyhow::Result<Config> {
    let path = match given {
        Some(p) => p.to_path_buf(),
        None => match default_path() {
            Some(p) if p.exists() => p,
            _ => return Ok(Config::default()),
        },
    };
    tracing::info!(path = %path.display(), "reading config");
    let text = fs::read_to_string(&path)
        .with_context(|| format!("cannot read config {}", path.display()))?;
    toml::from_str(&text).with_context(|| format!("bad config {}", path.display()))
}
import logging
import tomllib
from pathlib import Path

log = logging.getLogger("pygrep")


def load_config(path: Path | None) -> dict:
    if path is None:
        return {}
    log.info("reading config %s", path)
    with open(path, "rb") as f:  # tomllib wants bytes
        return tomllib.load(f)
$ TGREP_CONFIG=tgrep.toml tgrep --verbose todo notes.txt
 INFO tgrep::config: reading config path=tgrep.toml
1:TODO: write tests
3:todo: add config
$ tgrep --config bad2.toml todo notes.txt
tgrep: bad config bad2.toml: TOML parse error at line 1, column 1
  |
1 | ignorecase = true
  | ^^^^^^^^^^
unknown field `ignorecase`, expected one of `ignore_case`, `line_number`, `color`

Settings come from several places. The usual order, from strongest to weakest:

  1. Flags on the command line, like -i.
  2. Environment variables, like TGREP_CONFIG.
  3. The config file.
  4. Defaults in the code.

On Linux, config files live in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME, or in ~/.config when that variable is not set. This follows the XDG Base Directory rules. macOS and Windows have their own places. Crates like directories find the right folder on each system. tgrep uses the XDG path everywhere, which many command-line tools also do.

Note one limit. The file can switch ignore_case on, but no flag can switch it off again. Real tools add opposite flags, like --no-ignore-case, for this case.

Failing when the default config file does not exist. Most users never create one. A missing default file means "use defaults". A missing file that the user named with --config is an error.

Step 6: logs and progress output

--verbose turns on log lines. They go to stderr, so they never mix with the results.

fn init_logging(verbose: u8) {
    let level = match verbose {
        0 => tracing::Level::WARN,
        1 => tracing::Level::INFO,
        _ => tracing::Level::DEBUG,
    };
    tracing_subscriber::fmt()
        .with_max_level(level)
        .with_writer(io::stderr) // logs go to stderr, results to stdout
        .with_ansi(io::stderr().is_terminal()) // no color codes in log files
        .without_time()
        .init();
}
$ tgrep --verbose --verbose rust langs.txt - < notes.txt
DEBUG tgrep: searching file=langs.txt
DEBUG tgrep: searching file=(standard input)
langs.txt:rust and python work well together.

The first version of this function had no with_ansi line. Its log lines were full of color codes, even when stderr went into a file. Always ask "is a person watching?" before you add color.

A progress bar answers the same question. This example uses the indicatif crate. It pretends to search 40 files.

use std::io::{self, IsTerminal};
use std::thread::sleep;
use std::time::Duration;

use indicatif::{ProgressBar, ProgressStyle};

fn main() {
    let files: Vec<String> = (1..=40).map(|i| format!("log-{i:02}.txt")).collect();
    // The bar draws on stderr. indicatif hides it when stderr is not a terminal.
    let bar = ProgressBar::new(files.len() as u64);
    bar.set_style(
        ProgressStyle::with_template("{bar:30} {pos}/{len} files {msg}")
            .unwrap()
            .progress_chars("#>-"),
    );
    let mut total = 0;
    for f in &files {
        bar.set_message(f.clone()); // show which file we are on
        sleep(Duration::from_millis(20)); // pretend to search the file
        total += 3;
        bar.inc(1);
    }
    bar.finish_and_clear(); // remove the bar before the summary
    // Results go to stdout, so `> result.txt` gets only this line.
    println!("{total} matches (stderr is a terminal: {})", io::stderr().is_terminal());
}

In a terminal, the bar redraws one line in place. Here is one frame from the middle of the run:

###############>-------------- 20/40 files log-20.txt

With stderr sent to a pipe, the bar is hidden, and only the result remains:

120 matches (stderr is a terminal: false)

indicatif also hides the bar when the TERM variable is unset or dumb. In Python, the standard logging module writes to stderr by default. Libraries like rich and tqdm draw progress bars.

A progress bar in a CI log or a cron job. Each redraw becomes a new line, and the log fills with thousands of bars. Draw progress only when stderr is a terminal, and update it at most a few times per second. indicatif limits redraws to 20 per second.

Step 7: testing the tool

There are two levels. Unit tests call grep with a byte slice and a Vec<u8>. Integration tests run the real binary, like a user.

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    fn run(text: &str, pattern: &str, opts: Options) -> (u64, String) {
        let re = build_regex(pattern, false, false).unwrap();
        let mut out = Vec::new(); // a Vec<u8> is a Write: perfect for tests
        let n = grep(text.as_bytes(), &mut out, &re, &opts, None).unwrap();
        (n, String::from_utf8(out).unwrap())
    }

    const OPTS: Options = Options { invert: false, line_number: true, count: false, color: false };

    #[test]
    fn finds_lines_with_numbers() {
        let (n, out) = run("apple\nbanana\ncherry\n", "an", OPTS);
        assert_eq!((n, out.as_str()), (1, "2:banana\n"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn invert_and_count() {
        let opts = Options { invert: true, count: true, ..OPTS };
        assert_eq!(run("a\nb\na\n", "a", opts), (1, String::new()));
    }
}
use std::io::Write;
use std::process::{Command, Output, Stdio};

// Cargo builds the binary and tells the test where it is.
const BIN: &str = env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_tgrep");

fn tgrep(args: &[&str], stdin: &str) -> Output {
    let mut child = Command::new(BIN)
        .args(args)
        .env_remove("TGREP_CONFIG") // tests must not read the user's config
        .env("XDG_CONFIG_HOME", "/nonexistent")
        .stdin(Stdio::piped())
        .stdout(Stdio::piped())
        .stderr(Stdio::piped())
        .spawn()
        .unwrap();
    child.stdin.take().unwrap().write_all(stdin.as_bytes()).unwrap();
    child.wait_with_output().unwrap()
}

#[test]
fn errors_give_2_on_stderr() {
    let out = tgrep(&["a", "no-such-file"], "");
    assert_eq!(out.status.code(), Some(2));
    assert!(out.stdout.is_empty());
    assert!(String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stderr).starts_with("tgrep: no-such-file:"));
}

Three more integration tests check exit code 0 with output, exit code 1, and exit code 2 for a typo in a flag.

$ cargo test
     Running unittests src/main.rs
test search::tests::invert_and_count ... ok
test search::tests::finds_lines_with_numbers ... ok
test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.00s
     Running tests/cli.rs
test bad_usage_gives_2 ... ok
test no_match_gives_1 ... ok
test errors_give_2_on_stderr ... ok
test match_gives_0_and_prints_the_line ... ok
test result: ok. 4 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.30s

env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_tgrep") is set by Cargo for integration tests. No extra crate is needed. The crates assert_cmd and predicates make such tests shorter. In Python, call main(["-n", "b", path]) directly in pytest and check the returned number. Typer has typer.testing.CliRunner, which also checks the exit code.

Tests that read the developer's real config file or environment. They pass on one laptop and fail in CI. Clear the variables in the test, as env_remove does above.

Step 8: packaging the binary

A Rust tool ships as one file. The release profile decides how big it is.

[profile.release]
strip = true        # remove debug symbols from the binary
lto = true          # optimise across crates: smaller and faster
codegen-units = 1   # slower build, better code
panic = "abort"     # no unwinding code

Ways to ship it:

  • cargo install --path . builds in release mode and copies the binary to ~/.cargo/bin. After cargo publish, anyone can run cargo install tgrep.
  • rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl, then cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl. A musl build is static and runs on almost any Linux.
  • dist (formerly cargo-dist) builds archives and installers for many systems in CI.
  • clap_complete and clap_mangen generate shell completions and a man page from the same Cli struct.

The install, cross-compile and dist commands were not run here, because they install tools or need other systems. The two release builds were run.

A Python tool ships as a package with an entry point. Here pygrep.py became src/pygrep/__init__.py.

[project]
name = "pygrep"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Print lines that match a pattern"
requires-python = ">=3.11"

[project.scripts]
pygrep = "pygrep:run"   # the command name = module:function

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.10,<0.11"]
build-backend = "uv_build"
$ uv build
$ ls dist
pygrep-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
pygrep-0.1.0.tar.gz
$ uvx --from dist/pygrep-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl pygrep -n -i rust langs.txt
1:Rust is fast.
3:rust and python work well together.

uvx runs the command in a temporary environment. uv tool install . installs it for good. The user still needs a Python on the machine. The Rust binary needs nothing.

"What makes a CLI tool good in a pipeline?" Results only on stdout. Errors, logs and progress on stderr. Stable, documented exit codes. No color or progress when nobody watches. Quiet on a broken pipe. Streaming input, so big files work.

Shipping a debug build. It is several times bigger and often ten times slower. Always build tools with --release.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for command-line tools
PatternPurposeModelNote
#[derive(Parser)] struct CliArguments and help from one structlet cli = Cli::parse();Doc comments become help text.
#[arg(short, long)] x: boolAn on/off flag-i, --ignore-casePython: action="store_true".
#[derive(ValueEnum)]A fixed list of values--color auto|always|neverBad values get a clear error.
fn f<R: BufRead, W: Write>A core that works on any input and outputgrep(text.as_bytes(), &mut vec, ...)Easy unit tests.
No file or - means stdinWork in pipescat log | tgrep errorLabel it "(standard input)".
BufWriter::new(io::stdout().lock())Fast outputOne lock, big writesFlush at the end.
Quiet on BrokenPipeBehave well before headErr(e) if is_broken_pipe(&e) => ExitCode::SUCCESSprintln! would panic.
fn main() -> ExitCodeDocumented exit codesExitCode::from(2)Do not call process::exit deep inside.
eprintln!("tool: {thing}: {err}")Clear error messagestgrep: missing.txt: No such file...Always to stderr.
Flags, then env, then file, then defaultsPredictable settingscli.color.or(cfg.color).unwrap_or(Auto)A missing default file is fine.
is_terminal() before colorNo escape codes in filesio::stdout().is_terminal()Same for logs and progress.
env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_name")Run the real binary in testsCommand::new(BIN).args(["-n", "b"])Check stdout, stderr and the code.
[profile.release] tuningSmall, fast binariesstrip = true, lto = trueHere 3.4 MB became 1.8 MB.

Practice

Your tool finds an error in one of five files. Where does the message go?

  • stdout, next to the results
  • stderr
  • Nowhere: just change the exit code

Messages for people go to stderr, so they never mix with data in a pipe. The exit code then says that an error happened.

What exit code does grep give when it finds nothing and has no error?

  • 0
  • 1
  • 2

0 means a line was selected, 1 means none, 2 means an error. Scripts use this with if grep -q ....

In clap derive, which field makes an option that may appear several times and counts them?

  • verbose: bool
  • verbose: Vec<bool>
  • #[arg(long, action = ArgAction::Count)] verbose: u8

ArgAction::Count adds one for each time the flag appears. Python's twin is action="count".

A Rust tool uses println! and runs as tool | head -1. What happens after head exits?

  • The tool is killed silently by SIGPIPE.
  • The next println! panics with "Broken pipe", and the exit code is 101.
  • Nothing: the output is buffered forever.

Rust ignores SIGPIPE, so the write returns an error, and println! panics. Use writeln! and handle BrokenPipe.

To check whether stdout is a terminal, call io::stdout().?.

In pyproject.toml, the table that defines command names is [project.?].

  1. Add a flag -q, --quiet to Cli. It prints nothing and only sets the exit code.
    Answer 
    /// Print nothing; only set the exit code
#[arg(short, long)]
pub quiet: bool,

    In run, set count: cli.count || cli.quiet and skip the count lines when quiet is set. Even better, stop at the first match: the answer is already known. That is why grep -q is fast on big files.

  2. Write the same --quiet flag for pygrep with argparse.
    Answer

    p.add_argument("-q", "--quiet", action="store_true"). In grep, return 1 at the first selected line when args.quiet is set, and print nothing. In main, skip the count output when quiet.

  3. Why does tgrep print the error for missing.txt before the match from langs.txt?
    Answer

    stdout goes through a BufWriter, so the match waits in memory until the flush at the end. stderr is not buffered, so the error appears at once. Both streams are correct. Only their order on a shared screen differs.

  4. A user sets ignore_case = true in the config file. One day they need a case-sensitive search. What can they do today, and what would you add?
    Answer

    Today they can point --config or TGREP_CONFIG at an empty file. Better: add --no-ignore-case (or -s, --case-sensitive) that wins over the file. In clap, the two flags can be linked with overrides_with, so the last one on the command line wins.

  5. Expert. Your CLI runs in CI. The log is full of lines like ###>--- 3/40, and the output file contains \x1b[1;31m. Find both bugs.
    Answer

    The progress bar draws without checking for a terminal, or the code forces a draw target. Let indicatif use stderr and hide itself, or check io::stderr().is_terminal(). The color codes come from coloring without checking stdout. Default to --color auto with io::stdout().is_terminal(). Many tools also respect the NO_COLOR environment variable.

  6. Expert. You must search 10 GB of files as fast as possible. Name three changes to tgrep.
    Answer

    Search bytes with regex::bytes instead of decoding every line to a String. Read big blocks and search the whole block first, splitting into lines only around a match. Search several files in parallel with threads, and keep each file's output together. The tool ripgrep does all three, and more.

Key takeaways

  • The contract: arguments and stdin in, results on stdout, messages on stderr, and a meaningful exit code.
  • clap derive turns a struct into a parser with help. argparse and Typer do the same in Python. Usage errors exit with 2.
  • Keep the core generic over BufRead and Write. It streams big inputs and is easy to test.
  • Lock and buffer stdout, flush at the end, and stay quiet on a broken pipe.
  • Settings come from flags, then environment, then a config file, then defaults. Color, logs and progress respect the terminal.
  • Test the real binary with CARGO_BIN_EXE_.... Ship a tuned release build, or a Python package with an entry point.

Sources

  • clap 4.6 derive reference. Attributes, field types, ValueEnum and doc comments as help.
  • Command Line Applications in Rust: exit codes. Exit code conventions and the exitcode crate.
  • Python documentation: argparse. Exit status 2, and the new color and suggest_on_error options.
  • Typer release notes. Version 0.29.1 and the vendored copy of Click since 0.26.0.
  • indicatif: ProgressDrawTarget. Bars on stderr, hidden when nobody watches.
  • XDG Base Directory Specification. Where config files live on Linux.

Data, serde and databases

Programs pass data around all the time: JSON from an API, TOML config, CSV reports, rows from a database. In Rust, one library called serde handles the formats, and sqlx talks to PostgreSQL. In Python, Pydantic and a driver like psycopg do the same jobs.

  • Turn Rust structs into JSON, TOML and CSV and back with serde derive.
  • Control names, defaults, enums and custom field formats with serde attributes.
  • Store times and ids safely with UTC timestamps and UUIDs.
  • Query PostgreSQL from Rust with sqlx: pools, parameters, rows as structs, migrations and transactions.
  • Do the same in Python with Pydantic and psycopg, and compare the two.

One struct, many formats

Here is a service description. The same struct becomes JSON and TOML, and comes back again.

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Service {
    name: String,
    port: u16,
    tags: Vec<String>,
    tls: Option<Tls>, // None is left out of TOML, and is null in JSON
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Tls {
    cert: String,
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let svc = Service {
        name: "api".into(),
        port: 8080,
        tags: vec!["web".into(), "public".into()],
        tls: Some(Tls { cert: "/etc/api.pem".into() }),
    };
    // One derive, many formats.
    let json = serde_json::to_string(&svc)?;
    let text = toml::to_string(&svc)?;
    println!("{json}\n---\n{text}---");
    // And back again.
    let a: Service = serde_json::from_str(&json)?;
    let b: Service = toml::from_str(&text)?;
    println!("{}", a == svc && b == svc);
    Ok(())
}
import tomllib

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Tls(BaseModel):
    cert: str


class Service(BaseModel):
    name: str
    port: int
    tags: list[str]
    tls: Tls | None = None


svc = Service(name="api", port=8080, tags=["web", "public"], tls=Tls(cert="/etc/api.pem"))
text = svc.model_dump_json()  # a JSON string
print(text)
back = Service.model_validate_json(text)  # parse and check
cfg = tomllib.loads('name = "api"\nport = 8080\ntags = ["web"]\n')  # TOML -> dict
print(back == svc, Service.model_validate(cfg))
{"name":"api","port":8080,"tags":["web","public"],"tls":{"cert":"/etc/api.pem"}}
---
name = "api"
port = 8080
tags = ["web", "public"]

[tls]
cert = "/etc/api.pem"
---
true

Python prints the same JSON line, then True name='api' port=8080 tags=['web'] tls=None.

To serialize is to turn a value into text or bytes. To deserialize is the way back. serde splits the work in two halves, with a small shared language in the middle.

The versions used here: serde 1.0.229, serde_json 1.0.154, toml 1.2.1, csv 1.4.0, and Pydantic 2.14.3. Python's standard tomllib reads TOML but cannot write it.

Using serde_json::Value everywhere because it is easy. Then every access is v["user"]["id"].as_u64(), and typos become None at run time. Use Value only for data with no fixed shape. Give known data a struct.

Serde attributes: names, defaults and enums

Real JSON rarely matches Rust names. APIs use camelCase, fields go missing, and old names live on. Attributes fix this without hand-written code.

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]
struct User {
    user_id: u64, // JSON name: "userId"
    #[serde(alias = "mail")] // also accept the old name when reading
    email: String,
    #[serde(default)] // missing means false
    is_admin: bool,
    #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
    nickname: Option<String>,
    #[serde(rename = "created")] // one field with its own name
    created_at: String,
}

fn main() {
    let input = r#"{"userId": 7, "mail": "ann@example.com", "created": "2026-11-15"}"#;
    let user: User = serde_json::from_str(input).unwrap();
    println!("{user:?}");
    println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&user).unwrap());

    let typo = r#"{"userId": 7, "email": "a@b.c", "isAdmn": true, "created": "x"}"#;
    println!("{}", serde_json::from_str::<User>(typo).unwrap_err());
}
from pydantic import AliasChoices, BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError
from pydantic.alias_generators import to_camel


class User(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(alias_generator=to_camel, extra="forbid")
    user_id: int
    email: str = Field(validation_alias=AliasChoices("email", "mail"))
    is_admin: bool = False
    nickname: str | None = None
    created_at: str = Field(alias="created")


u = User.model_validate_json('{"userId": 7, "mail": "ann@example.com", "created": "2026-11-15"}')
print(u)
print(u.model_dump_json(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True))
try:
    User.model_validate_json('{"userId": 7, "email": "a@b.c", "isAdmn": true, "created": "x"}')
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.errors()[0]["type"], e.errors()[0]["loc"])
User { user_id: 7, email: "ann@example.com", is_admin: false, nickname: None, created_at: "2026-11-15" }
{"userId":7,"email":"ann@example.com","isAdmin":false,"created":"2026-11-15"}
unknown field `isAdmn`, expected one of `userId`, `email`, `mail`, `isAdmin`, `nickname`, `created` at line 1 column 40

Python prints the same model and JSON, and then extra_forbidden ('isAdmn',).

The attributes you use most
AttributeEffectPydantic twin
rename_all = "camelCase"All names in another casealias_generator=to_camel
rename = "x"One field gets another nameField(alias="x")
alias = "x"Also accept another name when readingAliasChoices
defaultMissing field gets Default::default()A default value
skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"Leave out empty valuesexclude_none=True
deny_unknown_fieldsUnknown keys are an errorextra="forbid"
flattenPut an inner struct's fields at the same levelModel inheritance

Four ways to write an enum

An enum needs a tag in the data, so the reader knows the variant. serde has four layouts. This program printed each one for Circle { r: 1.5 } and Dot:

// The usual choice for web APIs: internally tagged.
#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "lowercase")]
enum Shape {
    Circle { r: f64 },
    Rect { w: f64, h: f64 },
    Dot,
}
external:  {"Circle":{"r":1.5}}  "Dot"
internal:  {"type":"circle","r":1.5}  {"type":"dot"}
adjacent:  {"t":"Circle","c":{"r":1.5}}  {"t":"Dot"}
untagged:  {"r":1.5}  null
Rect { w: 2.0, h: 3.0 }
unknown variant `star`, expected one of `circle`, `rect`, `dot` at line 1 column 15
  • External (the default): {"Circle": {...}}. Good for Rust-to-Rust data.
  • Internal, #[serde(tag = "type")]: the tag sits beside the fields. Most JSON APIs look like this.
  • Adjacent, #[serde(tag = "t", content = "c")]: tag and data in two keys.
  • Untagged: no tag at all. serde tries each variant in order. Errors are vague, and the first variant that fits wins.

Pydantic calls the internal form a discriminated union:

class Circle(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["circle"]
    r: float


class Rect(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["rect"]
    w: float
    h: float


class Drawing(BaseModel):
    shape: Circle | Rect = Field(discriminator="type")  # like #[serde(tag = "type")]


print(Drawing.model_validate_json('{"shape": {"type": "rect", "w": 2, "h": 3}}'))
# shape=Rect(type='rect', w=2.0, h=3.0)

Combining deny_unknown_fields with flatten. The serde documentation says this combination is not supported, on the outer struct or the inner one. Pick one of the two for each struct.

Custom formats for single fields

Sometimes one field needs a special text form. An invoice sends money as "12.34", but your code wants whole cents. An email must be checked when it is read.

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

/// An email that was checked once, when it was read.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(try_from = "String", into = "String")]
struct Email(String);

impl TryFrom<String> for Email {
    type Error = String; // becomes the serde error message
    fn try_from(s: String) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
        if s.contains('@') { Ok(Email(s.to_lowercase())) } else { Err(format!("not an email: {s}")) }
    }
}

impl From<Email> for String {
    fn from(e: Email) -> String {
        e.0
    }
}

/// Money as whole cents in Rust, but as "12.34" in JSON.
mod money {
    use serde::{Deserialize, Deserializer, Serializer, de::Error};

    pub fn serialize<S: Serializer>(cents: &u64, s: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error> {
        s.serialize_str(&format!("{}.{:02}", cents / 100, cents % 100))
    }

    pub fn deserialize<'de, D: Deserializer<'de>>(d: D) -> Result<u64, D::Error> {
        let text = String::deserialize(d)?;
        let (whole, frac) = text.split_once('.').ok_or_else(|| D::Error::custom("expected 12.34"))?;
        let ok = frac.len() == 2;
        match (whole.parse::<u64>(), frac.parse::<u64>()) {
            (Ok(w), Ok(f)) if ok => Ok(w * 100 + f),
            _ => Err(D::Error::custom(format!("bad amount {text:?}"))),
        }
    }
}
#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Invoice {
    to: Email,
    #[serde(with = "money")]
    total: u64, // cents
}

fn main() {
    let inv: Invoice = serde_json::from_str(r#"{"to": "Ann@Example.com", "total": "12.34"}"#).unwrap();
    println!("{inv:?}");
    println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&inv).unwrap());
    for bad in [r#"{"to": "ann", "total": "1.00"}"#, r#"{"to": "a@b.c", "total": "1.5"}"#] {
        println!("{}", serde_json::from_str::<Invoice>(bad).unwrap_err());
    }
}
Invoice { to: Email("ann@example.com"), total: 1234 }
{"to":"ann@example.com","total":"12.34"}
not an email: ann at line 1 column 12
bad amount "1.5" at line 1 column 31
  • #[serde(try_from = "String", into = "String")] reads a String, then calls your TryFrom. An invalid email can never be built, not even from JSON. This is "parse, do not validate" from Structs, enums and pattern matching.
  • #[serde(with = "money")] points at a module with two functions, serialize and deserialize. Ready-made modules exist too, like chrono::serde::ts_seconds below.
  • D::Error::custom(...) makes an error in the format's own error type. serde_json adds the line and column for you.

Pydantic does the same with Annotated types. A BeforeValidator runs on the raw input, and a PlainSerializer writes the output.

from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, BeforeValidator, PlainSerializer, ValidationError


def check_email(v: str) -> str:
    if "@" not in v:
        raise ValueError(f"not an email: {v}")
    return v.lower()


def parse_cents(v: str) -> int:
    whole, _, frac = v.partition(".")
    if len(frac) != 2 or not (whole + frac).isdigit():
        raise ValueError(f"bad amount {v!r}")
    return int(whole) * 100 + int(frac)


Email = Annotated[str, BeforeValidator(check_email)]
Cents = Annotated[
    int,
    BeforeValidator(parse_cents),  # "12.34" -> 1234 when reading
    PlainSerializer(lambda c: f"{c // 100}.{c % 100:02}", return_type=str),  # and back
]


class Invoice(BaseModel):
    to: Email
    total: Cents


inv = Invoice.model_validate_json('{"to": "Ann@Example.com", "total": "12.34"}')
print(inv, inv.model_dump_json())
for bad in ['{"to": "ann", "total": "1.00"}', '{"to": "a@b.c", "total": "1.5"}']:
    try:
        Invoice.model_validate_json(bad)
    except ValidationError as e:
        print(e.errors()[0]["msg"])
to='ann@example.com' total=1234 {"to":"ann@example.com","total":"12.34"}
Value error, not an email: ann
Value error, bad amount '1.5'

A whole new data format means implementing serde's Serializer and Deserializer traits. The serde site has a guide for that. It is rare work: for almost every format, a crate already exists.

Storing money in f64. 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in binary floating point. Store whole cents in an integer, or use a decimal type like rust_decimal in Rust and decimal.Decimal in Python.

CSV: rows as structs

A sales file has one bad row. The program sums the good rows and reports the bad one.

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
struct Sale {
    city: String,
    amount: u32,
    #[serde(default)] // the column may be missing; an empty cell is None
    note: Option<String>,
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Total<'a> {
    city: &'a str,
    sales: u32,
    sum: u32,
}

const DATA: &str = "\
city,amount,note
Tokyo,120,
Osaka,80,first day
Tokyo,95,
Osaka,lots,typo here
";
import csv
import io
import sys
from collections import defaultdict

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

DATA = """city,amount,note
Tokyo,120,
Osaka,80,first day
Tokyo,95,
Osaka,lots,typo here
"""


class Sale(BaseModel):
    city: str
    amount: int  # "120" -> 120: pydantic converts the text
    note: str | None = None

The main part reads every row, sums the good ones and writes a new CSV table.

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let mut rdr = csv::Reader::from_reader(DATA.as_bytes()); // first line = headers
    let mut totals: std::collections::BTreeMap<String, (u32, u32)> = Default::default();
    for result in rdr.deserialize::<Sale>() {
        match result {
            Ok(sale) => {
                if let Some(n) = &sale.note {
                    eprintln!("note for {}: {n}", sale.city);
                }
                let t = totals.entry(sale.city).or_default();
                *t = (t.0 + 1, t.1 + sale.amount);
            }
            Err(e) => eprintln!("skipped: {e}"), // one bad row does not stop the file
        }
    }
    let mut wtr = csv::Writer::from_writer(std::io::stdout());
    for (city, (sales, sum)) in &totals {
        wtr.serialize(Total { city, sales: *sales, sum: *sum })?; // headers come from the struct
    }
    wtr.flush()?;
    Ok(())
}
totals: dict[str, list[int]] = defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0])
for line, row in enumerate(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(DATA)), start=2):
    row = {k: (v or None) for k, v in row.items()}  # empty cell -> None
    try:
        sale = Sale.model_validate(row)
    except ValidationError as e:
        print(f"skipped line {line}: {e.errors()[0]['msg']}", file=sys.stderr)
        continue
    totals[sale.city][0] += 1
    totals[sale.city][1] += sale.amount

w = csv.writer(sys.stdout, lineterminator="\n")
w.writerow(["city", "sales", "sum"])
for city in sorted(totals):
    w.writerow([city, *totals[city]])
note for Osaka: first day
skipped: CSV deserialize error: record 4 (line: 5, byte: 57): field 1: invalid digit found in string
city,sales,sum
Osaka,1,80
Tokyo,2,215

Python prints skipped line 5: Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer and the same table.

CSV has no types. Every cell is text. The struct gives the types: amount: u32 turns "120" into a number, or reports the row. The csv crate matches columns by header name, so the column order in the file does not matter. Its error says the record, line and byte, which helps a lot with big files.

Splitting CSV lines with split(','). A cell like "Tokyo, Japan" has a comma inside quotes, and your columns shift. Always use a real CSV reader: the csv crate or Python's csv module.

Times and ids

A user in Tokyo books a meeting. The program stores the time in UTC and gives the event a UUID.

use chrono::{DateTime, FixedOffset, Utc};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use uuid::Uuid;

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Event {
    id: Uuid,
    at: DateTime<Utc>, // always store and compare in UTC
    #[serde(with = "chrono::serde::ts_seconds")]
    expires: DateTime<Utc>, // as Unix seconds in JSON
}

fn main() {
    // A time from a user in Tokyo (+09:00).
    let local: DateTime<FixedOffset> = DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339("2026-11-15T09:30:00+09:00").unwrap();
    let at = local.with_timezone(&Utc);
    println!("{local} -> {at}");

    let ev = Event { id: Uuid::nil(), at, expires: at + chrono::Duration::days(30) };
    println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&ev).unwrap());

    // v4 is random. v7 starts with the time, so new ids sort after old ones.
    let (a, b) = (Uuid::now_v7(), Uuid::now_v7());
    println!("v{} v{} sorted: {}", Uuid::new_v4().get_version_num(), a.get_version_num(), a < b);
    println!("{}", "2026-13-01T00:00:00Z".parse::<DateTime<Utc>>().unwrap_err());
}
import uuid
from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Event(BaseModel):
    id: uuid.UUID
    at: datetime


local = datetime.fromisoformat("2026-11-15T09:30:00+09:00")
at = local.astimezone(UTC)
print(local, "->", at)
ev = Event(id=uuid.UUID(int=0), at=at)
print(ev.model_dump_json(), int((at + timedelta(days=30)).timestamp()))
a, b = uuid.uuid7(), uuid.uuid7()  # new in Python 3.14
print(f"v{uuid.uuid4().version} v{a.version} sorted: {a < b}")
try:
    datetime.fromisoformat("2026-13-01T00:00:00Z")
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
2026-11-15 09:30:00 +09:00 -> 2026-11-15 00:30:00 UTC
{"id":"00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000","at":"2026-11-15T00:30:00Z","expires":1797294600}
v4 v7 sorted: true
input is out of range

Python gives the same instant, the same JSON time, the same Unix number 1797294600, and month must be in 1..12, not 13.

Rules for time:

  • A point in time is stored in UTC. Convert to local time only to show it.
  • In JSON, write times as RFC 3339 text, like 2026-11-15T00:30:00Z. serde does this for DateTime<Utc>.
  • An offset like +09:00 is not a time zone. A zone like Asia/Tokyo has rules, such as summer time in other places. For zone rules, use chrono-tz or the newer crate jiff in Rust, and zoneinfo in Python.

Rust has three big time crates. chrono (0.4.45) is the oldest and most used. time (0.3.55) is smaller. jiff (0.2.44) is the newest and has strong time zone support. sqlx supports chrono and time as features. Its README does not list jiff, so this chapter uses chrono.

A UUID is an id you can create in the program, before the database sees the row. Version 4 is random. Version 7, from RFC 9562, starts with a millisecond timestamp. New v7 ids sort after older ones, so database indexes stay compact. The uuid crate has Uuid::now_v7(), and Python 3.14 added uuid.uuid7().

Storing local times without an offset, like 2026-03-29 02:30. In many European zones that hour does not exist on the day clocks move forward. Store UTC with TIMESTAMPTZ, and keep the zone name in a separate column if you need it.

SQL from Rust with sqlx

Now the data goes into PostgreSQL. A small bank has accounts and transfers. First, the table design as a migration:

-- Accounts hold money in cents. The CHECK keeps balances from going below zero.
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id            UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    owner         TEXT NOT NULL,
    balance_cents BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (balance_cents >= 0),
    meta          JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
    created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE transfers (
    id           BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    from_id      UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts (id),
    to_id        UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts (id),
    amount_cents BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (amount_cents > 0),
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The project uses sqlx 0.9.0, released in May 2026. It is async, so it runs on tokio.

[dependencies]
sqlx = { version = "0.9.0", features = ["runtime-tokio", "tls-rustls-ring-webpki", "postgres", "macros", "migrate", "uuid", "chrono", "json"] }
tokio = { version = "1.54", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
uuid = { version = "1.29.2", features = ["v7", "serde"] }
chrono = { version = "0.4.45", features = ["serde"] }
use std::time::Duration;

use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};
use serde::Serialize;
use sqlx::postgres::{PgPool, PgPoolOptions};
use sqlx::types::Json;
use uuid::Uuid;

/// One row of the accounts table. Field names match the column names.
#[derive(Debug, Serialize, sqlx::FromRow)]
pub struct Account {
    pub id: Uuid,                     // UUID
    pub owner: String,                // TEXT NOT NULL
    pub balance_cents: i64,           // BIGINT
    pub meta: Json<serde_json::Value>, // JSONB
    pub created_at: DateTime<Utc>,    // TIMESTAMPTZ
}

pub async fn connect(url: &str) -> Result<PgPool, sqlx::Error> {
    PgPoolOptions::new()
        .max_connections(10) // at most 10 open connections
        .acquire_timeout(Duration::from_secs(3)) // wait 3 s for a free one, then fail
        .connect(url)
        .await
}

Two functions write and read one account:

pub async fn create_account(pool: &PgPool, owner: &str, cents: i64) -> Result<Account, sqlx::Error> {
    sqlx::query_as::<_, Account>(
        "INSERT INTO accounts (id, owner, balance_cents)
         VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
         RETURNING id, owner, balance_cents, meta, created_at",
    )
    .bind(Uuid::now_v7()) // $1
    .bind(owner) // $2: sent apart from the SQL text, so no injection
    .bind(cents) // $3
    .fetch_one(pool)
    .await
}

pub async fn find_account(pool: &PgPool, id: Uuid) -> Result<Option<Account>, sqlx::Error> {
    sqlx::query_as("SELECT id, owner, balance_cents, meta, created_at FROM accounts WHERE id = $1")
        .bind(id)
        .fetch_optional(pool) // Ok(None) when no row matches
        .await
}

Four ideas sit in this code:

  1. The pool. A connection pool keeps connections open and lends them out. Opening a PostgreSQL connection takes several network round trips, so you do it rarely. In sqlx 0.9 the defaults are 10 connections at most, 0 at least, and a 30-second wait for a free one.
  2. Parameters. $1, $2 are placeholders. .bind(...) sends each value separately from the SQL text. The database never reads a value as SQL code.
  3. Rows as structs. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] maps each column to the field with the same name. query_as::<_, Account> returns Account values.
  4. How many rows? fetch_one wants exactly one row. fetch_optional gives Option. fetch_all gives a Vec. execute runs a statement and reports the rows changed.
PostgreSQL types and their Rust and Python twins
PostgreSQLRust (sqlx)Python (psycopg)
BIGINT / INTEGERi64 / i32int
TEXTStringstr
BOOLEANboolbool
UUIDuuid::Uuid (feature uuid)uuid.UUID
TIMESTAMPTZDateTime<Utc> (feature chrono)datetime with a zone
JSONBJson<T> or serde_json::Value (feature json)dict, write with Jsonb(...)

a column without NOT NULLOption<T>T | None

This code was checked with cargo check and cargo clippy against sqlx 0.9.0. It was not run here, because running it needs a PostgreSQL server.

Compile-time checked queries

sqlx has a second style. The macros query! and query_as! send your SQL to a real database while compiling. The compiler then knows every column type.

pub async fn owner_of(pool: &PgPool, id: uuid::Uuid) -> Result<String, sqlx::Error> {
    let row = sqlx::query!("SELECT owner FROM accounts WHERE id = $1", id)
        .fetch_one(pool)
        .await?;
    Ok(row.owner) // the macro knows the column is TEXT NOT NULL, so this is a String
}

Without a database, the build stops with this real message:

error: set `DATABASE_URL` to use query macros online, or run `cargo sqlx prepare` to update the query cache

So you choose. The macros catch a wrong column name or type at build time, but the build needs DATABASE_URL or a saved query cache. cargo sqlx prepare writes that cache into a .sqlx folder, which you commit, so CI can build without a database. The functions query_as and FromRow need no database at build time, but they check types only at run time.

Building SQL with format!, like format!("... WHERE owner = '{owner}'"). A name like x' OR '1'='1 changes the query: this is SQL injection. Since sqlx 0.9, a non-literal SQL string does not even compile:

error[E0277]: dynamic SQL strings should be audited for possible injections
    = help: the trait `SqlSafeStr` is not implemented for `&std::string::String`
    = note: prefer literal SQL strings with bind parameters or `QueryBuilder` to add dynamic data to a query.

Migrations and transactions

The main function applies the migrations, then moves money.

mod db;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let url = std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")?; // e.g. postgres://app:secret@localhost/bank
    let pool = db::connect(&url).await?;
    sqlx::migrate!().run(&pool).await?; // applies new files in ./migrations, once each

    let ann = db::create_account(&pool, "Ann", 10_000).await?;
    let bo = db::create_account(&pool, "Bo", 500).await?;
    let id = db::transfer(&pool, ann.id, bo.id, 2_500).await?;
    println!("transfer {id} done");

    match db::transfer(&pool, bo.id, ann.id, 1_000_000).await {
        Err(sqlx::Error::Database(e)) if e.is_check_violation() => println!("refused: not enough money"),
        other => println!("unexpected: {other:?}"),
    }
    let bo = db::find_account(&pool, bo.id).await?.expect("Bo exists");
    println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&bo)?);
    pool.close().await;
    Ok(())
}

sqlx::migrate!() puts the files from ./migrations into the binary at compile time. At start-up, it runs each new file once, in order, and records it in a table called _sqlx_migrations. The sqlx-cli tool creates new files with a timestamp in the name: sqlx migrate add create_accounts.

A transfer changes two rows and adds a third. Either all three changes happen, or none. That is a transaction.

/// Moves money between two accounts. All three statements succeed, or none.
pub async fn transfer(pool: &PgPool, from: Uuid, to: Uuid, cents: i64) -> Result<i64, sqlx::Error> {
    let mut tx = pool.begin().await?; // BEGIN
    let moved = sqlx::query("UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents - $1 WHERE id = $2")
        .bind(cents)
        .bind(from)
        .execute(&mut *tx) // run inside the transaction
        .await?; // the CHECK fails here if the balance would go below 0
    if moved.rows_affected() == 0 {
        return Err(sqlx::Error::RowNotFound); // tx is dropped: ROLLBACK
    }
    sqlx::query("UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents + $1 WHERE id = $2")
        .bind(cents)
        .bind(to)
        .execute(&mut *tx)
        .await?;
    let (id,): (i64,) = sqlx::query_as(
        "INSERT INTO transfers (from_id, to_id, amount_cents) VALUES ($1, $2, $3) RETURNING id",
    )
    .bind(from)
    .bind(to)
    .bind(cents)
    .fetch_one(&mut *tx)
    .await?;
    tx.commit().await?; // COMMIT: now other connections see the change
    Ok(id)
}

BEGIN

pool.begin() borrows one connection and starts a transaction on it.

First UPDATE

Bo has 3,000 cents. Taking 1,000,000 would give a negative balance.

The CHECK fires

PostgreSQL refuses the row. The ? returns the error at once.

Drop means ROLLBACK

The function leaves without commit(). When tx is dropped, sqlx rolls the transaction back.

Nothing changed

No balance moved and no transfer row exists. The connection goes back to the pool.

You can see the same rollback today without a server. SQLite runs inside your program, and sqlx supports it too. This version adds the money first, so you can see that the first change is undone.

use sqlx::sqlite::{SqlitePool, SqlitePoolOptions};

#[derive(Debug, sqlx::FromRow)]
struct Account {
    owner: String,
    balance: i64,
}

async fn transfer(pool: &SqlitePool, from: &str, to: &str, amount: i64) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> {
    let mut tx = pool.begin().await?;
    sqlx::query("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ?1 WHERE owner = ?2")
        .bind(amount)
        .bind(to)
        .execute(&mut *tx)
        .await?; // the money arrives first ...
    sqlx::query("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ?1 WHERE owner = ?2")
        .bind(amount)
        .bind(from)
        .execute(&mut *tx)
        .await?; // ... and this can fail the CHECK
    tx.commit().await
}

async fn show(pool: &SqlitePool) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> {
    let rows: Vec<Account> = sqlx::query_as("SELECT owner, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY owner")
        .fetch_all(pool)
        .await?;
    let line: Vec<String> = rows.iter().map(|a| format!("{}={}", a.owner, a.balance)).collect();
    println!("{}", line.join(" "));
    Ok(())
}
def transfer(frm: str, to: str, amount: int) -> None:
    with db:  # commit at the end, or roll back on an exception
        db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE owner = ?", (amount, to))
        db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE owner = ?", (amount, frm))


def show() -> None:
    rows = db.execute("SELECT owner, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY owner").fetchall()
    print(" ".join(f"{o}={b}" for o, b in rows))

The main part creates the table, makes one good transfer and one that must fail.

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> {
    // An in-memory database lives inside one connection, so the pool keeps one.
    let pool = SqlitePoolOptions::new().max_connections(1).connect("sqlite::memory:").await?;
    sqlx::query("CREATE TABLE accounts (owner TEXT PRIMARY KEY, balance INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0))")
        .execute(&pool)
        .await?;
    sqlx::query("INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('Ann', 100), ('Bo', 5)").execute(&pool).await?;

    transfer(&pool, "Ann", "Bo", 30).await?;
    show(&pool).await?;
    match transfer(&pool, "Bo", "Ann", 500).await {
        Err(sqlx::Error::Database(e)) if e.is_check_violation() => println!("refused: {}", e.message()),
        other => println!("unexpected: {other:?}"),
    }
    show(&pool).await // Ann did NOT get 500: the first UPDATE was rolled back
}
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", autocommit=False)  # Python 3.12+: explicit transactions
db.execute("CREATE TABLE accounts (owner TEXT PRIMARY KEY, balance INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0))")
db.execute("INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('Ann', 100), ('Bo', 5)")
db.commit()

# ... transfer() and show() from above ...

transfer("Ann", "Bo", 30)
show()
try:
    transfer("Bo", "Ann", 500)
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("refused:", e)
show()
Ann=70 Bo=35
refused: CHECK constraint failed: balance >= 0
Ann=70 Bo=35

Both programs ran and printed exactly these three lines. After the refused transfer, Ann still has 70, not 570.

Editing a migration file that already ran in production. sqlx stores a checksum of each applied file, and the next start fails because the file changed. Never edit an applied migration. Add a new one that changes the schema again.

Python: Pydantic and psycopg

The Python twin of the bank uses psycopg 3.3 with its pool package, and Pydantic models for rows.

import os
import uuid
from datetime import datetime

from psycopg.rows import class_row
from psycopg.types.json import Jsonb
from psycopg_pool import ConnectionPool
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Account(BaseModel):  # one row; pydantic checks the types
    id: uuid.UUID
    owner: str
    balance_cents: int
    meta: dict
    created_at: datetime


pool = ConnectionPool(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"], min_size=1, max_size=10, open=True)

The two functions match create_account and transfer in Rust:

def create_account(owner: str, cents: int) -> Account:
    with pool.connection() as conn:  # commits when the block ends without error
        cur = conn.cursor(row_factory=class_row(Account))  # rows become Account objects
        cur.execute(
            "INSERT INTO accounts (id, owner, balance_cents, meta) VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s)"
            " RETURNING id, owner, balance_cents, meta, created_at",
            (uuid.uuid7(), owner, cents, Jsonb({})),  # values travel apart from the SQL
        )
        return cur.fetchone()


def transfer(frm: uuid.UUID, to: uuid.UUID, cents: int) -> int:
    with pool.connection() as conn, conn.transaction():  # BEGIN ... COMMIT or ROLLBACK
        cur = conn.execute(
            "UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents - %s WHERE id = %s", (cents, frm)
        )
        if cur.rowcount == 0:
            raise LookupError(f"no account {frm}")  # leaves the block: ROLLBACK
        conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents + %s WHERE id = %s", (cents, to))
        row = conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO transfers (from_id, to_id, amount_cents) VALUES (%s, %s, %s) RETURNING id",
            (frm, to, cents),
        ).fetchone()
        return row[0]

This file was checked for syntax and imports with psycopg 3.3.9, psycopg-pool 3.3.3 and Pydantic 2.14.3. It was not run here, because it needs a PostgreSQL server.

  • psycopg uses %s as the placeholder, not $1. It still sends the values apart from the SQL.
  • class_row(Account) builds an Account from each row, like FromRow.
  • At the end of with pool.connection(), an open transaction is committed, or rolled back after an exception.
  • psycopg's docs say the default of open may change, so set it explicitly. For the async pool, opening in the constructor is deprecated.
Rust and Python side by side
JobRustPython
Describe the data#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]class M(BaseModel)
When are types checked?Compile time for your code, read time for the dataRead time, by Pydantic
Row to object#[derive(FromRow)]row_factory=class_row(M)
Check SQL before runningquery! macrosNo built-in way
Placeholder$1 (Postgres), ?1 (SQLite)%s (psycopg), ? (sqlite3)
Transactionpool.begin() ... tx.commit(), drop rolls backwith conn.transaction():
PoolPgPoolOptionspsycopg_pool.ConnectionPool

"How big should the pool be?" Small. PostgreSQL's default max_connections is 100, and each connection costs server memory. Ten app instances with 20 connections each already need 200. Start near 10 per instance, measure the wait time for a connection, and grow only if it matters. Keep transactions short, so connections return to the pool fast.

Doing slow work inside a transaction, like an HTTP call to a payment service. The transaction holds row locks and a pooled connection the whole time. Other requests wait, and the pool runs dry. Do the slow call first, then open a short transaction.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for data, serde and databases
PatternPurposeModelNote

#[serde(default)]Accept missing fieldsis_admin: boolUses Default.
#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]Catch typos in input"unknown field `isAdmn`"Not with flatten.
#[serde(tag = "type")]Enums the JSON way{"type":"circle","r":1.5}Pydantic: discriminated union.
#[serde(try_from = "String")]Check a value while readingstruct Email(String)Invalid values cannot exist.
#[serde(with = "module")]A custom text form for one fieldcents as "12.34"Never f64 for money.

Uuid::now_v7()Ids that sort by time.bind(Uuid::now_v7())Python 3.14: uuid.uuid7().
PgPoolOptions::new().max_connections(n)Reuse connectionsOne pool per processKeep it small.
