The Agent Skills format

An agent needs know-how, not only tools. A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file and optional scripts and references. The open specification is at agentskills.io. Here is a small skill:

---
name: release-notes
description: Writes release notes from merged pull requests. Use when the user asks for release notes, a changelog entry or a summary of what shipped.
license: MIT
metadata:
  author: book-example
  version: "1.0"
---

# Release notes

1. Run `scripts/list_prs.sh v1.2.0` to list merged pull requests since a tag.
2. Group them under Added, Changed, Fixed.
3. Write one short line per change. Link the pull request number.
4. If a change breaks old code, put it first under "Breaking".

The top part between the --- lines is YAML frontmatter. Two fields are required. name has 1 to 64 characters: lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens, not at the start or end. description has 1 to 1,024 characters and says what the skill does and when to use it. Optional fields include license, compatibility, metadata and an experimental allowed-tools.

Why this shape? Progressive disclosure. At start, the agent loads only the name and description of every skill, about 100 tokens each. It loads the body only when a task needs the skill, and a script only when a step needs it. With 50 skills, start-up costs about 50 \cdot 100 = 5{,}000 tokens. Loading 50 full bodies of up to 5,000 tokens could cost 250,000 tokens. This is the working-set idea from operating systems: keep in fast memory only what you use now.

A checker for the main rules, in both languages:

// Check a SKILL.md against the main rules of the Agent Skills format. Std only.
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::path::Path;

fn check(dir: &str) -> Vec<String> {
    let path = Path::new(dir).join("SKILL.md");
    let text = std::fs::read_to_string(&path).unwrap_or_default();
    let parts: Vec<&str> = text.split("---\n").collect();
    if !text.starts_with("---\n") || parts.len() < 3 {
        return vec!["SKILL.md must start with YAML frontmatter between --- lines".into()];
    }
    // Only top-level "key: value" lines. A real tool uses a YAML parser.
    let fields: HashMap<&str, &str> = parts[1].lines()
        .filter(|l| !l.starts_with(' '))
        .filter_map(|l| l.split_once(':'))
        .map(|(k, v)| (k.trim(), v.trim()))
        .collect();
    let (name, desc) = (fields.get("name").copied().unwrap_or(""), fields.get("description").copied().unwrap_or(""));
    let folder = Path::new(dir).file_name().unwrap().to_str().unwrap();
    let mut errors = Vec::new();
    let good_chars = name.chars().all(|c| c.is_ascii_lowercase() || c.is_ascii_digit() || c == '-');
    let good_hyphens = !name.starts_with('-') && !name.ends_with('-') && !name.contains("--");
    if name.is_empty() || name.len() > 64 || !good_chars || !good_hyphens {
        errors.push(format!("name '{name}': 1-64 of a-z 0-9 and single hyphens inside"));
    }
    if name != folder { errors.push(format!("name '{name}' must match the folder '{folder}'")); }
    if desc.is_empty() || desc.chars().count() > 1024 {
        errors.push("description: 1 to 1024 characters, say what and when".into());
    }
    if text.lines().count() > 500 { errors.push("warning: keep SKILL.md under 500 lines".into()); }
    errors
}

fn main() {
    for dir in std::env::args().skip(1) {
        let errors = check(&dir);
        if errors.is_empty() { println!("{dir} -> ok") } else { println!("{dir} -> {errors:?}") }
    }
}
"""Check a SKILL.md against the main rules of the Agent Skills format."""
import pathlib
import re
import sys


def check(skill_dir):
    path = pathlib.Path(skill_dir) / "SKILL.md"
    text = path.read_text()
    parts = text.split("---\n")
    if not text.startswith("---\n") or len(parts) < 3:
        return ["SKILL.md must start with YAML frontmatter between --- lines"]
    # Only top-level "key: value" lines. A real tool uses a YAML parser.
    fields = dict(line.split(":", 1) for line in parts[1].splitlines()
                  if ":" in line and not line.startswith(" "))
    fields = {k.strip(): v.strip() for k, v in fields.items()}
    name, desc = fields.get("name", ""), fields.get("description", "")
    errors = []
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*", name) or len(name) > 64:
        errors.append(f"name '{name}': 1-64 of a-z 0-9 and single hyphens inside")
    if name != path.parent.name:
        errors.append(f"name '{name}' must match the folder '{path.parent.name}'")
    if not 1 <= len(desc) <= 1024:
        errors.append("description: 1 to 1024 characters, say what and when")
    if len(text.splitlines()) > 500:
        errors.append("warning: keep SKILL.md under 500 lines")
    return errors


for d in sys.argv[1:]:
    print(d, "->", check(d) or "ok")
$ ./skillcheck release-notes Release_Notes
release-notes -> ok
Release_Notes -> ["name 'release--notes': 1-64 of a-z 0-9 and single hyphens inside", "name 'release--notes' must match the folder 'Release_Notes'", "description: 1 to 1024 characters, say what and when"]

Skills, AGENTS.md and MCP all belong to the same open movement. In December 2025 the Linux Foundation announced the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), with MCP, goose and AGENTS.md as its first projects. The list can grow, so check the AAIF site for the current projects.

A vague description such as "Helps with notes." The agent decides from the description alone whether to load the skill. Say what it does and when: "Writes release notes from merged pull requests. Use when ..."

A minimal MCP server

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets any agent use tools from any server. It uses JSON-RPC 2.0 messages. Over the stdio transport, the agent starts the server as a child process. Each message is one line on stdin or stdout. Logs must go to stderr, never stdout.

The current version of the protocol is 2026-07-28. It made MCP stateless. The old initialize handshake is gone. Every request carries its protocol version in _meta. Servers must answer server/discover. Every result has resultType, and list results carry cache hints ttlMs and cacheScope. Our server implements discover, tools/list and tools/call.

// A minimal MCP server (protocol 2026-07-28) over stdio, with serde_json.
use serde_json::{Value, json};
use std::io::{BufRead, Write};

const VERSION: &str = "2026-07-28";

fn tools() -> Value {
    json!([
        { "name": "add", "description": "Add two numbers a and b.",
          "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "required": ["a", "b"],
              "properties": { "a": { "type": "number" }, "b": { "type": "number" } } } },
        { "name": "word_count", "description": "Count the words in a text.",
          "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "required": ["text"],
              "properties": { "text": { "type": "string" } } } }
    ])
}

// Returns (text, is_error). A bad argument is a tool error, not a crash.
fn call_tool(name: &str, args: &Value) -> (String, bool) {
    if name == "add" {
        return match (&args["a"], &args["b"]) {
            (Value::Number(a), Value::Number(b)) => match (a.as_i64(), b.as_i64()) {
                (Some(a), Some(b)) => ((a + b).to_string(), false),
                _ => ((a.as_f64().unwrap() + b.as_f64().unwrap()).to_string(), false),
            },
            _ => ("a and b must be numbers".into(), true),
        };
    }
    let text = args["text"].as_str().unwrap_or("");
    (text.split_whitespace().count().to_string(), false)
}
"""A minimal MCP server (protocol 2026-07-28) over stdio. Standard library only."""
import json
import sys

VERSION = "2026-07-28"
META = {"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo": {"name": "tiny-tools", "version": "0.1.0"}}
TOOLS = [
    {"name": "add", "description": "Add two numbers a and b.",
     "inputSchema": {"type": "object", "required": ["a", "b"],
                     "properties": {"a": {"type": "number"}, "b": {"type": "number"}}}},
    {"name": "word_count", "description": "Count the words in a text.",
     "inputSchema": {"type": "object", "required": ["text"],
                     "properties": {"text": {"type": "string"}}}},
]


def call_tool(name, args):
    """Return (text, is_error). A bad argument is a tool error, not a crash."""
    if name == "add":
        a, b = args.get("a"), args.get("b")
        if not all(isinstance(x, (int, float)) and not isinstance(x, bool) for x in (a, b)):
            return "a and b must be numbers", True
        return str(a + b), False
    return str(len(str(args.get("text", "")).split())), False
fn handle(msg: &Value) -> Option<Value> {
    let id = msg.get("id")?.clone(); // no id: a notification, no reply
    let (method, params) = (msg["method"].as_str().unwrap_or(""), &msg["params"]);
    let error = |code: i64, message: String, data: Value| {
        let mut e = json!({ "code": code, "message": message });
        if !data.is_null() { e["data"] = data; }
        Some(json!({ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": id, "error": e }))
    };
    let ok = |mut result: Value| {
        result["resultType"] = json!("complete");
        result["_meta"] = json!({ "io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo": { "name": "tiny-tools", "version": "0.1.0" } });
        Some(json!({ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": id, "result": result }))
    };
    if method == "initialize" { // an old client: say which version we speak
        return error(-32601, format!("no initialize: this server speaks MCP {VERSION}"), Value::Null);
    }
    let asked = &params["_meta"]["io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion"];
    if asked != VERSION {
        return error(-32022, "Unsupported protocol version".into(), json!({ "supported": [VERSION], "requested": asked }));
    }
    match method {
        "server/discover" => ok(json!({ "supportedVersions": [VERSION], "capabilities": { "tools": {} },
                                        "ttlMs": 3600000, "cacheScope": "public" })),
        "tools/list" => ok(json!({ "tools": tools(), "ttlMs": 300000, "cacheScope": "public" })),
        "tools/call" => {
            let name = params["name"].as_str().unwrap_or("");
            if !tools().as_array().unwrap().iter().any(|t| t["name"] == name) {
                return error(-32602, format!("Unknown tool: {name}"), Value::Null);
            }
            let (text, is_error) = call_tool(name, &params["arguments"]);
            ok(json!({ "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": text }], "isError": is_error }))
        }
        _ => error(-32601, "Method not found".into(), Value::Null),
    }
}
def handle(msg):
    """Answer one JSON-RPC request. Return None for a notification."""
    if "id" not in msg:
        return None  # notifications get no reply
    rid, method, params = msg["id"], msg.get("method"), msg.get("params", {})

    def error(code, message, data=None):
        err = {"code": code, "message": message} | ({"data": data} if data else {})
        return {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rid, "error": err}

    def ok(result):
        return {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rid, "result": {"resultType": "complete", "_meta": META} | result}

    if method == "initialize":  # an old client: say which version we speak
        return error(-32601, f"no initialize: this server speaks MCP {VERSION}")
    asked = params.get("_meta", {}).get("io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion")
    if asked != VERSION:
        return error(-32022, "Unsupported protocol version", {"supported": [VERSION], "requested": asked})
    if method == "server/discover":
        return ok({"supportedVersions": [VERSION], "capabilities": {"tools": {}},
                   "ttlMs": 3600000, "cacheScope": "public"})
    if method == "tools/list":
        return ok({"tools": TOOLS, "ttlMs": 300000, "cacheScope": "public"})
    if method == "tools/call":
        if params.get("name") not in {t["name"] for t in TOOLS}:
            return error(-32602, f"Unknown tool: {params.get('name')}")
        text, is_error = call_tool(params["name"], params.get("arguments", {}))
        return ok({"content": [{"type": "text", "text": text}], "isError": is_error})
    return error(-32601, "Method not found")
fn main() {
    let mut out = std::io::stdout().lock();
    for line in std::io::stdin().lock().lines() { // one JSON message per line
        let line = line.expect("stdin closed");
        let reply = match serde_json::from_str::<Value>(&line) {
            Ok(msg) => handle(&msg),
            Err(_) => Some(json!({ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": null,
                                   "error": { "code": -32700, "message": "Parse error" } })),
        };
        if let Some(r) = reply {
            writeln!(out, "{r}").unwrap();
            out.flush().unwrap(); // the client waits for this line
        }
        eprintln!("handled {}...", line.chars().take(40).collect::<String>()); // logs: stderr
    }
}
for line in sys.stdin:  # one JSON message per line
    try:
        reply = handle(json.loads(line))
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        reply = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": None, "error": {"code": -32700, "message": "Parse error"}}
    if reply is not None:
        print(json.dumps(reply, separators=(",", ":"), sort_keys=True), flush=True)
    print(f"handled {line[:40].strip()}...", file=sys.stderr)  # logs go to stderr

To test it, we pipe eight requests into the server: discover, list, two calls of add, an unknown tool, an old version, an old initialize, and one notification.

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"server/discover","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"add","arguments":{"a":2,"b":3},"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"add","arguments":{"a":"two","b":3},"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":5,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"delete_all","arguments":{},"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":6,"method":"tools/list","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2025-11-25"}}}

Both servers print exactly the same bytes. I compared them with diff. Here are the replies, without the long reply to tools/list:

{"id":1,"jsonrpc":"2.0","result":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo":{"name":"tiny-tools","version":"0.1.0"}},"cacheScope":"public","capabilities":{"tools":{}},"resultType":"complete","supportedVersions":["2026-07-28"],"ttlMs":3600000}}
{"id":3,"jsonrpc":"2.0","result":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo":{"name":"tiny-tools","version":"0.1.0"}},"content":[{"text":"5","type":"text"}],"isError":false,"resultType":"complete"}}
{"id":4,"jsonrpc":"2.0","result":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo":{"name":"tiny-tools","version":"0.1.0"}},"content":[{"text":"a and b must be numbers","type":"text"}],"isError":true,"resultType":"complete"}}
{"error":{"code":-32602,"message":"Unknown tool: delete_all"},"id":5,"jsonrpc":"2.0"}
{"error":{"code":-32022,"data":{"requested":"2025-11-25","supported":["2026-07-28"]},"message":"Unsupported protocol version"},"id":6,"jsonrpc":"2.0"}
{"error":{"code":-32601,"message":"no initialize: this server speaks MCP 2026-07-28"},"id":7,"jsonrpc":"2.0"}

Read the replies one by one. A bad argument to add is a tool error: a normal result with isError: true, which the model can read and fix. An unknown tool is a protocol error with code -32602. The wrong version gets error -32022 with the list of supported versions. The notification gets no reply at all.

Give each part of a system only the rights it needs for its job, and nothing more.

In simple words: an agent with a delete_all tool can delete everything, by mistake or because a web page told it to. Expose few tools. Validate every input on the server. The MCP spec also says a human should be able to deny tool calls. The skill field allowed-tools follows the same idea.

Printing a debug line to stdout in a stdio server. The client tries to read it as JSON and the connection breaks. Use stderr, as both servers above do.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for agents and orchestration
PatternPurposeModelNote
Loop with a step limitRun a tool-calling agent safelyfor step in 1..=max_stepsReturn an error when the limit is reached.
Error as a resultLet the model fix its own mistakeToolResult { ok: false, text }Do not crash. Do not hide it.
Fake model in testsTest the loop with no key and no costasync fn fake_model(history)Script the replies from the history.
Reducer per keyMerge parallel writesAnnotated[list, operator.add]No reducer plus two writers is an error.
Checkpoint at the barrierResume after a crashwrite to .tmp, then renameKeep pending writes so good nodes do not re-run.
Semaphore limitRespect rate limitsSemaphore::new(3)Give the permit back before you sleep.
Timeout per tryStop a hanging calltimeout(300 ms, work())The cancelled work may have happened anyway.
Retry with back-offSurvive short failures20 ms, 40 ms, 80 ms plus jitterRetry only transient errors, and only idempotent work.
Store, search, forgetKeep context small and freshtop-k by cosine, strength by half-lifeAlways support delete on request.
Atomic claimOne worker per taskone conditional updateLocks need an expiry.
SKILL.md with a clear descriptionLoad know-how only when neededname + description in frontmatterName equals the folder name.
Stateless MCP requestCall tools on any server_meta with protocolVersionLogs go to stderr, never stdout.

Practice

A task has 5 steps and each step works with probability 0.9. The task works with probability about ? (two decimals).

One model call takes 4 seconds and you allow 8 calls at once. By Little's law the most you can do is ? calls per second.

A tool call fails because the model passed a wrong argument. What should the agent loop do?

  • Stop the program with a panic.
  • Send the error back to the model as a tool result.
  • Ignore it and continue without the result.

The model can read the error and correct the argument, as in step 2 of our run.

Nodes web and docs run in the same step and both write the key summary, which has no reducer. What happens in LangGraph?

  • The last node to finish wins.
  • The values are joined into a list.
  • An InvalidUpdateError is raised.

A key without a reducer accepts one value per step. Give it a reducer to accept more.

Which error should the orchestrator retry?

  • 400 bad input
  • 503 busy
  • 401 not allowed

5xx and timeouts are often short problems. 4xx errors repeat the same way every time.

  1. Why does our orchestrator give the semaphore permit back before the back-off sleep?
    Answer

    A sleeping job does no work. If it kept the permit, it would block a place, and fewer than 3 jobs would run. Giving it back keeps all 3 places busy.

  2. Use Amdahl's law: 40% of a job is sequential. What is the speed-up with 4 workers, and what is the limit?
    Answer

    f = 0.6. S(4) = 1/(0.4 + 0.6/4) = 1/0.55 \approx 1.82. The limit is 1/0.4 = 2.5.

  3. Three independent checkers each catch a bad answer with probability 0.8. You reject the answer if at least two of them say "bad". What is the chance to catch a bad answer?
    Answer

    0.8^3 + 3 \cdot 0.8^2 \cdot 0.2 = 0.512 + 0.384 = 0.896. This is the Condorcet jury theorem at work: a majority of independent voters, each right more than half the time, is right more often than one voter. Real model checkers often make the same mistakes, so the gain is smaller.

  4. Our graph node write sends an email. The run crashes after the email is sent but before the checkpoint. What happens on resume, and how do you fix it?
    Answer

    The step runs again, so the email is sent twice. Make it idempotent: give the email a fixed id from the thread id and step number, and let the mail service drop duplicates. Or record "email sent" in a durable store before you send, and check it first.

  5. Write the request line that asks an MCP 2026-07-28 server for its tools.
    Answer

    {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":9,"method":"tools/list","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28"}}} on one line, with no line breaks inside.

  6. Hard: two Paperclip-style agents claim tasks with "SELECT the task WHERE assignee IS NULL" and then "UPDATE SET assignee = me". What can go wrong, and what is the fix?
    Answer

    Both agents can read the same free task before either writes. Both then think they own it. Use one atomic statement: UPDATE tasks SET assignee = me WHERE id = 7 AND assignee IS NULL, and check that exactly one row changed. Add an expiry time so a dead agent does not hold the task forever.

Key takeaways

  • An agent is a loop around a model. Keep a step limit, and return tool errors as results.
  • A state graph runs in supersteps: parallel nodes on one snapshot, a barrier, reducers, then a checkpoint.
  • Checkpoints make resume possible. Pending writes and idempotent side effects make it correct.
  • An orchestrator needs a parallel limit, a timeout per try, and retries with back-off for transient errors only.
  • Little's law, Amdahl's law and the chain formula tell you speed and reliability before you build.
  • Skills load know-how step by step. MCP 2026-07-28 is stateless: every request names its version.

Sources

  • LangGraph on GitHub. The framework, its features and its inspirations.
  • LangGraph checkpointers. Supersteps, threads, pending writes and durability modes.
  • Paperclip on GitHub. Companies, goals, heartbeats, execution locks and budgets.
  • Agent Skills specification. SKILL.md fields, folders and progressive disclosure.
  • MCP 2026-07-28 key changes. Stateless requests, server/discover and resultType.
  • Linux Foundation: the Agentic AI Foundation. The founding projects MCP, goose and AGENTS.md.

Rust editions 2015, 2018, 2021, 2024

Rust promises that old code keeps working. But sometimes the language needs a breaking change, such as a new keyword. Editions solve this problem. This chapter shows what each edition changed, with real compiler output, and how to move a crate to the next one.

  • Explain what an edition is and what it is not.
  • Name the main changes of Rust 2018, 2021 and 2024, with a before and after example.
  • Predict how one file behaves under two different editions.
  • Move a crate to a new edition with cargo fix --edition, step by step.
  • Say what is known today about the next edition.

One file, two results

Here is a tiny program. It uses async as a variable name.

fn main() {
    let async = 3; // a normal name in 2015
    println!("{}", async + 1);
}

We compile the same file twice. Only the flag --edition changes.

4
error: expected identifier, found keyword `async`
 --> kw_async.rs:2:9
  |
2 |     let async = 3; // a normal name in 2015
  |         ^^^^^ expected identifier, found keyword
  |
help: escape `async` to use it as an identifier
  |
2 |     let r#async = 3; // a normal name in 2015
  |         ++

The compiler is the same. The source is the same. The result is different. The reason is the edition.

  • An edition is a set of language rules. It has a year as its name: 2015, 2018, 2021 or 2024.
  • Each crate chooses its own edition.
  • In 2018 async became a keyword. So it cannot be a variable name any more.
  • The help line shows the way out. A raw identifier like r#async is still a normal name.

Where you choose the edition

[package]
name = "shop"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"   # the rules for this crate
rustc --edition 2021 main.rs

cargo new always writes the newest edition. On this machine that is 2024. A wrong year is refused.

error: invalid value '2019' for '--edition <YEAR>'
  [possible values: 2015, 2018, 2021, 2024]

  tip: a similar value exists: '2021'

A Cargo.toml with no edition line does not mean "newest". It means 2015. Plain rustc without the flag also uses 2015. Always write the line.

The four editions

Every stable edition so far (checked on 15 November 2026)
EditionFirst Rust versionDateTheme
20151.0.015 May 2015stability: the default rules
20181.31.06 Dec 2018productivity: new paths and keywords
20211.56.021 Oct 2021consistency: small clean-ups
20241.85.020 Feb 2025the largest edition so far
  1. 15 May 2015 Rust 1.0. Rust 2015 starts. It gets its name only later, in 2017.
  2. 6 Dec 2018 Rust 1.31. Rust 2018, the first real edition.
  3. 21 Oct 2021 Rust 1.56. Rust 2021.
  4. 20 Feb 2025 Rust 1.85. Rust 2024.
  5. 26 Jun 2025 Rust 1.88. Let chains arrive, but only for Rust 2024.
  6. 12 Nov 2026 Rust 1.100. One 2024 rule, the never type fallback, now applies to every edition.

What an edition is not

Look at this list of features. Each came out in a normal release. Which edition do you need for it?

  • Non-lexical lifetimes, a smarter borrow checker. It came with Rust 2018 in 1.31. Then 1.36 gave it to Rust 2015 too.
  • async fn and .await came in 1.39. They need 2018 or later, only because of the keywords.
  • Const generics came in 1.51. They work in every edition.

So most new features land in all editions. An edition carries only the changes that would break old code.

An edition is

  • a choice for one crate
  • a small set of breaking rules
  • opt-in: you move when you want
  • supported by every newer compiler

An edition is not

  • a compiler version (1.99 is a version)
  • a new language or a fork
  • a list of all new features
  • a forced upgrade for your users

Rust 1.99 still compiles 2015 code. Later compilers will keep doing so. That is the promise of stable Rust.

Python made a different choice

Python also turned async into a keyword, in Python 3.7. But Python has no editions. So the change hit every file at once.

// Cargo.toml says edition = "2015":
let async = 3;     // still fine today

// Cargo.toml says edition = "2018" or later:
let r#async = 3;   // the raw name is needed
async = 3
print(async + 1)
  File "/home/you/kw.py", line 1
    async = 3
          ^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax

Python has a small tool with the same idea: from __future__ import .... It switches on new rules for one file. For example, annotations stores type hints as text.

An edition is like a house rule. Each family (crate) picks its rules. The families still visit each other and talk. They do not need the same rules for that.

"Rust 2024" is not a Rust version. You cannot install "Rust 2024". You install a compiler, such as 1.99.0. It supports 2015, 2018, 2021 and 2024.

How editions keep old code working

A program often has many crates. Your crate may use 2024. A dependency may use 2015. They still build into one program.

A crate of any edition must work together with crates of every other edition. So the choice of edition is private to each crate.

In simple words: you can move to 2024 today. Your users and your dependencies do not have to move with you. Example: a 2024 crate depends on a 2015 crate with a function named gen. In 2024 gen is a keyword. The 2024 crate simply calls r#gen().

This rule limits what an edition may change. The Edition Guide calls the changes "skin deep". All Rust code ends up in the same MIR. An edition can change how text is read. It cannot change what a type is.

Why a trait impl cannot depend on the edition

Assume [T; N]: IntoIterator existed only in 2021 crates. A 2018 crate and a 2021 crate could then disagree about one type. One generic function would behave in two ways. So Rust 1.53 added the impl for all editions. Only the method-call syntax array.into_iter() hides it in 2015 and 2018. The next section shows the result.

The tools that make it work

  • Every change has a lint. It warns about code that the next edition will read in a new way.
  • These lints form a group, such as rust_2024_compatibility.
  • cargo fix --edition applies their suggestions for you.
  • The fixed code works in both the old and the new edition. So you can migrate in small steps.

A macro follows the edition of the crate that defines it. It does not follow the crate that calls it. This matters for macro authors.

Rust 2015 and Rust 2018

Rust 2015 is the default edition. Its theme was stability. Nobody migrates to 2015. You only migrate away from it.

Rust 2018 arrived with Rust 1.31.0 on 6 December 2018. The edition system itself was created for it. Its theme was productivity.

Change 1: paths and modules

mod shapes {
    pub fn area(w: u32, h: u32) -> u32 { w * h }
}
mod report {
    use shapes::area; // starts at the crate root in 2015
    pub fn show() { println!("area = {}", area(2, 3)); }
}
fn main() { report::show(); }
area = 6
error[E0432]: unresolved import `shapes`
 --> paths.rs:5:9
  |
5 |     use shapes::area; // starts at the crate root in 2015
  |         ^^^^^^
  |
  = note: `use` statements changed in Rust 2018; read more at <https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/rust-2018/module-system/path-clarity.html>
help: a similar path exists
  |
5 |     use crate::shapes::area; // starts at the crate root in 2015
  |         +++++++
  • In 2018 a use path works like every other path. It starts with a crate name, crate, self or super.
  • crate::shapes::area means: start at the root of this crate. This form also works in 2015.
  • extern crate serde; is not needed any more. A dependency in Cargo.toml is enough.
  • A module foo.rs can sit next to a folder foo/. You do not need foo/mod.rs.

Change 2: new keywords

  • async, await and dyn became strict keywords.
  • try became a reserved keyword. It is kept for a future try block. So the old macro try! stopped working.
error: use of deprecated `try` macro
  = note: in the 2018 edition `try` is a reserved keyword, and the `try!()` macro is deprecated
help: you can use the `?` operator instead

Change 3: trait parameters need names

trait Scale {
    fn scale(&self, u32) -> u32; // no parameter name: a warning
}
trait Scale {
    fn scale(&self, _: u32) -> u32; // a name, even `_`, is required
}

Rust 2018 also changed some Cargo defaults for finding targets. And cargo install for the current folder now needs --path ..

Many people think dyn Trait is a 2018 feature. The syntax works in every edition since Rust 1.27. What changed later is the old form &Trait. It became an error in 2021.

Rust 2021

Rust 2021 arrived with Rust 1.56.0 on 21 October 2021. It is a small edition of clean-ups. Here are its changes.

Additions to the prelude

The prelude got TryFrom, TryInto and FromIterator.

Cargo resolver 2 by default

edition = "2021" means resolver = "2". Features of a dependency are no longer merged in every case.

IntoIterator for arrays

array.into_iter() now gives values, not references.

Disjoint capture in closures

A closure captures only the fields it uses, not the whole variable.

Panic macro consistency

panic! always reads its first argument as a format string, like println!.

Reserved syntax

prefix"text", prefix#name and prefix'c' are reserved for future syntax. Later, c"text" (1.77) and raw lifetimes like 'r#gen (1.83) used this room.

Warnings promoted to errors

Bare trait objects like &Trait and the range pattern 0...9 are errors.

Or patterns in macro_rules

The fragment $p:pat also matches A | B. The new $p:pat_param keeps the old meaning.

Before and after: arrays

fn type_of<T>(_: &T) -> &'static str {
    std::any::type_name::<T>()
}

fn main() {
    let scores = [10, 20, 30];
    for s in scores.into_iter() {
        println!("{}", type_of(&s)); // what type is one item?
        break;
    }
}
warning: this method call resolves to `<&[T; N] as IntoIterator>::into_iter` (due to backwards compatibility), but will resolve to `<[T; N] as IntoIterator>::into_iter` in Rust 2021
  = note: `#[warn(array_into_iter)]` (part of `#[warn(rust_2021_compatibility)]`) on by default
&i32
i32

The same line gives a different type. The warning in 2018 is the migration lint. It tells you before you move.

Before and after: closures

struct Order {
    id: String,
    total: u32,
}

fn main() {
    let order = Order { id: String::from("A-7"), total: 40 };
    let id = order.id; // move one field out
    let show = || println!("total = {}", order.total); // use another field
    show();
    println!("id = {id}");
}
error[E0382]: borrow of partially moved value: `order`
 --> capture.rs:9:16
  |
8 |     let id = order.id; // move one field out
  |              -------- value partially moved here
9 |     let show = || println!("total = {}", order.total); // use another field
  |                ^^                        ----------- borrow occurs due to use in closure
  |                |
  |                value borrowed here after partial move
total = 40
id = A-7

In 2018 the closure captures all of order. In 2021 it captures only order.total. The change can also change when values are dropped. So cargo fix may add a line like let _ = &order; to keep the old behaviour.

Before and after: panic, prelude and old syntax

More changes, tested with rustc 1.99.0
CodeEdition 2018Edition 2021
panic!("{}");warning, then panics with the text {}error: 1 positional argument in format string, but no arguments were given
big.try_into() with no use lineerror[E0599]: no method named try_intocompiles
0...49 => "fail"warning: ... range patterns are deprecatederror[E0783]
fn talk(a: &Speak)warning: trait objects without an explicit dyn are deprecatederror[E0782]: expected a type, found a trait

Do not pass a variable as the only argument of panic!. Write panic!("{}", msg). For a value that is not text, use std::panic::panic_any(value).

Rust 2024 in detail

Rust 2024 arrived with Rust 1.85.0 on 20 February 2025. The release post calls it the largest edition so far. This tree shows all its parts.

RPIT lifetime capture

// Return the letters of a word, one by one.
fn letters(word: &str) -> impl Iterator<Item = char> {
    word.chars() // this iterator borrows `word`
}

fn main() {
    let s = String::from("rust");
    println!("{:?}", letters(&s).collect::<Vec<_>>());
}
error[E0700]: hidden type for `impl Iterator<Item = char>` captures lifetime that does not appear in bounds
 --> rpit_a.rs:3:5
  |
2 | fn letters(word: &str) -> impl Iterator<Item = char> {
  |                  ----     -------------------------- opaque type defined here
  |                  |
  |                  hidden type `Chars<'_>` captures the anonymous lifetime defined here
help: add a `use<...>` bound to explicitly capture `'_`
['r', 'u', 's', 't']
  • RPIT means a function returns impl Trait. The real type behind it is the hidden type.
  • The rule in 2024: the hidden type may use every generic parameter in scope. This includes all lifetimes.
  • Before 2024, lifetimes were captured only when they appeared in the bounds.

The new default can capture too much. This function returns only numbers. But 2024 assumes the result still borrows v.

// `use<>` says: the result borrows nothing.
fn positions(v: &Vec<u32>) -> impl Iterator<Item = usize> + use<> {
    0..v.len()
}

fn main() {
    let mut v = vec![5, 6];
    let it = positions(&v);
    v.push(7); // allowed: `it` holds no borrow of `v`
    println!("{:?}", it.collect::<Vec<_>>());
}
[0, 1]

Without + use<>, edition 2024 says error[E0502]: cannot borrow `v` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable. The note says "Rust 2024 has adjusted the impl Trait lifetime capture rules". The chapter Lifetimes explains use<..> in depth.

if let temporary scope

use std::cell::RefCell;

fn main() {
    let cache: RefCell<Option<u32>> = RefCell::new(None);
    if let Some(n) = *cache.borrow() {
        println!("cached: {n}");
    } else {
        // Fill the cache. This needs a mutable borrow.
        *cache.borrow_mut() = Some(42);
        println!("filled");
    }
    println!("{:?}", cache.borrow());
}
thread 'main' (116758694) panicked at iflet.rs:9:16:
RefCell already borrowed
filled
Some(42)

cache.borrow() makes a temporary. In 2021 it lives until the end of the whole if let, including else. In 2024 it is dropped before else starts. With a RwLock, the 2021 rule can even cause a deadlock.

Tail expression temporary scope

use std::cell::RefCell;

fn name_len() -> usize {
    let name = RefCell::new(String::from("Ferris"));
    name.borrow().len() // a temporary `Ref` is made here
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", name_len());
}
error[E0597]: `name` does not live long enough
 --> tail.rs:5:5
  |
4 |     let name = RefCell::new(String::from("Ferris"));
  |         ---- binding `name` declared here
5 |     name.borrow().len() // a temporary `Ref` is made here
  |     ^^^^---------
  |     |
  |     borrowed value does not live long enough
  |     a temporary with access to the borrow is created here ...
6

The last expression of a block is its tail. In 2024, temporaries in the tail are dropped before the local variables. In 2021 they were dropped after. That order made this code fail.

The new rule can also break code. let x = { &String::from("1234") }.len(); works in 2021 but fails in 2024. The String is now dropped at the end of the block. Move the block into its own let.

Unsafe extern blocks and unsafe attributes

unsafe extern "C" {
    // `safe` is our promise: any i32 is fine for abs.
    safe fn abs(x: i32) -> i32;
}

// SAFETY: no other symbol in the program is called `add_one`.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn add_one(x: i32) -> i32 {
    x + 1
}

fn main() {
    println!("{} {}", abs(-7), add_one(1)); // no unsafe block for abs
}
7 2
  • An extern block lists foreign functions. Wrong types there cause undefined behaviour. So 2024 requires unsafe extern.
  • Inside, mark each item safe or unsafe. An item without a mark is unsafe.
  • Three attributes must now be written as unsafe: no_mangle, export_name and link_section. They change the global symbol names.
  • The old forms give "extern blocks must be unsafe" and "unsafe attribute used without unsafe" in 2024.

The chapter Unsafe Rust and FFI covers these in depth.

Three more rules about unsafe

Tested with rustc 1.99.0
CodeEdition 2021Edition 2024
std::env::set_var("MODE", "test");compileserror[E0133]: call to unsafe function set_var
let r = &COUNTER; on a static mutwarning: creating a shared reference to mutable staticerror (lint static_mut_refs is deny)
an unsafe call inside unsafe fn with no unsafe { }compileswarning[E0133] (lint unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn)

set_var and remove_var are not safe when other threads run. Calling them is now unsafe. The old CommandExt::before_exec is unsafe too.

The gen keyword

fn gen(n: u32) -> Vec<u32> {
    (0..n).collect()
}
fn r#gen(n: u32) -> Vec<u32> { // raw name
    (0..n).collect()
}

In 2024, gen is a reserved keyword. It is kept for future gen blocks, which will make iterators easy to write. The 2021 form gives "expected identifier, found reserved keyword `gen`". A common victim was the method rand::Rng::gen. The rand crate 0.9 renamed it to random.

Never type fallback

fn make<T: Default>() -> Result<T, String> {
    Ok(T::default())
}

fn run() -> Result<(), String> {
    make()?; // which T? Nothing here says it.
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", run());
}
warning: this function depends on never type fallback being `()`
note: in edition 2024, the requirement `!: Default` will fail
Ok(())
error: this function depends on never type fallback being `()`
  = note: `#[deny(dependency_on_unit_never_type_fallback)]` (part of `#[deny(rust_2024_compatibility)]`) on by default
help: use `()` annotations to avoid fallback changes
  |
6 |     make::<()>()?; // which T? Nothing here says it.
  |         ++++++
error[E0277]: the trait bound `!: Default` is not satisfied
 --> never.rs:6:5
  |
6 |     make()?; // which T? Nothing here says it.
  |     ^^^^^^ the trait `Default` is not implemented for `!`
  • The never type ! is the type of return, panic! and the error path of ?.
  • When the compiler cannot find a type, it uses a fallback. Before 2024 it was (). In 2024 it is !.
  • The fix works everywhere: name the type, as in make::<()>()?.

Rust 1.100.0 (12 November 2026) made the fallback ! in all editions. The Edition Guide now says this change is no longer edition-specific. This machine has 1.99.0, so the tabs above still show a difference. See Rust recent releases.

Small changes in the standard library and macros

Future and IntoFuture in the prelude

fn answer() -> impl Future<Output = u8> needs use std::future::Future; in 2021. In 2024 it compiles without it. If your own trait also has a method poll, a call can become unclear. cargo fix then writes the full trait path.

IntoIterator for Box<[T]>

For a Box<[u32]>, ids.into_iter() gives &u32 in 2021 and u32 in 2024. It is the same story as arrays in 2021.

The expr fragment in macro_rules

In 2024, $e:expr also matches const { ... } and _. Our test macro picked "rule 2" in 2021 and "rule 1" in 2024. The new fragment expr_2021 keeps the old meaning.

Match ergonomics reservations

In a pattern that skips references, you cannot write mut, ref or & on a binding. This keeps room for better rules later.

Let chains

if let Some(t) = input && let Ok(n) = t.parse::<i32>() && n > 0. Stable since 1.88, only in 2024. In 2021 the error is "let chains are only allowed in Rust 2024 or later". They need the new if let scope.

Reserved syntax

#"text"# without a prefix, and ##, are reserved for the future.

Cargo, rustdoc and rustfmt

  • edition = "2024" means resolver = "3". This resolver prefers dependency versions that fit your rust-version. See Cargo, crates and workspaces.
  • Double names are gone. Write [package], not [project]. Write dev-dependencies, not dev_dependencies.
  • default-features on a workspace dependency: Rust 1.85 to 1.98 rejected one case. Since 1.99, the package setting wins.
  • Doctests are compiled together into one program. Tests run much faster.
  • rustfmt has a style edition. Set style_edition = "2024" in rustfmt.toml to choose it on its own.

Migrate with cargo fix --edition

We take a real crate on edition 2021. It has six things that 2024 reads differently.

use std::cell::RefCell;

extern "C" {
    fn abs(x: i32) -> i32;
}

#[no_mangle]
pub extern "C" fn shop_version() -> u32 {
    3
}

fn gen(n: u32) -> Vec<u32> {
    (1..=n).collect()
}

fn main() {
    std::env::set_var("SHOP_MODE", "test");
    let stock: RefCell<Option<u32>> = RefCell::new(None);
    if let Some(n) = *stock.borrow() {
        println!("stock {n}");
    } else {
        println!("no stock yet");
    }
    let ids: Box<[u32]> = gen(3).into_boxed_slice();
    for id in ids.into_iter() {
        print!("{id} ");
    }
    println!("| {} {}", unsafe { abs(-5) }, shop_version());
}
  1. Commit your work. Run cargo update. Run cargo test. Everything must pass on the old edition.
  2. Keep edition = "2021". Run cargo fix --edition. It applies the migration lints.
  3. Read the result. Look for new comments that start with FIXME. Check every match that was an if let.
  4. Now change Cargo.toml to edition = "2024".
  5. Run cargo build and cargo test. Fix what is left by hand.
  6. Run cargo fmt. Commit the formatting on its own, so reviews stay clear.
   Migrating Cargo.toml from 2021 edition to 2024
    Checking shop v0.1.0 (/home/you/shop)
   Migrating src/main.rs from 2021 edition to 2024
       Fixed src/main.rs (7 fixes)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.14s

The flag --allow-no-vcs was needed only because this test folder is not a git folder. These are the seven fixes:

-extern "C" {
+unsafe extern "C" {
-#[no_mangle]
+#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
-fn gen(n: u32) -> Vec<u32> {
+fn r#gen(n: u32) -> Vec<u32> {
-    std::env::set_var("SHOP_MODE", "test");
+    // FIXME: Audit that the environment access only happens in single-threaded code.
+    unsafe { std::env::set_var("SHOP_MODE", "test") };
-    if let Some(n) = *stock.borrow() {
+    match *stock.borrow() { Some(n) => {
         println!("stock {n}");
-    } else {
+    } _ => {
         println!("no stock yet");
-    }
+    }}
-    let ids: Box<[u32]> = gen(3).into_boxed_slice();
-    for id in ids.into_iter() {
+    let ids: Box<[u32]> = r#gen(3).into_boxed_slice();
+    for id in ids.iter() {

After step 4 the program prints the same line as before: no stock yet, then 1 2 3 | 5 3. cargo fmt then turns the odd match into normal layout.

  • Each fix keeps the old meaning. The match keeps the borrow alive into the second arm, like 2021 did.
  • Here the old meaning is not needed. After the move you can turn the match back into if let.
  • The FIXME is real work. cargo fix cannot prove that no other thread runs.

Do not change Cargo.toml first. On a 2024 crate, cargo fix --edition only says: warning: `src/main.rs` is already on the latest edition (2024), unable to migrate further. Then it prints the right order of steps.

Bigger projects

  • A workspace: every package has its own edition. Move one package at a time.
  • Features and platforms: cargo fix sees one setup at a time. Run it with --all-features, and with --target for other platforms.
  • A fix fails: Cargo undoes it and warns. --broken-code keeps the broken result, so you can repair it.
  • One lint at a time: add #![warn(rust_2024_compatibility)], or one lint such as #![warn(if_let_rescope)]. Then run plain cargo fix.
  • Macros: cargo fix cannot always fix code that a macro makes. Procedural macros need manual work.

Is a next edition coming?

Ask the compiler first. rustc 1.99.0 knows a placeholder named future.

$ rustc --edition 2027 e.rs
error: argument for `--edition` must be one of: <2015|2018|2021|2024|future>. (instead was `2027`)

$ rustc --edition future e.rs
error: the crate requires edition future, but the latest edition supported by this Rust version is 2024

The facts on 15 November 2026:

  • The stable editions are 2015, 2018, 2021 and 2024. The Edition Guide has no fifth edition.
  • The Rust blog has announced no next edition. The Inside Rust blog has no such post either.
  • The Edition Guide says there is "roughly a three year window" between editions. The project never promised a fixed rhythm.
  • The edition team met on 29 September 2026. Its public notes say many people want an Edition 2027. They also discuss one edition every year. No decision is recorded.
  • A draft from October 2026 proposes a very small "Edition 2026". It says it is not approved yet.
  • One idea for a next edition is new range types. gen blocks do not need one, because 2024 already reserved the word.

A next edition is likely, but its year and content are not decided. Check the Edition Guide and the Rust blog before you plan for it.

Three answers impress. First, editions are per crate and crates of all editions link together. Second, most features are not edition-gated. Third, migration is cargo fix --edition, then the Cargo.toml change, then tests.

Four editions in four slides

Rust 2015: stability

Rust 1.0, May 2015. The default when no edition is written. Every newer compiler still supports it.

Rust 2018: productivity

Rust 1.31. New paths with crate::, no extern crate, the keywords async, await, dyn, and a reserved try.

Rust 2021: consistency

Rust 1.56. Arrays iterate by value, closures capture fields, panic! formats, TryInto in the prelude, dyn is required.

Rust 2024: the largest

Rust 1.85. New capture and drop rules, unsafe made visible, gen reserved, resolver 3, and let chains since 1.88.

The next one

Not decided on 15 November 2026. Discussed: Edition 2027, maybe yearly editions after that.

Patterns to remember

Edition patterns you will use
PatternPurposeModelNote
edition = "YEAR" in [package]Choose the rules for one crateedition = "2024"No line means 2015, not the newest.
rustc --edition YEAR file.rsTest one file under one editionrustc --edition 2021 tail.rsPlain rustc also defaults to 2015.
r#nameUse a name that became a keywordfn r#gen(n: u32)Works in every edition. A 2024 crate can call a 2015 gen.
use crate::module::item;Import from the root of this crateuse crate::shapes::area;Needed since 2018. It also works in 2015.
&dyn TraitName a trait objectfn talk(a: &dyn Speak)Bare &Speak is an error since 2021.
for x in arrayIterate over an array by valuefor s in [10, 20, 30]array.into_iter() gave &T before 2021.
panic!("{}", value)Panic with a message from a variablepanic!("{}", msg)panic!(msg) is an error in 2021.
impl Trait + use<..>Say exactly what a returned type keeps-> impl Iterator<Item = usize> + use<>2024 captures every lifetime by default.
unsafe extern "C" { safe fn ...; }Declare C functionssafe fn abs(x: i32) -> i32;Required in 2024. You still must check the types.
#[unsafe(attr)]Mark a risky attribute#[unsafe(no_mangle)]Required in 2024 for three attributes.
unsafe { std::env::set_var(..) }Change an environment variableunsafe { std::env::set_var("MODE", "test") }Only while no other thread runs.
func::<()>()?Avoid the never type fallbackmake::<()>()?;Name the type. Then no edition can change it.
cargo fix --edition, then edit Cargo.tomlMove a crate to the next editioncargo fix --edition && cargo testThe order matters. Fix first, then switch.
#![warn(rust_2024_compatibility)]See all migration warnings, one by one#![warn(if_let_rescope)]Good for a big crate that moves slowly.

Practice

A Cargo.toml has no edition line. Which edition does Cargo use?

  • The newest one, 2024
  • 2015
  • The edition of the compiler

A missing edition means 2015, for backward compatibility. Only cargo new writes the newest year.

Your crate uses 2024. Your dependency uses 2015. What happens?

  • Cargo refuses to build.
  • You must move the dependency to 2024 first.
  • It builds. Crates of different editions work together.

Editions do not split the ecosystem. Each crate is read with its own edition.

Which of these needed an edition change?

  • Const generics in 1.51
  • gen as a reserved word
  • LazyLock in 1.80

A new keyword breaks old code that uses the word as a name. New library types and new syntax that was an error before do not break anything.

Under edition 2021, this code panics with "RefCell already borrowed". Why?

if let Some(n) = *cache.borrow() { /* ... */ } else { *cache.borrow_mut() = Some(42); }
  • A RefCell cannot hold an Option.
  • The temporary from borrow() lives into the else block.
  • The else block runs twice.

In 2021 the temporary lives until the end of the if let. In 2024 it is dropped before else.

Rust 2021 arrived with Rust 1.?.

Rust 2024 arrived with Rust 1.?.

To use the name gen in a 2024 crate, write ?.

In 2024, edition = "2024" means Cargo resolver version ?.

  1. Explain the difference between "Rust 1.99" and "Rust 2024" in two sentences.
    Answer

    Rust 1.99 is a compiler version, released on 1 October 2026. Rust 2024 is an edition, a set of rules that a crate chooses, and Rust 1.99 supports it together with 2015, 2018 and 2021.

  2. This 2018 code must move to 2021. What does cargo fix --edition do with it, and why? 
    for s in scores.into_iter() { total += *s; }
    Answer

    In 2018 scores.into_iter() on an array gives references, so *s is needed. The lint array_into_iter suggests scores.iter(). That keeps the old meaning in both editions. After the move you may write for s in scores { total += s; }.

  3. A function compiles in 2021 but not in 2024. What is wrong, and what are two ways to fix it? 
    fn ids(v: &Vec<u32>) -> impl Iterator<Item = usize> { 0..v.len() }
// the caller keeps the iterator and then pushes to v
    Answer

    In 2024 the returned type captures the lifetime of v. So the caller still borrows v and cannot push. Fix one: write + use<> on the return type. Fix two: return a concrete type, such as std::ops::Range<usize>, which holds no borrow.

  4. After cargo fix --edition you see // FIXME: Audit that the environment access only happens in single-threaded code. What must you check? Name a safer design.
    Answer

    You must check that no other thread runs when set_var is called. A safer design sets the variable before any thread starts, for example first thing in main. Even better, pass the value as normal configuration, not as an environment variable. For a child process, use Command::env.

  5. Hard. Why can the never type fallback change in all editions in 1.100, when other 2024 rules stay edition-only?
    Answer

    Rust may change behaviour on every edition when the breakage is very rare and was warned about for a long time. Rust warned about such code for many releases. In 1.92 the warnings became errors on the older editions too. A change like a new keyword is different. It would break much working code, so it must stay behind an edition.

  6. Hard. Plan the move of a workspace with 12 crates from 2021 to 2024. Write five steps.
    Answer

    One: update dependencies and make all tests pass. Two: pick the leaf crates first, those that no other crate in the workspace uses. Three: for each crate run cargo fix --edition -p name --all-features, review the diff, set its edition, and test. Four: repeat for each platform with --target if the code has cfg parts. Five: run cargo fmt and commit format changes on their own. Each step is one small pull request.

Key takeaways

  • An edition is a set of language rules. Each crate chooses one in Cargo.toml.
  • The editions are 2015, 2018 (1.31), 2021 (1.56) and 2024 (1.85). A missing edition means 2015.
  • Crates of all editions build together. Every compiler supports every older edition.
  • Most new features come to all editions. Only breaking changes wait for an edition.
  • Rust 2024 changed capture rules, temporary scopes and unsafe syntax. It reserved gen and made resolver 3 the default.
  • Migrate with cargo fix --edition first. Then change Cargo.toml. Then test and review.
  • On 15 November 2026, no next edition is decided. An Edition 2027 is being discussed.

Sources

  • The Rust Edition Guide. The official guide to every edition and to migration. Read on 15 November 2026.
  • Announcing Rust 1.85.0 and Rust 2024. The release post of the 2024 edition.
  • Announcing Rust 1.56.0 and Rust 2021. The release post of the 2021 edition.
  • Announcing Rust 1.31 and Rust 2018. The first edition, with NLL and the new module paths.
  • The Cargo Book: cargo fix. All options of the migration command.
  • Edition team triage notes, 29 September 2026. Public meeting notes about Edition 2027. No decision yet.

Rust history: 1.0 to 1.74

Rust 1.0 came out on 15 May 2015. Since then a new stable version arrives every six weeks. This chapter explains that train and walks through the big steps from 1.0 to 1.74, each with a tiny program.

  • Explain the six-week release train and the three channels: stable, beta and nightly.
  • Use rustup to pick a channel or a fixed version.
  • Name the version that brought ?, impl Trait, async and await, const generics, let else and GATs.
  • Read old Rust code and guess its age from the features it uses.
  • Find any fact about a release in the official notes.

The release train

Look at the dates of three releases. Count the days between them.

Three releases from RELEASES.md
VersionDateDays since the one before
1.72.024 Aug 202342
1.73.05 Oct 202342
1.74.016 Nov 202342

42 days are six weeks. This is the release train. A release leaves on time, like a train. A feature that is not ready waits for the next one.

Three channels

Rust has three channels. Every change goes through all three.

  • Nightly is built every night from the main branch. Unfinished features live here.
  • Beta is the next stable version. For six weeks it only gets bug fixes.
  • Stable is what most people use. It promises that your code keeps compiling.

So a change merged today reaches stable in six to twelve weeks. A bug fix found in beta goes into nightly first. Then it is copied back into beta. This copy is a backport.

The train started on day one. Rust 1.0 and the beta of 1.1 came out on the same day, 15 May 2015.

Point releases

Sometimes a release has a serious bug. Then a point release follows, such as 1.52.1. It changes only the last number. From 1.0 to 1.74 there were 75 six-week releases and 30 point releases.

Some point releases and why they came
VersionDateReason
1.34.214 May 2019Security bug CVE-2019-12083. Error::type_id was made unstable again.
1.52.110 May 2021Incremental compilation was switched off. A new check had found hidden bugs in it.
1.58.120 Jan 2022Security bug CVE-2022-21658, a race in std::fs::remove_dir_all.
1.66.110 Jan 2023Cargo now checks SSH host keys for git URLs (CVE-2022-46176).
1.68.228 Mar 2023GitHub changed its leaked RSA host key. Cargo got the new key.
1.71.13 Aug 2023Security bug CVE-2023-38497. Cargo ignored the umask when it unpacked crates.

Do not stay on an old point version "because it works". Point releases often fix security bugs. Run rustup update often.

Stable, beta and nightly in practice

This machine has several toolchains. A toolchain is one rustc with its cargo and standard library.

rustup toolchain list
stable-aarch64-apple-darwin (active, default)
1.88.0-aarch64-apple-darwin
1.97.0-aarch64-apple-darwin
1.99.0-aarch64-apple-darwin
rustup update                    # get the newest stable
rustup toolchain install beta    # add the beta channel
rustup toolchain install nightly # add the nightly channel
cargo +beta test                 # run one command with beta
cargo +1.88.0 check              # run one command with an old version
rustup default stable            # choose the default
[toolchain]
channel = "1.74.0"

Why you cannot use nightly features on stable

#![feature(never_type)] // ask for an unstable feature

fn main() {}
error[E0554]: `#![feature]` may not be used on the stable release channel
 --> gate.rs:1:1
  |
1 | #![feature(never_type)] // ask for an unstable feature
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

An unfinished feature hides behind a feature gate. Only nightly opens the gate. This keeps stable code safe from features that may still change.

How a feature becomes stable

  1. Someone writes an RFC. The team discusses the design in public.
  2. The team accepts the RFC. Work starts on nightly, behind a feature gate.
  3. People test it on nightly. The design changes if needed. This can take years.
  4. The team agrees to stabilize. A last call for objections runs for ten days.
  5. The gate is removed on nightly. The feature then rides the train: beta, then stable.

Python does it differently. It ships one big release each year, in October. See Python versions.

Test your project on beta in CI. Then you find problems six weeks before your users do. You also help Rust find bugs early.

The big milestones at a glance

This table is the map of the chapter. Every date comes from RELEASES.md.

The big steps from 1.0 to 1.74
VersionDateMain change
1.015 May 2015the first stable Rust, and the stability promise
1.1310 Nov 2016the ? operator
1.152 Feb 2017custom #[derive]: Serde and Diesel on stable
1.2610 May 2018impl Trait, ..=, u128, main returns Result
1.316 Dec 2018Rust 2018, non-lexical lifetimes, const fn
1.364 Jul 2019Future trait, alloc crate, NLL for 2015
1.397 Nov 2019async and .await
1.5125 Mar 2021const generics, Cargo resolver 2
1.5621 Oct 2021Rust 2021, rust-version in Cargo.toml

1.653 Nov 2022GATs, let else, break from a labeled block
1.701 Jun 2023OnceCell, OnceLock, sparse crates.io index

  1. 2015 Stability. 1.0 in May. Six releases that year.
  2. 2016 Errors made easy. ? arrives in 1.13.
  3. 2017 Libraries grow. Custom derive lets Serde work on stable.
  4. 2018 Productivity. impl Trait, then Rust 2018 with NLL.
  5. 2019 Async. Future in 1.36, async and .await in 1.39.
  6. 2020 Polish. matches!, safe float casts, more const fn.
  7. 2021 Const generics and Rust 2021.
  8. 2022 Comfort. {name} in format strings, scoped threads, GATs and let else.
  9. 2023 Toward 1.74. OnceLock, faster crates.io access, lints in Cargo.toml.

2015 to 2017: the foundations

Rust 1.0 (15 May 2015): the promise

fn main() {
    let names = vec!["Ann", "Bo"];
    for name in &names {
        println!("Hello, {}!", name);
    }
}
Hello, Ann!
Hello, Bo!

Ownership, borrowing, traits and Cargo were all in 1.0. The main news was the promise. Code that compiles on stable 1.0 should compile on every later 1.x. The program above still compiles, eleven years later.

In semantic versioning, a new first number means breaking changes. Rust does not break stable code. So it stays at 1.x. Breaking changes go into editions instead. See Rust editions.

Rust 1.13 (10 November 2016): the question mark

use std::num::ParseIntError;

fn sum(a: &str, b: &str) -> Result<i32, ParseIntError> {
    let x = a.parse::<i32>()?; // on Err, return the error at once
    let y = b.parse::<i32>()?;
    Ok(x + y)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", sum("2", "40"));
    println!("{:?}", sum("2", "forty"));
}
def total(a: str, b: str) -> int:
    return int(a) + int(b)  # int() raises ValueError on bad text

print(total("2", "40"))
try:
    total("2", "forty")
except ValueError as e:
    print("error:", e)
Ok(42)
Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit })
42
error: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'forty'

Before 1.13 people wrote try!(a.parse::<i32>()). The ? does the same with one character. The chapter Error handling explains it fully.

Old code with try! fails in edition 2018 or later. try is a reserved keyword there. The compiler says: "use of deprecated `try` macro". Replace it with ?.

Rust 1.15 to 1.20 (2017): derive, shorthand, constants

struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}

impl Point {
    const ORIGIN: Point = Point { x: 0, y: 0 }; // 1.20: associated constant
}

fn make(x: i32, y: i32) -> Point {
    Point { x, y } // 1.17: field init shorthand
}

fn main() {
    let p = make(3, 4);
    println!("{} {} {}", p.x, p.y, Point::ORIGIN.x);
}
3 4 0
  • 1.15 (2 February 2017) made custom #[derive] stable. These are procedural macros. Now #[derive(Serialize)] from Serde worked on stable Rust.
  • 1.17 (27 April 2017) allowed Point { x, y } instead of Point { x: x, y: y }.
  • 1.20 (31 August 2017) added constants inside impl and traits.

2018: impl Trait and the 2018 edition

Rust 1.26 (10 May 2018): a big release

// 1.26: return "some iterator" without naming its type.
fn evens(limit: u32) -> impl Iterator<Item = u32> {
    (0..=limit).filter(|n| n % 2 == 0) // 1.26: ..= includes the end
}

fn main() -> Result<(), String> { // 1.26: main may return Result
    let list: Vec<u32> = evens(10).collect();
    println!("{:?}", list);
    let big = u64::MAX as u128 * 4; // 1.26: 128-bit integers
    println!("{}", big);
    if list.is_empty() {
        return Err(String::from("no numbers"));
    }
    Ok(())
}
[0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
73786976294838206460
  • impl Trait in return position hides a long type. The real type here is a Filter of a range with a closure. You cannot even write it by hand.
  • ..= is a range that includes its end. 0..=10 has 11 numbers.
  • u128 and i128 are new integer types.
  • main can return Result. An Err prints and ends the program with an error code.
  • Match ergonomics: matching on &Option<T> works without writing & and ref in the pattern.

Rust 1.27 to 1.30 (2018): dyn, SIMD and macros

  • 1.27 (21 June 2018) added the syntax dyn Trait for trait objects. It also made SIMD on x86 stable, in std::arch.
  • 1.30 (25 October 2018) made attribute and function-like procedural macros stable. It added raw identifiers like r#for and paths that start with crate::.

Rust 1.31 (6 December 2018): Rust 2018 and NLL

fn main() {
    let mut scores = vec![10, 20];
    let first = &scores[0]; // a shared borrow starts
    println!("first = {}", first); // the last use of `first`
    scores.push(30); // NLL: the borrow has ended, so this is fine
    println!("{:?}", scores);
}
first = 10
[10, 20, 30]
  • The old borrow checker rejected this program. For it, a borrow lived until the end of its block, the closing brace.
  • NLL means a borrow ends at its last use. So push is fine.
  • In 1.31, NLL worked only in Rust 2018. Rust 1.36 gave it to Rust 2015 too.
  • The same release brought Rust 2018 with its new module paths. It also brought const fn, a function that can run at compile time.
  • Clippy and rustfmt reached 1.0 on stable.

We cannot show the old error here. The old checker was removed completely in 1.63. Every edition uses NLL today.

2019 and 2020: async and await

Rust 1.36 (4 July 2019): the ground for async

  • The Future trait became stable. A future is a value that will be ready later.
  • The alloc crate became stable. Code without the full std can now use Vec and Box.
  • MaybeUninit replaced the dangerous mem::uninitialized.
  • HashMap got a new, faster inner design, based on the hashbrown crate.

Rust 1.39 (7 November 2019): async and await

use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::pin;
use std::task::{Context, Poll, Waker};

async fn price(item: &str) -> u32 { // 1.39: async fn
    if item == "tea" { 3 } else { 5 }
}

async fn bill() -> u32 {
    price("tea").await + price("cake").await // 1.39: .await
}

// A tiny runner, only for this page. Real code uses tokio.
fn block_on<F: Future>(fut: F) -> F::Output {
    let mut fut = pin!(fut); // pin! is from 1.68
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(Waker::noop()); // Waker::noop is from 1.85
    loop {
        if let Poll::Ready(v) = fut.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
            return v;
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("total = {}", block_on(bill()));
}
import asyncio

async def price(item: str) -> int:
    return 3 if item == "tea" else 5

async def bill() -> int:
    return await price("tea") + await price("cake")

print("total =", asyncio.run(bill()))
total = 8
  • async fn returns a future. .await waits for a future without blocking the thread.
  • Rust has no built-in runtime. You choose one, such as tokio. Python has asyncio in its standard library.
  • The keywords async and await need edition 2018 or later.

The chapter Async and await goes much deeper.

A future does nothing until someone polls it. bill(); alone does not run bill. You must .await it or give it to a runtime.

Small helpers from 1.34 to 1.46

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", u8::try_from(200_i32)); // 1.34: TryFrom
    println!("{}", u8::try_from(300_i32).is_err()); // too big for u8
    let c = 'x';
    println!("{}", matches!(c, 'a'..='z')); // 1.42: matches!
    println!("{}", 300.7_f64 as u8); // 1.45: saturates at 255
    println!("{}", f64::NAN as i32); // 1.45: NaN becomes 0
}
Ok(200)
true
true
255
0
1.32 (17 Jan 2019): dbg!

dbg!(a * 2) prints the file, the line, the expression and its value. Then it returns the value.

1.34 (11 Apr 2019): TryFrom and TryInto

Conversions that can fail return Result. Cargo also got alternative registries.

1.40 (19 Dec 2019): #[non_exhaustive] and todo!

A library can say "more variants may come". Users must then add a _ arm.

1.42 (12 Mar 2020): matches! and subslice patterns

matches!(x, pattern) gives a bool. Patterns like [first, .., last] work on slices.

1.45 (16 Jul 2020): safe float casts

Before, 300.7 as u8 was undefined behaviour. Now it saturates: too big gives the maximum, NaN gives 0.

1.46 (27 Aug 2020): if, match and loop in const fn

Also #[track_caller]: a panic message names the caller, not the helper.

2021 and 2022: const generics, Rust 2021, GATs

Rust 1.51 (25 March 2021): const generics

// 1.51: N is a value (a number), not a type.
fn sum<const N: usize>(values: [i32; N]) -> i32 {
    let mut total = 0;
    for v in values { // 1.53: arrays iterate by value
        total += v;
    }
    total
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", sum([1, 2, 3]));
    println!("{}", sum([10; 5])); // here N is 5
}
6
50
  • Const generics let one function work for arrays of every length.
  • This first version is a minimum. The value must be an integer, bool or char.
  • Cargo got feature resolver 2, written resolver = "2".
  • 1.53 (17 June 2021) made arrays iterable by value. It also allowed nested or-patterns like Some(1 | 2) and non-ASCII names.

Rust 1.56 (21 October 2021): Rust 2021

This release brought the 2021 edition. It also added the rust-version field to Cargo.toml. That is the oldest Rust your crate supports. The details are in Rust editions.

Rust 1.58 to 1.62 (2022): small comforts

#[derive(Debug, Default)]
enum Level {
    Low,
    #[default] // 1.62: the default variant of an enum
    Medium,
    High,
}

fn main() {
    let name = "Ferris";
    let age = 8;
    println!("{name} is {age}"); // 1.58: names inside the braces
    let (mut a, mut b) = (1, 2);
    (a, b) = (b, a); // 1.59: assign to a tuple pattern
    println!("{a} {b}");
    println!("{:?}", Level::default());
    let _others = [Level::Low, Level::High]; // use the other variants
}
Ferris is 8
2 1
Medium
  • 1.58 (13 January 2022): format strings can name a variable directly, like Python f-strings.
  • 1.59 (24 February 2022): destructuring assignment, and inline assembly with asm!.
  • 1.62 (30 June 2022): #[default] on an enum variant, and the command cargo add.

Rust 1.63 (11 August 2022): scoped threads

use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let words = vec!["red", "green", "blue"];
    let mut total = 0;
    thread::scope(|s| { // 1.63: scoped threads
        s.spawn(|| println!("first: {}", words[0])); // borrows `words`
        s.spawn(|| total = words.iter().map(|w| w.len()).sum());
    }); // every thread has ended here
    println!("letters: {total}");
}
first: red
letters: 12

A normal thread::spawn needs owned data or Arc. A scoped thread may borrow local data. The scope waits for all its threads at the end. See Threads and shared state.

1.64 (22 September 2022) came next. It added IntoFuture, C types in core::ffi, and workspace inheritance in Cargo. rust-analyzer also became a rustup component.

Rust 1.65 (3 November 2022): GATs and let else

fn port(text: &str) -> u16 {
    let Some((_, num)) = text.split_once(':') else { // 1.65: let else
        return 80; // the else block must leave the function
    };
    num.parse().unwrap_or(80)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", port("localhost:8080"));
    println!("{}", port("localhost"));
    let size = 'check: { // 1.65: break out of a labeled block
        if port("a:1") < 1024 {
            break 'check "small";
        }
        "large"
    };
    println!("{size}");
}
def port(text: str) -> int:
    _, sep, num = text.partition(":")
    if not sep:  # the same early return
        return 80
    return int(num) if num.isdigit() else 80

print(port("localhost:8080"))
print(port("localhost"))
8080
80
small

let ... else binds a pattern or leaves at once. The else block must not continue. It must return, break or panic. This removes one level of nesting.

// 1.65: an associated type with its own lifetime parameter (a GAT).
trait Lender {
    type Item<'a> where Self: 'a;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item<'_>>;
}

struct Pairs {
    data: Vec<i32>,
    pos: usize,
}

impl Lender for Pairs {
    type Item<'a> = &'a [i32]; // each item borrows from `self`
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<&[i32]> {
        let pair = self.data.get(self.pos..self.pos + 2)?;
        self.pos += 1;
        Some(pair)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut p = Pairs { data: vec![1, 2, 3], pos: 0 };
    while let Some(pair) = p.next() {
        println!("{:?}", pair);
    }
}
[1, 2]
[2, 3]

A GAT is an associated type with its own generic parameters. Here Item<'a> can borrow from the iterator itself. The normal Iterator trait cannot do that. The RFC for GATs was opened more than six and a half years before 1.65. See Advanced traits and types.

2023: the road to 1.74

Rust 1.68 and 1.70: faster Cargo, lazy globals

use std::sync::OnceLock;

static CONFIG: OnceLock<String> = OnceLock::new(); // 1.70

fn config() -> &'static str {
    CONFIG.get_or_init(|| {
        println!("loading config"); // runs only once
        String::from("mode=fast")
    })
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", config());
    println!("{}", config());
}
loading config
mode=fast
mode=fast
  • 1.68 (9 March 2023) added the sparse protocol for crates.io and the pin! macro.
  • 1.70 (1 June 2023) made sparse the default. Cargo no longer clones the whole crates.io index.
  • 1.70 also added OnceCell, OnceLock and IsTerminal. Before, you needed the once_cell crate.

Rust 1.71 to 1.73: FFI and clearer panics

fn main() {
    let items = vec![1, 2, 3, 4];
    assert_eq!(items.len(), 5, "wrong item count");
}
thread 'main' panicked at h173.rs:3:5:
assertion `left == right` failed: wrong item count
  left: 4
 right: 5
thread 'main' panicked at 'assertion failed: `(left == right)`
  left: `4`,
 right: `5`: wrong item count', h173.rs:3:5
  • 1.71 (13 July 2023) added the "C-unwind" ABI. A panic may then cross into C code and back in a defined way.
  • 1.73 (5 October 2023) made panic messages easier to read. The place comes first. Your message sits on its own line.
  • 1.73 also added get, set and take on thread locals that hold a Cell.

Rust 1.74 (16 November 2023): lints in Cargo.toml

[lints.rust]
unsafe_code = "forbid"

[lints.clippy]
enum_glob_use = "deny"
error: usage of an `unsafe` block
 --> src/main.rs:4:20
  |
4 |     println!("{}", unsafe { *p }); // not allowed by [lints]
  |                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = note: requested on the command line with `-F unsafe-code`
use std::num::Saturating;

fn main() {
    let mut stock = Saturating(250_u8); // 1.74
    stock += Saturating(10); // stops at 255: no overflow panic
    println!("{}", stock);
    let left = Saturating(3_u8) - Saturating(5_u8); // stops at 0
    println!("{}", left);
}
255
0
  • The [lints] table sets lint levels for the whole package. Before, you wrote #![deny(...)] in the code or used RUSTFLAGS.
  • Saturating<T> does maths that stops at the minimum and the maximum.
  • Cargo got registry authentication. Private registries can now ask for credentials.
  • async fn and impl Trait in return position may now mention Self and associated types.
  • Apple minimums went up: macOS 10.12 and iOS 10.

Six weeks later, on 28 December 2023, came 1.75 with async fn in traits. That story continues in Rust recent releases: 1.75 to today.

How the features grew

Big features rarely arrive in one release. They come in steps. Read each arrow as "made possible".

Ten milestones to remember

1. Rust 1.0 (2015)

The stability promise. Stable code keeps compiling on every later 1.x.

2. The ? operator (2016)

Pass an error up with one character. It replaced try!.

3. Custom derive (2017)

#[derive(Serialize)] on stable. Serde became the normal way to read and write data.

4. impl Trait (2018)

Return an iterator or a closure without naming its type.

5. Rust 2018 and NLL

New paths, new keywords and a smarter borrow checker.

6. async and await (2019)

Fast network code that reads like normal code. tokio grew around it.

7. Const generics (2021)

Code over array lengths. [T; N] got trait impls for every N.

8. Rust 2021

A small edition of clean-ups. Arrays iterate by value. Closures capture fields.

9. GATs and let else (2022)

A long-awaited type feature, and a simple way to leave early.

10. OnceLock and sparse (2023)

Lazy globals in std, and much faster crates.io access.

Patterns to remember

Patterns from the releases 1.0 to 1.74

Practice

How long is one trip of the release train?

  • One month
  • Six weeks
  • One year

A new stable version comes every six weeks, or 42 days. Python is the one with yearly releases.

You found a feature that exists only behind #![feature(...)]. Where can you use it?

  • On stable, with a warning
  • On beta
  • Only on nightly

Stable gives error E0554. Beta is a future stable, so it refuses too.

Old code uses try!(read()) and has no ?. When was it written, most likely?

  • Before November 2016
  • After Rust 2018
  • After 1.39

? came in 1.13, on 10 November 2016. After that most code moved to ?.

Which release brought non-lexical lifetimes to edition 2015?

  • 1.31
  • 1.36
  • 1.63

1.31 brought NLL for 2018 only. 1.36 extended it to 2015. 1.63 removed the old checker.

async and .await became stable in Rust 1.?.

Const generics became stable in Rust 1.?.

Let else and GATs became stable in Rust 1.?.

A small bug-fix release like 1.52.1 is called a ?.

  1. Rust 1.100 came out on 12 November 2026. When is 1.101 due? Show your sum.
    Answer

    Six weeks are 42 days. 12 November plus 18 days is 30 November. 24 more days give 24 December 2026. Check the official dates, because the plan can change.

  2. A merge into nightly happens one day after the beta branch was cut. In which stable version does it appear? Explain with the train.
    Answer

    It missed the current beta. It rides in the next beta, which starts in about six weeks. That beta becomes stable six weeks later. So it reaches stable in about twelve weeks, two versions after the current stable.

  3. Rewrite this function with let else. 
    fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str {
    match text.split_whitespace().next() {
        Some(w) => w,
        None => return "",
    }
}
    Answer 
    fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str {
    let Some(w) = text.split_whitespace().next() else {
        return "";
    };
    w
}

    first_word("hello world") gives "hello". first_word(" ") gives "".

  4. Why was the old borrow checker unhappy with the NLL example, and why is the new one happy?
    Answer

    The old checker tied the borrow first to its block. The borrow lived until the closing brace, so push collided with it. NLL looks at real uses. first is not used after the println!, so the borrow is over before push.

  5. Your crate must build on Rust 1.65. Which of these can you use: let else, OnceLock, [lints], scoped threads?
    Answer

    let else (1.65) and scoped threads (1.63) are fine. OnceLock needs 1.70. [lints] needs Cargo 1.74. Write rust-version = "1.65" and Clippy will warn about the newer ones.

  6. Hard. Rust never shipped a 2.0. Explain how the project can still remove a keyword clash or a bad default. Use one example from this chapter.
    Answer

    Breaking changes go into editions, which each crate chooses. Example: try! clashed with a future try block. Rust 2018 reserved try, while 2015 crates keep the old macro. Both kinds of crate still build together. So the version stays 1.x and no code breaks without the author's choice.

Key takeaways

  • A new stable Rust leaves every six weeks. 69 of the 74 gaps from 1.0 to 1.74 were exactly 42 days.
  • Changes flow from nightly to beta to stable. Unstable features need a feature gate on nightly.
  • From 1.0 to 1.74 there were 75 six-week releases and 30 point releases.
  • Key versions: ? 1.13, impl Trait 1.26, Rust 2018 and NLL 1.31, async 1.39, const generics 1.51, Rust 2021 1.56, GATs and let else 1.65.
  • Big features arrive in steps across many releases.
  • RELEASES.md and the release posts on the Rust blog are the sources of truth.

  • Announcing Rust 1.0. The stability promise and the six-week cycle.
