Rust recent releases: 1.75 to today

Rust gets a new stable version every six weeks. This chapter walks through every one, from 1.75.0 to 1.100.0. For each release you see the date, the main changes in simple words, and a small program that proves them.

  • Name the main change of each release from 1.75 to 1.100.
  • Use the new features, such as let chains, LazyLock and async closures.
  • Read the official release notes and find what matters for your code.
  • Check which Rust version a feature needs before you use it.
  • Upgrade a project step by step, without surprises.

Where Rust is today

Start with three commands. They show which Rust you have.

rustc --version
cargo --version
rustup toolchain list
rustc 1.99.0 (b940084d7 2026-09-28)
cargo 1.99.0 (5f94df478 2026-08-27)
stable-aarch64-apple-darwin (active, default)
1.88.0-aarch64-apple-darwin
1.97.0-aarch64-apple-darwin
1.99.0-aarch64-apple-darwin

Today is 15 November 2026. The newest stable Rust is 1.100.0. It came out on 12 November 2026. This machine still has 1.99.0, from 1 October 2026.

Rust ships a new release every six weeks. The chapter Rust history: 1.0 to 1.74 explains this train. This chapter starts where that one stops.

  • From 1.75.0 to 1.100.0 there are 26 six-week releases.
  • There are also 12 point releases, such as 1.77.2.
  • No release in this list broke the promise of stable Rust. Old code still compiles, with a few rare cases.

How this chapter marks its tests

  • ran on 1.99.0 The code was compiled and run on this machine. The compiler was rustc 1.99.0 with edition 2024, on an Apple silicon Mac.
  • not run here The feature is newer than 1.99.0. The text comes from the official release notes only.
  • Python twins ran on Python 3.14.3. Many changes here are only about Rust. They have no Python twin.

Four words you need

  • To stabilize a feature means to switch it on for everybody.
  • Nightly is the daily build. New features wait there first.
  • A lint is a compiler check. It gives a warning or an error.
  • An edition is a set of language rules. See Rust editions.

Rust 1.100 is not 1.1 and not 1.10. Each part of the version is a whole number. So 1.100 comes after 1.99.

How to read a release note

Each release has two official texts. The blog post shows the main changes with examples. The file RELEASES.md lists every change. It always has the same parts.

Language

New syntax and new rules of the language. Example: let chains in 1.88.

Compiler and Platform Support

New compiler flags and changes for each target. A target has a tier. Tier 1 is tested on every change.

Libraries and Stabilized APIs

New functions and types in the standard library. This is the longest list in most releases.

Cargo and Rustdoc

Changes in the build tool and in the documentation tool.

Compatibility Notes

Changes that can break old code or change its behaviour. Read this part before every upgrade.

The point releases

A point release changes only the last number. It fixes bugs. It adds no features. Always install it.

The 12 point releases in this range
VersionDateWhat it fixed
1.77.128 Mar 2024Windows builds: debug information was removed by default. This was undone.
1.77.29 Apr 2024A security bug, CVE-2024-24576. Arguments for Windows batch files were not escaped well.
1.80.18 Aug 2024Wrong machine code when comparing floats. A change to the dead_code lint was undone.
1.84.130 Jan 2025Compiler crashes, slow compilation with the new trait solver, wrong errors in incremental builds.
1.85.118 Mar 2025Merged doc tests of the 2024 edition. std::fs::rename on one old Windows 10 version.
1.91.110 Nov 2025File locking on illumos. Linker errors on WebAssembly targets.
1.93.112 Feb 2026A compiler crash that hit rustfmt. A wrong Clippy warning. Leaked file handles on wasm32-wasip2.
1.94.126 Mar 2026std::thread::spawn on one WebAssembly target. Cargo got a safer tar (CVE-2026-33055, CVE-2026-33056).
1.96.130 Jun 2026Cargo timeouts and retries. Security patches for libssh2. Wrong machine code from one optimization.
1.97.116 Jul 2026Wrong machine code from an LLVM optimization.
1.98.13 Sep 2026Wrong machine code when building vtables.
1.99.115 Oct 2026Wrong bool return values from C functions on x86-64. A missing symbol on UEFI. A linker path on macOS.

Four of the last five point releases fixed a miscompilation. This machine has 1.99.0, so it does not have the 1.99.1 fix. The cure is one command: rustup update stable.

How much grows in each release

The big moments

  1. 28 Dec 2023 1.75. Traits can have async fn.
  2. 25 Jul 2024 1.80. LazyLock arrives in the standard library.
  3. 17 Oct 2024 1.82. &raw and unsafe extern make unsafe code clearer.
  4. 20 Feb 2025 1.85. The 2024 edition and async closures.
  5. 15 May 2025 1.87. Ten years after Rust 1.0, to the day.
  6. 26 Jun 2025 1.88. Let chains.
  7. 18 Sep 2025 1.90. The LLD linker is the default on Linux x86-64.
  8. 16 Apr 2026 1.95. cfg_select! and if let guards.
  9. 9 Jul 2026 1.97. The v0 symbol names become the default.
  10. 12 Nov 2026 1.100. The never type ! is stable.

2023 and 2024: releases 1.75 to 1.83

These nine releases gave Rust async traits, lazy globals and safer unsafe code. Each block starts with a program. Then it lists what changed.

Rust 1.75.0 (28 December 2023): async fn in traits

use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::pin;
use std::task::{Context, Poll, Waker};

trait Store {
    // New in 1.75: an async fn inside a trait.
    async fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<u32>;
    // New in 1.75: `impl Trait` as a return type inside a trait.
    fn keys(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = &str>;
}

struct Memory(Vec<(&'static str, u32)>);

impl Store for Memory {
    async fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<u32> {
        self.0.iter().find(|(k, _)| *k == key).map(|(_, v)| *v)
    }
    fn keys(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = &str> {
        self.0.iter().map(|(k, _)| *k)
    }
}

// A tiny executor for this page. Real programs use tokio.
fn block_on<F: Future>(fut: F) -> F::Output {
    let mut fut = pin!(fut);
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(Waker::noop());
    loop {
        if let Poll::Ready(value) = fut.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
            return value;
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let store = Memory(vec![("ann", 31), ("bo", 27)]);
    println!("{:?}", block_on(store.get("bo")));
    println!("{:?}", store.keys().collect::<Vec<_>>());
}
Some(27)
["ann", "bo"]
  • A trait can now have an async fn. Before 1.75 you needed a helper crate for this.
  • A trait method can return impl Trait.
  • Raw pointers got methods that count in bytes, such as byte_add.
  • Option::as_slice and File::set_modified are new.
  • Cargo adds a new package to [workspace.members] for you.
  • The compiler itself got about 2% faster on Linux x86-64.

An async fn in a public trait gives a warning. The caller cannot ask for a Send future. Such a trait also does not work with dyn. The practice section shows the fix.

Rust 1.76.0 (8 February 2024): small helpers

use std::any::type_name_of_val;

fn main() {
    let evens = (1..10).filter(|n| n % 2 == 0);
    // New in 1.76: ask for the type name of a value.
    println!("{}", type_name_of_val(&evens));

    // New in 1.76: look at a value in the middle of a chain.
    let port = "80a"
        .parse::<u16>()
        .inspect_err(|e| println!("bad port: {e}"))
        .unwrap_or(8080);
    let name = Some("ann").inspect(|n| println!("found {n}"));
    println!("{port} {name:?}");
}
core::iter::adapters::filter::Filter<core::ops::range::Range<i32>, e176::main::{{closure}}>
bad port: invalid digit found in string
found ann
8080 Some("ann")
  • type_name_of_val prints the type of any value. It helps with closures and iterators.
  • inspect and inspect_err let you log a value and keep the chain.
  • Arc::unwrap_or_clone takes the value out, or clones it when others still share it.
  • ptr::addr_eq, ptr::from_ref and ptr::from_mut are new.
  • The docs now say which types have the same ABI. One new promise: char and u32 match.

Rust 1.77.0 (21 March 2024): C string literals

use std::ffi::CStr;
use std::mem::offset_of;

#[repr(C)]
struct Header {
    kind: u8,
    len: u32,
}

fn main() {
    // New in 1.77: a C string literal. The compiler adds the last 0 byte.
    let name: &CStr = c"rust";
    println!("{:?} is {} bytes with the 0", name, name.to_bytes_with_nul().len());

    // New in 1.77: at which byte does a field start?
    println!("kind: {}, len: {}", offset_of!(Header, kind), offset_of!(Header, len));

    // New in 1.77: cut a slice into runs of neighbours.
    let temps = [20, 21, 21, 25, 19, 22];
    for run in temps.chunk_by(|a, b| a <= b) {
        println!("{run:?}");
    }
}
"rust" is 5 bytes with the 0
kind: 0, len: 4
[20, 21, 21, 25]
[19, 22]
  • c"text" makes a &CStr. This helps with FFI. A zero byte in the middle is a compile error.
  • offset_of! gives the place of a field in bytes.
  • An async fn can call itself. The inner call must be boxed with Box::pin.
  • New slice methods: chunk_by, first_chunk, last_chunk.
  • File::create_new fails when the file already exists.
  • Cargo release builds now remove debug information. The binaries get smaller.

Rust 1.78.0 (2 May 2024): your own error messages

#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
    message = "`{Self}` cannot be saved",
    label = "this type has no `Save` impl",
    note = "write `impl Save for {Self}` first"
)]
trait Save {}

fn save(_item: impl Save) {}

fn main() {
    save(42_u8);
}
error[E0277]: `u8` cannot be saved
  --> e178.rs:11:10
   |
11 |     save(42_u8);
   |     ---- ^^^^^ this type has no `Save` impl
   |     |
   |     required by a bound introduced by this call
   |
   = help: the trait `Save` is not implemented for `u8`
   = note: write `impl Save for u8` first
  • #[diagnostic::on_unimplemented] lets a library write the error text for a missing trait.
  • Debug builds now check the rules of many unsafe library functions. A broken rule stops the program with a clear message.
  • pointer::align_offset and slice::align_to now give the same answer on every run.
  • The main Windows targets need Windows 10 or newer.
  • Cargo writes lockfile version 4. It also looks at rust-version when it writes the lockfile.

Rust 1.79.0 (13 June 2024): inline const

use std::fmt::Display;
use std::num::NonZero;

// New in 1.79: a bound on an associated type, written in place.
fn join_all<I: Iterator<Item: Display>>(items: I) -> String {
    items.map(|x| x.to_string()).collect::<Vec<_>>().join(", ")
}

fn main() {
    // New in 1.79: an inline const block. String is not Copy, but this works.
    let names: [String; 3] = [const { String::new() }; 3];
    println!("{names:?}");

    println!("{}", join_all([1.5, 2.5].into_iter()));

    // New in 1.79: one generic NonZero type for every integer type.
    let step = NonZero::new(4_u32).expect("not zero");
    println!("{} {:?}", 100 / step, NonZero::new(0_u8));
}
["", "", ""]
1.5, 2.5
25 None
  • const { ... } runs code at compile time, in the middle of normal code.
  • You can write Iterator<Item: Display>. No extra where line is needed.
  • Temporary values in if and match live longer. More code compiles.
  • New: NonZero<T>, path::absolute, utf8_chunks.
  • The standard library keeps frame pointers. Profilers can read the stack more easily.

Rust 1.80.0 (25 July 2024): LazyLock

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::LazyLock;

// New in 1.80: a global value that is built on first use.
static PORTS: LazyLock<HashMap<&str, u16>> = LazyLock::new(|| {
    println!("building the map");
    HashMap::from([("http", 80), ("https", 443)])
});

// New in 1.80: `a..b` in a pattern. The end is not included.
fn size_name(bytes: u64) -> &'static str {
    match bytes {
        0 => "empty",
        ..1_000 => "small",
        1_000..1_000_000 => "medium",
        1_000_000.. => "large",
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("start");
    println!("{:?}", PORTS.get("https"));
    println!("{:?}", PORTS.get("http"));
    println!("{} {} {}", size_name(0), size_name(999), size_name(1_000_000));
}
from functools import cache

# Python twin of LazyLock: the body runs on the first call only.
@cache
def ports() -> dict[str, int]:
    print("building the map")
    return {"http": 80, "https": 443}

def size_name(n: int) -> str:
    match n:
        case 0:
            return "empty"
        case _ if n < 1_000:
            return "small"
        case _ if n < 1_000_000:
            return "medium"
        case _:
            return "large"

print("start")
print(ports().get("https"))
print(ports().get("http"))
print(size_name(0), size_name(999), size_name(1_000_000))
start
building the map
Some(443)
Some(80)
empty small large
start
building the map
443
80
empty small large
  • LazyLock builds a value the first time you use it. It is safe with threads. LazyCell is the version for one thread.
  • Many projects used the once_cell or lazy_static crate for this. Now the standard library is enough.
  • Range patterns can leave out the end: a..b.
  • Cargo checks every cfg name and value. A typo gives the warning unexpected_cfgs.
  • size_of and align_of need no import any more.
  • New: Option::take_if, split_at_checked, trim_ascii.

Rust 1.80 added new ways to collect into Box<str>. Old versions of the time crate, before 0.3.35, then failed to compile. The fix was cargo update. Keep your dependencies fresh before you upgrade Rust.

Rust 1.81.0 (5 September 2024): expect and core::error

use std::fmt;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct TooBig(u32);

impl fmt::Display for TooBig {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "{} is too big", self.0)
    }
}

// New in 1.81: the Error trait lives in `core`. It works without `std`.
impl core::error::Error for TooBig {}

// New in 1.81: `expect` is like `allow`, but it warns when the lint stays silent.
#[expect(dead_code, reason = "we use it again next week")]
fn old_helper() {}

fn main() {
    let err: Box<dyn core::error::Error> = Box::new(TooBig(900));
    println!("{err}");
    // New in 1.81: one clear call to ask if a path exists.
    println!("{:?}", std::fs::exists("/no/such/file"));
    let mut v = vec![3, 1, 2];
    v.sort(); // 1.81 put new and faster sort code behind the same call
    println!("{v:?}");
}
900 is too big
Ok(false)
[1, 2, 3]

What happens when the lint does not fire any more? The compiler tells you. Then you delete the attribute.

#[expect(unused_variables, reason = "remove this line when the bug is fixed")]
fn main() {
    let total = 3;
    println!("{total}");
}
warning: this lint expectation is unfulfilled
 --> e181b.rs:1:10
  |
1 | #[expect(unused_variables, reason = "remove this line when the bug is fixed")]
  |          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = note: remove this line when the bug is fixed
  = note: `#[warn(unfulfilled_lint_expectations)]` on by default
  • #[expect(lint)] silences a lint and reminds you later. All lint attributes can take a reason.
  • core::error::Error makes the Error trait usable in no_std code.
  • Both sort functions got new and faster code. They may panic when your Ord is wrong.
  • A panic that leaves an extern "C" function now stops the program.
  • New: fs::exists, Duration::abs_diff, hint::assert_unchecked.

Rust 1.82.0 (17 October 2024): safer unsafe

use std::ffi::c_char;

// New in 1.82: `unsafe extern`, with `safe` or `unsafe` on every item.
unsafe extern "C" {
    pub safe fn abs(x: i32) -> i32; // we promise that this C function is safe
    pub unsafe fn strlen(s: *const c_char) -> usize;
}

#[repr(C, packed)]
struct Packet {
    tag: u8,
    value: u32, // not aligned: it starts at byte 1
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", abs(-7)); // no unsafe block is needed

    let p = Packet { tag: 1, value: 182 };
    // New in 1.82: `&raw const` makes a raw pointer and never a reference.
    let ptr = &raw const p.value;
    println!("{} {}", { p.tag }, unsafe { ptr.read_unaligned() });
    println!("{}", unsafe { strlen(c"hello".as_ptr()) });

    let age: Option<u32> = None;
    println!("{}", age.is_none_or(|a| a >= 18)); // new in 1.82
    println!("{}", [1, 2, 2, 9].is_sorted()); // new in 1.82
    println!("{}", std::iter::repeat_n("ab", 3).collect::<String>());
}
7
1 182
5
true
true
ababab
  • &raw const and &raw mut make a raw pointer directly. They replace the addr_of! macros.
  • An extern block can be unsafe extern. Each item inside is marked safe or unsafe.
  • Risky attributes are written as #[unsafe(no_mangle)].
  • use<..> says which lifetimes an impl Trait return type keeps. See Lifetimes.
  • cargo info shows facts about a crate in the terminal.
  • Floating-point maths works in const fn.
  • Apple silicon Macs became a Tier 1 target. This machine is one of them.

Do not write &p.value as *const u32 for a packed field. That makes a reference first, and the reference is not aligned. The compiler rejects it. Use &raw const p.value.

Rust 1.83.0 (28 November 2024): const code grows up

// New in 1.83: `&mut` works inside a const fn.
const fn squares(mut table: [u8; 5]) -> [u8; 5] {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < table.len() {
        let cell = &mut table[i]; // a mutable borrow at compile time
        *cell = (i * i) as u8;
        i += 1;
    }
    table
}

const SQUARES: [u8; 5] = squares([0; 5]);

static LIMIT: u32 = 25;
const LIMIT_REF: &u32 = &LIMIT; // new in 1.83: a const can point to a static

fn main() {
    println!("{SQUARES:?} {LIMIT_REF}");
    let mut cache: Option<Vec<u8>> = None;
    cache.get_or_insert_default().push(7); // new in 1.83
    println!("{cache:?}");
}
[0, 1, 4, 9, 16] 25
Some([7])
  • Const code can use &mut and mutable raw pointers.
  • A const can hold a reference to a static.
  • The list of functions that became usable in const code has 81 entries.
  • New: Option::get_or_insert_default, BufRead::skip_until, ControlFlow::break_value.
  • io::ErrorKind got many new kinds, such as StorageFull and NotADirectory.

2025: releases 1.84 to 1.92

This year brought the 2024 edition, async closures, trait upcasting and let chains. Cargo also learned to respect your Rust version.

Rust 1.84.0 (9 January 2025): Cargo knows your Rust version

[package]
name = "shop"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"
rust-version = "1.84"   # the oldest Rust that this crate supports
resolver = "3"          # new in 1.84: pick dependency versions that fit rust-version
fn main() {
    println!("{}", 99_u32.isqrt()); // new in 1.84: whole-number square root

    // New in 1.84: strict provenance. Hide one bit in a pointer without casts.
    let value = Box::new(5_u64);
    let ptr: *const u64 = &raw const *value;
    let tagged = ptr.map_addr(|a| a | 1); // u64 is aligned to 8, so bit 0 is free
    println!("{}", tagged.addr() & 1);
    let clean = tagged.map_addr(|a| a & !1);
    println!("{}", unsafe { *clean });
}
9
1
5
  • The MSRV is the oldest Rust that your crate supports. You write it as rust-version.
  • The new resolver prefers dependency versions that work with your MSRV.
  • The compiler started to use its next trait solver. For now it checks that trait impls do not overlap.
  • The strict provenance functions are stable: addr, map_addr, with_addr.
  • New: isqrt on integers, ptr::dangling, Pin::as_deref_mut.
  • The old target name wasm32-wasi is gone. Use wasm32-wasip1.

resolver = "3" needs Cargo 1.84. A crate with an older MSRV cannot use this line. Put the setting in .cargo/config.toml instead.

Rust 1.85.0 (20 February 2025): the 2024 edition

// `block_on` is the small helper from the 1.75 example.

// New in 1.85: the AsyncFn traits. This function takes an async closure.
async fn twice(job: impl AsyncFn(u32) -> u32) -> u32 {
    job(1).await + job(2).await
}

fn main() {
    let bonus = 10;
    // New in 1.85: an async closure. It borrows `bonus`.
    let add = async |n: u32| n + bonus;
    println!("{}", block_on(twice(add)));

    // New in 1.85: collect into three collections in one pass.
    let (ids, big, text): (Vec<u32>, Vec<u32>, Vec<String>) =
        (1..4).map(|n| (n, n * 100, format!("#{n}"))).collect();
    println!("{ids:?} {big:?} {text:?}");
}
import asyncio
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable

async def twice(job: Callable[[int], Awaitable[int]]) -> int:
    return await job(1) + await job(2)

async def main() -> None:
    bonus = 10

    async def add(n: int) -> int:  # an inner async function reads `bonus`
        return n + bonus

    print(await twice(add))

asyncio.run(main())
23
[1, 2, 3] [100, 200, 300] ["#1", "#2", "#3"]
23
  • The 2024 edition is stable. It is the biggest edition so far. The chapter Rust editions covers it.
  • An async closure is written async |x| { ... }. It can borrow from its surroundings.
  • The traits AsyncFn, AsyncFnMut and AsyncFnOnce need no import.
  • collect() can fill a tuple of up to 12 collections.
  • #[diagnostic::do_not_recommend] hides an impl from error messages.
  • New: Waker::noop, midpoint for floats and unsigned integers.

Rust 1.86.0 (3 April 2025): trait upcasting

use std::fmt::Debug;

trait Shape: Debug {
    fn area(&self) -> f64;
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Square(f64);

impl Shape for Square {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 {
        self.0 * self.0
    }
}

fn main() {
    let shape: Box<dyn Shape> = Box::new(Square(3.0));
    println!("{}", shape.area());
    // New in 1.86: go from `dyn Shape` up to its supertrait `dyn Debug`.
    let debug: Box<dyn Debug> = shape;
    println!("{debug:?}");

    // New in 1.86: two mutable borrows into one slice, checked at run time.
    let mut scores = [10, 20, 30];
    if let Ok([first, last]) = scores.get_disjoint_mut([0, 2]) {
        std::mem::swap(first, last);
    }
    println!("{scores:?} {}", scores.get_disjoint_mut([1, 1]).is_err());

    let mut stack = vec![1, 2, 8];
    println!("{:?} {stack:?}", stack.pop_if(|top| *top > 5)); // new in 1.86
}
9
Square(3.0)
[30, 20, 10] true
Some(8) [1, 2]
  • A supertrait is a trait that another trait needs. A trait object can now turn into its supertrait object.
  • get_disjoint_mut gives several &mut into one slice or one HashMap.
  • A safe function can carry #[target_feature].
  • Debug builds stop the program when code reads through a null pointer.
  • The lint missing_abi warns about a bare extern. Write extern "C".
  • New: Vec::pop_if, Once::wait, next_up and next_down on floats.

Rust 1.87.0 (15 May 2025): ten years of Rust, and pipes

use std::io::Read;
use std::process::Command;

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    // New in 1.87: an anonymous pipe. It joins stdout and stderr of a child.
    let (mut reader, writer) = std::io::pipe()?;
    let mut child = Command::new("sh")
        .args(["-c", "echo to-stdout; echo to-stderr 1>&2"])
        .stdout(writer.try_clone()?)
        .stderr(writer)
        .spawn()?;
    let mut text = String::new();
    reader.read_to_string(&mut text)?;
    child.wait()?;
    print!("{text}");

    // New in 1.87: take the matching items out of a Vec.
    let mut nums = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];
    let even: Vec<i32> = nums.extract_if(.., |n| *n % 2 == 0).collect();
    println!("{even:?} {nums:?}");
    println!("{} {}", 12_u32.is_multiple_of(4), 200_u8.cast_signed());
    Ok(())
}
to-stdout
to-stderr
[2, 4, 6] [1, 3, 5]
true -56
  • Rust 1.0 came out on 15 May 2015. Rust 1.87 came out exactly ten years later.
  • std::io::pipe() makes a pipe without a name. It works well with Command.
  • Many CPU intrinsics in std::arch are safe to call now. The target feature must be on.
  • asm! can jump to a labelled Rust block.
  • use<..> works in trait definitions.
  • New: Vec::extract_if, is_multiple_of, cast_signed, slice split_off.

Rust 1.88.0 (26 June 2025): let chains

use std::cell::Cell;

fn port_from(line: &str) -> Option<u16> {
    // New in 1.88 (2024 edition): `let` parts and tests joined with `&&`.
    if let Some((key, value)) = line.split_once('=')
        && key.trim() == "port"
        && let Ok(port) = value.trim().parse::<u16>()
        && port >= 1024
    {
        Some(port)
    } else {
        None
    }
}

fn main() {
    for line in ["port = 8080", "port = 80", "host = x"] {
        println!("{line:?} -> {:?}", port_from(line));
    }

    let hits = Cell::new(1);
    hits.update(|n| n + 1); // new in 1.88
    println!("{}", hits.get());

    // New in 1.88: cut a slice into arrays of one size, plus the rest.
    let (pairs, rest) = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].as_chunks::<2>();
    println!("{pairs:?} {rest:?}");
}
def port_from(line: str) -> int | None:
    key, sep, value = line.partition("=")
    # The walrus `:=` gives a name to a value inside the test.
    if (
        sep
        and key.strip() == "port"
        and (text := value.strip()).isdigit()
        and (port := int(text)) >= 1024
    ):
        return port
    return None

for line in ["port = 8080", "port = 80", "host = x"]:
    print(repr(line), "->", port_from(line))
"port = 8080" -> Some(8080)
"port = 80" -> None
"host = x" -> None
2
[[1, 2], [3, 4]] [5]
'port = 8080' -> 8080
'port = 80' -> None
'host = x' -> None
  • A let chain joins let patterns and normal tests with &&. It works in if and while.
  • Naked functions are stable. You write the whole body in assembly with naked_asm!.
  • cfg(true) and cfg(false) are allowed.
  • Cargo cleans its download cache by itself. It removes files that nobody used for months.
  • New: Cell::update, HashMap::extract_if, as_chunks.

Let chains need the 2024 edition. The same file with edition 2021 gives this error on rustc 1.99.0: error: let chains are only allowed in Rust 2024 or later.

Rust 1.89.0 (7 August 2025): let the compiler count

// New in 1.89: `_` for a const generic argument. The compiler finds the number.
fn zeros<const N: usize>() -> [u8; N] {
    [0; _]
}

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let row: [u8; 4] = zeros::<_>();
    println!("{row:?}");

    // New in 1.89: flatten a Result inside a Result.
    let nested: Result<Result<u8, String>, String> = Ok(Err("inner".to_string()));
    println!("{:?}", nested.flatten());

    // New in 1.89: lock a file, so two programs do not write at the same time.
    let file = std::fs::File::create("demo.lock")?;
    file.lock()?;
    println!("locked");
    file.unlock()?;
    Ok(())
}
[0, 0, 0, 0]
Err("inner")
locked

This release also added a lint about lifetimes that hide. Here is the warning for fn words(text: &str) -> std::str::Split<char>.

warning: hiding a lifetime that's elided elsewhere is confusing
 --> e189b.rs:1:16
  |
1 | fn words(text: &str) -> std::str::Split<char> {
  |                ^^^^     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the same lifetime is hidden here
  |                |
  |                the lifetime is elided here
  |
  = note: `#[warn(mismatched_lifetime_syntaxes)]` on by default
help: use `'_` for type paths
  |
1 | fn words(text: &str) -> std::str::Split<'_, char> {
  |                                         +++
  • _ can stand for a const generic argument, as in [0; _].
  • The lint mismatched_lifetime_syntaxes asks you to show hidden lifetimes with '_.
  • AVX-512 and more x86 CPU features are stable.
  • cargo test --doc --target runs doc tests for another target too.
  • New: File::lock, Result::flatten, NonNull::from_ref, OsString::leak.
  • This was the last release with Intel Macs as Tier 1.

Rust 1.90.0 (18 September 2025): faster linking on Linux

// New in 1.90: these float functions also run at compile time.
const ROWS: f64 = (10.0_f64 / 3.0).ceil();

fn main() {
    println!("{ROWS}");
    // New in 1.90: take a signed number from an unsigned one, with a check.
    let balance: u32 = 5;
    println!("{:?}", balance.checked_sub_signed(8));
    println!("{:?}", balance.checked_sub_signed(-8));
    println!("{}", balance.saturating_sub_signed(8));
    // New in 1.90: compare an owned C string with a borrowed one.
    let owned = std::ffi::CString::new("ok").unwrap();
    println!("{}", owned == c"ok");
}
4
None
Some(13)
0
true
  • The linker LLD is the default on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu. Linking gets faster. You can switch it off with -C linker-features=-lld.
  • cargo publish --workspace publishes all crates of a workspace in the right order.
  • Intel Macs moved from Tier 1 to Tier 2.
  • New: checked_sub_signed and its family. floor, ceil and round work in const code.

The LLD change is for Linux on x86-64. This machine is a Mac, so the linker change was not tested here.

Rust 1.91.0 (30 October 2025): Windows on ARM is Tier 1

use std::path::Path;
use std::time::Duration;

fn main() {
    // New in 1.91: add with a carry bit. Big-number code needs this.
    println!("{:?}", u8::MAX.carrying_add(1, true));
    println!("{:?}", Duration::from_mins(90)); // new in 1.91
    println!("{}", Duration::from_hours(2) == Duration::from_mins(120));
    // New in 1.91: the file name before the FIRST dot.
    let p = Path::new("backup.tar.gz");
    println!("{:?} {:?}", p.file_prefix(), p.file_stem());
    println!("{}", p == "backup.tar.gz"); // new in 1.91: Path == str

    // New in 1.91: `strict_*` panics on overflow in every build mode.
    let big: u8 = "250".parse().unwrap();
    println!("{}", big.strict_add(5));
    println!("{}", big.strict_add(6));
}

  • aarch64-pc-windows-msvc, Windows on ARM, is a Tier 1 target.
  • A new lint warns when a function returns a raw pointer to its own local variable.
  • The strict_* methods panic on overflow, also in release builds.
  • A panic message now shows the thread id. You can see it in the output above.
  • New: Duration::from_mins, Path::file_prefix, PathBuf::add_extension, BTreeMap::extract_if.
  • Cargo has the setting build.build-dir for its work files.

Rust 1.92.0 (11 December 2025): ready for the never type

use std::convert::Infallible;
use std::num::NonZero;
use std::sync::{RwLock, RwLockWriteGuard};

fn log(_msg: &str) -> Result<(), Infallible> {
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    log("start"); // since 1.92 there is no warning: this Result can never be Err

    let config = RwLock::new(1);
    let mut writer = config.write().unwrap();
    *writer += 1;
    // New in 1.92: turn a write lock into a read lock, with no gap between.
    let reader = RwLockWriteGuard::downgrade(writer);
    println!("{}", *reader);

    let items = NonZero::new(10_u32).unwrap();
    let per_page = NonZero::new(4_u32).unwrap();
    println!("{}", items.div_ceil(per_page)); // new in 1.92: divide and round up

    // New in 1.92: memory on the heap that is already full of zero bytes.
    let zeros: Box<[u8; 4]> = unsafe { Box::<[u8; 4]>::new_zeroed().assume_init() };
    println!("{zeros:?}");
}
2
3
[0, 0, 0, 0]
  • Two lints about the never type now give errors. They prepared the big change of 1.100.
  • unused_must_use is silent for Result<(), Infallible>. On rustc 1.88.0 the line log("start"); still gave a warning.
  • On Linux, backtraces work again with -Cpanic=abort.
  • New: RwLockWriteGuard::downgrade, Box::new_zeroed, NonZero::div_ceil.
  • iter::Repeat::count now panics. Before, it never returned.

2026: releases 1.93 to 1.100

The newest eight releases. The last one, 1.100.0, is three days old today. Its example is marked "not run here".

Rust 1.93.0 (22 January 2026): better static Linux builds

use std::collections::VecDeque;
use std::fmt;
use std::time::Duration;

fn main() {
    // New in 1.93: a slice becomes an array reference when the length fits.
    let bytes: &[u8] = &[1, 2, 3, 4];
    let four: Option<&[u8; 4]> = bytes.as_array();
    let five: Option<&[u8; 5]> = bytes.as_array();
    println!("{four:?} {five:?}");

    // New in 1.93: a Display value made from a closure. No new struct is needed.
    let label = fmt::from_fn(|f| write!(f, "{} items", bytes.len()));
    println!("{label}");

    let mut queue = VecDeque::from([3, 9, 4]);
    println!("{:?} {queue:?}", queue.pop_front_if(|n| *n < 5)); // new in 1.93
    println!("{:?}", Duration::from_nanos_u128(1_500_000_000)); // new in 1.93
    println!("{}", char::MAX_LEN_UTF8); // new in 1.93
}
Some([1, 2, 3, 4]) None
4 items
Some(3) [9, 4]
1.5s
4
  • The *-linux-musl targets ship musl 1.2.5. Static Linux programs get a better DNS client.
  • A global allocator written in Rust may use thread-local storage.
  • One line inside asm! can have its own #[cfg].
  • New: as_array, fmt::from_fn, VecDeque::pop_front_if, Vec::into_raw_parts.
  • #[test] on a wrong item, such as a struct, is now an error.

Rust 1.94.0 (5 March 2026): array windows

use std::sync::LazyLock;

static CONFIG: LazyLock<String> = LazyLock::new(|| "ready".to_string());

fn rising(temps: &[i32]) -> bool {
    // New in 1.94: windows that are arrays, so a pattern can take them apart.
    temps.array_windows().all(|[a, b]| a < b)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{} {}", rising(&[1, 4, 9]), rising(&[1, 9, 4]));

    // New in 1.94: look inside a LazyLock without starting it.
    println!("{:?}", LazyLock::get(&CONFIG));
    let _ = CONFIG.len(); // first use: the value is built now
    println!("{:?}", LazyLock::get(&CONFIG));

    // New in 1.94: take the next item only if it can be converted.
    let mut words = ["12", "7", "x", "5"].into_iter().peekable();
    let mut sum = 0;
    while let Some(n) = words.next_if_map(|w| w.parse::<i32>().map_err(|_| w)) {
        sum += n;
    }
    println!("{sum} {:?}", words.next());
    println!("{:.4}", std::f64::consts::GOLDEN_RATIO); // new in 1.94
}
from itertools import pairwise

def rising(temps: list[int]) -> bool:
    # pairwise gives (a, b), (b, c), ... like array_windows with size 2.
    return all(a < b for a, b in pairwise(temps))

print(rising([1, 4, 9]), rising([1, 9, 4]))
true false
None
Some("ready")
19 Some("x")
1.6180
True False
  • array_windows is like windows, but each window is an array of a fixed size.
  • LazyLock::get returns None when the value is not built yet.
  • Peekable::next_if_map tests and converts the next item in one step.
  • Cargo config files can pull in other files with include.
  • Cargo reads TOML 1.1. An inline table can span lines and end with a comma.
  • The standard library uses Unicode 17.

Rust 1.95.0 (16 April 2026): cfg_select! and if let guards

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, Ordering};

// New in 1.95: choose code at compile time, like a `match` on the target.
const OS: &str = cfg_select! {
    target_os = "macos" => "macOS",
    target_os = "linux" => "Linux",
    windows => "Windows",
    _ => "another system",
};

fn describe(input: Option<&str>) -> String {
    match input {
        // New in 1.95: `if let` inside a match guard.
        Some(text) if let Ok(n) = text.parse::<i32>() => format!("number {n}"),
        Some(text) => format!("text {text}"),
        None => "nothing".to_string(),
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{OS}");
    println!("{} / {} / {}", describe(Some("42")), describe(Some("hi")), describe(None));

    let mut names = vec!["ann".to_string()];
    let last = names.push_mut("bo".to_string()); // new in 1.95: push, then get `&mut`
    last.push('b');
    println!("{names:?}");

    let hits = AtomicU32::new(5);
    hits.update(Ordering::Relaxed, Ordering::Relaxed, |n| n * 2); // new in 1.95
    println!("{}", hits.load(Ordering::Relaxed));
    println!("{:?} {}", bool::try_from(1_u8), bool::try_from(2_u8).is_err()); // new in 1.95
}
import sys

OS = {"darwin": "macOS", "linux": "Linux", "win32": "Windows"}.get(sys.platform, "another system")

def describe(value: str | None) -> str:
    match value:
        # A guard with the walrus does the same job as `if let` in a Rust guard.
        case str() as text if (n := to_int(text)) is not None:
            return f"number {n}"
        case str() as text:
            return f"text {text}"
        case None:
            return "nothing"

def to_int(text: str) -> int | None:
    try:
        return int(text)
    except ValueError:
        return None

print(OS)
print(describe("42"), "/", describe("hi"), "/", describe(None))
macOS
number 42 / text hi / nothing
["ann", "bob"]
10
Ok(true) true
macOS
number 42 / text hi / nothing
  • cfg_select! is a macro. It keeps the first arm whose condition is true. Many projects used the cfg-if crate for this.
  • A match guard can contain if let. The guard does not count for the "all cases covered" check.
  • New: Vec::push_mut, update on atomics, bool::try_from for integers, hint::cold_path.
  • The module core::range starts here with RangeInclusive.
  • Apple tvOS, watchOS and visionOS targets moved to Tier 2.
  • Custom JSON target files are for nightly only again.

Rust picks the operating system when it compiles. Python picks it when the program runs. That is why the Rust twin is a const.

Rust 1.96.0 (28 May 2026): new ranges and assert_matches!

use core::assert_matches;
use core::range::Range;

// New in 1.96: this Range is Copy, so a struct that holds it can be Copy too.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
struct Span(Range<usize>);

impl Span {
    fn of(self, text: &str) -> &str {
        &text[self.0]
    }
}

fn parse(text: &str) -> Result<u8, std::num::ParseIntError> {
    text.parse()
}

fn main() {
    let span = Span(Range { start: 0, end: 4 });
    let copy = span; // a copy, not a move
    println!("{} | {}", span.of("rust 1.96"), copy.of("fast code"));

    // New in 1.96: assert that a value matches a pattern.
    assert_matches!(parse("7"), Ok(1..=9));
    assert_matches!(parse("300"), Err(_));
    println!("two asserts passed");
    assert_matches!(parse("70"), Ok(1..=9)); // this one fails
}
rust | fast
two asserts passed

 right: Ok(1..=9)

  • core::range::Range and its friends are new range types. They are Copy.
  • The syntax 0..4 still makes the old type. The release post says a future edition will change that.
  • assert_matches! checks a value against a pattern. On failure it prints the value.
  • You can loop over a range of NonZero integers.
  • WebAssembly targets: a symbol that is not defined is now a link error.
  • Cargo fixed two security bugs, CVE-2026-5222 and CVE-2026-5223. Users of crates.io were not affected.

assert_matches! needs an import: use std::assert_matches;. It is not loaded by default, because many crates already had a macro with this name.

Rust 1.97.0 (9 July 2026): new symbol names, strict Cargo

fn main() {
    let n: u32 = 0b0010_1100; // 44
    // New in 1.97: small helpers for bits.

    println!("{:?}", 0_u32.highest_one());
    const IS_CONTROL: bool = '\n'.is_control(); // works in const since 1.97
    println!("{IS_CONTROL}");

None
true

The big change is under the hood. A symbol is the name of a function in the compiled file. Mangling makes that name unique. Rust 1.97 uses the scheme "v0" by default. The same generic function gives these two names.

The old name hides the type u8 behind a hash. The new name keeps it as the letter h. Very old debuggers and profilers may not read the new names.

Rust 1.98.0 (20 August 2026): fast number text


use core::fmt::NumBuffer;

fn main() {
    // New in 1.98: write an integer as text into a small buffer on the stack.
    let mut buf = NumBuffer::<u64>::new();
    let text: &str = 1_234_567_u64.format_into(&mut buf);
    println!("{text} has {} digits", text.len());

    // New in 1.98: a sum that the compiler may reorder to go faster.
    let prices = [0.1_f64, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4];
    let total = prices.iter().fold(0.0_f64, |acc, p| acc.algebraic_add(*p));
    println!("{}", (total - 1.0).abs() < 1e-9);

    println!("{:?}", "[42]".strip_circumfix('[', ']')); // new in 1.98
    let line = "name=ann";
    let value = &line[5..];
    println!("{:?}", line.substr_range(value)); // new in 1.98
    println!("{:?}", (line.len() > 20).ok_or("too short")); // new in 1.98
    println!("{}", None::<&str>.map_or_default(|s| s.len())); // new in 1.98
}

  • format_into writes an integer as text without a String. The release post says it is about as fast as the itoa crate.
    • 
  
  • The algebraic_* float methods let the compiler reorder the maths. The result can differ in the last digits.
    • 
  
  • The docs now promise that a dropped Box inside ManuallyDrop may be moved.
    • 
  
  • New: strip_circumfix, substr_range, bool::ok_or, Option::map_or_default.
    • 
  
  • Five bare-metal ARM targets moved to Tier 2.
    • 



Do not use algebraic_add where every bit must be the same on every machine. Use it for speed in sums where a tiny difference is fine.



Rust 1.99.0 (1 October 2026): C-variadic functions


use std::collections::VecDeque;

// New in 1.99: write a C-style function that takes any number of arguments.
/// SAFETY: pass `count`, then exactly `count` values of type i32.
unsafe extern "C" fn sum(count: u32, mut args: ...) -> i32 {
    let mut total = 0;
    for _ in 0..count {
        // SAFETY: the caller promised that an i32 comes next.
        total += unsafe { args.next_arg::<i32>() };
    }
    total
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", unsafe { sum(3, 10_i32, 20_i32, 12_i32) });

    // New in 1.99: a boxed array gives its items by value in a `for` loop.
    let boxed: Box<[String; 2]> = Box::new(["a".to_string(), "b".to_string()]);
    for s in boxed {
        print!("{s} ");
    }
    println!();

    let mut recent = VecDeque::from([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
    recent.retain_back(2); // new in 1.99: keep only the last two
    println!("{recent:?}");

    // New in 1.99: repair bad UTF-8. Good bytes are not copied.
    println!("{}", String::from_utf8_lossy_owned(vec![b'o', b'k', 0xFF]));
}

a b
[4, 5]

  • A variadic function takes any number of arguments. Rust could call such C functions before. Now Rust can define them.
    • 
  
  • size_of_val_raw, align_of_val_raw and Layout::for_value_raw read the size behind a raw pointer.
    • 
  
  • The docs of Box::leak now say: do not free leaked memory later. Use Box::into_raw for that plan.
    • 
  
  • Cargo has a new profile named debug. Today it is the same as dev.
    • 
  
  • Cargo switches off incremental compilation when the variable CI is set.
    • 
  
  • The old modules such as std::i32 are deprecated. Write i32::MAX.

Rust 1.100.0 (12 November 2026): the never type


not run here This machine has rustc 1.99.0. The code below follows the release notes of 1.100.0.


use std::mem::DropGuard;
use std::num::ParseIntError;

// New in 1.100: `!` (the never type) can be written in any type position.
fn certain<T>(result: Result<T, !>) -> T {
    let Ok(value) = result; // the Err side can never exist
    value
}

fn parse_all(nums: &mut Vec<u32>, words: &[&str]) -> Result<(), ParseIntError> {
    let old_len = nums.len();
    // New in 1.100: the closure runs when the guard goes away.
    let mut nums = DropGuard::new(nums, move |nums| nums.truncate(old_len));
    for w in words {
        nums.push(w.parse()?); // on error, the guard removes the new items
    }
    DropGuard::dismiss(nums); // success: keep the new items
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", certain(Ok(5)));

    let mut nums = vec![1];
    println!("{} {nums:?}", parse_all(&mut nums, &["2", "x"]).is_err());
    println!("{} {nums:?}", parse_all(&mut nums, &["2", "3"]).is_ok());

    let mut light = false;
    light.toggle(); // new in 1.100
    println!("{light}");
    println!("{}", "v1.100".trim_prefix("v")); // new in 1.100
    println!("{:?}", Vec::from_fn(4, |i| i * i)); // new in 1.100
}

  • The never type ! is stable. It is the type of return, break and panic!.
    • 
  
  • Infallible is now another name for !.
    • 
  
  • The main parts of the allocator API are stable: the trait Allocator, Vec::new_in and Box::new_in.
    • 
  
  • DropGuard runs a closure on every way out of a function.
    • 
  
  • Cargo warns about dependencies that you never use.
    • 
  
  • Cargo can wait before it uses a brand-new crate version. This is a dependency cooldown.
    • 
  
  • New: bool::toggle, str::trim_prefix, Vec::from_fn, Box::map.
    • 
  
  • The standard library uses Unicode 18. wasm32-wasip3 is a Tier 2 target.
    • 



[registry]
global-min-publish-age = "3 days"


In 1.100 the never type "fallback" changed in every edition. A value with an unknown type in code that never returns is now !, not (). The release notes call the breaks rare. Also, Cargo has a new layout for its build folder. Tools that read that folder directly may fail.



The ten changes that matter most


This is the opinion of this book. It is not an official list. The order is the order of time.



  

    
1. Async fn in traits

    
A trait can say async fn get(&self). Async code now fits normal Rust design.

  

  

    
2. Inline const and stronger const code

    
const { ... } came in 1.79. &mut in const code came in 1.83. More work moves to compile time.

  

  

    
3. LazyLock

    
A global value that builds itself on first use. No extra crate is needed.

  

  

    
4. The expect attribute

    
#[expect(lint)] silences a warning today. It warns again when the reason is gone.

  

  

    
5. Clearer unsafe code

    
&raw, unsafe extern and #[unsafe(...)]. The word "unsafe" now sits where the risk is.

  

  

    
6. Cargo respects your Rust version

    
With rust-version and resolver 3, Cargo avoids dependencies that are too new for you.

  

  

    
7. The 2024 edition and async closures

    
A new set of language rules, and async |x| { ... } with the AsyncFn traits.

  

  

    
8. Trait upcasting

    
&dyn Shape becomes &dyn Debug with no helper method.

  

  

    
9. Let chains and if let guards

    
Let chains came in 1.88. Guards with if let came in 1.95. Deep nesting goes away.

  

  

    
10. The never type and allocators

    
! is a real type. Collections can use your own allocator. Both took many years of work.

  





The changes by theme

Clippy reads rust-version. It warns when you use a newer function. The docs of the standard library show the same fact. Each item has a small "since" version.



Upgrade in small steps



  
    
    
  1. Read the blog post of the new release. Then read "Compatibility Notes" in RELEASES.md.
    2. 
    
  2. Make sure your work is saved in git and all tests pass on the old version.
    3. 
    
  3. Run rustup update stable. Check with rustc --version.
    4. 
    
  4. Run cargo check and then cargo test. Read every new warning.
    5. 
    
  5. Run cargo clippy. New lints often point to real problems.
    6. 
    
  6. If a dependency fails, run cargo update for that crate and test again.
    7. 
    
  7. Raise rust-version only when you need a new feature.
    8. 
  




[toolchain]
channel = "1.99.0"



Changes that can bite



  
1.80: an old dependency stops compiling
New trait impls changed type inference. Old versions of the time crate failed. Update dependencies first.

  
1.81: sort may panic, panics in extern "C" stop the program
The new sort code can notice a broken Ord and panic. A panic that crosses extern "C" now ends the process.

  
1.90: another linker on Linux
LLD is the default on Linux x86-64. Rare link problems can show up. The flag -C linker-features=-lld switches back.

  
1.94: macro names can clash
Standard macros now come from the prelude. If you import your own matches! with a star import, the name is ambiguous.

  
1.97: symbol names look different
The v0 names are the default. Old debuggers and profilers may show raw names. Linker messages also become visible.

  
1.99: new deprecation warnings
std::i32::MAX and its friends now warn. With deny on warnings, the build fails. The fix is i32::MAX.

  
1.100: never type fallback
The fallback is ! in all editions. The lints of 1.92 warned about code that this change breaks.




A good answer names a feature, its version and its edition. Example: "Let chains are stable since 1.88, but only in the 2024 edition." Also know the term future-compatibility warning. Rust warns for several releases before it turns a mistake into an error.



Patterns to remember



  Patterns from the releases 1.75 to 1.100
  
PatternPurposeModelNote

  
    
const { expr }Run code at compile time, in place[const { String::new() }; 3]Since 1.79. The value must be known at compile time.

    
static X: LazyLock<T>A global that is built on first usestatic PORTS: LazyLock<HashMap<&str, u16>> = LazyLock::new(|| ...);Since 1.80. Do not add a crate for this first.

    
#[expect(lint, reason = "...")]Silence a lint and get a reminder later#[expect(dead_code, reason = "used next week")]Since 1.81. allow never reminds you.

    
&raw const placeMake a raw pointer with no referencelet ptr = &raw const p.value;Since 1.82. Needed for packed fields.

    
unsafe extern "C" { safe fn ...; }Declare C functions with a clear promisepub safe fn abs(x: i32) -> i32;Since 1.82. The 2024 edition requires unsafe extern.

    
async |x| { ... }Pass async code as an argumentasync fn twice(job: impl AsyncFn(u32) -> u32)Since 1.85. It may borrow local variables.

    
let up: Box<dyn Super> = sub;Go from a trait object to its supertraitlet debug: Box<dyn Debug> = shape;Since 1.86. No helper method is needed.

    
slice.get_disjoint_mut([i, j])Two mutable borrows into one sliceif let Ok([a, b]) = v.get_disjoint_mut([0, 2])Since 1.86. It gives Err when the indexes overlap.

Fill in the missing word: let ptr = &? const p.value;


The oldest Rust that a crate supports is its ?.


    
  
  1. Rewrite this function with a let chain. It has four levels of nesting.

    fn domain_old(user: Option<&User>) -> Option<&str> {
    if let Some(u) = user {
        if let Some(email) = &u.email {
            if let Some((_, domain)) = email.split_once('@') {
                if !domain.is_empty() {
                    return Some(domain);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    None
}
    
    
    Answer

    fn domain_new(user: Option<&User>) -> Option<&str> {
    if let Some(u) = user
        && let Some(email) = &u.email
        && let Some((_, domain)) = email.split_once('@')
        && !domain.is_empty()
    {
        return Some(domain);
    }
    None
}
    
    
    Both versions return Some("example.org") for the email ann@example.org. Both return None when there is no email.
    2. 
  
  2. Your crate has rust-version = "1.85". You want to use Vec::extract_if. What is the problem, and what are your two choices?
    
    Answer
    Vec::extract_if is stable since 1.87. A user with Rust 1.85 cannot compile the crate. Clippy warns about this. Choice one: raise rust-version to 1.87. Choice two: keep 1.85 and use an older method, such as retain.
    3. 
  
  3. A release note says: "Stabilize if let guards on match arms". In which part of RELEASES.md is this line? What does it mean for you?
    
    Answer
    It is in the part "Language" of version 1.95.0. The syntax is now allowed on stable Rust. You can use it when your MSRV is 1.95 or higher.
    4. 
  
  4. After an upgrade to 1.80, a build failed inside the time crate. Why can a new Rust break an old dependency? What is the fix?
    
    Answer
    New trait impls in the standard library can make type inference unclear. Old code that relied on one single impl then fails. The fix is cargo update, because newer versions of the crate say the type clearly.
    5. 
  
  5. This public trait gives a warning. Change it so that the future is always Send. Keep async fn in the impl.

    pub trait Store {
    async fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<u32>;
}
    
    
    Answer

    use std::future::Future;

pub trait Store {
    // The plain form of `async fn`, with a Send promise added.
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> impl Future<Output = Option<u32>> + Send;
}

pub struct Memory(pub Vec<(String, u32)>);

impl Store for Memory {
    // The impl may still use `async fn`.
    async fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<u32> {
        self.0.iter().find(|(k, _)| k == key).map(|(_, v)| *v)
    }
}
    
    
    The warning text itself suggests this form. The trait method returns impl Future with + Send. A test with a function that needs T: Send compiles.
    6. 
  
  6. Hard. A team uses RUSTFLAGS=-Dwarnings in CI and upgrades from 1.98 to 1.99. The build fails on std::u32::MAX. Explain why. Give a quick fix and a better setup.
    
    Answer
    Rust 1.99 fully deprecates the old integer modules. Deprecation is a warning, and the flag turns every warning into an error. The quick fix is to write u32::MAX. A better setup pins the toolchain with rust-toolchain.toml. Then a new Rust arrives only when the team chooses it. Since 1.97 the team can also use CARGO_BUILD_WARNINGS=deny. That setting does not throw away the build cache.
    7. 




Key takeaways


    
  
  • Rust released 26 six-week versions from 1.75.0 to 1.100.0, plus 12 point releases.
    • 
  
  • The newest stable version on 15 November 2026 is 1.100.0, from 12 November 2026.
    • 
  
  • The big steps were async fn in traits, LazyLock, the 2024 edition, let chains and the never type.
    • 
  
  • Most of each release is small library growth. Read "Stabilized APIs" to find new helpers.
    • 
  
  • A feature has a first version. Set rust-version and let Clippy check it.
    • 
  
  • Some features also need an edition. Let chains need 2024.
    • 
  
  • Read "Compatibility Notes" before you upgrade. Install point releases at once.

Python versions: 3.8 to today

Python gets one new feature release every October. This chapter walks through every version from 3.8 to 3.15. For each one you see the date, the main changes and a small program that was really run.

  • Explain the yearly release cycle and the five years of support.
  • Name the main features of each version from 3.8 to 3.15.
  • Use new syntax such as match, except*, type parameters, t-strings and lazy imports.
  • Check which Python version a feature needs before you use it.
  • Choose a Python version for a new project today.

Where Python is today

Start with two commands. They show which Python you have.

python3.14 -VV
python3.15 -VV
Python 3.14.3 (main, Mar 10 2026, 18:02:52) [Clang 21.1.4 ]
Python 3.15.0b2 (main, Jun 11 2026, 04:04:20) [Clang 22.1.3 ]

Today is 15 November 2026. The newest Python release is 3.15.2. It came out on 25 October 2026. The first 3.15 release, 3.15.0, came out on 9 October 2026.

This machine has Python 3.14.3 and a test version of 3.15, called 3.15.0b2. The plain python3 here is an old 3.9. So always type the full name, like python3.14.

How to read a version number

Take 3.15.2. It has three parts.

  • 3 is the major number. It has been 3 since 2008.
  • 15 is the minor number. A new minor number is a feature release. It comes once a year.
  • 2 is the micro number. It counts bugfix releases.

A bugfix release never adds features. So Python 3.14.3 and 3.14.10 have the same features. Before a feature release there are test versions. a means alpha, b means beta and rc means release candidate. So 3.15.0b2 is "3.15.0, beta 2".

Programs often need to check the version. Look at this example first.

import sys

print(sys.version_info[:3])
print(sys.version_info >= (3, 11))
print("3.10" < "3.9")      # strings: compared letter by letter
print((3, 10) < (3, 9))    # tuples: compared number by number
(3, 14, 3)
True
True
False

The third line is wrong. It says 3.10 is older than 3.9. Strings compare letter by letter, and "1" comes before "9". A tuple compares number by number, so 10 is bigger than 9. Always compare sys.version_info with a tuple.

Never compare version strings. "3.10" is not "3.1" and it is not smaller than "3.9". The same rule holds for Rust: 1.100 comes after 1.99.

How this chapter marks its tests

  • ran on 3.14.3 The code ran on this Mac with Python 3.14.3. All features of 3.8 to 3.14 work there. The newest 3.14.10 has the same features, so it gives the same result.
  • ran on 3.15.0b2 The code ran on the 3.15 beta. The final 3.15.2 is not installed, so these examples were not run on the final release. Features stop changing at beta 1. The text follows the official release notes.
  • not run here The text comes from the official release notes only.
  • Rust twins ran on rustc 1.99.0 with edition 2024. Python 3.8, 3.10 and 3.11 are not installed. Their features were tested on 3.14.3. A few "old Python" checks ran on 3.9.13, 3.12 and 3.13.

The yearly release cycle

Here is the life of one version, Python 3.15. All dates come from PEP 790, its official schedule.

  1. 7 May 2025. Work on 3.15 starts. On the same day, 3.14 reaches beta 1.
  2. 14 October 2025. Alpha 1. New features arrive during the eight alphas.
  3. 7 May 2026. Beta 1. This is the feature freeze. After it, only fixes go in.
  4. 4 August 2026. Release candidate 1. Three candidates came before the final.
  5. 9 October 2026. Python 3.15.0, the final release.
  6. About October 2028. The last bugfix release with installers.
  7. About October 2031. End of life. No more fixes.

The rule behind these dates is PEP 602. It started with Python 3.9.

  • One feature release comes out every year, in October.
  • Each version is developed for about 17 months. The next version starts at the beta 1 of the previous one.
  • After the release, a version gets five years of support in total.
  • For the first two years it gets bugfix releases. They come about every two months, with installers for Windows and macOS.
  • For the next three years it gets security fixes only. These releases are source code only. There are no new installers.

Versions 3.9 to 3.12 had 18 months of bugfixes, then three and a half years of security fixes. Two full years started with 3.13.

A deprecated feature first gets a warning. Python waits at least two releases before it removes it. So a warning in 3.13 gives you time until 3.15 or later.

The table shows the status of every version today. It comes from the official "Status of Python versions" page.

"Security" does not mean "fully supported". Python 3.12 still gets fixes, but no new installers. If a bug in 3.12 hurts you, the fix may never come. Plan to move up.
