Python 3.8 and 3.9

Both versions are end of life now. But you meet their features in almost every codebase. So learn them well.

3.8: the walrus and positional-only parameters

def area(width, height, /, *, unit="m"):
    # width and height: by position only. unit: by name only.
    return f"{width * height} {unit}2"

readings = [12, 7, 31, 4]
if (n := len(readings)) > 3:       # walrus: give n a value inside the test
    print(f"{n=} readings, too many")

print(area(3, 4, unit="cm"))
try:
    area(width=3, height=4)
except TypeError as err:
    print("TypeError:", err)
n=4 readings, too many
12 cm2
TypeError: area() got some positional-only arguments passed as keyword arguments: 'width, height'
  • := is the walrus operator. It gives n a value and tests it in one line.
  • The / makes width and height positional-only. You can rename them later without breaking callers.
  • The * is older. Parameters after it are keyword-only.
  • f"{n=}" prints the name and the value. It is great for quick debugging.

3.8 also added functools.cached_property, importlib.metadata and an async prompt with python -m asyncio. For type hints it added Literal, Final, Protocol and TypedDict. The chapter Type hints explains them.

readings = [12, 7, 31, 4]
if n := len(readings) > 3:      # no brackets: n gets the result of ">"
    print("n is", n)
if (n := len(readings)) > 3:    # brackets: n gets the length
    print("n is", n)
n is True
n is 4

The walrus binds weakly. Without brackets, n gets True, not 4. Always put brackets around (name := value) inside a test.

3.9: dict union and built-in generics

Here is the same merge in Rust and in Python. Rust comes first.

use std::collections::BTreeMap;

fn main() {
    let defaults = BTreeMap::from([("host", "localhost"), ("port", "8000")]);
    let user = BTreeMap::from([("port", "9000")]);
    let mut config = defaults.clone(); // copy, then add the user values
    config.extend(user); // the later value wins, like `|` in Python
    println!("{config:?}");
}
defaults = {"host": "localhost", "port": "8000"}
user = {"port": "9000"}
config = defaults | user     # a new dict: the right side wins
print(config)
defaults |= user             # change defaults in place
print(defaults == config)
{"host": "localhost", "port": "9000"}
{'host': 'localhost', 'port': '9000'}
True

3.9 also lets you write list[int] and dict[str, int] in type hints. Before, you had to import List and Dict from typing.

from datetime import datetime
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

def names(rows: list[dict[str, str]]) -> list[str]:   # no typing.List
    return [r["name"].removeprefix("Dr. ") for r in rows]

print(names([{"name": "Dr. Kim"}, {"name": "Ana"}]))

call = datetime(2026, 11, 15, 9, 0, tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Asia/Tokyo"))
print(call.astimezone(ZoneInfo("Europe/London")))
['Kim', 'Ana']
2026-11-15 00:00:00+00:00
  • str.removeprefix() and removesuffix() cut a known start or end.
  • zoneinfo gives real time zones from the IANA database.
  • CPython got a new parser (PEP 617). It made match possible one year later.
  • PEP 602 started the yearly cycle with this version.
python3.14 -c 'print("Dr. Drew".strip("Dr. "), "|", "Dr. Drew".removeprefix("Dr. "))'
ew | Drew

strip("Dr. ") is not removeprefix("Dr. "). strip removes any of those letters from both ends. So it eats too much and leaves "ew". Use removeprefix to cut one exact start.

Python 3.10 and 3.11

3.10 reached end of life on 1 October 2026. 3.11 still gets security fixes until October 2027. Both versions changed daily Python a lot.

3.10: structural pattern matching

Pattern matching came to Python in 3.10. Rust had it from the start. Compare them.

fn handle(command: &str) -> String {
    let words: Vec<&str> = command.split_whitespace().collect();
    match words.as_slice() {
        ["go", direction] => format!("walk {direction}"),
        ["take", items @ ..] if !items.is_empty() => format!("take {} items", items.len()),
        ["quit" | "exit"] => "bye".to_string(),
        _ => "unknown".to_string(),
    }
}

fn main() {
    for c in ["go north", "take key lamp", "exit", "dance"] {
        println!("{c} -> {}", handle(c));
    }
}
def handle(command: str) -> str:
    match command.split():
        case ["go", direction]:
            return f"walk {direction}"
        case ["take", *items] if items:
            return f"take {len(items)} items"
        case ["quit" | "exit"]:
            return "bye"
        case _:
            return "unknown"

for c in ["go north", "take key lamp", "exit", "dance"]:
    print(c, "->", handle(c))
go north -> walk north
take key lamp -> take 2 items
exit -> bye
dance -> unknown
  • ["go", direction] matches a list of two words. It puts the second word in direction.
  • *items takes the rest, like items @ .. in Rust.
  • if items is a guard. "quit" | "exit" means one or the other.
  • case _ matches anything. See Structs, enums and pattern matching for more.

The same file on Python 3.9 stops at once:

    match command.split():
          ^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax

3.10 also made unions short. Write int | None instead of Optional[int]. And zip() can now check the lengths.

def parse_port(text: str) -> int | None:     # X | Y instead of Optional[X]
    return int(text) if text.isdigit() else None

print(parse_port("8080"), parse_port("http"))

try:
    list(zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b"], strict=True))
except ValueError as err:
    print("ValueError:", err)
8080 None
ValueError: zip() argument 2 is shorter than argument 1

Other 3.10 changes: brackets around many with items, clearer error messages with "Did you mean", itertools.pairwise(), the built-ins aiter() and anext(), and int.bit_count().

DEFAULT = 80

def kind(port: int) -> str:
    match port:
        case DEFAULT:          # a bare name catches every value
            return "default"
        case 443:
            return "https"
    return "other"
  File ".../capture_bug.py", line 5
    case DEFAULT:          # a bare name catches every value
         ^^^^^^^
SyntaxError: name capture 'DEFAULT' makes remaining patterns unreachable

A bare name in a case is not a comparison. It catches the value and gives it that name. To compare with a constant, use a dotted name like Port.DEFAULT, or write the number.

3.11: faster, with exception groups and task groups

3.11 is the speed release. The official notes say it is 10 to 60 percent faster than 3.10. On the standard benchmark it is 1.25 times faster on average. The trick is a specializing adaptive interpreter (PEP 659). Your code does not change at all.

3.11 also added exception groups. A task group uses them. Look at this example.

import asyncio

async def fetch(name: str, delay: float) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    if name.startswith("bad"):
        raise ValueError(f"{name} failed")
    return name.upper()

async def main() -> None:
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:     # waits for all tasks
            ok = tg.create_task(fetch("api", 0.01))
            tg.create_task(fetch("bad-db", 0.02))
            tg.create_task(fetch("bad-cache", 0.02))
    except* ValueError as group:                  # catch part of a group
        for err in group.exceptions:
            print("caught:", err)
    print("first task:", ok.result())

asyncio.run(main())
caught: bad-db failed
caught: bad-cache failed
first task: API
  • TaskGroup starts tasks and waits for all of them. If one fails, it cancels the others.
  • Two tasks failed. So the group raised an ExceptionGroup with two errors inside.
  • except* catches the matching errors from the group. Other errors keep going up.
  • The chapter Generators and asyncio goes deeper.

Errors also got notes and sharper tracebacks. The marks under the code show the exact part that failed (PEP 657).

def read_port(env: dict[str, str]) -> int:
    try:
        return int(env["PORT"])
    except ValueError as err:
        err.add_note("Hint: PORT must be a whole number.")
        raise

read_port({"PORT": "ten"})
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../note.py", line 8, in <module>
    read_port({"PORT": "ten"})
    ~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File ".../note.py", line 3, in read_port
    return int(env["PORT"])
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'ten'
Hint: PORT must be a whole number.

The new tomllib module reads TOML. Many projects keep settings in pyproject.toml, so this helps a lot.

import tomllib

with open("app.toml") as f:          # text mode: wrong
    try:
        tomllib.load(f)
    except TypeError as err:
        print("TypeError:", err)

with open("app.toml", "rb") as f:    # binary mode: right
    print(tomllib.load(f))
TypeError: File must be opened in binary mode, e.g. use `open('foo.toml', 'rb')`
{'server': {'port': 8080}}

tomllib.load() needs a file opened with "rb". Also, tomllib can only read. To write TOML you need a package from PyPI.

More 3.11 additions: asyncio.timeout(), enum.StrEnum, the type hints Self, LiteralString and TypeVarTuple, and the -P option for a safer import path.

Python 3.12 and 3.13

Both versions get security fixes only now. Their features are new enough that you should check them before you use them in a library.

3.12: type parameter syntax and freer f-strings

A type parameter lets one function work with many types. Rust always wrote them in angle brackets. Since 3.12, Python writes them in square brackets.

type Pair<T> = (T, T); // a generic type alias

fn first<T: Copy>(items: &[T]) -> T {
    items[0]
}

fn swap<T>(pair: Pair<T>) -> Pair<T> {
    (pair.1, pair.0)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{} {:?}", first(&[3, 1, 2]), swap(("a", "b")));
}
type Pair[T] = tuple[T, T]           # a generic type alias

def first[T](items: list[T]) -> T:   # T is a type parameter
    return items[0]

def swap[T](pair: Pair[T]) -> Pair[T]:
    return (pair[1], pair[0])

print(first([3, 1, 2]), swap(("a", "b")))
3 ("b", "a")
3 ('b', 'a')

The type statement makes a type alias. Before 3.12, you needed TypeVar("T") at the top of the file. Python 3.9 does not know this syntax:

    type Pair[T] = tuple[T, T]           # a generic type alias
         ^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax

3.12 also rebuilt f-strings inside the grammar (PEP 701). Now you can reuse the same quotes inside the braces. Backslashes and comments inside braces work too.

from itertools import batched
from typing import override

songs = ["intro", "verse"]
print(f"Playlist: {", ".join(songs)}")   # same quotes inside: OK since 3.12
print(list(batched(range(7), 3)))         # groups of 3

class Job:
    def run(self) -> str:
        return "job"

class NightJob(Job):
    @override                  # a type checker warns if Job has no run()
    def run(self) -> str:
        return "night job"

print(NightJob().run())
Playlist: intro, verse
[(0, 1, 2), (3, 4, 5), (6,)]
night job
  • @override marks a method that replaces a parent method. A type checker warns if the parent has no such method.
  • One process can hold several interpreters. Now each one can have its own GIL (PEP 684). In 3.12 you could use this only from C code.
  • sys.monitoring (PEP 669) gives fast hooks for debuggers and coverage tools.
  • The old modules distutils, asyncore, asynchat and imp are gone.
python3.12 -c "import distutils"
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'distutils'

Old setup.py files often import distutils. On 3.12 and later this fails. Move the build to pyproject.toml with setuptools or another build tool. See Packaging and testing.

3.13: a new REPL, and two big experiments

The REPL is the prompt you get when you type python3.13. In 3.13 it was rewritten, based on code from PyPy.

  • You can edit a whole block of several lines, and history keeps it.
  • Type exit or help without brackets.
  • Prompts and tracebacks have colour.
  • F1 opens help, F2 shows history, F3 is paste mode.
  • Set PYTHON_BASIC_REPL to get the old prompt back.

3.13 also started two experiments.

  • The free-threaded build (PEP 703) has no GIL. Threads can run Python code on many cores at once. It is a separate program, usually called python3.13t.
  • A basic JIT compiler (PEP 744). It was off by default and the gains were small.
import copy
import sys
import sysconfig
from dataclasses import dataclass
from warnings import deprecated

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int

p = Point(1, 2)
print(copy.replace(p, y=5))     # a changed copy of a frozen object

@deprecated("Use area_v2() instead.")
def area() -> int:
    return 1

area()                          # Python warns at run time

print("free-threaded build:", sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED"))
print("GIL on now:", sys._is_gil_enabled())
Point(x=1, y=5)
.../py313.py:19: DeprecationWarning: Use area_v2() instead.
  area()                          # Python warns at run time
free-threaded build: 0
GIL on now: True

The same file gave the same lines on Python 3.13.12. This Mac has the normal build, so the GIL is on. On a free-threaded build the first value is 1.

  • 19 old "dead battery" modules were removed (PEP 594). Some are cgi, crypt, telnetlib and imghdr. The 2to3 tool is gone too.
  • New type hints: defaults for type parameters, ReadOnly and TypeIs.
  • iOS and Android became official platforms, at tier 3.
  • From 3.13, a version gets two full years of bugfixes.
python3.13 -c "import cgi"
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'cgi'

On Python 3.12 the same import still works. It only prints a warning:

python3.12 -c "import cgi"
<string>:1: DeprecationWarning: 'cgi' is deprecated and slated for removal in Python 3.13

An old script can work on 3.12 and fail on 3.13. People ignore the warning until the module is gone. Always read the "Removed" part of the release notes before you upgrade.

Python 3.14

Python 3.14.0 came out on 7 October 2025. The newest bugfix release is 3.14.10, from 25 October 2026. This machine runs 3.14.3.

Template strings

A template string looks like an f-string with a t. But it does not build a str. It gives you the parts, so you decide how to join them.

import html
from string.templatelib import Interpolation, Template

def safe_html(tpl: Template) -> str:
    parts = []
    for part in tpl:
        if isinstance(part, Interpolation):
            parts.append(html.escape(str(part.value)))   # user data: escape
        else:
            parts.append(part)                           # our own text: keep
    return "".join(parts)

user = "<script>alert(1)</script>"
tpl = t"<p>Hello {user}</p>"
print(type(tpl).__name__)
print(safe_html(tpl))
Template
<p>Hello &lt;script&gt;alert(1)&lt;/script&gt;</p>

The user text was escaped. Our own <p> tags were kept. Libraries can do the same for SQL, shell commands and logs. See Strings and text.

user = "Ann"
print(t"Hello {user}")       # a Template, not a str
Template(strings=('Hello ', ''), interpolations=(Interpolation('Ann', 'user', None, ''),))

A t-string is not text. Printing it shows its parts, not a nice sentence. You must pass it to a function that turns it into a result.

Deferred annotations, and except without brackets

An annotation is not computed when Python defines the function any more (PEP 649 and PEP 749). Python computes it only when someone asks. So a forward reference needs no quotes.

from annotationlib import Format, get_annotations

class Node:
    def add(self, child: Node) -> None:   # no quotes around Node
        pass

print(get_annotations(Node.add, format=Format.STRING))
print(Node.add.__annotations__)

try:
    int("x")
except ValueError, TypeError:            # no brackets needed (no "as")
    print("not a number")
{'child': 'Node', 'return': 'None'}
{'child': <class '__main__.Node'>, 'return': None}
not a number
  • The new annotationlib module reads annotations in three formats: VALUE, FORWARDREF and STRING.
  • You no longer need from __future__ import annotations for forward references.
  • PEP 758 allows except A, B: without brackets. With as err you still need brackets.

Subinterpreters in the standard library

A subinterpreter is a full Python inside your process. Each one has its own GIL since 3.12. The new concurrent.interpreters module (PEP 734) makes them usable from Python code.

from concurrent.futures import InterpreterPoolExecutor

def count_primes(limit: int) -> int:
    # Slow on purpose: pure Python work that needs the CPU.
    return sum(all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1)) for n in range(2, limit))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Each worker is a separate interpreter with its own GIL.
    with InterpreterPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
        print(list(pool.map(count_primes, [1_000, 10_000, 50_000])))
[168, 1229, 5133]

This works like a process pool, but inside one process. The notes list limits. Start-up is not fast yet, each interpreter uses extra memory, and many C extensions from PyPI do not support it yet.

Free-threading, the JIT and a new interpreter

  • Free-threading is officially supported (PEP 779). It is still optional, a separate build. Single-thread code runs about 5 to 10 percent slower on it.
  • The JIT ships in the Windows and macOS installers. It is off unless you set PYTHON_JIT=1. It is still experimental: from 10 percent slower to 20 percent faster.
  • A tail-call interpreter is a new way to build CPython. With Clang 19 or newer it is about 3 to 5 percent faster.
import sys

print("JIT built in:", sys._jit.is_available())
print("JIT on now:", sys._jit.is_enabled())
python3.14 jit.py
PYTHON_JIT=1 python3.14 jit.py
JIT built in: True
JIT on now: False
JIT built in: True
JIT on now: True

The leading underscore in sys._jit means "internal". It can change in any release. Use it for tests, not in a library.

One 3.14 story is a lesson for experts. 3.14.0 shipped a new incremental garbage collector. In production it used too much memory. So 3.14.5 went back to the old collector, and 3.15 keeps the old one. You can see it in the thresholds:

python3.14 -c "import gc; print(gc.get_threshold())"
python3.15 -c "import gc; print(gc.get_threshold())"
(2000, 10, 0)
(2000, 10, 10)

On 3.14.0 to 3.14.4 the third number is always 0. It has no meaning there. This is why you should test bugfix releases too, not only feature releases.

Smaller but useful

from compression import zstd

data = b"python " * 1000
packed = zstd.compress(data)
print(len(data), "->", len(packed))
print(zstd.decompress(packed) == data)
7000 -> 25
True
  • compression.zstd adds Zstandard, a fast modern compression format.
  • The REPL now colours your code as you type.
  • python -m asyncio ps PID and pstree PID show the tasks of a running program.
  • sys.remote_exec() lets a debugger attach to a running process safely (PEP 768).
  • Releases are no longer signed with PGP (PEP 761). Use Sigstore to check them.
def risky() -> str:
    try:
        raise RuntimeError("disk full")
    finally:
        return "all good"        # this hides the error

print(risky())
.../finally.py:5: SyntaxWarning: 'return' in a 'finally' block
  return "all good"        # this hides the error
all good
all good

A return inside finally throws the error away. The disk is full, but the function says "all good". Since 3.14, Python warns about this (PEP 765). Move the return out of the finally block.

Python 3.15, the newest

Python 3.15.0 came out on 9 October 2026. Then 3.15.1 came on 21 October. 3.15.2 followed on 25 October, as a fast security release. This machine only has beta 2. ran on 3.15.0b2 The examples below ran on that beta, not on the final 3.15.2. The features match the official release notes.

Lazy imports

A lazy import waits until you first use the name. Programs with many imports start faster (PEP 810).

lazy import json                 # a proxy now, the real import later
import sys

print("json loaded:", "json" in sys.modules)
print(json.dumps({"ok": True}))  # first use: Python imports json here
print("json loaded:", "json" in sys.modules)
json loaded: False
{"ok": true}
json loaded: True
  • lazy is a soft keyword. It works with import x and from x import y.
  • At first Python puts a small proxy in the name. The real import happens on first use.
  • Lazy imports are allowed only at module level. Inside a function, a class or a try block they are a SyntaxError.
  • -X lazy_imports=all or PYTHON_LAZY_IMPORTS=all makes all imports lazy.
  • For older versions, list names in __lazy_modules__. Then 3.15 makes those plain imports lazy.
  File ".../py315lazy.py", line 1
    lazy import json                 # a proxy now, the real import later
         ^^^^^^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax

Now look at a lazy import of a module that does not exist.

lazy import plugins_missing
print("started")
plugins_missing.run()
started
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../lazyfail.py", line 1, in <module>
    lazy import plugins_missing
ImportError: lazy import of 'plugins_missing' raised an exception during resolution

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../lazyfail.py", line 3, in <module>
    plugins_missing.run()
    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'plugins_missing'

With a lazy import, a missing module fails later. The error comes at the first use, not at the top of the file. The traceback shows both places, so read it to the end.

frozendict, sentinel and unpacking in comprehensions

MISSING = sentinel("MISSING")               # a unique marker value

settings = frozendict(host="localhost", port=8000)
cache = {settings: "loaded"}                # hashable, so it can be a key
print(cache[frozendict(port=8000, host="localhost")])

def port_of(cfg, default=MISSING):
    port = cfg.get("port", default)
    return "no port" if port is MISSING else port

print(port_of(settings), port_of(frozendict()))

rows = [[1, 2], [3], [4, 5]]
print([*row for row in rows])               # unpacking in a comprehension
parts = [{"a": 1}, {"b": 2}, {"a": 3}]
print({**d for d in parts})                 # later keys win

try:
    settings["port"] = 9000
except TypeError as err:
    print("TypeError:", err)
loaded
8000 no port
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
{'a': 3, 'b': 2}
TypeError: 'frozendict' object does not support item assignment
  • frozendict is a dict that cannot change (PEP 814). It is hashable when its keys and values are. Order does not matter for ==.
  • sentinel("MISSING") makes a unique sentinel (PEP 661). Compare it with is. It is clearer than object().
  • A comprehension can now use * and ** (PEP 798).

Rust flattens with an iterator method. Python 3.15 does it with a star.

fn main() {
    let rows = vec![vec![1, 2], vec![3], vec![4, 5]];
    let flat: Vec<i32> = rows.into_iter().flatten().collect();
    println!("{flat:?}");
}
rows = [[1, 2], [3], [4, 5]]
flat = [*row for row in rows]   # unpacking in a comprehension
print(flat)
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

frozendict is not a subclass of dict. So isinstance(x, dict) is False for it. Check collections.abc.Mapping if you want to accept both.

UTF-8 by default

An encoding decides how text becomes bytes. From 3.15, open() uses UTF-8 when you give no encoding (PEP 686). Before, it used the system setting. That was a common bug on Windows.

import sys

print(sys.version.split()[0], "UTF-8 mode:", sys.flags.utf8_mode)
LANG=en_US.UTF-8 python3.14 utf8.py
LANG=en_US.UTF-8 python3.15 utf8.py
LANG=en_US.UTF-8 python3.15 -X utf8=0 utf8.py
3.14.3 UTF-8 mode: 0
3.15.0b2 UTF-8 mode: 1
3.15.0b2 UTF-8 mode: 0

-X utf8=0 or PYTHONUTF8=0 brings the old way back. Still, the best rule has not changed. Always write encoding="utf-8", and your code works the same on every version.

Faster, and easier to inspect

  • The JIT got a big upgrade. The notes report 7 to 8 percent on x86-64 Linux. On Apple silicon macOS they report 11 to 12 percent over the tail-call interpreter. It is still experimental.
  • A new profiling package (PEP 799). profiling.tracing is the old cProfile. profiling.sampling is Tachyon, a new sampling profiler.
  • Frame pointers are on by default (PEP 831). Native tools like perf can walk the stack more easily.
  • New module math.integer holds integer functions such as isqrt and comb.
  • Type hints: TypedDict gets closed and extra_items. TypeForm and @disjoint_base are new.
  • Wheels for free-threading: one wheel can now target the stable ABI of free-threaded builds, called abi3t (PEP 803).
  • Installers: the official macOS installer now adds free-threading support by default.

The Tachyon command looks like this. not run here On this Mac the beta stopped with a permission error. macOS needs sudo to read another process.

python3.15 -m profiling.sampling run slow.py       # start and profile a script
python3.15 -m profiling.sampling attach 1234       # profile a running process

Error messages learned words from other languages. Here is the same file on two versions.

items = [1, 2, 3]
items.push(4)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../py315err.py", line 2, in <module>
    items.push(4)
    ^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'push'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../py315err.py", line 2, in <module>
    items.push(4)
    ^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'push'. Did you mean '.append'?
from typing import TypedDict

class Point(TypedDict, closed=True):     # no other keys allowed
    x: int
    y: int

class Labels(TypedDict, extra_items=str):  # any extra key, value is str
    name: str

print(Point.__closed__, Labels.__extra_items__)
True <class 'str'>

not run here PEP 829 adds .start files. They name a function that runs when Python starts. They replace the risky import lines in .pth files. Code inside .pth files is hard to audit, and this makes it clear.

What comes next

Work on 3.16 started on 7 May 2026. Alpha 2 came out on 10 November 2026. The final 3.16.0 is planned for early October 2027 (PEP 826). not run here Its features are not fixed until beta 1, in May 2027. So this book does not list them.

Which version to use today

Before you choose, review the big steps. Swipe through the ten changes that matter most.

The walrus

if (n := len(xs)) > 3: names a value inside a test.

Built-in generics and dict union

list[int] without imports. a | b merges two dicts.

match

Patterns test the shape of a value and take parts out.

Speed

1.25 times faster on average. Your code does not change.

TaskGroup and except*

Structured async code. Many errors travel together.

Type parameters

def first[T](xs: list[T]) -> T and type Pair[T] = ...

No-GIL and JIT experiments

The free-threaded build and a first JIT appear.

t-strings

Templates keep text and values apart. Safe HTML and SQL.

Deferred annotations

Forward references without quotes. Faster imports of typed code.

Lazy imports and UTF-8

lazy import x for fast start-up. UTF-8 is the default encoding.

A simple decision

  • A new application: 3.14 is the safe choice in November 2026. It has had a year of fixes. Popular packages have had a year to ship wheels for it. Choose 3.15 when all your important packages support it.
  • A library: support every version that still gets fixes. Today that is 3.11 to 3.15.
  • Science libraries: many follow SPEC 0. It drops a version three years after its release. So in late 2026 they may need 3.13 or newer.
  • An old application: 3.10 and older get no fixes, not even for security. Upgrade first, then add features.

Write your minimum version in pyproject.toml. Tools like pip and uv read it.

[project]
name = "report-tool"
version = "1.0.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"

Sometimes you must support two versions in one file. Check the version with a tuple.

import sys

if sys.version_info >= (3, 11):
    import tomllib
else:
    import tomli as tomllib      # the same API, from PyPI

print(tomllib.loads("workers = 4"))
{'workers': 4}

Upgrade in five steps

  1. Read the "Porting to Python 3.14" part of the What's New page. Also read "Removed" for 3.13 and 3.14.
  2. Run your tests on the old version with warnings as errors: python -W error::DeprecationWarning -m pytest. Fix every warning.
  3. Check that every package you need has wheels for the new version.
  4. Add the new version to your test matrix in CI. Run both versions for a while.
  5. Change requires-python, deploy, and drop the old version later.

Interviews often ask about the GIL. A good short answer: 3.12 gave each subinterpreter its own GIL. 3.13 added an experimental build without a GIL. 3.14 made that build officially supported, but it is still optional. Also know that 3.11 brought the big speed-up.

Is Python 3 "version 3" or "version 3.14"?

Both words are used. The language is Python 3. A release is a feature version like 3.14, plus a bugfix number.

Do bugfix releases ever break code?

They should not, but it can happen. The 3.14.5 garbage collector change is a real example. Pin the full version in production and test each upgrade.

Where do I find all changes of one version?

On docs.python.org, the "What's New in Python 3.X" page. The full list is in the changelog linked from it.

Patterns to remember

Version patterns for daily Python
PatternPurposeModelNote
sys.version_info >= (3, N)Check the running versionif sys.version_info >= (3, 11):Never compare version strings.
(name := value) (3.8)Name a value inside a testif (n := len(xs)) > 3:Brackets are needed.
def f(a, /, *, b) (3.8)Fix how callers pass argumentsdef area(w, h, /, *, unit="m"):Left of /: position only.
a | b on dicts (3.9)Merge two dictsconfig = defaults | userThe right side wins.
match x: case ...: (3.10)Test the shape of a valuecase ["go", direction]:A bare name captures. It does not compare.
T | None (3.10)An optional typedef find() -> int | None:Replaces Optional[int].
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg: (3.11)Run tasks and wait for alltg.create_task(fetch(url))Errors arrive as a group.
except* Error as group: (3.11)Catch part of a groupexcept* ValueError as g:Loop over g.exceptions.
def f[T](x: T) -> T (3.12)A generic functiondef first[T](xs: list[T]) -> T:No TypeVar needed.
type Name = ... (3.12)A type aliastype Pair[T] = tuple[T, T]The value is computed lazily.
t"...{x}..." (3.14)Keep text and values apartsafe_html(t"<p>{user}</p>")The result is a Template, not a str.

frozendict(...) (3.15)A dict that cannot changefrozendict(host="x", port=80)Not a subclass of dict.
[*xs for xs in rows] (3.15)Flatten in one step[*row for row in rows]Use ** for dicts.
requires-pythonState your minimum versionrequires-python = ">=3.11"Raise it when a version reaches end of life.

Practice

Which release came out on 9 October 2026?

  • Python 3.14.0
  • Python 3.15.0
  • Python 3.15.2
  • Python 3.16.0

3.15.0 came on 9 October 2026. 3.15.2 came on 25 October 2026. 3.16 is planned for 2027.

Which version reached end of life on 1 October 2026?

  • 3.9
  • 3.10
  • 3.11
  • 3.12

3.10 came out in October 2021. Five years later it reached end of life. 3.9 ended in October 2025.

What does {"a": 1, "b": 2} | {"b": 9} give?

  • {'a': 1, 'b': 2}
  • {'a': 1, 'b': 9}
  • A TypeError

Dict union (3.9) makes a new dict. The right side wins for the same key.

The walrus operator is written ? and came in Python ?.

A security-only version gets source releases but no new ?.

In 3.15, [*row for row in [[1], [2, 3]]] gives ?.

What does t"Hi {name}" return in Python 3.14?

  • A str
  • A bytes object
  • A Template object

A t-string keeps the text and the values apart. A function must turn it into a result.

  1. Why is if platform_version < "3.9": a bug? Fix it.
    Answer

    Strings compare letter by letter, so "3.10" is smaller than "3.9". Use a tuple: if sys.version_info < (3, 9):.

  2. Rewrite def find(key: str) -> Optional[List[int]]: in the style of Python 3.10.
    Answer

    def find(key: str) -> list[int] | None:. list[int] works since 3.9. X | None works since 3.10. No import from typing is needed.

  3. A match has case TIMEOUT: where TIMEOUT = 30. Every value now goes to that case. Why, and how do you fix it?
    Answer

    A bare name is a capture pattern. It catches any value. Use a dotted name such as Limits.TIMEOUT, or write case 30:.

  4. A team writes a library in November 2026. Which Python versions should its tests cover, and why?
    Answer

    3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14 and 3.15. These still get fixes. 3.10 reached end of life on 1 October 2026. A science library that follows SPEC 0 may start at 3.13.

  5. Your service on 3.14.3 uses much less memory after an upgrade to 3.14.6. Give a likely reason from this chapter.
    Answer

    3.14.0 to 3.14.4 used a new incremental garbage collector. It caused high memory use for some programs. 3.14.5 went back to the old collector.

  6. With lazy import plugins, the program starts fine but fails later with ModuleNotFoundError. Explain this.
    Answer

    A lazy import only makes a proxy. Python loads the module on first use. So a missing module fails at the first use. The traceback shows the use and the import line.

  7. Old code uses asyncio.gather() and loses errors after the first one. Which 3.11 tools help, and how?
    Answer

    Use asyncio.TaskGroup. It waits for all tasks and cancels the rest when one fails. All errors arrive in one ExceptionGroup. Catch them with except*.

Key takeaways

  • Python ships one feature release every October. Bugfix releases never add features.
  • Each version gets five years: two years of bugfixes, then three years of security fixes only.
  • Today 3.15.2 is the newest release. 3.11 to 3.15 get fixes. 3.10 and older are end of life.
  • Key steps: 3.10 match, 3.11 speed and TaskGroup, 3.12 type parameters, 3.14 t-strings, 3.15 lazy imports.
  • Free-threading and the JIT grew from 3.13 to 3.15. They are real now, but still optional.
  • Check versions with sys.version_info, write requires-python, and read "Removed" before each upgrade.

Sources

  • What's New in Python. The official release notes for every version, 3.8 to 3.15.
  • What's New in Python 3.15. Lazy imports, frozendict, sentinel, UTF-8 default and the JIT numbers.
  • Status of Python versions. Support phases, first release and end-of-life dates.
  • Python downloads. The date of every release, including 3.15.2 and 3.14.10.
  • PEP 602: Annual release cycle for Python. The yearly cycle and the five-year support window.
  • SPEC 0: Minimum supported dependencies. The three-year rule many science libraries follow.

The Python data model

The data model is the set of rules behind every Python value. It says what an object is, how names point to objects, and how len(), ==, for and with talk to your own classes. Learn it once, and Python stops surprising you.

  • Explain identity, type and value, and choose between is and ==.
  • Predict what happens when two names point to one mutable object.
  • Write special methods so your class works with len, indexing, for, in, ==, sets and with.
  • Follow the steps of attribute lookup, and use __getattr__ and __slots__ well.
  • Match each special method to the Rust trait that does the same job.

This part of the book is about Python. So Python comes first. Each important idea has a Rust tab next to it for comparison. The Rust chapters explain the Rust side in full. This chapter links to them.

Everything is an object

Start with a few lines. Look at what each one prints.

x = 42
print(type(x), id(x) > 0)
print(isinstance(x, object), isinstance(len, object), isinstance(int, object))
print(type(int), type(type))

a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
c = a
print(a == b, a is b)   # same value, two objects
print(a is c)           # two names, one object
print((42).bit_length(), "hi".upper(), len.__name__)
<class 'int'> True
True True True
<class 'type'> <class 'type'>
True False
True
6 HI len

A number is an object. A function is an object. Even a class like int is an object. Its type is type. So everything has methods and attributes. That is why (42).bit_length() works.

Every object has three parts.

The three parts of every object
PartMeaningHow to read itCan it change?
IdentityWhich object this isid(x), and x is yNever
TypeWhat the object can dotype(x)No
ValueThe data insidex == y, print(x)Only for mutable types

In CPython, id(x) is the memory address of the object. a is b asks "same object?". a == b asks "same value?". Two lists can have the same value and still be two objects.

import sys
# Even a small int carries a header: a type pointer and a reference count.
print(sys.getsizeof(1), sys.getsizeof(2**100), sys.getsizeof(1.0))
28 40 24
use std::mem::size_of;
fn main() {
    // A Rust number is just its bytes. No header, no identity.
    println!("{} {} {}", size_of::<i32>(), size_of::<i64>(), size_of::<f64>());
}
4 8 8

This is the first big difference. In Python every value is a full object on the heap. In Rust a value is only its data. Rust has no id() for an i32. The book compares memory in Ownership and borrowing.

Now the common mistake. Look at this test with is.

a = int("1000")
b = int("1000")
print(a == b, a is b)
c = int("7")
d = int("7")
print(c == d, c is d)   # small ints are cached in CPython
x = None
print(x is None)        # the right use of is
True False
True True
True

Do not use is to compare numbers or strings. CPython keeps one shared object for small ints from -5 to 256. So is seems to work for 7 and fails for 1000. This is a detail of CPython, not a rule. Python even warns when it compiles the line: SyntaxWarning: "is" with 'int' literal. Did you mean "=="? Use is only for None, True, False and your own sentinel objects.

Names and references

A Python variable is not a box. It is a name tag on an object. Run this and guess each line first.

def add_item(items, item):
    items.append(item)      # changes the caller's list

def replace(items):
    items = ["new"]          # rebinds the local name only

shop = ["milk"]
add_item(shop, "eggs")
replace(shop)
print(shop)

a = [1, 2]
b = a
a = a + [3]      # makes a NEW list, then rebinds a
print(a, b)
a = b
a += [3]         # changes the list in place
print(a, b)
['milk', 'eggs']
[1, 2, 3] [1, 2]
[1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3]

An assignment binds a name to an object. It never copies. A reference is that link. Function arguments work the same way. The Python FAQ says arguments are "passed by assignment". The parameter is a new name for the caller's object.

  • Change the object (items.append), and the caller sees it.
  • Rebind the name (items = [...]), and the caller sees nothing.
  • a = a + [3] builds a new list. a += [3] changes the old list. For a list, += calls __iadd__, which works in place.

grid = [[0] * 3] * 3 makes three references to one row. grid[0][0] = 9 then prints [[9, 0, 0], [9, 0, 0], [9, 0, 0]]. Build each row on its own: [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)].

Rust does the opposite by default. let b = a; moves the list, and a is no longer usable. Sharing needs a borrow (&a) or an Rc. See Ownership and borrowing and Smart pointers.

Mutable and immutable

Some objects can change after they are made. Others cannot. Here is a tuple that holds a list.

t = ("ann", [1, 2])
t[1].append(3)          # the list inside can change
print(t)
try:
    t[1] += [4]
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
print(t)                # surprise: the list changed anyway
try:
    hash(t)
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
('ann', [1, 2, 3])
TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
('ann', [1, 2, 3, 4])
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

A mutable object can change in place. An immutable object cannot. The tuple stays immutable. It always holds the same two objects. But one of those objects is a list, and the list can change.

Built-in types by mutability
ImmutableMutable
int, float, bool, complexlist
str, bytesbytearray
tuple, frozensetdict, set
None, rangeMost objects of your own classes

Why did t[1] += [4] fail and still work? It runs two steps. First t[1].__iadd__([4]) extends the list. Then t[1] = result tries to store it back into the tuple. That second step fails. The Python FAQ explains this exact case.

Immutability matters for hashable objects. Dict keys and set items must be hashable. A tuple is hashable only if everything inside is hashable.

names = ("ann",)          # tuple: this TYPE cannot change
names_list = ["ann"]      # list: this TYPE can change
names_list.append("bo")   # any name for this list may change it
fn main() {
    let names = vec![String::from("ann")];
    // names.push(String::from("bo")); // error[E0596]: cannot borrow `names` as mutable
    let mut names = names;             // the same Vec, now through a mut binding
    names.push(String::from("bo"));
    let view = &names;                 // shared borrow: read only
    println!("{view:?}");
}
["ann", "bo"]

In Python, the type decides if a value can change. A list can always change, through any name. In Rust, the binding or the borrow decides. The same Vec is read only through let or &, and writable through let mut or &mut.

s.upper() does not change s. Strings are immutable. Every string method returns a new string. Write s = s.upper() to keep the result.

Special methods: how Python talks to your class

You write len(p). Python runs type(p).__len__(p). Each piece of syntax has a special method behind it. People also call them dunder methods. Here is a class that has six of them.

class Playlist:
    def __init__(self, name, songs):
        self.name = name
        self.songs = list(songs)

    def __repr__(self):                 # for developers: repr(), the REPL
        return f"Playlist({self.name!r}, {self.songs!r})"

    def __str__(self):                  # for users: print(), str()
        return f"{self.name} ({len(self)} songs)"

    def __len__(self):                  # len(p), and truth: empty is False
        return len(self.songs)

    def __getitem__(self, i):           # p[0], p[-1], p[1:3]
        if isinstance(i, slice):
            return Playlist(self.name, self.songs[i])
        return self.songs[i]

    def __iter__(self):                 # for song in p
        return iter(self.songs)

    def __contains__(self, song):       # "x" in p
        return song in self.songs

p = Playlist("Focus", ["Intro", "Rain", "Deep", "Outro"])
print(repr(p))
print(p)
print(len(p), p[0], p[-1])
print(p[1:3])
print("Rain" in p, [s.lower() for s in p])
print(bool(Playlist("Empty", [])))
Playlist('Focus', ['Intro', 'Rain', 'Deep', 'Outro'])
Focus (4 songs)
4 Intro Outro
Focus (2 songs)
True ['intro', 'rain', 'deep', 'outro']
False
use std::fmt;
use std::ops::Index;

#[derive(Debug)] // like __repr__: written for us
struct Playlist {
    name: String,
    songs: Vec<String>,
}

impl fmt::Display for Playlist { // like __str__
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "{} ({} songs)", self.name, self.songs.len())
    }
}

impl Index<usize> for Playlist { // like __getitem__
    type Output = String;
    fn index(&self, i: usize) -> &String {
        &self.songs[i]
    }
}

impl<'a> IntoIterator for &'a Playlist { // like __iter__
    type Item = &'a String;
    type IntoIter = std::slice::Iter<'a, String>;
    fn into_iter(self) -> Self::IntoIter {
        self.songs.iter()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let songs = ["Intro", "Rain", "Deep"].map(String::from).to_vec();
    let p = Playlist { name: "Focus".into(), songs };
    println!("{p:?}");
    println!("{p}");
    println!("{}", p[1]);
    for s in &p {
        print!("{} ", s.to_lowercase());
    }
    println!();
}
Playlist { name: "Focus", songs: ["Intro", "Rain", "Deep"] }
Focus (3 songs)
Rain
intro rain deep

Step through what Python does for each line.

repr(p) and print(p)

repr calls __repr__. print and str call __str__. Without __str__, Python uses __repr__.

len(p)

Calls __len__. It must return an int that is 0 or more.

p[0] and p[1:3]

Both call __getitem__. A slice arrives as a slice object. Raise IndexError for a bad index.

for s in p

Calls iter(p), which calls __iter__. It must return an iterator.

"Rain" in p

Calls __contains__. Without it, Python loops with __iter__, which is slower.

if p:

Calls __bool__. Without it, Python uses __len__: 0 means false. With neither, the object is always true.

This is duck typing. Python does not ask "is this a list?". It asks "does it have __len__?". A set of special methods that work together is a protocol, like the iteration protocol.

The old iteration protocol

A class with only __getitem__ is still iterable. Python calls it with 0, 1, 2 and so on, until it raises IndexError.

class Squares:
    def __getitem__(self, i):        # only __getitem__, no __iter__
        if i >= 4:
            raise IndexError(i)      # this stops the for loop
        return i * i

sq = Squares()
print(list(sq), 9 in sq)
[0, 1, 4, 9] True

It works, but write __iter__ in new code. It is clear and it works for things without an index. The chapter Generators and asyncio shows the easy way to write __iter__ with yield.

Do not call special methods yourself. Write len(p), not p.__len__(). The built-in does extra checks. For example, len() raises ValueError if __len__ returns a negative number. It raises TypeError for a float.

Equality, hashing and operators

By default, == on your objects compares identity. Two points with the same numbers are "not equal". Add __eq__ to compare values.

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Point):
            return NotImplemented       # let Python try the other side
        return (self.x, self.y) == (other.x, other.y)

print(Point(1, 2) == Point(1, 2), Point(1, 2) == "p")
print(Point.__hash__)
try:
    {Point(1, 2)}
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

class HPoint(Point):
    def __hash__(self):
        return hash((self.x, self.y))   # the same fields as __eq__

print(len({HPoint(1, 2), HPoint(1, 2), HPoint(3, 4)}))
True False
None
TypeError: cannot use 'Point' as a set element (unhashable type: 'Point')
2

Three rules come from this example.

  1. If you write __eq__ and no __hash__, Python sets __hash__ to None. The objects are now unhashable.
  2. Equal objects must have equal hashes. So hash the same fields that __eq__ compares. A tuple of the fields is the easy way.
  3. Return NotImplemented for a type you do not know. Python then tries the other object, and finally falls back to identity. Do not return False and do not raise.

Here is the mistake that rule 2 is about. The hash uses a field that can change.

class Tag:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, Tag) and self.name == other.name
    def __hash__(self):
        return hash(self.name)      # depends on a field that can change

t = Tag("rust")
seen = {t}
t.name = "python"                   # the hash changes, the set does not know
print(t in seen, Tag("rust") in seen, len(seen))
False False 1

A set stores an object in a slot chosen by its hash. Change the hash later, and the set looks in the wrong slot. The object is lost but still inside. Only hash objects whose compared fields never change. A frozen dataclass does this for you: see Classes, dataclasses and protocols.

@dataclass(frozen=True)   # writes __eq__ and __hash__ from the fields
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int
#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)] // == and hashing from the fields
struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}

Rust has the same rule. The Hash documentation asks that k1 == k2 means equal hashes. Breaking it is a logic error: a HashMap may just fail to find keys. Deriving both traits together keeps them in step, like a frozen dataclass.

Operators and NotImplemented

a + b first calls a.__add__(b). If that returns NotImplemented, Python tries b.__radd__(a). The "r" means "reflected": the object on the right side.

class Money:
    def __init__(self, cents):
        self.cents = cents
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Money({self.cents})"
    def __add__(self, other):            # m + other
        if isinstance(other, Money):
            return Money(self.cents + other.cents)
        return NotImplemented            # "I cannot do this one"
    def __radd__(self, other):           # other + m, when other gave up
        if other == 0:                   # sum() starts with 0
            return self
        return NotImplemented

print(Money(150) + Money(50))
print(sum([Money(1), Money(2), Money(3)]))
try:
    Money(1) + "x"
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
Money(200)
Money(6)
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'Money' and 'str'

Rust uses the trait std::ops::Add for +, with an associated type Output. The compiler picks the impl from the types, so no "try the other side" step exists. See Traits and generics for impl Add for Point.

Context managers: __enter__ and __exit__

A with block runs setup code, your code, and then clean-up code. The clean-up runs even when an error happens.

import time

class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        print("start")
        return self                         # bound to the name after "as"

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):  # runs on every way out
        ms = (time.perf_counter() - self.start) * 1000
        print(f"end, error={exc_type.__name__ if exc_type else None}")
        return False                        # False: do not hide the error

with Timer() as t:
    total = sum(range(1000))
print(total, type(t).__name__)

try:
    with Timer():
        1 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("the error still reached us")
start
end, error=None
499500 Timer
start
end, error=ZeroDivisionError
the error still reached us
use std::time::Instant;

struct Timer {
    start: Instant,
}

impl Timer {
    fn new() -> Timer {
        println!("start");
        Timer { start: Instant::now() }
    }
}

impl Drop for Timer { // like __exit__: runs when the value goes away
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        let _ms = self.start.elapsed().as_millis();
        println!("end");
    }
}

fn main() {
    {
        let _t = Timer::new(); // a name keeps it alive to the end of the block
        let total: u64 = (0..1000).sum();
        println!("{total}");
    } // _t is dropped here, even on an early return or a panic
    println!("after the block");
}
start
499500
end
after the block

An object with __enter__ and __exit__ is a context manager.

  • __enter__ runs first. Its return value goes to the name after as.
  • __exit__ always runs. It gets three values: the error type, the error and the traceback. With no error, all three are None.
  • If __exit__ returns a true value, the error is suppressed. A false value lets it go on.

Rust ties clean-up to the end of a scope with Drop. This idea is called RAII. Python ties clean-up to a with block instead. You write with, or nothing happens. The next chapter, Functions, closures and decorators, shows the short way with contextlib.

Do not return True from __exit__ by habit. It hides every error inside the block. The program goes on as if nothing happened. Return None or False unless you want to swallow one known error type.

Attribute lookup

What does Python do for a.bank? It searches in a fixed order. This example shows the order at work.

class Account:
    bank = "Mint"                      # class attribute: shared

    def __init__(self, owner):
        self.owner = owner             # instance attribute: in __dict__

    @property
    def label(self):                   # a property is a data descriptor
        return f"{self.owner}@{self.bank}"

    def greet(self):                   # a plain method: non-data descriptor
        return "hi"

a = Account("ann")
print(a.__dict__)
print(a.bank, a.label)

a.bank = "Own"                         # makes a NEW instance attribute
print(a.bank, Account.bank, a.__dict__)

a.greet = lambda: "shadowed"           # the instance wins over a method
print(a.greet())
try:
    a.label = "x"                      # a property wins over the instance
except AttributeError as e:
    print("AttributeError:", e)
{'owner': 'ann'}
Mint ann@Mint
Own Mint {'owner': 'ann', 'bank': 'Own'}
shadowed
AttributeError: property 'label' of 'Account' object has no setter

Each object keeps its own attributes in a dict called __dict__. The class has its own __dict__ too. A descriptor is a class attribute with __get__, and maybe __set__. A data descriptor has __set__ or __delete__. Here is the order for obj.name.

  1. Search the class and its parents, in MRO order. Remember what you find.
  2. Is it a data descriptor, like a property? Then call its __get__. Done.
  3. Is name in obj.__dict__? Then return that value. Done.
  4. Is it a non-data descriptor, like a function? Call __get__. A function becomes a bound method. Done.
  5. Is it a plain class attribute? Return it. Done.
  6. Nothing found? Call __getattr__ if the class has one. Else raise AttributeError.

So a.bank = "Own" does not change the class. It adds a new entry to a.__dict__, which hides the class value. The steps above are inside object.__getattribute__. The chapter Classes, dataclasses and protocols explains the MRO.

__getattr__: a fallback for missing names

class Config:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self._data = data
    def __getattr__(self, name):         # only called when normal lookup fails
        try:
            return self._data[name]
        except KeyError:
            raise AttributeError(name) from None

c = Config({"host": "localhost", "port": 5432})
print(c.host, c.port)
print(hasattr(c, "user"))

class C:
    pass
obj = C()
obj.__len__ = lambda: 5                 # on the instance, not the class
print(obj.__len__())
try:
    len(obj)                            # len() looks on type(obj) only
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
localhost 5432
False
5
TypeError: object of type 'C' has no len()

__getattr__ runs only after the normal search fails. __getattribute__ runs for every access, so it is easy to break. Prefer __getattr__. Raise AttributeError for unknown names, so hasattr and getattr(obj, name, default) still work.

Special methods are looked up on the type, not on the object. len(obj) ignores obj.__len__ and skips __getattribute__. This keeps built-ins fast. So define special methods in the class body, never on one object.

Rust has no run-time attribute search. The compiler knows every field and method of a type. A missing field is a compile error, like error[E0609]: no field `z` on type `Point`.

__slots__: a fixed set of fields

A normal object can get new attributes at any time. That needs room for a dict. __slots__ gives the class a fixed list of fields instead.

import tracemalloc

class Plain:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

class Slotted:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y")             # a fixed list of fields
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

def measure(make, n=100_000):
    tracemalloc.start()
    objs = [make() for _ in range(n)]   # the list adds 8 bytes per object
    size, _ = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
    tracemalloc.stop()
    return size // n

def plain_with_dict():
    p = Plain(1, 2)
    p.__dict__                          # asking for __dict__ builds a real dict
    return p

print("Plain          ", measure(lambda: Plain(1, 2)))
print("Plain + __dict__", measure(plain_with_dict))
print("Slotted        ", measure(lambda: Slotted(1, 2)))

s = Slotted(1, 2)
try:
    s.z = 3                            # not in __slots__
except AttributeError as e:
    print("AttributeError:", e)
Plain           96
Plain + __dict__ 159
Slotted         56
AttributeError: 'Slotted' object has no attribute 'z' and no __dict__ for setting new attributes

__slots__ lists the only allowed attribute names. Python stores them at fixed places inside the object. There is no __dict__ and no __weakref__, unless you add those names to the list.

  • It saves memory. Here, 56 bytes instead of 96, or 159 once the dict exists.
  • It catches typos. s.z = 3 fails at once.
  • Since Python 3.11, CPython delays building the dict of a plain object. That is why plain objects got smaller. Slots still win.
  • The easy way today is @dataclass(slots=True).

Rust structs always work like this. The fields are fixed when the program compiles. A struct Point { x: i64, y: i64 } takes exactly 16 bytes. See Memory and performance.

You cannot give a slot a default value in the class body. x = 0 next to __slots__ = ("x",) raises ValueError: 'x' in __slots__ conflicts with class variable. Set defaults in __init__. Also, a subclass without its own __slots__ gets a __dict__ again.

Expert note: how a slot works

Each name in __slots__ becomes a data descriptor on the class. Try print(Slotted.x). It shows <member 'x' of 'Slotted' objects>, a member descriptor. Its __get__ and __set__ read and write a fixed place in the object. So slots use the same lookup steps as property. That is also why a class attribute with the same name would replace the slot.

The data model and Rust traits

A special method and a Rust trait solve the same problem. Both let your type plug into the language. This table pairs them.

Special methods and their Rust partners
PythonRustUsed by
__repr__Debugrepr(x) / {:?}
__str__, __format__Displayprint(x), f-strings / {}
__eq__PartialEq, Eq==
__lt__ and friendsPartialOrd, Ord<, sorted / sort()
__hash__Hashdict, set / HashMap, HashSet
__len__a len() method, by habitlen(x) / x.len()
__getitem__Index, IndexMutx[i]
__iter__, __next__IntoIterator, Iteratorfor loops
__add__Adda + b
__bool__none: Rust has no truthinessif x:
__enter__, __exit__Dropwith / end of scope
__call__Fn, FnMut, FnOncef(x)

The big difference is when the check happens.

  • Rust checks at compile time. for s in &p fails to compile if &Playlist has no IntoIterator.
  • Python checks at run time, on the line itself. A missing __iter__ gives TypeError: 'X' object is not iterable only when that line runs.
  • A type checker like mypy closes part of the gap. A Protocol describes the needed methods. See Type hints.

The current PCAP exam is PCAP-31-04. Its syllabus asks you to tell identity from equality with is, to read __dict__, and to write __str__. Trace names and objects on paper. Draw arrows, like the picture in this chapter. Check the official syllabus page: exam details can change.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for the Python data model
PatternPurposeModelNote
x is NoneTest for one special objectif result is None: ...Never use is for numbers or strings.
b = a.copy()Get a real second listbackup = items.copy()b = a only adds a name.
[[0] * n for _ in range(m)]Build a grid of new rows[[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)][[0] * 3] * 3 shares one row.
def __repr__(self)Clear output for developersreturn f"Point({self.x!r}, {self.y!r})"Make it look like code that rebuilds the object.
__len__ + __getitem__Make a sequencereturn self.songs[i]Raise IndexError for a bad index.
def __iter__(self)Make it work in forreturn iter(self.songs)Return an iterator, not a list.
__eq__ + __hash__Use objects as dict keysreturn hash((self.x, self.y))Hash the same fields that __eq__ compares.
return NotImplementedSay "not my type" in an operatorif not isinstance(other, Point): return NotImplementedReturn it, do not raise it.
__radd__ for 0Make sum() workif other == 0: return selfsum() starts from the int 0.
__enter__ / __exit__Clean up on every way outwith Timer() as t: ...A true return value hides errors.
def __getattr__(self, name)Fallback for missing attributesreturn self._data[name]Raise AttributeError, not KeyError.

Practice

a = [1], then b = a, then b.append(2). What is a?

  • [1]
  • [1, 2]
  • An error

b = a adds a second name for the same list. A change through one name shows through the other.

Which test should use is?

  • count is 0
  • name is "admin"
  • value is None

None is a single object. Numbers and strings need ==.

A class defines __eq__ but not __hash__. What happens on {obj}?

  • It uses the default hash from object.
  • TypeError: the type is unhashable.
  • It works, but every object gets hash 0.

Python sets __hash__ = None for you, to protect the rule that equal objects have equal hashes.

A class has __len__ but no __bool__. An empty object is used in if obj:. What happens?

  • It is always true.
  • It is false, because __len__ returns 0.
  • TypeError

Truth testing falls back to __len__. Zero means false.

for x in obj first calls the special method name.

If __exit__ returns a true value, the error inside the with block is word.

In Rust, the trait that plays the role of __getitem__ is trait.

  1. What does this print, and why? 
    def grow(xs):
    xs += [3]
    xs = [0]

nums = [1, 2]
grow(nums)
print(nums)
    Answer

    It prints [1, 2, 3]. xs += [3] changes the shared list in place. xs = [0] only rebinds the local name. The caller never sees it.

  2. Write a class Countdown(n) so that len(Countdown(3)) is 3 and list(Countdown(3)) is [3, 2, 1].
    Answer 
    class Countdown:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
    def __len__(self):
        return self.n
    def __iter__(self):
        return iter(range(self.n, 0, -1))
  3. A User has __eq__ on email. You want users in a set. What do you add, and what must stay true?
    Answer

    Add def __hash__(self): return hash(self.email). The email must not change while the user is in a set or a dict. A frozen dataclass is the safest way.

  4. Why does obj.__len__ = lambda: 5 not make len(obj) work?
    Answer

    Built-ins look up special methods on type(obj), not on the object. The instance attribute is ignored. Define __len__ in the class.

  5. Expert. A class has a property called size. You run obj.__dict__["size"] = 10. What does obj.size return now: the property or 10? Explain with the lookup steps.
    Answer

    The property. A property is a data descriptor. Data descriptors come before the instance __dict__ in the lookup order. A plain method is a non-data descriptor, so an instance value would win over it.

  6. Expert. You need 5 million small records with three fields. Name two Python choices that save memory, and the Rust choice.
    Answer

    In Python: a class with __slots__, or @dataclass(slots=True). A NamedTuple or a column store like a NumPy array also works. In Rust: a plain struct in a Vec. Its size is just the fields, with no per-object header.

Key takeaways

  • Every Python value is an object with an identity, a type and a value. is compares identity. == compares value.
  • Names are references. Assignment and argument passing never copy. Mutating shows through every name. Rebinding does not.
  • In Python the type decides mutability. In Rust the binding or the borrow decides.
  • Special methods connect your class to syntax: len, [], for, in, ==, +, with. Rust does the same with traits, checked at compile time.
  • Equal objects need equal hashes. __eq__ alone makes a class unhashable.
  • Attribute lookup goes: data descriptor, instance dict, other class attributes, then __getattr__. __slots__ fixes the fields and saves memory.
