Type hints

A type hint says what kind of value a name should hold. Python itself ignores hints when it runs. A separate tool reads them and finds bugs before the program runs. This chapter goes from the first hint to generics, overloads and narrowing, and compares it all with Rust.

  • Write hints for variables, functions, collections and optional values.
  • Build generic functions, classes and aliases with the Python 3.12 syntax.
  • Describe data and behaviour with TypedDict, Literal, Final, Self, Protocol and Callable.
  • Use overloads and narrowing so the checker knows the exact type in each branch.
  • Run mypy and pyright, and explain how gradual typing differs from Rust's static typing.

Why type hints

Look at this small program first. It has one hint per argument and one for the result.

def total_price(price: float, count: int) -> float:
    return price * count

print(total_price(2.5, 4))
print(total_price("2.5", 4))   # wrong type, but Python runs it
10.0
2.52.52.52.5

The second call is a bug. A string times 4 repeats the string. Python does not stop it, because Python does not check hints while it runs. Now ask a type checker.

uv run --with mypy mypy why.py
why.py:5: error: Argument 1 to "total_price" has incompatible type "str"; expected "float"  [arg-type]
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)

The checker found the bug without running the code. Rust does the same check, but inside the compiler, and you cannot skip it.

# Hints are notes for tools. Python runs the bad call anyway.
total_price("2.5", 4)
fn total_price(price: f64, count: u32) -> f64 {
    price * count as f64
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", total_price("2.5", 4)); // wrong type
}
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> why.rs:6:32
  |
6 |     println!("{}", total_price("2.5", 4)); // wrong type
  |                    ----------- ^^^^^ expected `f64`, found `&str`

So why write hints? There are four good reasons.

  • Fewer bugs. The checker finds wrong types, missing None checks and typos in names.
  • Better editors. Your editor uses hints for completion and safe renames.
  • Clear documents. A signature with hints tells the reader what goes in and what comes out.
  • Runtime tools. Libraries such as pydantic and FastAPI read hints to check and convert data. See The standard library you need.

A hint is not a check. def f(x: int) still accepts a string at run time. If you need a check while the program runs, write it with isinstance or use a library such as pydantic.

Basic hints

Here are the hints you write every day.

from typing import Any, reveal_type

name: str = "Ann"
scores: list[int] = [90, 85]
ages: dict[str, int] = {"Ann": 31}
point: tuple[float, float] = (1.0, 2.5)    # exactly two floats
row: tuple[int, ...] = (1, 2, 3)           # any number of ints

count = 3                     # no hint: the checker infers int
reveal_type(count)
reveal_type(ages.get("Bo"))

def shout(x: Any) -> str:
    return x.upper()          # Any: no check at all

def whisper(x: object) -> str:
    return x.lower()          # object: only methods every object has
basics.py:10: note: Revealed type is "int"
basics.py:11: note: Revealed type is "int | None"
basics.py:17: error: "object" has no attribute "lower"  [attr-defined]
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
Runtime type is 'int'
Runtime type is 'NoneType'

Read the example line by line.

  • Write the type after a colon: name: str. Write the result type after an arrow: -> str.
  • Use the built-in classes for collections: list[int], dict[str, int], set[str]. You do not need typing.List any more.
  • tuple[float, float] means exactly two items. tuple[int, ...] means any length.
  • The checker infers many types. So you rarely write hints for local variables.
  • reveal_type(x) asks the checker to print the type it sees. At run time it prints the real type.
  • A function that returns nothing has the result type None.

Any and object look alike, but they are opposites. Any switches checks off: every use is allowed. object is the parent of all classes: you can only use methods that every object has. Use object when you mean "any value, and I will check it".

Hint the edges of your code: function parameters, results and class fields. Let the checker infer the types inside function bodies.

Optional values and unions

A function often returns a value or nothing. Here the user may not exist.

USERS = {1: "Ann", 2: "Bo"}

def find_user(user_id: int) -> str | None:
    return USERS.get(user_id)        # None when the id is missing

name = find_user(3)
print(name.upper())                  # bug: name can be None
optional.py:7: error: Item "None" of "str | None" has no attribute "upper"  [union-attr]
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/you/typing/optional.py", line 7, in <module>
    print(name.upper())                  # bug: name can be None
          ^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'

str | None is a union. It means "a str or None". The old spelling is Optional[str] or Union[str, None]. They mean the same. The | form works since Python 3.10. The fix is one if:

USERS = {1: "Ann", 2: "Bo"}

def find_user(user_id: int) -> str | None:
    return USERS.get(user_id)

def greeting(user_id: int) -> str:
    name = find_user(user_id)
    if name is None:                 # after this line, name is str
        return "Hello, guest"
    return f"Hello, {name.upper()}"

print(greeting(1))
print(greeting(3))
Hello, ANN
Hello, guest
use std::collections::HashMap;

fn find_user(users: &HashMap<u32, &'static str>, id: u32) -> Option<&'static str> {
    users.get(&id).copied()
}

fn main() {
    let users = HashMap::from([(1, "Ann"), (2, "Bo")]);
    for id in [1, 3] {
        match find_user(&users, id) {   // you must handle None
            Some(name) => println!("Hello, {}", name.to_uppercase()),
            None => println!("Hello, guest"),
        }
    }
}
Hello, ANN
Hello, guest

Python's str | None plays the role of Rust's Option<&str>. In Rust the compiler forces you to handle None. In Python only the checker does, and only if you run it.

Optional does not make an argument optional. It only allows None. An argument is optional only when it has a default value.

from typing import Optional

def greet(name: Optional[str]) -> str:   # may be None, but must be passed
    return f"Hi {name or 'guest'}"

def wave(times: int = None) -> str:      # default None, type says int
    return "wave " * (times or 1)

print(greet())
optional_arg.py:6: error: Incompatible default for parameter "times" (default has type "None", parameter has type "int")  [assignment]
optional_arg.py:6: note: PEP 484 prohibits implicit Optional. Accordingly, mypy has changed its default to no_implicit_optional=True
optional_arg.py:9: error: Missing positional argument "name" in call to "greet"  [call-arg]

The right forms are def greet(name: str | None = None) and def wave(times: int | None = None).

Generics with the 3.12 syntax

A generic function works for many types but keeps them connected. The placeholder is a type parameter. Since Python 3.12 you write it in square brackets after the name.

from collections.abc import Sized

def first[T](items: list[T]) -> T:          # T: any type, chosen per call
    return items[0]

class Stack[T]:                              # a generic class
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._items: list[T] = []

    def push(self, item: T) -> None:
        self._items.append(item)

    def pop(self) -> T:
        return self._items.pop()

def longest[S: Sized](a: S, b: S) -> S:     # bound: S must have len()
    return a if len(a) >= len(b) else b

def add[N: (int, float)](a: N, b: N) -> N:  # constraint: int or float
    return a + b

type Pair[T] = tuple[T, T]                   # a generic type alias

s: Stack[str] = Stack()
s.push("job")
print(first([3, 1, 2]), s.pop(), longest("ab", "abc"), add(2, 3))
s.push(42)                                   # wrong: s holds str
longest(3, 4)                                # wrong: int has no len()
generics.py:27: error: Argument 1 to "push" of "Stack" has incompatible type "int"; expected "str"  [arg-type]
generics.py:28: error: Value of type variable "S" of "longest" cannot be "int"  [type-var]
Found 2 errors in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
struct Stack<T> {
    items: Vec<T>,
}

impl<T> Stack<T> {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Stack { items: Vec::new() }
    }
    fn push(&mut self, item: T) {
        self.items.push(item);
    }
    fn pop(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
        self.items.pop()
    }
}

fn first<T: Copy>(items: &[T]) -> T {   // T: Copy is a bound
    items[0]
}

fn main() {
    let mut s: Stack<&str> = Stack::new();
    s.push("job");
    println!("{} {:?}", first(&[3, 1, 2]), s.pop());
    // s.push(42); // error[E0308]: mismatched types
}
3 Some("job")

Python printed 3 job abc 5 and then crashed on longest(3, 4) with TypeError. The checker found both bugs first. Here are the four forms:

  • [T]: any type. Each call picks one type for T.
  • [S: Sized]: a bound. S must be a kind of Sized. This is like T: Trait in Rust.
  • [N: (int, float)]: a constraint. N is exactly int or exactly float.
  • type Pair[T] = tuple[T, T]: a generic type alias.

Since Python 3.13 a type parameter can have a default. Before 3.12 you declared every parameter with TypeVar. You still see that style in older code.

from typing import Generic, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")                     # before 3.12: declare T first

class OldBox(Generic[T]):
    def __init__(self, item: T) -> None:
        self.item = item

class Box[T = int]:                  # 3.13: T is int if not given
    def __init__(self, item: T) -> None:
        self.item = item

def show(b: Box) -> None:            # same as Box[int]
    print(b.item + 1)

show(Box(41))
print(Box.__type_params__, T.__name__)
42
(T,) T

Variance: why list[int] is not list[float]

An int is accepted where a float is expected. So is a list[int] a list[float]? Try it.

from collections.abc import Sequence

def mean(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    return sum(xs) / len(xs)

def mean_ro(xs: Sequence[float]) -> float:   # read-only view
    return sum(xs) / len(xs)

ints: list[int] = [1, 2, 3]
print(mean_ro(ints))   # fine
print(mean(ints))      # error: list is invariant
variance.py:11: error: Argument 1 to "mean" has incompatible type "list[int]"; expected "list[float]"  [arg-type]
variance.py:11: note: "list" is invariant -- see https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/common_issues.html#variance
variance.py:11: note: Consider using "Sequence" instead, which is covariant

A function that takes list[float] may append 2.5 to the list. Then your list of ints holds a float. So the checker refuses. This rule is called variance.

  • A invariant type, like list or dict, needs the exact parameter.
  • A covariant type, like Sequence or tuple, is read-only. So Sequence[int] fits Sequence[float].
  • With the 3.12 syntax the checker infers the variance of your own classes. You do not declare it.

Rust has the same rule. A shared reference &T is covariant in T. A mutable reference &mut T is invariant in T, for the same reason: you could write a wrong value through it. Rust applies variance mostly to lifetimes.

Accept the widest type you can, return the most exact one. Take Sequence[float] or Iterable[str] as a parameter. Return list[float].

Precise data: TypedDict, Literal, Final and Self

JSON data often arrives as a dict. A plain dict[str, object] says almost nothing. These four tools say much more.

from typing import Final, Literal, NotRequired, ReadOnly, Self, TypedDict

class Movie(TypedDict):
    title: str
    year: ReadOnly[int]              # 3.13: checkers forbid changes
    rating: NotRequired[float]       # this key may be missing

type Mode = Literal["read", "write"]
MAX_RETRIES: Final = 3

def open_db(path: str, mode: Mode) -> str:
    return f"{path} opened for {mode}"

class Query:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.parts: list[str] = []

    def where(self, cond: str) -> Self:   # returns the same class
        self.parts.append(cond)
        return self

m: Movie = {"title": "Dune", "year": 2021}
print(m, type(m).__name__)
print(open_db("app.db", "read"))
print(Query().where("age > 30").where("city = 'Oslo'").parts)

bad: Movie = {"title": "Up", "yeer": 2009}   # typo in a key
m["year"] = 2024                             # read-only key
open_db("app.db", "delete")                  # not an allowed value
MAX_RETRIES = 5                              # Final cannot change
{'title': 'Dune', 'year': 2021} dict
app.db opened for read
['age > 30', "city = 'Oslo'"]
records.py:27: error: Missing key "year" for TypedDict "Movie"  [typeddict-item]
records.py:27: error: Extra key "yeer" for TypedDict "Movie"  [typeddict-unknown-key]
records.py:28: error: ReadOnly TypedDict key "year" TypedDict is mutated  [typeddict-readonly-mutated]
records.py:29: error: Argument 2 to "open_db" has incompatible type "Literal['delete']"; expected "Literal['read', 'write']"  [arg-type]
records.py:30: error: Cannot assign to final name "MAX_RETRIES"  [misc]
Found 5 errors in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
  • A TypedDict lists the keys of a dict and the type of each value. At run time it is a normal dict, as the output shows. NotRequired marks a key that may be missing. ReadOnly (3.13) marks a key that must not change.
  • A Literal type allows only listed values. It is great for modes, states and options.
  • Final says a name never changes. Python still lets you change it at run time. Only the checker complains.
  • Self is the type of the current class. A child class that calls where() gets the child type back. This keeps chained calls typed.
class Movie(TypedDict):
    title: str
    rating: NotRequired[float]
type Mode = Literal["read", "write"]
MAX_RETRIES: Final = 3
struct Movie {
    title: String,
    rating: Option<f32>, // a field that may be empty
}
enum Mode { Read, Write } // only these values exist
const MAX_RETRIES: u32 = 3;

Rust gets these guarantees from struct, enum and const, and they hold at run time too. For your own classes in Python, a dataclass is often better than a TypedDict. See Classes, dataclasses and protocols.

Python 3.15 adds closed TypedDicts (PEP 728). class Point(TypedDict, closed=True) allows no other keys. class Tags(TypedDict, extra_items=str) allows other keys with str values. I ran this on the 3.15 beta. pyright 1.1.414 checked it correctly. mypy 2.4.1 did not know extra_items yet. Check your checker's release notes: this can change.

Protocol and Callable: types for behaviour

Sometimes you care what an object can do, not what class it is. A Protocol describes that. Traits and generics shows the basics. Here is a typical use: a fake clock for tests.

import time
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Protocol

def apply(f: Callable[[int], str], value: int) -> str:
    return f(value)

class Clock(Protocol):               # any object with now() -> float fits
    def now(self) -> float: ...

class RealClock:
    def now(self) -> float:
        return time.time()

class FakeClock:                     # for tests: no inheritance needed
    def now(self) -> float:
        return 100.0

def stamp(clock: Clock) -> str:
    return f"t={clock.now():.0f}"

def timed[**P, R](f: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]:
    def wrapper(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
        start = time.perf_counter()
        result = f(*args, **kwargs)
        print(f"{f.__name__} took {time.perf_counter() - start:.1f}s")
        return result
    return wrapper

@timed
def resize(path: str, width: int) -> str:
    return f"{path} -> {width}px"

print(apply(hex, 255), stamp(FakeClock()))
print(resize("cat.png", width=640))
resize("cat.png", width="big")       # wrong type, even through the decorator
0xff t=100
resize took 0.0s
cat.png -> 640px
resize took 0.0s
callables.py:36: error: Argument "width" to "resize" has incompatible type "str"; expected "int"  [arg-type]
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
  • Callable[[int], str] is a function that takes one int and returns a str. The built-in hex fits. Import Callable from collections.abc.
  • FakeClock fits Clock only because it has now(). This is structural typing.
  • **P is a ParamSpec. It copies the parameter list of the wrapped function. So the decorator keeps the real signature, and the checker still sees the bad width="big".

The last call ran without an error, and the checker caught it. Decorators themselves are in Functions, closures and decorators.

def apply(f: Callable[[int], str], value: int) -> str: ...
class Clock(Protocol):
    def now(self) -> float: ...
trait Clock {
    fn now(&self) -> f64;
}

struct FakeClock;
impl Clock for FakeClock {           // Rust needs an explicit impl
    fn now(&self) -> f64 {
        100.0
    }
}

fn apply(f: impl Fn(i32) -> String, value: i32) -> String {
    f(value)
}

fn stamp(clock: &impl Clock) -> String {
    format!("t={:.0}", clock.now())
}

fn main() {
    println!("{} {}", apply(|n| format!("{n:#x}"), 255), stamp(&FakeClock));
}
0xff t=100

A decorator typed as Callable[..., Any] loses the signature. Every call through it is accepted, even a wrong one. Use [**P, R] and Callable[P, R] instead.

Overloads and narrowing

Overloads: the result type depends on the arguments

This load() returns text by default and bytes with binary=True. Without help, the checker only knows str | bytes.

from pathlib import Path

def load(path: str, binary: bool = False) -> str | bytes:
    p = Path(path)
    return p.read_bytes() if binary else p.read_text()

print(load("note.txt") + "!")     # we know it is str. The checker does not.
nooverload.py:7: error: Unsupported operand types for + ("bytes" and "str")  [operator]
nooverload.py:7: note: Left operand is of type "str | bytes"

An overload lists each case with its own signature. The checker picks the case that matches the call.

from pathlib import Path
from typing import Literal, overload, reveal_type

@overload
def load(path: str, binary: Literal[False] = False) -> str: ...
@overload
def load(path: str, binary: Literal[True]) -> bytes: ...
def load(path: str, binary: bool = False) -> str | bytes:   # the real body
    p = Path(path)
    return p.read_bytes() if binary else p.read_text()

Path("note.txt").write_text("hi")
text = load("note.txt")
data = load("note.txt", binary=True)
reveal_type(text)
reveal_type(data)
print(text.upper(), data[0])
overloads.py:15: note: Revealed type is "str"
overloads.py:16: note: Revealed type is "bytes"
Success: no issues found in 1 source file

HI 104
// Rust has no overloading. Use two names, or a generic with a trait.
fn load_text(path: &str) -> std::io::Result<String> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path)
}
fn load_bytes(path: &str) -> std::io::Result<Vec<u8>> {
    std::fs::read(path)
}

The @overload lines are only for the checker. Their body is .... The last definition, without @overload, is the one Python runs. If a generic can say the same thing, prefer the generic. Overloads are for cases where the result type depends on a value, such as a Literal flag.

Narrowing: the type changes inside a branch

You already saw if name is None. After that test the checker knows more. This is narrowing. It also works with isinstance, == on literals, in and match.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import assert_never, reveal_type

@dataclass
class Circle:
    r: float

@dataclass
class Square:
    side: float

@dataclass
class Triangle:
    base: float
    height: float

type Shape = Circle | Square | Triangle

def area(s: Shape) -> float:
    match s:
        case Circle(r=r):
            return 3.14159 * r * r
        case Square(side=a):
            return a * a
        case _:
            reveal_type(s)        # only Triangle is left here
            assert_never(s)       # error: we forgot Triangle

def describe(x: int | str | None) -> str:
    if x is None:
        return "nothing"
    if isinstance(x, int):
        reveal_type(x)
        return f"number {x}"
    reveal_type(x)                # not None, not int: str
    return f"text {x!r}"
narrowing.py:26: note: Revealed type is "narrowing.Triangle"
narrowing.py:27: error: Argument 1 to "assert_never" has incompatible type "Triangle"; expected "Never"  [arg-type]
narrowing.py:33: note: Revealed type is "int"
narrowing.py:35: note: Revealed type is "str"
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
enum Shape {
    Circle { r: f64 },
    Square { side: f64 },
    Triangle { base: f64, height: f64 },
}

fn area(s: &Shape) -> f64 {
    match s {
        Shape::Circle { r } => 3.14159 * r * r,
        Shape::Square { side } => side * side,
        // Triangle is missing
    }
}
error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `&Shape::Triangle { .. }` not covered
 --> shapes.rs:8:11
  |
8 |     match s {
  |           ^ pattern `&Shape::Triangle { .. }` not covered

Never is the type with no values. If every case is handled, nothing is left for assert_never(s), so the call is fine. If you forget a case, that case is left, and the checker reports it. This gives you Rust's exhaustive match, but only from the checker.

You can write your own narrowing function with TypeIs (3.13) or the older TypeGuard (3.10).

from typing import TypeGuard, TypeIs, reveal_type

def is_int(x: object) -> TypeIs[int]:
    return isinstance(x, int)

def is_int_guard(x: object) -> TypeGuard[int]:
    return isinstance(x, int)

def check(v: int | str) -> None:
    if is_int(v):
        reveal_type(v)
    else:
        reveal_type(v)          # TypeIs: the else branch is str
    if is_int_guard(v):
        reveal_type(v)
    else:
        reveal_type(v)          # TypeGuard: still int | str
typeis.py:11: note: Revealed type is "int"
typeis.py:13: note: Revealed type is "str"
typeis.py:15: note: Revealed type is "int"
typeis.py:17: note: Revealed type is "int | str"

TypeIs narrows both branches, like isinstance. TypeGuard narrows only the true branch. But TypeIs has one rule: the new type must be part of the old type. So list[object] to list[str] needs TypeGuard. mypy says Narrowed type "list[str]" is not a subtype of input type "list[object]" if you try TypeIs.

Running mypy and pyright

Two checkers are used most. mypy is the original checker. pyright also powers the Pylance plugin in VS Code. Run either one with uv run --with, so you install nothing globally.

def discount(price, percent):          # no hints at all
    return price - price * percent / 100

def label(price: float) -> str:
    return "Price: " + price           # bug: str + float

def report():
    return "Total: " + 10              # bug inside an untyped function
uv run --with mypy mypy shop.py
shop.py:5: error: Unsupported operand types for + ("str" and "float")  [operator]
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
uv run --with mypy mypy --strict shop.py
shop.py:1: error: Function is missing a type annotation  [no-untyped-def]
shop.py:5: error: Returning Any from function declared to return "str"  [no-any-return]
shop.py:5: error: Unsupported operand types for + ("str" and "float")  [operator]
shop.py:7: error: Function is missing a return type annotation  [no-untyped-def]
shop.py:8: error: Unsupported operand types for + ("str" and "int")  [operator]
Found 5 errors in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
uv run --with pyright pyright shop.py
/home/you/typing/proj/shop.py
  /home/you/typing/proj/shop.py:5:12 - error: Operator "+" not supported for types "Literal['Price: ']" and "float" (reportOperatorIssue)
  /home/you/typing/proj/shop.py:8:12 - error: Operator "+" not supported for types "Literal['Total: ']" and "Literal[10]" (reportOperatorIssue)
2 errors, 0 warnings, 0 informations

Look at line 8. It is a clear bug, but plain mypy is silent. By default mypy does not check the body of a function without hints. --strict turns on that check and many more, and it asks for hints everywhere. pyright checks every body by default. One bug can give two lines in strict mode: line 5 shows the bad + and also a result of type Any.

Put the settings in pyproject.toml, so every person and every CI run uses the same rules.

[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.14"
strict = true                 # all the extra checks on

[[tool.mypy.overrides]]
module = ["legacy.*"]         # old code: check it later
ignore_errors = true

[tool.pyright]
pythonVersion = "3.14"
typeCheckingMode = "strict"
Success: no issues found in 1 source file
0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 informations

When one line must stay as it is, silence only that error and say which one: x = old_api() # type: ignore[no-untyped-call]. A bare # type: ignore hides every future error on that line too.

Run the checker as it is

Run plain mypy on the code. Fix the real bugs it finds. Do not add hints yet.

Put it in CI

Pin the checker version. Write the settings in pyproject.toml. Now no new error can enter.

Hint the shared code first

Start with the helpers and data classes that many modules import. Every caller gets better checks.

Check untyped bodies

Turn on check_untyped_defs = true. Old functions are now checked inside.

Hints for all new code

Set disallow_untyped_defs = true for finished modules. New functions must have hints.

Go strict

Turn on strict = true module by module. Use overrides for the old parts that are left.

Gradual typing compared with Rust

Python lets you add hints a little at a time. This is gradual typing. The price is Any. A value of type Any fits everywhere, so a bug can pass through it.

import json
from typing import cast, reveal_type

raw = json.loads('{"port": 8080}')
reveal_type(raw)                       # Any: the checker knows nothing
cfg = cast(dict[str, int], raw)        # trust me: no check at run time
reveal_type(cfg["port"])
port = raw["port"] + "1"               # no error from mypy
gradual.py:5: note: Revealed type is "Any"
gradual.py:7: note: Revealed type is "int"
Success: no issues found in 1 source file

TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
use std::any::Any;

fn main() {
    let raw: Box<dyn Any> = Box::new(8080_i32);
    // let port = raw + 1;  // error[E0369]: cannot add `{integer}` to `Box<dyn Any>`
    match raw.downcast_ref::<i32>() {  // you must check the real type
        Some(p) => println!("port {}", p + 1),
        None => println!("not an i32"),
    }
}
port 8081

Even --strict passed this file, and it crashed at run time. json.loads returns Any, and cast only tells the checker to trust you. Rust's dyn Any is the opposite. It allows nothing until you check the real type.

Gradual typing in Python and static typing in Rust
QuestionPython with hintsRust
Who checks?A separate tool, if you run itThe compiler, always
Checked at run time?No. Hints are only dataNot needed: the types are proven
Code without types?Allowed. It becomes AnyNot possible. Types are inferred or written
Escape hatchAny, cast, # type: ignoreunsafe, checked downcast
Fit ruleBy shape (Protocol) or by classBy explicit impl Trait
Missing case in matchError only with assert_never and a checkerError E0004, always
Different checkers?Yes. They can disagree on edge casesOne compiler, one answer

Rust is a strict teacher who reads every page before you hand it in. Python with hints is a helper you can call when you want. The helper is good, but it cannot see pages marked Any.

A common question is "Does Python check type hints?". The answer: not at run time. Hints are stored in __annotations__. Tools such as mypy and pyright check them before running. Libraries such as pydantic read them at run time on purpose. Since 3.14, Python computes annotations only when someone asks, as Python versions shows.

Patterns to remember

Type hint patterns
PatternPurposeModelNote
name: T, -> THint a parameter and a resultdef area(w: float, h: float) -> float:Python does not check it at run time.
list[T], dict[K, V]Hint a collectionages: dict[str, int] = {}No need for typing.List.
T | None = NoneAn optional argumentdef wave(times: int | None = None):The type alone does not make it optional.
if x is None: returnNarrow away Noneif user is None: return "guest"After the test, x has the plain type.
def f[T](x: T) -> TA generic functiondef first[T](xs: list[T]) -> T:No TypeVar needed since 3.12.
[T: Bound]Limit a type parameterdef longest[S: Sized](a: S, b: S) -> S:[T: (A, B)] means exactly A or B.
Sequence[T] as inputAccept many collection typesdef mean(xs: Sequence[float]):list is invariant.
class X(TypedDict)Type a dict with fixed keysrating: NotRequired[float]It is a plain dict at run time.
Literal["a", "b"]Allow only some valuestype Mode = Literal["read", "write"]Good for flags and states.
-> SelfReturn the current classdef where(self, c: str) -> Self:Child classes get their own type.
class P(Protocol)Type by behaviourdef stamp(clock: Clock) -> str:No inheritance needed.
[**P, R] with Callable[P, R]Type a decoratordef timed[**P, R](f: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]:Callable[..., Any] loses all checks.
@overloadResult type depends on an argumentdef load(p: str, binary: Literal[True]) -> bytes: ...The last definition has the real body.
case _: assert_never(x)Make a match exhaustiveassert_never(shape)Works only when a checker runs.
# type: ignore[code]Silence one known errorold() # type: ignore[no-untyped-call]Always give the error code.

Practice

What does Python do when it runs def f(x: int) -> int: return x * 2 with f("ab")?

  • It raises a TypeError because of the hint.
  • It returns "abab".
  • It refuses to start the program.

Python does not check hints while running. A string times 2 repeats it. Only a checker would report the bug.

Which hint means "a string or nothing"?

  • str = None
  • str | None
  • Optional
  • Any

str | None is the same as Optional[str]. Any allows everything and switches checks off.

The Python 3.12 way to write a generic function is def first<span class="blank" data-answer="[T]">?</span>(items: list[T]) -> T:.

A type checker prints the type it sees for x when you call ?.

By default, mypy does not check the body of a function without ?.

Why does mypy refuse mean(ints) when mean takes list[float] and ints is a list[int]?

  • Because int is never accepted as float.
  • Because list is invariant: mean could put a float into your int list.
  • Because lists cannot hold numbers in typed code.

A mutable list must match exactly. Take Sequence[float], which is read-only and covariant.

A function returns TypeIs[int] and is called with v: int | str. What is the type of v in the else branch?

  • int | str
  • int
  • str
  • Never

TypeIs narrows both branches. With TypeGuard the else branch would stay int | str.

  1. Fix this signature so the argument is really optional: def connect(timeout: Optional[float]) -> None.
    Answer

    def connect(timeout: float | None = None) -> None:. The default value makes it optional. The type float | None allows the default.

  2. Write a generic function last that returns the last item of a list, with the 3.12 syntax. What does the checker infer for last(["a", "b"])?
    Answer

    def last[T](items: list[T]) -> T: return items[-1]. For ["a", "b"] the checker infers T = str, so the result is str.

  3. An API returns dicts like {"id": 7, "email": "x@example.com"}, and sometimes a "phone" key. Write a TypedDict for it.
    Answer

    class User(TypedDict): with id: int, email: str and phone: NotRequired[str]. At run time it is still a plain dict, so validate real input with a library such as pydantic.

  4. Your decorator is typed def retry(f: Callable[..., Any]) -> Callable[..., Any]. A wrong call through it passes the checker. Why, and what is the fix?
    Answer

    ... and Any accept every call, so the real signature is lost. Use a ParamSpec: def retry[**P, R](f: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R], and type the wrapper as (*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R.

  5. You add a Hexagon class to type Shape = Circle | Square | Triangle. How can the checker show every match that forgot it?
    Answer

    End each match with case _: assert_never(s). After you add Hexagon to the alias, the checker reports each place where Hexagon reaches assert_never. Rust reports E0004 without any extra code.

  6. A teammate says: "mypy --strict passes, so our JSON config code cannot have type bugs." Explain why this is wrong, and what Rust does differently.
    Answer

    json.loads returns Any, and Any fits every type. cast also only asks the checker to trust you. So a wrong type can pass and crash at run time. Validate the data at the edge, for example with pydantic, or with isinstance checks. In Rust, serde must parse the data into a real type, and a wrong type gives an error value you must handle.

Key takeaways

  • Hints are notes for tools. Python ignores them at run time. mypy and pyright check them before running.
  • Use built-in generics (list[int]), X | None for optional values and a default for optional arguments.
  • Since 3.12, write generics as def f[T], class C[T] and type Alias[T] = .... Bounds use [T: Bound].
  • TypedDict, Literal, Final and Self make data precise. Protocol and Callable type behaviour, and **P keeps decorator signatures.
  • Overloads tie result types to arguments. Narrowing and assert_never give a checked, exhaustive match.
  • Gradual typing lets you start small, but Any lets bugs through. Rust checks every type, always, in the compiler.

Sources

  • typing: Support for type hints. The official reference, with the version that added each feature.
  • The Python typing specification. The shared rules for all checkers, including narrowing with TypeIs and TypeGuard.
  • PEP 695: Type Parameter Syntax. The 3.12 syntax for generics, bounds, constraints and type aliases.
  • mypy: Using mypy with an existing codebase. The steps for adding types to old code, and the strict options.
  • pyright: Type concepts, advanced. All narrowing forms pyright supports.
  • What's New in Python 3.15. Closed TypedDicts (PEP 728), TypeForm (PEP 747) and other typing changes.

Generators and asyncio

A generator is a function that can pause and continue later. That one idea gives Python lazy loops, data pipelines and, in the end, async and await. This chapter goes from for loops to tasks, timeouts and queues in asyncio, and compares each step with Rust.

  • Explain the iterator protocol and write iterators and generators.
  • Build lazy pipelines with generators, generator expressions and itertools.
  • Explain how a coroutine and the event loop work together.
  • Use tasks, TaskGroup, gather, timeouts, queues, async with and async for.
  • Mix sync and async code safely, and compare it with Rust iterators and futures.

Iterables and iterators

Start with a list and two calls: iter() and next().

colors = ["red", "green"]          # a list is an iterable
it = iter(colors)                  # ask it for an iterator
print(next(it))
print(next(it))
try:
    next(it)                       # nothing left
except StopIteration:
    print("StopIteration: the iterator is used up")

print(iter(colors) is iter(colors))   # a new iterator each time
print(iter(it) is it)                 # an iterator returns itself
red
green
StopIteration: the iterator is used up
False
True

Two words matter here.

  • An iterable can make an iterator. Lists, strings, dicts, files and ranges are iterables. Each iter() call gives a fresh iterator.
  • An iterator gives one value per next() call. When it has no more values, it raises StopIteration. It can be used only once.

A for loop is just these two calls. Python turns for c in colors: print(c) into this:

colors = ["red", "green"]
_it = iter(colors)
while True:
    try:
        c = next(_it)
    except StopIteration:
        break
    print(c)

Your own class becomes an iterator with two special methods: __iter__ returns the iterator, and __next__ returns the next value. The data model chapter explains special methods.

class Countdown:
    def __init__(self, start: int) -> None:
        self.n = start

    def __iter__(self) -> "Countdown":
        return self

    def __next__(self) -> int:
        if self.n <= 0:
            raise StopIteration     # "no more values"
        self.n -= 1
        return self.n + 1

print(list(Countdown(3)))
[3, 2, 1]
struct Countdown {
    n: u32,
}

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {   // None means "no more"
        if self.n == 0 {
            return None;
        }
        self.n -= 1;
        Some(self.n + 1)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let v: Vec<u32> = Countdown { n: 3 }.collect();
    println!("{v:?}");
}
[3, 2, 1]

Python ends with an exception. Rust ends with None. The idea is the same. The full Rust side is in Iterators and closures.

You loop over an iterator twice and the second loop is empty. No error appears. A list can be looped many times. An iterator, a generator or an open file cannot. Make a list with list(it) if you need two passes.

Generators and yield

Writing __next__ by hand is long. A generator does the same work in a few lines.

def countdown(n: int):
    print("start")
    while n > 0:
        yield n                    # pause here and hand out n
        n -= 1
    print("done")

g = countdown(2)                   # nothing runs yet
print(type(g).__name__)
print(next(g))                     # runs to the first yield
print(next(g))                     # resumes after the yield
print(list(g))                     # runs to the end
generator
start
2
1
done
[]

Watch the order. Calling countdown(2) runs no code. It only makes a generator object. Each next() runs the body until the next yield, then pauses. The local variable n survives the pause. At the end of the body, the generator raises StopIteration for you.

Lazy pipelines

Generators can feed each other. Each stage takes one item, works on it and passes it on. So a huge file never sits in memory.

from collections.abc import Iterator

def read_lines(path: str) -> Iterator[str]:
    with open(path) as f:           # the file stays open while we iterate
        for line in f:
            yield line.rstrip("\n")

def errors(lines: Iterator[str]) -> Iterator[str]:
    for line in lines:
        if line.startswith("ERROR"):
            yield line.removeprefix("ERROR ")

def numbered(items: Iterator[str]) -> Iterator[str]:
    for i, item in enumerate(items, start=1):
        yield f"{i}. {item}"

for row in numbered(errors(read_lines("app.log"))):
    print(row)
1. disk full
2. timeout
# A generator keeps its state in local variables.
def countdown(n):
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1
fn countdown(mut n: u32) -> impl Iterator<Item = u32> {
    std::iter::from_fn(move || {      // the closure keeps the state
        if n == 0 {
            return None;
        }
        n -= 1;
        Some(n + 1)
    })
}

fn main() {
    let errors: Vec<String> = ["INFO start", "ERROR disk full", "ERROR timeout"]
        .into_iter()
        .filter_map(|l| l.strip_prefix("ERROR ")) // lazy, like a generator
        .enumerate()
        .map(|(i, e)| format!("{}. {e}", i + 1))
        .collect();
    println!("{:?} {errors:?}", countdown(3).collect::<Vec<_>>());
}
[3, 2, 1] ["1. disk full", "2. timeout"]

Stable Rust has no yield yet. On rustc 1.99.0 a gen { yield 1; } block fails with error[E0658]: gen blocks are experimental. The 2024 edition reserves the word gen for it. Today you use std::iter::from_fn or adapter chains instead.

yield from, send and the return value

Generators have three more tools. You need them rarely in daily code. But they explain how async works.

from collections.abc import Generator

def inner() -> Generator[int, None, str]:
    yield 1
    yield 2
    return "inner done"            # becomes the value of "yield from"

def outer() -> Generator[int, None, None]:
    result = yield from inner()    # pass on every value of inner()
    print("got:", result)
    yield 3

print(list(outer()))

def running_average() -> Generator[float, float, None]:
    total, count = 0.0, 0
    average = 0.0
    while True:
        value = yield average      # receive a value with send()
        total += value
        count += 1
        average = total / count

avg = running_average()
next(avg)                          # "prime" it: run to the first yield
print(avg.send(10), avg.send(20), avg.send(60))
avg.close()                        # raises GeneratorExit inside, then stops
got: inner done
[1, 2, 3]
10.0 15.0 30.0
  • yield from inner() hands out every value of inner(). Its result is the return value of inner().
  • gen.send(x) resumes the generator, and yield gives back x. So values flow in both directions.
  • gen.close() stops it. A finally block inside the generator still runs.
  • The hint Generator[Y, S, R] lists the yield type, the send type and the return type.

Never raise StopIteration inside a generator to stop it. Since Python 3.7 this becomes RuntimeError: generator raised StopIteration (PEP 479). Use return.

Generator expressions and itertools recipes

A generator expression looks like a list comprehension with round brackets. Compare the memory.

import sys

squares_list = [n * n for n in range(1_000_000)]   # all values now
squares_gen = (n * n for n in range(1_000_000))    # one value at a time
print(sys.getsizeof(squares_list), sys.getsizeof(squares_gen))
print(sum(n * n for n in range(1_000_000)))        # no extra brackets needed
print(max(len(w) for w in ["a", "abc", "ab"]))
8448728 208
333332833333500000
3

The list needs about 8 MB for its slots alone. The generator needs 208 bytes, whatever the length. When a function takes one iterable, like sum or max, you can drop the extra brackets.

The itertools module has lazy building blocks. Iterators and closures lists them with their Rust twins. The official docs also give recipes. These recipes are not in the module, so you copy them or install the more-itertools package. Here are four useful ones, plus newer tools.

from collections import deque
from itertools import batched, chain, groupby, islice, tee

def take(n, iterable):                      # first n items as a list
    return list(islice(iterable, n))

def sliding_window(iterable, n):            # (a,b,c), (b,c,d), ...
    it = iter(iterable)
    window = deque(islice(it, n - 1), maxlen=n)
    for x in it:
        window.append(x)
        yield tuple(window)

def unique_everseen(iterable):              # drop repeats, keep order
    seen = set()
    for x in iterable:
        if x not in seen:
            seen.add(x)
            yield x

def flatten(list_of_lists):                 # one level deep
    return chain.from_iterable(list_of_lists)

print(take(3, unique_everseen("abracadabra")))
print(list(sliding_window([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 3)))
print(list(flatten([[1, 2], [3], []])))
print(list(batched("abcdefg", 3)))
a, b = tee([1, 2, 3])                       # two independent copies
print(list(a), list(b))
['a', 'b', 'r']
[(1, 2, 3), (2, 3, 4), (3, 4, 5)]
[1, 2, 3]
[('a', 'b', 'c'), ('d', 'e', 'f'), ('g',)]
[1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3]

take works on an endless iterator too, because islice stops early. batched is new in 3.12. Since 3.13, batched(xs, 3, strict=True) raises ValueError: batched(): incomplete batch when the last group is short.

groupby groups only neighbours with the same key. Sort first, by the same key.

from itertools import groupby

words = ["apple", "bean", "avocado", "banana"]
print([(k, list(g)) for k, g in groupby(words, key=lambda w: w[0])])
print([(k, list(g)) for k, g in groupby(sorted(words), key=lambda w: w[0])])
[('a', ['apple']), ('b', ['bean']), ('a', ['avocado']), ('b', ['banana'])]
[('a', ['apple', 'avocado']), ('b', ['banana', 'bean'])]

Coroutines: from generators to async def

A generator pauses at yield and continues on next(). Now imagine many paused functions, each waiting for the network. One small loop wakes each one when its data is ready. That is the whole idea of asyncio. Here is a tiny version, built only from generators.

import time
from collections import deque

def sleep(seconds):                    # a tiny "awaitable": yields a wake-up time
    yield time.monotonic() + seconds

def job(name, seconds):
    print(f"{name} starts")
    yield from sleep(seconds)          # pause; the loop runs other jobs
    print(f"{name} ends after {seconds}s")

def run(*jobs):                        # a tiny event loop
    ready = deque((0.0, j) for j in jobs)
    while ready:
        wake, j = ready.popleft()
        if wake > time.monotonic():    # not time yet: put it back
            ready.append((wake, j))
            continue
        try:
            ready.append((next(j), j)) # run until the next pause
        except StopIteration:
            pass                       # this job is finished

start = time.monotonic()
run(job("A", 0.2), job("B", 0.1))
print(f"total {time.monotonic() - start:.1f}s")
A starts
B starts
B ends after 0.1s
A ends after 0.2s
total 0.2s

Two waits of 0.2 s and 0.1 s took 0.2 s in total, on one thread. The jobs waited at the same time. The real asyncio loop is smarter: it sleeps until the next timer and asks the operating system which network sockets are ready. But the shape is the same.

Python 3.5 gave this pattern its own syntax. A function defined with async def is a coroutine function. await plays the role of yield from.

import asyncio

async def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"hello {name}"

c = greet("Ann")                   # nothing runs: we get a coroutine object
print(type(c).__name__)
try:
    c.send(None)                   # drive it by hand, like the event loop
except StopIteration as stop:
    print("result:", stop.value)   # the return value travels in StopIteration

greet("Bo")                        # created, never awaited
print(asyncio.run(greet("Cy")))    # the normal way
coroutine
result: hello Ann
/home/you/gen/coro1.py:13: RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'greet' was never awaited
  greet("Bo")                        # created, never awaited
RuntimeWarning: Enable tracemalloc to get the object allocation traceback
hello Cy
async fn greet(name: &str) -> String {
    format!("hello {name}")
}

fn main() {
    greet("Bo"); // creates a future, never polled
    println!("main ends");
}
warning: unused implementer of `Future` that must be used
 --> lazyfut.rs:6:5
  |
6 |     greet("Bo"); // creates a future, never polled
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = note: futures do nothing unless you `.await` or poll them

In both languages, calling an async function does nothing by itself. Python gives a coroutine object. Rust gives a future. Something must drive it: the event loop in Python, the runtime in Rust. Rust warns at compile time. Python warns only at run time.

You forget await before an async call. The call returns a coroutine object, not the result, and the work never happens. Look for the "never awaited" warning. mypy and pyright also report an unused coroutine.
