The event loop, tasks, gather and TaskGroup

Two fake network calls take 0.3 s and 0.2 s. Here are four ways to run them.

import asyncio
import time

async def fetch(name: str, seconds: float) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(seconds)          # stands for a network call
    return f"{name}:{seconds}"

async def main() -> None:
    t = time.perf_counter()
    a = await fetch("users", 0.3)         # one after the other
    b = await fetch("orders", 0.2)
    print(a, b, f"sequential {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s")

    t = time.perf_counter()
    ta = asyncio.create_task(fetch("users", 0.3))   # both start now
    tb = asyncio.create_task(fetch("orders", 0.2))
    print(await ta, await tb, f"tasks {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s")

    t = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(fetch("users", 0.3), fetch("orders", 0.2))
    print(results, f"gather {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s")

    t = time.perf_counter()
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tu = tg.create_task(fetch("users", 0.3))
        to = tg.create_task(fetch("orders", 0.2))
    print(tu.result(), to.result(), f"TaskGroup {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s")

asyncio.run(main())
users:0.3 orders:0.2 sequential 0.5s
users:0.3 orders:0.2 tasks 0.3s
['users:0.3', 'orders:0.2'] gather 0.3s
users:0.3 orders:0.2 TaskGroup 0.3s
  • asyncio.run(main()) creates the event loop, runs main() and closes the loop. Call it once, at the top of your program.
  • await coro runs the coroutine and waits. Nothing else in this function happens meanwhile.
  • A task starts a coroutine in the background. create_task starts it at once. You get the result later with await task.
  • gather runs many awaitables and returns the results in the same order.
  • A TaskGroup waits for all its tasks at the end of the async with block.

Take a ready task

The loop takes the first task from the ready queue.

Run it to the next await

The task runs normal Python code until it awaits something slow, like sleep or a socket read.

Park it

The task gives control back. The loop notes what it waits for: a timer or a socket.

Run the others

The loop runs the next ready tasks in the same way.

Ask the operating system

When no task is ready, the loop sleeps until a timer ends or a socket has data.

Wake the task

The waiting task goes back to the ready queue. It continues right after its await.

When a task fails

Here two tasks fail and one is slow. TaskGroup and gather react in different ways.

import asyncio

async def fetch(name: str, seconds: float, fail: bool = False) -> str:
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(seconds)
        if fail:
            raise ConnectionError(f"{name} is down")
        return name
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print(f"{name} was cancelled")
        raise                              # always re-raise CancelledError

async def main() -> None:
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tg.create_task(fetch("users", 0.1, fail=True))
            tg.create_task(fetch("orders", 0.1, fail=True))
            tg.create_task(fetch("stock", 1.0))
    except* ConnectionError as group:
        for err in group.exceptions:
            print("failed:", err)

    results = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch("users", 0.1, fail=True), fetch("stock", 0.2),
        return_exceptions=True,            # errors become results
    )
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())
stock was cancelled
failed: users is down
failed: orders is down
[ConnectionError('users is down'), 'stock']
  • When one task in a TaskGroup fails, the group cancels the others. Then it raises all errors together in an ExceptionGroup. You catch it with except*.
  • Plain gather passes on the first error and does not cancel the other awaitables. With return_exceptions=True, errors come back as items of the result list.
  • This is structured concurrency. Prefer TaskGroup in new code.
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
    tg.create_task(fetch("users", 0.3))
    tg.create_task(fetch("orders", 0.2))
# here both tasks are finished
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};
use tokio::task::JoinSet;

async fn fetch(name: &'static str, ms: u64) -> String {
    tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(ms)).await;
    format!("{name}:{ms}")
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let t = Instant::now();
    let mut set = JoinSet::new();          // like a TaskGroup
    set.spawn(fetch("users", 300));
    set.spawn(fetch("orders", 200));
    while let Some(res) = set.join_next().await { // in finish order
        println!("{}", res.unwrap());
    }
    println!("JoinSet {:.1}s", t.elapsed().as_secs_f64());
}
orders:200
users:300
JoinSet 0.3s

You call asyncio.create_task(job()) and keep no reference. The loop holds tasks only weakly, so the task can vanish before it ends, and its error is lost. Start tasks in a TaskGroup, or keep them in a set.

Since Python 3.14, asyncio.get_event_loop() raises RuntimeError when no loop is running. Old code that called it at the top of a file breaks. Use asyncio.run(), or asyncio.get_running_loop() inside a coroutine. 3.14 also added python -m asyncio ps PID and pstree PID to see what a running program waits for.

Timeouts and cancellation

A slow server must not hang your program. Set a time limit.

import asyncio

async def slow_query() -> str:
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(5)
        return "rows"
    finally:
        print("cleanup: connection closed")   # runs on cancel too

async def main() -> None:
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.2):       # 3.11+
            await slow_query()
    except TimeoutError:
        print("timeout after 0.2s")

    try:
        await asyncio.wait_for(slow_query(), timeout=0.1)  # older style
    except TimeoutError:
        print("wait_for timed out")

    task = asyncio.create_task(slow_query())
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    task.cancel()                              # ask the task to stop
    try:
        await task
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("task cancelled:", task.cancelled())

asyncio.run(main())
cleanup: connection closed
timeout after 0.2s
cleanup: connection closed
wait_for timed out
cleanup: connection closed
task cancelled: True

Cancellation in Python is an exception. The loop raises CancelledError inside the task, at its current await. So finally blocks and async with blocks still clean up. asyncio.timeout() turns that cancel into a TimeoutError outside the block.

In Rust you cancel a future by dropping it. No code runs inside it, except the Drop of its values. See Async and await for tokio::time::timeout and cancellation safety.

Never swallow CancelledError. Look what happens to the timeout.

import asyncio

async def stubborn() -> None:
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(5)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("ignored the cancel")            # wrong: no re-raise

async def main() -> None:
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.1):
            await stubborn()
        print("no timeout reported!")
    except TimeoutError:
        print("timeout")

asyncio.run(main())
ignored the cancel
no timeout reported!

The timeout fired, but the task ate the cancel. So the timeout never reached your code. If you catch CancelledError to log or clean up, always end with raise. A bare except Exception is safe here: CancelledError is a BaseException, not an Exception.

Queues: producers and workers

A queue connects tasks that make work with tasks that do work. Here one producer makes five URLs and two workers download them.

import asyncio

async def producer(q: asyncio.Queue[str]) -> None:
    for url in ["a.com", "b.com", "c.com", "d.com", "e.com"]:
        await q.put(url)                   # waits when the queue is full
        print("queued", url)
    q.shutdown()                           # 3.13: no more items will come

async def worker(name: str, q: asyncio.Queue[str]) -> None:
    while True:
        try:
            url = await q.get()
        except asyncio.QueueShutDown:      # empty and shut down: stop
            return
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)           # pretend to download
        print(f"{name} got {url}")
        q.task_done()

async def main() -> None:
    q: asyncio.Queue[str] = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=2)   # backpressure
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tg.create_task(producer(q))
        for i in range(2):
            tg.create_task(worker(f"w{i}", q))
    print("all done")

asyncio.run(main())
queued a.com
queued b.com
queued c.com
queued d.com
w0 got a.com
w1 got b.com
queued e.com
w0 got c.com
w1 got d.com
w0 got e.com
all done
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::sync::mpsc;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<&str>(2); // capacity 2: backpressure
    let producer = tokio::spawn(async move {
        for url in ["a.com", "b.com", "c.com"] {
            tx.send(url).await.unwrap(); // waits when the channel is full
        }
        // tx is dropped here: the channel closes
    });
    while let Some(url) = rx.recv().await { // None when closed and empty
        tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)).await;
        println!("got {url}");
    }
    producer.await.unwrap();
    println!("all done");
}
got a.com
got b.com
got c.com
all done

Read the Python output with the queue size in mind.

  • The workers took a.com and b.com at once. So c.com and d.com fit in the queue.
  • Then the queue was full. put("e.com") waited until a worker took an item. This is backpressure. Without maxsize, a fast producer can fill all your memory.
  • shutdown() (3.13) says "no more items". Workers empty the queue, then get() raises QueueShutDown and they stop. Before 3.13 people put a special "stop" value in the queue for each worker.
  • task_done() and await q.join() let a producer wait until every item is done.

In Rust, the channel closes when the last sender is dropped. Then recv() returns None. Python needs the explicit shutdown() call.

asyncio.Queue is not thread-safe. Use it only between tasks on the same loop. Between threads use queue.Queue.

async with and async for

Some setup and cleanup must wait for the network: open a connection, close it. Some loops must wait for each next item: messages from a socket. Python has async versions of with and for for this.

import asyncio
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

@asynccontextmanager
async def connection(name: str) -> AsyncIterator[str]:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)              # pretend to connect
    print("open", name)
    try:
        yield name                         # the body of "async with" runs here
    finally:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)          # pretend to close
        print("close", name)

async def ticks(n: int) -> AsyncIterator[int]:   # an async generator
    for i in range(n):
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)          # wait for the next message
        yield i

async def main() -> None:
    async with connection("db") as conn:
        async for t in ticks(3):
            print(conn, "tick", t)
    squares = [t * t async for t in ticks(4)]     # async comprehension
    print(squares)

asyncio.run(main())
open db
db tick 0
db tick 1
db tick 2
close db
[0, 1, 4, 9]
  • async with calls await obj.__aenter__() and await obj.__aexit__(...). @asynccontextmanager builds both from one async generator. It is the async twin of @contextmanager from Functions, closures and decorators.
  • An async generator has both await and yield. async for calls await it.__anext__() for each item.
  • An async comprehension collects the items into a list.

Rust has no async for in the stable language yet. You use a Stream from the futures or tokio-stream crates with while let Some(x) = stream.next().await. There is no async Drop either, so cleanup that must await needs an explicit call.

Limit how many run at once

A hundred tasks can open a hundred connections. A server may block you. A semaphore sets a limit, and you use it with async with.

import asyncio
import time

limit = asyncio.Semaphore(3)               # at most 3 at the same time
active = 0

async def download(i: int) -> None:
    global active
    async with limit:
        active += 1
        print(f"start {i} (active {active})")
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
        active -= 1

async def main() -> None:
    t = time.perf_counter()
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        for i in range(7):
            tg.create_task(download(i))
    print(f"7 downloads in {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s")

asyncio.run(main())
start 0 (active 1)
start 1 (active 2)
start 2 (active 3)
start 3 (active 1)
start 4 (active 2)
start 5 (active 3)
start 6 (active 1)
7 downloads in 0.3s

Never more than three ran at once. Seven downloads of 0.1 s took three rounds, so 0.3 s. Note that active += 1 is safe here without a lock. Only one task runs at a time, and it cannot be paused between two awaits.

Mixing sync and async code

Async code and normal blocking code do not mix by themselves. This example has a heartbeat task that should print every 0.1 s.

import asyncio
import time

def read_sensor() -> int:                  # old blocking code
    time.sleep(0.3)
    return 42

async def heartbeat() -> None:
    for _ in range(3):
        print(f"  beat at {time.perf_counter() - START:.1f}s")
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)

async def bad() -> None:
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tg.create_task(heartbeat())
        await asyncio.sleep(0)             # let heartbeat start
        print("blocking call:", read_sensor())         # freezes the loop

async def good() -> None:
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tg.create_task(heartbeat())
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        print("to_thread:", await asyncio.to_thread(read_sensor))

START = time.perf_counter()
print("bad")
asyncio.run(bad())
START = time.perf_counter()
print("good")
asyncio.run(good())
bad
  beat at 0.0s
blocking call: 42
  beat at 0.3s
  beat at 0.4s
good
  beat at 0.0s
  beat at 0.1s
  beat at 0.2s
to_thread: 42

In bad() the heartbeat stopped for 0.3 s. time.sleep holds the only thread, so the loop cannot run any task. In good(), asyncio.to_thread (3.9) runs the blocking function in a worker thread, and the loop stays free. The same problem comes from requests.get, a big file read or a slow database driver. Use an async library or to_thread.

Debug mode finds such calls for you. It reports every step that holds the loop for more than 0.1 s.

import asyncio
import time

async def main() -> None:
    time.sleep(0.2)                        # blocking call inside async code

asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)            # or: PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1
Executing <Task finished name='Task-1' coro=<main() done, defined at /home/you/gen/debugmode.py:4> result=None created at .../asyncio/runners.py:109> took 0.211 seconds

Threads help with waiting, not with heavy maths. With the normal GIL, CPU work in a thread still blocks other Python code. Send CPU work to other processes with run_in_executor.

import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

def count_primes(limit: int) -> int:       # pure CPU work
    return sum(all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1)) for n in range(2, limit))

async def main() -> None:
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:    # other processes: other cores
        jobs = [loop.run_in_executor(pool, count_primes, n) for n in (10_000, 50_000)]
        print(await asyncio.gather(*jobs))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
[1229, 5133]

The other direction also has a trap. Sync code may call asyncio.run() only when no loop is running. Inside async code it fails with RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop. Inside async code, just await. Async code spreads upward, so plan where the one asyncio.run() goes. More on threads and processes is in Threads and shared state.

Which tool for which job
SituationPythonRust (tokio)
Start async from sync codeasyncio.run(main())#[tokio::main] or Runtime::block_on
Blocking call inside async codeawait asyncio.to_thread(f)spawn_blocking(f).await
CPU-heavy workrun_in_executor(ProcessPoolExecutor(), f)spawn_blocking or rayon
Wait without blockingawait asyncio.sleep(s)tokio::time::sleep(d).await
Never use inside async codetime.sleep, requests.getstd::thread::sleep, blocking I/O

Python and Rust compared

Iterators and futures in both languages
IdeaPythonRust
Next value__next__, ends with StopIterationnext(), ends with None
Easy lazy sequenceGenerator with yieldfrom_fn, adapters (gen blocks are unstable)
Use twiceSecond loop is silently emptyCompile error: value moved (E0382)
Calling an async functionGives a coroutine object, does nothingGives a future, does nothing
Who drives itThe built-in event loopA runtime crate such as tokio
ThreadsOne loop on one threadTasks move between worker threads
CancelCancelledError raised inside, finally runsThe future is dropped
Forgot to awaitWarning at run timeWarning at compile time

"Is asyncio parallel?" No. It is concurrent: tasks take turns on one thread while they wait. It helps with many slow network calls. For CPU work, use processes, or free-threaded Python, or move the hot loop to Rust.

Patterns to remember

Generator and asyncio patterns
PatternPurposeModelNote
def f(): ... yield xA lazy sequencedef read_lines(p): ... yield lineCalling it runs nothing yet.
g(f(source))A pipeline of generatorsnumbered(errors(read_lines("app.log")))One item flows at a time.
sum(x for x in xs)Aggregate without a listsum(n * n for n in range(10))Can be used only once.
yield from inner()Pass on another generatorresult = yield from inner()Gives the inner return value.
groupby(sorted(xs, key=k), key=k)Group items by a keygroupby(sorted(words), key=lambda w: w[0])Without sorting, only neighbours group.
asyncio.run(main())Start async codeasyncio.run(main())Once, at the top. Never inside a loop.
async with TaskGroup() as tg:Run tasks and wait for alltg.create_task(fetch(url))One failure cancels the others.
gather(..., return_exceptions=True)Collect results and errorsawait asyncio.gather(a(), b(), return_exceptions=True)Plain gather does not cancel on error.
async with asyncio.timeout(s):Limit the waiting timeasync with asyncio.timeout(2): await q()Catch TimeoutError outside the block.
except CancelledError: ...; raiseClean up on cancelexcept asyncio.CancelledError: log(); raiseNever swallow it.
Queue(maxsize=n) + shutdown()Producer and workersq = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=100)shutdown needs 3.13.
async with Semaphore(n):Limit how many run at onceasync with limit: await get(url)Create it once, share it.
@asynccontextmanagerAsync setup and cleanupasync with connection("db") as c:Put cleanup in finally.
await asyncio.to_thread(f, x)Call blocking code from async codeawait asyncio.to_thread(read_sensor)Helps waiting, not CPU work.

Practice

What does g = countdown(3) do when countdown contains yield?

  • It runs the body and returns a list.
  • It creates a generator object. No code in the body runs yet.
  • It runs the body up to the first yield.

The body starts only on the first next(g). That call runs it up to the first yield.

gen = (x * 2 for x in [1, 2, 3]). What is (sum(gen), sum(gen))?

  • (12, 12)
  • (12, 0)
  • An error on the second sum

A generator can be used once. The second sum finds it empty and returns 0, with no error.

An iterator signals the end by raising ?. A Rust iterator returns ?.

To run a blocking function from async code without freezing the loop, write await asyncio.<span class="blank" data-answer="to_thread">?</span>(read_sensor).

The Python 3.13 method that tells an asyncio.Queue "no more items" is ?.

Three tasks are in a TaskGroup. One raises ValueError. What happens?

  • The other two keep running. The error is printed and ignored.
  • The other two are cancelled. The error is raised in an ExceptionGroup when the block ends.
  • The program stops at once without cleanup.

TaskGroup cancels the rest and waits for them. Catch the errors with except* ValueError.

Two awaits in a row wait 1 s and 2 s. The same two calls in a TaskGroup take how long?

  • 3 s
  • About 2 s
  • About 1 s

Tasks wait at the same time. The total is the longest wait, not the sum.

  1. Write a generator evens(limit) that yields 0, 2, 4, ... below limit. Then get the first three even squares with a generator expression and islice.
    Answer

    def evens(limit): n = 0; while n < limit: yield n; n += 2 (on separate lines). Then list(islice((x * x for x in evens(100)), 3)) gives [0, 4, 16].

  2. A teammate reads a 20 GB log with lines = open(p).readlines() and filters it. The server runs out of memory. Rewrite the idea.
    Answer

    Iterate the file object, which is lazy: with open(p) as f: errors = (l for l in f if l.startswith("ERROR")), and use the generator inside the with block. Only one line is in memory at a time.

  3. Your async web scraper uses requests.get(url) inside async def functions. It is not faster than the sync version. Why? Give two fixes.
    Answer

    requests.get blocks the only thread, so tasks cannot wait at the same time. Fix 1: use an async client such as httpx.AsyncClient. Fix 2: wrap the call in await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, url).

  4. A worker catches except asyncio.CancelledError: pass. Now asyncio.timeout(5) around it never raises. Explain and fix.
    Answer

    The timeout works by cancelling the task. The worker swallows the cancel, so the timeout never sees it. Do the cleanup, then raise again, or use finally for cleanup instead of catching the error.

  5. You must call 500 URLs, but the server allows only 10 connections at once. Sketch the code.
    Answer

    Create limit = asyncio.Semaphore(10). In fetch(url), write async with limit: around the request. Start all 500 with tg.create_task(fetch(u)) inside a TaskGroup. Another way: a Queue with 10 worker tasks.

  6. Explain why asyncio.Queue needs shutdown() while a tokio mpsc channel closes by itself.
    Answer

    In Rust the channel knows how many senders exist. When the last sender is dropped, ownership rules close the channel and recv() returns None. Python's queue has no owners. It cannot know that no one will put more items, so you must say it with shutdown() (3.13) or a stop value.

Key takeaways

  • A for loop calls iter() once and next() until StopIteration. Iterators work once.
  • A generator pauses at yield and keeps its local variables. Chained generators make memory-light pipelines.
  • Coroutines are generators grown up. The event loop runs one ready task at a time until it awaits.
  • Use TaskGroup for tasks, asyncio.timeout for limits, queues for producers and workers, and a semaphore for limits on how many run.
  • Never block the loop: use async libraries, to_thread for blocking calls and processes for CPU work.
  • Rust has the same ideas: next() returns Option, futures are lazy, and tasks are cancelled by dropping them.

Sources

  • asyncio: Coroutines and Tasks. TaskGroup, gather, timeouts, to_thread and the warning about task references.
  • asyncio: Queues. maxsize, task_done, join and shutdown (3.13).
  • itertools. The building blocks and the official recipes.
  • Python reference: yield expressions. How yield, send, close and async generators work.
  • PEP 492: Coroutines with async and await syntax. Why async def was added and how it relates to generators.
  • What's New in Python 3.14. The asyncio call graph tools and other changes.

The standard library you need

Python comes with a large standard library. It reads files, parses JSON, handles time zones, runs programs and tests your code. This chapter shows the modules you will use every week, the mistakes people make with them, and the five outside packages that almost every project adds.

  • Work with files, folders, JSON, CSV and TOML using pathlib, shutil, json, csv and tomllib.
  • Handle dates and time zones correctly with datetime and zoneinfo.
  • Use collections, re, dataclasses, subprocess, logging and argparse in small tools.
  • Test code with unittest.mock and run work in parallel with concurrent.futures.
  • Choose the right module for a task, and know when httpx, pydantic, numpy, pandas or FastAPI is better.

Files and folders: pathlib, os and shutil

Here is a small script that makes a folder, writes a file, finds it, copies it and deletes everything.

import os
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

base = Path("demo")
(base / "logs").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)   # no error if it exists
report = base / "logs" / "report.txt"                # "/" joins path parts
report.write_text("ok\n", encoding="utf-8")

print(report, report.name, report.stem, report.suffix, report.parent)
print(report.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip())
print([p.as_posix() for p in base.rglob("*.txt")])   # search all subfolders
backup = report.copy(base / "backup.txt")            # 3.14: Path.copy
print(backup.exists(), backup.stat().st_size, "bytes")

print(os.environ.get("APP_MODE", "dev"))             # an environment variable
print(shutil.which("git") is not None)               # is git on the PATH?
shutil.rmtree(base)                                  # delete the whole tree
print(base.exists())
demo/logs/report.txt report.txt report .txt demo/logs
ok
['demo/logs/report.txt']
True 3 bytes
dev
True
False

Each module has its own job.

  • pathlib gives a Path object. You join parts with /, read and write files, and search with glob and rglob. Use it for almost all path work.
  • os talks to the operating system: environment variables, the process id, low-level file calls. os.environ is a dict of the environment.
  • shutil works on whole files and trees: copy, move, delete a folder, find a program with which, check free disk space with disk_usage.

Python 3.14 added Path.copy(), Path.move() and their _into() forms. On older versions use shutil.copy2 and shutil.move.

report = Path("demo") / "logs" / "report.txt"
report.write_text("ok\n", encoding="utf-8")
use std::fs;
use std::path::Path;

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let base = Path::new("demo_rs");
    fs::create_dir_all(base.join("logs"))?;
    let report = base.join("logs").join("report.txt");
    fs::write(&report, "ok\n")?;
    println!("{:?} {:?} {:?}", report.file_name(), report.extension(), report.parent());
    println!("{}", fs::read_to_string(&report)?.trim());
    fs::copy(&report, base.join("backup.txt"))?;
    println!("{}", std::env::var("APP_MODE").unwrap_or("dev".into()));
    fs::remove_dir_all(base)?;
    println!("{}", base.exists());
    Ok(())
}
Some("report.txt") Some("txt") Some("demo_rs/logs")
ok
dev
false

Rust splits the same work between std::path for names and std::fs for disk work. Every disk call returns a Result, so the ? shows where errors can happen. In Python they raise exceptions such as FileNotFoundError.

You call open(p) or read_text() without encoding="utf-8". Then Python uses the system's default encoding, which can differ on Windows. Always pass the encoding for text files. Python 3.15 makes UTF-8 the default, but older versions do not.

Data formats: json, csv and tomllib

import csv
import json
import tomllib
from datetime import date

order = {"id": 7, "items": ["tea", "cake"], "paid": True, "note": None}
text = json.dumps(order, indent=2)                # Python -> JSON text
back = json.loads(text)                           # JSON text -> Python
print(back == order, type(back["items"]).__name__)

try:
    json.dumps({"day": date(2026, 11, 15)})
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
print(json.dumps({"day": date(2026, 11, 15)}, default=str))   # fallback

with open("people.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["name", "age"])
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows([{"name": "Ann", "age": 31}, {"name": "Bo, Jr.", "age": 7}])
with open("people.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
print(open("people.csv").read().strip())
print(rows[1], type(rows[1]["age"]).__name__)    # every value is a str

with open("pyproject.toml", "rb") as f:          # tomllib wants binary mode
    cfg = tomllib.load(f)
print(cfg["project"]["name"], cfg["tool"]["app"]["retries"])
True list
TypeError: Object of type date is not JSON serializable
{"day": "2026-11-15"}
name,age
Ann,31
"Bo, Jr.",7
{'name': 'Bo, Jr.', 'age': '7'} str
shop 3
  • json: dumps and loads work with strings. dump and load work with files. JSON true, null and arrays become True, None and lists.
  • JSON knows only strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays and objects. A date, a set or your own class fails. Pass default=str, or convert first.
  • csv: DictReader and DictWriter use the header row as keys. The module adds quotes when a value holds a comma, like "Bo, Jr.". Every value you read back is a string.
  • tomllib (3.11) reads TOML. It cannot write TOML. Use the tomli-w package for that. In 3.15 it reads TOML 1.1.

You open a CSV file without newline="". On Windows every row then gets an extra empty line. The csv module handles line endings itself, so always pass newline="".

order = json.loads(text)      # a dict: no check of the fields
order["id"] + 1               # works only if "id" really is a number
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Order {
    id: u32,
    items: Vec<String>,
    paid: bool,
    note: Option<String>, // null becomes None
}

fn main() -> Result<(), serde_json::Error> {
    let text = r#"{"id": 7, "items": ["tea", "cake"], "paid": true, "note": null}"#;
    let order: Order = serde_json::from_str(text)?; // checks every field
    println!("{order:?}");
    println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&order)?);
    let bad = serde_json::from_str::<Order>(r#"{"id": "7"}"#);
    println!("{}", bad.unwrap_err());
    Ok(())
}
Order { id: 7, items: ["tea", "cake"], paid: true, note: None }
{"id":7,"items":["tea","cake"],"paid":true,"note":null}
invalid type: string "7", expected u32 at line 1 column 10

Python's json gives you plain dicts and checks nothing. Rust's serde parses straight into a typed struct and rejects wrong data. In Python, pydantic gives you the serde style. You meet it at the end of this chapter.

Dates and times: datetime and zoneinfo

Time bugs are common and expensive. Look at one meeting time in three places.

from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

meeting = datetime(2026, 11, 15, 9, 30, tzinfo=UTC)     # an aware time
tokyo = meeting.astimezone(ZoneInfo("Asia/Tokyo"))
new_york = meeting.astimezone(ZoneInfo("America/New_York"))
print(tokyo.isoformat())
print(new_york.isoformat())
print(tokyo == new_york)                                # the same moment
print(f"{tokyo:%d %b %Y, %H:%M %Z}")

naive = datetime(2026, 11, 15, 9, 30)                   # no time zone
try:
    print(naive < meeting)
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

ny = ZoneInfo("America/New_York")
before = datetime(2026, 3, 7, 12, 0, tzinfo=ny)         # the day before DST
after = before + timedelta(days=1)                      # same wall clock time
print(after, after - before)
print(after.astimezone(UTC) - before.astimezone(UTC))   # real elapsed time
print(datetime.fromisoformat("2026-11-15T18:30:00+09:00").astimezone(UTC))
2026-11-15T18:30:00+09:00
2026-11-15T04:30:00-05:00
True
15 Nov 2026, 18:30 JST
TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes
2026-03-08 12:00:00-04:00 1 day, 0:00:00
23:00:00
2026-11-15 09:30:00+00:00
  • An aware datetime has a time zone. A naive one does not. Python refuses to compare the two.
  • zoneinfo (3.9) gives real zones from the IANA time zone database, such as "Asia/Tokyo". Windows has no system copy, so install the tzdata package there.
  • On 8 March 2026 New York moved its clocks forward one hour for DST. Adding one day kept the wall clock at 12:00. But only 23 real hours passed. Do time maths in UTC when you need real durations.
  • isoformat() and fromisoformat() are the safe way to store and read times as text.

You use datetime.utcnow(). It returns a naive time that only looks like UTC. It is deprecated since 3.12. Write datetime.now(UTC) instead. Store UTC, and convert to a local zone only when you show the time to a person.

Rust's standard library has only SystemTime and Duration. For dates and zones, Rust projects add a crate such as chrono or jiff.

Everyday tools: collections, re and dataclasses

collections

from collections import ChainMap, Counter, defaultdict, deque, namedtuple

words = "the cat and the dog and the bird".split()
counts = Counter(words)                       # count anything hashable
print(counts.most_common(2))

by_letter = defaultdict(list)                 # missing key -> new empty list
for w in words:
    by_letter[w[0]].append(w)
print(dict(by_letter))

recent = deque(maxlen=3)                      # keeps only the last 3
for page in ["home", "shop", "cart", "pay"]:
    recent.append(page)
print(recent)

Point = namedtuple("Point", "x y")            # a light, read-only record
p = Point(2, 5)
print(p.x + p.y, p)

defaults = {"port": 8080, "debug": False}
user = {"debug": True}
config = ChainMap(user, defaults)             # look in user first
print(config["port"], config["debug"])
[('the', 3), ('and', 2)]
{'t': ['the', 'the', 'the'], 'c': ['cat'], 'a': ['and', 'and'], 'd': ['dog'], 'b': ['bird']}
deque(['shop', 'cart', 'pay'], maxlen=3)
7 Point(x=2, y=5)
8080 True
counts = Counter(words)
recent = deque(maxlen=3)
use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};

fn main() {
    let words = "the cat and the dog and the bird".split_whitespace();
    let mut counts: HashMap<&str, u32> = HashMap::new();
    for w in words {
        *counts.entry(w).or_default() += 1; // like Counter / defaultdict
    }
    let mut top: Vec<_> = counts.into_iter().collect();
    top.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(&a.1).then(a.0.cmp(b.0)));
    println!("{:?}", &top[..2]);

    let mut recent = VecDeque::with_capacity(3); // no maxlen: trim by hand
    for page in ["home", "shop", "cart", "pay"] {
        if recent.len() == 3 {
            recent.pop_front();
        }
        recent.push_back(page);
    }
    println!("{recent:?}");
}
[("the", 3), ("and", 2)]
["shop", "cart", "pay"]

Rust's entry() API does the work of Counter and defaultdict. Collections covers both languages in depth.

re: regular expressions

A regular expression finds text by its shape. Here we pull fields out of log lines.

import re

log = "2026-11-15 09:30:12 ERROR db timeout after 30s; 2026-11-15 09:31:02 WARN slow"
pattern = re.compile(r"(?P<date>\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}) (?P<time>[\d:]{8}) (?P<level>[A-Z]+)")

for m in pattern.finditer(log):              # every match, with groups
    print(m["level"], m["time"])

print(re.findall(r"\d+s\b", log))            # all durations
print(re.sub(r"\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}", "<time>", log)[:40])

print(re.match(r"\d+", "abc 123"))           # match: only at the start
print(re.search(r"\d+", "abc 123"))          # search: anywhere
print(re.fullmatch(r"[a-z]+", "abc1"))       # fullmatch: the whole string
print("\d" == r"\d", len("\n"), len(r"\n"))  # why we write r"..."
/home/you/std/regex.py:15: SyntaxWarning: "\d" is an invalid escape sequence. Such sequences will not work in the future. Did you mean "\\d"? A raw string is also an option.
  print("\d" == r"\d", len("\n"), len(r"\n"))  # why we write r"..."
ERROR 09:30:12
WARN 09:31:02
['30s']
2026-11-15 <time> ERROR db timeout after
None
<re.Match object; span=(4, 7), match='123'>
None
True 1 2
  • (?P<name>...) is a named group. Read it with m["name"].
  • re.compile builds the pattern once. Use it when you reuse a pattern in a loop.
  • match checks only the start. search looks anywhere. fullmatch needs the whole string. Python 3.15 adds prefixmatch as a clearer name for match.
  • Always write patterns as raw strings: r"\d". In a normal string, Python reads the backslash first. You see the warning above, and "\n" becomes one newline character instead of two characters.

Regular expressions are good for small, flat text. For JSON, HTML, CSV or dates, use the real parser. It handles quotes, escapes and edge cases for you. In Rust, the regex crate gives the same syntax with guaranteed linear time.

dataclasses

import json
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field, replace

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Server:
    host: str
    port: int = 8080
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # a new list each time

s = Server("db.local", tags=["prod"])
print(s)
print(json.dumps(asdict(s)))                         # dataclass -> dict -> JSON
print(replace(s, port=5432))                         # a changed copy
print(Server(**json.loads('{"host": "x", "port": 1}')))
Server(host='db.local', port=8080, tags=['prod'])
{"host": "db.local", "port": 8080, "tags": ["prod"]}
Server(host='db.local', port=5432, tags=['prod'])
Server(host='x', port=1, tags=[])

A dataclass writes the boring methods for you. asdict turns it into a dict for JSON. replace makes a changed copy of a frozen object. A dataclass does not check types at run time: Server(**data) accepts a string port too. The full story is in Classes, dataclasses and protocols.

Running other programs: subprocess

import subprocess
import sys

r = subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, "-c", "print('hello from a child')"],   # a list, no shell
    capture_output=True, text=True, check=True, timeout=10,
)
print(r.returncode, r.stdout.strip())

try:
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", "import sys; sys.exit(3)"], check=True)
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
    print("failed with code", e.returncode)

try:
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", "import time; time.sleep(5)"], timeout=0.5)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    print("killed after 0.5s")

name = "x; echo HACKED"                          # imagine this came from a user
print(subprocess.run(["echo", name], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip())
print(subprocess.run(f"echo {name}", shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip())
0 hello from a child
failed with code 3
killed after 0.5s
x; echo HACKED
x
HACKED

subprocess.run is the one function you need most of the time. Learn its options.

  • Pass the command as a list: ["git", "status"]. Each item is one argument.
  • capture_output=True keeps the output. text=True gives str instead of bytes.
  • check=True raises CalledProcessError when the exit code is not 0. Without it, failures pass silently.
  • timeout= kills a program that hangs.

Never build a command string from user input and pass shell=True. The shell reads ; as "run another command". The last line above ran echo HACKED. This is called command injection. With a list, the same input was harmless text.

subprocess.run(["echo", name], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
use std::process::Command;

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let out = Command::new("echo").arg("x; echo HACKED").output()?; // no shell
    println!("{} {}", out.status.code().unwrap(), String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stdout).trim());
    let status = Command::new("sh").args(["-c", "exit 3"]).status()?;
    println!("success: {}, code: {:?}", status.success(), status.code());
    Ok(())
}
0 x; echo HACKED
success: false, code: Some(3)

Rust's Command never uses a shell unless you start one yourself. A failed exit code is not an error there either. You must check status.success(), like check=True.

Command-line tools: argparse and logging

A real tool needs options and good messages. argparse reads the options. logging prints messages with levels. Here is a tool that lists big files.

import argparse
import logging
from pathlib import Path

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)              # one logger per module

def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="tidy", description="Find big files.",
                                     suggest_on_error=True)   # 3.14
    parser.add_argument("folder", type=Path, help="where to look")
    parser.add_argument("--min-kb", type=int, default=100, help="size limit")
    parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true")
    parser.add_argument("--sort", choices=["name", "size"], default="size")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    logging.basicConfig(                       # configure once, in main
        level=logging.DEBUG if args.verbose else logging.INFO,
        format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s",
    )
    log.debug("args: %s", args)                # lazy: formatted only if shown
    big = [p for p in args.folder.rglob("*") if p.is_file()
           and p.stat().st_size >= args.min_kb * 1024]
    log.info("found %d big files in %s", len(big), args.folder)
    key = (lambda p: p.name) if args.sort == "name" else (lambda p: -p.stat().st_size)
    for p in sorted(big, key=key):
        print(f"{p.stat().st_size // 1024:>6} KB  {p}")
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
python3.14 tidy.py data -v --min-kb 1
DEBUG __main__: args: Namespace(folder=PosixPath('data'), min_kb=1, verbose=True, sort='size')
INFO __main__: found 2 big files in data
   292 KB  data/big.bin
     1 KB  data/mid.bin
python3.14 tidy.py --help
usage: tidy [-h] [--min-kb MIN_KB] [-v] [--sort {name,size}] folder

Find big files.

positional arguments:
  folder              where to look

options:
  -h, --help          show this help message and exit
  --min-kb MIN_KB     size limit
  -v, --verbose
  --sort {name,size}
python3.14 tidy.py data --sort siz
usage: tidy [-h] [--min-kb MIN_KB] [-v] [--sort {name,size}] folder
tidy: error: argument --sort: invalid choice: 'siz', maybe you meant 'size'? (choose from name, size)
  • argparse writes the help text and the error messages for you. type=Path and type=int convert the text. choices limits the values.
  • suggest_on_error=True (3.14) adds the "maybe you meant" hint. In 3.15 it is on by default. Help text is in colour since 3.14.
  • main(argv) takes a list, so a test can call main(["data", "-v"]) directly.
  • Get a logger with getLogger(__name__) in every module. Configure logging once, in main. A library should never call basicConfig.

Logging has five levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR and CRITICAL. Inside except, use log.exception. It logs at ERROR level and adds the traceback.

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s",
                    datefmt="%H:%M:%S")
log = logging.getLogger("shop.pay")

log.debug("not shown: the level is INFO")
log.info("user %s paid %.2f", "ann", 12.5)    # pass values, not an f-string
try:
    1 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    log.exception("price calculation failed")  # ERROR level + traceback
09:55:20 INFO shop.pay: user ann paid 12.50
09:55:20 ERROR shop.pay: price calculation failed
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/you/std/logs.py", line 10, in <module>
    1 / 0
    ~~^~~
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

You write log.debug(f"data: {big_object}"). Python builds that string even when DEBUG is off. Write log.debug("data: %s", big_object). Then the string is built only if the message is shown. Log tools can also group messages by the fixed text.

Read the options

Make an ArgumentParser. Give each option a type, a default and a help text.

Set up logging

Call logging.basicConfig once in main. Choose the level from --verbose.

Work with paths

Turn input into Path objects. Use rglob, stat and read_text(encoding="utf-8").

Read and write data

Load settings with tomllib. Write results with json or csv.

Return an exit code

Return 0 for success and another number for failure. End with raise SystemExit(main()), so shells and CI see the result.

Testing with unittest.mock

Tests must not call real servers. A mock replaces a slow or risky function during a test. Here advice() calls the network through fetch_temp().

import json
from urllib.request import urlopen

def fetch_temp(city: str) -> float:
    url = f"https://api.example.com/temp/{city}"
    with urlopen(url, timeout=5) as r:
        return json.load(r)["temp"]

def advice(city: str) -> str:
    try:
        temp = fetch_temp(city)
    except TimeoutError:
        return "no data"
    return "take a coat" if temp < 10 else "t-shirt"
from weather import fetch_temp   # copies the name

def banner(city: str) -> str:
    return f"{city}: {fetch_temp(city)} C"
import unittest
from unittest.mock import patch

import app
import weather

class AdviceTest(unittest.TestCase):
    @patch("weather.fetch_temp", autospec=True)     # replace where it is used
    def test_cold(self, fake):
        fake.return_value = 3.0
        self.assertEqual(weather.advice("Oslo"), "take a coat")
        fake.assert_called_once_with("Oslo")

    @patch("weather.fetch_temp", autospec=True, side_effect=TimeoutError)
    def test_timeout(self, fake):
        self.assertEqual(weather.advice("Oslo"), "no data")

    def test_wrong_signature(self):
        with patch("weather.fetch_temp", autospec=True) as fake:
            with self.assertRaises(TypeError):     # autospec checks arguments
                fake("Oslo", "extra")

    def test_patch_where_used(self):
        with patch("app.fetch_temp", return_value=21.0):   # app has its own name
            self.assertEqual(app.banner("Rome"), "Rome: 21.0 C")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()
test_cold (test_weather.AdviceTest.test_cold) ... ok
test_patch_where_used (test_weather.AdviceTest.test_patch_where_used) ... ok
test_timeout (test_weather.AdviceTest.test_timeout) ... ok
test_wrong_signature (test_weather.AdviceTest.test_wrong_signature) ... ok

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 4 tests in 0.003s

OK
  • patch("module.name") swaps a name for a mock during one test, then puts the real one back.
  • return_value sets what the mock returns. side_effect can raise an error, return values from a list one by one, or call a function.
  • assert_called_once_with checks how your code used the mock.
  • autospec=True copies the real signature. A call with wrong arguments fails, like the real function would.

The most important rule: patch the name where it is looked up, not where it is defined. app.py did from weather import fetch_temp. That made a second name, app.fetch_temp. Patch weather.fetch_temp in a test of app.banner, and the real function still runs.

urllib.error.URLError: <urlopen error [Errno 8] nodename nor servname provided, or not known>
Ran 1 test in 0.047s
FAILED (errors=1)

Rust has no monkey patching. You pass the dependency in as a trait object or a generic, and give a fake in the test. Python can do that too: a Protocol and a fake class, as in Type hints. Many teams prefer it to patch. pytest, the most used test runner, is in Packaging and testing.

Running work in parallel: concurrent.futures

concurrent.futures gives one simple interface for a pool of threads or a pool of processes.

import time
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed

def download(url: str) -> str:                 # waits: good for threads
    time.sleep(0.2)
    if url.endswith(".bad"):
        raise ValueError(f"cannot load {url}")
    return f"{url}: 200"

def count_primes(limit: int) -> int:           # computes: needs processes
    return sum(all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1)) for n in range(2, limit))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    urls = ["a.com", "b.com", "c.bad", "d.com"]
    t = time.perf_counter()
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
        futures = {pool.submit(download, u): u for u in urls}
        for fut in as_completed(futures):      # in the order they finish
            try:
                print(fut.result())            # re-raises the worker's error
            except ValueError as e:
                print("error:", e)
    print(f"threads: {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s for 4 downloads")

    for Pool in (ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor):
        t = time.perf_counter()
        with Pool(max_workers=4) as pool:
            results = list(pool.map(count_primes, [300_000] * 4))
        print(f"{Pool.__name__}: {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s {results[0]}")
b.com: 200
error: cannot load c.bad
d.com: 200
a.com: 200
threads: 0.2s for 4 downloads
ThreadPoolExecutor: 1.69s 25997
ProcessPoolExecutor: 0.45s 25997
  • submit returns a Future. result() waits for it and raises the worker's error in your thread.
  • as_completed gives futures as they finish. map keeps the input order.
  • Four waits of 0.2 s took 0.2 s with threads. Threads are good for waiting.
  • For the prime counting, threads took 1.69 s. One call after the other took 1.57 s, so threads gave nothing. The GIL lets one thread run Python code at a time. Processes took 0.45 s, because each one has its own interpreter.

On Linux, ProcessPoolExecutor now starts workers with forkserver instead of fork. macOS and Windows still use spawn. So the work function must be importable, and the start code must sit under if __name__ == "__main__":. 3.14 also added InterpreterPoolExecutor, a pool of subinterpreters in one process. See Python versions.

with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(count_primes, [300_000] * 4))
use std::thread;

fn count_primes(limit: u32) -> usize {
    (2..limit).filter(|&n| (2..).take_while(|d| d * d <= n).all(|d| n % d != 0)).count()
}

fn main() {
    let results: Vec<usize> = thread::scope(|s| {
        let handles: Vec<_> = (0..4).map(|_| s.spawn(|| count_primes(300_000))).collect();
        handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).collect()
    }); // real threads on real cores: no GIL
    println!("{results:?}");
}
[25997, 25997, 25997, 25997]

Rust threads run on all cores with no GIL, so plain threads are enough. For waiting on many network calls, Python also has asyncio. See Generators and asyncio, and Threads and shared state for the Rust side.
