print(client.post("/items", json={"name": "tea", "price": 2.5}).json())
bad = client.post("/items", json={"name": "tea", "price": "cheap"})
print(bad.status_code, bad.json()["detail"][0]["msg"])
{'saved': 'tea'}
422 Input should be a valid number, unable to parse string as a number
  • httpx has the same style as requests, plus AsyncClient for asyncio. MockTransport fakes a server, so the example needs no network. Always set a timeout.
  • httpx2: httpx has had no stable release since 0.28.1 in December 2024. Only test versions of 1.0 came out (1.0.dev1 to 1.0.dev6). In 2026 the pydantic team published httpx2, a fork of 0.28.1 with the same API (2.16.0 on 15 November 2026). Write import httpx2 as httpx to switch. Starlette 1.10, under FastAPI's TestClient, now warns when you use plain httpx. I could not find an official statement from the original httpx author. Check the project pages before you choose.
  • pydantic checks data at run time and converts it when safe: "7" became 7. It reports every problem at once. This is the Python version of serde.
  • numpy runs one operation on a whole array in compiled code. It is much faster than a Python loop. Performance and how CPython works measures it.
  • pandas 3.0 (January 2026) stores text in a real string type, so the dtype prints str. It also makes copy-on-write the default. Polars is a fast, Rust-based option for big tables.
  • FastAPI reads your type hints to check the request, and answers 422 for bad input. TestClient calls the app directly, with no server. For the Rust side, see Web services with axum.

"When do you add a dependency?" A good answer: when the standard library cannot do the job well, and the package is well kept. Check the release history, the number of maintainers and the license. Pin versions in a lock file, for example with uv lock.

Patterns to remember

Standard library patterns
PatternPurposeModelNote
Path(a) / bJoin path partsPath("data") / "users.csv"Works on every operating system.
p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")Read a small text filePath("a.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8")Always pass the encoding.
json.dumps(x, default=str)Write JSON with odd typesjson.dumps({"day": today}, default=str)JSON has no dates or sets.
open(p, newline="") + DictReaderRead a CSV filerows = list(csv.DictReader(f))Every value is a string.
tomllib.load(open(p, "rb"))Read TOML configcfg = tomllib.load(f)Binary mode. Read only.
datetime.now(UTC)Get the current timestamp = datetime.now(UTC).isoformat()Not utcnow(): it is naive.
dt.astimezone(ZoneInfo(z))Show a time in a zonet.astimezone(ZoneInfo("Asia/Tokyo"))Store UTC, convert for people.
Counter(xs).most_common(n)Count and rankCounter(words).most_common(3)Works for any hashable item.
re.compile(r"(?P<n>...)")Reuse a pattern with named groupsm["level"]Always a raw string.
subprocess.run([..], check=True)Run a program safelyrun(["git", "pull"], check=True, timeout=60)A list, never shell=True with input.
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)Log from a modulelog.info("got %d rows", n)Values as arguments, not f-strings.
main(argv=None) + argparseA testable command-line toolraise SystemExit(main())Tests call main([...]).
patch("user_module.name", autospec=True)Fake a dependency in a test@patch("app.fetch_temp")Patch where the name is looked up.
ThreadPoolExecutor / ProcessPoolExecutorRun work in parallelpool.map(f, items)Threads for waiting, processes for CPU.

Practice

Which line joins a folder and a file name correctly on every system?

  • "data" + "/" + "users.csv"
  • Path("data") / "users.csv"
  • os.environ["data"] + "users.csv"

pathlib uses the right separator for each system and gives you a Path object with useful methods.

You read a CSV with DictReader. What is the type of row["age"]?

  • int
  • str
  • It depends on the value.

CSV has no types. Every value comes back as a string. Convert it yourself, or let pydantic or pandas do it.

To get the current time with a time zone, write datetime.now(<span class="blank" data-answer="UTC|timezone.utc|datetime.UTC">?</span>).

The subprocess option that raises an error for a non-zero exit code is <span class="blank" data-answer="check=True|check">?</span>.

tomllib.load needs a file opened in ? mode.

report.py does from db import query. A test of report.build() must fake query. What do you patch?

  • patch("db.query")
  • patch("report.query")
  • patch("query")

The import made a name report.query. build() looks up that name, so you patch it there.

You must resize 10 000 images with pure Python code on an 8-core machine. Which pool is the better first choice?

  • ThreadPoolExecutor
  • ProcessPoolExecutor
  • No pool: a plain loop is always fastest.

This is CPU work. With the GIL, threads run Python code one at a time. Processes use all cores.

  1. Write code that prints the names of all .log files under logs, in all subfolders, sorted.
    Answer

    for p in sorted(Path("logs").rglob("*.log")): print(p.name). rglob searches all subfolders. sorted works because paths can be compared.

  2. A service stores datetime.now() in the database. Users in Tokyo and Berlin see wrong times. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
    Answer

    datetime.now() is naive local time of the server. It has no zone, so nobody knows what it means. Store datetime.now(UTC), and convert with astimezone(ZoneInfo(user_zone)) only when you show it.

  3. Rewrite this safely: subprocess.run(f"convert {filename} out.png", shell=True). The file name comes from an upload.
    Answer

    subprocess.run(["convert", filename, "out.png"], check=True, timeout=60). With a list there is no shell, so ; or $(...) in the name is just text. Also check that the name is a real file, and add "--" before it if the tool supports it, so a name that starts with - is not read as an option.

  4. Count the five most common words in a text file, ignoring case. Use the standard library only.
    Answer

    words = re.findall(r"[a-z']+", Path("book.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8").lower()), then Counter(words).most_common(5).

  5. Your team logs with print(). List three things logging gives you that print does not.
    Answer

    Levels you can switch on and off without code changes. Time stamps and module names in a fixed format. Handlers that send messages to files, the console or a log service. Also log.exception adds the traceback for you.

  6. An API returns JSON orders. A teammate wants plain dicts. You want pydantic. Give the main argument, and the Rust equivalent.
    Answer

    Plain dicts check nothing, so a wrong type crashes later, far from the cause. A pydantic model checks and converts at the edge and lists every problem at once. It also gives type hints for mypy. The Rust equivalent is serde: serde_json::from_str::<Order> parses into a struct or returns an error.

Key takeaways

  • Use pathlib for paths and small files, shutil for whole trees, and os for the environment. Always pass encoding="utf-8".
  • json, csv and tomllib read the common formats. None of them checks types. CSV values are always strings.
  • Store aware UTC times. Use zoneinfo to show local times. Do duration maths in UTC.
  • Run programs with subprocess.run([...], check=True, timeout=...). Never pass user input to shell=True.
  • Build tools with argparse and logging. Patch names where they are looked up. Use threads for waiting and processes for CPU work.
  • Add httpx (or httpx2), pydantic, numpy, pandas or FastAPI when the standard library is not enough, and pin the versions.

Sources

  • The Python Standard Library. The official reference for every module in this chapter.
  • What's New in Python 3.14. Path.copy and move, argparse suggestions, the forkserver default and InterpreterPoolExecutor.
  • unittest.mock. patch, autospec, side_effect and the "where to patch" rule.
  • subprocess. run, check, timeout and the security notes about the shell.
  • What's new in pandas 3.0.0. The string dtype, copy-on-write and the January 2026 release.
  • httpx2: migration guide. The fork of httpx 0.28.1 and how to switch.

Performance and how CPython works

Python is easy to write, but it can be slow. This chapter opens the engine. You see how CPython runs your code, how it frees memory and why one thread often runs at a time. Then you learn to measure, and to make slow code fast.

  • Read the bytecode of a function with dis and explain the interpreter loop.
  • Explain reference counting, the cycle collector and the 3.14.5 change.
  • Describe the GIL, the free-threaded build, the specialising interpreter and the JIT.
  • Measure code with timeit, cProfile and py-spy before you change it.
  • Choose a faster data structure, NumPy, processes or Rust for a slow part.

What happens when you run a .py file

Start with a tiny function. Then look at what Python really runs.

import dis

def total(prices):
    s = 0
    for p in prices:
        s += p
    return s

dis.dis(total)      # show the instructions inside total
  3           RESUME                   0

  4           LOAD_SMALL_INT           0
              STORE_FAST               1 (s)

  5           LOAD_FAST_BORROW         0 (prices)
              GET_ITER
      L1:     FOR_ITER                11 (to L2)
              STORE_FAST               2 (p)

  6           LOAD_FAST_BORROW_LOAD_FAST_BORROW 18 (s, p)
              BINARY_OP               13 (+=)
              STORE_FAST               1 (s)
              JUMP_BACKWARD           13 (to L1)

  5   L2:     END_FOR
              POP_ITER

  7           LOAD_FAST_BORROW         1 (s)
              RETURN_VALUE

Python does not run your text directly. First a compiler turns it into bytecode. The left column is the line number in your file. The middle column is the instruction name.

  • LOAD_FAST_BORROW puts a local variable on a stack.
  • BINARY_OP takes two values from the stack, adds them and puts the result back.
  • STORE_FAST takes the top value and saves it in a local variable.
  • JUMP_BACKWARD goes back to the start of the loop.

The bytecode lives in a code object. Every function has one, in total.__code__. When you import a module, Python saves its bytecode in a .pyc file. The next import skips the compile step.

printf 'def double(x):\n    return x * 2\n' > shop.py
python3.14 -c "import shop; print(shop.double(21))"
ls __pycache__
42
shop.cpython-314.pyc

The interpreter loop

The interpreter is a loop written in C. It does three things again and again.

  1. Read the next instruction.
  2. Jump to the C code for that instruction.
  3. Run that code, then go back to step 1.

Each step has a small cost. A loop over one million items runs millions of instructions. That is the main reason why pure Python loops are slow. Rust compiles the same loop to a few machine instructions.

Python 3.14 added a new way to build this loop. In the tail-call interpreter, every instruction is a small C function. The notes say it is 3 to 5 percent faster with Clang 19 or newer. The Python 3.14.3 on this laptop was built this way.

A .pyc file does not make your program run faster. It only makes the import faster. Also, bytecode is an inside detail of CPython. Instruction names change in every version, so never build a tool that depends on them.

Reference counting and the garbage collector

Every Python object has a counter. It counts how many names and containers point to it. Look at the count go up and down. Rust does the same thing, but only for values you put in an Rc.

use std::rc::Rc;

fn main() {
    let data = Rc::new(vec![1, 2, 3]);
    println!("{}", Rc::strong_count(&data)); // one owner
    let alias = Rc::clone(&data); // a second owner, same vector
    println!("{}", Rc::strong_count(&data));
    drop(alias); // remove the second owner
    println!("{}", Rc::strong_count(&data));
} // count reaches 0 here: the vector is freed
import sys

data = [1, 2, 3]
print(sys.getrefcount(data))   # the call itself adds one reference
alias = data                   # a second name for the same list
print(sys.getrefcount(data))
box = {"k": data}              # the dict holds one more reference
print(sys.getrefcount(data))
del alias, box                 # remove two references
print(sys.getrefcount(data))
1
2
1
2
3
4
2

This is reference counting. When the count reaches zero, Python frees the object at once. Most objects die this way, quickly and in a known order. Python shows one extra reference, because the argument of getrefcount is a reference too.

Some objects never change their count. None, True and small integers are immortal since Python 3.12. This saves work and helps threads.

Cycles need a second helper

import gc

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.other = None
    def __del__(self):
        print("free", self.name)

gc.collect()               # start clean
a = Node("a")
del a                      # count drops to 0: freed at once
print("after del a")

b, c = Node("b"), Node("c")
b.other, c.other = c, b    # a cycle: b -> c -> b
del b, c                   # each count is still 1: nothing is freed
print("after del b, c")
print("found:", gc.collect())   # the cycle finder frees them
free a
after del a
after del b, c
free b
free c
found: 2

Two objects that point to each other form a reference cycle. Their counts never reach zero. So CPython has a garbage collector too. It looks for groups of objects that only point to each other.

  • The collector uses generations. Most objects die young, so young objects are checked most often.
  • A collection of the youngest group starts after about 2000 new objects. gc.get_threshold() shows the numbers.
  • gc.collect() runs a full collection. It returns how many objects it found.
  • The weakref module makes a reference that does not count. It breaks cycles, like Weak in Rust.
python3.14 -c "import gc; print(gc.get_threshold())"
(2000, 10, 0)

Here is a true story for experts. Python 3.14.0 shipped a new incremental collector. It made pauses much shorter. But many users saw high memory use in production. So 3.14.5 went back to the 3.13 collector. On 3.14.0 to 3.14.4 the third number above is ignored. The chapter Python versions tells the whole story.

Do not put cleanup work in __del__. You do not know when it runs. An object in a cycle waits for the collector, and some objects live until the program ends. Close files and connections with with instead.

The specialising interpreter and the JIT

Run a function many times with whole numbers. Then look at its bytecode again, with adaptive=True.

import dis

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

for _ in range(1000):
    add(1, 2)              # warm up with int values

dis.dis(add, adaptive=True)
  3           RESUME_CHECK             0

  4           LOAD_FAST_BORROW_LOAD_FAST_BORROW 1 (a, b)
              BINARY_OP_ADD_INT        0 (+)
              RETURN_VALUE

The general BINARY_OP became BINARY_OP_ADD_INT. Python saw only integers here. So it switched to a fast version for integers. Warm up with floats, and you get BINARY_OP_ADD_FLOAT.

This is the specialising interpreter from PEP 659. It came in Python 3.11 and gave the big speed-up of that version. Each fast instruction starts with a guard. If the guard fails, Python goes back to the general instruction. Later it may choose a new fast version.

for _ in range(1000):
    add(1, 2)                 # ints: Python picks the int version
for _ in range(1000):
    add("ab", "cd")           # now strings: the guess is wrong

dis.dis(add, adaptive=True)
              BINARY_OP_ADD_UNICODE    0 (+)

Hot code that always sees the same types stays fast. A function that gets ints, then strings, then floats keeps changing its mind. Keep the types in a hot loop the same.

The JIT

A JIT compiler goes one step further. It finds hot loops. It turns the loop into small steps called micro-ops. Then it glues ready-made pieces of machine code together. This method is called copy-and-patch (PEP 744). LLVM is needed to build a CPython with a JIT, but not to run it.

PYTHON_JIT=1 python3.14 adaptive4.py | grep JUMP
              JUMP_BACKWARD_JIT       13 (to L1)

Without PYTHON_JIT=1 the same line says JUMP_BACKWARD_NO_JIT. The backward jump counts how often a loop runs. When the loop is hot, the JIT starts.

The table times a prime counter, hot.py. Its code is in the last section of this chapter. Later sections time the same job.

The prime-count loop of this chapter, best of 5 (one laptop run, a busy machine)
PythonJIT offJIT on
3.14.30.400 s0.538 s
3.15.0b20.362 s0.206 s

On 3.14 the JIT made this loop slower. On the 3.15 beta it made it almost twice as fast. This fits the official notes. They say the 3.14 JIT is from 10 percent slower to 20 percent faster. The 3.15 JIT is much better, but still experimental.

Do not turn on the JIT in production because a blog says "faster". Measure your own program on your own Python. The JIT also uses more memory. In 3.14 and 3.15 it is an experiment.

Measure first: timeit, cProfile and py-spy

Guessing is the most common way to waste a day. Measure first. Start with timeit. It runs a small piece of code many times.

python3.14 -m timeit -s "items = list(range(10_000))" "9_999 in items"
python3.14 -m timeit -s "items = set(range(10_000))" "9_999 in items"
5000 loops, best of 5: 58 usec per loop
20000000 loops, best of 5: 16.6 nsec per loop

The -s code runs once, as setup. It is not timed. Searching a list checks every item. Searching a set uses a hash, so it is about 3500 times faster here. timeit reports the best run, because other programs only make runs slower.

cProfile: which function is slow?

A profiler watches a whole program. cProfile is in the standard library. Here is a report script with a hidden problem.

import random

def load(n):
    rng = random.Random(42)
    return [f"user{rng.randrange(n)}@example.com" for _ in range(n)]

def unique(emails):
    seen = []                    # a list: "in" checks every item
    for e in emails:
        if e not in seen:
            seen.append(e)
    return seen

def domains(emails):
    return {e.split("@")[1] for e in emails}

def main():
    emails = load(20_000)
    print(len(unique(emails)), len(domains(emails)))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
python3.14 -m cProfile -s cumulative report.py
12591 1
         146123 function calls (146100 primitive calls) in 1.098 seconds

   Ordered by: cumulative time

   ncalls  tottime  percall  cumtime  percall filename:lineno(function)
      3/1    0.000    0.000    1.098    1.098 {built-in method builtins.exec}
        1    0.000    0.000    1.098    1.098 report.py:1(<module>)
        1    0.000    0.000    1.093    1.093 report.py:17(main)
        1    1.068    1.068    1.070    1.070 report.py:7(unique)
        1    0.004    0.004    0.019    0.019 report.py:3(load)
  • ncalls is how many times the function ran.
  • tottime is the time inside the function itself, without the functions it calls.
  • cumtime also counts the functions it calls.

unique takes 1.068 of 1.098 seconds. Change one line: return list(dict.fromkeys(emails)). A dict keeps the first order and uses hashing. The whole program then took 0.026 seconds, about 40 times faster.

py-spy: look inside a running program

cProfile records every call. That is a tracing profiler. It slows code with many small calls. py-spy is a sampling profiler. It reads the program from outside, about 100 times a second. So it adds almost no cost, and it can attach to a live server.

uv run --with py-spy py-spy record -o profile.svg -- python3.14 report.py
uv run --with py-spy py-spy top --pid 12345      # a live view, like top
uv run --with py-spy py-spy dump --pid 12345     # the stack of every thread, now
This program requires root on OSX.
Try running again with elevated permissions by going 'sudo !!'

On macOS py-spy always needs sudo, so the flame graph was not made here. On Linux, record -- python3.14 ... works without root. Attaching to another process with --pid usually needs root. In Docker, add the capability SYS_PTRACE.

record writes a flame graph. Each box is a function. A wide box means much time. Useful flags are --rate, --subprocesses and --native for C and Rust code.

Python 3.15 adds a profiling package. profiling.sampling is a built-in sampling profiler, and profiling.tracing is the old cProfile. See Python versions.

You time one run with time.time() on a busy laptop. Then you believe a 5 percent gain. Use time.perf_counter(), run the code several times and keep the best. For serious work, use the pyperf package.

Faster data structures

The fastest fix is often a better container. Look at two common jobs: a queue and building a long text.

import timeit
from collections import deque

N = 10_000

def queue_list():
    q = list(range(N))
    while q:
        q.pop(0)              # moves every other item one step left

def queue_deque():
    q = deque(range(N))
    while q:
        q.popleft()           # takes the first item in one step

def text_plus():
    s = ""
    for i in range(N):
        s = s + str(i) + ","  # may copy the text again and again
    return s

def text_join():
    return ",".join(str(i) for i in range(N)) + ","

for f in (queue_list, queue_deque, text_plus, text_join):
    best = min(timeit.repeat(f, number=10, repeat=5)) / 10
    print(f"{f.__name__:12} {best * 1000:7.3f} ms")
queue_list     5.261 ms
queue_deque    0.234 ms
text_plus      9.350 ms
text_join      0.601 ms

Speed depends on how the work grows with the size n. We write this with big-O. O(1) means the same work for any size. O(n) means work grows with the size.

Cost of common operations (average case)
JobSlow choiceFast choice
Is x in the group?x in list: O(n)x in set: O(1)
Take from the frontlist.pop(0): O(n)deque.popleft(): O(1)
Remove duplicates, keep orderloop with a list: O(n^2)dict.fromkeys(xs): O(n)
Count thingsxs.count(x) for each xcollections.Counter(xs)
Always get the smallestmin(xs) again and againheapq: O(\log n) per item
Find in a sorted listloop over all itemsbisect: O(\log n)
Build a long texts = s + part in a loop"".join(parts)

Memory matters too. A list of floats holds a pointer to a separate float object for each number. A typed array holds the raw 8-byte numbers side by side.

list of floats   32.4 MB
array('d')        8.2 MB
numpy float64     8.0 MB

For many small objects of one class, __slots__ also saves memory. The chapter The Python data model shows it.

In a quick test, s += part took 1.02 ms, but s = s + part + "," took 9.9 ms. CPython has a hidden trick for some += forms. Other forms and other Pythons do not get it. Do not depend on the trick. Use "".join().

Vectorising with NumPy

Here is one job done three ways: count random points inside a circle. This gives an estimate of pi.

import numpy as np
# xs and ys are lists of 1_000_000 random floats; ax and ay are the same as arrays

def loop_python():
    inside = 0
    for x, y in zip(xs, ys):
        if x * x + y * y <= 1.0:
            inside += 1
    return inside

def loop_numpy_items():
    inside = 0
    for i in range(N):                  # a Python loop over numpy items
        if ax[i] * ax[i] + ay[i] * ay[i] <= 1.0:
            inside += 1
    return inside

def vectorised():
    return int(np.count_nonzero(ax * ax + ay * ay <= 1.0))  # one call
uv run --with numpy python3.14 vec.py
loop_python       785634  best     40.4 ms
loop_numpy_items  785634  best    298.0 ms
vectorised        785634  best      1.1 ms
pi is about 3.142536

To vectorise means to give NumPy the whole array at once. The loop then runs in C, over numbers that sit side by side in memory. Here it was about 37 times faster than the Python loop.

  • An array has one dtype. All items have the same type and size.
  • ax * ax makes a new array. <= 1.0 makes an array of True and False.
  • Broadcasting lets arrays of different shapes work together.
import numpy as np

prices = np.array([[10.0, 20.0, 30.0],     # 2 shops x 3 products
                   [12.0, 18.0, 33.0]])
tax = np.array([1.10, 1.08, 1.10])         # one rate per product
print(prices * tax)                         # tax is stretched over each row
print(prices.mean(axis=0))                  # average per product (down each column)
[[11.   21.6  33.  ]
 [13.2  19.44 36.3 ]]
[11.  19.  31.5]

A Python loop over NumPy items is the worst choice. It was 7 times slower than plain lists above. Each ax[i] makes a new NumPy scalar object. Give NumPy whole arrays, or stay with plain Python.

A second trap: NumPy integers have a fixed size. They wrap around without an error.

import numpy as np

big = np.array([3_000_000_000, 4_000_000_000])   # int64
print((big * big).tolist())                         # wraps around, no error
print([int(v) * int(v) for v in big])               # Python int: exact
[9000000000000000000, -2446744073709551616]
[9000000000000000000, 16000000000000000000]

The GIL and the free-threaded build

Four threads add 1 to the same counter, one million times each. The right answer is 4,000,000. Run it on the normal build and on the free-threaded build.

import sys
import threading

count = 0

def work():
    global count
    for _ in range(1_000_000):
        count += 1          # read, add, write: three steps, not one

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print("GIL enabled:", sys._is_gil_enabled(), "count:", count)
python3.14 race.py
python3.14t race.py
GIL enabled: True count: 4000000
GIL enabled: False count: 1096667

The free-threaded build lost almost three million updates. Three runs gave 1,096,667, then 1,247,098, then 945,656. This is a race condition. Two threads read the same old value, and both write back old value plus one.

The normal build has the GIL. Only one thread runs bytecode at a time. A thread lets go of the GIL every 5 ms, or when it waits for the disk or the network. So here the GIL hid the bug. It does not make your code safe. Fix it with a lock, and share less.

lock = threading.Lock()

def work():
    global count
    local = 0
    for _ in range(1_000_000):
        local += 1          # private to this thread: no sharing
    with lock:              # one short locked step at the end
        count += local
GIL enabled: True count: 4000000
GIL enabled: False count: 4000000

Why the free-threaded build matters

The free-threaded build came as an experiment in 3.13 (PEP 703). Since 3.14 it is officially supported (PEP 779), but it is still a separate program, python3.14t. Threads can now use many CPU cores for pure Python work.

The prime-count job split over 4 threads, best of 3 (one laptop run)
Build1 thread4 threads
3.14.3 normal (GIL)0.400 s0.403 s
3.14.3 free-threaded0.418 s0.158 s
  • Check the build: sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED") is 1, and python3.14t -VV says "free-threading build".
  • Check the running state: sys._is_gil_enabled().
  • An old C extension can turn the GIL back on when you import it. Python prints a warning. PYTHON_GIL=0 or -X gil=0 forces it off.
  • One thread runs a bit slower. What's New in 3.14 says 5 to 10 percent. The free-threading guide says from about 1 percent on macOS arm to 8 percent on x86-64 Linux.
  • In 3.14 the free-threaded build has no JIT. You choose one or the other.
  • Built-in list, dict and set have small inside locks. Your own code still needs locks, as the race shows.

"The GIL makes my code thread-safe." No. It protects CPython's own data, not your logic. count += 1 is several bytecode steps. The race was only hidden. On 3.14t it appears at once.

Multiprocessing

The other way past the GIL is more processes. Each process has its own interpreter and its own GIL.

import sys
import time
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, ThreadPoolExecutor

from hot import count_primes   # the prime counter from the last section of this chapter

def run(pool_class, workers=4, hi=300_000, parts=16):
    step = hi // parts                      # 16 small parts keep 4 workers busy
    los = [i * step for i in range(parts)]
    his = [lo + step for lo in los]
    start = time.perf_counter()
    with pool_class(max_workers=workers) as pool:
        total = sum(pool.map(count_primes, los, his))
    return total, time.perf_counter() - start

if __name__ == "__main__":                  # needed: workers import this file
    print("GIL enabled:", sys._is_gil_enabled())
    for pool_class in (ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor):
        total, _ = run(pool_class)
        best = min(run(pool_class)[1] for _ in range(3))
        print(f"{pool_class.__name__:20} {total} primes, best {best:.3f} s")
GIL enabled: True
ThreadPoolExecutor   25997 primes, best 0.403 s
ProcessPoolExecutor  25997 primes, best 0.167 s
  • Arguments and results travel between processes as bytes. Python uses pickle for this. Big data costs time to send.
  • Starting a process takes time. Give each worker a big piece of work.
  • The start method is spawn on macOS and Windows. Since 3.14, Linux uses forkserver by default, not fork.
  • The last part of the range has the most work. Many small parts let free workers take the next part.

Two errors come up again and again. Without the __main__ guard, each new worker runs the pool code again:

RuntimeError:
        An attempt has been made to start a new process before the
        current process has finished its bootstrapping phase.

And a lambda cannot travel to another process, because pickle cannot find it by name:

_pickle.PicklingError: Can't pickle <function <lambda> at 0x10101ba00>: it's not found as __main__.<lambda>

Use a normal def function at the top level of a module. Put pool code under if __name__ == "__main__":. For threads that wait on the network, and for subinterpreters, see Threads and shared state.

When to move a hot loop to Rust

Here is the same prime counter in both languages. Rust comes first.

fn is_prime(n: u64) -> bool {
    if n < 2 {
        return false;
    }
    let mut d = 2;
    while d * d <= n {
        if n % d == 0 {
            return false;
        }
        d += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn count_primes(lo: u64, hi: u64) -> usize {
    (lo..hi).filter(|&n| is_prime(n)).count()
}
// main() times count_primes(0, 300_000), best of 5
def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2:
        return False
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return False
        d += 1
    return True

def count_primes(lo, hi):
    return sum(1 for n in range(lo, hi) if is_prime(n))

# __main__ times count_primes(0, 300_000), best of 5
25997 primes, best 0.010 s
25997 primes, best 0.400 s

A hot loop with branches and small numbers is the best case for Rust. Here Rust was about 40 times faster. The chart puts all the results of this chapter side by side.

Do not jump to Rust first. Climb the ladder one step at a time, and measure after each step.

Measure

Find the hot spot with cProfile or py-spy. Often it is not where you guessed.

Fix the algorithm

A set instead of a list made report.py 40 times faster. This costs nothing.

Use a library

NumPy, the standard library and collections already run in C.

Use more cores

Processes, or threads on the free-threaded build. The gain is at most the number of free cores.

Move the loop to Rust

Write the whole hot loop in Rust with PyO3. Call it once with a lot of data.

Rust pays off when one call does a lot of work. Good examples are parsers, text scanning, graph searches and simulations. Each call across the border has a cost. Converting a Python list into a Rust Vec also has a cost. So move the whole loop, not one small function. The chapter Rust and Python together builds such a module with PyO3 and maturin.

You rewrite a function in Rust before you profile. The program is not faster, because the time went to a database call. Or you move a tiny function that runs a million times. Now the border cost is bigger than the work. Profile first, then move a big piece.

Interviews ask: "How do you make Python code faster?" A strong answer has an order. Measure, fix the algorithm, use C-backed libraries, use processes or free threads, and only then write an extension in Rust or C.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for fast Python
PatternPurposeModelNote
dis.dis(f, adaptive=True)See bytecode and its fast versionsdis.dis(add, adaptive=True)Names change in every version.
python -m timeit -s SETUP CODETime a small piece of code-s "s = set(r)" "5 in s"Setup is not timed.
python -m cProfile -s cumulative app.pyFind the slow function-s tottime for own timeIt slows code with many calls.
py-spy record -o out.svg -- python app.pyFlame graph with almost no costpy-spy dump --pid 123Needs sudo on macOS.
x in setFast membership testif email in seen:A list checks every item.
list(dict.fromkeys(xs))Remove duplicates, keep orderlist(dict.fromkeys(emails))set(xs) loses the order.
deque.popleft()A fast queueq = deque(); q.popleft()list.pop(0) is O(n).
"".join(parts)Build a long text",".join(names)Do not depend on the += trick.
np.op(whole_array)Vectorise a numeric loopnp.count_nonzero(a * a <= 1)Never loop over NumPy items.
with lock:Protect shared data in threadswith lock: count += localThe GIL does not protect your logic.
ProcessPoolExecutor().map(f, xs)Use many cores for CPU workpool.map(count_primes, los, his)Needs a __main__ guard and no lambdas.
PYTHON_JIT=1 python3.14 app.pyTry the experimental JITsys._jit.is_enabled()Measure: it can be slower.

Practice

What does Python save in a .pyc file?

  • Machine code for your CPU
  • The bytecode of a module
  • The values of your variables

A .pyc file holds compiled bytecode. It skips the compile step on the next import. It does not make the code run faster.

When does CPython free a list that no name or container points to, and that is not in a cycle?

  • At once, when its reference count reaches zero
  • At the next garbage collection
  • When the program ends

Reference counting frees most objects at once. The garbage collector is only needed for cycles.

Four threads run pure Python CPU work on the normal 3.14 build. What do you expect?

  • About four times faster than one thread
  • About the same time as one thread
  • A crash

The GIL lets one thread run bytecode at a time. The test above gave 0.400 s and 0.403 s.

sys.getrefcount(x) shows one more than you expect, because its ? is also a reference.

After warm-up with whole numbers, a + b becomes the instruction ?.

On macOS and Windows the default start method of multiprocessing is ?.

  1. In a cProfile report, a function has tottime 0.01 s and cumtime 3.2 s. Where is the time going?
    Answer

    Almost all the time is in functions it calls. Look at the functions below it in the call chain. The function itself is cheap.

  2. Your code checks if user_id in banned: for one million users. banned is a list of 50,000 ids. Make it fast.
    Answer

    Turn it into a set once: banned = set(banned). Each check is then O(1) on average instead of up to 50,000 comparisons.

  3. A teammate writes for i in range(len(a)): out[i] = a[i] * 2 with NumPy arrays. Why is it slow, and what is the fix?
    Answer

    It is a Python loop, and each a[i] makes a NumPy scalar object. Write out = a * 2. The loop then runs in C over the whole array.

  4. A counter shared by threads is right on Python 3.14 but wrong on 3.14t. Explain, and give two fixes.
    Answer

    count += 1 is a read, an add and a write. Without the GIL, threads mix these steps and lose updates. Fix 1: protect the update with a threading.Lock. Fix 2: count in a local variable in each thread and add the results once at the end.

  5. A service on Python 3.14.2 used much less memory after an upgrade to 3.14.6. Give a likely reason.
    Answer

    3.14.0 to 3.14.4 used a new incremental garbage collector. Some programs kept much more garbage in memory with it. 3.14.5 went back to the 3.13 collector.

  6. You must speed up a log parser. It reads lines and matches many small rules in a Python loop. NumPy does not fit. Plan the work in order.
    Answer

    First profile it to find the hot part. Then check the algorithm, for example compile regular expressions once and use sets for lookups. Next try processes over chunks of the file. If the parse loop is still the hot spot, move the whole loop into Rust with PyO3. Pass a big batch of lines in one call, not one line per call.

Key takeaways

  • CPython compiles your code to bytecode. A loop in C reads and runs one instruction at a time.
  • Reference counting frees most objects at once. The garbage collector frees cycles. 3.14.5 went back to the 3.13 collector.
  • The specialising interpreter (3.11) makes hot code fast for the types it sees. The JIT is still experimental in 3.14 and 3.15.
  • The GIL lets one thread run bytecode at a time. The free-threaded build removes it, and then races appear.
  • Measure first with timeit, cProfile and py-spy. Then fix the algorithm, use NumPy, use processes, and move a big hot loop to Rust last.

Sources

  • What's New in Python 3.14. Free-threading, the JIT in the installers, the tail-call interpreter, the garbage collector revert and the new start method.
  • Python support for free threading. How to check the build, the GIL switches and the single-thread cost.
  • dis: disassembler for Python bytecode. Instructions, the adaptive view and the warning that bytecode changes.
  • PEP 744: JIT compilation. Copy-and-patch, micro-op traces and the rules for leaving the experiment.
  • py-spy on GitHub. The sampling profiler: record, top, dump, flags and permissions.
  • NumPy: broadcasting. How arrays of different shapes work together.

Packaging and testing

A script works on your laptop. A package works on every laptop, and its tests prove it. In this chapter you build one small package from an empty folder. You add tests, checks and a CI pipeline, and you build a file that anyone can install.

  • Set up a project with the src layout and a clear pyproject.toml.
  • Use uv for environments, dependencies, lock files and tools.
  • Write pytest tests with fixtures, parametrize and mocks.
  • Check code with ruff and mypy, locally and in CI.
  • Build a wheel and publish it safely with trusted publishing.

Project layout

We build a tool called wordtally. It finds the most common words in a text. Start with one command.

uv init --lib --vcs none --author-from none --python 3.14 wordtally
cd wordtally
Initialized project `wordtally` at `/home/you/wordtally`
  • --lib makes a library. It adds a py.typed file, which tells type checkers that the package has type hints.
  • --vcs none skips git init. Without it, uv also starts a git repository.
  • --author-from none keeps your name and email out of the file.

After all the steps of this chapter, the project looks like this.

The code lives in src/wordtally/. This is the src layout. The other choice is the flat layout. Since uv 0.12, a plain uv init also makes the src layout. Why is it better? Look at this test.

python3.14 -c "import wordtally"
uv run python -c "import wordtally; print(wordtally.__file__)"
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'wordtally'
/home/you/wordtally/src/wordtally/__init__.py

Plain Python cannot see the package from the project folder. Only the project's virtual environment can. There, uv installed the package in editable mode. So your tests always use the installed package, the same way your users will.

With a flat layout, Python can import the package straight from the current folder. Tests pass on your laptop. But a file may be missing from the built package, and users get an ImportError. The src layout finds this problem early.

pyproject.toml, table by table

This is the final pyproject.toml of the project. The chapter Cargo, crates and workspaces compares it with Cargo.toml. Here we go deeper.

[project]
name = "wordtally"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Count the most common words in a text."
readme = "README.md"
license = "MIT"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = [
    "httpx>=0.28",
]

[project.scripts]
wordtally = "wordtally.cli:main"     # the command calls main()

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.13.8,<0.14.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "mypy>=2.4.1",
    "pytest>=9.2.0",
    "ruff>=0.17.5",
]

[tool.pytest]
testpaths = ["tests"]
strict = true

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 88

[tool.mypy]
strict = true
files = ["src"]
What each table does
TableWho reads itWhat it says
[project]every tool, PyPIName, version, description and what users need to install.
[project.scripts]the installerCommands to create. wordtally runs wordtally.cli:main.
[build-system]uv, pip, buildWhich build backend makes the package.
[dependency-groups]uv, pip 25.1 and newerTools for developers only. Users never get them.
[tool.NAME]that one toolSettings for pytest, ruff, mypy and others.
  • license = "MIT" is an SPDX expression (PEP 639). The old table form license = {text = "MIT"} is deprecated.
  • requires-python = ">=3.11" is the oldest Python you support. uv uses it when it locks.
  • "httpx>=0.28" is a version specifier. A library gives a lower limit and stays open above.
  • [project.optional-dependencies] holds extras. Users install them with wordtally[web]. Dependency groups are never published.

A library writes dependencies = ["httpx==0.28.1"]. Now every app that uses it must use exactly 0.28.1, and the installer finds conflicts. Pin exact versions in the lock file, not in a library's dependencies. Also keep pytest and ruff out of dependencies. They belong in the dev group.

uv: environments, dependencies, lock files and tools

Add the one real dependency, then the developer tools.

uv add 'httpx>=0.28'
uv add --dev pytest ruff mypy
Using CPython 3.14.3
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Resolved 8 packages in 195ms

      Built wordtally @ file:///home/you/wordtally
Prepared 1 package in 25ms
Installed 8 packages in 11ms

One command did four jobs. It wrote the dependency into pyproject.toml. It made .venv. It resolved the versions and wrote them to uv.lock. Then it installed them. uv tree shows the result.

wordtally v0.1.0
├── httpx v0.28.1
│   ├── anyio v4.16.0
│   │   ├── idna v3.20
│   │   └── typing-extensions v4.16.0
│   ├── certifi v2026.10.23
│   ├── httpcore v1.0.9

│   │   └── h11 v0.16.0

└── ruff v0.17.5 (group: dev)

The lock file

A lock file makes installs the same everywhere. Here is the entry for httpx in uv.lock.

[[package]]
name = "httpx"
version = "0.28.1"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
dependencies = [
    { name = "anyio" },
    { name = "certifi" },
    { name = "httpcore" },
    { name = "idna" },
]
wheels = [
    { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/.../httpx-0.28.1-py3-none-any.whl", hash = "sha256:d909...", size = 73517 },
]
  • Every file has a hash. A changed or fake file fails the install.
  • The lock is universal. One uv.lock works for Linux, macOS and Windows, and for Python 3.11 to 3.15.
  • Commit uv.lock to git. uv writes it. Never edit it by hand.
  • Other tools cannot read uv.lock. uv export --format pylock.toml writes the standard lock format of PEP 751.

What if someone changes pyproject.toml and forgets the lock? Here a line "rich>=14" was added by hand.

uv sync --locked
Resolved 23 packages in 129ms
error: The lockfile at `uv.lock` needs to be updated, but `--locked` was provided.

hint: To update the lockfile, run `uv lock`.

This is exactly what CI should do. It stops a build with an old lock file.

uv commands for every day
CommandWhat it does
uv syncMakes .venv match the lock file exactly.
uv run CMDSyncs if needed, then runs the command in .venv.
uv lock --upgrade-package httpxMoves one package to its newest allowed version.
uv remove httpxRemoves a dependency from the file, the lock and .venv.
uv python pin 3.14Writes the Python version for this project into .python-version.
uv run --python 3.12 pytestRuns once with another Python version.

Tools outside the project

Some tools do not belong to any project. uv runs them in a temporary environment.

uv tool run ruff@0.17.5 --version     # the same as: uvx ruff@0.17.5 --version
uv run --with numpy python3.14 -c "import numpy; print(numpy.__version__)"
ruff 0.17.5
2.5.4

uvx runs a command-line tool. uv run --with adds a package for one run. uv tool install ruff installs a tool for your user account for good.

You run pip install rich inside .venv. It works today. But rich is not in pyproject.toml or uv.lock, and the next uv sync removes it. Always use uv add.

Tests with pytest

Here is the code we test, in src/wordtally/__init__.py.

"""Count the words in a text."""

import re
from collections import Counter

WORD = re.compile(r"[a-z']+")


def words(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Split text into lower-case words."""
    return WORD.findall(text.lower())


def top_words(text: str, n: int = 3) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
    """Return the n most common words, most common first."""
    if n < 1:
        raise ValueError("n must be at least 1")
    return Counter(words(text)).most_common(n)

Now the same two tests in both languages. Rust comes first. The Rust file also holds Rust versions of words and top_words. Only its tests are shown.

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn words_are_lower_case() {
        assert_eq!(words("The cat. THE dog!"), ["the", "cat", "the", "dog"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn top_words_counts() {
        let want = vec![("b".to_string(), 3), ("a".to_string(), 2)];
        assert_eq!(top_words("b a b c b a", 2), want);
    }
}
from wordtally import top_words, words


def test_words_are_lower_case():
    assert words("The cat. THE dog!") == ["the", "cat", "the", "dog"]


def test_top_words_counts():
    assert top_words("b a b c b a", n=2) == [("b", 3), ("a", 2)]
running 2 tests
test tests::words_are_lower_case ... ok
test tests::top_words_counts ... ok

test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.00s
============================= test session starts ==============================
platform darwin -- Python 3.14.3, pytest-9.2.0, pluggy-1.7.0
rootdir: /home/you/wordtally
configfile: pyproject.toml
plugins: anyio-4.16.0
collected 2 items

tests/test_words.py ..                                                   [100%]

============================== 2 passed in 0.01s ===============================

pytest finds tests by name. It looks for files called test_*.py and functions called test_*. A test is a plain function with a plain assert. There is no class and no special method.

The real power shows when a test fails. Here a test expects "world-wide" to stay one word.

    def test_hyphen_word():
>       assert words("A world-wide web") == ["a", "world-wide", "web"]
E       AssertionError: assert ['a', 'world', 'wide', 'web'] == ['a', 'world-wide', 'web']
E
E         At index 1 diff: 'world' != 'world-wide'
E         Left contains one more item: 'web'
E         Use -v to get more diff

pytest rewrites each assert before it runs. So it can show both sides and the first difference. Now you decide: is the code wrong, or the test?

pytest 9 reads settings from a [tool.pytest] table with real TOML types. The older [tool.pytest.ini_options] still works, but you cannot use both. strict = true turns on several checks, for example an error for a misspelled marker.

You name a file words_test.py or a function check_words(). pytest does not collect it and says nothing. The tests never run. Always start file and function names with test_.

Fixtures and parametrize

Many tests need the same thing, for example a text file. A fixture makes it. Put shared fixtures in tests/conftest.py. pytest finds them by name.

import pytest


@pytest.fixture
def sample_file(tmp_path):
    """A small text file in a fresh temporary folder."""
    path = tmp_path / "poem.txt"
    path.write_text("the sun and the moon and the sea", encoding="utf-8")
    return path
import sys

import pytest

from wordtally.cli import main


def test_cli_prints_top_words(sample_file, monkeypatch, capsys):
    monkeypatch.setattr(sys, "argv", ["wordtally", str(sample_file)])
    main()
    out = capsys.readouterr().out  # what main() printed
    assert out.splitlines() == ["   3 the", "   2 and", "   1 sun"]


def test_cli_needs_one_file(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(sys, "argv", ["wordtally"])
    with pytest.raises(SystemExit, match="usage"):
        main()

The test asks for fixtures by naming them as parameters. Four are used here.

  • sample_file is ours. It uses another fixture, tmp_path.
  • tmp_path is built in. Each test gets a new empty folder.
  • monkeypatch changes a value for one test, here sys.argv. It puts the old value back after the test.
  • capsys catches what the code prints.

A fixture can also clean up. Write yield instead of return. The code after yield runs after the test, even when the test fails.

@pytest.fixture
def db():
    conn = {"open": True, "rows": []}
    print("\nsetup: open")
    yield conn                      # the test runs here
    conn["open"] = False            # teardown: runs even if the test fails
    print("teardown: closed")


def test_insert(db):
    db["rows"].append("sun")
    print("test: rows =", db["rows"])
    assert db["open"]
setup: open
test: rows = ['sun']
.teardown: closed

1 passed in 0.00s

By default a fixture runs again for every test. @pytest.fixture(scope="session") makes it once for the whole run. Use that for slow things, like a database server.

One test, many inputs

Parametrize runs one test with a table of inputs. Each row becomes its own test.

import pytest

from wordtally import top_words, words


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    ("text", "expected"),
    [
        ("The cat. THE dog!", ["the", "cat", "the", "dog"]),
        ("don't stop", ["don't", "stop"]),
        ("", []),
        ("2026 is a year", ["is", "a", "year"]),
    ],
    ids=["mixed-case", "apostrophe", "empty", "digits"],
)
def test_words(text, expected):
    assert words(text) == expected


def test_top_words_counts():
    assert top_words("b a b c b a", n=2) == [("b", 3), ("a", 2)]


def test_top_words_rejects_zero():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="at least 1"):
        top_words("a b", n=0)
tests/test_cli.py::test_cli_prints_top_words PASSED                      [ 12%]
tests/test_cli.py::test_cli_needs_one_file PASSED                        [ 25%]
tests/test_words.py::test_words[mixed-case] PASSED                       [ 37%]
tests/test_words.py::test_words[apostrophe] PASSED                       [ 50%]
tests/test_words.py::test_words[empty] PASSED                            [ 62%]
tests/test_words.py::test_words[digits] PASSED                           [ 75%]
tests/test_words.py::test_top_words_counts PASSED                        [ 87%]
tests/test_words.py::test_top_words_rejects_zero PASSED                  [100%]

The ids give each case a readable name. You can run one case: uv run pytest "tests/test_words.py::test_words[empty]". pytest.raises checks that an error happens. match checks its message with a regular expression.

You put a loop inside one test: for text, want in cases: assert .... The first failure stops the loop, so you never see the other cases. With parametrize, each case passes or fails on its own.

Mocking

A test must not call the real internet. It is slow, and it fails when the network is down. Here is the code that fetches a page.

"""Count the words of a web page."""

import httpx

from wordtally import top_words


def top_words_at(url: str, n: int = 3) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
    response = httpx.get(url, timeout=10)
    response.raise_for_status()  # an HTTP error becomes an exception
    return top_words(response.text, n)

We replace httpx.get with a fake during the test. This is called mocking. There are two common ways.

from unittest.mock import Mock, patch

import httpx

from wordtally import web


class FakeResponse:
    text = "red green red blue red green"

    def raise_for_status(self):
        pass  # pretend the status was 200


def test_top_words_at_with_monkeypatch(monkeypatch):
    def fake_get(url, timeout):
        return FakeResponse()

    monkeypatch.setattr(httpx, "get", fake_get)  # no network in tests
    assert web.top_words_at("https://example.com", n=1) == [("red", 3)]


def test_top_words_at_with_mock():
    response = Mock(text="a b a")  # a Mock accepts any call
    with patch("wordtally.web.httpx.get", return_value=response) as get:
        assert web.top_words_at("https://example.com") == [("a", 2), ("b", 1)]
    get.assert_called_once_with("https://example.com", timeout=10)
    response.raise_for_status.assert_called_once()
  • monkeypatch with a small fake class. It is simple and clear. The fake has only what the code needs.
  • unittest.mock.patch with a Mock. A Mock remembers every call. So you can check how the code used it, with assert_called_once_with.

The hardest rule of mocking: patch the name where it is used. Look at this module. It copies the name get into itself.

from httpx import get          # copies the name get into this module


def page_length(url: str) -> int:
    return len(get(url, timeout=2).text)

# ---- test_fetch.py ----
from unittest.mock import Mock, patch

import fetch


def test_wrong_target():
    with patch("httpx.get", return_value=Mock(text="abc")):   # wrong place
        assert fetch.page_length("https://wordtally.invalid") == 3


def test_right_target():
    with patch("fetch.get", return_value=Mock(text="abc")):   # where it is used
        assert fetch.page_length("https://wordtally.invalid") == 3
FAILED test_fetch.py::test_wrong_target - httpx.ConnectError: [Errno 8] noden...
1 failed, 1 passed in 0.19s

The wrong test called the real network. patch("httpx.get") changed the name inside httpx. But fetch still had its own copy. The .invalid address made the mistake fail fast.

A plain Mock accepts any call, even a wrong one. Your test can pass while the real function would fail. Use patch(..., autospec=True). Then the mock checks the arguments against the real function. And mock only the border of your code: the network, the clock, the disk.

ruff and type checking

Tests check behaviour. A linter and a type checker find other bugs. The chapter Testing and tooling shows their Rust twins, clippy and rustfmt. Here is a messy new module.

import os
from typing import List


def add_word(word: str, seen: List[str] = []) -> List[str]:
    seen.append(word)
    return seen


def load(path: str) -> str:
    try:
        return open(path).read()
    except:
        return ""
uv run ruff check --output-format concise src/wordtally/messy.py
src/wordtally/messy.py:1:8: F401 [*] `os` imported but unused
src/wordtally/messy.py:2:1: UP035 `typing.List` is deprecated, use `list` instead
src/wordtally/messy.py:5:31: UP006 [*] Use `list` instead of `List` for type annotation
src/wordtally/messy.py:5:43: B006 Do not use mutable data structures for argument defaults
src/wordtally/messy.py:5:50: UP006 [*] Use `list` instead of `List` for type annotation
src/wordtally/messy.py:13:5: E722 Do not use bare `except`
Found 6 errors.
[*] 3 fixable with `--fix` (1 unsafe fix available with `--fix --unsafe-fixes`).

ruff check --fix fixed four problems. Two stayed, because a human must decide: the shared list default (B006) and the bare except (E722). Ruff 0.16.0, from July 2026, raised the default rule set from 59 to 413 rules. So pin the ruff version in your dev group, or a new release can fail your CI.

ruff format is the formatter. In CI, ruff format --check changes nothing. It only shows what it would change:

unformatted: File would be reformatted
  --> src/wordtally/web.py:10:34
   |
9  |     response = httpx.get(url, timeout=10)
   -     response.raise_for_status()          # an HTTP error becomes an exception
10 +     response.raise_for_status()  # an HTTP error becomes an exception
11 |     return top_words(response.text, n)
   |

mypy finds what ruff cannot

from wordtally import top_words


def first_word(text: str, n: str) -> str:
    return top_words(text, n)[0]          # two bugs here


def count_words(text):                    # no type hints at all
    return len(text.split())
src/wordtally/extra.py:5: error: Incompatible return value type (got "tuple[str, int]", expected "str")  [return-value]
src/wordtally/extra.py:5: error: Argument 2 to "top_words" has incompatible type "str"; expected "int"  [arg-type]
src/wordtally/extra.py:8: error: Function is missing a type annotation  [no-untyped-def]
Found 3 errors in 1 file (checked 4 source files)

ruff check said "All checks passed!" for this file. Ruff looks at patterns. mypy follows the types through calls. You need both. With strict = true, every function needs type hints. That is a good rule for new code. Other type checkers are pyright and ty. ty comes from the ruff team. It was still a beta (0.0.104) in November 2026.

You add # type: ignore or # noqa to make the red go away. Now a real bug hides there. Fix the code. If you must ignore, name the exact rule, like # noqa: E722, and write why.

A user does not want your source folder. They want a wheel. First choose the version, then build.

# wordtally

Count the most common words in a text file or a web page.

There are no tests in the wheel. They stay in your repository. Now install the wheel in a fresh environment, outside the project, and use the command.

printf 'the sun and the moon and the sea\n' > poem.txt

Publishing

not run here Publishing needs a PyPI account, so these steps were not run for this book. They follow the uv guide. Practise on TestPyPI first. Add this index to pyproject.toml:

[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "testpypi"
url = "https://test.pypi.org/simple/"
publish-url = "https://test.pypi.org/legacy/"
explicit = true      # only packages that ask for this index use it
uv publish --index testpypi        # asks for a TestPyPI token
uv publish                         # the real PyPI

A token on your laptop can leak. Trusted publishing is safer. On PyPI you name your GitHub repository, the workflow file and an environment. PyPI then accepts uploads only from that workflow. It gets a short-lived token through OpenID Connect.

name: release
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]

jobs:
  pypi:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: pypi
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write       # PyPI checks this identity: no token is stored
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.3
      - run: uv build --no-sources
      - run: uv publish

uv publish finds the trusted identity by itself. The uv guide goes one step further. It builds in one job and publishes in a second job. Then only the small publish job holds the id-token permission.

You fix a typo and upload the same version again. PyPI refuses it. A file name can be used only once, even after you delete the release. Bump the version with uv version --bump patch for every upload. Never paste a PyPI token into code or a workflow file.

CI and the whole project, from empty folder to tested package

CI runs your checks on every push. Here is the workflow for GitHub Actions. not run here The YAML was checked with a parser, and the same commands ran on this laptop.

name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.3
        with:
          enable-cache: true
      - run: uv sync --locked          # fail if uv.lock is out of date
      - run: uv run ruff check
      - run: uv run ruff format --check
      - run: uv run mypy

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.11", "3.12", "3.13", "3.14", "3.15"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.3
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
          enable-cache: true
      - run: uv sync --locked
      - run: uv run pytest
  • The lint job runs once. The test job runs once per Python version in the matrix.
  • python-version tells uv which Python to use. It wins over .python-version.
  • The actions are pinned to full versions. The setup-uv README pins a commit hash, which is even safer.

The same steps on this laptop:

Here is the whole road again. Swipe through it.

Create

uv init --lib wordtally makes the src layout and pyproject.toml.

Add dependencies

uv add httpx for users. uv add --dev pytest ruff mypy for you.

Write the code

Small functions with type hints in src/wordtally/. A command in [project.scripts].

Write tests

Fixtures in conftest.py, parametrize for many inputs, mocks for the network.

Check

ruff check, ruff format --check and mypy until all are clean.

Automate

A CI workflow with uv sync --locked and a Python matrix.

Build and try

uv build, then install the wheel in a fresh environment and run it.

Release

Bump the version, push a tag, and let trusted publishing upload it.

Interviews ask: "How do you make a Python build reproducible?" Name three things. A lock file with hashes, committed to git. uv sync --locked in CI. And pinned versions of the tools and the CI actions.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for packaging and testing
PatternPurposeModelNote
uv init --lib NAMEStart a package with the src layoutuv init --lib wordtallyPlain uv init adds a command.
uv add PKG / uv add --dev PKGAdd a user or developer dependencyuv add --dev pytestNever pip install into .venv.
uv sync --lockedInstall exactly the lock filefirst step in CIFails if the lock is old.
uv lock --upgrade-package PKGUpgrade one dependencyuv lock --upgrade-package httpxCommit the new uv.lock.
uvx TOOL@VERSIONRun a tool without installing ituvx ruff@0.17.5 checkPin the version for repeatable runs.
@pytest.fixture + yieldSet up and clean upyield connCode after yield is the teardown.
@pytest.mark.parametrizeOne test, many inputsparametrize(("text", "expected"), [...])Add ids for readable names.
pytest.raises(E, match=...)Check that an error happenspytest.raises(ValueError, match="at least")match is a regular expression.
monkeypatch.setattr(obj, name, fake)Replace a value for one testmonkeypatch.setattr(httpx, "get", fake_get)It restores the value after the test.
patch("module.name")Mock with call checkspatch("wordtally.web.httpx.get")Patch where the name is used.
ruff check --fix / ruff formatLint and formatuv run ruff format --check in CIPin ruff: default rules change.
[tool.mypy] strict = trueStrict type checksuv run mypyRuff does not check types.
uv build --no-sources + uv publishBuild and upload a releasetrusted publishing in CIEach version can be uploaded once.

Practice

Where should pytest go in a library's pyproject.toml?

  • [project] dependencies
  • [dependency-groups] dev
  • [build-system] requires

Users of the library do not need pytest. Dependency groups are for developers and are never published.

CI fails with "The lockfile at uv.lock needs to be updated, but --locked was provided". What happened?

  • PyPI is down.
  • Someone changed pyproject.toml but did not run uv lock.
  • The tests failed.

--locked refuses to change the lock file. Run uv lock locally and commit the new uv.lock.

app.py has from time import sleep and calls sleep(5). Which target makes the test fast?

  • patch("time.sleep")
  • patch("app.sleep")
  • Both work the same way

Patch the name where the code looks it up. The import copied the name sleep into app. Patching time.sleep does not change that copy.

pytest collects files whose names start with ?.

The fixture that gives each test a fresh empty folder is called ?.

In a fixture, the code after ? runs as teardown.

  1. Write a parametrized test for top_words with these cases: "a a b" with n=1 gives [("a", 2)], and "x y" with n=5 gives [("x", 1), ("y", 1)].
    Answer

    @pytest.mark.parametrize(("text", "n", "expected"), [("a a b", 1, [("a", 2)]), ("x y", 5, [("x", 1), ("y", 1)])]), then def test_top(text, n, expected): assert top_words(text, n) == expected. A larger n than the number of words is fine. most_common returns all of them.

  2. A teammate's tests pass on their laptop, but the published package fails with ModuleNotFoundError: wordtally.web. The project uses a flat layout. What is a likely cause, and how does the src layout help?
    Answer

    Python imported the package from the current folder, so tests did not use the built package. The file was missing from the wheel. With the src layout, tests can only import the installed package, so a missing file fails at once. Also test the built wheel in a fresh environment.

  3. Why does the CI workflow use uv sync --locked and not plain uv sync?
    Answer

    Plain uv sync may update the lock file when pyproject.toml changed. Then CI tests versions nobody reviewed. --locked fails instead, so the lock file in git is always the one that was tested.

  4. Ruff passes, but mypy reports Argument 2 to "top_words" has incompatible type "str". Why did ruff not see it?
    Answer

    Ruff checks patterns in each file. It does not follow types through function calls. mypy reads the hints of top_words and sees that the call passes a str where an int is needed.

  5. Your release workflow uploads with a token saved as a GitHub secret. Suggest a safer setup and list the steps.
    Answer

    Use trusted publishing. On PyPI, add a trusted publisher with your repository, the workflow file name and an environment. In the workflow, give the publish job permissions: id-token: write and run uv publish without a token. Then delete the old token on PyPI.

  6. A test for top_words_at uses a plain Mock, and it passes. Later someone renames the parameter timeout of the real function they call. The test still passes, but production breaks. What would catch this?
    Answer

    Use patch(..., autospec=True). The mock then has the same signature as the real function. A call with wrong arguments fails in the test. A small integration test against a local test server also helps.

Key takeaways

  • Use the src layout. Tests then use the installed package, like your users do.
  • pyproject.toml holds the project, the build backend, the dev groups and the tool settings. Libraries give lower limits, not exact pins.
  • uv manages .venv, uv.lock and tools. Commit the lock and use uv sync --locked in CI.
  • pytest gives plain asserts with clear diffs, fixtures for setup, parametrize for many inputs and monkeypatch or mock for borders.
  • Ruff finds patterns and formats code. mypy finds type bugs. Pin both versions.
  • Build with uv build, test the wheel in a fresh environment, and publish with trusted publishing.

Sources

  • uv: Building and publishing a package. Version bumps, uv build, uv publish, TestPyPI and trusted publishing.
  • uv: Using uv in GitHub Actions. setup-uv, Python matrix, caching and uv sync --locked.
  • PyPA: Writing your pyproject.toml. The tables, license expressions, scripts and dependency groups.
  • pytest: How to use fixtures. Fixtures, conftest.py, yield teardown and scopes.
  • unittest.mock: Where to patch. Why you patch the name where it is looked up.
  • Ruff documentation. The linter and formatter, its rules and settings.

Algorithms 1: arrays, strings, hashing, searching, sorting

An interview problem is often small. But a slow answer and a fast answer can differ by hours of computer time. This chapter is hands-on practice. For each technique you solve one real problem, in Rust and in Python, and you measure the cost.

  • Estimate the cost of code with big-O and check it with a doubling test.
  • Solve array and string problems with hash maps, two pointers and sliding windows.
  • Use a stack, a queue and binary search, including binary search on the answer.
  • Sort with a custom order in both languages and avoid the common sort bugs.
  • Build a linked list in Rust with Option<Box<Node>> and explain why it is hard.

The Computer Science book teaches the theory behind this chapter. Its chapters "Discrete maths for computer science", "Data structures" and "Sorting, searching, divide and conquer" have the definitions and the proofs. Here we practise. We write code, run it and look at the numbers.

Big-O in simple words

Here is a simple question. Does a list of numbers have a repeat? There are two ways to answer it. Way one compares every pair. Way two remembers each number in a set. Let us time both, and double the size each time.

use std::collections::HashSet;
use std::hint::black_box;
use std::time::Instant;

// Way one: compare every pair.
fn has_repeat_pairs(v: &[u64]) -> bool {
    for i in 0..v.len() {
        for j in i + 1..v.len() {
            if v[i] == v[j] {
                return true;
            }
        }
    }
    false
}

// Way two: remember what we saw.
fn has_repeat_set(v: &[u64]) -> bool {
    let mut seen = HashSet::new();
    v.iter().any(|x| !seen.insert(x)) // insert is false for a repeat
}

fn main() {
    for n in [1_000u64, 2_000, 4_000, 8_000] {
        // all different numbers: the worst case, no early stop
        let v: Vec<u64> = (0..n).map(|i| i * 7919 % 1_000_003).collect();
        let t = Instant::now();
        let a = has_repeat_pairs(black_box(&v));
        let pairs = t.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1e3;
        let t = Instant::now();
        let b = has_repeat_set(black_box(&v));
        let set = t.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1e3;
        println!("n={n:>5}  pairs {pairs:8.3} ms   set {set:6.3} ms   {a} {b}");
    }
}
import time

def has_repeat_pairs(v):
    for i in range(len(v)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(v)):
            if v[i] == v[j]:
                return True
    return False

def has_repeat_set(v):
    seen = set()
    for x in v:
        if x in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(x)
    return False

for n in [1_000, 2_000, 4_000, 8_000]:
    v = [i * 7919 % 1_000_003 for i in range(n)]
    t = time.perf_counter()
    a = has_repeat_pairs(v)
    pairs = (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1e3
    t = time.perf_counter()
    b = has_repeat_set(v)
    set_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1e3
    print(f"n={n:>5}  pairs {pairs:8.3f} ms   set {set_ms:6.3f} ms   {a} {b}")
n= 1000  pairs    0.164 ms   set  0.048 ms   false false
n= 2000  pairs    0.693 ms   set  0.088 ms   false false
n= 4000  pairs    2.734 ms   set  0.138 ms   false false
n= 8000  pairs   10.157 ms   set  0.272 ms   false false

Python printed this on the same machine:

n= 1000  pairs    8.389 ms   set  0.040 ms   False False
n= 2000  pairs   40.010 ms   set  0.083 ms   False False
n= 4000  pairs  158.273 ms   set  0.323 ms   False False
n= 8000  pairs  656.026 ms   set  0.272 ms   False False

Look at the pairs column. When n doubles, the time grows about four times. Look at the set column. When n doubles, the time only doubles. This is a doubling test. It is the fastest way to check a cost on a real machine. Very small times are noisy, like the Python set column. Trust the big numbers more.

We describe this growth with big-O notation. The pairs way does about \frac{n(n-1)}{2} comparisons. We drop the constant and the small term. We say it is O(n^2). The set way does one step per number. It is O(n).

The costs you meet most often
Big-ONameTypical codeSteps for n = 1,000,000
O(1)constantread v[i], a hash lookup1
O(\log n)logarithmicbinary searchabout 20
O(n)linearone loop over the data1,000,000
O(n \log n)n log na good sortabout 20,000,000
O(n^2)quadratica loop inside a loop1,000,000,000,000
O(2^n)exponentialtry every subsettoo many to finish

How to read the cost of code

  • One loop over n items is O(n).
  • A loop inside a loop multiplies: O(n \cdot m).
  • Two loops one after the other add: O(n + m). Keep the bigger one.
  • A loop that halves the range each time is O(\log n).
  • Big-O usually means the worst case. Way one stops early if it finds a repeat. We still call it O(n^2).

Memory has a cost too. We call it space complexity. The set way uses O(n) extra memory. The pairs way uses O(1). Fast code often buys speed with memory.

One line can hide a loop. x in my_list, v.contains(&x), v.remove(0) and s.chars().nth(i) are all O(n). Put one of them inside a loop and your code becomes O(n^2). Read every library call and ask: does this walk the whole collection?

Arrays, strings and hash maps

The first problem is the most famous interview question. You get a list of numbers and a target. Find two positions whose numbers add up to the target.

Input [2, 7, 11, 15] and target 9. Answer: positions 0 and 1, because 2 + 7 = 9. Each position can be used only once.

The slow answer tries every pair: O(n^2). The fast answer walks once. For each number x it asks a hash map: did I already see target - x?

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn two_sum(nums: &[i32], target: i32) -> Option<(usize, usize)> {
    let mut seen: HashMap<i32, usize> = HashMap::new(); // value -> position
    for (i, &x) in nums.iter().enumerate() {
        // Ask first, then insert. So x never pairs with itself.
        if let Some(&j) = seen.get(&(target - x)) {
            return Some((j, i));
        }
        seen.insert(x, i);
    }
    None
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", two_sum(&[2, 7, 11, 15], 9));
    println!("{:?}", two_sum(&[3, 2, 4], 6));
    println!("{:?}", two_sum(&[3, 3], 6));
    println!("{:?}", two_sum(&[1, 2], 7));
}
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}  # value -> position
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        j = seen.get(target - x)
        if j is not None:  # not "if j:", because j can be 0
            return (j, i)
        seen[x] = i
    return None

print(two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9))
print(two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6))
print(two_sum([3, 3], 6))
print(two_sum([1, 2], 7))
Some((0, 1))
Some((1, 2))
Some((0, 1))
None

Python prints (0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 1) and None. The time is O(n). The extra memory is O(n) for the map.

Insert first and ask second, and [3, 2, 4] with target 6 gives (0, 0). The 3 found itself. In Python, if j: is also a bug. Position 0 is "false", so the pair at position 0 is lost.

Strings: bytes or characters?

The next problem: are two words anagrams? "listen" and "silent" are. Count the letters of both words and compare the counts.

use std::collections::HashMap;

// Fast path: only the letters a to z. One array of 26 counters.
fn is_anagram_ascii(a: &str, b: &str) -> bool {
    if a.len() != b.len() {
        return false;
    }
    let mut count = [0i32; 26];
    for (x, y) in a.bytes().zip(b.bytes()) {
        count[(x - b'a') as usize] += 1; // b'a' is the byte 97
        count[(y - b'a') as usize] -= 1;
    }
    count.iter().all(|&c| c == 0)
}

// General path: any Unicode text. Count chars in a map.
fn is_anagram(a: &str, b: &str) -> bool {
    let mut count: HashMap<char, i32> = HashMap::new();
    for c in a.chars() {
        *count.entry(c).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }
    for c in b.chars() {
        *count.entry(c).or_insert(0) -= 1;
    }
    count.values().all(|&n| n == 0)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", is_anagram_ascii("listen", "silent"));
    println!("{}", is_anagram_ascii("rat", "car"));
    println!("{}", is_anagram("über", "rübe")); // ü needs the char version
    println!("{} {}", "über".len(), "über".chars().count()); // bytes, chars
}
from collections import Counter

def is_anagram(a, b):
    return Counter(a) == Counter(b)  # counts every character

print(is_anagram("listen", "silent"))
print(is_anagram("rat", "car"))
print(is_anagram("über", "rübe"))
print(len("über".encode()), len("über"))  # bytes, characters
true
false
true
5 4

Python prints True, False, True and 5 4. A Rust &str is UTF-8 bytes. The letter ü takes 2 bytes. So len() counts bytes, not characters. Python's len counts characters. The chapter Strings and text explains this in depth.

In Rust, s[i] on a string does not compile. Many people then write s.chars().nth(i) inside a loop. That walks the string from the start each time: O(n^2). Convert once instead: let cs: Vec<char> = s.chars().collect(); or use s.as_bytes() for plain ASCII text.

Prefix sums: many range totals fast

A shop has sales for each day. People ask many questions like "total sales from day 2 to day 5". A prefix sum answers each question in O(1).

fn main() {
    let sales = [5, 3, 8, 6, 2, 7];
    // pre[i] = total of the first i days. pre has one extra item.
    let mut pre = vec![0; sales.len() + 1];
    for i in 0..sales.len() {
        pre[i + 1] = pre[i] + sales[i];
    }
    println!("{pre:?}");
    // Total of days lo..hi (hi not included) is pre[hi] - pre[lo].
    let (lo, hi) = (2, 5);
    println!("days 2 to 4: {}", pre[hi] - pre[lo]);
}
from itertools import accumulate

sales = [5, 3, 8, 6, 2, 7]
pre = [0, *accumulate(sales)]  # [0, 5, 8, ...]
print(pre)
lo, hi = 2, 5
print("days 2 to 4:", pre[hi] - pre[lo])
[0, 5, 8, 16, 22, 24, 31]
days 2 to 4: 16

The build costs O(n) once. Then each question costs O(1): 8 + 6 + 2 = 16. Python prints the same.

Two pointers

Here is two sum again, with one change: the list is sorted. Now we need no hash map at all. Put one pointer at each end.

fn pair_sum_sorted(a: &[i32], target: i32) -> Option<(usize, usize)> {
    if a.is_empty() {
        return None; // a.len() - 1 would underflow below
    }
    let (mut lo, mut hi) = (0, a.len() - 1);
    while lo < hi {
        let sum = a[lo] + a[hi];
        if sum == target {
            return Some((lo, hi));
        } else if sum < target {
            lo += 1; // need a bigger sum
        } else {
            hi -= 1; // need a smaller sum
        }
    }
    None
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", pair_sum_sorted(&[1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11], 10));
    println!("{:?}", pair_sum_sorted(&[1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11], 13));
    println!("{:?}", pair_sum_sorted(&[1, 2], 9));
    println!("{:?}", pair_sum_sorted(&[], 9));
}
def pair_sum_sorted(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1  # hi is -1 for an empty list: the loop skips
    while lo < hi:
        s = a[lo] + a[hi]
        if s == target:
            return (lo, hi)
        if s < target:
            lo += 1
        else:
            hi -= 1
    return None

print(pair_sum_sorted([1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11], 10))
print(pair_sum_sorted([1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11], 13))
print(pair_sum_sorted([1, 2], 9))
print(pair_sum_sorted([], 9))
Some((2, 3))
None
None
None

Each step moves one pointer, so there are at most n steps: O(n) time and O(1) extra memory. Why is it safe to drop the right number when the sum is too big? The left number is the smallest one left. If even the smallest partner is too big for a[hi], no partner works. So a[hi] can never be in the answer.

The second kind: read and write pointers

Both pointers can also move in the same direction. One pointer reads every item. The other marks where the next kept item goes. Here we remove repeats from a sorted list in place.

// Keep one copy of each value. Return the new length.
fn dedup_sorted(v: &mut Vec<i32>) -> usize {
    if v.is_empty() {
        return 0;
    }
    let mut write = 1; // v[..write] holds the kept values
    for read in 1..v.len() {
        if v[read] != v[write - 1] {
            v[write] = v[read];
            write += 1;
        }
    }
    v.truncate(write);
    write
}

fn main() {
    let mut v = vec![1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 7];
    let n = dedup_sorted(&mut v);
    println!("{n} {v:?}");
    let mut w = vec![1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 7];
    w.dedup(); // the standard library does the same
    println!("{w:?}");
}
def dedup_sorted(v):
    if not v:
        return 0
    write = 1
    for read in range(1, len(v)):
        if v[read] != v[write - 1]:
            v[write] = v[read]
            write += 1
    del v[write:]
    return write

v = [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 7]
n = dedup_sorted(v)
print(n, v)
4 [1, 2, 3, 7]
[1, 2, 3, 7]
