Python prints 4 [1, 2, 3, 7]. Rust's Vec::dedup uses the same idea inside.

In Rust, a.len() - 1 on an empty slice does not give -1. The type is usize, which has no negative values. A debug build panics with "attempt to subtract with overflow". Check for an empty input first.

Sliding window

Find the length of the longest part of a string with no repeated character. In "pwwkew" the answer is 3, for "wke". The part must be one piece. Such a piece is called a substring.

A sliding window keeps a start and an end. The end moves right one step at a time. When the window breaks the rule, the start jumps right until the rule holds again.

Read p

Window "p". No repeat. Best length 1.

Read w

Window "pw". No repeat. Best length 2.

Read the second w

We saw w at position 1, inside the window. The start jumps to position 2. Window "w". Best stays 2.

Read k

Window "wk". Best stays 2.

Read e

Window "wke". Best length 3.

Read the last w

We saw w at position 2, inside the window. The start jumps to 3. Window "kew". Best stays 3.

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn longest_unique(s: &str) -> usize {
    let mut last: HashMap<char, usize> = HashMap::new(); // char -> last position
    let (mut start, mut best) = (0, 0);
    for (i, c) in s.chars().enumerate() {
        if let Some(&j) = last.get(&c) {
            if j >= start {
                start = j + 1; // jump past the old copy
            }
        }
        last.insert(c, i);
        best = best.max(i + 1 - start);
    }
    best
}

fn main() {
    for s in ["pwwkew", "abcabcbb", "bbbbb", "", "abba", "día día"] {
        println!("{s:?} -> {}", longest_unique(s));
    }
}
def longest_unique(s):
    last = {}  # char -> last position
    start = best = 0
    for i, c in enumerate(s):
        if last.get(c, -1) >= start:
            start = last[c] + 1
        last[c] = i
        best = max(best, i + 1 - start)
    return best

for s in ["pwwkew", "abcabcbb", "bbbbb", "", "abba", "día día"]:
    print(f'"{s}" -> {longest_unique(s)}')
"pwwkew" -> 3
"abcabcbb" -> 3
"bbbbb" -> 1
"" -> 0
"abba" -> 2
"día día" -> 4

Python prints the same lines. Each character enters the window once and the start only moves forward. So the work is O(n), not O(n^2).

Drop the test j >= start and "abba" gives 3, which is wrong. At the last "a", the old "a" is at position 0. That is outside the window already. Without the test, the start jumps back from 2 to 1. A window start must never move left.

A fixed-size window

Some windows have a fixed size. "What is the best total of 3 days in a row?" Add the new day and subtract the day that leaves.

fn best_k_sum(v: &[i64], k: usize) -> Option<i64> {
    if k == 0 || k > v.len() {
        return None;
    }
    let mut sum: i64 = v[..k].iter().sum();
    let mut best = sum;
    for i in k..v.len() {
        sum += v[i] - v[i - k]; // one day in, one day out
        best = best.max(sum);
    }
    Some(best)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", best_k_sum(&[5, 3, 8, 6, 2, 7, 9], 3));
}
def best_k_sum(v, k):
    if k == 0 or k > len(v):
        return None
    s = best = sum(v[:k])
    for i in range(k, len(v)):
        s += v[i] - v[i - k]
        best = max(best, s)
    return best

print(best_k_sum([5, 3, 8, 6, 2, 7, 9], 3))
Some(18)

Python prints 18. The best window is 2, 7, 9.

Stack and queue

A stack is a pile of plates. You add and take at the top. A queue is a line at a shop. You join at the back and leave at the front. In Rust a Vec is a good stack and a VecDeque is a good queue. In Python, use a list as a stack and collections.deque as a queue.

Problem: balanced brackets

Is "{[()]}" balanced? Each closing bracket must match the last open bracket that is still open. "The last one still open" is exactly the top of a stack.

fn balanced(s: &str) -> bool {
    let mut stack: Vec<char> = Vec::new();
    for c in s.chars() {
        match c {
            '(' | '[' | '{' => stack.push(c),
            ')' | ']' | '}' => {
                let want = match c {
                    ')' => '(',
                    ']' => '[',
                    _ => '{',
                };
                if stack.pop() != Some(want) {
                    return false; // wrong bracket, or nothing open
                }
            }
            _ => {} // ignore other characters
        }
    }
    stack.is_empty() // something still open means false
}

fn main() {
    for s in ["{[()]}", "(]", "((", ")(", "f(a[1]) { }"] {
        println!("{s:12} {}", balanced(s));
    }
}
PAIRS = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}

def balanced(s):
    stack = []
    for c in s:
        if c in "([{":
            stack.append(c)
        elif c in PAIRS:
            if not stack or stack.pop() != PAIRS[c]:
                return False
    return not stack

for s in ["{[()]}", "(]", "((", ")(", "f(a[1]) { }"]:
    print(f"{s:12} {str(balanced(s)).lower()}")
{[()]}       true
(]           false
((           false
)(           false
f(a[1]) { }  true

Python prints the same. Time O(n), memory O(n) for the stack.

Problem: the next warmer day (a monotonic stack)

For each day, how many days until a warmer day? Temperatures [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73] give [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]. The slow way looks ahead from each day: O(n^2). The fast way keeps a stack of days that still wait for an answer. The temperatures on that stack always go down from bottom to top. Such a stack is a monotonic stack.

fn days_until_warmer(t: &[i32]) -> Vec<usize> {
    let mut answer = vec![0; t.len()];
    let mut waiting: Vec<usize> = Vec::new(); // positions of colder days
    for (i, &temp) in t.iter().enumerate() {
        // Today answers every waiting day that is colder.
        while let Some(&j) = waiting.last() {
            if t[j] >= temp {
                break;
            }
            waiting.pop();
            answer[j] = i - j;
        }
        waiting.push(i);
    }
    answer // days still waiting keep 0
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", days_until_warmer(&[73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]));
}
def days_until_warmer(t):
    answer = [0] * len(t)
    waiting = []  # positions of colder days
    for i, temp in enumerate(t):
        while waiting and t[waiting[-1]] < temp:
            j = waiting.pop()
            answer[j] = i - j
        waiting.append(i)
    return answer

print(days_until_warmer([73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]))
[1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]

There is a while inside a for. Is it O(n^2)? No. Each day is pushed once and popped at most once. So all the pops together cost at most n. The total is O(n). This kind of counting is called amortized analysis.

Problem: requests in the last minute (a queue)

A server logs the time of each request in seconds. After each request, it asks: how many requests came in the last 60 seconds? Old times leave at the front. New times join at the back.

use std::collections::VecDeque;

struct RecentCounter {
    times: VecDeque<u64>,
}

impl RecentCounter {
    fn hit(&mut self, now: u64) -> usize {
        self.times.push_back(now);
        while let Some(&old) = self.times.front() {
            if old + 60 > now {
                break; // still inside the last 60 seconds
            }
            self.times.pop_front();
        }
        self.times.len()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut c = RecentCounter { times: VecDeque::new() };
    for t in [1, 10, 59, 60, 61, 130] {
        print!("{} ", c.hit(t));
    }
    println!();
}
from collections import deque

class RecentCounter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.times = deque()

    def hit(self, now):
        self.times.append(now)
        while self.times[0] + 60 <= now:
            self.times.popleft()
        return len(self.times)

c = RecentCounter()
print(*[c.hit(t) for t in [1, 10, 59, 60, 61, 130]])
1 2 3 4 4 1

At time 61, the hit at time 1 is 60 seconds old, so it leaves. At time 130 only the new hit is left. Python prints the same numbers.

A Python list as a queue with pop(0) moves every item: O(n) per pop. Use deque.popleft(), which is O(1). The same holds for Vec::remove(0) in Rust.

Binary search

Think of a number from 1 to 100. I guess 50. You say "higher". I guess 75. You say "lower". Each answer removes half of the numbers. After at most 7 guesses I know your number, because 2^7 = 128 \ge 100. This is binary search. It needs sorted data, or a yes/no question whose answers go "no, no, ..., yes, yes".

The safe way to write it

Most bugs come from the edges. Use one clear rule. Keep a range lo..hi with hi not included. Everything before lo is "no". Everything from hi on is "yes". Stop when the range is empty.

// First position whose value is >= target (the "lower bound").
fn lower_bound(a: &[i32], target: i32) -> usize {
    let (mut lo, mut hi) = (0, a.len()); // the answer is in lo..=hi
    while lo < hi {
        let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; // never overflows
        if a[mid] < target {
            lo = mid + 1; // mid is a "no"
        } else {
            hi = mid; // mid is a "yes"
        }
    }
    lo
}

fn main() {
    let a = [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10];
    println!("{} {} {}", lower_bound(&a, 8), lower_bound(&a, 6), lower_bound(&a, 99));
    // The standard library has it: partition_point.
    let first = a.partition_point(|&x| x < 8);
    let after = a.partition_point(|&x| x <= 8);
    println!("8 is at {first}..{after}");
    println!("{:?} {:?}", a.binary_search(&10), a.binary_search(&6));
}
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

def lower_bound(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2  # Python ints never overflow
        if a[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo

a = [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10]
print(lower_bound(a, 8), lower_bound(a, 6), lower_bound(a, 99))
print(f"8 is at {bisect_left(a, 8)}..{bisect_right(a, 8)}")
3 1 6
8 is at 3..5
Ok(5) Err(1)

Python prints the first two lines the same. partition_point in Rust and bisect_left in Python give the first "yes" position. binary_search gives Ok(position) or Err(where it would go). The value 8 sits at positions 3 and 4. So the range is 3..5.

Binary search on the answer

This is the expert move. Sometimes the list is not the thing you search. You search the answer itself.

Parcels with weights 1, 2, ..., 10 must leave in this order. A truck makes one trip per day. What is the smallest truck capacity that ships everything in 5 days?

  1. Ask a yes/no question: "Can capacity c do it in 5 days?" A bigger truck never hurts. So the answers go no, no, ..., yes, yes.
  2. The answer is at least 10, the heaviest parcel. It is at most 55, the total weight. Search in 10 to 55.
  3. Try 32: 2 days. Yes. Try 21: 3 days. Yes. Try 15: 5 days. Yes.
  4. Try 12: 6 days. No. Try 14: 6 days. No.
  5. The range is now empty. The answer is 15.
// How many days does capacity cap need? One greedy pass.
fn days_needed(w: &[u32], cap: u32) -> u32 {
    let (mut days, mut load) = (1, 0);
    for &x in w {
        if load + x > cap {
            days += 1; // start a new day
            load = 0;
        }
        load += x;
    }
    days
}

fn smallest_truck(w: &[u32], days: u32) -> u32 {
    let mut lo = *w.iter().max().unwrap(); // a parcel cannot be split
    let mut hi: u32 = w.iter().sum();      // one day for everything
    while lo < hi {
        let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        let ok = days_needed(w, mid) <= days;
        println!("try {mid:2}: {} days {}", days_needed(w, mid), if ok { "yes" } else { "no" });
        if ok { hi = mid } else { lo = mid + 1 }
    }
    lo
}

fn main() {
    let w: Vec<u32> = (1..=10).collect();
    println!("answer {}", smallest_truck(&w, 5));
}
def days_needed(w, cap):
    days, load = 1, 0
    for x in w:
        if load + x > cap:
            days += 1
            load = 0
        load += x
    return days

def smallest_truck(w, days):
    lo, hi = max(w), sum(w)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        ok = days_needed(w, mid) <= days
        print(f"try {mid:2}: {days_needed(w, mid)} days {'yes' if ok else 'no'}")
        if ok:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo

print("answer", smallest_truck(list(range(1, 11)), 5))
try 32: 2 days yes
try 21: 3 days yes
try 15: 5 days yes
try 12: 6 days no
try 14: 6 days no
answer 15

Python prints the same trace. The cost is O(n \log S), where S is the total weight. Each check is one pass over the n parcels.

In a language with fixed-size integers, (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow when both are big. Write lo + (hi - lo) / 2. A second classic bug is lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1. When hi = lo + 1, mid equals lo, and the loop never ends.

Sorting and custom order

Sorting is often the first step of a fast answer. After a sort, repeats stand together, two pointers work, and binary search works. A good sort is O(n \log n). The CS book proves that no comparison sort can do better in the worst case.

Sort by several keys

Sort people by age, youngest first. Break ties by name.

use std::cmp::Reverse;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u32,
}

fn main() {
    let mut people: Vec<Person> = [("Cy", 30), ("Ann", 25), ("Bo", 30), ("Di", 25)]
        .into_iter()
        .map(|(n, a)| Person { name: n.to_string(), age: a })
        .collect();

    // Age first, then name. then_with runs only on a tie.
    people.sort_by(|a, b| a.age.cmp(&b.age).then_with(|| a.name.cmp(&b.name)));
    let names: Vec<&str> = people.iter().map(|p| p.name.as_str()).collect();
    println!("{names:?}");

    // Oldest first. Reverse flips the order of one key.
    people.sort_by_key(|p| Reverse(p.age)); // stable: names stay sorted
    let names: Vec<&str> = people.iter().map(|p| p.name.as_str()).collect();
    println!("{names:?}");

    // Floats are not Ord, because of NaN. Use total_cmp.
    let mut xs: [f64; 4] = [2.5, -1.0, 9.75, 0.0];
    xs.sort_by(|a, b| a.total_cmp(b));
    println!("{xs:?}");
}
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Person:
    name: str
    age: int

people = [Person(n, a) for n, a in [("Cy", 30), ("Ann", 25), ("Bo", 30), ("Di", 25)]]

people.sort(key=lambda p: (p.age, p.name))  # a tuple key: age, then name
print([p.name for p in people])

people.sort(key=lambda p: p.age, reverse=True)  # still stable
print([p.name for p in people])

xs = [2.5, -1.0, 9.75, 0.0]
print(sorted(xs))
["Ann", "Di", "Bo", "Cy"]
["Bo", "Cy", "Ann", "Di"]
[-1.0, 0.0, 2.5, 9.75]

Python prints the same names, with single quotes. Both sorts are stable. In the second sort Bo and Cy are both 30. They keep the order from the first sort. Rust also has sort_unstable. It can be faster and needs no extra memory, but equal items may change places.

Problem: merge meeting times

Meetings [1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18] overlap. Merge them into [1,6], [8,10], [15,18]. Sort by start time first. Then each meeting either joins the last group or starts a new one.

fn merge(mut v: Vec<(i32, i32)>) -> Vec<(i32, i32)> {
    v.sort_unstable(); // sorts by start, then end
    let mut out: Vec<(i32, i32)> = Vec::new();
    for (s, e) in v {
        match out.last_mut() {
            Some(last) if s <= last.1 => last.1 = last.1.max(e), // overlap: grow
            _ => out.push((s, e)),                               // gap: new group
        }
    }
    out
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", merge(vec![(8, 10), (1, 3), (15, 18), (2, 6)]));
    println!("{:?}", merge(vec![(1, 4), (4, 5)])); // touching counts
    println!("{:?}", merge(vec![(1, 10), (2, 3)])); // inside another
}
def merge(v):
    out = []
    for s, e in sorted(v):
        if out and s <= out[-1][1]:
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)
        else:
            out.append([s, e])
    return out

print(merge([(8, 10), (1, 3), (15, 18), (2, 6)]))
print(merge([(1, 4), (4, 5)]))
print(merge([(1, 10), (2, 3)]))
[(1, 6), (8, 10), (15, 18)]
[(1, 5)]
[(1, 10)]

Python prints lists like [[1, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]. The sort costs O(n \log n). The loop costs O(n). Note max in the overlap case. Without it, [1,10] and [2,3] would shrink to [1,3].

A comparison you cannot write as a key

Arrange numbers to make the largest number. [3, 30, 34, 5, 9] gives "9534330". Put a before b when the text a + b is bigger than b + a. This compares two items, so it is not a key. Rust takes a compare function. Python needs functools.cmp_to_key.

fn largest(nums: &[u32]) -> String {
    let mut s: Vec<String> = nums.iter().map(|n| n.to_string()).collect();
    // b+a vs a+b: the bigger joined text goes first
    s.sort_by(|a, b| format!("{b}{a}").cmp(&format!("{a}{b}")));
    let out = s.concat();
    if out.starts_with('0') { "0".to_string() } else { out } // [0, 0] -> "0"
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", largest(&[3, 30, 34, 5, 9]));
    println!("{}", largest(&[10, 2]));
    println!("{}", largest(&[0, 0]));
}
from functools import cmp_to_key

def largest(nums):
    s = [str(n) for n in nums]
    # negative: a first. positive: b first.
    s.sort(key=cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: (b + a > a + b) - (b + a < a + b)))
    out = "".join(s)
    return "0" if out.startswith("0") else out

print(largest([3, 30, 34, 5, 9]))
print(largest([10, 2]))
print(largest([0, 0]))
9534330
210
0

Python prints the same three lines.

A compare function must be consistent. If it says a < b and b < c, it must also say a < c. Since Rust 1.81, the standard sorts may panic when they detect a broken order. Before that, they gave a strange order. Also avoid a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap() for floats. It panics on NaN. total_cmp never panics.

Rust's sort is stable and O(n \log n) in the worst case. Since Rust 1.81 both sorts use new, faster algorithms. Python's sort is Timsort. Since Python 3.11 it merges its runs in the "powersort" order, which is close to optimal. Both are fast on data that is already partly sorted.

Linked lists in Rust, and why they are hard

A linked list is a chain. Each node holds a value and a link to the next node. The last node links to nothing.

In Rust a link is Option<Box<Node>>. The Box puts the node on the heap and owns it. The Option says "maybe there is no next node". Here is the classic problem: reverse the list.

struct Node {
    val: i32,
    next: Option<Box<Node>>,
}

fn from_slice(v: &[i32]) -> Option<Box<Node>> {
    let mut head = None;
    for &x in v.iter().rev() {
        head = Some(Box::new(Node { val: x, next: head })); // add at the front
    }
    head
}

fn reverse(mut head: Option<Box<Node>>) -> Option<Box<Node>> {
    let mut prev: Option<Box<Node>> = None;
    while let Some(mut node) = head {
        head = node.next.take(); // cut the link, keep the rest of the chain
        node.next = prev;        // point this node backwards
        prev = Some(node);
    }
    prev
}

fn to_vec(mut cur: &Option<Box<Node>>) -> Vec<i32> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    while let Some(node) = cur {
        out.push(node.val);
        cur = &node.next; // walk with a shared borrow
    }
    out
}

fn main() {
    let list = from_slice(&[1, 2, 3, 4]);
    let rev = reverse(list);
    println!("{:?}", to_vec(&rev));
    println!("{:?}", to_vec(&reverse(None)));
}
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

def from_list(v):
    head = None
    for x in reversed(v):
        head = Node(x, head)
    return head

def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    while head:
        head.next, prev, head = prev, head, head.next
    return prev

def to_list(cur):
    out = []
    while cur:
        out.append(cur.val)
        cur = cur.next
    return out

print(to_list(reverse(from_list([1, 2, 3, 4]))))
print(to_list(reverse(None)))
[4, 3, 2, 1]
[]

Python prints the same. The key Rust tool is Option::take. It moves the value out and leaves None behind. You cannot just move node.next out of a node and leave a hole. Every place must always hold a valid value. take fills the hole with None.

Adding at the tail: a mutable cursor

To add at the end, walk with a &mut cursor to the last empty link. Then write into it.

struct Node {
    val: i32,
    next: Option<Box<Node>>,
}

fn push_back(head: &mut Option<Box<Node>>, val: i32) {
    let mut cur = head;
    while let Some(node) = cur {
        cur = &mut node.next; // move the cursor one link forward
    }
    *cur = Some(Box::new(Node { val, next: None })); // cur is the empty link
}

fn main() {
    let mut head = None;
    for x in [1, 2, 3] {
        push_back(&mut head, x);
    }
    let mut cur = &head;
    while let Some(node) = cur {
        print!("{} ", node.val);
        cur = &node.next;
    }
    println!();
}
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

def push_back(head, val):
    if head is None:
        return Node(val)  # a new list
    cur = head
    while cur.next:
        cur = cur.next
    cur.next = Node(val)
    return head

head = None
for x in [1, 2, 3]:
    head = push_back(head, x)
cur = head
while cur:
    print(cur.val, end=" ")
    cur = cur.next
print()
1 2 3

Python prints the same. Each push_back walks the whole list: O(n). A real queue keeps a pointer to the tail. In Python that is one more field. In safe Rust it is hard, because the tail node would then have two owners: the node before it and the tail pointer.

Why linked lists are hard in Rust

  • One owner. Each node has exactly one owner. A doubly linked list has two links into each node. You need Rc, RefCell and Weak, or unsafe code. The chapter Smart pointers builds one.
  • No holes. You cannot move a field out and leave it empty. You use take, replace or mem::swap.
  • Borrow rules. You cannot hold a &mut to a node and also read its neighbour through another path.
  • Drop. Dropping a long list drops node 1, which drops node 2, and so on. The default drop is recursive. A very long list can overflow the stack.
struct Node {
    val: i32,
    next: Option<Box<Node>>,
}

struct List {
    head: Option<Box<Node>>,
}

impl Drop for List {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        // Free the nodes one by one in a loop, not by recursion.
        let mut cur = self.head.take();
        while let Some(mut node) = cur {
            cur = node.next.take();
        } // node is freed here, and its next is already None
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut list = List { head: None };
    for i in 0..1_000_000 {
        list.head = Some(Box::new(Node { val: i, next: list.head.take() }));
    }
    println!("top value {}", list.head.as_ref().unwrap().val);
    drop(list); // safe: our loop frees the million nodes
    println!("freed");
}
top value 999999
freed

Remove the impl Drop block and run it again. On this machine the program then crashes:

top value 999999

thread 'main' (118102435) has overflowed its stack
fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting

The book "Learning Rust With Entirely Too Many Linked Lists" builds several linked lists in Rust and explains every problem on the way. Its advice is clear. Almost always, use a Vec or a VecDeque. Rust's standard LinkedList exists, but the documentation also says Vec and VecDeque are usually faster. In interviews, linked list questions are still common. Now you can answer them in both languages.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for arrays, strings, searching and sorting
PatternPurposeModelNote
Doubling testCheck the real cost of codeTime n = 1000, 2000, 4000. Four times slower each time means O(n^2).Use the worst-case input, and a release build in Rust.
Hash map of "seen" valuesTurn a pair search into one passif let Some(&j) = seen.get(&(target - x))Ask first, insert second.
Counting arrayCount letters fastlet mut count = [0; 26];Only for a small known alphabet. Use a map for Unicode.
Prefix sumAnswer many range totalspre[hi] - pre[lo]pre has one more item than the data.
Two pointers from both endsPair search in sorted dataif sum < target { lo += 1 } else { hi -= 1 }Check for an empty slice before len() - 1.
Read and write pointersFilter a list in placev[write] = v[read]; write += 1;Rust has dedup and retain for this.
Sliding windowBest substring or subarrayif j >= start { start = j + 1 }The start never moves left.
Stack for matchingBrackets, undo, nestingif stack.pop() != Some(want) { return false }Check that the stack is empty at the end.
Monotonic stackNext bigger or smaller itemwhile t[top] < temp { pop and answer }O(n): each item is pushed and popped once.
Queue of timesCount events in a time windowpush_back(now), pop old ones from the frontPython: deque, never list.pop(0).
Half-open binary searchFirst "yes" positiona.partition_point(|&x| x < t)Python: bisect_left(a, t).
Binary search on the answerSmallest value that worksif ok(mid) { hi = mid } else { lo = mid + 1 }The test must go no, no, yes, yes.
Sort by several keysOrder recordsa.age.cmp(&b.age).then_with(|| a.name.cmp(&b.name))Python: key=lambda p: (p.age, p.name).
Option::takeMove out of a linked nodehead = node.next.take();Leaves None behind, so no hole.

Practice

You double the input. The time goes from 1 second to about 2 seconds. What is the likely cost?

  • O(\log n)
  • O(n)
  • O(n^2)

Linear code takes twice the time for twice the data. O(n^2) would take about 4 seconds.

Which line hides a loop over the whole list?

  • v[i]
  • v.push(x)
  • v.contains(&x)

contains checks the items one by one: O(n). Indexing and push are O(1).

In the sliding window for "longest substring with no repeat", what must never happen?

  • The end moves right.
  • The start moves left.
  • The map gets a new key.

The window only moves forward. A start that jumps back counts old characters again. "abba" then gives 3 instead of 2.

Which Rust collection is the right queue for "requests in the last 60 seconds"?

  • Vec with remove(0)
  • VecDeque
  • BTreeMap

You add at the back and remove at the front. VecDeque does both in O(1).

In Rust, the first position with x >= 8 in a sorted slice is a.?(|&x| x < 8).

The Python twin of that call is bisect.?(a, 8).

To move a node out of node.next and leave None, call node.next.?.

  1. Write is_palindrome with two pointers. Skip characters that are not letters or digits, and ignore case. "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" is a palindrome.
    Answer 
    fn is_palindrome(s: &str) -> bool {
    let cs: Vec<char> = s
        .chars()
        .filter(|c| c.is_alphanumeric())
        .flat_map(|c| c.to_lowercase())
        .collect();
    let (mut i, mut j) = (0, cs.len());
    while i + 1 < j {
        if cs[i] != cs[j - 1] {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
        j -= 1;
    }
    true
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"));
    println!("{}", is_palindrome("race a car"));
}
    true
false

    In Python: cs = [c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum()], then return cs == cs[::-1]. The Rust version keeps j one past the end. So it never computes 0 - 1 on an empty input.

  2. Count the subarrays whose sum is exactly k. [1, 2, 3, -1, 1] with k = 3 has 3 of them. Use prefix sums and a hash map in O(n).
    Answer 
    def count_k(v, k):
    seen = {0: 1}  # prefix total -> how many times we saw it
    total = count = 0
    for x in v:
        total += x
        count += seen.get(total - k, 0)  # earlier prefixes that make k
        seen[total] = seen.get(total, 0) + 1
    return count

print(count_k([1, 2, 3, -1, 1], 3))
    3

    A subarray from i to j has sum pre[j] - pre[i]. We want pre[i] = pre[j] - k. The map counts the earlier prefixes. The three subarrays are [1, 2], [3] and [3, -1, 1]. A sliding window fails here because of the negative number.

  3. Your binary search loops forever on [1, 2]. The code says lo = mid. Explain the bug with numbers.
    Answer

    With lo = 0 and hi = 1, mid = 0. If the test says "no", we set lo = mid = 0. Nothing changed, so the loop repeats forever. Write lo = mid + 1, because mid itself is already known to be a "no".

  4. Expert. Why is for i in 0..n { s.chars().nth(i) } slow in Rust, and why is Python's s[i] fast?
    Answer

    A Rust string is UTF-8. A character takes 1 to 4 bytes. To find character i, Rust must walk from the start: O(i), so the loop is O(n^2). CPython stores each string with one fixed width per character: 1, 2 or 4 bytes for every character in that string. So it can jump straight to character i.

  5. Expert. Find the middle node of a linked list in one pass, in Python. Then say why the same idea is harder with &mut in Rust.
    Answer

    Use a slow pointer and a fast pointer. The slow one moves one node, the fast one moves two: while fast and fast.next: slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next. When the fast one reaches the end, the slow one is in the middle. In Rust, two shared borrows &Option<Box<Node>> work fine. But two &mut cursors into the same list are not allowed. To change the middle node, find its position first, then walk again with one &mut cursor.

Key takeaways

  • Big-O says how cost grows. Check it with a doubling test on real data.
  • Most "make it faster" answers use a hash map, a set or a sort.
  • Two pointers and sliding windows turn many O(n^2) searches into O(n).
  • A stack matches nested things. A queue keeps things in arrival order. Use Vec and VecDeque, or list and deque.
  • Binary search needs a no-then-yes test. Use a half-open range and lo = mid + 1.
  • In Rust a linked list is Option<Box<Node>>, moved with take. It is hard because each node has one owner. In real code, use a Vec.

Sources

  • Rust standard library: slices. sort, sort_unstable, binary_search, partition_point and dedup.
  • Announcing Rust 1.81.0. The new sort algorithms and the panic on a broken order.
  • Python: Sorting techniques. Key functions, stability and cmp_to_key.
  • Python: bisect. bisect_left, bisect_right and the key argument.
  • Learning Rust With Entirely Too Many Linked Lists. Why linked lists are hard in Rust, and when to use them.
  • CPython commit: switch to the powersort merge strategy. The change behind Python 3.11's list sort.

Algorithms 2: trees, graphs, dynamic programming

Many real problems are about links: files in folders, roads between cities, tasks that wait for other tasks. Trees and graphs model these links. Dynamic programming solves problems that repeat the same small question many times. This chapter solves one real problem per technique, in Rust and in Python.

  • Build a binary tree in Rust and Python and walk it in four orders.
  • Use a heap as a priority queue: BinaryHeap in Rust and heapq in Python.
  • Store a graph as an adjacency list and run BFS, DFS, topological sort, Dijkstra and union-find on it.
  • Write a backtracking search that cuts dead branches early.
  • Solve dynamic programming problems with a five-step recipe, and build a trie for autocomplete.

This chapter is practice. The Computer Science book has the theory. Its chapter "Graph algorithms" proves that BFS finds shortest paths and that Dijkstra is correct. "Data structures" explains heaps, tries and why union-find is almost constant time. "Dynamic programming and greedy algorithms" explains Bellman's principle. Read those for the why. Read this chapter for the how.

Binary trees and traversal

A tree starts at one top node, the root. In a binary tree each node has at most two children: left and right. A binary search tree (BST) adds a rule. Everything on the left is smaller than the node. Everything on the right is bigger.

In Rust a child link is Option<Box<Node>>, as in the linked list of Algorithms 1. A tree is a list with two links per node.

use std::collections::VecDeque;

struct Node {
    val: i32,
    left: Option<Box<Node>>,
    right: Option<Box<Node>>,
}

type Tree = Option<Box<Node>>;

// Smaller values go left, others go right.
fn insert(root: &mut Tree, val: i32) {
    match root {
        None => *root = Some(Box::new(Node { val, left: None, right: None })),
        Some(n) if val < n.val => insert(&mut n.left, val),
        Some(n) => insert(&mut n.right, val),
    }
}

// Left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree.
fn inorder(root: &Tree, out: &mut Vec<i32>) {
    if let Some(n) = root {
        inorder(&n.left, out);
        out.push(n.val);
        inorder(&n.right, out);
    }
}

fn preorder(root: &Tree, out: &mut Vec<i32>) {
    if let Some(n) = root {
        out.push(n.val); // the node first
        preorder(&n.left, out);
        preorder(&n.right, out);
    }
}
from collections import deque

class Node:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def insert(root, val):
    if root is None:
        return Node(val)
    if val < root.val:
        root.left = insert(root.left, val)
    else:
        root.right = insert(root.right, val)
    return root

def inorder(root, out):
    if root:
        inorder(root.left, out)
        out.append(root.val)
        inorder(root.right, out)

def preorder(root, out):
    if root:
        out.append(root.val)
        preorder(root.left, out)
        preorder(root.right, out)

The second half adds the depth and the level order. Level order uses a queue.

fn depth(root: &Tree) -> usize {
    match root {
        None => 0,
        Some(n) => 1 + depth(&n.left).max(depth(&n.right)),
    }
}

// Row by row, with a queue of borrowed nodes.
fn levels(root: &Tree) -> Vec<Vec<i32>> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    let mut queue: VecDeque<&Node> = root.as_deref().into_iter().collect();
    while !queue.is_empty() {
        let mut row = Vec::new();
        for _ in 0..queue.len() { // exactly the nodes of this row
            let n = queue.pop_front().unwrap();
            row.push(n.val);
            queue.extend(n.left.as_deref());
            queue.extend(n.right.as_deref());
        }
        out.push(row);
    }
    out
}

fn main() {
    let mut root: Tree = None;
    for v in [8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7, 13] {
        insert(&mut root, v);
    }
    let (mut a, mut b) = (Vec::new(), Vec::new());
    inorder(&root, &mut a);
    preorder(&root, &mut b);
    println!("inorder  {a:?}");
    println!("preorder {b:?}");
    println!("depth {}  levels {:?}", depth(&root), levels(&root));
}
def depth(root):
    if root is None:
        return 0
    return 1 + max(depth(root.left), depth(root.right))

def levels(root):
    out = []
    queue = deque([root] if root else [])
    while queue:
        row = []
        for _ in range(len(queue)):
            n = queue.popleft()
            row.append(n.val)
            queue.extend(c for c in (n.left, n.right) if c)
        out.append(row)
    return out

root = None
for v in [8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7, 13]:
    root = insert(root, v)
a, b = [], []
inorder(root, a)
preorder(root, b)
print("inorder ", a)
print("preorder", b)
print(f"depth {depth(root)}  levels {levels(root)}")
inorder  [1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14]
preorder [8, 3, 1, 6, 4, 7, 10, 14, 13]
depth 4  levels [[8], [3, 10], [1, 6, 14], [4, 7, 13]]

Python prints the same. The inorder walk of a BST gives the values sorted. That is a useful test. as_deref() turns a &Option<Box<Node>> into an Option<&Node>. A postorder walk visits both children first and the node last. You use it to free a tree or to add up sizes from the bottom.

Problem: is this really a BST?

Someone gives you a tree. Check the BST rule. The obvious test compares each node with its two children. That test is wrong.

struct Node {
    val: i32,
    left: Option<Box<Node>>,
    right: Option<Box<Node>>,
}

fn node(val: i32, left: Option<Box<Node>>, right: Option<Box<Node>>) -> Option<Box<Node>> {
    Some(Box::new(Node { val, left, right }))
}

// Wrong: looks only at direct children.
fn naive(t: &Option<Box<Node>>) -> bool {
    let Some(n) = t else { return true };
    n.left.as_ref().is_none_or(|l| l.val < n.val)
        && n.right.as_ref().is_none_or(|r| r.val > n.val)
        && naive(&n.left)
        && naive(&n.right)
}

// Right: every node must fit in the range (lo, hi) from all its ancestors.
fn valid(t: &Option<Box<Node>>, lo: Option<i32>, hi: Option<i32>) -> bool {
    let Some(n) = t else { return true };
    if lo.is_some_and(|lo| n.val <= lo) || hi.is_some_and(|hi| n.val >= hi) {
        return false;
    }
    valid(&n.left, lo, Some(n.val)) && valid(&n.right, Some(n.val), hi)
}

fn main() {
    // 5 has right child 7. 7 has left child 4. But 4 is smaller than 5!
    let t = node(5, node(3, None, None), node(7, node(4, None, None), None));
    println!("naive {}  valid {}", naive(&t), valid(&t, None, None));
}
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def naive(t):
    if t is None:
        return True
    if t.left and t.left.val >= t.val:
        return False
    if t.right and t.right.val <= t.val:
        return False
    return naive(t.left) and naive(t.right)

def valid(t, lo=None, hi=None):
    if t is None:
        return True
    if (lo is not None and t.val <= lo) or (hi is not None and t.val >= hi):
        return False
    return valid(t.left, lo, t.val) and valid(t.right, t.val, hi)

t = Node(5, Node(3), Node(7, Node(4)))
print(f"naive {naive(t)}  valid {valid(t)}")
naive true  valid false

Python prints naive True valid False. The 4 sits on the right side of 5, so it must be bigger than 5. Each step down the tree makes the allowed range smaller. The cost is O(n): one visit per node.

Insert 1, 2, 3, ... in sorted order and the BST becomes one long line. Its depth is n. Recursive code then goes n calls deep. Python stops at 1000 calls by default:

import sys

class Node:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, None, None

def insert(root, val):
    if root is None:
        return Node(val)
    if val < root.val:
        root.left = insert(root.left, val)
    else:
        root.right = insert(root.right, val)
    return root

print(sys.getrecursionlimit())
root = None
try:
    for v in range(2000):  # sorted input: the tree is a line
        root = insert(root, v)
except RecursionError as e:
    print("RecursionError:", e)
1000
RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded

Rust has no such limit, but a very deep recursion overflows the stack and the program aborts. The fixes are the same in both languages. Use a loop with your own stack, or use a balanced tree. Rust's BTreeMap is balanced. Python has no balanced tree in the standard library.

On LeetCode, a Rust tree node is Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>. That type lets many places share and change one node. It is more general, but it is harder to read. When one owner holds the whole tree, Option<Box<Node>> is enough.

Heaps and priority queues

A hospital does not treat patients in arrival order. The most urgent patient goes first. A priority queue works like that. The usual way to build one is a heap.

Rust's BinaryHeap is a max-heap. Python's heapq works on a plain list and is a min-heap. To flip the order, Rust wraps items in std::cmp::Reverse. Python stores negative numbers, or, since Python 3.14, uses the new heappush_max and heappop_max.

use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::BinaryHeap;

fn main() {
    let mut max = BinaryHeap::from([3, 9, 1, 7]);
    max.push(5);
    println!("peek {:?}", max.peek()); // the biggest, without removing it
    print!("pop order:");
    while let Some(x) = max.pop() {
        print!(" {x}");
    }
    println!();

    let mut min = BinaryHeap::new(); // Reverse makes it a min-heap
    for x in [3, 9, 1, 7] {
        min.push(Reverse(x));
    }
    let Reverse(smallest) = min.pop().unwrap();
    println!("smallest {smallest}");
}
import heapq

h = [3, 9, 1, 7]
heapq.heapify_max(h)  # Python 3.14: max-heap functions
heapq.heappush_max(h, 5)
print("peek", h[0])
print("pop order:", *[heapq.heappop_max(h) for _ in range(len(h))])

m = [3, 9, 1, 7]
heapq.heapify(m)  # the classic min-heap, in place, O(n)
print("smallest", heapq.heappop(m))
peek Some(9)
pop order: 9 7 5 3 1
smallest 1

Python prints peek 9, the same pop order and smallest 1.

Problem: the k closest points

A delivery app has many drivers. Find the 2 drivers closest to the shop at (0, 0). Sorting all of them costs O(n \log n). A heap that never holds more than k items costs O(n \log k). Keep the k best so far. When the heap grows to k + 1, throw out the worst one, which is the farthest. So we need the biggest distance on top: a max-heap.

use std::collections::BinaryHeap;

fn k_closest(points: &[(i32, i32)], k: usize) -> Vec<(i32, i32)> {
    let mut heap = BinaryHeap::new(); // max-heap of (distance squared, point)
    for &(x, y) in points {
        heap.push((x * x + y * y, (x, y))); // no sqrt needed to compare
        if heap.len() > k {
            heap.pop(); // drop the farthest point
        }
    }
    // into_sorted_vec gives the smallest distance first
    heap.into_sorted_vec().into_iter().map(|(_, p)| p).collect()
}

fn main() {
    let drivers = [(1, 3), (-2, 2), (5, 8), (0, 1), (3, 3)];
    println!("{:?}", k_closest(&drivers, 2));
}
import heapq

def k_closest(points, k):
    heap = []  # min-heap of (-distance, point): the farthest is on top
    for x, y in points:
        heapq.heappush(heap, (-(x * x + y * y), (x, y)))
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
    return [p for _, p in sorted(heap, reverse=True)]

drivers = [(1, 3), (-2, 2), (5, 8), (0, 1), (3, 3)]
print(k_closest(drivers, 2))
print(heapq.nsmallest(2, drivers, key=lambda p: p[0] ** 2 + p[1] ** 2))
[(0, 1), (-2, 2)]

Python prints [(0, 1), (-2, 2)] twice. heapq.nsmallest does the same job in one call. Compare squared distances. The square root is slow and gives floats, and it does not change the order.

Iterating over a heap does not give sorted order. for x in &heap in Rust and for x in h in Python walk the inner array as it is. Only pop, into_sorted_vec or sorted(h) give sorted order.

Graphs: adjacency lists, BFS and DFS

A graph has nodes and edges. A road map is a graph: cities are nodes and roads are edges. The usual way to store a graph in code is an adjacency list: for each node, the list of its neighbours. It uses O(V + E) memory for V nodes and E edges.

BFS visits the start, then all nodes 1 step away, then 2 steps, and so on. It uses a queue. In a graph without weights, BFS finds the shortest path, counted in edges.

use std::collections::VecDeque;

fn build(n: usize, edges: &[(usize, usize)]) -> Vec<Vec<usize>> {
    let mut adj = vec![Vec::new(); n];
    for &(a, b) in edges {
        adj[a].push(b); // no direction: add both ways
        adj[b].push(a);
    }
    adj
}

// Returns the distance and the parent of every node.
fn bfs(adj: &[Vec<usize>], start: usize) -> (Vec<Option<usize>>, Vec<Option<usize>>) {
    let mut dist = vec![None; adj.len()];
    let mut parent = vec![None; adj.len()];
    let mut queue = VecDeque::from([start]);
    dist[start] = Some(0);
    while let Some(u) = queue.pop_front() {
        for &v in &adj[u] {
            if dist[v].is_none() { // mark when we add, not when we pop
                dist[v] = Some(dist[u].unwrap() + 1);
                parent[v] = Some(u);
                queue.push_back(v);
            }
        }
    }
    (dist, parent)
}

fn main() {
    let adj = build(7, &[(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3), (3, 4), (5, 6)]);
    let (dist, parent) = bfs(&adj, 0);
    println!("{dist:?}");
    let mut path = vec![4]; // walk the parents back from 4
    while let Some(p) = parent[*path.last().unwrap()] {
        path.push(p);
    }
    path.reverse();
    println!("path {path:?}");
}
from collections import deque

def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]  # not [[]] * n: that shares one list
    for a, b in edges:
        adj[a].append(b)
        adj[b].append(a)
    return adj

def bfs(adj, start):
    dist = [None] * len(adj)
    parent = [None] * len(adj)
    dist[start] = 0
    queue = deque([start])
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        for v in adj[u]:
            if dist[v] is None:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
                parent[v] = u
                queue.append(v)
    return dist, parent

adj = build(7, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3), (3, 4), (5, 6)])
dist, parent = bfs(adj, 0)
print(dist)
path = [4]
while parent[path[-1]] is not None:
    path.append(parent[path[-1]])
print("path", path[::-1])
[Some(0), Some(1), Some(1), Some(2), Some(3), None, None]
path [0, 1, 3, 4]

Python prints [0, 1, 1, 2, 3, None, None] and the same path. Nodes 5 and 6 have no distance: they cannot be reached. BFS costs O(V + E). Each node enters the queue once, and each edge is looked at twice.

Mark a node as seen when you add it to the queue, not when you take it out. Otherwise the same node can enter the queue many times. In a dense graph the queue then grows huge. In Python, [[]] * n makes n names for one single list. Use a comprehension.

Problem: count the islands (DFS)

DFS goes deep first. It follows one path to its end, then comes back and tries the next. It uses a stack: the call stack in a recursive version, or your own Vec. Here is a map: 1 is land and 0 is water. How many islands are there? Land cells touch up, down, left or right.

fn islands(map: &[&str]) -> usize {
    let mut g: Vec<Vec<u8>> = map.iter().map(|r| r.bytes().collect()).collect();
    let (h, w) = (g.len(), g[0].len());
    let mut count = 0;
    for r in 0..h {
        for c in 0..w {
            if g[r][c] != b'1' {
                continue;
            }
            count += 1; // a new island: sink all of it
            let mut stack = vec![(r, c)];
            g[r][c] = b'0';
            while let Some((y, x)) = stack.pop() {
                let near = [(y.wrapping_sub(1), x), (y + 1, x), (y, x.wrapping_sub(1)), (y, x + 1)];
                for (ny, nx) in near {
                    // wrapping_sub turns -1 into a huge number, so < h fails
                    if ny < h && nx < w && g[ny][nx] == b'1' {
                        g[ny][nx] = b'0';
                        stack.push((ny, nx));
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    count
}

fn main() {
    let map = ["11000", "11000", "00100", "00011"];
    println!("{}", islands(&map));
}
def islands(rows):
    g = [list(r) for r in rows]
    h, w = len(g), len(g[0])
    count = 0
    for r in range(h):
        for c in range(w):
            if g[r][c] != "1":
                continue
            count += 1
            stack = [(r, c)]
            g[r][c] = "0"
            while stack:
                y, x = stack.pop()
                for ny, nx in ((y - 1, x), (y + 1, x), (y, x - 1), (y, x + 1)):
                    if 0 <= ny < h and 0 <= nx < w and g[ny][nx] == "1":
                        g[ny][nx] = "0"
                        stack.append((ny, nx))
    return count

print(islands(["11000", "11000", "00100", "00011"]))
3

Both print 3. We use our own stack, not recursion, so a big map cannot hit the recursion limit. Change stack.pop() to queue.pop_front() on a VecDeque and the same code becomes BFS. For counting islands, both work.

BFS or DFS?
QuestionUseWhy
Fewest steps from A to B, no weightsBFSIt visits nodes in order of distance.
Can I reach B at all? How many groups?eitherBoth visit every reachable node once.
Cycles, order of tasks, all pathsDFSIt knows the current path from the start.
Cheapest path with weightsDijkstraBFS ignores the weights.

Topological sort: an order for tasks

You plan a study path. "Intro" comes before "Data" and "Algo". "Algo" comes before "Graphs". Some courses wait for others. The edges have a direction, from "first" to "then". A topological order lists the courses so that no course comes before its prerequisite. It exists only when there is no cycle.

Kahn's algorithm is simple. Count how many prerequisites each course has. Start with the courses that have none. Each time you finish a course, its followers wait for one course less.

use std::collections::VecDeque;

fn topo(n: usize, edges: &[(usize, usize)]) -> Option<Vec<usize>> {
    let mut adj = vec![Vec::new(); n];
    let mut waits = vec![0; n]; // number of prerequisites still open
    for &(a, b) in edges {
        adj[a].push(b); // a must come before b
        waits[b] += 1;
    }
    let mut ready: VecDeque<usize> = (0..n).filter(|&v| waits[v] == 0).collect();
    let mut order = Vec::new();
    while let Some(u) = ready.pop_front() {
        order.push(u);
        for &v in &adj[u] {
            waits[v] -= 1;
            if waits[v] == 0 {
                ready.push_back(v);
            }
        }
    }
    // A cycle never reaches zero, so some nodes are missing.
    if order.len() == n { Some(order) } else { None }
}

fn main() {
    let names = ["Intro", "Data", "Algo", "Graphs", "ML", "Project"];
    let mut edges = vec![(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 5)];
    let order = topo(6, &edges).unwrap();
    println!("{:?}", order.iter().map(|&i| names[i]).collect::<Vec<_>>());
    edges.push((5, 0)); // Project before Intro: a cycle
    println!("{:?}", topo(6, &edges));
}
from collections import deque
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter, CycleError

def topo(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    waits = [0] * n
    for a, b in edges:
        adj[a].append(b)
        waits[b] += 1
    ready = deque(v for v in range(n) if waits[v] == 0)
    order = []
    while ready:
        u = ready.popleft()
        order.append(u)
        for v in adj[u]:
            waits[v] -= 1
            if waits[v] == 0:
                ready.append(v)
    return order if len(order) == n else None

names = ["Intro", "Data", "Algo", "Graphs", "ML", "Project"]
edges = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 5)]
print([names[i] for i in topo(6, edges)])
print(topo(6, edges + [(5, 0)]))

# The standard library: map each node to its prerequisites.
ts = TopologicalSorter({"Data": {"Intro"}, "Algo": {"Intro"}, "Intro": {"Algo"}})
try:
    print(list(ts.static_order()))
except CycleError as e:
    print("cycle:", e.args[1])
["Intro", "Data", "Algo", "ML", "Graphs", "Project"]
None

Python printed this. The last line comes from graphlib:

['Intro', 'Data', 'Algo', 'ML', 'Graphs', 'Project']
None
cycle: ['Intro', 'Algo', 'Intro']

The cost is O(V + E). Python's graphlib (since 3.9) does the same job. Its dict maps each node to its prerequisites, not to its followers. On a cycle it raises CycleError and shows the cycle. Build tools and package managers use this exact algorithm to order their work.

A topological order is usually not unique. "Data" could come before or after "Algo". Do not test for one fixed order. Test the rule instead: for every edge a to b, a comes first.

Dijkstra: the cheapest path

Now the edges have costs, for example minutes of driving. BFS counts edges, so it is no longer enough. Dijkstra's algorithm always takes the closest unfinished node next. It uses a min-heap of (cost so far, node).

Start

A costs 0. The heap holds (0, A). Every other node costs "unknown".

Pop A, cost 0

The road to C gives 1. The road to B gives 4. Push (1, C) and (4, B).

Pop C, cost 1

B through C costs 1 + 2 = 3. That beats 4, so push (3, B). D through C costs 6. Push (6, D).

Pop B, cost 3

D through B costs 3 + 1 = 4. That beats 6, so push (4, D).

Pop (4, B): old news

B is already done with cost 3. This entry is stale. Skip it.

Pop D, cost 4

E through D costs 7. Push (7, E). Later, (6, D) is stale and is skipped too.

Pop E, cost 7

The heap is empty. Final costs: A 0, C 1, B 3, D 4, E 7.

use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::BinaryHeap;

fn dijkstra(adj: &[Vec<(usize, u64)>], start: usize) -> (Vec<u64>, Vec<usize>) {
    let mut dist = vec![u64::MAX; adj.len()]; // MAX means "not reached"
    let mut prev = vec![usize::MAX; adj.len()];
    let mut heap = BinaryHeap::from([Reverse((0, start))]); // min-heap
    dist[start] = 0;
    while let Some(Reverse((d, u))) = heap.pop() {
        if d > dist[u] {
            continue; // stale: we already found a cheaper way to u
        }
        for &(v, w) in &adj[u] {
            let nd = d + w;
            if nd < dist[v] {
                dist[v] = nd;
                prev[v] = u;
                heap.push(Reverse((nd, v)));
            }
        }
    }
    (dist, prev)
}

fn main() {
    let names = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"];
    let mut adj = vec![Vec::new(); 5];
    for (a, b, w) in [(0, 1, 4), (0, 2, 1), (2, 1, 2), (1, 3, 1), (2, 3, 5), (3, 4, 3)] {
        adj[a].push((b, w)); // directed roads
    }
    let (dist, prev) = dijkstra(&adj, 0);
    println!("{dist:?}");
    let mut path = vec![4];
    while prev[*path.last().unwrap()] != usize::MAX {
        path.push(prev[*path.last().unwrap()]);
    }
    let names: Vec<&str> = path.iter().rev().map(|&i| names[i]).collect();
    println!("{}", names.join(" -> "));
}
import heapq

def dijkstra(adj, start):
    dist = [float("inf")] * len(adj)
    prev = [None] * len(adj)
    dist[start] = 0
    heap = [(0, start)]
    while heap:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue  # stale entry
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            nd = d + w
            if nd < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = nd
                prev[v] = u
                heapq.heappush(heap, (nd, v))
    return dist, prev

names = "ABCDE"
adj = [[] for _ in range(5)]
for a, b, w in [(0, 1, 4), (0, 2, 1), (2, 1, 2), (1, 3, 1), (2, 3, 5), (3, 4, 3)]:
    adj[a].append((b, w))
dist, prev = dijkstra(adj, 0)
print(dist)
path = [4]
while prev[path[-1]] is not None:
    path.append(prev[path[-1]])
print(" -> ".join(names[i] for i in reversed(path)))
[0, 3, 1, 4, 7]
A -> C -> B -> D -> E

Python prints the same. Neither heap can lower the cost of an item that is already inside. So we push a new entry and skip the old one when it comes out. This is called lazy deletion. The Rust standard library's own Dijkstra example does the same. The cost is O((V + E) \log V).

Dijkstra is wrong when an edge has a negative cost. A node is "done" when it leaves the heap. A negative edge found later could still make it cheaper. For negative costs use Bellman-Ford. The CS book chapter "Graph algorithms" explains it and proves why Dijkstra needs costs of zero or more.

Union-find: who is in the same group?

A network team adds cables between computers one by one. They want to know: does a new cable make a loop? Union-find answers this almost instantly. Each group has one leader. find(x) returns the leader of x. union(a, b) joins two groups.

struct Dsu {
    parent: Vec<usize>,
    size: Vec<usize>,
}

impl Dsu {
    fn new(n: usize) -> Self {
        Dsu { parent: (0..n).collect(), size: vec![1; n] } // everyone leads alone
    }

    fn find(&mut self, mut x: usize) -> usize {
        while self.parent[x] != x {
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]; // path halving
            x = self.parent[x];
        }
        x
    }

    // Returns false if a and b were already in one group.
    fn union(&mut self, a: usize, b: usize) -> bool {
        let (mut ra, mut rb) = (self.find(a), self.find(b));
        if ra == rb {
            return false;
        }
        if self.size[ra] < self.size[rb] {
            std::mem::swap(&mut ra, &mut rb); // hang the small tree under the big one
        }
        self.parent[rb] = ra;
        self.size[ra] += self.size[rb];
        true
    }
}

fn main() {
    let cables = [(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (1, 4), (1, 5)];
    let mut dsu = Dsu::new(6);
    for (a, b) in cables {
        if !dsu.union(a, b) {
            println!("cable {a}-{b} makes a loop");
        }
    }
    println!("same group 2 and 5: {}", dsu.find(2) == dsu.find(5));
}
class Dsu:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))
        self.size = [1] * n

    def find(self, x):
        while self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]  # path halving
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x

    def union(self, a, b):
        ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return False
        if self.size[ra] < self.size[rb]:
            ra, rb = rb, ra
        self.parent[rb] = ra
        self.size[ra] += self.size[rb]
        return True

dsu = Dsu(6)
for a, b in [(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (1, 4), (1, 5)]:
    if not dsu.union(a, b):
        print(f"cable {a}-{b} makes a loop")
print("same group 2 and 5:", str(dsu.find(2) == dsu.find(5)).lower())
cable 1-4 makes a loop
same group 2 and 5: true

Python prints the same. Two tricks make it fast. Path halving makes the trees flat while find walks. Union by size keeps the trees short. With both tricks each operation is almost O(1). The exact bound uses the inverse Ackermann function, which is below 5 for any real input. The CS book chapter "Data structures" proves it.

Union-find only joins groups. It cannot split them. For "add and remove links", you need other tools. Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm is union-find plus a sort of the edges by cost.

Backtracking: try, go deeper, undo

Some problems ask for every answer, or for one answer among very many choices. Backtracking builds an answer one choice at a time. After each choice it goes deeper. When it comes back, it undoes the choice and tries the next one. The shape is always the same: choose, explore, undo.

Warm-up: all subsets

fn subsets(items: &[i32], i: usize, current: &mut Vec<i32>, out: &mut Vec<Vec<i32>>) {
    if i == items.len() {
        out.push(current.clone()); // one full answer
        return;
    }
    subsets(items, i + 1, current, out); // choice 1: skip items[i]
    current.push(items[i]); // choice 2: take items[i]
    subsets(items, i + 1, current, out);
    current.pop(); // undo the choice
}

fn main() {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    subsets(&[1, 2, 3], 0, &mut Vec::new(), &mut out);
    println!("{} {out:?}", out.len());
}
def subsets(items):
    out, current = [], []
    def go(i):
        if i == len(items):
            out.append(current.copy())  # copy! current keeps changing
            return
        go(i + 1)
        current.append(items[i])
        go(i + 1)
        current.pop()
    go(0)
    return out

out = subsets([1, 2, 3])
print(len(out), out)
8 [[], [3], [2], [2, 3], [1], [1, 3], [1, 2], [1, 2, 3]]

Python prints the same. n items have 2^n subsets, so the cost is O(n \cdot 2^n). Backtracking is never fast in the worst case. Its power is pruning.

Problem: the N queens

Place n chess queens on an n \times n board. No two may attack each other: not in one row, one column or one diagonal. How many ways are there? We place one queen per row. Before we go deeper, we check the column and both diagonals. A bad branch is cut at once. This cutting is called pruning.

struct Board {
    n: usize,
    cols: Vec<bool>,
    diag1: Vec<bool>, // row + col is the same on one diagonal
    diag2: Vec<bool>, // row - col + n - 1 is the same on the other
}

fn place(b: &mut Board, row: usize) -> u64 {
    if row == b.n {
        return 1; // all queens placed: one solution
    }
    let mut count = 0;
    for col in 0..b.n {
        let (d1, d2) = (row + col, row + b.n - 1 - col);
        if b.cols[col] || b.diag1[d1] || b.diag2[d2] {
            continue; // prune: this square is attacked
        }
        b.cols[col] = true; b.diag1[d1] = true; b.diag2[d2] = true; // choose
        count += place(b, row + 1); // explore
        b.cols[col] = false; b.diag1[d1] = false; b.diag2[d2] = false; // undo
    }
    count
}

fn main() {
    for n in 1..=8 {
        let mut b = Board { n, cols: vec![false; n], diag1: vec![false; 2 * n], diag2: vec![false; 2 * n] };
        print!("{} ", place(&mut b, 0));
    }
    println!();
}
def queens(n):
    cols, d1, d2 = set(), set(), set()
    def place(row):
        if row == n:
            return 1
        count = 0
        for col in range(n):
            if col in cols or row + col in d1 or row - col in d2:
                continue  # prune
            cols.add(col); d1.add(row + col); d2.add(row - col)
            count += place(row + 1)
            cols.remove(col); d1.remove(row + col); d2.remove(row - col)
        return count
    return place(0)

print(*[queens(n) for n in range(1, 9)])
1 0 0 2 10 4 40 92

Python prints the same: 92 solutions for the normal 8 by 8 board. Without pruning there are 8^8, about 16.8 million, ways to put one queen in each row. With pruning, the search makes only 2,057 calls of place. We counted them with a small counter.

Forgetting the undo step. Then the marks from one branch stay on the board and block the next branch. A second classic bug is in Python: out.append(current) without .copy(). Every saved answer is then the same list, and it ends empty.

Dynamic programming step by step

Count the ways to climb 30 stairs if each step goes up 1 or 2 stairs. The direct recursion asks the same question again and again. Let us count the calls.

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn ways_slow(n: u64, calls: &mut u64) -> u64 {
    *calls += 1;
    if n <= 1 { return 1; }
    ways_slow(n - 1, calls) + ways_slow(n - 2, calls)
}

// Same recursion, but remember every answer.
fn ways_memo(n: u64, memo: &mut HashMap<u64, u64>, calls: &mut u64) -> u64 {
    *calls += 1;
    if n <= 1 { return 1; }
    if let Some(&w) = memo.get(&n) { return w; }
    let w = ways_memo(n - 1, memo, calls) + ways_memo(n - 2, memo, calls);
    memo.insert(n, w);
    w
}

fn main() {
    for n in [10, 20, 25, 30] {
        let (mut slow, mut fast) = (0, 0);
        let a = ways_slow(n, &mut slow);
        let b = ways_memo(n, &mut HashMap::new(), &mut fast);
        println!("n={n}: {a} ways  slow calls {slow:>7}  memo calls {fast}");
        assert_eq!(a, b);
    }
}
from functools import cache

calls = 0

def ways_slow(n):
    global calls
    calls += 1
    return 1 if n <= 1 else ways_slow(n - 1) + ways_slow(n - 2)

@cache  # remembers every answer: memoization in one line
def ways_memo(n):
    return 1 if n <= 1 else ways_memo(n - 1) + ways_memo(n - 2)

for n in [10, 20, 25, 30]:
    calls = 0
    a = ways_slow(n)
    print(f"n={n}: {a} ways  slow calls {calls:>7}  memo {ways_memo(n)}")
print(ways_memo.cache_info())
n=10: 89 ways  slow calls     177  memo calls 19
n=20: 10946 ways  slow calls   21891  memo calls 39
n=25: 121393 ways  slow calls  242785  memo calls 49
n=30: 1346269 ways  slow calls 2692537  memo calls 59

Python printed this. The last line shows 31 misses: ways_memo computed each n from 0 to 30 only once.

n=10: 89 ways  slow calls     177  memo 89
n=20: 10946 ways  slow calls   21891  memo 10946
n=25: 121393 ways  slow calls  242785  memo 121393
n=30: 1346269 ways  slow calls 2692537  memo 1346269
CacheInfo(hits=31, misses=31, maxsize=None, currsize=31)

The slow version is exponential. The memo version is O(n). This is the whole idea of dynamic programming (DP). It works when a problem has overlapping subproblems and the best answer is built from best answers of smaller problems. Storing answers in a recursive function is called memoization. Filling a table from small to big is called bottom-up DP.

  1. State. Say in words what one table cell means. "best[a] = the fewest coins that make the amount a."
  2. Choice. What is the last decision? "The last coin is one of the coin values c."
  3. Recurrence. Write the cell from smaller cells. best[a] = 1 + \min_c best[a - c].
  4. Base and order. best[0] = 0. Fill a = 1, 2, 3, ... so smaller cells are ready first.
  5. Answer. Read best[amount]. If no coins fit, say so.

Problem: the fewest coins

fn fewest_coins(coins: &[usize], amount: usize) -> Option<u32> {
    let mut best: Vec<Option<u32>> = vec![None; amount + 1]; // None: impossible
    best[0] = Some(0);
    for a in 1..=amount {
        for &c in coins {
            if c <= a {
                if let Some(prev) = best[a - c] {
                    let cand = prev + 1; // use one coin c on top of best[a - c]
                    best[a] = Some(best[a].map_or(cand, |b| b.min(cand)));
                }
            }
        }
    }
    best[amount]
}

fn greedy(coins: &[usize], mut amount: usize) -> u32 {
    let mut n = 0; // always take the biggest coin that fits
    for &c in coins.iter().rev() {
        n += (amount / c) as u32;
        amount %= c;
    }
    n
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?} {:?}", fewest_coins(&[1, 2, 5], 11), fewest_coins(&[2], 3));
    println!("greedy {}  dp {:?}", greedy(&[1, 3, 4], 6), fewest_coins(&[1, 3, 4], 6));
}
from functools import cache

def fewest_coins(coins, amount):
    @cache
    def best(a):  # top-down: the same recurrence, as a function
        if a == 0:
            return 0
        options = [best(a - c) for c in coins if c <= a]
        options = [o for o in options if o is not None]
        return 1 + min(options) if options else None
    return best(amount)

def greedy(coins, amount):
    n = 0
    for c in sorted(coins, reverse=True):
        n += amount // c
        amount %= c
    return n

print(fewest_coins([1, 2, 5], 11), fewest_coins([2], 3))
print("greedy", greedy([1, 3, 4], 6), " dp", fewest_coins([1, 3, 4], 6))
Some(3) None
greedy 3  dp Some(2)

Python prints 3 None and greedy 3 dp 2. For 11 the answer is 5 + 5 + 1. With coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6, greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1. DP finds 3 + 3. Greedy is fast, but it is right only for some coin systems. The cost of DP is O(\text{amount} \times \text{coins}).

Problem: edit distance (a 2D table)

How many single-letter edits turn "sunday" into "saturday"? An edit is an insert, a delete or a replace. Spell checkers and the diff tool use this number. The state is d[i][j]: the edits that turn the first i letters of one word into the first j letters of the other.

fn edit_distance(a: &str, b: &str) -> usize {
    let (a, b): (Vec<char>, Vec<char>) = (a.chars().collect(), b.chars().collect());
    let mut d = vec![vec![0; b.len() + 1]; a.len() + 1];
    for i in 0..=a.len() { d[i][0] = i; } // delete everything
    for j in 0..=b.len() { d[0][j] = j; } // insert everything
    for i in 1..=a.len() {
        for j in 1..=b.len() {
            let same = a[i - 1] == b[j - 1];
            d[i][j] = (d[i - 1][j] + 1)                          // delete a[i-1]
                .min(d[i][j - 1] + 1)                            // insert b[j-1]
                .min(d[i - 1][j - 1] + if same { 0 } else { 1 }); // keep or replace
        }
    }
    d[a.len()][b.len()]
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", edit_distance("sunday", "saturday"));
    println!("{}", edit_distance("kitten", "sitting"));
    println!("{}", edit_distance("", "abc"));
}
def edit_distance(a, b):
    prev = list(range(len(b) + 1))  # only the last row is needed
    for i in range(1, len(a) + 1):
        cur = [i] + [0] * len(b)
        for j in range(1, len(b) + 1):
            same = a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]
            cur[j] = min(prev[j] + 1, cur[j - 1] + 1, prev[j - 1] + (0 if same else 1))
        prev = cur
    return prev[-1]

print(edit_distance("sunday", "saturday"))
print(edit_distance("kitten", "sitting"))
print(edit_distance("", "abc"))
3
3
3

Python prints the same. Here is the full table for a small pair, "sun" and "satu". Each cell is the edit distance between a row prefix and a column prefix. For example, row "u" and column "u" hold 2: "su" becomes "satu" with two inserts. The cell in the bottom right is the answer.

Edit distance table for "sun" (rows) and "satu" (columns)
""satu
""01234
s10123
u21122
n32223

The answer is 3. Check it by hand: insert "a", insert "t", then delete "n". Each cell needs only three neighbours: left, up and up-left. So the Python version keeps only two rows. That cuts memory from O(nm) to O(m). It is a common follow-up question in interviews.

Off-by-one indexes. The table has len + 1 rows and columns, because row 0 means "the empty prefix". So letter i of the word is a[i - 1]. Write the meaning of a cell in a comment before you write any loop.

Tries: search by prefix

A search box suggests words while you type. After "car" it shows "card", "care" and "cart". A trie stores words letter by letter. Words with the same start share the same path. Finding all words with a prefix of length m takes O(m) steps to reach the prefix, plus the size of the answer.

use std::collections::BTreeMap;

#[derive(Default)]
struct Trie {
    children: BTreeMap<char, Trie>, // sorted, so results come out in order
    end: bool,                      // a word ends here
    count: usize,                   // words that pass through here
}

impl Trie {
    fn insert(&mut self, word: &str) {
        let mut node = self;
        node.count += 1;
        for c in word.chars() {
            node = node.children.entry(c).or_default();
            node.count += 1;
        }
        node.end = true;
    }

    fn find(&self, prefix: &str) -> Option<&Trie> {
        let mut node = self;
        for c in prefix.chars() {
            node = node.children.get(&c)?; // no child: no such prefix
        }
        Some(node)
    }

    fn collect(&self, buf: &mut String, out: &mut Vec<String>) {
        if self.end {
            out.push(buf.clone());
        }
        for (&c, child) in &self.children {
            buf.push(c);
            child.collect(buf, out);
            buf.pop(); // backtracking again: undo the letter
        }
    }
}
class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}
        self.end = False
        self.count = 0

    def insert(self, word):
        node = self
        node.count += 1
        for c in word:
            node = node.children.setdefault(c, Trie())
            node.count += 1
        node.end = True

    def find(self, prefix):
        node = self
        for c in prefix:
            node = node.children.get(c)
            if node is None:
                return None
        return node

    def collect(self, prefix, out):
        if self.end:
            out.append(prefix)
        for c in sorted(self.children):
            self.children[c].collect(prefix + c, out)
fn main() {
    let mut t = Trie::default();
    for w in ["car", "card", "care", "cart", "cat", "dog"] {
        t.insert(w);
    }
    let count = t.find("car").map_or(0, |n| n.count);
    println!("words starting with car: {count}");
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    if let Some(n) = t.find("ca") {
        n.collect(&mut "ca".to_string(), &mut out);
    }
    println!("{out:?}");
    println!("is ca a word? {}", t.find("ca").is_some_and(|n| n.end));
}
t = Trie()
for w in ["car", "card", "care", "cart", "cat", "dog"]:
    t.insert(w)
node = t.find("car")
print("words starting with car:", node.count if node else 0)
out = []
node = t.find("ca")
if node:
    node.collect("ca", out)
print(out)
node = t.find("ca")
print("is ca a word?", str(bool(node and node.end)).lower())
words starting with car: 4
["car", "card", "care", "cart", "cat"]
is ca a word? false

Python prints the same, with single quotes. In Rust the children live inside a BTreeMap, which is already on the heap. So no Box is needed. The loop node = node.children.entry(c).or_default() moves a &mut one level down each time. That is the same cursor trick as in the linked list.

A trie uses more memory than a hash set of words. Use it when prefixes matter: autocomplete, IP routing tables, word games. For "is this exact word in the list?", a HashSet is simpler and faster.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for trees, graphs and dynamic programming
PatternPurposeModelNote
type Tree = Option<Box<Node>>A tree with one ownerSome(n) if val < n.val => insert(&mut n.left, val)Use Rc<RefCell<..>> only when nodes are shared.
Recursion with a rangeCheck a BSTvalid(&n.left, lo, Some(n.val))Comparing with children only is wrong.
Level order with a queueVisit a tree row by rowfor _ in 0..queue.len() { ... }Read the length before the loop.
Heap of size kTop k items in O(n \log k)heap.push(x); if heap.len() > k { heap.pop(); }Keep the worst of the best on top.
Reverse(x)Min-heap in RustBinaryHeap::from([Reverse((0, start))])Python's heapq is a min-heap already.
Adjacency listStore a graphlet mut adj = vec![Vec::new(); n];Python: [[] for _ in range(n)], not [[]] * n.
BFS with a queueFewest steps, no weightsif dist[v].is_none() { mark; push_back(v) }Mark when you push, not when you pop.
DFS with your own stackFlood fill, groupswhile let Some(cell) = stack.pop()No recursion limit to hit.
Kahn's algorithmOrder tasks, find cycleswaits[v] -= 1; if waits[v] == 0 { ready.push_back(v) }Fewer than n nodes out means a cycle.
Dijkstra with lazy deletionCheapest pathsif d > dist[u] { continue; }No negative costs.
Union-findGroups and loop checksif !dsu.union(a, b) { loop found }Use path halving and union by size.
Choose, explore, undoBacktrackingpush(x); go(i + 1); pop();Prune early. Copy the answer when you save it.
Five-step DP recipeTurn a recursion into a tablebest[a] = 1 + min(best[a - c])Write what a cell means first.
@cacheMemoize in Python@cache def best(a): ...Deep recursion can still hit the limit.
TriePrefix searchnode = node.children.entry(c).or_default();For exact words only, a set is simpler.

Practice

You need the fewest train changes between two stations. Every ride counts as 1. Which algorithm?

  • BFS
  • DFS
  • Topological sort

All edges cost the same, so BFS finds the shortest path. Dijkstra also works, but it is slower and not needed.

A road has cost -3. What happens with Dijkstra?

  • It still works, only slower.
  • It can give a wrong answer.
  • It does not compile.

Dijkstra treats a node as finished when it leaves the heap. A negative edge found later could still lower that cost. Use Bellman-Ford.

What does Rust's BinaryHeap::pop return?

  • The smallest item
  • The biggest item
  • The oldest item

BinaryHeap is a max-heap. Wrap items in Reverse to get the smallest first.

Kahn's algorithm outputs 4 nodes for a graph with 6 nodes. What does that mean?

  • Two nodes have no edges.
  • The graph has a cycle.
  • The queue was too small.

Nodes on a cycle wait for each other, so their count never reaches zero. They never enter the queue.

In Python, heapq.?(h) removes and returns the smallest item.

The inorder walk of a binary search tree gives the values in ? order.

  1. Merge k sorted lists into one sorted list in O(N \log k). Write it in Rust with a min-heap.
    Answer 
    use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::BinaryHeap;

fn merge_k(lists: &[Vec<i32>]) -> Vec<i32> {
    // (value, which list, position in that list)
    let mut heap: BinaryHeap<Reverse<(i32, usize, usize)>> = lists
        .iter()
        .enumerate()
        .filter(|(_, l)| !l.is_empty())
        .map(|(i, l)| Reverse((l[0], i, 0)))
        .collect();
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    while let Some(Reverse((v, i, j))) = heap.pop() {
        out.push(v);
        if j + 1 < lists[i].len() {
            heap.push(Reverse((lists[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))); // next from the same list
        }
    }
    out
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", merge_k(&[vec![1, 4, 7], vec![2, 5], vec![], vec![0, 9]]));
}
    [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9]

    The heap never holds more than k items, one per list. In Python, heapq.merge(*lists) does this for you and returns a lazy iterator.

  2. House robber. Houses in a row hold money [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]. You cannot rob two neighbours. What is the most money? Use the five-step recipe.
    Answer

    State: best[i] = the most money from the first i houses. Choice: rob house i or not. Recurrence: best[i] = max(best[i-1], best[i-2] + money[i]). Only two numbers are needed at a time:

    def rob(money):
    skip, take = 0, 0  # best without and with the last house
    for m in money:
        skip, take = max(skip, take), skip + m
    return max(skip, take)

print(rob([2, 7, 9, 3, 1]))
    12

    Rob houses 1, 3 and 5: 2 + 9 + 1 = 12.

  3. Your BFS on a grid is very slow on a big empty map. You mark cells as seen when you pop them. Why is it slow?
    Answer

    A cell can be pushed by each of its 4 neighbours before it is popped. On an open map the queue fills with many copies of the same cells. Mark a cell when you push it. Then each cell enters the queue once, and BFS is O(V + E) again.

  4. Expert. Find the longest increasing subsequence of [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]. The plain DP is O(n^2). Give an O(n \log n) answer.
    Answer

    Keep a list tails. tails[k] is the smallest last value of any increasing subsequence of length k + 1. For each number, binary search its place in tails and replace that item, or append it at the end:

    fn lis(v: &[i32]) -> usize {
    let mut tails: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    for &x in v {
        let i = tails.partition_point(|&t| t < x); // first tail >= x
        if i == tails.len() { tails.push(x) } else { tails[i] = x }
    }
    tails.len()
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", lis(&[10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]));
}
    4

    One answer is 2, 3, 7, 18. Note that tails itself is not always a real subsequence. Only its length is the answer. Python: use bisect_left(tails, x).

  5. Expert. Why does the trie insert compile in Rust, when node is a &mut that is replaced inside the loop?
    Answer

    node.children.entry(c).or_default() borrows node and returns a &mut to a child. We assign that new reference to node. The old borrow is no longer used after this line. The borrow checker (non-lexical lifetimes) sees that only one usable &mut exists at any time. So the code is safe and accepted.

Key takeaways

  • A Rust tree is Option<Box<Node>>. Recursion is short, but deep trees need a loop or a balanced tree.
  • BinaryHeap is a max-heap and heapq is a min-heap. A heap of size k finds the top k in O(n \log k).
  • Store graphs as adjacency lists. BFS gives fewest steps, DFS explores deep, Kahn orders tasks, Dijkstra finds the cheapest path with costs of zero or more.
  • Union-find joins groups and finds loops in almost constant time.
  • Backtracking is choose, explore, undo. Pruning makes it practical.
  • DP stores the answers to small subproblems. Write what a cell means, then the recurrence, then the order.

Sources

  • Rust standard library: binary_heap. BinaryHeap, Reverse, and the official Dijkstra example with stale entries.
  • Python: heapq. The min-heap functions and the new max-heap functions of Python 3.14.
  • Python: graphlib. TopologicalSorter, static_order and CycleError.
  • Python: functools. cache and lru_cache for memoization.
  • Rust standard library: collections. VecDeque, BTreeMap and when to use each collection.

Three projects in both languages

Small examples teach one idea at a time. Real programs mix many ideas, and they must handle bad input, crashes and many users. This chapter builds three complete small programs, each in Rust and in Python, step by step and with tests. At the end we compare what each language made easy and what it made hard.

  • Build a command-line word counter with clear exit codes and tests.
  • Build a key-value store that keeps its data in an append-only log file and survives a crash.
  • Build a tiny HTTP API on top of that store with only the standard library.
  • Test all three in-process, without a real terminal, disk crash or network server.
  • Compare Rust and Python on code size, safety, speed and comfort, with real numbers.

How we build each project

All three projects follow the same four steps.

  1. Write the contract. What goes in, what comes out, and what happens on bad input.
  2. Build a pure core. The core works on values and streams that it receives. It never opens the real terminal or the real network itself.
  3. Add a thin shell. main connects the core to the real world: arguments, files, stdin, sockets. It has almost no logic.
  4. Test the core first. Tests call the core with fake input. Then one test runs the real program.
