This split has a name: functional core, imperative shell. It is the reason we can test an HTTP server without starting one.

The folders

A Cargo workspace holds the three Rust crates. Each crate has a lib.rs with the core and a small main.rs with the shell. The third project uses the second one as a library. No crate needs anything outside the standard library.

[workspace]
members = ["wcount", "kvlog", "kvhttp"]
resolver = "3"
[package]
name = "kvhttp"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
kvlog = { path = "../kvlog" } # project 2, used as a library
use_small_heuristics = "Max"  # keep short items on one line

The other two crates have the same Cargo.toml with their own name and no dependencies. The rustfmt.toml file only makes the code shorter on the page. The Python side needs no configuration. Each module is one file, and pytest finds every test_*.py file.

cd projects/rust && cargo test          # all three crates, 18 tests
cd projects/python && uv run --with pytest python3.14 -m pytest -q

Each Rust project builds a big target folder. Several projects can share one build folder: set CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/home/you/.cache/cargo-target in your shell. A workspace already shares one folder between its own crates.

Project 1: a word counter

The Unix tool wc counts lines, words and bytes. We build our own version, wcount. It does one thing more: it lists the most common words.

The contract of wcount
InputOutput
wcount a.txt b.txtOne row per file: lines, words, bytes, name. Then a total row.
wcount with no filesCount stdin. The row has no name.
--top NAlso print the N most common words, in lower case.
A file is missingPrint an error to stderr, count the other files, exit with 1.
A bad optionPrint the usage to stderr and exit with 2.

An exit code tells the shell what happened. 0 means success. Python's argparse exits with 2 when the command line is wrong, and grep uses 2 for errors too. We follow that habit: 1 when an input file fails, 2 when the command is wrong. Scripts depend on these numbers, so they are part of the contract.

Step 1: the counting core

A Counts value holds three numbers. Counts::of counts one block of bytes. We count bytes, not characters, as wc does. For words we need text, so we decode the bytes first.

//! wcount: count lines, words and bytes, and find the most common words.
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::fs;
use std::io::{self, Read, Write};

#[derive(Debug, Default, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
pub struct Counts {
    pub lines: usize,
    pub words: usize,
    pub bytes: usize,
}

impl Counts {
    pub fn of(data: &[u8]) -> Counts {
        let text = String::from_utf8_lossy(data); // bad bytes become U+FFFD
        Counts {
            lines: data.iter().filter(|&&b| b == b'\n').count(),
            words: text.split_whitespace().count(),
            bytes: data.len(),
        }
    }

    pub fn add(&mut self, other: Counts) {
        self.lines += other.lines;
        self.words += other.words;
        self.bytes += other.bytes;
    }
}
"""wcount: count lines, words and bytes, and find the most common words."""
import argparse
import re
import sys
from collections import Counter
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Counts:
    lines: int = 0
    words: int = 0
    bytes: int = 0

    @classmethod
    def of(cls, data: bytes) -> "Counts":
        text = data.decode("utf-8", errors="replace")  # bad bytes become U+FFFD
        return cls(data.count(b"\n"), len(text.split()), len(data))

    def add(self, other: "Counts") -> None:
        self.lines += other.lines
        self.words += other.words
        self.bytes += other.bytes

A file may hold bytes that are not valid UTF-8. String::from_utf8_lossy in Rust and decode(errors="replace") in Python replace each bad part with the character U+FFFD. The program never crashes on strange files. The #[derive(Default)] in Rust and the = 0 defaults in the Python dataclass give an all-zero Counts for the total.

Step 2: the most common words

/// The n most common words, in lower case. Ties are sorted by the word.
pub fn top_words(text: &str, n: usize) -> Vec<(String, usize)> {
    let mut counts: HashMap<String, usize> = HashMap::new();
    let words = text
        .split(|c: char| !(c.is_alphanumeric() || c == '\''))
        .map(|w| w.trim_matches('\'')) // 'quoted' -> quoted, don't stays
        .filter(|w| !w.is_empty());
    for w in words {
        *counts.entry(w.to_lowercase()).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }
    let mut pairs: Vec<(String, usize)> = counts.into_iter().collect();
    pairs.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(&a.1).then_with(|| a.0.cmp(&b.0)));
    pairs.truncate(n);
    pairs
}

/// One output row, like wc: a space, then each number 7 wide.
fn line(c: Counts, name: &str) -> String {
    let mut s = format!(" {:>7} {:>7} {:>7}", c.lines, c.words, c.bytes);
    if !name.is_empty() {
        s.push(' ');
        s.push_str(name);
    }
    s
}
WORD = re.compile(r"(?:[^\W_]|')+")  # letters, digits and ' (no underscore)


def top_words(text: str, n: int) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
    words = (w.strip("'").lower() for w in WORD.findall(text))
    counts = Counter(w for w in words if w)
    return sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:n]


def line(c: Counts, name: str) -> str:
    s = f" {c.lines:>7} {c.words:>7} {c.bytes:>7}"
    return f"{s} {name}" if name else s

A word is a run of letters, digits and apostrophes. So "don't" stays one word, and "'the'" becomes "the". We sort by count, biggest first, and then by the word. Without the second key, two words with the same count could come out in any order, and the tests would sometimes fail. The cost is O(n \log n) for the sort. A heap of size N would make it O(n \log N), as in Algorithms 2. For a few thousand different words the simple sort is fine.

In Python, \w in a regular expression also matches the underscore. Rust's char::is_alphanumeric does not. Then "snake_case" is one word in Python and two words in Rust. The pattern [^\W_] means "a word character, but not the underscore". Small details like this make two versions disagree.

Step 3: the command line

pub const USAGE: &str = "usage: wcount [--top N] [FILE]...";

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
pub struct Options {
    pub top: Option<usize>,
    pub files: Vec<String>,
}

pub fn parse_args(args: &[String]) -> Result<Options, String> {
    let mut opts = Options { top: None, files: Vec::new() };
    let mut it = args.iter();
    while let Some(arg) = it.next() {
        match arg.as_str() {
            "--top" => {
                let n = it.next().ok_or("--top needs a number")?;
                let n = n.parse().map_err(|_| format!("--top: not a number: {n}"))?;
                opts.top = Some(n);
            }
            s if s.starts_with('-') => return Err(format!("unknown option {s}")),
            _ => opts.files.push(arg.clone()),
        }
    }
    Ok(opts)
}
def make_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="wcount")
    parser.add_argument("--top", type=int, metavar="N", help="also print the N most common words")
    parser.add_argument("files", nargs="*")
    return parser

Here the languages differ a lot. Python has argparse in its standard library. Five lines give us parsing, error messages and a --help page. Rust's standard library has no argument parser. We write a small one by hand. In a real tool you would add the clap crate, as the chapter Command-line tools does.

Step 4: run and report

run is the whole program as a function. It receives the arguments and three streams, and it returns the exit code. It never calls std::process::exit or sys.exit itself. That is why tests can call it.

/// The whole program. main() only connects it to the real stdin and stdout.
pub fn run(args: &[String], stdin: &mut dyn Read, out: &mut dyn Write, err: &mut dyn Write) -> i32 {
    let opts = match parse_args(args) {
        Ok(o) => o,
        Err(msg) => {
            let _ = writeln!(err, "wcount: {msg}\n{USAGE}");
            return 2; // 2 = the user typed something wrong
        }
    };
    let mut inputs: Vec<(String, Vec<u8>)> = Vec::new();
    let mut code = 0;
    if opts.files.is_empty() {
        let mut data = Vec::new();
        if let Err(e) = stdin.read_to_end(&mut data) {
            let _ = writeln!(err, "wcount: stdin: {e}");
            return 1;
        }
        inputs.push((String::new(), data));
    }
    for name in &opts.files {
        match fs::read(name) {
            Ok(data) => inputs.push((name.clone(), data)),
            Err(e) => {
                let _ = writeln!(err, "wcount: {name}: {e}");
                code = 1; // remember the error, but count the other files
            }
        }
    }
    match report(&inputs, opts.top, out) {
        Ok(()) => code,
        Err(e) => {
            let _ = writeln!(err, "wcount: {e}");
            1
        }
    }
}
def main(argv=None, stdin=None, out=None, err=None) -> int:
    stdin = sys.stdin.buffer if stdin is None else stdin
    out = sys.stdout if out is None else out
    err = sys.stderr if err is None else err
    try:
        args = make_parser().parse_args(argv)
    except SystemExit as e:  # argparse exits on bad input: keep control
        return e.code
    inputs, code = [], 0
    if not args.files:
        inputs.append(("", stdin.read()))
    for name in args.files:
        try:
            with open(name, "rb") as f:
                inputs.append((name, f.read()))
        except OSError as e:
            print(f"wcount: {name}: {e.strerror}", file=err)
            code = 1  # remember the error, but count the other files
    try:
        report(inputs, args.top, out)
    except OSError as e:  # for example, the reader closed the pipe
        print(f"wcount: {e}", file=err)
        return 1
    return code
fn report(inputs: &[(String, Vec<u8>)], top: Option<usize>, out: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut total = Counts::default();
    for (name, data) in inputs {
        let c = Counts::of(data);
        total.add(c);
        writeln!(out, "{}", line(c, name))?;
    }
    if inputs.len() > 1 {
        writeln!(out, "{}", line(total, "total"))?;
    }
    if let Some(n) = top {
        let texts: Vec<_> = inputs.iter().map(|(_, d)| String::from_utf8_lossy(d)).collect();
        for (word, count) in top_words(&texts.join("\n"), n) {
            writeln!(out, " {count:>7} {word}")?;
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}
def report(inputs: list[tuple[str, bytes]], top: int | None, out) -> None:
    total = Counts()
    for name, data in inputs:
        c = Counts.of(data)
        total.add(c)
        print(line(c, name), file=out)
    if len(inputs) > 1:
        print(line(total, "total"), file=out)
    if top is not None:
        text = "\n".join(d.decode("utf-8", errors="replace") for _, d in inputs)
        for word, n in top_words(text, top):
            print(f" {n:>7} {word}", file=out)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

In Rust, &mut dyn Read and &mut dyn Write accept any stream: the real stdin, a file, or a byte slice in a test. In Python, any object with read or write works. That is duck typing. The Python argparse raises SystemExit on bad input. We catch it, so main still returns a code instead of ending the process.

The Rust main.rs is the thin shell. It only connects run to the real streams.

use std::io;
use std::process::ExitCode;

fn main() -> ExitCode {
    let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().skip(1).collect(); // skip the program name
    let code =
        wcount::run(&args, &mut io::stdin().lock(), &mut io::stdout().lock(), &mut io::stderr());
    ExitCode::from(code as u8)
}

Do not print errors to stdout. A user may write wcount *.txt > counts.txt. Errors on stdout end up inside the file and break the next program in the pipeline. Errors go to stderr, so the user still sees them.

Project 1: tests and a real run

Unit tests call the core functions directly. They need no files except one small temporary file.

// Integration tests: start the real binary as a child process.
use std::io::Write;
use std::process::{Command, Stdio};

#[test]
fn the_binary_counts_stdin() {
    let mut child = Command::new(env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_wcount")) // Cargo sets this path
        .args(["--top", "2"])
        .stdin(Stdio::piped())
        .stdout(Stdio::piped())
        .spawn()
        .unwrap();
    child.stdin.take().unwrap().write_all(b"to be or not to be\n").unwrap();
    let out = child.wait_with_output().unwrap(); // stdin is closed by now
    assert!(out.status.success());
    let text = String::from_utf8(out.stdout).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(text, "       1       6      19\n       2 be\n       2 to\n");
}

#[test]
fn a_bad_option_exits_with_2() {

Now a real run on two small files and one missing file:

cargo run -q -p wcount -- --top 3 notes.txt todo.txt missing.txt; echo "exit $?"

Python prints the same rows and the same exit code. Only its error message is shorter: wcount: missing.txt: No such file or directory. The system wc notes.txt todo.txt prints the same three count rows. That is a good check that our counts are right. A bad option shows the two styles of error message:

wcount: --top needs a number
usage: wcount [--top N] [FILE]...
usage: wcount [-h] [--top N] [files ...]
wcount: error: argument --top: expected one argument

The first two lines come from our hand-written Rust parser. The last two come from argparse. Both programs exit with 2.

Project 2: a key-value store with a log file

A key-value store saves a value under a key, and finds it again later. Redis and many databases are key-value stores at heart. Ours keeps all data in a HashMap or dict in memory. Every change is also written to a file, so the data survives a restart.

The file is an append-only log. We never change old lines. Each change adds one line at the end:

set lang Rust
set year 2015
set lang Rust and Python
del year

To rebuild the data after a restart, we replay the log from the top. Why a log? Adding at the end of a file is a very fast kind of disk write. A crash can damage at most the last line. And the log is a full history of changes. Real systems use the same idea: databases call it a write-ahead log.

set lang Rust

The map is empty. Now it holds lang = "Rust".

set year 2015

The map holds lang = "Rust" and year = "2015".

set lang Rust and Python

The same key again. The new value replaces the old one. The value may contain spaces: it is the rest of the line.

del year

year leaves the map. Only lang = "Rust and Python" is left.

Rewrite the log

Four lines describe one key. Compaction writes a new log with one line per live key: set lang Rust and Python.

Step 1: keys and escapes

The format must be able to hold every value. A value can contain a newline, and a newline ends a log line. So we escape it: a newline becomes the two characters \n, and a backslash becomes \\. Keys are simpler. We only allow letters, digits, -, _ and ., so a key never contains a space.

//! kvlog: a key-value store that writes every change to an append-only log.
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::fs::{self, File, OpenOptions};
use std::io::{self, BufRead, BufReader, BufWriter, Write};
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};

pub struct Store {
    path: PathBuf,
    file: File,                    // the log, open for appending
    data: HashMap<String, String>, // the current value of every key
    lines: usize,                  // lines in the log, old ones included
}

/// Keys are short and simple: letters, digits, '-', '_' and '.'.
pub fn valid_key(key: &str) -> bool {
    !key.is_empty()
        && key.len() <= 200
        && key.bytes().all(|b| b.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || b"-_.".contains(&b))
}

// A value may hold any text. Only '\' and newline need an escape.
fn escape(v: &str) -> String {
    v.replace('\\', "\\\\").replace('\n', "\\n")
}

fn unescape(v: &str) -> Result<String, String> {
    let mut out = String::with_capacity(v.len());
    let mut chars = v.chars();
    while let Some(c) = chars.next() {
        if c != '\\' {
            out.push(c);
            continue;
        }
        match chars.next() {
            Some('\\') => out.push('\\'),
            Some('n') => out.push('\n'),
            other => return Err(format!("bad escape {other:?}")),
        }
    }
    Ok(out)
}
"""kvlog: a key-value store that writes every change to an append-only log."""
import os
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

KEY = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,200}")


def valid_key(key: str) -> bool:
    return KEY.fullmatch(key) is not None


def _escape(v: str) -> str:
    return v.replace("\\", "\\\\").replace("\n", "\\n")


def _unescape(v: str) -> str:
    out, chars = [], iter(v)
    for c in chars:
        if c != "\\":
            out.append(c)
            continue
        match next(chars, None):
            case "\\":
                out.append("\\")
            case "n":
                out.append("\n")
            case other:
                raise ValueError(f"bad escape {other!r}")
    return "".join(out)

Step 2: apply one line

/// Apply one log line, "set KEY VALUE" or "del KEY", to the map.
fn apply(data: &mut HashMap<String, String>, line: &str) -> Result<(), String> {
    match line.split_once(' ') {
        Some(("set", rest)) => {
            let (key, value) = rest.split_once(' ').ok_or("set without a value")?;
            data.insert(key.to_string(), unescape(value)?);
        }
        Some(("del", key)) => {
            data.remove(key);
        }
        _ => return Err(format!("unknown line {line:?}")),
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn invalid(kind: io::ErrorKind, msg: String) -> io::Error {
    io::Error::new(kind, msg)
}
def _apply(data: dict, line: str) -> None:
    match line.split(" ", 2):
        case ["set", key, value]:
            data[key] = _unescape(value)
        case ["del", key]:
            data.pop(key, None)
        case _:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown line {line!r}")

Rust's split_once and Python's split(" ", 2) with match read almost the same. A line we do not understand is an error, not something to skip in silence. A store that skips lines can lose data without anyone noticing.

Step 3: open and replay, and survive a crash

impl Store {
    /// Open the log, or create it, and replay every line into memory.
    pub fn open(path: impl AsRef<Path>) -> io::Result<Store> {
        let path = path.as_ref().to_path_buf();
        let (mut data, mut lines, mut good) = (HashMap::new(), 0, 0u64);
        if path.exists() {
            let mut reader = BufReader::new(File::open(&path)?);
            let mut line = String::new();
            loop {
                line.clear();
                let n = reader.read_line(&mut line)?;
                if n == 0 || !line.ends_with('\n') {
                    break; // the end, or a torn last line from a crash
                }
                apply(&mut data, &line[..line.len() - 1]).map_err(|msg| {
                    let msg = format!("{}: line {}: {msg}", path.display(), lines + 1);
                    invalid(io::ErrorKind::InvalidData, msg)
                })?;
                lines += 1;
                good += n as u64; // bytes of complete lines so far
            }
        }
        let file = OpenOptions::new().create(true).append(true).open(&path)?;
        file.set_len(good)?; // cut off a torn tail, or the next line glues onto it
        Ok(Store { path, file, data, lines })
    }
class Store:
    def __init__(self, path):
        self.path = Path(path)
        self.data: dict[str, str] = {}
        self.lines = 0
        good = 0  # bytes of complete lines
        if self.path.exists():
            with open(self.path, "rb") as f:
                for raw in f:  # binary lines keep their b"\n"
                    if not raw.endswith(b"\n"):
                        break  # a torn last line from a crash
                    try:
                        _apply(self.data, raw[:-1].decode("utf-8"))
                    except ValueError as e:  # also catches bad UTF-8
                        raise ValueError(f"{self.path}: line {self.lines + 1}: {e}") from None
                    self.lines += 1
                    good += len(raw)
        self.file = open(self.path, "ab")
        self.file.truncate(good)  # cut off a torn tail

    def close(self) -> None:
        self.file.close()

    def __enter__(self):
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc) -> None:
        self.close()

Imagine the power fails while we write set b 2\n. The file may end with set b 2 and no newline. That last line is torn. We stop the replay there. The change was never confirmed to the user, so dropping it is correct.

There is a trap. If we leave the torn bytes in the file, the next write goes after them. Then the file holds set b 2set c 3, and that broken line sits in the middle forever. So open cuts the file back to the last full line: set_len(good) in Rust, truncate(good) in Python. A test below checks exactly this case.

Project 2: writes, compaction and tests

Step 4: set, get and delete

    pub fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<&str> {
        self.data.get(key).map(String::as_str)
    }

    pub fn set(&mut self, key: &str, value: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
        if !valid_key(key) {
            return Err(invalid(io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput, format!("bad key {key:?}")));
        }
        self.append(&format!("set {key} {}\n", escape(value)))?; // disk first
        self.data.insert(key.to_string(), value.to_string()); // then memory
        Ok(())
    }

    /// Returns false when the key was not there.
    pub fn delete(&mut self, key: &str) -> io::Result<bool> {
        if !self.data.contains_key(key) {
            return Ok(false);
        }
        self.append(&format!("del {key}\n"))?;
        self.data.remove(key);
        Ok(true)
    }

    fn append(&mut self, line: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
        self.file.write_all(line.as_bytes())?; // File has no buffer of its own
        self.file.sync_data()?; // ask the OS to put the bytes on the disk now
        self.lines += 1;
        Ok(())
    }
    def get(self, key: str) -> str | None:
        return self.data.get(key)

    def set(self, key: str, value: str) -> None:
        if not valid_key(key):
            raise ValueError(f"bad key {key!r}")
        self._append(f"set {key} {_escape(value)}\n")  # disk first
        self.data[key] = value  # then memory

    def delete(self, key: str) -> bool:
        if key not in self.data:
            return False
        self._append(f"del {key}\n")
        del self.data[key]
        return True

    def _append(self, line: str) -> None:
        self.file.write(line.encode("utf-8"))
        self.file.flush()  # Python's buffer -> the OS
        os.fsync(self.file.fileno())  # the OS -> the disk
        self.lines += 1

The order matters: disk first, memory second. If the disk write fails, the map is unchanged, and the error goes back to the caller. Then memory and disk always agree.

A write passes through two buffers before it reaches the disk. Python's file object has its own buffer: flush empties it into the operating system. A Rust File has no buffer of its own, so it needs no flush. The operating system also keeps the bytes in memory for a while. sync_data in Rust and os.fsync in Python ask it to write them to the disk now.

That safety has a price. We measured 1,000 small writes in Rust on this machine. Without sync_data, one write took about 1.6 µs. With it, one write took about 2.3 ms: more than a thousand times slower. Real databases group many changes into one sync. This is called group commit. Your numbers depend on your disk and operating system.

Step 5: compaction

The log grows with every change, even when the data does not. 100 updates of one key make 100 lines for one value. Compaction rewrites the log with one line per key.

    /// All keys, sorted, so the output is stable.
    pub fn keys(&self) -> Vec<&str> {
        let mut keys: Vec<&str> = self.data.keys().map(String::as_str).collect();
        keys.sort_unstable();
        keys
    }

    pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
        self.data.len()
    }

    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        self.data.is_empty()
    }

    pub fn log_lines(&self) -> usize {
        self.lines
    }

    /// Rewrite the log with one line per live key. Old lines disappear.
    pub fn compact(&mut self) -> io::Result<()> {
        let tmp = self.path.with_extension("compact");
        let mut out = BufWriter::new(File::create(&tmp)?);
        for key in self.keys() {
            writeln!(out, "set {key} {}", escape(&self.data[key]))?;
        }
        let file = out.into_inner().map_err(|e| e.into_error())?; // flush the buffer
        file.sync_all()?; // the new log is on the disk
        fs::rename(&tmp, &self.path)?; // atomic swap: old log or new log, never half
        self.file = OpenOptions::new().append(true).open(&self.path)?;
        self.lines = self.data.len();
        Ok(())
    }
}
    def keys(self) -> list[str]:
        return sorted(self.data)

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self.data)

    def compact(self) -> None:
        tmp = self.path.with_suffix(".compact")
        with open(tmp, "wb") as f:
            for key in self.keys():
                f.write(f"set {key} {_escape(self.data[key])}\n".encode("utf-8"))
            f.flush()
            os.fsync(f.fileno())  # the new log is on the disk
        os.replace(tmp, self.path)  # atomic swap: old log or new log, never half
        self.file.close()
        self.file = open(self.path, "ab")
        self.lines = len(self.data)

We never write the new log over the old one. A crash in the middle would leave half a file. We write a new file, sync it, and then rename it over the old one. On Unix-like systems a rename is atomic: a reader sees the old log or the new log, never a mix.

On Linux, the rename itself is only durable after you also sync the folder that holds the file. Careful databases open the folder and call sync on it. We skip that step here to keep the code short.

Step 6: a small command-line shell

use std::error::Error;
use std::process::ExitCode;

const USAGE: &str = "usage: kvlog FILE (set KEY VALUE | get KEY | del KEY | keys | compact)";

fn run(args: &[String]) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let [file, cmd, rest @ ..] = args else {
        return Err(USAGE.into());
    };
    let mut store = kvlog::Store::open(file)?;
    match (cmd.as_str(), rest) {
        ("set", [key, value]) => store.set(key, value)?,
        ("get", [key]) => match store.get(key) {
            Some(value) => println!("{value}"),
            None => return Err(format!("{key}: not found").into()),
        },
        ("del", [key]) => {
            if !store.delete(key)? {
                return Err(format!("{key}: not found").into());
            }
        }
        ("keys", []) => store.keys().iter().for_each(|k| println!("{k}")),
        ("compact", []) => {
            let before = store.log_lines();
            store.compact()?;
            println!("log lines: {before} -> {}", store.log_lines());
        }
        _ => return Err(USAGE.into()),
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> ExitCode {
    let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().skip(1).collect();
    match run(&args) {
        Ok(()) => ExitCode::SUCCESS,
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("kvlog: {e}");
            ExitCode::FAILURE
        }
    }
}
USAGE = "usage: kvlog.py FILE (set KEY VALUE | get KEY | del KEY | keys | compact)"


def cli(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    if len(argv) < 2:
        print(USAGE, file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    with Store(argv[0]) as store:
        match argv[1:]:
            case ["set", key, value]:
                store.set(key, value)
            case ["get", key]:
                value = store.get(key)
                if value is None:
                    print(f"kvlog: {key}: not found", file=sys.stderr)
                    return 1
                print(value)
            case ["del", key]:
                if not store.delete(key):
                    print(f"kvlog: {key}: not found", file=sys.stderr)
                    return 1
            case ["keys"]:
                for key in store.keys():
                    print(key)
            case ["compact"]:
                before = store.lines
                store.compact()
                print(f"log lines: {before} -> {store.lines}")
            case _:
                print(USAGE, file=sys.stderr)
                return 1
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(cli(sys.argv[1:]))

Rust matches the argument slice with patterns like [file, cmd, rest @ ..]. Python 3.10 and newer match a list with case ["set", key, value]. The two look almost the same. Here is a real session with the Rust binary:

kvlog data.log set lang Rust
kvlog data.log set year 2015
kvlog data.log set lang "Rust and Python"
kvlog data.log get lang
kvlog data.log del year
kvlog data.log get year
kvlog data.log compact
cat data.log
Rust and Python
kvlog: year: not found
log lines: 4 -> 1
set lang Rust and Python

The get year line exits with 1. The Python version wrote a byte-for-byte equal log file. So the Python store can open a log that Rust wrote, and the other way round. A simple text format is easy to share between languages.

Step 7: tests

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    // A fresh folder for each test, so tests can run in parallel.
    fn temp_log(name: &str) -> PathBuf {
        let dir = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("kvlog-{}-{name}", std::process::id()));
        let _ = fs::remove_dir_all(&dir);
        fs::create_dir_all(&dir).unwrap();
        dir.join("data.log")
    }

    #[test]
    fn set_get_delete_and_reopen() {
        let path = temp_log("basic");
        let mut s = Store::open(&path).unwrap();
        s.set("a", "1").unwrap();
        s.set("b", "2").unwrap();
        s.set("b", "3").unwrap(); // a new value for b
        assert!(s.delete("a").unwrap());
        assert!(!s.delete("zzz").unwrap());
        drop(s);
        let s = Store::open(&path).unwrap(); // replay the log
        assert_eq!((s.get("a"), s.get("b")), (None, Some("3")));
        assert_eq!(s.log_lines(), 4);
    }

    #[test]
    fn any_text_survives_the_round_trip() {
        let path = temp_log("odd");
        let odd = "two\nlines, a \\ backslash and ü";
        Store::open(&path).unwrap().set("k", odd).unwrap();
        Store::open(&path).unwrap().set("empty", "").unwrap();
        let s = Store::open(&path).unwrap();
        assert_eq!((s.get("k"), s.get("empty")), (Some(odd), Some("")));
    }
import pytest

from kvlog import Store


def test_set_get_delete_and_reopen(tmp_path):
    path = tmp_path / "data.log"
    with Store(path) as s:
        s.set("a", "1")
        s.set("b", "2")
        s.set("b", "3")  # a new value for b
        assert s.delete("a")
        assert not s.delete("zzz")
    with Store(path) as s:  # replay the log
        assert (s.get("a"), s.get("b")) == (None, "3")
        assert s.lines == 4


def test_any_text_survives_the_round_trip(tmp_path):
    path = tmp_path / "data.log"
    odd = "two\nlines, a \\ backslash and ü"
    with Store(path) as s:
        s.set("k", odd)
        s.set("empty", "")
    with Store(path) as s:
        assert (s.get("k"), s.get("empty")) == (odd, "")


def test_a_torn_last_line_is_cut_off(tmp_path):
    path = tmp_path / "data.log"
    path.write_text("set a 1\nset b 2")  # the crash came mid-line
    with Store(path) as s:
        assert (s.get("a"), s.get("b")) == ("1", None)
        s.set("c", "3")
    assert path.read_text() == "set a 1\nset c 3\n"
    #[test]
    fn a_torn_last_line_is_cut_off() {
        let path = temp_log("torn");
        fs::write(&path, "set a 1\nset b 2").unwrap(); // the crash came mid-line
        let mut s = Store::open(&path).unwrap();
        assert_eq!((s.get("a"), s.get("b")), (Some("1"), None));
        s.set("c", "3").unwrap();
        assert_eq!(fs::read_to_string(&path).unwrap(), "set a 1\nset c 3\n");
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_bad_line_in_the_middle_is_an_error() {
        let path = temp_log("bad");
        fs::write(&path, "set a 1\noops\nset b 2\n").unwrap();
        let err = Store::open(&path).err().unwrap();
        assert!(err.to_string().ends_with("line 2: unknown line \"oops\""));
    }

    #[test]
    fn bad_keys_are_refused() {
        let mut s = Store::open(temp_log("key")).unwrap();
        let err = s.set("has space", "x").unwrap_err();
        assert_eq!(err.kind(), io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput);
    }

    #[test]
    fn compact_keeps_the_data_and_drops_old_lines() {
        let path = temp_log("compact");
        let mut s = Store::open(&path).unwrap();
        for i in 0..100 {
            s.set("counter", &i.to_string()).unwrap();
        }
        s.set("name", "kv").unwrap();
        assert_eq!(s.log_lines(), 101);
        s.compact().unwrap();
        s.set("after", "yes").unwrap(); // the new file still takes appends
        let s = Store::open(&path).unwrap();
        assert_eq!((s.get("counter"), s.log_lines(), s.len()), (Some("99"), 3, 3));
    }
}

running 6 tests
test tests::a_bad_line_in_the_middle_is_an_error ... ok
test tests::bad_keys_are_refused ... ok
test tests::a_torn_last_line_is_cut_off ... ok

test result: ok. 6 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.15s

Rust tests run in parallel threads. So each test gets its own folder, named after the test and the process id. Python's pytest gives each test a fresh folder through the tmp_path fixture. The torn-line test writes a broken file by hand. That is how you test a crash without crashing anything.

Project 3: a tiny HTTP API

Now other programs should use the store over the network. We build a small HTTP API on top of project 2. We use only the standard library, so you can see every byte. In real work you would use axum in Rust or FastAPI in Python, as in Web services with axum.

The contract of kvhttp
RequestAnswer
GET /health200 with ok
GET /kv200 with all keys as a JSON list, like ["a","b"]
GET /kv/KEY200 with the value, or 404
PUT /kv/KEY with a body204: the body is now the value
DELETE /kv/KEY204, or 404 if the key was not there
A wrong method on a known path405 with an Allow header
Broken or too large requests400, 413, 431 or 501

An HTTP/1.1 request is plain text. It has a request line, header lines, an empty line, and then the body. Each line ends with the two bytes \r\n. The standard RFC 9112 describes this format.

Step 1: the request type

//! kvhttp: a tiny HTTP API over the kvlog store. Standard library only.
use kvlog::Store;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, BufReader, Read, Write};
use std::sync::Mutex;

const MAX_LINE: usize = 8 * 1024; // the longest request line or header line
const MAX_HEADERS: usize = 100;
const MAX_BODY: usize = 1024 * 1024; // 1 MiB

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Request {
    pub method: String,
    pub path: String,
    pub headers: Vec<(String, String)>, // names in lower case
    pub body: Vec<u8>,
}

impl Request {
    pub fn header(&self, name: &str) -> Option<&str> {
        self.headers.iter().find(|(k, _)| k == name).map(|(_, v)| v.as_str())
    }
}
"""kvhttp: a tiny HTTP API over the kvlog store. Standard library only."""
import json
import socketserver
import threading
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from http import HTTPStatus

from kvlog import Store, valid_key

MAX_LINE = 8 * 1024  # the longest request line or header line
MAX_HEADERS = 100
MAX_BODY = 1024 * 1024  # 1 MiB


class HttpError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, status: int, why: str):
        super().__init__(why)
        self.status = status


@dataclass
class Request:
    method: str
    path: str
    headers: dict[str, str]  # names in lower case
    body: bytes = b""

Step 2: read one line, with limits

A server must never trust the client. A client can send a line of 10 GB, or never finish its line. So every read has a limit.

/// A request we refuse: the status code and a short reason.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
pub struct HttpError(pub u16, pub &'static str);

/// One line without its line end. Ok(None) means the input has ended.
fn read_line(r: &mut impl BufRead) -> Result<Option<String>, HttpError> {
    let mut buf = Vec::new();
    let limit = (MAX_LINE + 1) as u64; // never read more than this
    let n = r
        .by_ref()
        .take(limit)
        .read_until(b'\n', &mut buf)
        .map_err(|_| HttpError(400, "read error"))?;
    if n == 0 {
        return Ok(None);
    }
    if buf.len() > MAX_LINE {
        return Err(HttpError(400, "line too long"));
    }
    if buf.pop() != Some(b'\n') {
        return Err(HttpError(400, "line cut off"));
    }
    if buf.last() == Some(&b'\r') {
        buf.pop(); // HTTP lines end with \r\n
    }
    String::from_utf8(buf).map(Some).map_err(|_| HttpError(400, "not UTF-8"))
}
def _read_line(rfile) -> str | None:
    raw = rfile.readline(MAX_LINE + 1)  # never read more than this
    if not raw:
        return None
    if len(raw) > MAX_LINE:
        raise HttpError(400, "line too long")
    if not raw.endswith(b"\n"):
        raise HttpError(400, "line cut off")
    try:
        return raw[:-1].removesuffix(b"\r").decode("utf-8")
    except UnicodeDecodeError:
        raise HttpError(400, "not UTF-8") from None

take(limit) in Rust and readline(limit) in Python stop after 8 KiB, even without a newline. Without that limit, one bad client could fill all the memory of the server.

Step 3: headers and the whole request

/// Header lines up to the empty line. Names become lower case.
fn read_headers(r: &mut impl BufRead) -> Result<Vec<(String, String)>, HttpError> {
    let mut headers = Vec::new();
    loop {
        let line = read_line(r)?.ok_or(HttpError(400, "headers cut off"))?;
        if line.is_empty() {
            return Ok(headers); // an empty line ends the headers
        }
        if headers.len() == MAX_HEADERS {
            return Err(HttpError(431, "too many headers"));
        }
        let (name, value) = line.split_once(':').ok_or(HttpError(400, "bad header"))?;
        headers.push((name.trim().to_ascii_lowercase(), value.trim().to_string()));
    }
}
def _read_headers(rfile) -> dict[str, str]:
    headers = {}
    while True:
        line = _read_line(rfile)
        if line is None:
            raise HttpError(400, "headers cut off")
        if line == "":
            return headers  # an empty line ends the headers
        if len(headers) == MAX_HEADERS:
            raise HttpError(431, "too many headers")
        name, sep, value = line.partition(":")
        if not sep:
            raise HttpError(400, "bad header")
        headers[name.strip().lower()] = value.strip()
/// Read one request. Ok(None) means the client sent nothing at all.
pub fn read_request(r: &mut impl BufRead) -> Result<Option<Request>, HttpError> {
    let Some(first) = read_line(r)? else {
        return Ok(None);
    };
    let parts: Vec<&str> = first.split(' ').collect();
    let [method, path, version] = parts[..] else {
        return Err(HttpError(400, "bad request line"));
    };
    if version != "HTTP/1.1" && version != "HTTP/1.0" {
        return Err(HttpError(400, "bad request line"));
    }
    let headers = read_headers(r)?;
    let mut req = Request { method: method.into(), path: path.into(), headers, body: Vec::new() };
    if req.header("transfer-encoding").is_some() {
        return Err(HttpError(501, "chunked bodies are not supported"));
    }
    if let Some(len) = req.header("content-length") {
        let len: usize = len.parse().map_err(|_| HttpError(400, "bad Content-Length"))?;
        if len > MAX_BODY {
            return Err(HttpError(413, "body too large"));
        }
        req.body = vec![0; len];
        r.read_exact(&mut req.body).map_err(|_| HttpError(400, "body cut off"))?;
    }
    Ok(Some(req))
}
def read_request(rfile) -> Request | None:
    first = _read_line(rfile)
    if first is None:
        return None  # the client sent nothing at all
    parts = first.split(" ")
    if len(parts) != 3 or parts[2] not in ("HTTP/1.1", "HTTP/1.0"):
        raise HttpError(400, "bad request line")
    headers = _read_headers(rfile)
    req = Request(parts[0], parts[1], headers)
    if "transfer-encoding" in headers:
        raise HttpError(501, "chunked bodies are not supported")
    if "content-length" in headers:
        length = headers["content-length"]
        if not (length.isascii() and length.isdigit()):
            raise HttpError(400, "bad Content-Length")
        if int(length) > MAX_BODY:
            raise HttpError(413, "body too large")
        req.body = rfile.read(int(length))
        if len(req.body) != int(length):
            raise HttpError(400, "body cut off")
    return req

Header names are not case-sensitive, so we store them in lower case. We read the body with read_exact: exactly Content-Length bytes, or an error. We refuse Transfer-Encoding with 501. A real HTTP/1.1 server must understand the chunked format. Our tiny server says honestly that it does not.

Step 4: the response

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Response {
    pub status: u16,
    pub headers: Vec<(&'static str, String)>,
    pub body: Vec<u8>,
}

impl Response {
    pub fn text(status: u16, body: &str) -> Response {
        let ct = "text/plain; charset=utf-8".to_string();
        Response { status, headers: vec![("Content-Type", ct)], body: body.into() }
    }

    pub fn empty(status: u16) -> Response {
        Response { status, headers: Vec::new(), body: Vec::new() }
    }

    pub fn write_to(&self, w: &mut impl Write) -> io::Result<()> {
        write!(w, "HTTP/1.1 {} {}\r\n", self.status, reason(self.status))?;
        for (name, value) in &self.headers {
            write!(w, "{name}: {value}\r\n")?;
        }
        if self.status != 204 {
            write!(w, "Content-Length: {}\r\n", self.body.len())?; // never on a 204
        }
        write!(w, "Connection: close\r\n\r\n")?; // one request per connection
        w.write_all(&self.body)
    }
}
@dataclass
class Response:
    status: int
    body: bytes = b""
    headers: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)

    @classmethod
    def text(cls, status: int, body: str) -> "Response":
        return cls(status, body.encode("utf-8"), {"Content-Type": "text/plain; charset=utf-8"})

    def to_bytes(self) -> bytes:
        lines = [f"HTTP/1.1 {self.status} {HTTPStatus(self.status).phrase}"]
        lines += [f"{name}: {value}" for name, value in self.headers.items()]
        if self.status != 204:
            lines.append(f"Content-Length: {len(self.body)}")  # never on a 204
        lines.append("Connection: close")  # one request per connection
        return ("\r\n".join(lines) + "\r\n\r\n").encode("ascii") + self.body

Python gets the reason phrases, like "Not Found", from http.HTTPStatus. Rust's standard library has no HTTP types, so we write the table ourselves:

fn reason(status: u16) -> &'static str {
    match status {
        200 => "OK",
        204 => "No Content",
        400 => "Bad Request",
        404 => "Not Found",
        405 => "Method Not Allowed",
        413 => "Content Too Large",
        431 => "Request Header Fields Too Large",
        500 => "Internal Server Error",
        501 => "Not Implemented",
        _ => "Unknown",
    }
}

Two rules from the HTTP standard RFC 9110 are in this code. A 204 response must not have a Content-Length header. And a 405 response must have an Allow header. Status 413 is called "Content Too Large" since RFC 9110. Older texts call it "Payload Too Large".

Step 5: the router

/// The router: pick the action from the method and the path.
pub fn handle(store: &Mutex<Store>, req: &Request) -> Response {
    let path = req.path.split('?').next().unwrap_or(""); // ignore a query string
    let parts: Vec<&str> = path.trim_start_matches('/').split('/').collect();
    // If another thread panicked while it held the lock, keep going anyway.
    let mut store = store.lock().unwrap_or_else(|poisoned| poisoned.into_inner());
    match (req.method.as_str(), parts.as_slice()) {
        ("GET", ["health"]) => Response::text(200, "ok\n"),
        ("GET", ["kv"]) => {
            // Keys hold only letters, digits, '-', '_' and '.': no JSON escapes needed.
            let quoted: Vec<String> = store.keys().iter().map(|k| format!("\"{k}\"")).collect();
            let mut r = Response::text(200, &format!("[{}]", quoted.join(",")));
            r.headers = vec![("Content-Type", "application/json".into())];
            r
        }
        ("GET", ["kv", key]) => match store.get(key) {
            Some(value) => Response::text(200, value),
            None => Response::text(404, "no such key\n"),
        },
        ("PUT", ["kv", key]) => put(&mut store, key, &req.body),
        ("DELETE", ["kv", key]) => match store.delete(key) {
            Ok(true) => Response::empty(204),
            Ok(false) => Response::text(404, "no such key\n"),
            Err(e) => Response::text(500, &format!("{e}\n")),
        },
        (_, ["health"] | ["kv"] | ["kv", _]) => {
            let allow = if parts.len() == 2 { "GET, PUT, DELETE" } else { "GET" };
            let mut r = Response::text(405, "method not allowed\n");
            r.headers.push(("Allow", allow.into())); // a 405 must say what is allowed
            r
        }
        _ => Response::text(404, "not found\n"),
    }
}
def handle(store: Store, lock: threading.Lock, req: Request) -> Response:
    parts = req.path.split("?", 1)[0].lstrip("/").split("/")
    with lock:  # one request at a time touches the store
        match req.method, parts:
            case "GET", ["health"]:
                return Response.text(200, "ok\n")
            case "GET", ["kv"]:
                body = json.dumps(store.keys(), separators=(",", ":"))
                return Response(200, body.encode(), {"Content-Type": "application/json"})
            case "GET", ["kv", key]:
                value = store.get(key)
                if value is None:
                    return Response.text(404, "no such key\n")
                return Response.text(200, value)
            case "PUT", ["kv", key]:
                if not valid_key(key):
                    return Response.text(400, "bad key\n")
                try:
                    store.set(key, req.body.decode("utf-8"))
                except UnicodeDecodeError:
                    return Response.text(400, "body is not UTF-8\n")
                return Response(204)
            case "DELETE", ["kv", key]:
                if store.delete(key):
                    return Response(204)
                return Response.text(404, "no such key\n")
            case _, ["health"] | ["kv"] | ["kv", _]:
                allow = "GET, PUT, DELETE" if len(parts) == 2 else "GET"
                resp = Response.text(405, "method not allowed\n")
                resp.headers["Allow"] = allow  # a 405 must say what is allowed
                return resp
            case _:
                return Response.text(404, "not found\n")

Both languages match on a pair: the method and the path split into parts. ("GET", ["kv", key]) reads like the contract table. The store sits behind a mutex, so only one request at a time changes it. In Rust the Mutex owns the store: you cannot touch the store without the lock. In Python the lock and the store are two separate objects. Nothing stops you from forgetting the with lock:.

Step 6: one connection, and the server

fn put(store: &mut Store, key: &str, body: &[u8]) -> Response {
    if !kvlog::valid_key(key) {
        return Response::text(400, "bad key\n");
    }
    let Ok(value) = std::str::from_utf8(body) else {
        return Response::text(400, "body is not UTF-8\n");
    };
    match store.set(key, value) {
        Ok(()) => Response::empty(204),
        Err(e) => Response::text(500, &format!("{e}\n")),
    }
}

/// Serve one connection: read one request, write one response.
/// It works on anything that can read and write: a TcpStream or a test fake.
pub fn handle_connection<S: Read + Write>(mut stream: S, store: &Mutex<Store>) -> io::Result<()> {
    let response = {
        let mut reader = BufReader::new(&mut stream);
        match read_request(&mut reader) {
            Ok(Some(req)) => handle(store, &req),
            Ok(None) => return Ok(()), // the client sent nothing
            Err(HttpError(status, why)) => Response::text(status, &format!("{why}\n")),
        }
    }; // the reader ends here, so we can use the stream again
    response.write_to(&mut stream)?;
    stream.flush()
}
def handle_connection(rfile, wfile, store: Store, lock: threading.Lock) -> None:
    """Read one request, write one response. Works on sockets and on BytesIO."""
    try:
        req = read_request(rfile)
        if req is None:
            return
        resp = handle(store, lock, req)
    except HttpError as e:
        resp = Response.text(e.status, f"{e}\n")
    except OSError as e:  # the disk failed
        resp = Response.text(500, f"{e}\n")
    wfile.write(resp.to_bytes())
    wfile.flush()

handle_connection is generic. In Rust it takes any S: Read + Write. In Python it takes any two objects with read and write. The server gives it a real socket. The tests give it bytes in memory. Here is the shell that starts the server:

use std::net::TcpListener;
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let store = Arc::new(Mutex::new(kvlog::Store::open("kv.log")?));
    let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:8099")?;
    println!("listening on http://127.0.0.1:8099");
    for stream in listener.incoming() {
        let Ok(stream) = stream else { continue }; // one failed accept is not fatal
        stream.set_read_timeout(Some(Duration::from_secs(5)))?; // slow clients give up
        let store = Arc::clone(&store); // one more owner of the same store
        thread::spawn(move || {
            if let Err(e) = kvhttp::handle_connection(stream, &store) {
                eprintln!("connection error: {e}");
            }
        });
    }
    Ok(())
}
class Handler(socketserver.StreamRequestHandler):
    timeout = 5  # seconds: slow clients give up

    def handle(self) -> None:
        handle_connection(self.rfile, self.wfile, self.server.store, self.server.lock)


def serve(path: str = "kv.log", port: int = 8099) -> None:
    with socketserver.ThreadingTCPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), Handler) as server:
        server.store = Store(path)
        server.lock = threading.Lock()
        print(f"listening on http://127.0.0.1:{port}")
        server.serve_forever()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    serve()

Each connection gets its own thread. In Rust, Arc lets all threads own the same store. In Python, ThreadingTCPServer starts the threads for you. Both set a read timeout of 5 seconds, so a slow client cannot keep a thread busy forever. We did not start these servers for this book. To try one yourself, run it, then use curl in a second terminal:

cargo run -p kvhttp            # or: python3.14 kvhttp.py
curl -i -X PUT --data 'hello world' http://127.0.0.1:8099/kv/greeting
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8099/kv/greeting

Project 3: testing without a server

A test that opens a real port is slow, and it can fail because the port is busy. We do not need one. handle_connection only needs something that reads and writes bytes. So the test gives it a fake connection.

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use std::sync::Arc;
    use std::thread;

    // A fake connection: bytes in from a Vec, bytes out into a Vec. No network.
    struct FakeStream {
        input: io::Cursor<Vec<u8>>,
        output: Vec<u8>,
    }

    impl Read for FakeStream {
        fn read(&mut self, buf: &mut [u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
            self.input.read(buf)
        }
    }

    impl Write for FakeStream {
        fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
            self.output.write(buf)
        }
        fn flush(&mut self) -> io::Result<()> {
            Ok(())
        }
    }

    fn call(store: &Mutex<Store>, raw: &str) -> String {
        let mut s = FakeStream { input: io::Cursor::new(raw.into()), output: Vec::new() };
        handle_connection(&mut s, store).unwrap();
        String::from_utf8(s.output).unwrap()
    }
import io
import threading

import pytest

from kvhttp import handle_connection
from kvlog import Store

LOCK = threading.Lock()


@pytest.fixture
def store(tmp_path):
    with Store(tmp_path / "kv.log") as s:
        yield s


def call(store, raw: bytes) -> bytes:
    """A fake connection: bytes in from one BytesIO, bytes out into another."""
    out = io.BytesIO()
    handle_connection(io.BytesIO(raw), out, store, LOCK)
    return out.getvalue()

In Rust the fake is a small struct with the Read and Write traits. In Python, two io.BytesIO objects are enough. Now the tests read like a conversation with the server:

    fn temp_store(name: &str) -> Mutex<Store> {
        let dir = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("kvhttp-{}-{name}", std::process::id()));
        let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(&dir);
        std::fs::create_dir_all(&dir).unwrap();
        Mutex::new(Store::open(dir.join("kv.log")).unwrap())
    }
    #[test]
    fn put_get_delete() {
        let store = temp_store("crud");
        let put = "PUT /kv/greeting HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: 11\r\n\r\nhello world";
        assert_eq!(call(&store, put), "HTTP/1.1 204 No Content\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n");
        let got = call(&store, "GET /kv/greeting HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n");
        print!("{got}"); // shown with: cargo test -- --nocapture
        assert!(got.starts_with("HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n"));
        assert!(got.ends_with("\r\n\r\nhello world"));
        assert!(call(&store, "DELETE /kv/greeting HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n").starts_with("HTTP/1.1 204 "));
        assert!(call(&store, "GET /kv/greeting HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n").starts_with("HTTP/1.1 404 "));
    }

    #[test]
    fn list_keys_as_json() {
        let store = temp_store("list");
        for key in ["b", "a"] {
            call(&store, &format!("PUT /kv/{key} HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: 1\r\n\r\nx"));
        }
        assert!(call(&store, "GET /kv HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n").ends_with("\r\n\r\n[\"a\",\"b\"]"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn an_empty_connection_gets_no_answer() {
        assert_eq!(call(&temp_store("empty"), ""), "");
    }
def test_put_get_delete(store):
    put = b"PUT /kv/greeting HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: 11\r\n\r\nhello world"
    assert call(store, put) == b"HTTP/1.1 204 No Content\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n"
    got = call(store, b"GET /kv/greeting HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n")
    print(got.decode())  # shown with: pytest -s
    assert got.startswith(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n")
    assert got.endswith(b"\r\n\r\nhello world")
    assert call(store, b"DELETE /kv/greeting HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n").startswith(b"HTTP/1.1 204 ")
    assert call(store, b"GET /kv/greeting HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n").startswith(b"HTTP/1.1 404 ")


def test_list_keys_as_json(store):
    for key in ["b", "a"]:
        call(store, f"PUT /kv/{key} HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: 1\r\n\r\nx".encode())
    assert call(store, b"GET /kv HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n").endswith(b'\r\n\r\n["a","b"]')


def test_an_empty_connection_gets_no_answer(store):
    assert call(store, b"") == b""

With cargo test -- --nocapture, the test prints the real response bytes for the GET. Each line ends with \r\n:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 11
Connection: close

hello world

One table of bad requests checks every error status:

    #[test]
    fn bad_requests_get_the_right_status() {
        let store = temp_store("errors");
        let cases = [
            ("hello\r\n\r\n", "400 Bad Request"),
            ("GET /kv HTTP/9\r\n\r\n", "400 Bad Request"),
            ("GET /nope HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n", "404 Not Found"),
            ("POST /kv/a HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n", "405 Method Not Allowed"),
            ("PUT /kv/bad%20key HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: 1\r\n\r\nx", "400 Bad Request"),
            ("PUT /kv/a HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: 5\r\n\r\nab", "400 Bad Request"),
            ("PUT /kv/a HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: 9999999\r\n\r\n", "413 Content Too Large"),
            ("PUT /kv/a HTTP/1.1\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n", "501 Not Implemented"),
        ];
        for (raw, want) in cases {
            let got = call(&store, raw);
            assert!(got.starts_with(&format!("HTTP/1.1 {want}\r\n")), "{raw:?} gave {got:?}");
        }
        assert!(
            call(&store, "POST /kv/a HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n").contains("Allow: GET, PUT, DELETE\r\n")
        );
    }
@pytest.mark.parametrize("raw, want", [
    (b"hello\r\n\r\n", "400 Bad Request"),
    (b"GET /kv HTTP/9\r\n\r\n", "400 Bad Request"),
    (b"GET /nope HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n", "404 Not Found"),
    (b"POST /kv/a HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n", "405 Method Not Allowed"),
    (b"PUT /kv/bad%20key HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: 1\r\n\r\nx", "400 Bad Request"),
    (b"PUT /kv/a HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: 5\r\n\r\nab", "400 Bad Request"),
    (b"PUT /kv/a HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: 9999999\r\n\r\n", "413 Content Too Large"),
    (b"PUT /kv/a HTTP/1.1\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n", "501 Not Implemented"),
])
def test_bad_requests_get_the_right_status(store, raw, want):
    assert call(store, raw).startswith(f"HTTP/1.1 {want}\r\n".encode())


def test_405_says_what_is_allowed(store):
    assert b"Allow: GET, PUT, DELETE\r\n" in call(store, b"POST /kv/a HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n")

Last, a test with real threads. Eight threads send 25 PUT requests each, all at the same time. If the lock were missing, writes could mix in the log, or keys could get lost. The test checks that all 200 keys arrived.

    #[test]
    fn many_threads_share_one_store() {
        let store = Arc::new(temp_store("threads"));
        let workers: Vec<_> = (0..8)
            .map(|t| {
                let store = Arc::clone(&store);
                thread::spawn(move || {
                    for i in 0..25 {
                        let raw =
                            format!("PUT /kv/t{t}-{i} HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nok");
                        assert!(call(&store, &raw).starts_with("HTTP/1.1 204 "));
                    }
                })
            })
            .collect();
        workers.into_iter().for_each(|w| w.join().unwrap());
        assert_eq!(store.lock().unwrap().len(), 200);
    }
}
def test_many_threads_share_one_store(store):
    def work(t):
        for i in range(25):
            raw = f"PUT /kv/t{t}-{i} HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nok".encode()
            assert call(store, raw).startswith(b"HTTP/1.1 204 ")

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=work, args=(t,)) for t in range(8)]
    for th in threads:
        th.start()
    for th in threads:
        th.join()
    assert len(store) == 200
running 5 tests
test tests::an_empty_connection_gets_no_answer ... ok
test tests::bad_requests_get_the_right_status ... ok
test tests::list_keys_as_json ... ok
test tests::put_get_delete ... ok
test tests::many_threads_share_one_store ... ok

test result: ok. 5 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.28s

The Python suite prints 25 passed. That number is higher than the Rust count because pytest counts each row of the parametrized table as its own test.

In Python, an assert that fails inside a threading.Thread does not fail the test. The exception stays in that thread, and pytest only prints a warning. That is why our test checks len(store) == 200 in the main thread at the end. In Rust, join().unwrap() passes a panic from the thread on to the test.

What each language makes easy and hard

We wrote the same three programs twice. Here are real numbers from this machine. We counted lines of code without tests, comments and blank lines.

Then we ran both word counters on a generated text file of 18.4 MB: 400,000 lines and 3.2 million words. The Rust binary was a release build.

$ time ./target/release/wcount --top 3 big.txt
  400000 3200000 18401467 big.txt
  200817 tool
  200716 runs
  200395 program
real 0.22
$ time python3.14 wcount.py --top 3 big.txt
  400000 3200000 18401467 big.txt
  200817 tool
  200716 runs
  200395 program
real 1.27
$ time wc big.txt
  400000 3200000 18401467 big.txt
real 0.03

Rust took about 0.22 seconds. Python took about 1.27 seconds, so Rust was almost 6 times faster here. The system wc was faster than both, but it does much less work: it does not count words in a map.

Python made these easy

  • Arguments: argparse is in the standard library.
  • JSON: json.dumps. Rust needs the serde_json crate, or hand-written code.
  • HTTP names: http.HTTPStatus knows every reason phrase.
  • Tests: tmp_path, capsys and parametrize come with pytest.
  • Fake streams: any object with read and write works.

Rust made these easy

  • Shared state: the Mutex owns the store, so a missing lock does not compile.
  • Errors: Result and ? show every place that can fail.
  • Refactoring: when we split read_headers out, the compiler checked every caller.
  • Speed: about 6 times faster with no extra work.
  • Shipping: one binary file. Python needs an interpreter on the target machine.

Each language also had its own hard parts. In Rust, handle_connection needs an inner block. The BufReader borrows the stream, and that borrow must end before we can write the answer. You must understand borrows to see why. In Python, the risks hide until run time. The underscore in \w and the silent thread assertion are both bugs that a type checker cannot find. Only careful tests can.

"Design a key-value store" is a common interview question. Talk about the same points as this chapter: an append-only log, replay on start, torn writes, fsync and its cost, compaction with an atomic rename, and a lock for many clients. Then name the next steps: an index of file offsets instead of keeping all values in memory, checksums on each line, and group commit.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for small complete programs
PatternPurposeModelNote
Functional core, imperative shellMake the program testablefn run(args, stdin, out, err) -> i32main only connects real streams.
Exit codes 0, 1, 2Tell scripts what happenedExitCode::from(code as u8)2 means "the command was typed wrong".
Errors to stderrKeep stdout clean for pipeswriteln!(err, "wcount: {name}: {e}")Start the message with the program name.
Sort with a tie-breakerStable, testable outputb.1.cmp(&a.1).then_with(|| a.0.cmp(&b.0))Never test the order of a HashMap.
Append-only logSave changes safely and fastOpenOptions::new().create(true).append(true)Replay it on start.
Disk first, memory secondKeep both in agreementself.append(&line)?; self.data.insert(k, v);A failed write changes nothing.
Cut a torn tailRecover after a crashfile.set_len(good)?Or the next line glues onto the broken one.
Write, sync, renameReplace a file atomicallyfile.sync_all()?; fs::rename(&tmp, &path)?Python: os.replace(tmp, path).
Limit every readProtect a server from bad clientsr.by_ref().take(limit).read_until(b'\n', &mut buf)Python: rfile.readline(limit).
Match on method and pathA small router("GET", ["kv", key]) => ...Add a 405 arm with an Allow header.
Generic connection handlerTest a server without a networkfn handle_connection<S: Read + Write>(stream: S, ..)Python: pass two BytesIO objects.
Mutex that owns the dataShare state between threadsArc<Mutex<Store>>Python: a separate threading.Lock. Do not forget it.

Practice

Why does run return an exit code instead of calling std::process::exit?

  • It is faster.
  • Tests can call it and check the code.
  • Rust does not allow exit in a library.

process::exit ends the whole process, including the test runner. A returned number is easy to check.

The log file ends with set b 2 and no newline. What does Store::open do?

  • It returns an error.
  • It sets b to 2.
  • It ignores the line and cuts it off the file.

A line without its newline is a torn write from a crash. The change was never confirmed, so we drop it. Then we cut the file, so the next line starts clean.

Which response must not have a Content-Length header?

  • 200 OK
  • 204 No Content
  • 404 Not Found

RFC 9110 says a server must not send Content-Length in a 204 response.

In the Python server, what happens if you forget with lock: in handle?

  • The code does not run.
  • It runs, but two threads can write to the store at the same time.
  • pytest refuses to start.

Python cannot see that the store belongs to the lock. In Rust the store is inside the Mutex, so you cannot reach it without locking.

To replace a file in one atomic step, Python calls os.?(tmp, path).

A Python file object has its own buffer. Empty it into the OS with f.?, then sync it with os.fsync.

  1. Add a -l option to wcount that prints only the line count. Which functions change in each language?
    Answer

    In Rust: add lines_only: bool to Options, a "-l" arm in parse_args, and a branch in line or report. In Python: one more add_argument("-l", action="store_true"), then a branch in report. Add one test per language. The core stays pure, so the tests stay short.

  2. Put an LRU cache in front of a slow lookup. Show it in Python with the standard library, and say what Rust needs.
    Answer 
    from collections import OrderedDict

class LRU:
    def __init__(self, cap):
        self.cap, self.data = cap, OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.data:
            return None
        self.data.move_to_end(key)  # now the most recently used
        return self.data[key]

    def put(self, key, value):
        self.data[key] = value
        self.data.move_to_end(key)
        if len(self.data) > self.cap:
            self.data.popitem(last=False)  # drop the least recently used

c = LRU(2)
c.put("a", 1); c.put("b", 2); c.get("a"); c.put("c", 3)
print(list(c.data))
    ['a', 'c']

    "b" was used least recently, so it left. Rust's standard library has no ordered map like this. You can use a HashMap plus a linked list stored in a Vec with indexes instead of pointers, or the lru crate. For whole function results, Python also has functools.lru_cache.

  3. The store syncs after every write, and a bulk import of 100,000 keys is slow. Design a faster import that is still safe at the end.
    Answer

    Add a set_many method. It writes all lines with one buffered writer, then calls sync_data once, then updates the map. One sync instead of 100,000 saves almost all the time. If the process crashes during the import, replay keeps the complete lines and drops the torn one. So the caller must treat the import as done only after set_many returns.

  4. Expert. Our server closes the connection after one request. What must change to support keep-alive, where one connection carries many requests?
    Answer

    Loop in handle_connection: read a request, answer it, and read the next one with the same BufReader, because it may already hold bytes of the next request. Send Connection: keep-alive or leave the header out. Stop when the client sends Connection: close or the read times out. The body length must always be exact, or the next request is read from the wrong place.

  5. Expert. A test sends PUT /kv/a with Content-Length: 5 but only 2 body bytes. In production the client could simply wait. What protects our server, and what would be better?
    Answer

    In the test the input ends, so read_exact fails and we answer 400. In production the read would wait. The 5-second read timeout on the socket ends the wait. But each waiting client still holds one thread. A better server uses a thread pool with a fixed size, or async I/O, and limits the total time per request. This is exactly what frameworks like axum, hyper and uvicorn handle for you.

Key takeaways

  • Put the logic in a core that takes its inputs and outputs as arguments. Keep main thin. Then everything is testable.
  • Exit codes, stderr and stable output order are part of a tool's contract.
  • An append-only log with replay is a simple, safe way to store data. Handle torn tails, sync when it matters, and compact with write, sync, rename.
  • An HTTP server is a line reader with limits, a router and a response writer. Never trust the client.
  • A generic connection handler lets you test a server with bytes in memory, without a port.
  • Python was shorter and had more in its standard library. Rust was faster and caught more mistakes before the program ran.

Sources

  • RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1. The message format, Content-Length and the chunked rule.
  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics. Status codes, the 405 Allow rule and 413 Content Too Large.
  • Rust standard library: File. sync_all, sync_data, set_len and why errors on drop are lost.
  • The Cargo Book: Workspaces. One lock file and one build folder for several crates.
  • Python: socketserver. ThreadingTCPServer, StreamRequestHandler and its timeout.
  • Python: os. fsync and the atomic os.replace.

Certificate and interview level

This is the last chapter of the book. It shows the real Python certificates and the honest truth about Rust certificates. Then you test yourself with 60 quiz questions and 25 interview questions.

  • Choose the right Python Institute exam and check its current version.
  • Explain why there is no official Rust certificate and show Rust skill in other ways.
  • Rate your own Rust level with a checklist from beginner to expert.
  • Answer exam questions by tracing code by hand.
  • Give short, clear model answers in a technical interview.

How to use this last chapter

Here is an example. Mia has a job interview in three weeks. She also wants a Python certificate this year. She does not know where to start.

This chapter gives her a plan in four steps.

  1. Pick a target. Read about the Python exams and the Rust situation.
  2. Find your level. Go through the Rust skill checklist. Be honest with yourself.
  3. Test yourself. Do the 30 Rust and 30 Python quiz questions. They go from easy to hard.
  4. Practise speaking. Answer the 25 interview questions out loud. Then read the model answer.

Every quiz answer has a link to the chapter that teaches the idea. A wrong answer is useful. It shows you exactly what to read again.

All quiz code ran on rustc 1.99.0 and Python 3.14.3 on 15 November 2026. The exam facts come from the official pages on the same day.

A certificate says you passed a test. An interview checks how you think and explain. You need both skills. This chapter trains both.

Do not read the answers first. Cover them. Answer, then check. Reading answers feels like learning. It is not the same thing.

Python Institute certificates in 2026

Start with an example. Ana wants to prove her Python skill. She wants to buy a voucher for "PCAP". But which PCAP? On 15 November 2026 two versions exist: PCAP-31-03 and PCAP-31-04. The letters are the same. The topics are not.

The Python Institute is part of OpenEDG. It owns the best-known Python exams. Its main path has four levels. Click the tree to open it.

Each exam has an exam code. The code names one version of the exam. You buy a voucher for one exam code.

New versions and old versions

The Python Institute changed its exams this autumn.
