How the Python exams ask questions

Here is a question in the exam style. We wrote it for this book.

x = [1, 2, 3]
y = x
y += [4]
print(len(x))

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b = b + [4]
print(len(a))
4
3

Why two different answers? y = x makes a second name for the same list. += on a list changes that list in place. But b + [4] builds a new list. Then b points to the new list, and a keeps the old one.

To trace code means to follow it line by line on paper. Many exam questions test this skill. The PCAP page says the exam puts weight on reading code. The new pages list these question types:

  • Single-select. Choose one answer.
  • Multiple-select. Choose two or more answers.
  • Interactive. The old PCEP page names drag and drop, gap fill, sort and code insertion.
  • Code-based. Read code and give its result. PCAP-31-04 lists this type.
  • Scenario-based. A short story about a task. You choose the best action.

Use these steps for every code question.

  1. Read the last line first. Know what the program prints.
  2. Draw a small table with one row for each name.
  3. Go line by line. Write the new value after each line.
  4. Look for the classic traps: one object with two names, // with negative numbers, a mutable default, a loop else, the order of except clauses.
  5. Check each option against your table. Remove the impossible options first.

Time matters too. Divide the minutes by the number of questions.

Do not run code in your head too fast. A wrong answer often comes from one skipped line. Draw the table, even when the code looks easy.

Is there an official Rust certificate?

An example first. You search the web for "Rust certification". You find many offers. One page sells a "Rust Foundation Certified Rust Developer" course. It looks official. Is it?

No. On 15 November 2026 there is no official Rust certificate for developers. The Rust project does not offer one. The Rust Foundation does not offer one. Here is the short history.

  1. 2015 Rust 1.0. The language is stable. No exam exists.
  2. Nov 2023 A plan. The Rust Foundation says it will build a training and certification program.
  3. Jun 2026 RFTT starts. On 25 June the Foundation starts Rust Foundation Trusted Training. It checks training companies.
  4. Nov 2026 Still no personal exam. The RFTT page says it accredits providers, "not individuals or courses at this time".

RFTT is an accreditation. It checks companies, not people. The first five accredited companies are Doulos, Ferrous Systems, Integer 32, Mainmatter and Wyliodrin.

So what exists? Three kinds of paper, and none is an official Rust exam.

  • Course certificates. The Linux Foundation sells a four-day live course, "Programming in Rust" (LFD480). You get a certificate of completion and a digital badge. Its free course "Getting Started with Rust" (LFEL1002) gives a badge for 70% on the final exam.
  • Training from accredited companies. The RFTT companies can give their own course certificates.
  • Tool certificates. Ferrocene is a Rust compiler from Ferrous Systems. It is qualified for safety standards such as ISO 26262. That certifies the tool, not you.

These papers show that you learned something. They do not show that you can build software.

Do not pay for an "official Rust certificate". If a site says "Rust Foundation certified developer", check rustfoundation.org first. Today no such personal certificate exists. This can change, so check again before you pay.

What proves Rust skill instead

Two people apply for one Rust job. Ben writes "Rust: expert" on his CV. Chen sends one link. It is a small command-line tool on GitHub. It has a README, tests, CI and clean clippy output. Who gets the interview? Chen. The link is proof. The word "expert" is only a claim.

Good proof is something a reviewer can open and check. Here is a rough order, from weak to strong.

What do these steps mean?

  • Exercises. Rustlings and the Exercism Rust track are good practice. As proof they are weak, because everybody solves the same tasks.
  • A finished project. One small tool or service with tests, docs and CI. The three projects chapter gives you three ideas.
  • A published crate. Publish it on crates.io. The docs appear on docs.rs.
  • Merged pull requests. Fix a bug in a known open-source crate. A maintainer reviewed your code, so it counts a lot.
  • Rust at work. Say what you built and give a measured result. For example: "the import job went from 9 minutes to 40 seconds".

A reviewer often runs these commands on your project first. Make sure they all pass.

cargo fmt --check                            # is the code formatted?
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings    # any lint warnings?
cargo test                                   # do all tests pass?
cargo doc --no-deps                          # do the docs build?

What the reviewer checks

  • A README with one command to run the project.
  • Tests for the normal case and the edge cases.
  • Result for errors, not unwrap, in library code.
  • A green CI badge.

What builds trust

  • Small commits with clear messages.
  • Doc comments with examples that run as doc tests.
  • One measured claim, with the benchmark code.
  • Issues that you closed with a clear answer.

Ten unfinished toy projects do not help. A big project with no tests does not help either. One small finished project beats ten half projects.

A Rust skill checklist from beginner to expert

Here is how to use it. Read each card. Count the lines you can do without help. If you can do four of five, go to the next card. Each line links to the chapter that teaches it.

Beginner: you can write small programs

  • Use cargo new, run, check and test. (Setup)
  • Write functions, structs, enums and match. (Structs and enums)
  • Use Vec, HashMap, String and &str. (Collections, Strings)
  • Return Result and use ?. (Error handling)
  • Read a compiler error and fix it alone.

Proof: a small command-line tool with three tests.

Intermediate: you work with the borrow checker

  • Explain move, Copy, Clone and the borrow rules. (Ownership)
  • Add lifetime annotations when elision is not enough. (Lifetimes)
  • Write generic code with trait bounds. Implement Display and From. (Traits)
  • Write iterator chains and closures. (Iterators)
  • Choose between Box, Rc, Arc and RefCell. (Smart pointers)

Proof: a library crate with docs, clippy clean, in a workspace. (Cargo, Testing)

Advanced: you write concurrent code

  • Use threads, Send, Sync, Arc<Mutex> and channels. (Threads)
  • Write async code with tokio: tasks, select!, timeouts. (Async)
  • Use associated types, GATs and trait objects well. (Advanced traits)
  • Write a small macro_rules! macro. (Macros)
  • Design a public API with good error types. (API design)

Proof: a concurrent tool that is tested under load.

Professional: you ship services

  • Build a JSON API with axum, tracing and graceful shutdown. (Web services)
  • Build a command-line tool with clap. (CLI tools)
  • Use serde and sqlx with PostgreSQL. (Data and databases)
  • Write a Python module in Rust with PyO3. (PyO3)
  • Measure and speed up code with a profiler. (Performance)

Proof: a deployed service with tests, metrics and a measured result.

Expert: you review and teach

  • Write unsafe code with safety comments and test it with Miri. (Unsafe and FFI)
  • Explain layout, monomorphisation and binary size. (Performance)
  • Move a crate to a new edition and follow new releases. (Editions, Recent releases)
  • Build hard systems from scratch, like vector search or agents. (Vector search, Agents)
  • Review pull requests and mentor other people.

Proof: merged pull requests in known crates, talks or posts.

The levels follow the parts of this book. Level 1 is the first part. Level 5 uses the hard parts. The 15 patterns chapter is a good review for levels 2 and 3.

Many people skip level 2. They jump to async and unsafe code. Then every bug looks like magic. Learn ownership and traits first. The rest becomes much easier.

How to answer interview questions

An example first. The interviewer asks: "What is Arc<Mutex<T>>?" Compare two answers.

"It is for threads. You use it when the compiler complains."

"Arc is a pointer with a reference count that many threads can share. Mutex lets only one thread change the value at a time. Together they give shared state that threads can change. Example: a hit counter for four threads. The cost is an atomic count and a lock. If threads only read, I use Arc alone. With many writers, a channel or an atomic can be faster."

The strong answer has four parts. Use this shape for most questions.

  1. Define. Say what it is in one or two sentences.
  2. Example. Give one small, real example.
  3. Trade-off. Name one trade-off: a cost, a limit or a risk.
  4. Alternative. Say what you use instead, and when.

A live coding task needs a different shape. Talk while you work.

Interviewer: Find two numbers in a list that add up to a target.

You: Can the list be empty? Can a number appear twice?

Interviewer: Yes to both. Return the two positions.

You: The simple way checks every pair. That is quadratic time. I can do one pass with a hash map. That is linear time and linear memory.

Interviewer: Good. Please write it.

You: Done. Now I test an empty list, the pair 3 and 3, and a list with no answer.

Notice the order. Ask about the input. Say the simple solution and its cost. Improve it. Write it. Test the edge cases out loud. The full code is in interview question 19.

Do not say "it depends" and stop. Say what it depends on. For example: "It depends on the workload. For I/O-bound work I use asyncio. For CPU-bound work I use processes or Rust."

Patterns to remember

Patterns for exams and interviews
PatternPurposeModelNote
Trace names, then valuesCode output questionsb = a gives one list with two namesDraw arrows from names to objects.
Compile time or run time?Rust "what happens" questionsA second borrow_mut on a RefCell panics at run timeThe borrow checker never panics. RefCell can.
Read the error codeRust compile errorsE0382 moved value, E0502 borrow conflictrustc --explain E0502 prints a full lesson.
Top to bottom, first match winsmatch arms, except clauses, the MROexcept Exception before except ValueErrorPut the specific case first.
Lazy until pulledIterators, generators, futuresmap(...) prints nothing before sum()A Python generator works only once.
Define, example, trade-off, alternativeAny interview question"Arc shares, costs atomics, use Rc in one thread"Stop after four parts.
Big-O for time and memoryAlgorithm questionsTwo-sum: O(n) time, O(n) memorySay the simple solution first.
Name the versionFacts that change"Let chains: Rust 1.88, edition 2024"An old answer can be wrong today.
Check the exam codeBuying a voucherPCAP-31-04, not PCAP-31-03Old versions end on 30 November 2027.
Proof by linkShowing Rust skillA repo with tests and green CIA badge shows learning, not building.
Edge cases out loudLive codingEmpty list, one item, duplicates, UnicodeTest them before the interviewer asks.
I/O-bound or CPU-bound?Concurrency questions1,000 HTTP calls: asyncio. Resize images: processes.Normal Python threads do not speed up CPU work.

Practice: 30 Rust questions

The questions go from easy to hard. Each answer links to the chapter that teaches the idea. All programs use edition 2024 and ran on rustc 1.99.0.

Easy: R1 to R10

R1. You only want to know if your code compiles. You do not need a program to run. Which command is fastest?

  • cargo build --release
  • cargo check
  • cargo run

cargo check runs the compiler checks but makes no binary. We checked: no file appeared in target/debug. Read: Setup and first programs.

R2. What does this program print?

fn main() {
    let x = 5;
    let x = x * 2;
    {
        let x = x + 1;
        println!("{x}");
    }
    println!("{x}");
}
  • 11 then 10
  • 11 then 11
  • It does not compile, because x is not mut.

Each let makes a new x. This is shadowing, not mutation. The inner x lives only inside the braces. Read: Variables and types.

R3. What does this print?

fn main() {
    let a: u8 = 255;
    let b = a.wrapping_add(1);
    let c = a.checked_add(1);
    println!("{b} {c:?}");
}
  • 0 None
  • 256 Some(256)
  • It panics.

A u8 holds 0 to 255. wrapping_add goes round to 0. checked_add returns None on overflow. A plain + that overflows panics in a debug build and wraps in a release build. Read: Variables and types.

R4. What does this print?

fn main() {
    let mut n = 1;
    let r = loop {
        n *= 3;
        if n > 20 {
            break n;
        }
    };
    println!("{r}");
}
  • 9
  • 27
  • It does not compile: a loop has no value.

n becomes 3, 9, then 27. Now n > 20, so break n gives 27 to r. Only loop can break with a value. Read: Control flow.

R5. What happens?

fn next(x: i32) -> i32 {
    x + 1;
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", next(1));
}
  • It prints 2.
  • It prints 0.
  • It does not compile: error E0308, mismatched types.

The semicolon turns x + 1 into a statement. The body then gives (), but the signature promises i32. Remove the semicolon. Read: Functions and modules.

R6. What does this print?

fn main() {
    let s = "héllo";
    println!("{} {}", s.len(), s.chars().count());
}
  • 5 5
  • 6 5
  • 5 6

len counts bytes. The letter é takes 2 bytes in UTF-8. chars().count() counts characters. Read: Strings and text.

R7. What happens?

fn main() {
    let s = String::from("héllo");
    let part = &s[0..2];
    println!("{part}");
}
  • It prints hé.
  • It prints h.
  • It compiles, then panics at run time.

é uses bytes 1 and 2. Index 2 cuts it in half. The panic says the end byte index 2 is not a char boundary. Use s.get(0..2), which returns None here. Read: Strings and text.

R8. What does this print?

fn main() {
    let n = 7;
    let kind = match n {
        0 => "zero",
        x if x % 2 == 0 => "even",
        1..=9 => "small odd",
        _ => "big odd",
    };
    println!("{kind}");
}
  • even
  • small odd
  • big odd

Arms are tried from top to bottom. 7 is not 0. The guard x % 2 == 0 is false. The range 1..=9 matches. Read: Structs, enums and pattern matching.

R9. What does the second line print?

use std::num::ParseIntError;

fn add(a: &str, b: &str) -> Result<i32, ParseIntError> {
    Ok(a.parse::<i32>()? + b.parse::<i32>()?)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", add("4", "5"));
    println!("{:?}", add("4", "five"));
}
  • Ok(4)
  • Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit })
  • The program panics.

The first line prints Ok(9). In the second call, ? returns the error to the caller at once. Nothing panics. Read: Error handling.

R10. This does not compile (E0382). Which fix is best?

fn shout(s: String) -> usize {
    s.len()
}

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("Ann");
    let n = shout(name);
    println!("{name} {n}");
}
  • Call shout(name.clone()).
  • Change it to fn shout(s: &str) and call shout(&name).
  • Write let mut name.

shout(name) moves the String, so name is gone. A function that only reads should borrow. A clone also works, but it copies the text for no reason. The fixed program prints Ann 3. Read: Ownership and borrowing.

Medium: R11 to R20

R11. What happens?

fn main() {
    let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let first = &v[0];
    v.push(4);
    println!("{first}");
}
  • It prints 1.
  • It does not compile: error E0502.
  • It panics at run time.

first borrows v. A push may move the buffer to new memory. Then first would point to freed memory. The borrow checker stops this at compile time. Read: Ownership and borrowing.

R12. Why does this signature fail with E0106, missing lifetime specifier?

fn longest(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}
  • A function cannot return &str.
  • The compiler cannot tell if the result borrows from a or from b.
  • Both strings must be 'static.

Elision can copy the lifetime of one input reference, or of &self, to the output. Here there are two inputs and no self. Write fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str. Read: Lifetimes.

R13. What does this print?

trait Greet {
    fn name(&self) -> String;
    fn hello(&self) -> String {
        format!("Hello, {}", self.name())
    }
}
struct Ann;
struct Bo;
impl Greet for Ann {
    fn name(&self) -> String { "Ann".into() }
}
impl Greet for Bo {
    fn name(&self) -> String { "Bo".into() }
    fn hello(&self) -> String { "Hi!".into() }
}
fn main() {
    let all: Vec<Box<dyn Greet>> = vec![Box::new(Ann), Box::new(Bo)];
    for g in &all {
        println!("{}", g.hello());
    }
}
  • Hello, Ann then Hello, Bo
  • Hello, Ann then Hi!
  • It does not compile: a trait with a default method cannot be dyn.

Ann uses the default method. Bo overrides it. Each Box<dyn Greet> calls through a vtable, so each value runs its own method. Read: Traits and generics.

R14. Which sentence is true about this code?

struct Meters(f64);

impl From<f64> for Meters {
    fn from(v: f64) -> Self {
        Meters(v)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let a = Meters::from(1.5);
    let b: Meters = 2.5.into();
    println!("{}", a.0 + b.0);
}
  • You must also write impl Into<Meters> for f64.
  • It compiles and prints 4. From gives you into() for free.
  • into() works only for built-in number types.

The standard library has a blanket impl: if U: From<T>, then T: Into<U>. So you implement From and get Into. Read: API design and idioms.

R15. In which order do the lines appear?

fn main() {
    let v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4];
    let it = v.iter().map(|x| {
        println!("see {x}");
        x * 10
    });
    println!("before");
    let total: i32 = it.take(2).sum();
    println!("{total}");
}
  • see 1, see 2, see 3, see 4, before, 30
  • before, see 1, see 2, 30
  • before, see 1, see 2, see 3, see 4, 30

map is lazy. Nothing runs until sum pulls items. take(2) stops after two items, so 3 and 4 are never seen. Read: Iterators and closures.

R16. call_twice must accept a closure that changes count and call it two times. Which bound fits?

fn call_twice<F: ???>(mut f: F) {
    f();
    f();
}

fn main() {
    let mut count = 0;
    call_twice(|| count += 1);
    println!("{count}");
}
  • F: Fn()
  • F: FnMut()
  • F: FnOnce()

The closure changes a captured variable, so it is FnMut. With Fn you get E0594. FnOnce allows one call only, so the second call gives E0382. With FnMut it prints 2. Read: Iterators and closures.

R17. What happens?

use std::cell::RefCell;

fn main() {
    let c = RefCell::new(vec![1]);
    let r = c.borrow();
    c.borrow_mut().push(2);
    println!("{r:?}");
}
  • It does not compile: two borrows.
  • It compiles, then panics: "RefCell already borrowed".
  • It prints [1, 2].

RefCell moves the borrow rules to run time. r still holds a shared borrow, so borrow_mut panics. Drop r first, or use try_borrow_mut. Read: Smart pointers and interior mutability.

R18. Your Cargo.toml says this. Which versions can Cargo choose?

[dependencies]
serde = "1.0.200"
  • Only 1.0.200
  • 1.0.200 or newer, but below 2.0.0
  • 1.0.200 or newer, but below 1.1.0

A plain version is a caret requirement. Cargo may pick any semver-compatible version. Cargo.lock then pins the exact one. We tested this rule with the semver crate: 1.9.0 matches, 2.0.0 does not. Read: Cargo, crates and workspaces.

R19. Run only the tests whose name contains parse, and show their println! output. Which command is right?

  • cargo test --nocapture parse
  • cargo test parse -- --nocapture
  • cargo run --test parse

Arguments before -- go to Cargo. Arguments after -- go to the test program. parse is a name filter. The first command fails with an unexpected argument error. On Rust 1.99, --no-capture also works. Read: Testing and tooling.

R20. What does this print?

fn main() {
    let v = [1, 3, 5, 7];
    println!("{:?} {:?}", v.binary_search(&5), v.binary_search(&4));
}
  • Ok(2) None
  • Ok(2) Err(2)
  • Ok(3) Err(3)

A found value gives Ok(index). A missing value gives Err(index): the place where you can insert it and keep the order. It costs O(log n) and needs a sorted slice. Read: Algorithms 1.

Hard: R21 to R30

R21. What happens?

use std::rc::Rc;
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let data = Rc::new(5);
    let h = thread::spawn(move || println!("{data}"));
    h.join().unwrap();
}
  • It prints 5.
  • It does not compile: Rc<i32> cannot be sent between threads safely (E0277).
  • It panics at run time.

Rc changes its count without atomic operations. So Rc is not Send. Use Arc. Read: Threads and shared state.

R22. What does this print?

async fn hello() {
    println!("hello");
}

fn main() {
    let f = hello();
    println!("made");
    drop(f);
}
  • hello then made
  • Only made
  • made then hello

Calling an async fn only builds a future. A future does nothing until someone polls it, with .await or an executor. Here we drop it without polling. Read: Async and await.

R23. This uses tokio 1.54. What does it print?

use std::time::{Duration, Instant};
use tokio::time::sleep;

async fn job(ms: u64) -> u64 {
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(ms)).await;
    ms
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let t = Instant::now();
    let (a, b) = tokio::join!(job(300), job(200));
    println!("{a} {b} {:.1}s", t.elapsed().as_secs_f64());
    let t = Instant::now();
    let a = job(300).await;
    let b = job(200).await;
    println!("{a} {b} {:.1}s", t.elapsed().as_secs_f64());
}
  • 300 200 0.5s then 300 200 0.5s
  • 300 200 0.3s then 300 200 0.5s
  • 200 300 0.3s then 300 200 0.5s

join! polls both futures at the same time. The waits overlap, so it takes as long as the longest one. The results come back in argument order. Two .await lines in a row take 0.3 + 0.2 seconds. Read: Async and await.

R24. What does this print?

fn sum<const N: usize>(a: [i32; N]) -> i32 {
    a.iter().sum()
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", sum([1, 2, 3]) + sum([10; 2]));
}
  • 26
  • 16
  • It does not compile: the arrays have different lengths.

N is part of the type. The compiler makes one sum for 3 and one for 2. [10; 2] means [10, 10]. So 6 + 20 = 26. Read: Advanced traits and types.

R25. let s: Box<dyn Store> = Box::new(Log); fails with E0038. Why?

use std::fmt::Debug;

trait Store {
    fn put<T: Debug>(&self, v: T);
}
  • Store has no default method.
  • put is generic, so it cannot go into a vtable.
  • Box cannot hold a trait.

A vtable needs one function pointer per method. A generic method has one copy per type T. So the trait is not dyn compatible. Take v: &dyn Debug instead. We tested that version: it compiles and prints 1. Read: Advanced traits and types.

R26. What does total!(1, 2, 3,) print?

macro_rules! total {
    ($($x:expr),* $(,)?) => { 0 $(+ $x)* };
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", total!(1, 2, 3,));
}
  • 6
  • It does not compile because of the last comma.
  • 0

$(...),* repeats for each expression. $(,)? accepts one optional comma at the end. The call expands to 0 + 1 + 2 + 3. Read: Macros.

R27. Which line needs an unsafe block?

fn main() {
    let x = 5;
    let p = &raw const x;   // line A
    let y = unsafe { *p };  // line B
    println!("{y}");
}
  • Line A
  • Line B
  • Both lines

Making a raw pointer is safe. Reading through it is one of the five unsafe powers. Without unsafe, line B gives E0133. Read: Unsafe Rust and FFI.

R28. On a 64-bit machine, what does this print?

use std::mem::size_of;

fn main() {
    println!(
        "{} {} {}",
        size_of::<Box<u8>>(),
        size_of::<Option<Box<u8>>>(),
        size_of::<Option<u8>>()
    );
}
  • 8 16 2
  • 8 8 2
  • 8 9 1

A Box is never null. So Rust uses the null value to mean None. This is the niche optimisation. A u8 has no free value, so Option<u8> needs an extra byte. Read: Memory and performance.

R29. This uses serde and serde_json. What does it print?

use serde::Serialize;

#[derive(Serialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
struct User {
    user_id: u32,
    #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
    nick: Option<String>,
}

fn main() {
    let u = User { user_id: 7, nick: None };
    println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&u).unwrap());
}
  • {"user_id":7,"nick":null}
  • {"userId":7}
  • {"userId":7,"nick":null}

rename_all = "camelCase" renames the fields. skip_serializing_if leaves out nick when it is None. Read: Data, serde and databases.

R30. Which sentence is true?

fn main() {
    let a = Some(3);
    let b = Some(4);
    if let Some(x) = a && let Some(y) = b && x < y {
        println!("{}", x + y);
    }
}
  • It prints 7 in every edition.
  • It prints 7, but only in the 2024 edition.
  • It never compiles: && is not allowed after if let.

Let chains became stable in Rust 1.88, for the 2024 edition only. With edition 2021 the compiler says let chains are only allowed in Rust 2024 or later. Read: Rust editions and Rust recent releases.

Practice: 30 Python questions

These questions use the style of the Python Institute exams. They are our own questions, not real exam items. All programs ran on Python 3.14.3.

Easy: P1 to P10

P1. What does this print?

print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, -7 // 2)
  • 3.5 3 -3
  • 3.5 3 -4
  • 3 3 -4

/ always gives a float. // is floor division. It rounds down, toward minus infinity. So -7 // 2 is -4. Read: Variables and types.

P2. What does this print?

items = [0, "", [], "0", None, 0.0]
print(sum(1 for x in items if x))
  • 0
  • 1
  • 2

0, the empty string, the empty list, None and 0.0 are all false. The string "0" is not empty, so it is true. Read: Control flow.

P3. What does this print?

for n in [3, 5, 7]:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        print("even found")
        break
else:
    print("no even")
  • even found
  • no even
  • Nothing

The else of a loop runs when the loop ends without break. Read: Control flow.

P4. What does this print?

s = "Python"
print(s[::-1], s[1:4], s[-2:])
  • nohtyP yth on
  • nohtyP ytho on
  • nohtyP yth n

A step of -1 reverses the string. [1:4] takes index 1, 2 and 3. [-2:] takes the last two characters. Read: Strings and text.

P5. What does this print?

x = 3.14159
print(f"{x:.2f}|{42:>5}|{7:03d}")
  • 3.14|42 |007
  • 3.14| 42|007
  • 3.1| 42|7

.2f gives two decimals. >5 puts the value on the right of 5 spaces. 03d pads with zeros to 3 digits. Read: Strings and text.

P6. What does this print?

d = {"b": 1, "a": 2}
d["c"] = 3
d["b"] = 9
print(list(d))
  • ['a', 'b', 'c']
  • ['b', 'a', 'c']
  • ['a', 'c', 'b']

A dict keeps insertion order. A new value for an old key does not move the key. Read: Collections.

P7. What does this print?

a = {1, 2, 3}
b = {2, 3, 4}
print(a & b, a | b, a - b)
  • {2, 3} {1, 2, 3, 4} {1}
  • {2, 3} {1, 2, 3, 2, 3, 4} {1}
  • {1, 4} {1, 2, 3, 4} {4}

& keeps items in both sets. | joins them without repeats. - keeps items of a that are not in b. Read: Collections.

P8. What does this print?

def add(x, items=[]):
    items.append(x)
    return items

add(1)
print(add(2))
  • [2]
  • [1, 2]
  • A TypeError

The default list is made once, when def runs. Every call shares it. Write items=None and make a new list inside. Read: Functions and modules.

P9. What does this print?

def f():
    try:
        return "try"
    finally:
        print("finally")

print(f())
  • Only try
  • try then finally
  • finally then try

finally runs before the function really returns. Then print shows the returned value. Read: Error handling.

P10. What does this print?

try:
    int("x")
except Exception:
    print("general")
except ValueError:
    print("value")
  • value
  • general
  • general then value

Python checks except clauses from top to bottom. ValueError is a subclass of Exception, so the first clause catches it. Put the specific clause first. Read: Error handling.

Medium: P11 to P20

P11. What does this print?

a = [1, 2]
b = a
c = [1, 2]
print(a == c, a is c, a is b)
  • True False True
  • True True True
  • False False True

== compares values. is compares identity. c is an equal but different list. Read: The Python data model.

P12. What does this print?

grid = [[0] * 2] * 2
grid[0][0] = 9
print(grid)
  • [[9, 0], [0, 0]]
  • [[9, 0], [9, 0]]
  • An IndexError

The outer * 2 copies the reference to one inner list. Both rows are the same object. Write [[0] * 2 for _ in range(2)]. Read: The Python data model.

P13. What does this print?

class Money:
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Money({self.v})"
    def __str__(self):
        return f"${self.v}"

m = Money(5)
print(m, [m], f"{m!r}")
  • $5 [$5] $5
  • $5 [Money(5)] Money(5)
  • Money(5) [Money(5)] $5

print uses __str__. A list shows its items with __repr__. !r asks for __repr__ in an f-string. Read: The Python data model.

P14. What happens?

x = 10

def f():
    print(x)
    x = 5

f()
  • It prints 10.
  • It prints 5.
  • UnboundLocalError

x = 5 makes x local in the whole function. So print(x) reads a local name that has no value yet. Pass x as a parameter instead. Read: Functions, closures and decorators.

P15. What does this print?

fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fs])
  • [0, 1, 2]
  • [2, 2, 2]
  • [3, 3, 3]

Each lambda looks up i when it runs, not when it is made. After the loop, i is 2. Fix it with lambda i=i: i. Read: Functions, closures and decorators.

P16. What does this print?

import functools

def log(fn):
    @functools.wraps(fn)
    def inner(*args, **kwargs):
        print("call", fn.__name__)
        return fn(*args, **kwargs)
    return inner

@log
def area(w, h):
    return w * h

print(area(2, 3), area.__name__)
  • Only 6 area
  • call area then 6 inner
  • call area then 6 area

The wrapper prints first, then returns 6. functools.wraps copies __name__ from area to inner. Read: Functions, closures and decorators.

P17. What does the first line print?

class A:
    def who(self): return "A"
class B(A):
    def who(self): return "B" + super().who()
class C(A):
    def who(self): return "C" + super().who()
class D(B, C):
    def who(self): return "D" + super().who()

print(D().who())
print([k.__name__ for k in D.__mro__])
  • DBA
  • DBCA
  • DCBA

super() follows the MRO, not the parent class. The second line prints ['D', 'B', 'C', 'A', 'object']. So the super() in B calls C. Read: Classes, dataclasses and protocols.

P18. What does this print?

class Box:
    def __init__(self):
        self.__secret = 1
        self._hint = 2

b = Box()
print(hasattr(b, "__secret"), hasattr(b, "_Box__secret"), b._hint)
  • True False 2
  • False True 2
  • An AttributeError for _hint

Inside a class, __secret becomes _Box__secret. This is name mangling. One underscore is only a convention. Read: Classes, dataclasses and protocols.

P19. What does this print?

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Tagged:
    x: int
    tags: list = field(default_factory=list)

t = Tagged(1)
t.tags.append("a")
print(t, Tagged(1) == Tagged(1))
  • FrozenInstanceError
  • Tagged(x=1, tags=['a']) True
  • Tagged(x=1, tags=[]) True

frozen=True blocks t.x = 2 with FrozenInstanceError. It does not freeze the list inside. Frozen is shallow. Use a tuple for real immutability. Read: Classes, dataclasses and protocols.

P20. What happens at run time, and what does mypy say?

def first(xs: list[int]) -> int | None:
    return xs[0] if xs else None

n = first([3])
print(n + 1)
  • A TypeError at run time.
  • It prints 4. mypy reports an error: unsupported operand types for +.
  • It prints 4, and mypy finds no problem.

Type hints do nothing at run time. mypy sees int | None and wants a check for None first. Read: Type hints.

Hard: P21 to P30

P21. Which Python version first accepts this syntax?

def last[T](xs: list[T]) -> T:
    return xs[-1]

print(last([1, 2, 3]), last(["a", "b"]))
  • 3.10
  • 3.12
  • 3.14

PEP 695 added this type parameter syntax in Python 3.12. Before, you wrote T = TypeVar("T"). It printed 3 b on 3.12 and on 3.14. Read: Type hints and Python versions.

P22. What does this print?

g = (x * x for x in range(4))
print(sum(g), sum(g))
  • 14 14
  • 14 0
  • A StopIteration error

A generator runs once. The first sum uses all items: 0 + 1 + 4 + 9. The second sum gets nothing. Read: Generators and asyncio.

P23. What does this print?

def gen():
    yield 1
    yield from [2, 3]
    return 4

print(list(gen()))
  • [1, 2, 3, 4]
  • [1, 2, 3]
  • [1, [2, 3]]

yield from passes on each item of the list. The return value 4 goes into StopIteration.value. list() ignores it. Read: Generators and asyncio.

P24. What does this print?

import asyncio
import time

async def job(name, d):
    await asyncio.sleep(d)
    print(name)
    return d

async def main():
    t = time.perf_counter()
    r = await asyncio.gather(job("a", 0.2), job("b", 0.1))
    print(r, round(time.perf_counter() - t, 1))

asyncio.run(main())
  • a, b, [0.2, 0.1] 0.3
  • b, a, [0.2, 0.1] 0.2
  • b, a, [0.1, 0.2] 0.2

The sleeps overlap, so the total is the longest sleep. b finishes first and prints first. gather returns results in argument order. Compare question R23. Read: Generators and asyncio.

P25. What does this print?

import asyncio

async def bad():
    raise ValueError("boom")

async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tg.create_task(bad())
    except* ValueError as eg:
        print(type(eg).__name__, len(eg.exceptions))

asyncio.run(main())
  • ValueError 1
  • ExceptionGroup 1
  • Nothing. The error is lost.

A TaskGroup collects the errors of its tasks into an ExceptionGroup. except* matches the ValueError parts inside it. Read: Generators and asyncio.

P26. What does this print?

from collections import Counter

c = Counter("banana")
print(c.most_common(2))
  • [('a', 3), ('n', 2)]
  • [('b', 1), ('a', 3)]
  • {'a': 3, 'n': 2}

Counter counts each letter. most_common(2) returns a list of the two biggest counts, as pairs. Read: The standard library you need.

P27. What does this print?

import heapq

h = [5, 1, 4]
heapq.heapify(h)
heapq.heappush(h, 2)
print([heapq.heappop(h) for _ in range(3)])
  • [5, 1, 4]
  • [1, 2, 4]
  • [1, 4, 5]

heapq is a min-heap. heappop always returns the smallest item. Push and pop cost O(log n). Dijkstra uses exactly this. Read: Algorithms 2.

P28. On the normal build of Python 3.14, what does this print?

import sys

print(sys._is_gil_enabled())
  • True
  • False
  • An AttributeError

The normal build of 3.14 still has the GIL. The free-threaded build, python3.14t, is a separate build. There it normally prints False. Read: Performance and how CPython works.

P29. In a new uv project you run uv add httpx. Which two files change?

  • requirements.txt and setup.py
  • pyproject.toml and uv.lock
  • Only .python-version

uv writes "httpx>=0.28.1" into the dependencies list in pyproject.toml. It updates the lock file with exact versions. It also installs the package into .venv. We saw this with uv 0.10.12. Read: Packaging and testing.

P30. What does this print on Python 3.14?

name = "Bo"
t = t"Hi {name}!"
print(type(t).__name__, t.strings, t.values)
  • str Hi Bo!
  • Template ('Hi ', '!') ('Bo',)
  • A SyntaxError

A t-string (PEP 750, new in 3.14) does not make a str. It makes a Template. It keeps the fixed text and the values apart. On Python 3.13 the same line is a SyntaxError. Read: Python versions.

Practice: 25 interview questions

Say your answer out loud first. Use the four-part shape. Then open the model answer. The model answers are short on purpose. In a real interview, add one example from your own work.

  1. Rust What is ownership? Why does Rust not need a garbage collector?
    Model answer

    Each value has one owner, usually a variable. When the owner goes out of scope, Rust drops the value and frees its memory. You can move ownership, or lend the value with a borrow. The compiler checks all of this before the program runs.

    So memory is freed at a known point. A garbage collector finds unused memory while the program runs. That costs time and can pause the program. Python uses reference counting plus a cycle collector. See Ownership and borrowing.

  2. Rust State the borrow rules. Which bug do they prevent?
    Model answer

    At one moment you have either many shared references or one mutable reference. And a reference must never outlive its value.

    Example bug: you keep a reference into a Vec, then you push. The push may move the buffer. The reference would point to freed memory. In C++ this is called iterator invalidation. Rust rejects it with E0502. The same rules also stop data races between threads. See Ownership and borrowing.

  3. Rust A function needs text. Do you take String or &str?
    Model answer

    String owns its text on the heap. &str is a borrowed view of UTF-8 text. If the function only reads, I take &str. Then callers can pass a &String, a literal or a slice.

    I take String when the function keeps the text, for example in a struct. Another option is impl Into<String>. Then the caller decides to move or to copy. See Strings and text and API design.

  4. Rust What does a lifetime annotation do?
    Model answer

    It does not change how long a value lives. It only describes a relation between references. fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str says: the result is valid only while both inputs are valid.

    The borrow checker then checks every caller. Most of the time, the elision rules write lifetimes for you. If the annotations get very hard, owning the data is often simpler. See Lifetimes.

  5. Rust Compare Result with exceptions. When do you panic?
    Model answer

    Result<T, E> is a normal return value. The type shows that a call can fail. The compiler makes you handle it. The ? operator passes the error up with one character.

    Python exceptions do not appear in the signature. Any line can raise one. I panic only for bugs, like a broken rule inside my own code. In tests and small scripts, unwrap or expect is fine. In library code, I return Result. See Error handling.

  6. Rust Generics or trait objects: how do you choose?
    Model answer

    A generic function like fn show<T: Display>(x: T) uses static dispatch. The compiler makes one copy for each type. Calls are fast and can be inlined. But the binary grows.

    A trait object like Box<dyn Display> uses dynamic dispatch through a vtable. There is one copy of the code and a small cost per call. I use it for mixed types in one list, or for plugins. The trait must be dyn compatible. See Traits and generics and Advanced traits.

  7. Rust What are Send and Sync? Why is Rc not Send? Show shared state.
    Model answer

    Send means a value can move to another thread. Sync means a shared reference can be used from many threads. The compiler adds both traits by itself. Rc updates its count without atomic operations. Two threads could break the count, so Rc is not Send. Arc uses atomic counts.

    use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let hits = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0)); // shared, thread-safe counter
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..4 {
        let hits = Arc::clone(&hits); // one handle per thread
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for _ in 0..1000 {
                *hits.lock().unwrap() += 1; // lock, add, unlock at end of line
            }
        }));
    }
    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
    println!("{}", *hits.lock().unwrap());
}
    4000
    import threading

hits = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def work():
    global hits
    for _ in range(1000):
        with lock:  # without the lock, updates can be lost
            hits += 1

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print(hits)
    4000

    In Python the lock matters too. hits += 1 is several steps, not one. See Threads and shared state.

  8. Rust How does async work in Rust?
    Model answer

    An async fn returns a future. A future is a state machine. It does nothing on its own. An executor, like the tokio runtime, calls poll on it. When the future must wait, it returns Pending. It keeps the waker that came with the poll call. When the data is ready, the waker asks the executor to poll again.

    So many tasks share a few threads. Two rules: never block inside async code, and remember that futures are lazy. For blocking work, use spawn_blocking. Pin exists because some futures point into themselves and must not move. See Async and await.

  9. Rust When do you use Box, Rc, Arc and RefCell?
    Model answer

    Box<T>: one owner, value on the heap. I use it for recursive types and trait objects. Rc<T>: many owners in one thread. Arc<T>: many owners across threads.

    RefCell<T> lets me change a value behind a shared reference. It checks borrows at run time and panics on a conflict. Common pairs are Rc<RefCell<T>> in one thread and Arc<Mutex<T>> across threads. Weak breaks cycles, for example a child that points to its parent. See Smart pointers.

  10. Rust What does unsafe allow? How do you keep unsafe code safe?
    Model answer

    unsafe gives five extra powers. Dereference a raw pointer. Call an unsafe function. Use a mutable static. Implement an unsafe trait. Read the fields of a union. The borrow checker still runs inside unsafe.

    I keep unsafe blocks small and put a safe API around them. Each block gets a // SAFETY: comment that says why the rules hold. I run the tests under Miri, which finds undefined behaviour. See Unsafe Rust and FFI.

  11. Rust Your Rust service is slow. What do you do?
    Model answer

    First I measure. I never guess. I check that it runs as a release build. Then I write a benchmark with criterion, or I profile with perf and a flamegraph. I look at the hottest function.

    Common causes are many small allocations, clone in a loop, a bad algorithm, or a lock that many threads wait for. I fix one thing and measure again. Later steps are LTO, codegen-units = 1 or PGO. See Memory and performance.

  12. Rust How do you design errors for a library, an application and a command-line tool?
    Model answer

    In a library I make an error enum. Callers can match on each case. The thiserror crate writes the Display and From code. In an application I often use anyhow. It wraps any error and adds context, like "while reading config.toml".

    In a command-line tool, errors go to stderr, not stdout. The exit code is not zero. main can return a Result or an ExitCode. See Error handling and Command-line tools.

  13. Rust What is a Rust edition? How do releases work?
    Model answer

    A new stable Rust comes out every six weeks. Changes move from nightly to beta to stable. An edition is a different thing. It is a set of opt-in changes that you choose per crate in Cargo.toml. The editions so far are 2015, 2018, 2021 and 2024.

    Crates of different editions work together in one program. So moving your crate to a new edition does not break your dependencies. cargo fix --edition does most of the work. See Rust editions, Rust history and Recent releases.

  14. Python Explain is and ==, mutable and immutable, and the mutable default bug.
    Model answer

    == compares values by calling __eq__. is checks identity: are both names the same object? I use is only for None and other singletons.

    Lists, dicts and sets are mutable. Ints, strings and tuples are immutable. A default argument is made once, when def runs. So a default list is shared by all calls. I write items=None and make a new list inside. See The Python data model.

  15. Python What is a decorator? Write one that takes an argument.
    Model answer

    A decorator takes a function and returns a new function. @retry(3) above def fetch means fetch = retry(3)(fetch). With an argument you need three levels: the factory, the decorator and the wrapper. functools.wraps keeps the name and the docstring. Rust has no decorators. A function that takes a closure does the same job.

    // Rust has no decorators. A function that takes a closure does the job.
fn retry<T, E: std::fmt::Display>(times: u32, mut f: impl FnMut() -> Result<T, E>) -> Result<T, E> {
    let mut last = f();
    for n in 1..times {
        match &last {
            Ok(_) => break,
            Err(e) => println!("try {n} failed: {e}"),
        }
        last = f();
    }
    last
}

fn main() {
    let mut calls = 0;
    let r = retry(3, || {
        calls += 1;
        if calls < 3 { Err("busy") } else { Ok(calls) }
    });
    println!("{r:?}");
}
    try 1 failed: busy
try 2 failed: busy
Ok(3)
    import functools

def retry(times):
    def deco(fn):
        @functools.wraps(fn)
        def inner(*args, **kwargs):
            for n in range(1, times):
                try:
                    return fn(*args, **kwargs)
                except Exception as e:
                    print(f"try {n} failed: {e}")
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)  # last try: errors go to the caller
        return inner
    return deco

calls = 0

@retry(3)
def fetch():
    global calls
    calls += 1
    if calls < 3:
        raise RuntimeError("busy")
    return calls

print(fetch())
    try 1 failed: busy
try 2 failed: busy
3

    See Functions, closures and decorators.

  16. Python Threads, processes or asyncio: how do you choose?
    Model answer

    It depends on the kind of work. For I/O-bound work with many waits, like 1,000 HTTP calls, I use asyncio or threads. For CPU-bound work in the normal build, threads do not run Python code in parallel. The GIL stops that. So I use multiprocessing, numpy, or a Rust extension.

    Python 3.13 added a free-threaded build without the GIL. In 3.14 it is officially supported. It is still a separate build, and some C extensions are not ready. See Performance and CPython and Generators and asyncio.

  17. Python Dataclass, NamedTuple or pydantic?
    Model answer

    A dataclass writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for me. It checks nothing at run time. A NamedTuple is an immutable tuple with field names. pydantic checks and converts input at run time, for example JSON from an API.

    My rule: dataclasses for internal data, pydantic at the edges where untrusted data comes in. In Rust, a struct with serde derive reads the JSON and checks the types in one step. See Classes and dataclasses and Data and databases.

  18. Python How do you set up and test a new project?
    Model answer

    I run uv init, then uv add for each dependency. pyproject.toml holds the metadata and tool settings. uv.lock pins exact versions. I put code in src/ and tests in tests/.

    pytest runs the tests, with fixtures and parametrize. ruff lints and formats. mypy or pyright checks the type hints. CI runs all of them on every pull request. See Packaging and testing, Type hints and Testing and tooling.

  19. Algorithms Find two numbers that add up to a target. Make it fast.
    Model answer

    The simple way checks all pairs. That is O(n^2) time. Better: walk the list once and keep a hash map from value to index. For each number, look for the target minus that number in the map. A lookup is O(1) on average, so the total is O(n) time and O(n) memory.

    use std::collections::HashMap;

// Return the positions of two numbers that add up to target.
fn two_sum(nums: &[i32], target: i32) -> Option<(usize, usize)> {
    let mut seen: HashMap<i32, usize> = HashMap::new(); // value -> index
    for (i, &n) in nums.iter().enumerate() {
        if let Some(&j) = seen.get(&(target - n)) {
            return Some((j, i));
        }
        seen.insert(n, i);
    }
    None
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", two_sum(&[2, 7, 11, 15], 9));
    println!("{:?}", two_sum(&[3, 3], 6));
    println!("{:?}", two_sum(&[1, 2], 7));
}
    Some((0, 1))
Some((0, 1))
None
    def two_sum(nums: list[int], target: int) -> tuple[int, int] | None:
    seen: dict[int, int] = {}  # value -> index
    for i, n in enumerate(nums):
        if target - n in seen:
            return seen[target - n], i
        seen[n] = i
    return None

print(two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9))
print(two_sum([3, 3], 6))
print(two_sum([1, 2], 7))
    (0, 1)
(0, 1)
None

    The tests cover the edge cases: a repeated value and no answer. See Algorithms 1.

  20. Algorithms BFS, DFS or Dijkstra: when do you use each one?
    Model answer

    BFS visits nodes level by level with a queue. On a graph without weights, it finds shortest paths. DFS goes deep first, with a stack or recursion. I use it for cycles, connected parts and topological sort.

    Dijkstra finds shortest paths when no edge weight is negative. It uses a priority queue, usually a min-heap. With a binary heap it costs O((V + E) \log V). With negative weights I use Bellman-Ford. See Algorithms 2.

  21. Design Design an LRU cache.
    Model answer

    An LRU cache keeps recently used items. When it is full, it drops the item that was used longest ago. The classic answer is a hash map plus a doubly linked list. Then get and put are O(1).

    In Python, OrderedDict has move_to_end and popitem, so the code is short. In Rust, a safe doubly linked list is hard. In an interview I use a HashMap plus a BTreeMap of "last used" ticks. That costs O(log n) per call. I say this, and I name the lru crate for production.

    use std::collections::{BTreeMap, HashMap};
struct Lru {
    cap: usize,
    tick: u64,                        // a clock that only goes up
    map: HashMap<String, (i32, u64)>, // key -> (value, last use)
    age: BTreeMap<u64, String>,       // last use -> key, oldest first
}
impl Lru {
    fn touch(&mut self, key: &str) {
        self.tick += 1;
        if let Some(e) = self.map.get_mut(key) {
            self.age.remove(&e.1);
            e.1 = self.tick;
            self.age.insert(self.tick, key.to_string());
        }
    }
    fn get(&mut self, key: &str) -> Option<i32> {
        self.touch(key);
        self.map.get(key).map(|e| e.0)
    }
    fn put(&mut self, key: &str, value: i32) {
        if !self.map.contains_key(key)
            && self.map.len() == self.cap
            && let Some((_, old)) = self.age.pop_first()
        {
            self.map.remove(&old); // evict the least recently used key
        }
        self.map.entry(key.to_string()).or_insert((value, 0)).0 = value;
        self.touch(key);
    }
}
fn main() {
    let mut c = Lru { cap: 2, tick: 0, map: HashMap::new(), age: BTreeMap::new() };
    c.put("a", 1);
    c.put("b", 2);
    c.get("a"); // now "b" is the oldest
    c.put("c", 3); // evicts "b"
    println!("{:?} {:?} {:?}", c.get("a"), c.get("b"), c.get("c"));
}
    Some(1) None Some(3)
    from collections import OrderedDict

class Lru:
    def __init__(self, cap: int):
        self.cap = cap
        self.data: OrderedDict[str, int] = OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key: str) -> int | None:
        if key not in self.data:
            return None
        self.data.move_to_end(key)  # mark as newest
        return self.data[key]

    def put(self, key: str, value: int) -> None:
        self.data[key] = value
        self.data.move_to_end(key)
        if len(self.data) > self.cap:
            self.data.popitem(last=False)  # drop the oldest

c = Lru(2)
c.put("a", 1)
c.put("b", 2)
c.get("a")
c.put("c", 3)
print(c.get("a"), c.get("b"), c.get("c"))
    1 None 3

    The Rust version uses a let chain, so it needs edition 2024. See Three projects.

  22. Design Design a small JSON web API in Rust.
    Model answer

    I use axum on the tokio runtime. Routes map a path and a method to a handler function. Extractors like Json<T>, Path and State read the request. Shared state, like a database pool, goes into State.

    My error type implements IntoResponse, so each error gives the right status code. tower middleware adds tracing, timeouts and limits. On Ctrl+C the server finishes open requests, then stops. This is graceful shutdown. Tests send requests to the router directly, without a real network. In Python, FastAPI with pydantic models plays the same role. See Web services with axum.

  23. Design When do you move Python code to Rust with PyO3?
    Model answer

    Only after a profiler shows one hot loop in pure Python. And only if numpy or a better algorithm cannot fix it. PyO3 lets me write the Python module in Rust. maturin builds the wheel.

    During long Rust work I release the GIL, so other Python threads can run. I also check the cost of the border: converting a big list takes time too. I measure before and after. If the gain is small, I keep the code in Python. See Rust and Python together.

  24. Design Exact vector search or HNSW: what is the trade-off?
    Model answer

    Exact search compares the query with every vector. That is O(n \cdot d) per query, and recall is 100%. HNSW builds a graph with layers. A search walks greedily from the top layer down to the nearest neighbours.

    HNSW is much faster on big data, but it can miss some true neighbours. So I measure recall at k against exact search. A setting like ef_search trades speed for recall. Quantisation saves memory: 8-bit codes turn 4 bytes per value into 1 byte. See Vector search from scratch.

  25. Design Design a safe tool-calling agent loop.
    Model answer

    The loop sends the messages to the model. If the model asks for a tool, the loop runs the tool and adds the result to the messages. This repeats until the model gives a final answer.

    For safety I add a step limit, so the loop cannot run forever. Each call gets a timeout and a few retries with backoff. Only allowed tools can run, and I check their arguments. A checkpoint after each step lets the agent resume after a crash. For tests, a fake model returns fixed replies, so no API key is needed. See Agents and orchestration in code.

Key takeaways

  • The main Python Institute path is PCEP, PCAP, PCPP1 and PCPP2. New versions came in autumn 2026: PCEP-30-03, PCAP-31-04, PCPP1-32-102 and PCPP2-32-202.
  • The old versions stay active until 30 November 2027. Check the exact exam code before you pay.
  • On 15 November 2026 there is no official Rust certificate for developers. RFTT accredits training companies, not people.
  • Prove Rust skill with links: a finished, tested project, a crate, merged pull requests.
  • In exams, trace the code by hand. In interviews, define, give an example, name a trade-off and an alternative.
  • Every quiz answer points to a chapter. Read it, then try the question again a few days later.
